As for the two types of clothing—those washed and those rained upon—it is not necessary that they be restricted by acceptance.
If one were to claim that they must be accepted, then would there not be other surplus garments that could not be washed or kept? Therefore, the following provides a summary.

[Commentary]: Now, using two points of reasoning to determine the sequence [of the offenses], among the thirty [offenses] of the *madhyama-āpatti*, there is no transgression that is not primarily due to greed;

moreover, the methods for acquiring objects are improper, obstructing the Path and inviting censure. Because the fault is grave, the rule of relinquishment (*niḥsargika*) was established to counteract the fundamental greed. This is not the case for the ninety [minor offenses] (*navati-praty-āpatti*);

even when an offense is committed on account of wealth, it arises from the improper manner of performing or utilizing the object, rather than from the intent to hoard through greed. Therefore, the rule of relinquishment was not established for them.
Regarding the abandonment of the two types of detachment, although it is not greed or hoarding, it constitutes a slighting of the holy teachings and a violation of the established rules;
its abandonment and confession restore purity so that one may maintain the precepts.

Now, in the first part of the section on the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture), three points are generally indicated, followed by a detailed explanation. First, it clarifies that there are four types of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, the first being those arising from a greedy mind.
Second, taking [the precepts] into one's possession; third, obstructing the Path; fourth, inviting derision. Next, the ninety *anuttara* (unexcelled) offenses are explained according to two meanings:

obstructing the Path and inviting derision. These do not necessarily require both conditions to be met simultaneously. To address potential objections, the text separately demonstrates these two exclusions.
[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the identity or difference of those who commit the offense:

there is no doubt that a single person commits this [offense]. As for the Saṃgha of the four directions, one never commits [the offense of] taking what is not given, because [the property] has no personal owner;
it is intended for the universal transformation [of all beings], and while one may enjoy its use, it cannot belong to oneself.
In the first section of the second explanation, there are two parts: first, it clarifies individual offenses;

second, it clarifies that the Saṃgha incurs no offense, because since the property of the four quarters of the Saṃgha is held in trust for perpetual use, there is no sense in which it can be "received" or "possessed," and thus no offense can be committed.
[Commentary] Question: Since the Saṃgha does not commit an offense, why does the Vinaya state that certain persons commit a *naiḥsargika* offense? Answer:
Whether it be the Saṃgha, a group of many people, or a single individual—this clarifies that the Saṃgha may indeed commit an offense; why then do you say there is none? Answer:

There are four categories of the Saṃgha, as already distinguished in the precept on theft (*adattādāna*). Here, the term "Saṃgha" refers specifically to the *saṃmukhībhūta-saṃgha* (the present Saṃgha).

In the initial question-and-answer section of the subsequent classification, the four positions regarding the precept on stealing refer to two types of permanent property and two types of present property;
here, we concern ourselves only with present property, as there is the sense of joint transgression within the category of present property.

[Commentary: If this is so, how does this differ from "co-residing" (sahajīvin)? The answer is that in the case of co-residing, few and many share [the property] in common; in the case of being present before [the donor], many share it while few do not.
Furthermore, because the two categories of "being present before" and "co-residing" might be confused, the answer specifies "few and many sharing in common."
Because there is no separate distribution [of the precepts], there is much that is common and little that is distinct;

since each has their own portion, [the text says]: "Now, the explanation of 'living together' (sahavāsa) is that the five precepts are not shared in their violation; the two [precepts] regarding the rainy-season robe (varṣāśāṭī)—not storing it for more than six years and not folding it—are both matters of personal observance (dhāraṇa), and thus have no sense of being jointly maintained. How could my separation cause them to incur an offense? [Commentary: Now, the explanation of "living together" is that the five precepts are not shared in their violation.

The two [precepts] regarding the rainy-season robe—namely, not storing it for more than six years and not folding it—are both matters of personal observance (*dhāraṇa*), and thus have no sense of being jointly maintained. How could my separation cause them to incur an offense?

In the first section of the following analysis, the reason why the five precepts shared among co-residents (*sahavāsin*) are not common [to all] is that because they involve the ritual of formal undertaking (*upasaṃpadā*), there is no sense of commonality.
[Commentary]:

There are seven precepts whose transgressions are indeterminate; for example, regarding the five cases of "long robes," "washing," "seizing," and so forth, how could one who is currently living together [with others] incur [a fault]?
If one has not committed an offense, there must necessarily be other conduct; first, one must be made to confess it, and if one does not confess, one commits an offense.

As for others, if they take away [the robe] for washing or accept it for keeping, and their bodies are seen not to have committed an offense regarding the *dīrgha* (extra) robes and so forth, yet they act in concert, they too may be considered to have committed the same offense.
Next, regarding the seven precepts, the text is divided into two parts: first, a general indication that they are the same as those below; second, a detailed explanation.

First, the five items of long-term storage (pañca-dīrgha) may be understood through their similarities and differences—namely, the ten days, the full moon, the emergency gift, the bowl, and the medicine.

Following this, it explains the forfeiture, washing, receiving, and holding [of these items], noting that while there is no commonality regarding long-term storage, there is commonality in sharing, joint use, and joint forfeiture, which entails a common offense.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "present Sangha," there are seven types of offenses that should be committed [together], such as collectively making cotton robes, black or white bedding, carrying wool, storing precious items, trading precious items, and taking back robes.
Next, regarding the "Manifest" [category], the first seven cases are easily understood.

[Commentary: As for the remaining eighteen, if one does not act in concert with others, there is no offense even if such acts occur—such as encountering bandits on a journey and having one's robes seized, or receiving more than the permitted amount while the owner is unaware of it.
What constitutes a shared offense? It refers to those who act together, suffer loss together, and jointly calculate the excess.
The *pratigraha* (acceptance) should further increase by three.
Among the eighteen [cases], the first clarifies the differences; having first cited the fault of losing one's robes, the acceptance of the remainder is explained by analogy.
Now, below, the common meaning is shown. "Common" (*sādhāraṇa*) refers to a joint plot. The three increases should be as previously cited: if it is the Saṃgha...

Whether it be many people or a single individual, this increases the three points within the text; here, it clarifies that they commit the offense together, thereby manifesting the principle of communal (*saṃgha*) transgression.
Therefore, it says "for now" (*jiǎ yīng*). [Commentary]:
Some say, "Why must one speak at such length? To describe it in so many ways never exhausts the root; now, let us explain it through a single principle."
This establishes the fundamental principles: if one does not recount the words of the past, one will not revere the teachings of the future.

Why is this? Among the thirty [offenses], there are those involving formal acceptance (*parigraha*); in these cases, the offense is incurred differently. For those who have accepted [the robe], if they share the same intention, they incur the offense together; if their intentions differ, they incur it separately.

For example, if a nun has the intention to have a robe washed and subsequently has it washed, she incurs the offense; however, if she initially had no such intention and the nun simply washed it on her own initiative, she does not.
The Buddha did not prohibit [certain practices]; this can be applied by analogy to other cases.

Next, the Master first refutes the prolixity [of previous views], and now below he demonstrates the essentials. First, he sets forth a single principle, which is the subsequent application of the mind’s identity and difference.

If one does not recount [the preceding points], how can one demonstrate the intent of the ancient citations? Below, he correctly clarifies the practice of receiving and maintaining [the precepts]. As it says: "If... [and so forth].
Regarding the aforementioned five precepts, when the mind is the same but the intention differs, there should be an increase of three instances of transgression for each of the three positions.

As illustrated by the examples cited below, it is evident that the determination of whether a transgression occurs depends on the presence or absence of mental intent; the various characters [used here] are merely rhetorical particles.
[Commentary] Third, regarding the number of people taught:

among the thirty [offenses], if one teaches others but does not do it oneself, the person who can teach incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), as there is no acquisition of wealth or the intercalary month [of merit].
The first section of the third gate concerns the thirty *pārājika* offenses common to all.

[Commentary]: Among those offenses committed for one's own sake, there are thirteen precepts. When instructing another to perform an act for one’s own benefit, if the completion of the act depends upon the physical karma (*kāyakarman*) of that other person as a distinct condition, and the offense is not established by one’s own vocal karma (*vākkarman*), then among the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), the offense is incurred spontaneously (*svarasataḥ*). According to the Vinaya, there are five such cases.

The seven rules regarding spreading out [a robe], taking back a robe, receiving precious objects, and the *Saṃghāṭi*; the five rules regarding sending a messenger to take a nun’s robe, washing an old robe, carding wool, exceeding the limit, and begging for thread;
and the five rules regarding driving [a weaver] and weaving—most of these involve praising the weaving, and sending a messenger also constitutes an offense.

Next, regarding the thirteen rules of the *Prātimokṣa* that are combined under the heading of "forming grave offenses," they are discussed as follows. These can be understood from the separate versions of the Vinaya as seven rules:

(1) the *Mahāsāṃghika* rule on requesting clothing beyond the limit, which refers to urgent requests for robes; (2) the rule on begging yarn; (3) the rule on driving a weaver, which concerns even a non-relative weaver;
(4) the rule from the *Mahīśāsaka* Vinaya on praising weaving, which means encouraging a weaver to increase the price; [and so forth].
[Commentary: Regarding the remaining seventeen precepts, when one instructs others for one's own sake, it does not necessarily accord with one's own mind; one incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).

Among these light offenses, some lack the sense of "for one's own sake," such as the two types of *pārājika* involving separation [from robes]; others do involve "for one's own sake," such as the category of keeping extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) and so forth.
One may ascertain their presence or absence by carefully examining each of the precepts.
[Commentary]: Regarding the fourth point, whether there is a possibility of repeated offenses:
among the thirty [rules], four precepts admit of repeated offenses—namely, those concerning washing clothes, carrying and folding rain-cloths, and so forth.
When these items are currently in use, they may be subject to repeated offenses; the text states that ordering another to wash, dye, or beat them constitutes three *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.

In the first section of the fourth gate, regarding the gravity [of offenses], it is explained that for both washing and splitting [wool], there are three matters each; for carrying wool, there is the transgression of exceeding the limit;

for rain-cloths, there is the offense of using them before the proper time or using them improperly; and for the concluding text on the commission of offenses, it cites scriptural evidence based on the washing and dyeing [of wool], while the other three categories apply universally.
[Commentary]: Regarding the remaining twenty-six precepts, there is no principle of "repeated offense. How is this known? First, there is no "seizure" nor "repeated seizure";

second, there is no "separation" nor "repeated separation"; third, regarding the five transgressions and six accomplishments—namely, the five types of spreading [the robes] and the request for thread—there is neither transgression nor accomplishment;

fourth, regarding the fourteen acceptances, there is no "repeated acceptance," meaning that taking robes from a nun, requesting robes beyond the limit, the first and second instances of dwelling, and the excessive solicitation for acceptance [are not repeated offenses].

These include trading jewels for jewels, selling bowls, praising one's own weaving, receiving rain-cloths prematurely, receiving urgent offerings prematurely, and diverting the property of the Saṃgha;
together with the previous thirty, these may be inferred.

Next, regarding the five faults of "no re-duplication" (*an-anvaya*) and the six cases of "completion": the five faults refer to the five instances of spreading out [the robe] and the request for thread;
as for the completion without fault, it should be stated that there are five faults of no re-duplication and six cases of completion without re-duplication.

In total, these comprise fourteen precepts and fourteen instances of receiving [the robe]. The subsequent sections on the bath-robe (*snāna-śāṭī*) follow the text; the section on "prior use" (*pūrva-prayoga*) precedes the section on "dropping" (*patana*).
Regarding the repetition of offenses, after the immediate transgressions (*sadyah-pāyantika*), one is restrained by the subsequent five categories of offenses.
Because these two precepts each encompass two regulations, although twenty-six were previously indicated, there are actually twenty-eight; it is for this reason as well.
Generally showing what follows below, some versions list thirty-two, which likely corresponds to the aforementioned count.
[Commentary] Question: Once something has been taken by force, there can be no further taking back of it; why then does the Vinaya text state that it may be hidden in various places?

Answer: This refers to cases where the person is not present before one's face; thus, there is a distinction between two types of "taking back. The establishment of the rule must be such, even though the nature of the offense itself is not so.
In the question, the Vinaya states: "If one seizes [the object] oneself or instructs another to seize it and then conceals it, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).

It further states: "If one places it upon a tree or similar location and it moves from its place, one commits a *pāyattika*. Since these texts appear to describe two separate offenses, the question seeks clarification.

In the answer, it is judged that there are two distinct cases for seizing: if the seizure occurs face-to-face, the offense is determined by the act of concealment; if the seizure does not occur face-to-face, the offense is determined by the displacement [of the object].

In the section concerning the offenses (*āpatti*), the phrase "not face-to-face" refers to a subsequent judgment, whereas "present before [the assembly]" refers to the initial judgment; since the Vinaya sets forth the characteristics of the offense, it is said that the establishment of the rule must be thus.
However, this does not mean that the act of committing the offense is not repeated. Therefore, it is said that the matter of the offense is not otherwise.

[Commentary] Fifth, regarding the explanation of the methods for relinquishing and repenting: although there are many varieties according to their specific names and characteristics, when condensed and synthesized, they comprise only three types of relinquishment.
First, it clarifies the relinquishment of material wealth as the condition for departing from transgression; for if one lacks such wealth, the transgression does not arise.
Second, it clarifies the relinquishment of the mind as the cause for departing from transgression; it is due to greed and arrogance that one comes to violate the Holy One.
This teaches the abandonment of offenses and the removal of karma that obstructs the Path through the Three Knowledges (*traividyā*).
In the fifth section, which sets forth the divisions: "wealth" refers to the object of the offense, and is thus called the "condition of the offense";

"mind" refers to the basis for the commission of karma, and is thus called the "cause of the offense"; and since the offense itself is an impediment to entering the Path, it is termed "karma that obstructs."

[Commentary]: Regarding the preceding explanation of material wealth, it is categorized according to the five types found in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, differentiated by their respective objects. [Commentary]:
First, relinquishing without regard for the object—such as cotton clothing—is not a matter of the substance itself, but rather because its nature causes harm to living beings;

unless it is cut and destroyed, how can this greed be exhausted? Second, regarding relinquishing with regard to the object, there is a distinction between the monastic and the lay: such as keeping or trading two types of precious items, where the substance is valuable and increases greed.
This is by no means what is possessed or used by those who have left the household life; it causes one to abandon [such things] to laypeople, manifesting that these are not the practices of the Way.

As for the remaining types of relinquishment, they all pertain to the stage of being "on the Path" (in the monastic order), with various distinctions between general and specific categories as detailed extensively in the *Shan-chao* (Commentary).

There are five types of relinquishing material goods (*cīvara*): first, regarding the initial classification, one type does not involve a specific recipient—namely, silk floss—while the others all involve a specific recipient.

Second, among those involving a recipient, two types concern precious objects given to laypeople, while the others are all given to the Sangha. Regarding the begging for a bowl: this occurs within the *śīla-saṃgha* (the community of precept-holders);
the distribution of a bowl does not apply to an individual alone, whereas the other cases do apply. Thus, it is said that there are differences between the general and the particular.

[Commentary]: Second, regarding the distinction between total destruction of the substance and relinquishment: in the case of silk, because the harm is permanently ceased upon its destruction, it is relinquished;
in other cases, it is entirely relinquished because there is still benefit from the physical object.
Of these two, only in the case of silk does one destroy it by cutting it up and mixing it with mud.

[Commentary] Third, regarding the discussion of locations: either through the ritual of spontaneous formation (*svayaṃ-kṛta-vidhi*), the fundamental dwelling, the distinct dwelling, the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), and the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) each correspond to their respective precepts;
by being drawn forth together, they manifest the characteristics [of the boundaries].
Among these three, only the begging of a bowl is restricted to formal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) because it requires such a rite;

furthermore, because the penalized bowl must be placed in the kitchen, it is restricted to the primary residence and not permitted on the boundary of the training ground (*sīmā*). All other precepts apply universally.
[Commentary]: Fourth, the differences in the assembly of the community: the three types of precepts do not involve such an assembly because they are forfeited by one’s own actions toward laypeople.
Among the four [categories], the three types of precepts are the same as those discussed above regarding the object (*ālambana*).

[Commentary]: Fifth, the differences in the restitution of property. There are five types: first, returning the item; second, changing it into secular goods and returning the value; third, entering the Sangha [to dispose of it].

4. Returning to the owner and not using it for its original purpose, as in the case of begging for a bowl; 5. Entering the Sangha or entering secular life and returning it to the owner so that it is no longer used, as in the case of the seven-day medicine—these five cases all involve returning to the owner.

Among these five, the first involves returning after transformation, which refers to the destruction of silk by cutting it; the *Yìchāo* (Commentary on the Meaning) uses the character "huài" (destroyed), though I suspect this character [may be a scribal error].
Regarding the four cases where [an item] enters the Sangha or enters secular hands, returning it to the original owner constitutes three types of judgment.

Among the five cases, excluding the aforementioned five types, all others are returned to the original owner; as for surplus items among them, they may be returned after one night has passed, or returned through a series of intermediaries, while the remainder are returned immediately on the spot.

[Commentary]: The preceding discussion has addressed how the five aspects of forfeiture differ according to our own Vinaya. However, if one follows other Vinayas, when various items are forfeited and enter the Sangha, they are not for the personal use of the individual who forfeited them.

Now, if there is one who commits an offense and, failing to contemplate the gravity of their karma, merely wishes to perform the ritual of forfeiture and confession while the defiled mind remains unabandoned, how can such a person be called a pure disciple of the Buddha?
I shall not extensively cite other schools here, but will rely instead on the case of money and precious objects.
The world abounds in such corruptions; let us examine how other Vinayas resolve this matter.

In the first section of another school, the first two phrases conclude the preceding text, while the subsequent portion indicates that other school’s approach. This section further has three parts: first, a general indication;
second, a refutation of erroneous practices; and third, an indication of the source from which [the present text] is derived.

[Commentary: Therefore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, regarding the possession and trading of precious objects: if the amount is small, it must be permanently relinquished; if the amount is large, it is relinquished to a pure attendant (*śucika-purusa*) who shares the same resolve.
The pure attendant then relinquishes them as bedding for the Sangha of the four directions.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the character "wu" (無) is missing above the word for "pure person" (*karmadāna*). It states: "If one cannot obtain a pure person, one may use [the property] as bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions.

[Commentary]: In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it says that items such as jewels must be permanently relinquished to the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha shall appoint a person to discard them permanently; it does not permit a pure person to do so.
Regarding the exchange of clothing and food for the consumption of the Saṃgha, it is improper for the original owner alone; this is because one fears that [the act] would fulfill their own desire.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, "improper for the original owner" means they do not share in the consumption.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when precious items are relinquished as an offering to the Saṃgha, they enter into the category of "inexhaustible wealth" (*akṣayanīvi*). Any interest generated from this must be used to provide clothing for the monastic dwellings;
it may not be divided out for individual use, as this serves to subdue the greedy mind of the original owner.
The inexhaustible wealth of the Saṃgha is the perpetual treasury of longevity; "monastic garments" refers to items such as curtains and canopies.
[Commentary] The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: regarding gold, silver, and so forth, if there is no pure person (*śuci-puruṣa*) available, one should cast them away.
The Saṃgha shall appoint a person who knows the five dharmas to close their eyes and cast them out, without recording the location.
One who skillfully perceives the five dharmas does not harbor attachment or aversion, etc., and fifthly, knows what is to be relinquished and what is not.
[Commentary: Based on these various texts, it is known that in all schools, "relinquishment" (praṇāśana) means complete relinquishment and not self-deception;

the *Dharmaguptaka* school is also like this. Because it is a complete relinquishment, one only needs to know how to repent for one's offenses; the Saṃgha itself shall deliberate on what is appropriate. One must carefully examine whether one is practicing the Path or seeking external hindrances.
Because it was made specifically through the power of karma and is used for the same purpose as when it was newly acquired, there is no sense of wrongful deprivation;

therefore, the Vinaya texts state that if one abandons it and does not return it, or uses it for another purpose, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* offense and no grave transgression. This is explained in the text.

Among the three [sections], the first establishes the general framework for the various texts; the four divisions below specifically demonstrate the primary section. First, it clarifies the intent of relinquishing:

since it is determined by the measure of the Saṃgha, it is clear that relinquishing the whole carries the same meaning as relinquishing to the entire community; hence it says, "it is likewise. Below, regarding the Saṃgha, it demonstrates the intent of returning:

fearing that seeking [rewards] would obstruct one's practice is the fundamental purpose of the teaching; to be crooked, burdensome, or contrary is what is meant. Therefore, below, it cites scriptural evidence regarding the Saṃgha.
If one does not return [the stolen object], it is a violation of the teachings (ājñā-vyatikrama) that incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, yet it is not a grave offense;

from this, we know that the prior resolution to relinquish [the object] was clear. My private interpretation is that relinquishing wealth and repenting for the offense is intended to sever the mind of greed. Other schools maintain that once [the object] is permanently discarded, the severance of greed is not required;

however, our own school prescribes its return, which conversely demonstrates that greed must indeed be severed. Furthermore, although the commission of the offense is caused by the defilement of the object, it fundamentally arises from the mind; therefore, one should merely relinquish the object to eliminate the offense.
The mind and matter thus become pure; this is why the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) excels other schools, precisely because of this.
When the text says "as explained later," it refers to the subsequent commentary.

[Commentary: If one establishes the method for re-donating robes after repeated offenses, among the thirty rules, the two rules concerning cotton garments and the three rules concerning the two treasures do not apply.

Among the twenty-seven monastic precepts, those four that are relinquished before the Sangha are returned immediately—namely, the two rules regarding separation [from robes], the two rules regarding hair, and the rule against improper dyeing—because although these involve dyeing, they are restricted to external bodily use and must be returned on the same day. As for the four rules concerning keeping [robes] beyond the permitted period, one may keep them overnight because the continuity of possession persists.
Regarding the remaining eighteen rules, which are relinquished individually, there is no need to wait overnight, as they do not involve a desire for hoarding.

Next, regarding the method for returning [the forfeiture] when a transgression is repeated: this refers to the fact that among the various "long" (dīgha) items, there may be the possibility of defilement through repeated offenses;

therefore, they must be distinguished at the outset. The first category consists of two separations and two types of hair; because these involve a violation of the teachings and a departure from the Dharma, and are not due to greed or accumulation, the seven-day period applies.
Together with the four lower precepts, these constitute the five long medicines. Since these are for external use only, they do not require overnight storage. As for the remaining ten:
Regarding the separate relinquishment of the eight precepts without staying overnight, it is possible for them to be relinquished together while staying overnight, as will be explained below.
[Commentary] Now, I shall clarify their characteristics by examining how the four precepts mutually defile one another.

[Commentary]: If one considers the twenty-three rules regarding the *atireka-cīvara* (extra robe) when it must be relinquished at the end of the month, during the *pāṭihārika-dāna* (special offering), or after the passing of the [robe season], six of these rules are immediately restored:
the two types of separation, the two rules concerning hair, the medicine, and the bowl.

As for the remainder, because they involve keeping the robe overnight, even if one has previously committed a separate offense and already relinquished the material, once the time comes to restore the property through the *posadha* (confession ceremony), the "extra" status is not yet established as having been kept overnight.

Because the defiled mind arises again toward the newly discarded robe and further defiles it, it causes [the robe] to remain overnight; thus, it increases together with the others and is returned as one.
Next, in the first section of the separate assignment, among the twenty-seven items, four long robes are excluded, leaving twenty-three.

The three types of long robes (*atireka-cīvara*) that serve as the "stained" objects are themselves the six precepts that act as the "stainers. The latter four [precepts] do not stain, as previously explained.

Regarding medicine, there is the seven-day limit and the bowl; because these two are distinct in substance, they do not mutually stain one another. The remaining seventeen precepts below clarify the method of confession and purification.

While it may appear that the category of "long" robes could involve mutual staining, according to the original rule, this is restricted to the point of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*), as it follows the specific rule regarding the "long" robe.
Therefore, they share the same overnight stay.

[Commentary]: If twenty-three of the precepts involve the forfeiture of the long bowl together with the bowl itself, one must request the bowl and stay overnight; for the remainder, it is returned immediately.

Next, regarding the extra bowl (*atireka-pātra*), one should beg for only a single bowl; because it has been dyed, the bowl kept overnight (*rātri-vipravāsa*)—which has not been dyed with cloth—is returned immediately.

[Commentary]: If the twenty-three rules are combined with the rules on extra medicine (*atireka-bhaiṣajya*) and discarded all at once, they are collectively returned because they pertain to food and clothing.

Because internal and external requisites are distinct and do not mutually defile one another, among the three categories, the superior ones are designated as fourfold. To clarify the mutual defilement of characteristics, the long-term medicines—whether they have been kept overnight or not—are included within the scope of what is defiled.

What is clarified here does not concern whether they have been kept overnight; rather, it concerns the fact that medicines generally fall into three categories, and the relinquishing of two of them constitutes giving.

Fearing that others might think these items were being abandoned due to defilement, he must distinguish them and show that the medicine must be given to another while the remainder is returned to the original owner;
thus it says, "all are returned. Below this, the reason for non-defilement is demonstrated.

In the summary title, it should have been stated as "twenty-two rules," because the long-term medicine was extracted from the twenty-three to serve as the defiling factor; thus one should reflect upon this.
[This concludes the section on] this. Second, the clarification of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).

[Commentary]: Among the offenses involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), the abandonment of what has been stored is the basis; while repenting the offense is very easy, purifying the mind is difficult. Since there is already a clear explanation...

The meaning of the text cannot be readily concealed; as it is explained extensively in the *Karmavācanā-saṃskāra* and the *Xingshichao*, I have re-explained it here for fear that those texts might not be seen.

Regarding the second section, "The Arising of the Mind of Renunciation," the first two phrases indicate the main body of the repentance, while the following two phrases clarify the mind of renunciation.
It is difficult [to escape] because the beginningless habituation to greed cannot be liberated from without a wise antidote; thus, the following passage indicates the necessity of renunciation.
[The character] "shū" (疏) is pronounced with a level tone (*píngshēng*), meaning "principle.

[Commentary: Regarding the five long-term precepts, one commits an offense due to the desire to store [possessions]; therefore, one must relinquish them. To reverse that greedy mind, one must not [retain them].

If the day returns to the owner, there must be some other circumstance as permitted in the text; as stated in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, one may receive extraordinary wealth on that very same day without incurring the fault of "storing" (*saṃnidhi*), because the mind has severed [the attachment].
This is why the original property cannot be received: since it has already been subject to the fault of storage, the mind must be separated by a night's interval.
If one does not sever [the attachment], then even after many nights, it constitutes an offense. This differs from the case of medicine, which must be used on the same day.
One may obtain [the robe] back and cease wearing it.

This correctly clarifies the initial intent for relinquishing the five types of long robes (*atireka-cīvara*) due to external conditions; that they are difficult to assemble, involve traveling afar, and require returning is as indicated below.
Regarding the relinquishment of the mind, the first point clarifies obtaining and receiving extraordinary wealth, which corresponds to the third phrase below.
The following demonstrates that one does not open the original container, nor does one set aside long-term medicines, because they are stored together with greed and are not kept overnight.
[Commentary] Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun) provides a sixfold analysis.

[Commentary]: Initially, although the robe has been relinquished and the offense confessed, because the intention to possess it has not been severed, one subsequently accepts another robe that is tainted by the previous one.

Since the intention to seek [the robe] has not been severed, even if one month passes—whether one obtains the sought-after robe or an unexpected robe—one commits a transgression of defilement, as the mind of non-relinquishment persists.

Next, regarding the enumeration of phrases, there are two distinctions within the first two: first, the distinction of harboring the intention to seek; second, the distinction of the duration of time, whether long or short.

[Commentary]: Regarding the four subsequent phrases, because the mind has severed [the connection], one is not defiled; that is, there is no offense for the preceding object, while the subsequent mind incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light transgression).

1. Having relinquished the three robes and repented for the offense, and having severed the intention to keep them, if one obtains a robe on that very day, there is no offense, because the intention was severed. 2.

Having relinquished the four robes and repented for the offense, and having severed the intention to keep them, if one subsequently seeks and obtains another robe on a later day, there is no offense, because the intention to keep them had been relinquished in the interim.

3. When the time for the ground [of the robe] has ended, having relinquished the robe, repented for the offense, and severed the intention to keep it, if one seeks and obtains another robe toward evening, there is no offense.

Regarding the offense of *duṣkṛta* for having already relinquished the six robes but not yet confessed the transgression: if one harbors the intention to keep them and, even after many days have passed, obtains a robe, one commits a *duṣkṛta*.
In the latter four phrases, the first provides a general indication of the three [cases], while the following two specifically list the second and sixth; both refer to the acquisition of a robe.
Having already repented of one's offenses, the distinction between the fourth and fifth [stages] both concerns seeking again;
yet, since the subsequent day differs from the previous day, by examining these numerical citations, one knows that the resolve to relinquish is the root of repentance.
[Commentary: The third [section] concerns the methods for relinquishing offenses.

[Commentary: Some masters establish the doctrine that thirty types of relinquishing offenses all require the assembly of the Sangha; because these are grave matters requiring the presence of the community, they are not accomplished if the assembly is not convened.
Regarding the three types of relinquishment for offenses, according to the initial master’s interpretation, all thirty [offenses] must be addressed before the Saṃgha;

because they differ from the *pāyattika* (sbyor ba gcig pa), even though the relinquishment of silk, cotton, and the two kinds of precious objects does not require the Saṃgha, the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) must still be confessed individually, and all members must assemble.
[Commentary] A master says: because one may not abandon the property while being apart from the assembly, the text states that one must not abandon it while apart from the assembly.

If the abandonment were invalid and thus no offense incurred, then those individuals who are excluded would likewise fall into the offense of being apart from the assembly. Therefore, [the rule applies].

Next, the textual evidence for the master’s position regarding the forfeiture of property to the Saṃgha is very clear: the forfeiture of offenses and their subsequent falling away from purity are treated as one category rather than separate sections.

[The *Shu* (Commentary) states: Some masters say that according to the Vinaya text it is better to follow the rule where, as with the two types of precious items such as cotton robes, the forfeiture is not performed before the Saṃgha;

therefore, the text does not explicitly state that the confession is made before the Saṃgha. All other prohibitions are established in relation to the Saṃgha, whether involving a large group or a single individual.

Later, the Master [Daoxuan] followed the Vinaya: for the remaining offenses, one confesses before the Sangha; however, for silk and the two treasures (gold and silver), one confesses individually. This is because among the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, only the rule concerning silk from silkworms and the two treasures do not provide a method for confession through forfeiture (*pratikarman*).

[Commentary: My current interpretation is that since these thirty precepts involve material objects as the causal condition for the offense, one must forfeit the object first. Furthermore, it would be difficult to perform the confession and forfeiture if one were to withdraw the object after the initial step. How could this be?

Regarding the forfeiture of property (*cīvara*) and the removal of offenses (*āpatti*), these must be performed separately from the Saṃgha. In accordance with the Vinaya, whatever property has been committed as an offense must be forfeited;

the removal of the offense must necessarily be before the Saṃgha, even if it consists of only one person within a single boundary (*sīmā*), for this is not a separate assembly (*gaṇa*), but rather a "Saṃgha of one.

As for the three precepts not being listed in the *Vinayamūla*, this is simply because the forfeiture of property is distinct, and the repentance for transgressions is not explicitly clarified; it does not mean that their separate removal is not permitted, for there is no such text in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and various schools state that because this offense must be confessed within the Saṃgha, it is brought up again in the main text; other details are as found in the *Śāstra* and commentaries.
In the current explanation, since the method of confession is first set forth, the previous section was extracted separately as the ninety [offenses].

As for the phrase "how could one possibly," it refers to the fact that the two difficulties regarding property and offenses cannot be treated in isolation. Following the subsequent passage, the present judgment first correctly demonstrates that even if there were but a single person...
This confession (*pratideśanā*) applies to all three stages; because there is no *saṃgha* present, it is permitted for an individual alone.

Although one may face a single person, the boundary must be fully assembled, as there is nothing that is not the *saṃgha*-dharma, as explained below in the *Vinaya*. Regarding the removal of obstacles concerning cotton garments and the two treasures, the *Vinaya* does not clarify the procedure for confession.

Later masters relied on this to establish their positions based on the literal text; therefore, it must be resolved through a comprehensive interpretation. First, the intent of the *Vinaya* is shown: the property is distinct.

Regarding "renunciation": as for cotton, it must be cut and destroyed; as for the two treasures (gold and silver), they are not permitted for commoners because they belong to the Saṃgha. Thus, "depending on" (*yīng*) means "due to" (*yīn*).

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, states: "Gold, silver, and money may not be grasped at all; if one grasps them, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, which must be confessed before the Saṃgha.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Duolun) states: "All precious valuables must be renounced to a trustworthy lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*); the offense is to be confessed before the Saṃgha."
The section on repentance concludes with the following brief indication of what remains.
[Commentary] The sixth section concerns the methods for maintaining and violating the precepts.
Among the thirty precepts, nine are *kṛta-dhāraṇa* (active observances), wherein the mere cessation of the action constitutes a violation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the five rules concerning "extra" items—such as extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), the monthly expectation for an extra bowl, extra medicine, and the lapse of the "urgent offering" (*ātyayika-dāna*)—the Buddha commanded that these be purified through formal dedication (*pariṣkāra-pariṇāmanā*) and accepted according to the Dharma.

To practice in accordance with these instructions is called "observance through action" (*karaṇa-samvara*); to not transgress the Buddha’s regulations is called "observance through restraint" (*vāraṇa-samvara*).

"Action" refers to the diligent cultivation and implementation of the teaching, while "restraint" refers to acting in accordance with the instruction without overstepping it. Thus, their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct; to violate them would constitute a transgression.
Not speaking [the truth] is termed a transgression of omission (*āpatti-āśraya*), while exceeding the time limit is termed a transgression of commission (*āpatti-kriyā*);

these are also said to have distinct natures (*svabhāva*) as they are mutually contrasted to reveal themselves, as explained above in the section on observance and transgression in the previous fascicle.
In the sixth section, among the five "long" [categories], the first part enumerates the individual precepts; from here below, the two-fold observance is shown collectively.

Because there is pure giving (*śuddhadeya*), the practice is divided into two distinct parts. Specifically, the following indicates the names and essences: first, it shows that the two types of observance—cessation (*saṃvara*) and action (*kriyā*)—are distinct practices;
"not transgressing" refers to the distinctness of their essence. Below, it clarifies that while the two offenses are identical in essence, the names for cessation and action are distinct.
It is not said that the transgression (*vyatikrama*) is distinct from the essence (*tattva*), for by maintaining the distinction, the offense is established; thus it is said "self-evident.
According to the tradition of the ancient masters, the two types of maintenance (*dhāraṇa*) differ in name and essence, while the two offenses differ in name but are one in essence.

This has been detailed and refuted in the upper section (*pūrvabhāga*). Here, it is further pointed out and indicated, either referring to the general meaning of the first fascicle or to the second [fascicle] on the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.

[Commentary]: Second, regarding the separation from the six [faults], these three precepts are termed "active observance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) because they are obtained through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*). They are termed "restraint observance" (*vārita-dhāraṇa*) because they accord with the teaching and do not contradict it.
To act contrary to the teaching and oppose restraint is termed "active transgression. To be unwilling to rely on the Dharma is termed "restraint transgression.
Thus, it is exceedingly clear.

[Commentary: Regarding the first precept against hoarding precious objects, it is called "observance through active practice" (*zhi-chí*) when one entrusts them to a lay patron; it is called "observance through abstention" (*zhì-chí*) when there is no violation because one refrains from possessing them.
In the following two sections, the enumeration of the precepts and the explicit instructions for their practice are largely the same as those previously mentioned.
[Commentary]: Regarding the other precepts, such as when someone takes a nun’s robe and offers it, one examines oneself and others;

seeing that there is no benefit, one stops the mind and does not accept it, fearing the violation of the precept. This is called "stopping and maintaining" (*zhi-chi*). It is not merely the absence of mental engagement that is termed "stopping.

This stopping is neutral (*avyākṛta*) and is not itself a following of the precept. Conversely, accepting and receiving [the gift] is called "acting and violating" (*zuo-fan*). A violation necessarily depends upon [this acceptance].
This records the accomplishment of karma.

Next, regarding the single maintenance [of the precepts], the first phrase provides a general indication of the twenty-one precepts, which will be shown individually below. Furthermore, there are two parts:

first, clarifying the maintenance through restraint (*śīla-dhāraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "one's own measure" (*svamāna*) and so forth, this means that one first observes, which is wisdom (*jñāna*), and subsequently...
"Not undertaking" is itself practice; it is not merely the opposite of what the ancients called "spontaneous non-action," which they termed "maintaining through cessation.

This has already been refuted above. Here, I shall decisively refute their argument. Upon reaching these words, I could not help but sigh with deep regret that those of the past did not hear this, and rejoice that I have encountered its transmission in this later age.
It may truly be said that the essential purport of the Vinaya teachings is now as clear as the bright moon.

At present, the cultivation of the myriad practices is straightforward and well-founded; I address those who study these teachings: let them reflect upon them thoroughly. To reverse this and act with clarity [in violation] constitutes an offense.
[Commentary: Seventh, regarding the differences between monks and nuns.
[Commentary]: Among the thirty rules, eighteen are offenses committed equally by both monks and nuns;
when listed individually in the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, there are twelve rules that differ in three respects.
In the general introduction of the seventh section, first it points to the *bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa* being the same as the monks' rules;

that is, the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* shares the same precepts as the monks (*bhikṣu*), and while the origins (*nidāna*) and detailed explanations are not recounted, the specific characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) alone are listed. Below this, the distinct precepts are indicated.

However, this is merely an explanation of the differences by contrasting them with the monks' precepts; as for the eighteen [precepts] listed prior to the thirty [specific *bhikṣuṇī*-only precepts], they are the same as those of the monks.

Furthermore, these twelve items listed below differ entirely from those for the *saṃgha*; although the practice of keeping an alms bowl is the same, the allowance of ten days is also a point of difference in the precepts.
One may see this for oneself by consulting the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

[Commentary]: Regarding the initial differences between the existence or non-existence [of certain rules for nuns]: as previously discussed, the two precepts concerning the rain-clothing and the six-night limit in the *araṇya* (forest hermitage) apply to the Saṃgha;

however, they do not apply to nuns. This is because the bathing-cloth is used constantly, and since the Buddha granted this exception for nuns, it is not subject to the restrictive regulations regarding time limits.
Furthermore, because nuns are physically weak and do not practice in the *araṇya*, there is no offense of separation [from their robes].

In the first section of the separate exposition, the initial part raises the precept and its underlying intent; following "bathing," the reason for the general explanation is provided. First, the rain-cloak for nuns is explained;
next, the separation from the robe in the *araṇya* (wilderness) is explained.

[Commentary]: Second, regarding the "identity of offense" (*pratibandha*) despite differences in conditions (*pratyaya*): when a monk and a nun both possess one bowl and commit an offense by possessing an extra bowl, it is called an "identity of offense.
The limit for monks is ten days, whereas for nuns it is restricted to one night; this is termed a "difference in conditions."
The subsequent section explaining the characteristics can be understood.
[Commentary] Why is this? Because the *saṃgha* consists of many individuals, a ten-day period is permitted for the purpose of accumulating and dispersing.
In the explanation of the reason, the first point regarding "accumulating and dispersing" refers to the act of transferring the gift to others.
[Commentary: Furthermore, whereas for monks it is not prescribed to have a companion and they are permitted to seek a pure nun on the day [of the ceremony], this is the opposite of the previous case.

Next, regarding the explanation of the established thesis: "seeking a pure [nun]" means selecting a pure object to serve as the counterpart (*pratimukha*), or it may mean seeking a person to whom one declares the purification;
thus it says "pure nun. Because the rule prescribes that a companion must be present, it says "the opposite of the previous."
[Commentary: If this were so, one might argue that when a nun keeps an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) with a companion, she should not be held to the same standard as the monks regarding the bowl.
However, the bowl is not like the robe; since the robe is not yet finished, there is no offense for keeping it as "extra. Once the bowl is finished, it must be formally dedicated (*pāriśuddhi*).

As for robes, even while they are being prepared and not yet finished, there is the fault of having an "extra" item. Because a robe cannot be completed by sewing with a single day’s worth of pins, the ten-day period is permitted.

In resolving this objection, [it is argued that] the rule for a nun’s extra robe (atireka-cīvara) is likewise opened for ten days; however, if one considers the principle of having a companion, that [analogy] does not hold.

In the response, it is explained that regarding the bowl, once it has been properly treated by fumigation and so forth, there is no offense; whereas regarding the extra robe, the substance of the cloth itself becomes an offense once the ten-day limit has passed. Therefore, they are not the same.

[Commentary]: If that is so, why is it that an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) which has not yet been completed but has a companion for the formal declaration (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*), being similar to an alms bowl, cannot be [retained]?

Furthermore, the permission for an extra robe for ten days refers specifically to those who possess only the three robes; within these ten days, its completion is permitted without the need for formal dedication (*pariṣkāra-dāna*).
If one does perform the formal dedication, it is likewise restricted to a single day.

In the subsequent commentary, the first section revisits and refutes the previous interpretation: although the former divided [the rule] into two parts, it did not fully account for the meaning of "companions. Furthermore, the latter section establishes the correct position:
for those who possess only the three robes, because they have not performed the *śuddhi* (purification/declaration), a ten-day period is permitted; for others, it is not permitted.

[Commentary]: If that is so, why is it that the permission granted for ten days applies equally? Once the permission has been granted, [the period] extends equally until the tenth day. This is understood by analogy:
just as the permission for gruel granted to those who are ill also applies to those who are not ill.

Regarding the resolution of objections: as for the current allowance for keeping an elder, it should not be permitted; however, in the response, what was explained above refers to the original allowance.
Once the exception has been granted, it is treated as a general permission, and the example cited makes this clear.

[Commentary]: Third, regarding the difference in gravity: taking a nun’s robe from among the five types of spread-out robes is a *pāyattika* offense for a nun and a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for a monk; washing it, carrying it, or spreading it out [for her] is likewise different.
The reasons for these differences will be further explained in the text itself.

Regarding the three categories of light and heavy offenses, first the names are listed; there are nine precepts in total. The following sections refer to the intent of these rules, which will be explained in the text as needed.

According to what follows, many of them are not further commented upon here. Now, examining the five cases of spreading out [robes]: because a *bhikṣuṇī* receives sparse and meager offerings, the offense is light in all such instances.

Regarding taking a *bhikṣuṇī*’s robe, it is stated below that since the Saṃgha is the most venerable, the gift is rare and thus the offense is light. As for washing and beating [the robe], there is no mention of this in the section below.
If one were to follow the superior principle of "shouldering the burden," then women would suffer much humiliation; for this reason, they differ from the *saṃgha*.
[Commentary] Regarding the eighth, the "spontaneous" *śrāmaṇera*:

within the eighth category, there are two types of *śrāmaṇeras*. First, those whose physical form is that of a *śrāmaṇera*; even if they receive the five precepts, their essence remains the same [as a layperson].

The secular world does not clarify this point; as for the second [point], since the dharma is the same for a śrāmaṇera who receives the ten precepts immediately, all preceding and succeeding discussions are based on this alone.
[Commentary: Before receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), one first instructs the person to undertake the fifteen precepts.

[Commentary]: This refers to the four precepts concerning extra robes and alms bowls that have been kept beyond the monthly limit. These pertain to the period after one has received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

If one counts more than ten days from the time wealth was accepted while still a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), it constitutes an offense of *pāyattika* (transgression) within the three categories of intentional offenses. Regarding the method for medicine:

it is not the case that once the two forms of acceptance—by hand and by mouth—are completed while one is a novice, the legal status of the acceptance is lost immediately upon advancing to full ordination.
Therefore, there is no spontaneous occurrence.

Regarding the four long sections in the first division, according to the *Yìchāo* (Excerpts on Meaning), there are two senses: receiving [the offense] after counting the transgressions is the first sense;
that is, receiving them collectively for what preceded is the second sense. The *Yìchāo* states: "Alternatively, it may also apply to the preceding number of days."

Regarding the phrase "after ten days are full," this refers to the combined period; alternatively, examining it closely, two meanings exist, and here the latter meaning is adopted to explain the aforementioned transgression of exceeding ten days, thus stating that it includes the prior period of receiving [the medicine].
However, one must further distinguish between two types of offenses: first, the offense of exceeding the day of formal reception;

second, the offense of reaching the limit after reception has concluded—both constitute offenses regardless of the three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral). The subsequent section distinguishes this from the case of long-term medicinal substances, even though...

These "extra" [robes] are counted because they are subject to the rules regarding possession (*parigraha*); they differ from the aforementioned four types of possessed items because their status (*avasthā*) is distinct.
If that is so, then when one was a *śrāmaṇera*, one kept extra robes, and after receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), the status likewise changed;
why, then, are those former items included in the count? Please explain this.

[Commentary: Furthermore, there are eleven offenses committed as a śrāmaṇera: teaching others how to prepare the five types of bedding, holding robes for a nun, washing, beating, or dyeing her robes, weaving robes for her, taking back robes, and having already initiated the preparatory effort (prayoga), subsequently committing the offense automatically upon completion.

Next, regarding the text on the training for persons, eleven precepts are listed: taking a robe and giving it to a nun to wash means washing a used garment; beating it means beating it with one's hand;

hair exceeding [the limit] means hair that has grown past the cord; "immediately" means to urgently seek the robe; "a nun’s robe" means taking a robe belonging to a nun who is not a relative; the remainder is understandable.
[Commentary: Regarding the remaining precepts, they must be formally received once more.
Next, among the fifteen precepts that do not arise spontaneously (*anupātta*), if one relies on the two types of abstention (*virati*), there is no sense of transgression;
however, as for those that must be formally received, this reveals that transgression is established through one's own action, and thus they do not arise spontaneously.
*Commentary on the Essentials of Practice of the Annotated Prātimokṣa of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Three, Part Two;
*Commentary on the Essentials of Practice of the Annotated Prātimokṣa of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Three, Part Three.
[Vinaya] First: The precept against keeping extra robes beyond the limit.
[Commentary: Regarding the first [category], the four points concerning the precept on keeping extra robes are the same as before.

As for the original intent of the initial prohibition: it was because the faculties and retributions of sentient beings differ and their strengths are unequal, that the Great Sage employed skillful means to establish permissions and prohibitions from beginning to end, resulting in six distinct types of supplementary regulations.

In the first section of the general introduction concerning the establishment of the precepts, there are two parts: the initial section on the provisional opening and closing of prohibitions—where "closing" refers to the establishment of the precepts—and the subsequent section on the hearing [of permission].

The first is the fundamental establishment; in relation to the second, it is termed "hearing. The second is the establishment of the prohibition, which necessarily requires an opening. The following four cases are all openings, yet each opening has its corresponding prohibition.

Since the final six types involve the provisional opening and establishment of the precepts according to the capacities of sentient beings, the text says "will supplement"; "will" (jiāng) here means...

This is an auxiliary [explanation]. [Commentary]: For those of superior capacity (*uttamapuruṣa*), the power of their karmic retribution is extraordinary; the fetal membranes grow along with them, so they do not require external sustenance.

Furthermore, when about to enter the Dharma, they vow never to consume anything else. Thus, the Tathāgata, in accordance with their capacities, permits them to rely solely on this [practice] to spontaneously pacify conditions and cultivate the means of salvation.

Regarding the "King on the Face" among the types of rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*): the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xianyu jing*) states that he has the character for "king" (*rāja*) upon his face.
According to the *Treatise on the Analysis of Merit* (*Fenbie gongde lun*), this person was born with a celestial crown (*mukuṭa*) upon his head, and thus the Brahmans conferred this name upon him.
Known as Māṇava, when he went forth from home, he donned a single white woolen cloth and went to where the World-Honored One was, seeking to become a seeker of the Way.
The Buddha said, "Welcome," and he immediately became a śramaṇa. He took the very white woolen cloth he had been wearing and dyed it into a *kāṣāya* robe, not using any other garment.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "I wish to wear this one robe for the rest of my life; may the Buddha grant me his permission."
The Buddha then silently consented; based on this, it appears that this was not the *jarāyu* (afterbirth). However, according to the *Zhangfu yi* (Ritual for Robes), it states:

"The Śākya sons wear their 'face-kings' (*mianwang*) garments as they go. From this, it is clear that the *jarāyu* is indeed intended. Furthermore, in the *Fofa zang zhuan* (Biographies of the Dharma-treasury Transmitters), Śāṇakavāsin is also said to have worn the *jarāyu*.
Yet, these accounts concern events after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; thus, citing them as evidence for the original intent of the regulation is entirely inconsistent.
"Requisites" refers to external support; "sustaining" means providing maintenance. The following two lines refer to the aforementioned going forth and addressing the Buddha.
The two lines beginning with "The Tathāgata" signify his silent consent. The two lines beginning with "Then" express the intention to go out and listen.
"Tranquil by nature, seeking nothing else" means that for the purpose of relief, a single robe is already sufficient.
[Commentary]: Second, as for those whose karmic retribution of the faculties is next strongest, they are capable of enduring cold and hardship;

they practice giving according to circumstances without regarding it as difficult, because the Great Sage, having measured their capacity, determined that they are fit to engage in the practice. Therefore, he prescribed the three robes, which must all be maintained and honored.
Should any be missing, they must be provided.
Of these two [sections], the first describes the conditions for the recipient; as it is inferior compared to what precedes it yet superior compared to what follows, it is called "next-strong.

"The act of bestowing" refers to the actual practice of advancement. Next, the lower section clarifies the prescribed rules: those who must possess [the requisites] will incur an offense on each day if they lack them, specifically regarding the deficiency of robes.

[Commentary]: Third, although it was prescribed that one possess three robes, because their physical strength remains insufficient and their mental vigor weak, they are oppressed by the suffering of cold;

thus their spirits are distracted and they lack mindfulness as they go about. Therefore, the Tathāgata again assessed their capacities and dispositions, and permitted them to keep one hundred and one items for identification and maintenance.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Among the one hundred and one items, the three robes and the alms bowl must necessarily be maintained; the remaining external items..."
If one has received [the precepts], it is permissible not to receive them again;

there is no fault. Among the three [sections], the first describes those of inferior capacity; the second clarifies that the Buddha permitted those of lower [capacity]; the third section is identical in structure to the first.

In the first, because their strength is thin, they are oppressed by cold and suffering; because their minds are weak, their spirits and faculties are disordered. Following this, the second section clarifies the permission, recording the recognition [of the rule].

This means that one merely receives and maintains [the precepts] without adding dharmas; as for "adding dharmas," it is because [the addition] is not necessarily required for the three robes, as can be seen in the treatise. [Commentary:
As for the fourth person, their physical constitution is weak and their mental faculties are not sharp; they depend upon time and place, requiring warmth and...
It is well if one obtains provisions so that one may advance in practice; however, if they are restricted as before, it leads to the decline of the Path and the commission of evil.
Therefore, the keeping of surplus goods is permitted, provided they are accepted according to what is offered, so that the donor may obtain merit and the recipient may gain sustenance for the Path.
Regarding the first two phrases among the fourth type of capacity: when both body and mind are inferior, one requires warmth as a counteragent, meaning one cannot endure the suffering of cold;

one requires a favorable environment, meaning one cannot tolerate lowly or humble conditions. If one is provided with these supports and is able to advance in practice, it clearly shows that such provisions are beneficial.
Conversely, if one retreats from the Path when subjected to the same restrictions as above, it demonstrates that such restrictions are detrimental.
Therefore, the following clarifies that by opening [the allowance], both self-benefit and benefit for others are accomplished.

[Commentary] As for the fifth type of person, their faculties and powers are extremely weak; they must rely on substantial objects to be able to alleviate suffering, sustain their bodies, and advance upon the Path.
Because there may be gradual stages [of progress], it is permitted to keep bedding, carriages, and other heavy objects in accordance with the teachings, as these matters are of great importance.
Therefore, one does not permit the giving of pure offerings (*śuddha-dāna*).

Regarding the fifth capacity, "suffering" refers to the fact that as long as one possesses a physical body, how could there be peace? Thus, the subsequent explanation of the prohibition can be understood.
[Commentary: As for the sixth person, they must obtain rooms adorned with various jewels before they can find peace of mind; this is as explained in the *Vibhaṅga*.
In the *Gongde lun*, it is said that when the deva Subhūti heard it was taught that one could enter the Path with coarse clothing, he refused to do so and instead sought various precious dwellings.
The Buddha ordered that all the royal requisites be lent to him, and by using them for a single night, the bhikṣu attained the Way.

The Buddha said, "You should know that awakening to the Way depends on the mind and is not restricted by outward form or dress. From this day forward, those who require such things shall be permitted to have them."
Regarding the first section of the six [divisions], the initial part describes the suitability of the capacity, as indicated below by citing the Buddha’s regulations:

"Among the Buddha’s disciples, there were two Subhūtis—one of royal lineage and one of householder lineage (namely, Śūnyatā-janman). Since this one is of royal lineage, the term 'deva' is added to distinguish him.
This refers to his birth in the world through the transformation-response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) as a constant teaching being (*saṃsāra-śāstṛ*) for five hundred lifetimes.
When the World-Honored Buddha returned to his native land, King Śuddhodana (also known as Janaka) exhorted five hundred members of the Śākya clan to leave the household life;
this bhikṣu was among their number. At the time of their renunciation, the Buddha instructed the bhikṣus:

"Those who practice the Way must all restrain themselves and maintain their integrity, wearing coarse garments, eating poor food, using grass and straw for beds, and taking excrement and urine as medicine. This bhikṣu...
Having heard this, he thought to himself: "I was born into a noble and wealthy family where food, clothing, and dwellings were provided naturally;

my palaces and garments were most exquisitely adorned, yet even so my desires were not fully satisfied. How much less could I endure wearing these five-layered hempen robes? I shall return home to fulfill my original intention.
He then went to the Buddha's presence, took leave of Ānanda, and said: "Please stop for a moment [as I have received the Buddha’s instruction]."
That night, he went to the king’s residence and borrowed various types of seating, banners, canopies, flowers, incense, lamps, and oil;
he prepared everything with great magnificence so that this bhikṣu might stay there overnight. By the final watch of the night, [the bhikṣu] attained the fruit of arhatship.
Ānanda informed the Buddha, and the Buddha replied as recorded in the commentary.
[Commentary: Although the preceding [passage] generally permits [the use of requisites], it is not for the sake of nourishing the karmic retribution.
As the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-nirdeśa* (The Sūtra on the Appearance of the Tathāgata) states: "The Tathāgata appears in the world to eliminate the notion of 'self.
If one does not do so, even while remaining within my Dharma, one shall not be permitted to enjoy even a single cup of water or a single robe. This is explained as follows.

Those who have escaped from affliction are like those in *nirvāṇa*; even if there are a hundred thousand such people, one should not consider that number large. A practitioner must measure themselves and determine their own station.

As the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If one lacks virtuous conduct yet accepts clothing and food, if they do not go to hell, then the clothing shall leave their body and the food shall burst through their belly.
These words are most grave; how can one deceive oneself? It is as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
It is said that for three reasons this precept was established: first, because of the accumulation of surplus, one becomes greedy for worldly gain and thereby destroys the wealth of the path’s merit;
second, because one loses the faith and respect of laypeople, as the bhikṣu’s hoarding becomes no different from that of a layperson;
and third, because it violates the Buddha’s four reliances and constitutes a practice lacking in frugality.
The subsequent section also has two parts. First, it demonstrates the intent of the allowance, as shown below; second, it cites scriptural evidence, which also has two parts.

First, it cites the *Buddhapiṭaka* to clarify that this is not an intended allowance. It further states: "If a monk who has broken the precepts cannot even digest one part-in-a-thousand-billion of an offering when a single hair is split into a thousand billion parts, how much less could he digest the four requisites? This is for the sake of liberation. Next, it cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
To clarify the correct meaning and open the mind, that sutra states: "I permit the bhikṣus to possess clothing, food, and bedding, each worth one hundred thousand pieces of gold.

This also permits their possession [of such items]. By previously citing a single hair to illustrate the small by means of the great, this clarifies the hundred thousand [pieces of gold] by illustrating the few through the many.
Since they have already attained liberation, how could they possess even a hundred thousand? Whether suppressing or exalting [the point], the intent remains the same.

There is nothing that does not entice practitioners; following this, the text cites a warning for those who lack self-reflection, fearing that upon hearing such permissions they may fail to grasp the Buddha’s intent and instead become arrogant and self-important—a phenomenon common in the final age, all resulting from a failure to examine oneself.

Regarding the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, "not heading toward hell" means one is fortunately spared from future retribution; "clothes remaining detached from the belly" means one must undergo suffering in the present life. Next...

Among these three intentions: first, if one is greedy for worldly gain, one will surely ruin the wealth of the Path; second, if one loses the trust of the laity, one will surely incur censure and defamation;
third, if one violates the four reliances, one will surely become intent on luxury and indulgence. Thus, by establishing three benefits, one overturns these three faults.

[Commentary] Second, regarding the explanation of the names: to store and use for one's own benefit is called "keeping" (*śikṣāpada*); to exceed the limit by retaining what remains after distribution is called "long-term";
because it exceeds the prescribed time limit, it is termed the "precept against keeping long-term or exceeding the limit."

Second, regarding the explanation of the name and its limitations: "the remainder" refers either to the three robes (*tricīvara*) or to those items outside the "one hundred and one" [permitted articles].
"Exceeding the time limit" means exceeding ten days.
[Commentary: There are three reasons why this is placed at the beginning.

In the second column of the sequence, the heading states: "The first master [classifies] the transgression of long robes as one offense that extends laterally to all other precepts, making two categories; the latter master considers the joy in committing offenses as common to all, making three.

[Commentary]: The first view holds that the single offense of possessing long robes can laterally extend to all other prohibitions, yet only nine precepts involve the fault of being stained by the transgression of long robes.
"Stained" (*yōu*) refers to two [types of] robes, two [types of] hair, two [types of] precious items, two bowls, and leftover medicine.

Regarding "horizontal extension" (*pángtōng*), the ancient interpretation of the first section states that "horizontal" (*páng*) means "transverse. According to the *Yìchāo*, taking a nun’s robe and so forth after the day has passed constitutes the offense of "excess" (*cháng*);

this is called "horizontal extension," meaning that one first commits the offense of excess regarding the extra robe, and subsequently takes the nun’s robe and so forth, thereby being stained by that excess.
The name "nine secondary defilements" refers to the fact that the first four dharmas do not defile [the precepts], while the latter five differ in their physical manifestation.

[Commentary] Question: How is this known? Answer: The Vinaya states that if one exchanges a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* robe for another without having relinquished the former, there is one *pāyattika* offense and one *duṣkṛta* offense.
Is this not the case? This means that although the material object has been relinquished, the mind of possession remains defiled, thereby constituting an offense.
Regarding the next section on the inquiry, the response from the cited text states that if one commits an offense involving the forfeiture of a robe and exchanges it for a new one,
the subsequent robe constitutes one *pāyattika*— which is the offense of "excess"— and one *duṣkṛta*, which is the offense of wearing it.

[Commentary: If one maintains this interpretation, then when robes belonging to a *bhikṣuṇī* are purchased and come into one's possession, one would be required to perform the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity) for them; yet, if one fails to do so, one incurs the offense of exceeding the limit (*atireka-dosa*) and further commits the offense of keeping an extra robe (*dīrgha-dosa*).
This current explanation is not so. Since the substance of such purchased wealth is defiled, it is improper to perform the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* for it to make it into the three robes (*tricīvara*).

As the Vinaya states: "A robe obtained through an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) is unfit to be accepted as pure. Based on this, if it is not pure, how could there be any defilement [of the robes]? Furthermore, since the wealth itself has no dual forfeiture, [the distinction between pure and impure does not apply].
