If [the time] has passed, there is a grave offense; this is consistent with the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Based on the common conditions, I shall rely on the "appearance of light" (*prabhāta-lakṣaṇa*) for now, and the rest shall be omitted.

Among the three [types of offenses], only the "storing overnight within" (*antar-śayana*) is explained, as the rules for oneself and others differ. First, I shall demonstrate the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* to show the underlying intent behind that regulation.

In the next section, when the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* first clarifies the fault regarding sentient beings, it should be understood as being identical to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* in its clarification of the "temporary separation" (i.e., going outside to avoid them) when dawn is about to break;

thus, one does not violate the restrictive rules. Below, the text demonstrates the flexibility of the Vinaya: since the food is not specifically assigned [to a particular category], it is said to be a "universal condition" (*sāmānya-pratyaya*).

[Commentary] Regarding the fourth point, the characteristics of the offense incurred for what is to be separated from: according to the sub-commentary on the Vinaya, with the exception of three items, the rest constitute a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

My current interpretation is as follows: regarding the "one hundred and one requisites," since there are those that may be kept and those that may be separated from, one incurs a minor offense [for failing to separate them].

As for the remaining items that have been "purified" (*viśuddha*) by designating another person as the owner, how could there be an offense for separation? This is as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "One should accept and keep the three robes, the undergarment, and the cloak."

The rain-bath garment, the wound-covering cloth, the mosquito net, the walking screen, the louse-removing cloth, the thigh-and-ankle protector, the head-wiping cloth, the hand-towel, the face-towel, and various bags—if they resemble robes, they should all be formally received and maintained;
the details regarding the keeping of these surplus items are also as explained in the *Śāstra*.

Regarding the initial summary in the section on the characteristics of offenses, the following now provides the correct interpretation to clarify the errors of the ancients. The ancients maintained that all instances of being separated from the "one hundred and one" types of robes constituted an offense of *duṣkṛta* (light transgression).

This [text], however, simply sets forth the correct explanation to demonstrate the inadequacy of those ancient views. As for the various robes cited as evidence below, they are all included within the "one hundred and one";
this is indicated by the reference to the *Śrīlāta-vinaya-vibhāṣā* (the *Chao*) in the section on the two robes.
[Vinaya]: Except by means of a formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma). [Commentary]:

Regarding the sixth point in the text, "except by means of a formal act of the Saṃgha," this clarifies that one may be separated from the robe through the acquisition of a specific dharma. [Annotation]:
At that time, a bhikṣu suffered from the disease of consumption (yakṣman); his discarded saṃghāṭī robe was extremely heavy. There was a matter of necessity [for him to be separated from it].

While traveling, he was unable to maintain his practice and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha ordered him to perform three formal requests (*jñapti*) followed by a motion and resolution (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to separate from the group.
[Commentary] Following the listing of the causes for illness, the method of requesting is explained; in total, there are five underlying intentions.

[Commentary]: First, the explanation of the opening conditions is as stated in the text. Regarding the reason for [the Buddha] wandering among those afflicted by illness, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there are four intentions:
first, because there are sentient beings with karmic conditions who should receive transformation; second, because it is appropriate to wander among those damaged by illness;
third, to seek a place to practice the Path; and fourth, to subdue, inspire faith, and lead them to realization. As for why Śāriputra was ill, there are likewise four meanings.
1. Because he troubled people in previous lives; 2. Because he deeply contemplated the Dharma with wisdom; 3. Because he was diligent in his practice and did not lie down; 4.

Because this is his final body and his past karma is already exhausted, yet through his supernormal power he turned the trichiliocosm and, out of a heart of great compassion, requested the Holy One to establish the prohibitions.
Regarding the two dharmas that constitute an offense: it must involve a person and a disease; when the clothing is heavy, the offense is established; for other persons or diseases, it is not.
Mutually, there is no single-sided establishment of what is called "old age"; generally, those over seventy years of age are designated as old.

Regarding the aforementioned four benefits, one may even seek them out regarding the Three Jewels. Furthermore, concerning the separation from robes—whether many or few—in this context, it refers specifically to the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If one leaves behind [a robe], provided it is done together and not through a formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*), all constitute the offense of separation (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*); however, it is permitted to leave [them] behind."
Regarding the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), one must not leave openings at the top or bottom that could provide an opportunity for thieves; rather, one should leave it as it is when it fits well.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* agree on this point. Fourth, concerning the duration of the days: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* does not permit opening [the retreat] during the summer season, whereas the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* allows for the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*) in nine months and the later retreat (*paścimavarṣā*) in eight months.
The *Samantapāsādikā* states that if an illness has not yet been cured, one may remain; however, if the illness is cured, one must return immediately, even if encountering difficulties.

Regarding the non-forfeiture and non-creation of the intention to forfeit the robe, it is generally said: if, after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one becomes too ill to go and later goes, the previous *karmavācanā* remains valid.

If one’s transformation [of the mind] is not yet complete, or while still seeking robes and medicine for the Three Jewels, and the month has already ended because of such difficulties, there is no offense as the conditions have ceased.
If [the monk] dies, these robes may be given to the five types of attendants.

The *Chongjia buduolun* (Treatise on Further Additions) states: "If the original robe has been offered to the Triple Gem and one seeks to obtain another robe, regardless of its weight or value, one should perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for its addition; this applies even up to the ninth month."

The sixth section explains the five intentions of the commentary. Regarding the first intention, there are two parts: first, citing the text; second, providing the explanation. First, the explanation of "wandering":

the first four points concern benefiting others—namely, those who are easily transformed; the fourth concerns those who are difficult to transform, and thus require subduing so that they may develop faith and realization.
The latter two points both concern self-benefit: "disease" refers to harm, which is to say, reduction. Next follows the explanation of "contracting illness."
Because of Śāriputra, it was necessary to clarify the intention regarding the beginning and end; concerning past karma, two points were established based on present practice.
That treatise asks: "If Śāriputra possesses the supernatural power of *ṛddhi* such that he can rotate the trichiliocosm in his hand, why does he say the saṃghāṭī robe is heavy?
The passage beginning with "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) is the answer given therein for the sake of future generations.
Because he manifested [the illness] despite being aged and infirm, it is called "Great Compassion. Of the two [aspects], the first shows that he did not fall ill due to the weight of his robes;

the second, regarding those who possess the requisite conditions, shows that only they are fit to receive the Dharma. Below, the explanation of the marks of aging is discussed in the *Madhyama Āgama*, where "seventy" is the correct reading (the variant "thirty" is an error).
The four benefits are the same as before. The passage beginning with "wandering" indicates the specific [details].

Question: Based on this, is it not necessary that one must be old or ill to be granted permission to manage monastic affairs? Question: If a youth is ill, is he permitted to leave [his duties] to attend to his condition?
Answer: The two conditions of being old and being ill do not overlap. Some say that if one is ill but not old, this may still be permitted;

however, as for one who is old but not ill, such a case is certainly not allowed. Our current view is otherwise: "old" refers to the decline of physical strength and does not necessarily require [the presence of illness].

Regarding the three types of robes among the "sicknesses" (ābādha), the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) herein refers to the *Mūla-vinaya*, as noted in the commentary on the first section of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.

As for the statement that "separating from them all constitutes an offense," it says there that to separate from all three robes when they have not been formally relinquished through *karmavācanā* is an offense because one has falsely applied the ritual formula to what was not permitted;
thus, the action is contrary to the Dharma and fails to be established, resulting in the lower grade of the offense (*pāyattika*). As for the upper grade:
The *saṃghāṭī* is for entering a village to generate wholesome merit; the "lower" refers to the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṇṭhaka*), as it is not permitted to wear only that alone.

Second, one must not keep [the robes] below [the waist]; this clarifies that in times of difficulty there are no restrictions. The "lower" refers to the two texts being identical, hence they are not cited separately.

Among the four [texts], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* both clarify that the time is not restricted; those who enter the *pūrvavarṣā* (early rains retreat) are exempt from the three-month period.

Regarding those who observe the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), with the exception of the four-month period, according to the principle established in the *Madhyama-āgama*, the suspension [of the precepts] is permitted as soon as the retreat is completed; thus, the timing is not fixed.

Next, citing the *Jianlun* (Sūtra on Seeing), it clarifies that during the middle [period], even if one recovers from an illness or does not recover, or encounters difficulties, the [retreat] is not lost; it says:

"If the road is dangerous and one cannot return, yet one constantly maintains the intention to return, even if one departs, the [retreat] is not lost. Subsequently, citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it clarifies other miscellaneous matters.

Regarding the three aspects: first, it clarifies that after the initial [period], the subsequent application of the rule does not require a renewed request; second, it clarifies that there is no offense when the transformation of others is difficult;

and third, it clarifies the case where the transformation is not yet complete—meaning one goes to teach them because the number of people is large or the location is distant—and thus the month ends while the task remains unfinished, such as when nine or eight months have elapsed. "The conditions having ceased" refers to the completion of the undertaking.

If the provisions are prepared outside the month due to specific circumstances, the summer limit is also permitted to be extended. If one dies while away from home, the responsibility for the funeral expenses falls upon those to whom they belong;
if there are caregivers for the deceased while abroad, they may request compensation for their services. Regarding the five types of robes, the primary robe is obtained first according to the rules.
As for the subsequent robes, regardless of whether they are light or heavy, they are permitted to be kept due to the opening of the allowance based on specific circumstances.
Because it has already been made without discrimination. [Vinaya] *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
[Commentary] The two phrases regarding the seventh and eighth items concern the two aspects of relinquishing the offense.
The two items, numbers seven and eight, are *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, which means they are offenses involving forfeiture (*śeṣa-pāyattika*). [Note:
If one is separated from any robes other than the three [allowable] robes, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; this applies equally to nuns as it does to monks.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary states: "The remaining robes and their light offenses are as explained above.
Regarding the explanation of the transgressions, "the remaining robes" refers to the aforementioned fourth section of the sub-commentary, which states: "For nuns, it is the same;
furthermore, if they [use] the *saṃkakṣikā*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the five robes [inappropriately], all constitute an offense."
[Note] There is no offense if the Saṃgha has performed the *karmavācanā*, if the dawn has not yet appeared, if one holds the robe in hand, if one has discarded the robe,
if one has reached the point where a thrown stone would land, if there is the perception that it has been taken away, if the path by water or land is cut off due to urgent distress,

if one is seized by bandits, wild beasts, or powerful persons, or if there is danger to life or to the *brahmacarya*; or if one does not discard the robe and does not reach the point where a thrown stone would land.
[This constitutes] an offense.

[Commentary: Among those cases where there is no offense, it is explained generally that there are seven ways in which there is no offense: (1) separating by means of an individual ritual, whether through face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*) or mental recitation (*manasikāra*);
(2) separating by means of a ritual before the Sangha, which has two parts. Regarding the first, there is the request for the ritual when there is a specific reason, as explained above.

2. The shared *kaṭhina* ritual involving separation from the three [types of robes]; 3. Separation by means of performing the ritual at a designated location, which does not result in the loss of the robe-boundary, as detailed in the *Jie-mo-shu-chao*;
4. Separation due to fear in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*); 5. Separation due to obstacles on royal roads or for reasons such as life or the *brahmacarya*, as explained below in the opening section;
6. Separation through the distribution of rewards during the *kārttika* month; 7. As described in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding superior conditions concerning the Saṃgha or the stūpa.

Furthermore, in the second section explaining the seven cases of non-offense regarding separation, the initial phrase "generally clarifying" means that it encompasses all conditions and does not apply exclusively to this one.
First, as noted in the commentary, this refers to the case where one discards the robe. Second, regarding the Sangha, there are two methods of requesting [permission]. Thus...

The commentary states: When the *saṃgha* performs the *karmavācanā*, the three pairs of locations previously mentioned as "open conditions" (*mukta-pratyaya*) are separated; this constitutes the binding of the *cīvara-sīmā*.

Prior to the binding, one merely relies on the monastery grounds (*vihāra*). Once the binding has been completed, it extends throughout both the interior and exterior of the monastery grounds, so that there is no loss [of the robe's validity] for either party.
Since this is not clarified here, it is referred to as being in the *Jiejie chao* (Manual on the Binding of Boundaries), as found in other commentaries.
Regarding the two robes: the fourth and seventh appear together in this section; they are explained in detail later in the twenty-ninth precept.
The fifth is as noted in the commentary; the sixth appears in the rules for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).

[Commentary: Regarding these seven types of relinquishment involving both existent and non-existent objects (*dharmin*), the first three constitute relinquishment of an existent object (*dharmasat*), while the latter three constitute relinquishment of a non-existent object (*dharmanāstitva*).

The intermediate case of the six-night period spent in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) and then sent back to a village constitutes relinquishment of a non-existent object due to the fear of losing [the robe]. The "remote relinquishment" (*dūrasaṃnyāsa*) is relinquishment of an existent object.

In the initial section of the *Liaojian*, regarding the first three items, there are dharmas that must be distinguished as being different. The ritual procedure of the "Individualists" (Bie-ren) involves the relinquishing of the robe and the loss of the dharma;

it is not an allowance for separation from the *kāṭhina*. This is for the purpose of receiving robes oneself at the designated location and binding the boundary (*sīmābandha*) based on one's own conditions;

only the method of requesting [permission] constitutes a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) that permits separation. Furthermore, although the seven types of separation share the same name, they themselves possess three distinct categories.
The first type of separation consists of relinquishing; the third consists of non-loss. As for the remaining five, they all pertain to non-loss in a different location.
These constitute the distinctions regarding separation for those in training; one should examine them carefully and not confuse them as one.
[Commentary: Regarding whether an offense is incurred or not: in the second, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh [cases], there is definitively no offense because there is a valid cause.
In the fifth case, it is due to being obstructed or forgetting to maintain the vow; thus, the loss of the vow does not accord with the explanation given in the text.

Next, the section on the five kinds of faultless [cases] distinguishes the loss of the dharma; while the other four are certainly not lost, the fifth may or may not be lost, as can be seen in the text itself.

Regarding the subsequent section on "forgetting and severing," according to the *Chao* (Commentary), it should be read as the character "wàng" (to look toward/expect), meaning the thought of losing it.
First, the case of a guilty loss of the dharma is clear. Third, regarding the "place of opposition," there may be three obstacles to separation.

Regarding the loss of the offense, it should be divided into three grades: the first grade (the upper five) is exclusively non-existent; the third grade is exclusively existent; and the middle grade is indeterminate as to existence or non-existence. [Commentary]:

When the Saṃgha performs the *karmavācanā*, this constitutes the attainment of the dharma that separates one from the prior state of being without the dharma. This occurs before the appearance of the dawn light.
When reaching the place where the stone was thrown, one should instead interpret this as "opening what was previously closed.

If one has the thought of taking [the robe] away, yet the robe is actually present and one forgets to give rise to that thought of taking it away, even if a night passes, the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) is lost; however, because the intention lacked the resolve for loss, there is no offense.

Since the mind lacks the fault of intentional relinquishment (*tyāga*), one does not commit the offense of abandonment. If the path by water or land is cut off, this includes even cases of forceful seizure or being obstructed by barriers.
Alternatively, it may be that the Buddha’s prohibition against descending [to this level] was due to the obstruction of emotional defilement, rather than because of arrogance; thus, they do not meet.

In the first section of the commentary on the text, there are five parts: first, explaining the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) which opens up what previously lacked a rule—this refers to the aforementioned stage of transgression;

second, explaining the "running protection" (*pārivāsika*) which reverses the previous opening—this refers to the three conditions for opening up concealment already listed in the preceding note; third... [and so forth].

To illustrate this, it is said that "reversing the interpretation" (fǎnjiě) involves three explanations: first, the removal of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and the loss of dharmas are both without fault;

second, they share the same meaning as being obstructed and cut off from hope; third, "forgetting" (*wàng*) should be taken as "delusion" (*wàng*), referring to false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*). The fourth and fifth sections can be understood by correlating them with the three obstructions (*āvaraṇa*).

[Commentary] Question: These various obstacles all exist within the state of "opening" (the opportunity for transgression); regarding those who have incurred a fault or committed an offense, how should they be adjudicated? Answer:

The manifestations of these signs are extremely numerous. Now, based on the gravity or mildness of the mental transgression and the conduct involved—if one has constantly maintained careful restraint and was unintentionally separated from the offense, yet suddenly encounters difficult circumstances where the person's clothing becomes different and one leaves it behind without conscious intent, but merely because the matter is obstructed—then according to this treatise, one must examine the mind.

It is not termed an offense if, due to mental indolence or laziness, one relinquishes the robes through various circumstances; there is relinquishment when the robes are separated from one's person, and there is an offense as described above in the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* regarding the rule of unlimited purification.
Regarding the question of "loss" (*hāni*) and "offense" (*āpatti*): "loss" refers to the loss of the Dharma, while "offense" refers to committing a transgression.

In the response, the first part provides a general indication, while the subsequent section offers a specific explanation. First, regarding the urgency of practice, it generally permits what is otherwise obstructive—that is, what would normally be a hindrance.

Second, regarding the laxity of disposition, it again restricts according to the text; therein, the two instances of the character "捨" (*śe*, to relinquish) refer precisely to "loss. As indicated below, this cites the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* by analogy.
If one does not perform the *śuddhi-vācanā* (declaration of purity), the ten-day period is not opened.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the conditions for exemptions from the precepts, how are diligence and indolence distinguished? Answer: The various exemptions regarding the characteristics of the precepts are all intended for those who practice them with devotion;
there must certainly be indolence in study for one to commit a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). These are not universal exemptions.

In the text of the "Difficulties" (Zhuan nan), it is not stated what the intention behind forcibly distinguishing [the cases] is; therefore, in the "Response" (Da), this is used as a basis to resolve all [such instances].
This opening of the text is not limited to this alone. [Commentary: Question:

Regarding the allowance for extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), this case involves forgetting [the rules]; is this an allowance? Answer: It is also like the previous two perspectives; one must diligently uphold [the precepts], and forgetting [them] constitutes an offense.

If one cannot learn [the ritual] and suddenly remembers it at night, one may take it up for the sake of understanding; there is no fault in seeking it out the next morning. It is neither a forfeiture nor an offense.

If it were lost through abandonment, the mind would be separated from the object and the conditions would differ, thus resulting in loss rather than an offense. An offense follows the intent and the teaching; if one originally forgot [the ritual], there is no transgression.
Next, in the inquiry, because one wishes to use the precedent of "long-term forgetting" to open up the case of "separation from robes," this question and answer are presented.

Within these, there are two perspectives based on the previous [distinction between] diligence and negligence. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, it clarifies that because the obstructing conditions prevent the mind from being interrupted, it is neither a loss nor an offense;

second, it clarifies that if the perception of loss occurs—meaning the aforementioned perspective is severed—it constitutes a loss of the formal rule, yet not an offense. This is based on the preceding [analysis].
To know that one has fallen [into transgression] is both a loss and an offense.
[Commentary: Regarding the two precepts of food and clothing, the *shu* (commentary) states that in the final age, people maintain only these two;

as for the remaining precepts, most are abandoned. Between food and clothing, there is not a single day they are not observed. As for those who observe them, they do so in accordance with the Dharma. It is simply that—
It suffices to say that you should not take offense at this abundance, nor should you feel that my intent is not fully expressed;

for regarding the two matters of clothing and food, there are extensive authentic teachings in the *Shōsho* (Commentary on the Essentials) and the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (Exegesis on the Ritual Procedures) that I have compiled, whereas all other matters are treated only briefly, and I know them merely in outline.
In the second part of the *Jiegu* (The Exhortation), there are two sections. First, it clarifies the reason why broad detail is required regarding the precepts on clothing and food.

As for these precepts: the various chapters following the *Tisheng* (Upāli) section mostly derive from clothing and food. On one hand, they are triggered by greedy desires; on the other, they are practices to be performed daily.

Because these precepts are explained with meticulous detail, it is said that [the Buddha] "held them in particular regard," meaning he paid his closest attention to them. "Mutual maintenance" refers to the restraint applied according to specific circumstances.
"Protection" refers precisely to what was previously called the "Dharma of the Bequeathed Teaching," wherein only the formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the practice (*caryā*) are emphasized.
As for the remaining precepts, those not regulated by matters of food and clothing are mostly omitted from discussion because their transgressive objects are not frequently encountered;

thus, for those who observe them according to the Dharma, there is no need for further mention. Conversely, this serves to clarify that few are able to observe them according to the Dharma, which is why it must be stated: "Do not [be lax]."

Second, regarding the *Lüshìchão* (Abridged Commentary on Ritual Matters), the sections on the precepts concerning leaving the assembly (*li-cháng-biézhòng*) and so forth, as well as the commentary in the second fascicle on the two robes, the four medicines, responding to invitations, and so on—namely, the texts concerning the two realms of food and clothing, as well as the receiving and purification of robes and medicines—are all extensive and detailed. Those who have already heard these may understand them;
however, those who have not yet heard them should examine themselves closely, for they are merely at the beginning of their study.
*Commentary on the Essentials of Practice of the Annotated Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Part Three, Lower One;
*Commentary on the Essentials of Practice of the Annotated Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Part Three, Lower Two.
[Vinaya] The precept concerning the three-month limit for keeping extra robes.
[Commentary] The third [section] concerns the precept on receiving robes at the full moon of the third month;
it is also called "Understanding the Intent of the Regulation.
Regarding the intent of the regulation: although one receives clothing according to the season to support the body, even if there are old garments, they may not be fit for wear.
It is because they merely accept and maintain [the robes] that the Noble One permitted their possession for the purpose of exchange;

however, as these were few and insufficient to wait for the full [period], he again permitted a one-month extension. Once the robes were sufficient, it was only right that they be accepted and replaced.
To possess them beyond this limit violates the Noble Teaching and destroys the dharma of few desires; therefore, this rule was established.

The first two lines of the introductory section provide a general account of clothing and requisites according to the seasons, namely cold and heat. The section beginning with "Although" specifically clarifies the present precept, which is further divided into two parts:

first, the explanation of the intent behind the allowance; second, the explanation of the intent behind the prohibition. Regarding the former, the section beginning with "Since" provides the narrative of the intent for the allowance; following this, the section beginning with "Now" clarifies the intent for the prohibition.

[Commentary: Five conditions constitute the offense: 1) because it is a single robe from one's original possession; 2) if the three robes are worn out, yet one keeps a new or fine set, one commits the aforementioned precept;
3) if one is permitted to keep surplus wealth intended as a replacement for those robes; 4) if one already possesses sufficient material for the robes and does not cut them into the required strips;
5) if there is no valid cause or condition, and one exceeds the time limit, one commits the offense.

Regarding the first of the requisite conditions: this rule for the *śīla-mūla* (root of the precepts) is established because when a robe is worn out and needs replacement, a one-month period is permitted for obtaining a robe.
If the robe is new and in good condition, it is not permitted. Furthermore, among the three robes (*tricīvara*), the permission applies if any one of them is worn out;

it is not necessary for all three to be worn out simultaneously. Third, regarding "common property" (*sādhāraṇa-vitta*): this refers to those whose physical substance and color are identical. As for the phrase "already sufficient," this is to be understood according to the following three positions.
According to the first two cases, if the third case occurs—regardless of whether it is asked or not, and whether it is sufficient or not—one commits an offense.
The rest are all as follows. [Note:
When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu with only three robes who had a saṃghāṭī that was worn out; for ten days...

In the meantime, they were unable to distinguish between what was permitted and what was not; because they wished to possess extra robes for the sake of fulfillment, the group of six bhikṣus took robes that were insufficient, washed, dyed, and marked them as purified, and then entrusted them to others while traveling abroad. A bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established the precept.

[Commentary]: Within the context of dependent origination, wood is [analogous to] the three robes; because one breaks the rule regarding robes for the sake of clothing, even if one obtains robe-material within the ten-day period, it is not yet complete.
Therefore, one must store it until the end of the month to fulfill the requirement.

When the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) heard this, they consequently committed an offense by taking robes that were incomplete; as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, "because the color and substance differ."
Because they are dissimilar, the present regulation is violated; yet, since it merely permits the making [of robes], why wait for the color and substance to be identical?

In the explanation of the conditions for the precept, the initial account describes the original allowance: because those who possess only the three robes do not store extra garments, this specific allowance was made for them.
As for the bhikṣu who stores extra robes, if he were not subject to this teaching, there would be no offense. This is as explained below when citing the rule on "identical robes."
He asked: "If one first obtains a blue garment and later obtains a yellow or red one, the colors are different;

furthermore, if one first obtains hemp and later obtains *kambala* or *kārpāsa*, the substances are dissimilar—does this constitute an offense? Now, following the above based on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the conditions for the precept are determined.

Question: In the previous section on the requisite conditions, it was stated that the property must be of the same kind (*samāna-dhana*). What is the answer to this? [The answer follows: The preceding...

Based on the first two positions, the same [category] is taken to fulfill this precept; however, regarding the offenses committed by the group of six within these conditions, it is actually based on the latter position that they are said to "wear the same robes.
Therefore, one must cite the definitive resolution to clearly understand that there is no distinction made [between the cases].
[Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu has finished making his robes.
[Commentary]: The precept text consists of nine phrases.
[Commentary]: First, the offender.

[Commentary: Having finished the section on the sufficiency of the two or three robes being of the same substance, if all three robes are ruined, then although the two-month period may be full for each of the three distinct types, one must immediately perform the ritual of receiving [a new robe]; if even one is not yet full, one must wait until it is full.
Regarding the second phrase of the *Prātimokṣa*, there are three distinct cases of expectation: namely, when each [period] has reached its full term of one month or two months.

This means that if the first two robes have reached their full month, one must make them immediately; as for the remaining one, it may be kept, but if it exceeds the month, it is likewise considered a defiled offense.
[Vinaya] The kaṭhina robe has been removed.

[Commentary] Regarding the three occasions for the removal of the kaṭhina, this refers to the cessation of the conditions that permit [the wearing of the robe]. Although the person did not formally accept the permission, because it was indeed permitted, there is no offense.
The third [point] states that such a person does not accept the dispensation because they are one who possesses only the three robes and does not accept the five privileges.
[The Vinaya says: "If a bhikṣu obtains out-of-season robe-cloth..."

[Note] "The proper time" refers to one month after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony when the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, or five months after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony when the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread.
"The improper time" refers to exceeding these limits.

[Commentary]: Regarding the fourth [category], "out-of-season robes" (*akālacīvara*): the annotation explains this in terms of time. Because they are outside of the permitted season, they are called "out-of-season.

Since within the permitted season [the use of such robes] is generally allowed without restriction regarding substitution, the current prohibition applies specifically during the out-of-season period, hence the one-month limit.
Among the four [categories], the "specified times" refer to one month and five months. Times other than these are called "non-specific times. Regarding "without clothing," it refers to eleven months;
regarding "with clothing," it refers to seven months. The following clarifies the reasons for distinguishing these times.
[The Vinaya: "If one desires [a robe], one may accept it; having accepted it, it should be completed quickly.

If it is sufficient, that is well. [The Commentary: "If within ten days the robe-material is sufficient, one should cut and sew it as described above. If not, then upon reaching the eleventh day, according to the amount of material, one commits an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya)."
[Commentary]: "If one desires it, one may accept it" indicates the characteristics of the robe being completed. Regarding the term "completed quickly":

since the cloth obtained on the first day was insufficient, it must be completed on the very day it becomes sufficient upon reaching the tenth day; otherwise, at dawn the following day, one would incur an offense.
Therefore, it is called "quickly. This is divided into three stages. The first stage is explained here as a general allowance, as stated in the commentary.

In the first part of the fifth section, there is a general indication; in the subsequent specific explanation, it is said that because one fears exceeding ten days, [the robe] must be completed quickly.
This refers to the indication of the stages below, which constitutes the first stage. As for the "remaining two stages" mentioned in the next section, this refers to what is generally permitted:
namely, that the *dīrghacīvara* (extra robe) is always permitted.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If one lacks sufficient [robes], one may keep them for one month in order to complete the set.
[Commentary] If one lacks the full set of robes, until the eleventh day—if on the eleventh day the full set of robes is obtained—one must act as prescribed above.
Should one fail to do so, by the twelfth day one incurs an offense regarding each robe; this applies likewise up to the twenty-ninth day.

When the thirtieth day arrives, whether the [robe] is sufficient or insufficient, whether it is the same cloth or not, on that very day they shall all be dealt with according to the aforementioned rule.
[Vinaya]: Should one keep it beyond this period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

[Note] Regarding whether bhikṣuṇīs commit the same offense or not: if within ten days they share the same robe and it is sufficient for making [a robe], or even if up to thirty days have passed and the robe is made on that very day, there is no offense;
otherwise, it is the same as the rule regarding long robes (*atirekacīvara*) when there is a valid reason.
[Commentary]: If it is insufficient, one may keep it for one month. This refers to the second stage, from the eleventh day to the twenty-ninth day, during which one may combine similar items;
on that very day, one may perform the ritual of non-similarity, and furthermore, one is permitted to look toward the following day.
This is based on the observance of the precepts according to the days. Furthermore, as explained in the commentary, the same applies to the twenty-ninth day.
Regarding the third case, up until the thirtieth day, whether one has received [the precepts] or not, it is said that they are held together; from the first day thereafter, they are no longer opened.

Because there is insufficient time in the sixth [case], twenty days are further opened to be combined as the first month’s release. First, the explanation of the [first] month: [Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on monastic disciplinary rules (*vinaya*), specifically concerning the calculation of the *poṣadha* (confession) period and the duration for which the precepts are maintained.]
If two positions together total nineteen days and the same type of robe is obtained, it is equivalent to having a sufficient robe; one should act on that very day.

If one does not act then, one commits an offense on the following day for obtaining a different robe. Furthermore, there is an opening for the following day, which refers to the subsequent position of thirty days.
Regarding the observance of the rules based on the number of days: in the initial position, it is still permissible within ten days to complete [the acquisition], starting from the tenth.

Because the limit for going away is only one day, it is also urgent. Alternatively, fearing that [the rite] might not be accomplished, one is instructed to perform the coarse practice and finish quickly.
After receiving the empowerment, one further pricks the third location with a fine needle. Only one day is permitted; if it is not obtained, one obtains it through *adhiṣṭhāna* (empowerment);
if it is not obtained, one performs the *viśuddhi* (purification). Otherwise, on the following day, one incurs an offense at the same time. If this is so...
Question: Do those who possess only the three robes also keep extra robes? Answer: Since this is a superior practice, there is certainly no room for negligence;

even if one were to perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) for them, it would not contradict the general principle that they are permitted [to keep extra robes], so there is no harm. Let students examine this further in detail.

[Commentary: This precept is established similarly to the previous rule regarding extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), as it concerns merely the robe itself; the remainder of the text is easily understood.

Within the section clarifying similarities and differences, the first two lines indicate the similarity, meaning that the characteristics of the offense (*āpatti-lakṣaṇa*) are no different from those previously stated; the latter two lines...

This specifically clarifies that [the allowance] applies only to those who possess the three robes; as for the previous opening regarding the storage of extra robes, the rest is easily understood, since the characteristics are clearly explained in the notes following the three subsequent sentences.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The precept against taking the robe of a non-relative nun.
[Commentary] The fourth precept concerning taking the robe of a nun.

[Commentary] There are three faults in its establishment: generally, when the inferior shows reverence to the superior, their feelings of devotion are earnest; they think of giving away what they possess, yet calculate that they have nothing left.

First, out of stinginess toward the Great Sangha, one recklessly accepts the wealth of others because they are not relatives; this causes their resources to be depleted, leading them to the distress of poverty and suffering.

Second, as the forms of men and women are distinct, it is logically impossible for them to become defiled by passion; yet now that their wealth and goods are intermingled, their emotional bonds become biased toward those who are close through such exchanges.
Because these interactions lead to defilement, there is the danger of violating the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); facing such perilous circumstances is truly most fearsome. Third.
One's conduct may involve worldly censure and invite slander; when one's purity is difficult to distinguish, there is no way to extricate oneself.
Because these various faults exist, this rule was established.
There are three intentions behind the fourth rule: first, it is for the sake of joy [in restraint]; second, it is to prevent defilement; and third, it is to ward off censure. Furthermore...
The first [type of stinginess] harms others; the second harms oneself; and the third harms both oneself and others. Within the first, "intense" (*yīn*) means grave;
"hoarding" (*qì*) means to store away; "depletion" (*qì*) means to exhaust; and "lack" (*qì*) means to be destitute. The two subsequent phrases summarize these points.
[Commentary] Five conditions constitute an offense.

[Commentary] First, regarding the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya), it states that taking [robes] from the two lower assemblies constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense); this is based on the distinction of their status.

However, if one takes [robes] out of defilement, there is no difference from a *bhikṣuṇī*, as stated in the *Mahā-saṃghika-vinaya* (Many-Section Vinaya), where washing robes and carding wool are offenses of the same category.

Falling into two categories of non-relatives: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, because they are relatives, one may take five parts by measure; yet even if they are relatives, taking [more] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Third, regarding "measured robes" (*pramāṇika-cīvara*), four parts are permitted as explained in the *Nidāna*. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, taking small items such as bowls does not constitute an offense.
Why is it that robes are considered "heavy"? Because people generally like to give many robes, they are heavy. As for the bowl, since there is only one, the offense is light.

Fourth, if one sends [an item] with an empty mind to obtain it by begging, there is no offense; however, upon receiving it, one commits an offense. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vibhaṅga* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mahāvibhāṣā*, if ten monks take one robe from a nun, all ten fall into the offense;
if ten nuns hold one robe and give it to one monk, all ten fall into the offense. The remainder is as explained in the *Vinayaviniścaya-ṭīkā*.

Regarding the first part of the "Requisites" (*pratyaya*), the citation from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* which distinguishes the two lower assemblies is identical to our own school. Below this, the meaning is determined:

the first phrase concludes the preceding section, while the latter part demonstrates a specific judgment. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, washing and beating constitute the same offense; this serves as a clear precedent.

Regarding the second point, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one must take the measure of a relative, meaning one must necessarily deliberate upon whether they exist or not; there is no falsehood in this principle.

Because it was taken [by force], there is no offense. Although the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that even taking from a relative is auspicious, in the end this invites censure; the intent is to sever both [possibilities].

Regarding the three cases, the origin story (*nidāna*) in the *Caturvargika-vinaya* concerns expensive Dharma robes, a *piṇḍapātra* (alms bowl), and small items—meaning there is no offense for stealing a *pātayantika* [offense] regarding small items.
"Small items" refers to those that are not of standard measure. Why? Below, the text raises a question to demonstrate the meaning of the weightiness or lightness of robes and bowls.
Fourth, "emptying the mind" means to exhaust one's sincerity and focus one's intent; it does not mean that the mind is insincere.

Fifth, regarding the ten *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses for monks, taking even one constitutes a downfall because their circumstances are identical; for nuns, ten are required to constitute one downfall because the counterparts differ. For details, refer to the *Śrī-vinaya-saṃgraha*, where the application according to specific characteristics is very extensive.
[Note] When the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, the nun Utpalavarṇā took food to the mountain to offer it to the senior monks (*sthavira*).
There, a certain bhikṣu, wearing worn-out robes, exchanged his expensive garments for those worn by the nun; he subsequently put on the worn-out clothes.
The Buddha, finding this strange, questioned and rebuked that bhikṣu, and based on this incident, he established this precept.

[Commentary]: Within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is explained that regarding the causes and conditions for the color of her flowers, according to the Vinaya, she shared a husband with her mother over many distant eons.
Because she covered food with flowers and offered it to a *pratyekabuddha*, she made a vow to always be handsome and respected by others; furthermore, she attained the merit of a *śramaṇa*.
Due to this impure vow, she now shares a husband; because she attained merit, her outflows (*āsrava*) have now been exhausted.
In the section on the conditions for the precepts, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* is first cited to clarify the circumstances regarding human beings. The Vinaya states:
When her parents were first married to a man from the country of Udyāna, they later gave birth to a daughter. Her husband had an illicit affair with her mother.

Having heard of this, Yaśodharā reproached herself, saying, "How can a mother and daughter share the same husband? She subsequently went to the city of Vārāṇasī and was married by an elder. Later, the elder...
He went to the country of Ujjayinī and, having gathered a hundred measures of gold, obtained a girl and returned to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī;
she was the daughter of Yaśodharā. When Yaśodharā asked about her origins and learned that she was her own daughter, she reproached herself and immediately sent her away.

She traveled to the city of Rājagṛha, where she saw the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and attained the fruit [of Arhatship]; she then requested to leave the household life. Next, he led [the next person].
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* demonstrates that there are two types of vows made based on past conditions: first, the vow for physical beauty;

second, the vow to attain the merits of a śramaṇa, namely the four fruits of śrāmaṇya. Because the correspondence between cause and effect is unfailing, the retributions experienced from these lower [vows] are likewise twofold.
[The Vinaya] states: "If a bhikṣu [accepts a robe] from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.
[Note]: "Not a relative" means she is not related by blood on the mother's or father's side, nor is she a relative within seven generations ascending to the ancestors.
If she is not a relative, one does not deliberate whether she is so or not; if she is a relative, then one deliberates to know whether it is permissible to accept it or not.
One must not take [a robe] based on whether it is good or bad, new or old, and so forth.
[Vinaya] Taking a robe.
[Commentary] There are ten kinds of robes; when a nun wore a worn-out robe and informed the World-Honored One, the Buddha said: "It should not be done thus; I allow [the following]."
If one possesses five robes that are complete and sturdy, any remaining robes may be given away as pure gifts (pariśuddha-dāna) or bestowed upon others at will. Why is this?
Even when women wear fine upper garments, they still do not appear beautiful; how much less so when wearing tattered and worn-out ones?
[Sūtra]: "Except for trade. [Commentary]:

At that time, the two divisions of the Saṃgha obtained robes and divided them between the two groups, having received them by mistake. The Buddha said: "I allow you to exchange robes with one another.
Regarding "trade": it means exchanging robe-material for robe-material; or exchanging non-robe-material for robe-material—such as needles or tubes.
Whether it be a knife, thread, a small object, or even a single pill of medicine used to trade for clothing—this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense according to the Vinaya. [Commentary:
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a *duṣkṛta* offense; there is no offense if she takes clothing from a relative bhikṣuṇī, or if she obtains it through trade.
If one takes [an object] for the sake of the Saṃgha or for a Buddhist stūpa, there is no offense.
[Commentary: The precept text consists of six phrases.
[Commentary: First, the offender; second, a non-relative. Regarding the seven generations of parents mentioned in the note, it is as already explained in the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing).

Regarding the body, one should include those four generations above reaching up to the great-great-grandfather, as well as those on the side including the four sisters, and those below including children and grandchildren;
for the mother’s side, it should be explained in a similar manner. If they are not relatives, one should clearly deliberate whether it is appropriate to associate with them or not.
Third, "taking clothing" refers to the object of the transgression against the precept. In the commentary, it says "one should not do so," because the female form is base and false.
Adorning the public thoroughfares is like wearing tattered clothing while preaching the Dharma to others; it is as if using a foul vessel to hold fine food. Fourth, regarding trade:

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states there are two benefits: first, the nun obtains suitable clothing without the need for the exertion of seeking after it, thereby attaining peace and joy in the cultivation of the Path;
second, since trading is permitted, she is freed from the distraction of such pursuits. Fifth, the regulation on relinquishment.

Regarding the six offenses of expiation (*pāyattika*) listed in the commentary, it is stated that when a nun takes a robe from a monk, it is merely a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) because the monk is a superior (*upariṣṭha*) and his property is rare;
therefore, the offense is light. If this is so, then in the section on the ninety offenses below, why is it established as a *pāyattika* when a monk gives a robe to a nun? The answer is:
that case was prohibited because it would lead to censure and fault.
In the second sentence of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, regarding the initial explanation of "relatives," it first indicates paternal kin:

taking one's own person as the first generation, there are four generations above—first, the father; second, the grandfather (*nī*, meaning the beginning); third, the great-grandfather (*zēng*, meaning the layer above);

and fourth, the great-great-grandfather (*gāo*, meaning the highest point). Taking four generations below, including sons and grandsons, these together constitute seven generations. Extending laterally to the fourth degree includes siblings.

Regarding "brothers and sisters," one calls them by their given names; "seven generations vertically" refers to the lineage from father to son, while "four horizontally" refers to those spoken of in relation to siblings. Thus, it is called "lateral.

In each of these seven vertical generations, there are likewise these four types of mothers; as explained by analogy with the father, the seven vertical and four horizontal relations are identical for both parents.

Third, at the beginning of the section, the phrase prior to the main text refers to the realm of persons (*pudgala-viṣaya*), whereas this [current passage] refers to the realm of things (*vastu-viṣaya*).
In the commentary, "tongdao" (passing through the way) means "broad" (hong). This clarifies the intent behind the Buddha’s reproach in the commentary.

Among the four [points], "trade" refers to the exchange of goods; the *Lun* (Treatise) sets forth the meaning of opening [the allowance]. First is for the sake of practicing the path; second is for the sake of abandoning faults.

In the commentary, first it cites the *Pratītyasamutpāda*, and next it clarifies that the Buddha’s opening [of the rule] does not apply to non-clothing, as explained above. Regarding the six [sections], the first explains the lightness of the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī*.
In the subsequent citation of examples within the response to the objection, the basis for the distinction is taken from the relative scarcity of numbers:
while the number of monks is common and that of nuns is rare, when it comes to the incitement of public censure, monks are many and nuns are few; this is why they differ.
[Vinaya] The fifth precept: Prohibiting the commissioning of a nun who is not a relative to wash old robes.
[Commentary] The fifth precept: Prohibiting the commissioning of a nun to wash old robes.

The reason this was established is that while it is natural for those of superior rank to command those of inferior status to perform tasks, and subordinates often respect their superiors, they frequently fail to exercise due deliberation.

Whether the measurement is appropriate or inappropriate, it causes distress, derails one’s work, and the resulting harm is not slight; furthermore, it gives rise to defiled habits and incurs the reproach of the world.
Therefore, it was regulated by means of the characteristics of washing, dyeing, and beating. These three precepts were established together because they arise from the same garment used by nuns;
thus, they were not formulated separately.
The fifth section, "Restraining the Mind," has two parts. First, the enumeration of faults, which has three sub-sections. The first is the fault of causing harm and vexation.
This begins by clarifying the matter of monks employing nuns as messengers; next, it addresses how nuns show respect to monks without discrimination between the ordinary and the capable.

Those who possess capability can avoid such faults, whereas those lacking capability do not know the proper timing, thereby causing vexation and giving rise to defilement—this constitutes the second fault.
To incur public reproach is the third fault, which is the same as above; because there are three intentions regarding the taking of robes, it is pointed out as before.
Next, to clarify the matter of separating from the bundle: one must separate based on the robe itself, hence the term "separating."
[Commentary] Five conditions constitute the offense: first, it is a nun; second, she is not a relative; third, it is an old garment;

fourth, one washes it oneself or causes another to do so—as extensively cited in the *Śrīgharā-vinaya* (Caoshu) regarding the four permutations; fifth, the offense is committed upon the completion of washing, dyeing, or beating.

Regarding the first section on the requisite conditions, the *Sishichao* (Commentary on the Four Sentences) states that there are four cases: (1) giving it oneself and having another person receive it;

(2) having another person give it and receiving it oneself; (3) giving it oneself and receiving it oneself; and (4) having another person give it and having another person receive it. In all these instances, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense.

[Commentary] Question: Since both [the robe] and the bowl involve transgressions, why was the bowl not subject to regulation? Answer: Because washing and dyeing were frequently practiced [with robes], it was regulated; as for the bowl, this was not the case, so it was not formally established [as a rule].

Regarding the word "transgression" (*guò*) in the section on resolving doubts, it is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùhū*). In the answer, "frequently practiced" (*xián*) refers to the fact that nuns frequently practiced [washing and dyeing]; this meaning does not apply to the bowl.
Furthermore, matters are distinguished as either grave or light, which is why they are categorized separately.

[Note: While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the monk Kālodāyin and the nun Thullanandā—both of whom were handsome and mutually attracted—sat together and lost their semen, staining their lower robes (antarvāsaka). They then had the nun wash it for them; because of this transgression, the bhikṣu [was reprimanded].
He informed the Buddha, who, because of this reproach, established the precept.
[Commentary]: Within the context of the causal conditions for the precept, because impurity causes defilement, he was ordered to wash it.
By explaining the specific manifestations of the fault within the causal conditions of the precept, the necessity for its establishment is demonstrated.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative (as described above above) [wash, dye, or beat an old robe].
[Commentary] If he has a non-relative śikṣamāṇā or śrāmaṇerī wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Washing old clothes.
[Commentary] Regarding "old clothes": even down to those that have been worn on the body once, if one washes, dyes, or beats new clothes, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If one dyes or beats them, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
[Note] If one instructs [a servant] to wash, dye, or beat [the robe], or if one performs all three oneself, there are three *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.

If one does not perform them [for oneself or others], there is a *duṣkṛta* offense for each instance. There is no offense in cases such as: when one is ill and instructs [another] to dye, wash, or beat;
when performing the work for the Saṃgha or a Buddhist monastery (*stūpa*); or when borrowing another's robe to wash, dye, or beat it.
[Commentary]: The six phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consist of: (1) one person, (2) a non-relative, and (3) washing old clothes—these constitute the objective basis (*ālambana*) of the precept.

(4) Dyeing and beating clearly define the essential characteristics of the action (*karmalakṣaṇa*), as explained above in the sub-commentary. Regarding the three cases where an offense occurs according to the words spoken:

(3) "not following" [the instruction] results in a mere *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) because there is only verbal karma and no physical action; this constitutes a "stalled preparatory effort" (*upakrama-avasthita*).

Regarding the explanation of the text within the four sections of the *Prātimokṣa*, the reference to "the above" points to the preceding detailed explanation of the conditions (*pratyaya*). As for the three types of offenses mentioned in the commentary according to the literal phrasing:
this refers to cases where the instigation is combined such that the full offense is incurred. Alternatively, if the instigation occurs sequentially, the former is grave and the latter is light;

or if the instigation is not combined, the determination of the offense varies accordingly. Regarding those that do not follow the [standard] transgression of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), there are again two types, such as when the instigation is combined.

If one intends to perform three actions but performs two, or intends to employ two messengers but employs one, or intends to perform one action but does not do so, one commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) based on what was actually performed;

if nothing was performed, it is a minor fault (*dukkaṭa*). Furthermore, if one instructs someone to wash a garment for the purpose of dyeing it, or to dye it for the purpose of beating it, because the mental intention and the actual act do not correspond, one should also incur a light offense.
This applies to verbal actions as well, when one employs another through expedient means.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Precept Six: Begging for Robes from a Layperson Who Is Not a Relative.
[Commentary] The sixth precept concerns begging for robes from a layperson who is not a relative.

[Commentary] Any world-transcending practitioner must adhere to having few desires as their fundamental disposition; now, with the three robes complete, one is capable of obtaining the necessary provisions.
When traveling on the road, one should stop at a suitable place to beg for alms;

however, because seeking excessively increases the fetter of greed, disturbs donors, and incurs no small fault, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that begging is prohibited for four reasons: first, to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish;
second, to prevent disputes and litigation; third, to extinguish the unwholesome minds of others; and fourth, to cause sentient beings to...
Because one gives rise to faith and joy within the True Dharma.
Regarding the sixth point, "Restraining the Mind," the first part describes how excessive greed for robes harms oneself by causing agitation and harms others;

the subsequent section cites and demonstrates four reasons: first, because even in the Buddha-dharma one should still have few desires; second, because lay households vary in status, being either high or low.
Third, because begging from them would inevitably give rise to contempt; fourth, because such mental contempt leads to a lack of faith in the True Dharma.
These latter two points concern the conditions of views and precepts; the present regulation of this precept reverses these faults to produce benefit.
[Commentary: There are six conditions that constitute an offense: (1) possessing the three robes; (2) being without a valid reason; (3) [requesting from] a householder who is not a relative.
Regarding the first three conditions, "being without a valid reason" refers to the absence of circumstances such as confiscation or loss.

Among the three conditions, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if one asks a relative for a fine robe, or if they are impoverished, or if they give little while one demands much, it is all a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

[Commentary]: Fourth, regarding begging for one's own sake, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that it is an offense even to employ skillful means—such as feigning the conditions of cold or heat—to obtain a robe of measured size.

Among these four [categories], "measured" refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which holds that obtaining a robe of four cubits (*hasta*) or more constitutes an offense; anything below that is permissible.
In mild cold, the cold manifests as thin; in heat, it manifests as thick.
[Commentary: Judging by this, those who practice the Way today truly have no Way to practice. They merely maintain worldly merit;

though their mouths recite sutras and preach the Dharma, and though their bodies sit upon the platform with composed countenances, their mental paths are constantly planning for when the session will end, as if they were already leaving me.
How can those who grasp at things in such a manner not violate the precepts on wrong livelihood? Therefore, Right Livelihood is established as a regulation.

This first section, which refutes what is not the Middle Way, is further divided into three parts. First, it sets forth the heading: "To practice the Way through speech and conduct yet to lack the Way" means to have the name but no reality.
To have no Way that can be practiced means one does not examine one's own mind; thus, one merely preserves worldly merit. But...

Regarding the "External Rituals" (wàiyí), there are two interpretations for the first two lines: the first indicates the preservation of merit, while the subsequent three lines clarify the absence of the Way.
The conclusion below summarizes the faults.

[Commentary]: When contemporary lecturers reach this point, they often dare not speak, because they have personally practiced these things; feeling ashamed to speak of them to others, how could they not remain silent?

If one does not practice it and remains hidden from the Way, what harm is there? Yet if someone were to practice it, this precept might be upheld by a single person during the Dharma-ending age. Be careful! Be careful!

In the first section of the following analysis, the reason for concealing and suppressing [the truth] is clarified: "to personally practice" refers to one's own transgressions. To feel shame yet remain silent is a contradiction between what is said and what is practiced;
therefore, this points out that while people at that time were still capable of knowing shame, nowadays there is no sense of shame.

When the body commits an offense while the mouth speaks otherwise, what is there left to discuss? Regarding the phrase "How can it be...": the ancient text reads "it can be stopped," though it is not practiced here, it is explained as follows.
"One must clearly manifest [the teachings] so that others may practice them; otherwise, in the Dharma-ending age, it is impossible to expect even a single person [to attain realization].
These words are most earnest in their exhortation. How should those of us who have recently entered the study listen and seek [the truth]?
The subsequent admonition that lecturers must not conceal the teachings is a further expression of extreme caution and warning.

[Commentary]: In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is stated that there is no offense for begging for minor items such as small supplementary clothing or hand-towels, provided one does not manifest the signs [of begging].
However, if one forms the thought, "I shall beg only for small things," yet receives a full set that was offered, this also constitutes an offense.
If one previously had no intention [to receive more], there is no offense. Could this not be considered a matter of mental state?
Among the three [cases], in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one requests without forming the mental sign (*nimitta*), it is not an evil mind; therefore, one does not incur an offense.
If one forms the thought of "receiving," this is an evil mind; therefore, one incurs an offense in all such cases.
[Commentary] In the fifth and sixth [cases], one incurs an offense immediately upon receiving.

[Note] When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Upāli (Bhadanta Upananda) preached the Dharma for a person and asked him for the garment he was wearing. After a brief hesitation, [the man] gave him his single-layered robe.
Upon entering the city, [Upāli] immediately claimed that he had been robbed by thieves in the Jeta Grove. The laypeople criticized and disparaged him.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who then established the precept.

[Commentary]: Within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it was taught that taking robes due to craving leads to fault and transgression; now, while these various difficulties cannot be avoided, they are also easy to examine and rectify.
However, since this single craving arises simultaneously with [the other factors], can it be extinguished together with them?

In the commentary on the section concerning the conditions for the precepts, it is noted that when one bows and yields to another because the matter is unavoidable, and enters the city in a single robe, if people ask the reason and he says, "I have been robbed by bandits," this refers to Kāṭhila (Bhadanta). Using the Dharma as a pretext to seek another's property is no different from white-robed robbery;
thus, he should be given this name. In the sub-commentary (*śū*), the underlying intent is followed to issue a warning and exhortation, which is difficult [to disregard].
"Exemption" refers to the worldly flow and change; "examination" means to encourage those who possess the Way.

However, as for the greedy person, one must point out the root of their affliction so that they may clearly recognize it for themselves. Since this beginningless habit of greed is innate, it ought to be restrained;
how can one instead indulge it and die together with it?

【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu begs for clothing from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative (the explanation of the text is as above), except during the [permitted] times, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. (The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.)
[Commentary: Within the *Śīla-sūtra* (the core precepts), there are six phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, a non-relative layman or laywoman; third, the begging for robes;
fourth, the allowance for specific circumstances;
the remainder is easily understood. Under the third phrase of the *Śīla-sūtra* section, a note points back to the aforementioned meaning of "non-relative."
[The Vinaya] states: "An exceptional occasion (*akāla*) refers to when one's robes have been stolen.
[The Commentary] states: At that time, a bhikṣu was stripped of his robes by bandits and went about naked. The Buddha said: "It is not so; he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If such a situation occurs, one should cover one's body with soft grass or tree leaves and proceed to the vicinity of a monastery, or take long [robes]."
If there is none among one's acquaintances, one may ask for it from within the Saṃgha; this may be shared clothing. If there is still none, one may ask for a robe or bedding belonging to the Saṃgha.
If they do not give it, one may personally open the storehouse and look inside. If there are mats, rugs, blankets, or covers, one may unfasten and dismantle them to cut and sew them into robes.
Having gone outside to beg for robes, once they have been obtained, one should wash, dye, and sew them, then properly place them back in their original location. If...
If one does not return to the original place, one shall be dealt with according to the law.
[Vinaya] Losing a robe, having a robe burned, or having a robe washed away (the circumstances are the same as above)—these are called "exceptional times.

[Commentary] There is no offense if, due to circumstances such as being robbed or losing [a robe], one begs from a person who is not a relative; or if one begs from a relative; or if one obtains it from a renunciant.

If one begs for oneself from one's own family, or begs for another on behalf of that other person, or begs for oneself on behalf of another, or obtains something without having asked, none of these are termed an offense.
[Commentary] "Other times" is a re-explanation of the previously mentioned exemptions.
[Commentary]: The phrase "having one's robes taken away" explains its characteristics very clearly. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: "While traveling, one sees bandits;

taking one's robe and bowl, one gives them to a youth and flees. Consequently, one is stripped by the bandits and obtains white cloth, five-colored cloth that has not been cut [for the saṃghāṭī], or the robes of non-Buddhists;
wearing these incurs no offense. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) states: "If one's robes are taken and later returned to their original place, they are empty."
If there is no one present, a monk residing nearby may wear it; however, if the person who previously stayed at the temple returns, he should take it back and place it in its original location.

Since the ownership of the location is thus settled, it cannot be transferred or altered. Without following the monastic rules (*saṃghadharma*), there is no basis for taking it out, as this would incur two faults.
Regarding the loss of robes, there are ten types: loss by the king, by thieves, by women, by those with lustful intent, or by one's parents.

Regarding the four types of forfeiture for returning to secular life (*pravrajyā-tyāga*) and the three types of forfeiture for losing [robes], there are ten [cases] due to long-term deterioration from wind, fire, and water.
As stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if robes are ruined, one is permitted to beg for them;

this includes cases where they are burned by household fires, wild fires, ghost fires, or celestial fires. Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, those ruined by being scorched by the sun are also termed [forfeited].
"Burning the robes" and "washing the robes" refer to wind and water, respectively.
Next, the conditions for the forfeiture [of robes] are explained; there are four such cases. Regarding the first—confiscation of the robes—the initial commentary provides a detailed explanation.

Within that commentary, first is the prohibition against being naked, followed by the instruction on expedient means: first taking one's own belongings, then borrowing the property of others. Finally...

Borrowing monastic property has two parts: first, clarifying the permissible taking of divisible items; these are the bedding and furniture currently present for the ten directions, which are the permanent property of the Saṃgha.
Second, clarifying the method for returning such items to the Saṃgha. Next, citing texts to demonstrate this, there are two sections:

first, citing the *Sāmagrī-vinaya* (Shanjian lü piposha) to clarify the method when encountering bandits; second, citing the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong lü) to clarify the method for returning property to the Saṃgha. This is because it is a constant practice.
Abiding in permanence and being unchangeable, as can be seen in the text;

regarding the two explanations of the faults, in the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya], among the ten faults, the "seizing" is divided into four, where the king and thieves are treated as two separate faults, while wind, water, and fire constitute the two conditions of drifting and burning—this differs from the current *Dharmaguptaka* [Vinaya] only in the combination and separation of the four conditions for seizing. In the *Pañcavargika*, the destruction of the robe is...

This is the same as the latter two of the three offenses in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Regarding "burning" and "flooding," they can be understood; the note stating that "the conditions are the same" means that taking or borrowing robes, and so forth, are all identical to the section on the forfeiture of robes (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
[Vinaya] The Vinaya merely clarifies the forfeiture for other categories;
the detailed exposition can be seen in the corresponding commentary.
[Vinaya] The seventh offense: the precept concerning taking extra clothing.
[Commentary] The seventh precept concerns receiving more clothing than permitted.

The reason this rule was established to prohibit excess is that when an ordained bhikṣu encounters four circumstances that cause him to lose his three robes, he has no means to advance in his practice.
When those of sincere faith hear of this, they exhaust their poverty to give alms; [the bhikṣu] ought to receive these according to what is given, thereby manifesting his own integrity.
Internally possessing a mind of integrity and frugality, one externally does not cause distress to the donor; this principle is clear and manifest.
Now, since the three robes are already sufficient, to take more than required is an excess that destroys faith and is utterly improper. This is why the rule was established.

As for the determination of the offense, it depends on the circumstances of the time; however, the offense is defined simply by the act of exceeding the proper measure, thereby binding oneself to the transgression.

The seventh section, "Restraining the Mind," has two parts. First, the intention for establishing the precept, which further has three sub-sections. First, a narrative on the loss incurred by failing to possess robes;

next, an explanation of the principle that one should receive a reduced amount; finally, a revelation of the faults of receiving more than necessary—namely, that it increases greed and destroys faith, thereby resulting in the extreme loss of both benefits.
Following this is the conclusion regarding the intent of the offense, though the text does not specify exactly how many robes constitute the limit.
Regarding the conditions for the completion of the offense, because the amount lost or forfeited cannot be fixed, it is called "excessive.
This means that in the text, if one exceeds [the limit], losing one and receiving one, up to losing three and receiving three, all constitute an excess.

[Commentary: Six conditions constitute an offense: (1) a bhikṣu who has lost his three robes; (2) a householder who is not a relative; (3) the gift is given specifically because [the bhikṣu] has lost them;
(4) if it is not accepted in accordance with the circumstances, there is no offense; (5) knowing that it was given because he had lost them, he accepts it.
[Commentary: The fifth fault regarding contentment refers to exceeding the limit, such as losing one [robe] and receiving another.
Among the five requisite conditions, because one may not receive [a new robe] once a robe has been lost, receiving one when it is not lost constitutes an excess.
