If this is so, how can one possess the three robes? The answer is: provided they are not being seized by others, seeking them separately is permissible.

[Answer: It is so. [Commentary] Question: Why is it that regarding robes there is a transgression for exceeding the limit, whereas for the bowl it is not the same? Answer: Regarding robes, because the three types are indefinite, one loses the joy [of the precept] by receiving them in excess;
as for the bowl, there is only one type, and since receiving it in excess is rare, even if such a case occurs, the offense is light.
The questions and answers are easy to understand.
[Commentary] Six: Incurring an offense through acceptance.
[Note] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, many bhikṣus encountered bandits and lost their robes; they came to the Jetavana where there were lay followers who had heard the news.
When many people sent robes to a bhikṣu, he told them to stop, saying, "I have already received offerings; I have my three robes, so I do not need more.

However, the group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) urged him to accept them, saying, "Take them and give them to me. He then accepted them again. The bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established a precept.
[Commentary]: Regarding the conditions for this precept, when the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks caused others to take [food] on their behalf, they themselves had already finished eating;
yet, because they seized more than was needed, they subsequently engaged in sexual intercourse, thereby violating the intention of the donor.

In the commentary on the section concerning the causes for the precepts, it is noted that because the six groups of monks (ṣaḍvargika) accepted [the practice] that the three robes of a bhikṣu were sufficient for their own needs, it is said that they were performing human affairs. [The Vinaya states:
"If a bhikṣu loses his robe, has it seized, has it burned, or has it carried away by water."

[Note] If one robe is lost, it should not be taken [as a replacement]. If two robes are lost and one remains—whether it be double-layered, triple-layered, or four-layered—it should be torn down to make a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, or an antarvāsaka.
[Commentary] The precept text consists of eight phrases.
[Commentary] First, the person who commits the offense.
[Commentary] Second, the four cases such as loss and confiscation; regarding these, if one loses even a single robe and it should not be taken back, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "In total..."

If one loses the three robes, one may take only the upper and lower garments; the remaining one must be sought elsewhere. This is because the donor at the place where the robe was lost possesses a generous heart, and it would be improper to take it all.

The commentary states that one should only be permitted to take [the remaining robe] as a last resort, provided that one first attempts to combine the pieces by disassembling and rejoining them to make a complete set of robes, and such a solution is entirely impossible.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative (both explained as above) [invites one to] the *pravāraṇā* and offers many robes. [Commentary] If,
at the *pravāraṇā*, one is offered many robes that are fine, thin, or not durable, one should accept them and make them into double layers.
If there are three or four layers, one should arrange them with a border; they should be folded over the shoulder at the soiled area, and hooks and ties should be attached.
If there is any remainder, one should ask the layperson: "What shall this remaining cloth be cut and made into?
If the donor says, "I did not give this to you because I lost my own clothes; I am giving it to you, Venerable Sir," then if one wishes to accept it, one should accept it.
[The Vinaya] states:
This bhikṣu should receive robes with contentment. [Commentary]:
If his three robes are all lost, he should receive robes with contentment. There are two kinds of contentment; for laypeople...
One who is content accepts whatever robes are given by laypeople; for an ordained person, contentment consists of the three robes.
[Vinaya] If one exceeds this (meaning that losing one and receiving another, or losing all three received ones), it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
[Note] Regarding whether a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense or not when she acts in concert with others: if she takes clothing knowing her own sufficiency; or if she takes less than her sufficiency;

or if the donor gives much clothing; or if the clothing is thin, coarse, or not durable; or if it is made in two or three layers and there is a surplus—as stated above, if she knows these things, she does not commit an offense.
[Commentary]: Third, those who are not relatives; fourth, laymen and laywomen. [Commentary]:

Fifth, "those who act according to their own will" (*svairin*) clarifies that the gift is not given for the purpose of deprivation; thus it is called "acting according to one's own will. Within the explanation of the commentary, these points do not mutually clarify one another.

Regarding the first section of the fifth phrase of the *Prātimokṣa*: if we consider this precept in terms of the offense of "seizing what has been offered," it refers to acting at will (*svairacārin*).

However, upon examining the intent of the text, it appears one wishes to clarify that if one should practice contentment even when not seizing what is offered, how much more so when it is offered as a gift after having been seized?
Let the student examine this further.

[Commentary]: "This bhikṣu should be content" refers to the loss of two out of three types of acceptance. This note explains the contentment of both monastics and laity to clarify the two characteristics.
Contentment for the laity means one cannot measure for oneself but follows whatever they may bestow. Contentment for those who have left home is restricted solely to the three robes;
this is because the Buddha has already formally prohibited [the possession of more], resulting in the loss of two types of acceptance and the retention of only one.
In the initial section of this division, the main text first explains the passage, followed by the commentary. Practicing giving while remaining a householder is itself contentment;

it is not something to be measured by oneself, as it arises from others. Therefore, this raises the case of the householder to contrast it with the different nature of contentment in the monastic life.
Regarding the text on the precepts, contentment specifically concerns the monastic.
[Commentary: If one exceeds this [limit], the meaning of the remaining text can be understood. [Commentary:

Regarding the previous precept, the opening for "this" and "that" refers to begging for this [robe] on behalf of another so that it may be received by oneself; the offense arises because of a deceitful mind.
If one were acting solely for another without such personal attachment, one would not necessarily take the robe.
Regarding the preceding section of the *Jianzhong*, since the opening of this precept for others was not permitted, it is specifically indicated here;
those who act out of deceitful intent know that they may not transgress by receiving [the precept] on another's behalf, as this would manifest a fondness for sentient beings.
[Vinaya] The eighth precept: Exhorting a lay devotee to increase the price of robe-cloth.
[Commentary] The eighth precept: Exhorting a lay devotee to increase the price of robe-cloth.

[Commentary] When a devout lay devotee has resolved their mind to give and the limit of the price has already been fixed, there is no principle for further increasing or continuing it; one ought to comply accordingly.

To give and receive does not diminish the Dharma; yet, to now feel dissatisfied with what is small and urge others to increase their offerings beyond measure, thereby receiving more for oneself, is an extreme transgression that destroys the donor's faith and respect. Therefore, this rule was established.
Eighth, regarding the initial section on "Restraint of the Mind," the first part explains the combined proclamation; next follows the manifestation of the characteristics of the offense.

[Commentary: There are six conditions for committing this offense: (1) a non-relative householder sincerely offers a price; (2) there is an intention regarding a time limit; (3) one knows that a time limit exists;
(4) out of dislike for a low amount, one urges an increase; (5) the other person increases the price of the thread; (6) one accepts it, thereby committing the offense.

[Commentary] Question: Among the robes, there is an exhortation to increase [the number], yet for the bowl there is no such increase. Answer: The robe serves as a support for the body in a broad sense, and because one delights in increasing them, they are regulated;
the bowl serves as a support for food in a narrow sense, and because it is something sought after, it is not so regulated.
[Commentary: If that were so, the offense for begging for a bowl should not be the same as that for begging for robes. [Answer: A bowl has no many uses;

because begging for it entirely causes deep affliction, this rule was established to encourage moderation. Even if one begs for more than a single bowl, though it constitutes an offense, it is merely light.
Regarding the conditions for the offense, the questions and answers, the shifting of the burden, and the distinctions concerning the bowl are all clearly visible in the text.
[Note: While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a householder and his wife were discussing how to provide robes, saying, "Bhadanta Upananda is an old friend of ours;
let us purchase a robe with this price and give it to him. When a bhikṣu who was on alms-round heard this, he informed others, and they subsequently went to that house.

[The Buddha] exhorted [the monks], saying that they must have [robes] that are vast, new, fine, and durable. When laypeople criticized and disparaged them, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, who then established the precept.

[Commentary]: Within the context of the causal conditions for this precept, from the beginning up to the point "durable," this explains the origin of the transgression; from "laypeople criticized" onwards, it concerns the [establishment of the rule].
Regarding the characteristics [of the response]:
in the context of the conditions for the precepts, the character *zhì* (緻) is pronounced as *zhì*, meaning "dense" or "compact.
[The Vinaya states: If a householder or a householder’s wife—as described above—procures the price for a robe for a bhikṣu.
[Commentary] This refers to using coins, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, jade, precious stones, necklaces, raw or wrought metal,
or even the ten kinds of robes.
[Vinaya] Having provided the price for such robes to a certain bhikṣu, that bhikṣu has not previously accepted an invitation to accept them at his own discretion.
[Commentary] If, during the *pravāraṇā*, one asks what kind of robe is required, the Buddha permitted bhikṣus who possess few desires and know contentment to seek one that is inferior.
[Vinaya] Upon arriving at the house of a layperson (*gṛhapati*), one should speak thus: "Excellent, layperson! Buy such a robe for me and give it to me."
"I do so for the sake of excellence.
[Note] There are two kinds of "seeking": seeking the price refers to when a donor provides a garment of great value, or even seeking an increase of one *māṣaka* or a sixteenth part thereof;
seeking the garment itself refers to speaking to a householder, saying, "Make a garment that is wide and long."
"Even to the extent of adding one additional line":
[The Vinaya] states that if a nun obtains such a robe, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

[The Commentary] notes that regarding whether this offense applies equally to both monks and nuns: if she first accepts an invitation for a meal and then goes to seek [robes], she incurs no offense provided she knows moderation.
Regarding seeking, one should diminish such efforts as seeking from kinsmen, seeking from renunciants, seeking for others, or having others seek for oneself;
rather, one should accept whatever is obtained without seeking.
[Commentary] The precept text consists of seven phrases.
[Commentary] First, "a person.

[Commentary] Second, "a layperson who is not a relative. Since the text does not clarify whether one is a relative or a non-relative, nor does it provide an allowance for non-offenses, we know that relatives are excluded.

Furthermore, the fact that the two versions of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra do not clarify the distinction between relatives and non-relatives differs from the preceding precept, which specifically designates "non-relatives. Therefore, one should determine the meaning by referring to the provisions for exceptions found below;
the text here is merely abbreviated.

[Commentary]: Third, to distinguish the value of the robes. In the notes, various gold and jewels are listed; these belong to the original regions [of India], whereas in this land [China], there are only coins and silk, as other precious items are rare.

Among the three [types of offerings], the listing of various precious substances refers to images made of gold and silver, which are merely different names for the same material. Regarding the ten types of clothing, they are explained as before.
"The original region" refers to India; it is not that such items do not exist here [in China], but because coins and silk are used more frequently, these [offerings] are said to be rare.
[Commentary]: The passage beginning with "The fourth is for bhikṣus" refers to the characteristic of increasing the price.

[Commentary]: The note states that "requesting something inferior is permitted" because it involves few desires and conserves effort; however, if the labor involved is great, even a layperson would commit an offense.
As the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* records, when someone gave him fine [cloth], he said: "I am one who dwells in the forest as a forest-dweller (*araṇyaka*) and a practitioner of asceticism (*dhūta*)."
If the items received are of inferior quality, the offense is likewise grave.

Regarding the four [cases], the commentary on the preceding section first restates and explains that even if much effort is expended, it is still an offense; for although one requested [the items], because they were inferior, it resulted in a waste of resources.
As the citation below provides proof, this demonstrates the wasting of effort. The *Chao* (Excerpts) states: "Because one describes one's own virtues, an offense is committed."
[Commentary: Regarding the two types of "seeking" mentioned in the sub-commentary, although the *Prātimokṣa* itself does not contain the word "seeking," the sense of seeking is present;

thus, it is listed as one of the sixteen [offenses], namely, "increasing the price. Similarly, "broad and long" refers to increasing the amount of thread. Even today there are those who commit this offense:
for instance, when a layperson agrees to provide a bolt of silk, [the monk] instructs them to purchase a better quality one; this is identical to this precept (the tenth).
Regarding the recitation, there are three types; if the price is increased, it constitutes an offense of *pāyattika*.
In the first section of the latter part, there are three subsections. First, the text cites and explains the meaning of "having a request," stating:

"To say 'give it to me for a good price' is itself a request. Below this text, the first explanation of "increasing the price" includes a note stating: "One *qián* refers to the ancient large copper coin."
One *qián* (coin) is worth sixteen [small coins]; thus, one-sixteenth of it is a single small coin. This is also an increase in price, as will be explained below regarding the "increase of robes.
Now, the determination of the matter of holding [the robe] is the same as this precept; that is, it is an increase in price. The "ten" below indicates the similarities and differences:
in our own school (*benzong*), there is simply no increase in color. Within the text, the two types of increase refer to price and quantity.

[Commentary: Regarding the characteristics of the transgression of this precept, the essential point lies in the original object; if one encourages the acquisition of something additional, it belongs to the preceding category of begging for [extra] requisites.

The subsequent section discusses the transgression in terms of encouraging the acquisition of more, restricting the offense to the original item itself; if the substance of the object is exchanged, it does not constitute an "increase. Thus, it is not [a transgression of] this precept.

[Commentary] Question: In the section on encouraging the increase of precepts, a single thread constitutes an offense; whereas in the section on begging for robes, one must have a full strip to constitute an offense. Why are these two cases different? Answer:

In the case of begging from the original donor, since the donor has no intention to give and the amount is left to their discretion, the sense of causing distress is slight; therefore, an offense is incurred only upon obtaining a full strip.

In the case of encouraging the increase [of robes], one has already made a formal determination and limit based on a sincere heart; if one does not accept it and instead complains that it is too small and demands more, an offense is incurred.
Because the affliction of excessive greed is the most serious, it causes one to commit an offense regardless of whether the amount is large or small.
In the question, since the quantity of robes requested differs from the previous case, the phrase "a single piece" refers to the allowance for one set of the *kāṣāya*.
In the answer, two precepts are distinguished because the gravity of the underlying mental transgression differs; thus, the regulations are established as two separate categories.
[Commentary] All other points are easily understood.
Regarding the summary of the conclusion, it refers to the three phrases beginning with "if one obtains the robe.
[Vinaya] The ninth precept concerning the two families increasing the price of a robe through repeated exhortation.
[Commentary: The ninth [section] exhorts the two householders to increase their offerings of robes for the Sangha.
The intent of the regulation and the conditions for its transgression are the same as before; the only difference is that the two families together shall produce a single robe.
In the first section of the ninth general explanation, where the conditions for the offense are the same, only the first case is modified by adding "two non-related householders.
[Commentary] Question: If one encourages two householders to jointly provide the price for a single robe, and the original amount is not increased, is there an offense? Answer: As follows.
The text states that increasing or not increasing [the portion] does not constitute an offense.

Regarding the two [cases], the initial question concerns merely encouraging the two families to combine [their portions] without increasing them; this too should be considered an offense. In the response concerning the offense, it must be based on whether there is an increase;
if there is no increase, it is not an offense. The text says, "for the sake of excellence," which is precisely what constitutes an increase. Therefore, [the former case] is indeed an offense.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the encouragement to combine two [offenses] into one—whether there is an increase or no increase—in which precept is this subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed under the latter precept. Although there is no increase in the offense, it is not a transgression;
as for the "increase," it is because they have been combined into one.
Next, the question is asked: "If one family does not increase [the number of] two precepts, what would they include? In the answer, since it involves two families, it cannot be the former precept.
[Commentary]: The question asks why only the combination of two is prescribed and not three; the answer is that examples can be cited to make this clear.

In the three question-and-answer sections, only two schools are cited; the same applies to the third and fourth, though they are not explicitly clarified because there is no *nidāna* (introductory narrative).

[Commentary] Question: Each of the three schools wishes to perform the distribution (*bhūta*), yet now they are ordered to combine the coarse with the fine. Is this not a violation? Under which precept is it subsumed?
Answer: Combining three [threads] to make a fine [fabric] differs from its original substance and is subsumed under the preceding precept.

Fourth, regarding the question of whether combining cloth to make a fine [fabric] also constitutes an increase in value and must be determined as belonging to a specific category: the answer is that while the substance is changed, it does not constitute an "increase" (ādhika), and the meaning is the same as the previous explanation.

[Commentary]: In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, because the Saṃgha is numerous, if even one person acts together [with others], they commit the same offense of a *pāyattika* as when the Saṃgha collectively commits it.

Among the three types of Saṃgha offenses, there are three distinct positions regarding the encouragement to increase [the number of participants]; all incur the offense simultaneously, for there is no difference in the principle that this increases greed and causes affliction.
The "lower reference" (*he-xia zhi*) refers to the aforementioned section on the categories of meaning.
[Note: While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, two lay devotees, husband and wife, were discussing how they wished to purchase robes for Baddhālita.

Upon hearing this, a *bhikṣu* who went begging for food informed them in detail. When they arrived at their home, he spoke to them, instructing them to prepare the robes together; the lay devotees then voiced their reproach.
A bhikṣu was criticized for his transgression, and the Buddha, having rebuked him, established the precept.

[Vinaya]: If two laymen or a layman and his wife provide the price for a robe for a bhikṣu, intending to purchase such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation to choose freely, goes to the house of those two laymen...

If one says, "Excellent! Householder, it would be good to provide such a price for robes so that we may together make one robe," and if the robe is obtained, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (the characteristics of the offense, its fulfillment, and the exceptions are as in the preceding rule).
[Commentary] The seven clauses of the precept text are no different from those previously mentioned.
[Vinaya] The precept concerning the excessive urgency in demanding robes.
[Commentary] The tenth precept: the precept concerning the excessive demand for the price of robes.
[Commentary]: However, precious gems and refined jewels are esteemed by worldly sentiment; they foster greed, obstruct the Path, and give rise to deep-seated afflictions.

Thus, they are particularly unsuitable for those who have left the household life to possess. Yet, fearing that one might commit an offense by accepting them when a donor offers them as the price for robes, [the monk] hands them over to a layperson’s custody so that it may be known as pure property (*śuddha-vastu*). When the search becomes urgent and pressing, there is no room for hesitation or delay.
Because they urge and harass others by means of such constraints— mandating three words followed by six silences—
and because these minor prohibitions result in grave transgressions and deep obstructions, how could it be permissible not to establish regulations?
Tenth, regarding the four sections within the "Regulation of Intent": First, it describes how worldly treasures give rise to affliction;
next, it clarifies that when laypeople practice pure giving, because they transfer truly pure objects to the recipient, this constitutes an offense against this precept.

Third, it explains that if one suddenly demands something urgently upon being asked, yet had previously been slow to respond, this constitutes an offense. Fourth, it clarifies the limits of transgression regarding the three types of offenses.
The six cases of verbal [transgression] and the instances of silence are clarified below.
[Commentary]: There are five conditions that constitute an offense: first, a donor sends gold, silver, coins, or jewels; second, for the purpose of trading for robes;

third, not accepting them from the person delivering them while intending to know they are pure objects; fourth, exceeding the legal limit; and fifth, having them come into one's possession—this constitutes an offense.
Among the conditions for the offense, the first two belong to the preceding donor, while the latter three all belong to the fault of the offender;
the limit of the legal procedure (*dharmavibhāga*) refers precisely to the aforementioned speech and silence.
[Commentary] Question: Since the price for robes is restricted by a maximum limit, why is the price for a bowl not so restricted? Answer: A single bowl is sufficient; there is no further need.
Because there is no excessive use, there is no fault of seeking beyond what is needed. If one has no bowl at all, even if one obtains hundreds or thousands, there is no offense.
However, because one already possesses one and seeks another, it falls under the offense of begging for a bowl; therefore, it is not permitted.
In the initial part of the question-and-answer section, the distinction is made by contrasting with robes;
if [the robe] is absent, there is no fault in requesting many, whereas if it is present, it is not included here.
[Note: While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a high minister of Rājagṛha, who had a close and frequent relationship with Baddhananda, sent [a gift].
Having entrusted the price for the robe to a steward, [the monk] urgently demanded it due to a pressing matter; consequently, he was penalized and became an object of reproach among the laity.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha established a precept because of it.

[Commentary: Within the context of the conditions for the precept, this first clarifies those whom the high minister favored; subsequently, it clarifies the conditions for the arising of transgressions resulting from the pursuit of punishment.
The passage beginning with "the common people’s censure" clarifies the reprimand and the subsequent regulation. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* state:

"Vadanyadeva was known during his lay life for his expertise in archery and military strategy. King Bimbisāra sent five hundred men to study under him, who mastered the arts and became highly proficient."

When wealth arrives, one should repay its kindness by bestowing treasures upon the house of a lay follower (*upāsaka*). If the family is poor and borrows [the goods] to present them at the government office, and when they are reclaimed, the borrower is dragged away and held accountable along with ordinary people.

Regarding the initial point in the context of the precepts: it refers to a high minister who was highly favored; "thick" (*hou*) here means "heavy" (*zhong*). Thus, because of the demand for repayment, one incurs punishment.
The Vinaya clarifies that because the steward was punished by the authorities with a fine of five hundred coins, the monks [appointed him] next.

Regarding the method of archery, he was skilled in bow and arrow; regarding military arts, he understood matters of warfare and combat. Having studied these, he attained mastery—"mastery" here meaning thorough comprehension.

[Commentary]: Question: If one suddenly demands clothing, does this constitute an offense against the King or his ministers, or does it constitute an offense against the *śuddhasthāna* (pure master)? Answer: Although the individuals involved were originally the King or his ministers, because they subsequently acted as *śuddhasthāna* masters and caused distress through their demands, the prohibition was established specifically regarding those later persons.
In the questions and answers, it is stated that all instances of causing distress or incurring punishment are due to the *viśuddhika* (steward), and thus they cause harm to those who come after.

[Commentary]: This precept ought to follow the precept on keeping precious objects (*ratnagrahaṇa*), as it regulates the *viśuddhika*. That it appears earlier in the sequence is either because the compilers did not maintain the proper order, or because those who transmitted the tradition lost the original intent.
Among the three [sections], regarding the section on "Possessing Precious Objects," it begins by explaining the causes for purification;

having explained the purification, it then addresses transgressions, the summoning of witnesses, and the compilation of the canon in an improper order, subsequently pointing out the discrepancies among the masters of the various schools and the failure in the transmission of the teachings, thereby holding the translators accountable for their errors.
【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu, or a king (one who possesses sovereign power and has no master), or a great minister (who stands at the king’s side), or a brāhmaṇa (one born into the brāhmaṇa caste),
or a householder (excluding kings, great ministers, and brāhmaṇas; referring to all other laypeople), or a householder’s wife (a laywoman),

sends a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a bhikṣu— as described above— and that messenger arrives before the bhikṣu with the price for such a robe, intending to give it to a certain bhikṣu...
The messenger says to the bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, for your sake I have sent this price for robes; please accept it. The bhikṣu should say to that messenger:
"I should not accept this price for robes. If I need a robe, and it is the proper time and the acquisition is pure, I shall accept it.
The messenger says to the bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, do you have anyone who attends to your affairs? The bhikṣu should say: [Yes].
If one says, "There is a monastery attendant or a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who serves as the steward for the bhikṣus;
when he is constantly performing services for the bhikṣus, I have sent a messenger to that steward and given him the price for the robe.
Having said this, he returns to the place where the bhikṣu is and speaks thus: "Venerable sir, I have already given the price for the robe to the steward named so-and-so whom you indicated."

A virtuous monk who knows the proper time should go there and obtain robes; a monk in need of robes should go to the person in charge of affairs and, after reminding them twice or thrice, should say: "I require robes."

[Note]: "Recollection" means that whether it be an attendant, a householder, one in the marketplace, or one at a place of work, one should go to that person's location and say once, twice, or three times: "I now require a robe; please give me one made for me. This is what is meant.
【Vinaya】 If, after being reminded two or three times, he obtains the robe, it is well;
if he does not obtain the robe, he should stand silently before him four, five, or six times.
[Note: If that attendant, whether at home, in the marketplace, or at his place of work, stands silently before him, the monk should say nothing.
When the attendant asks, "For what reason do you stand here? the monk should reply, "You yourself should know. If the person says, "I do not know now;
someone else knows," the monk should tell that person, "Know this. This is the manner of remaining silent.
[Vinaya] If, after being invited four times, five times, or six times, one remains silent before [the donor] and receives the robe, it is well.
[Commentary] If one speaks once, it breaks two instances of silence; likewise, up to speaking three times, it breaks six instances of silence.

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If one does not obtain a robe and seeks to obtain a robe beyond this [limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture). [This applies equally to Bhikṣuṇīs as for the Saṃgha.
If one does not obtain a robe, one may either go in person or send a messenger to the place where the price for the robe was obtained, saying:
"Previously you sent a messenger with the price for a robe to give to a certain Bhikṣu; that Bhikṣu has ultimately not obtained the robe; please return it."
"Take it; do not let this opportunity be lost.

[Note] There is no offense if one sends a messenger to inform them, or if the other says, "I do not need it now, I shall give it to you as a gift," and the bhikṣu, at that time, uses gentle speech and skillful means to request the robe, or if it is given for the purpose of making a *pārikkāra* (miscellaneous requisites).
If one requests [the object] at the proper time with gentle words, or obtains it through skillful means:

[The Commentary] explains that the six phrases of the precept text are as follows: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the circumstances regarding the owner of the treasure, such as a king and so forth;

third, the formation of the karmic act and the establishment of the offense by requesting beyond the limit; fourth, the relinquishment of the object; fifth, the formal conclusion of the offense; and sixth, the prohibition against proceeding further if the object is not obtained.
[Commentary] Regarding the second section on the characteristics of establishing the rule (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there are eight phrases. First, there are five stages:

[1] the patron sends a messenger with jewels to give to a bhikṣu; [2] that messenger arrives at the bhikṣu’s location (this clarifies the manner in which the messenger receives the jewels and delivers them);
[3] the bhikṣu speaks to the messenger (this clarifies the fear of committing the offense of possessing jewels and thus not accepting them immediately).

1. Regarding the characteristics of acceptance: Four [points] concerning the messenger’s speech to the bhikṣu; below, it clarifies that the messenger also knows the bhikṣu is not one who accepts precious objects.

2. Questioning the person in charge: Five points concerning what the bhikṣu should say to the person in charge; below, it clearly indicates the location where the person in charge is found. 3. At that time, the messenger goes there:

Below, it clarifies the manner of giving the precious object and entrusting it to the pure master (*śuci-pati*). 4. Returning to the place of the bhikṣu: Below, it clarifies that the object has already been entrusted.

The section on the Jewel concludes; it returns to inform the world’s messengers that they may likewise act in this manner. In the second part of the *Śīlaskandha-vibhāṣā*, the first sub-section clarifies the establishment of the rules regarding the eight requirements for robes, including the procedures for their procurement and distribution.
Within this, the first category consists of the five types of persons who hold office, namely kings, ministers, and so forth.
"Those who are the 'treasure-holders' (ratnapāla)" refers to those mentioned in the text as follows: "the monastery attendants" (ārāmika) refers to those who guard the garden;

"lay devotees" (upāsaka) refers to lay householders and secular officials who are trusted by the world; and "messengers" (dūta) refers to those capable of going back and forth to serve as envoys, which is naturally how it should be.

[Commentary]: Within the section on requesting the formal procedure (*dharmatā*), first is explained the manner of requesting three times by means of speech; second, if the robe is not obtained, the manner of remaining silent from the fourth or fifth time onwards.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one requests once by speech, the pure owner shall come within one month; thus it continues up to the third [request]."
The month may not exceed ten days; [it may be] four, three, two, or one day, down to a mere moment—it must not exceed three.
If there is even a single instance of silence, the precedent should be understood as above.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is stated in full: "If a bhikṣu goes to the place of a donor to request a robe, saying, 'Long-lived one, give me the price for a robe,' and the donor replies, 'Venerable sir, come back in one month,' and the bhikṣu returns after exactly one month to request it again;
if the donor says, 'Venerable sir, come back in another month,' and the bhikṣu returns after [another] month..."
If one goes to request [an item] once a month, and after three months it is not given, one may not request it again.

If it is said, "Come in half a month," or "in ten days," or even "for a brief moment," as long as more than three [months] have passed, one may not request it again. The case of requesting in silence follows the same principle regarding the months and days;
it is simply that one does not speak.
[Commentary] The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "One who remains silent does not speak with the mouth; when called to sit, he does not sit; when given food, he does not accept it;
and regarding preaching the Dharma or offering prayers for blessings, he does nothing at all. If asked, 'For what reason have you come here? he replies, 'Householder, you should know this yourself.'"
The *Shanjian* (Sudarsana-vibhāṣā) indicates that "silence" (*mo*) and "note" (*zhu*) are largely identical.

[Commentary: When using pure speech to go and solicit, there are six instances where one does not commit an offense; when using pure silence to go and solicit, there are twelve. Because silence is interspersed with contrary speech, there are nine instances.
As for the four or five instances mentioned in the Vinaya text, these follow the momentum of the preceding speech and connect to the subsequent four or five cases, provided the action is carried out.
At the time of the formal act, because there are one or two initial intentions, six instances of silence are formed.
Within the three divisions [of the procedure], the first demonstrates the three positions; however, a single instance of speech corresponds to two instances of silence.

In the lower section of the Vinaya, the text of the precepts is punctuated so that the *Prātimokṣa* itself correctly correlates the three instances of speech and six instances of silence to clarify the nature of the offense, as previously explained in points two and three.

If one reverses [the sequence] and speaks, one seeks the latter four, five, and six; if one reverses it again, one borrows the former one, two, and three, joining them with the latter four, five, and six to form six silent [counts]. Therefore, it is said that "one receives the previous words," and so forth.

As for "if performing the ritual acts" and so on, although the translated text is abbreviated, when employing the silent seeking, one proceeds from one to six. According to the meaning, it should properly be stated as "if one reversal."
[The text continues] up until: "If one stands silently before [the preceptor] for six repetitions, the textual signs will then become manifest.
[Commentary: Regarding the characteristics of those who keep and receive [the precepts], they are as explained in the section on the Jewel Precepts (Ratna-śīla).
Since the keeping and receiving [of the precepts] by means of three fingers is not appropriate here, it need not be clarified.
[Commentary: "If one does not obtain the robe" refers to the primary action (*karmavastu*) of this precept. From here on, the characteristics of the precept are easy to recognize.
Regarding the marking of the other phrases: the first mark indicates the third phrase; from here on, it points to the remaining three phrases—namely, the four abandonments and the five offenses.

The passage from "if one does not obtain the robe" down to the end of the text constitutes the sixth phrase, which concerns the failure to go and inform [the donor] regarding the robe after having requested it.
The commentary on the primary term clarifies that there is no offense if one immediately dispatches a messenger to inform the owner of the robe;
since the owner does not accept it and one employs skillful means rather than forcibly demanding it, the exemption from offense is granted.
[Vinaya] The eleventh precept: making bedding from cotton wool.
[Commentary] The eleventh precept: begging for cotton wool to make the three robes.

[Commentary] Regarding the intent of the regulation: cotton wool is a product of living beings; to obtain it while not harboring a path of compassion that avoids taking life, yet to seek it out extensively, is prohibited.
To outwardly incur reproach and shame while inwardly losing the root of goodness constitutes an offense of extreme depth; therefore, the Sage specifically prohibited it.

Although other offenses involving the relinquishment of property through wealth may be expiated, in this case, one must cut and destroy [the object] to forever exhaust the source of greed. Since the world shares in the dust and evil, aiding one another in vice, everything used for personal clothing and service does nothing but harm life;
yet people claim to practice compassion with their mouths—how can anyone truly uphold such a precept? Thus, the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* says:
There are four reasons: first, to stop slander; second, to increase faith and respect; third, to attain peace and happiness for the sake of practicing the Path;
and fourth, to avoid harming the lives of sentient beings.

Regarding the first section of the eleven points on "restraining the mind," it is divided into three parts. First, describing the faults and explaining the conditions that give rise to the restraint: sentient beings...

Because it is that which is accomplished [by the precepts], the following sections demonstrate the differences in the rules for forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) and the subsequent censure of worldly attire as being identical to secular dust—that is, being mired in mundane affairs and unable to transcend them—and the mutual complicity of evil, meaning that both parties practice together without recognizing each other’s faults.

Regarding the four intentions in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the first two are the reverse of the conditions for the precepts; the third is the absence of begging; and the fourth is... [the absence of]... [seeking].

[This constitutes] the fulfillment of compassionate conduct. [Commentary: Regarding the characteristics of the Vinaya teachings, there are three points to be sought; where there is slight deviation, it is opened up as non-offense.

Now, based on the causal conditions of the precept, [the Buddha] went to a family raising silkworms to beg for silk floss and watched them boiling [the cocoons]. Worldly people mocked and reviled him, considering this the ultimate extreme of generating faults through one’s livelihood.
In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the section on miscellaneous rules and the detailed explanation regarding wild silkworms both stipulate that [the offender] must destroy them.

Furthermore, in the subsequent reconciliation (*saṃgraha*), the detailed explanation of the causal conditions for the precepts is found throughout the commentary (*ṭīkā*). In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the miscellaneous rules and the case of wild silkworms cite minor instances to illustrate the gravity of the offense;
this clarifies that in all three instances—preceding, following, and intermediate—the matter is urgent, thereby manifesting the severity of the transgression.

[Commentary: People today all violate [the rules regarding] clothing, yet why is this so? It is because they are deluded by names. Since the text says "to make bedding," they assume it refers to things such as quilts.

Now, by definitively establishing the terminology, one will know that I have committed an offense. For while the three robes (*tricīvara*) are known by their general name, in this land they did not previously exist;
people merely heard of making *saṃghāṭī* robes out of cotton, but since this land originally lacked them, no one knew what they were.

Because these objects are spread out extensively and share this quality of being laid down, they are thus termed "reversals"; alternatively, they are called "bedding" (*śayanāsana*) or "spreading materials.

Within the first section of the threefold classification of names, it is divided into two parts: first, it indicates the offenses; all such offenses are generally permitted by way of this [explanation]. Thus it is said.
Because it is formed by joining and then cutting away, the following section now correctly names it; the three robes mentioned above are what is established here.

However, below this, the original translation is presented: first, it is noted that there was no direct translation for this term, and next, it explains the translation based on its characteristics, clarifying that the character "zhāng" (張) is an error and should be "cháng" (長).

[Commentary]: Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that "requisites" (*śayanāsana*) refers to the name for the three robes. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that the "six-year bedding" is precisely the three robes.
If it were not the three robes, how could the procedure for requesting them be as described?

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* also says that when an aged or ill bhikṣu holds a woolen *saṃghāṭī*—which here is translated as "bedding"—is this not the same case? Whether black or white bedding, they are all identical to this.
In the cited evidence, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* provides explicit clarification; how could this not be a reliable authority?

Furthermore, the six-year rule for bedding and requisites mentioned in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*—how could these possibly refer to blankets and quilts? Moreover, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* cited here also concerns the causal conditions for requesting [robes] every six years.

The *Vinayamātṛkā* states that "bedding" (*śayanāsana*) refers to the *saṃghāṭī*, making it clear they are not different. Thus, the two rules concerning black and white hair, as well as the four preceding precepts, all pertain to the three robes alone.

[Commentary]: As for the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) mentioned later, this exists in our own region; its material composition is inverted [compared to the robes], and its physical characteristics are clearly defined.

Since the three robes (*tricīvara*) do not exist here, there is a risk of confusion, and people of the world are collectively deluded regarding the terminology, universally referring to it as a "spreading mat" (*āstaraṇa*). Were it not for seeing this [sitting mat], by what means could one distinguish [it from the robes]?

The term *niṣīdana* (translated here as "sitting mat") is confused with the three robes (*tricīvara*). Because both the sitting mat and the couches or stools used here in this land are used as supports for sitting, there is a potential for confusion;
however, the three robes cannot be so translated because they do not function in that way. This point of confusion is precisely what is being addressed in the present text.

[Commentary: Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or *Bahudhātuka-vibhaṅga*) states: "The term 'reclining equipment' (*śayanāsana*) is a name for clothing. In foreign lands, clothing is made from cotton; there are generally two types:

those that are finely split like felt, and those woven from spun thread. It is because [one uses such materials] that an offense is incurred. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* all refer to it as *kauśeya*.
The treatise states: "This is the name for cotton obtained from raising silkworms, similar to what is found in the land of Qin."
Regarding the Dharma:

in the initial citation from the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), the name and substance are demonstrated. It is described as being finely split like felt, resembling the "wool-floss" (*yù*) of today; when made into threads and woven, it becomes like the fine silk of today.

The subsequent four passages cited clarify only the substance. As for *kauśeya* (silk): *Note: The provided text fragment appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on the Vinaya or Abhidharma, specifically discussing the nature and classification of fabrics, such as *kauśeya* (silk).*

Regarding "transforming silkworm cocoons" and "the first silk": the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that these are merely different names for cotton. The phrase "such as in the land of Qin" refers to this region [China].
[Commentary] There are five conditions that constitute an offense: 1) it is cotton from silkworms; 2) one personally solicits it; 3) one makes it into a robe; 4) it is for one's own use.
The fifth [offense] is committed immediately upon the action.
Among the conditions for the offense, regarding those who make robes, other garments should be lighter [in weight].
[Note: When the Buddha was in the country of Kalandaka, the group of six bhikṣus went to a family raising silkworms and requested raw silk that had not yet been processed as well as [processed silk].
He used cotton mixed with wild silkworm silk to make bedding. Furthermore, while observing and exposing cocoons, he was criticized by householders who said, "He harms living beings;
there is no true Dharma here. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established a precept.
[Commentary]: The conditions for the precept are as explained above.
This is because the conditions for the precept were already indicated in the previous three sections.
[Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding using wild silk cotton (mixed with either wool, cotton, cloth, or other fibers), it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Qi* (In this context, "abandoning" refers to using an axe or a hatchet to chop and slice [wood] and mixing it with mud to plaster a wall), constitutes a *pāyattika*. [Note:

If one performs the act oneself or instructs another, one commits an offense if the work is completed; if not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one causes another to perform the work for oneself, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one obtains something already completed and chops it with an axe to mix with mud for plastering a mound.
[The Commentary] The Prātimokṣa consists of five parts.
[The Commentary] First, the person who commits the offense.

[Commentary: Second, regarding mixed wild silk-cotton: this refers to the household context for the primary precept. If one commits an offense even with mixed materials, how much more so with pure ones?

If one commits an offense even with wild silk, how much more so with domestic silk? This is because the distant [wild] is regulated by the near [domestic]. As for what is called "mixed," it is explained in detail in the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Vinaya-saṃgraha*).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If wool is interwoven between the warp and woof, it is also an offense. It is seen that even a single hair of *kauśeya* silk mixed [with other fibers] constitutes an offense.
Furthermore, regarding the transgression involving *kauseya* (silk): the finest particles within the silk are, by the standards of this region, called *hu*.
The first part of the second sentence of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* generally indicates that mixed [silk] is considered distant while pure domestic [silk] is considered near;

since it constitutes an offense even for the distant, how much more so for the near? Wild silkworms are those born naturally, which produce cocoons upon trees; there are those who take these to make cotton.
Regarding the passage "the items listed below are explained as indicated in the notes," the notes state that *kṣauma* (linen) and *kārpāsa* (cotton) are mixed together.
As for the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* rule concerning weaving with alternating threads, it says:

if the warp is *kauśeya* (silk) and the weft is wool, or if the warp is wool and the weft is *kauśeya*, whether one does it oneself or causes another to do it, it constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
"Fall into the next [level], within the *Sudarśana* [Heaven], even a single hair's breadth" means as much as a single hair. Below, the Sanskrit name is shown:
a *hu* (忽) is that which first emerges from the mouth of a silkworm; ten *hu* make one *si* (絲). This is it.
[Commentary]: Third, making bedding is an act that constitutes an offense.
Among the three [types of robes], "bedding" refers specifically to the *kāṣāya* (monastic robe).
[Commentary]: Fourth, *niḥsargika* refers to the rule of forfeiture. The passage concerning the characteristics of forfeiture within the commentary is extremely clear.

Among the four, the characteristics of "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) differ from those in other precepts. The note states that "jīn" (斤) is equivalent to a "knife" (*dātra*), and "cuò" (挫) is written as "cuò" (剉), with the phonetic gloss "cūo" (麤) and the tone indicator "wò" (臥).
[Commentary] The fifth category consists of the *pāyattika* (波逸提) offenses, which are transgressions of the Dharma.

[Commentary]: Regarding "not committing an offense," if one has already obtained [the object], it must still be cut with an axe; this statement is intended for those who are negligent. How can it be interpreted otherwise?

In the first passage of the fifth explanation of the commentary, the phrase "this statement is intended for those who are negligent" means that the admonition and restraint are extremely urgent. How could it be otherwise?
Generally speaking, there is certainly no permission [to accept such items].

[The *Śū* (Commentary) states: As the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says, "If another has already completed the act of giving, one still commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). Regarding the two sections on the five parts [of robes], the texts of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* differ, which has led to various interpretations.
[Commentary]: Some explain that while the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* agrees with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it differs from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.

However, in the text of the Vinaya, regarding the case of obtaining a robe that is already finished, there is no provision for leniency; it merely states that one must cut or destroy it. How can one set aside the prohibition and instead employ the leniency granted by another school?

They are not the same. Regarding the first section among the three, the ancients claimed that because the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* lists [the case] as non-offensive, it is the same as the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*;

however, the subsequent refutation is incorrect, for the commentary cites the Vinaya and clearly states that "an axe chopping" precisely accords with the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. Thus, it says they are not the same.
I know that the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is lax and cannot be relied upon.

[Commentary: Furthermore, while participating in the translation work, I personally observed that from the country of Tang (China) westward and southward to the great ocean, among the monks of more than a hundred countries, those robes currently worn are none of them made of cotton or silk;
they are neither felt nor woven cloth, yet they constitute dharma-robes according to the established law.
Question: For what reason does this [act] constitute direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for the purpose of ceasing killing? What is the use of empty words?
One should know that what is manifest cannot be dismissed as non-existent, and what is not [manifest] cannot be confused with being existent.

Of these two [sections], the first recounts what was personally heard: when Xuanzang returned from the West, he selected ten monks at Ci'en Monastery to assist in the translation of the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*, and the Master (Paramārtha) was among them;
hence it says, "participated in the translation. Regarding the phrase "west and south," these were all foreign lands outside the borders of the Tang.
"Fur" refers to animal hair, which constitutes one's "birth-share" (*jāti-bhāga*); however, this refers to shearing rather than killing, as will be clarified below.
To reprimand those below for their erroneous understanding of manifest phenomena, it is said that "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is *man*, meaning "false.
To dismiss what is evident as non-existent may still be excusable; however, to mistake what is not for what is, how can one avoid being deemed ignorant?

[Commentary] Question: Since it is said that what is not the Dharma cannot be received and maintained, does it become [an offense]? Answer: As the Vinaya universally prohibits this, it simply states that the five great colors (pañcamahāvarṇa) do not constitute valid acceptance and maintenance.

Regarding the substance of the material itself, there is no explicit text on whether it may be obtained or not. If one follows the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, when silk or cotton is brought and offered to a precept-holder, one should not accept it;
if one accepts it, it is not out of compassion, yet it does not constitute a breaking of the precepts. One should deliberate based on this.
In the first question-and-answer section, the initial point relies on the Vinaya’s lack of a formal ruling.

If one follows the Sūtras below to deliberate upon the case of Aṅgulimāla—specifically that which has been adapted from a Mahāyāna Sūtra—the rule states that one should not accept [offerings] from those who are not from silkworm-keeping families; this is a prohibition found within the Sūtras.

If one were to accept such offerings, it would contradict the teachings on transformation (*huàjiào*). Not breaking the precepts means not violating the regulations of the formulated teachings (*zhìjiào*). This pertains to the Mahāyāna.
For a Bodhisattva, compassionate conduct is primary; thus, if one wears silk garments, one is stained by the aspect of killing sentient beings.

Therefore, this is not compassion. The Śrāvaka vehicle takes the elimination of faults as its foundation; however, because they merely distance themselves from the actual killer and the conditions for the offense are incomplete, their precepts are not considered broken.

According to the Vinaya, following this principle, such actions may be established as lawful; yet, when deeply considering the intent of the Sūtras, these ultimately do not accord with the Dharma, and therefore one must exercise careful discernment.

In the *Zhuoye Zhangfu Yi* (The Ritual of the Robes and Garments for the Seasoned Practitioner), it says: "From the words of morning until the speech of grief, [the practice] shall finally be permanently severed.
The intention of the Patriarch can thus be seen clearly.

[Commentary] Question: Since both the black and white *mian-yi* (cotton garments) share the same conditions for transgression, why is it that one is classified as *ruoshe* (to be discarded) while the other is classified as *quanhuai* (completely ruined)? Answer: Regarding the *mian-yi*...
Since damaging one's life fundamentally contravenes the Sage’s intent, the source must be severed to eliminate future transgressions forever;
however, if the hair on the body is not black or white, and the degree of damage is slight and the obstruction minor, the use [of such items] is permitted.
Next, he asks the cotton to cut and destroy the black and white hairs; having discarded them, he returns them to their owner. Therefore, he questions this to resolve the matter:
because the hair does not damage life, it is different from the cotton, and thus they are separated by weight and discarded.

[Commentary]: If this is so, then there are currently those who make cotton; as they wait for insects to fly out, they do not intend to harm their lives, and thus there should be no transgression. Answer:
Originally, the causal conditions were present, and the intent was fundamentally one of harm. Even if the cotton does not kill them, because the instances are few, it is not taken into account.
In the initial two lines of the response to this difficult objection, it is shown that the Buddha’s original intent in establishing the rule was to effect permanent cessation;
thus, one need not inquire whether insects are present or not, for any silk from silkworms inevitably involves harm. The final two lines clarify the reason why no such distinction is made.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the two precious items (wool and medicine) and the four permitted transgressions of the precepts, why are they restated after the renunciation [of the precepts], and why are they used again after the renunciation?

[Śāstra] The twelfth precept concerning bedding made of black wool.
The twelve pairs [of rules] are named after the subsequent precepts.
[Commentary: Since the substance of this wool is precious, it is inappropriate to wear it; doing so would cause the waste of donated goods and increase the fetters of greed.
Furthermore, because one would personally engage in its manufacture, inviting public censure and obstructing the Path, it would deeply hinder one's fundamental practice; therefore, it was prohibited.

The regulation of the mind is summarized into six points: first, wasteful expenditure; second, excessive greed; third, worldly management; fourth, inviting censure; fifth, obstructing the Path; and sixth, hindering one's vocation.
These can be seen by referring to the respective texts. Regarding the value of the substance [of robes], as clarified in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: [text follows].

[Commentary: Four conditions constitute an offense: 1) using pure black wool; 2) making it into three robes (excluding the case of making blankets, covers, or bedding, which do not fall under this precept);
3) for one's own use; 4) making it oneself. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"The bhikṣus all made blankets, the three robes, and sitting mats, with the sole exception of water-strainers. Because they begged for such large quantities of wool, they were resented by others; furthermore, the wool was coarse."
One *liang* of this [precious substance] requires two or three *jin* of gold; its fine and soft texture causes tears to flow from the eyes of those who encounter it.
Because it is sought after by people, some are ruined or die, and because it destroys household wealth and livelihoods, it is relinquished for the sake of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the second point concerning the conditions for an offense: because it was formerly confused with the name [of another rule], it is distinguished from woolen blankets, as those are not subject to this precept.

Its substance is a heavy object, and by its nature, one would logically incur a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* below cites and demonstrates that there are two intentions behind the formulation of this rule:

first, seeking it oneself causes the laity to feel revulsion; second, requesting others to seek it causes them to break their [productive] karma. First, it clarifies that the substance is precious to manifest its [significance].
Regarding the difficulty of obtaining a human birth and seeking its equivalent:
a wife of a merchant caravan told Śāriputra, "My husband and his kinsmen have sometimes returned home and sometimes died without returning, all for the sake of seeking this wool.
Because this demonstrates the gravity of the transgression, the Buddha prohibited it.
[Note] While the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, many Licchavis engaged in improper conduct; they wore black woolen blankets over their bodies and walked about at night so that others would not see them.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw them, they intentionally imitated this behavior. The Licchavis criticized and disparaged the bhikṣus, who reported the matter to the Buddha.
Consequently, the Buddha established a precept.

In the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), "Licchavis" refers to non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), and "wrong practice" (*mithyācāra*) refers to their non-Buddhist doctrines. Those who despise the Licchavis do so because they [the Licchavis] indiscriminately identify with them.

[The Vinaya states: If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding (*śayanāsana*) using entirely new wool from a black sheep (whether naturally black or dyed black), [he commits an offense]. If it is a bhikṣuṇī... [the same applies].

Saṃghāvaśeṣa. [Note] The characteristics of committing an offense by doing it oneself, instructing another to do it, or acting on behalf of another are all as in the preceding precepts. It is no offense for a nun in the case of:
if she obtains one that is already finished; if she cuts, tears, or damages it; or if she makes it double-layered by folding thin material; or if it is a small sitting mat.
If one makes a mattress, a hat, sleeves, a heat-retaining cloth, or a cloth for wrapping leather sandals, there is no offense in any of these cases.
[Commentary] The precept text consists of five phrases.
[Commentary]: One person. [Commentary]:
Second, the object is that which is made from newly acquired, purely black wool of the *urabhraka* (small sheep). "Pure" means unmixed;
if mixed, it does not constitute an offense. "*Urabhraka*" refers to a small lamb.
In the second phrase of the *Prātimokṣa*, the character "róu" (羺)—pronounced as "nú gōu" (奴鈎)—refers to a wild sheep (*húyáng*). The text states that those which are small have fine wool.
[Commentary: The third point, the formal offense regarding the making of bedding, refers specifically to Dharma robes (*dharmakāya*). If one makes other types of clothing, it is as described above.

Regarding the offense [of making a mattress], it was committed because, among the robes permitted by the rules, the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) was intended for wearing over one’s shoulders when traveling at night;

since the bhikṣus imitated this practice, they knew it was not the lower garment (*antarvāsaka*), let alone a mattress. Thus, this constitutes a violation of the precepts. Therefore, the following provision permits the use of a mattress, as it is not an offense.

In the third sentence, regarding the citation and explanation: first, the definition and essence are established as above; next, the conditions are listed as below, citing the conditions to provide proof.

Since it is worn externally and reveals [the body], it is a *kāṣāya*. Regarding the explanation of the name within the secular context: that which is worn on the upper body is called *yi* (upper garment), and that which is worn on the lower body is called *shang* (lower garment).
Since this is for the upper body, it is not the lower *shang*. Furthermore, the *shang* does not constitute an offense, nor is a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) used for wearing.
Therefore it says, "How much more so.
[Commentary] Formerly, because these were used as the five types of bedding and mats, the precept was established stating: "This wool is a precious material;

it is not appropriate to use it for inferior purposes, lest it be wasted on useless expenses. This statement is precisely that. However, the current practice is different, as it pertains to the timing within the aforementioned meaning.

Regarding the "reclining requisites" (*śayanāsana*): fearing that a revision might cause confusion, I have preserved the ancient terminology for now. If readers understand this to be incorrect, there will be no great fault.
Among the ancient commentaries, the initial citation shows that the four types of reclining requisites do not include the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*);

they are collectively termed the "five *śayyā*. The formulation of the precepts follows the intent described in the ancient commentaries; since those [ancient texts] refer to blankets and quilts, it says "used below" (*adhaḥprayoga*) here.
The following passage clarifies that it is not the first phrase; the marker below points back to the preceding text.

According to the ancient edition, the character "竝" (ping) above is likely an error in the transmitted text for the character "然" (ran). This means that in the previous section on the gates of meaning, it frequently states "five arrangements" (五敷);
this follows the ancient version to indicate what must be known.
[Commentary]: The two phrases regarding the fourth and fifth [offenses] are explained as above.
"The fourth and fifth are as above" refers to the forfeiture and the offense.
[Commentary]: The sub-commentary states: "If one has already obtained it, this is an opening provision; it differs from the preceding precept. If one has already obtained it..."
If it is completed, one incurs the offense of cutting; this precept is an exception (*kai*), and thus there is no textual passage regarding cutting. Furthermore, it says:

"If one cuts or destroys [the robe]" refers to when, at the time of making it, one intends for it to be destroyed later; since the original intention was not to destroy it, the offense is incurred once it is completed.
This same twofold interpretation applies by analogy to the cases of thin, light, or double-layered robes among the various subsequent precepts.

In the commentary, the first part explains what has already been established; next, it analyzes "cutting" and "destroying" by way of the presence or absence of intention (*citta*) to clarify the two characteristics;
finally, it probes and examines the subsequent precepts.
[Vinaya] The thirteenth precept concerning bedding with white hair.
[Commentary]: The thirteenth [precept] concerns the rule for making the three robes from white hair.

The intent behind this regulation is the same as in the *Pañcavargika* and *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, where because black hair was not permitted under the preceding precepts, small amounts of white and brindled hair were mixed in;
consequently, the rule was established to have the three types of hair intermingled.

Regarding the first phrase of the thirteen rules for regulating the mind: although they share the same essence, because the obstruction to one's practice caused by greed for construction is no different from other such hindrances, they must be regulated and restricted.

The fifth section below demonstrates the difference from the original school: while that school established the rule only when the object was purely white, this school establishes it even when there is a slight admixture.
Because of that slight admixture, the limits of the prohibition are set; "pure white" and "mottled" mean that the latter does not consist of many [mixed colors].
The character *māng* (尨) has the phonetic component *jiǎng* (江). If one follows the dictionaries, it refers to a dog with much hair;
some say it should be written as *náng* (牻), which is explained as "variegated. However, this is actually the name for a variegated-colored ox and does not mean "variegated" [in general].
Now, according to the commentary, where the head, feet, and other parts are coarse-haired and a pale yellow color, such is called *māng-máo* (尨毛).
[Commentary]: There are five conditions for the offense to be established: first, three hairs; second, the act of making; third, the intention to make it into a robe; fourth, for one's own use;
and fifth, increasing the quality or decreasing the inferiority by at least one *liang*. When these are fulfilled, the offense is committed.
The fourth condition for an offense: if the excellence increases, it is black hair; if the defect decreases, it is white or brindled hair. [Commentary] Question:

Since both black and white constitute an offense, why was the case of black hair not prohibited earlier when it was mixed? Answer: The two precepts clarify that the textual description of mixing would be redundant;
therefore, following the latter example, mixing with black does not constitute an offense.
In the initial question-and-answer, since white [hair] has diminished and good [hair] has been permitted, while black must necessarily be interspersed with brindled [hair], there is no fault;
thus it is said that "the latter serves as an analogy for the former.

[Commentary]: Question: Since all three types of hair are interspersed, why is black hair predominant while brindled hair is scarce? Answer: Because the precept was established based on white hair, black [hair]...

Bahuśruta says that according to the previous [text], the black and white [wool] must also be in large quantities; he further states that although black is noble, it conforms to the appearance of a dharma-robe, whereas white is a secular garment, and for this reason it is used in small amounts.
Next, he asks: since the text of the precepts states that there are two parts of black wool and one part each of white and variegated wool, how is this so?

The middle section simply states "māṅ" (variegated), but its meaning must necessarily include "white. In the answer, first there is an explanation by way of contrasting the characteristics of the prohibitive precepts;
next, there is an explanation by way of following or violating the color of the hair.
[Note: While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus made new bedding exclusively from white hair. Laypeople...
Regarding the censure [of the Buddha] as being like that of a king or a great minister: when a bhikṣu was accused of an offense, the Buddha, because of this, rebuked him and established the precept.
