To repair it, one should pull and stretch it until it is taut, then cut out a square measuring one *vitasti* (a span) and patch it onto the new material.
If the patch is applied to the edge or the center, it is because the old material has become discolored.
[The Vinaya states: "If one makes a new sitting mat, one must take a piece of the old one measuring one *vitasti* in length and breadth and patch it onto the new material."
To alter the color [of a robe] constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. [Note:

Whether one does it oneself, instructs another, or has it done for oneself, the offense is as described above; for a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases:

if it is for the purpose of cutting [excess material], if it is to fold a new [robe], if the original is worn out and one makes a new one, if another person makes it for one, or if one obtains [a new one].
If it is already completed, or if it is made of pure [old] material, there is no offense.

[Commentary: Regarding the establishment of the precept text, there are three points for the violation of the rule and four points for the violation of the teaching. "If a bhikṣu" refers to the person who commits the act;

second, "making a new sitting mat" is the objective condition (*ālambana*) of this precept; third, one should take up the following to clarify the characteristics of the established rule, namely, the term "worn out."
Regarding "form" (*rūpa*), it is because one must sever attachment to it. As for the subsequent aspects of transgression, they may be sought through the underlying intention.
In the text of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, there is first a general division, followed by a detailed explanation.

First, the establishment of the rule is explained: a span of one *vitasti*—that is, one cubit of the Buddha, meaning two feet on each of the four sides. The method of measuring described in the commentary is extremely detailed; as for the words: [The text continues with the specific measurements and instructions.]
Regarding "severing attachment," attachment refers to craving. Following this, the text next explains the violation of the teachings in four points: first, "new" refers to the object of the offense;
second, "not taking up" refers to the violation of the Dharma; third, "abandoning"; and fourth, "the offense. Thus, there are four phrases.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "because it was taken up for measurement" in the note: this means that even if the formal act has not yet been performed, because one already possesses the intention to count [the stalks], it constitutes an offense.
Conversely, if one ultimately does not proceed to count them, the offense is likewise established accordingly.

The commentary on the first section explains that because the new [material] must first be completed before it can be folded, the explanation regarding the mental intention (*citta*) for its use also establishes the circumstances under which there is no offense. [The Sub-commentary] states:

"This is what is added by the sacred Dharma; it is intended for constant use as a seat. It does not refer to woolen cloth or other items used for ordinary purposes, but rather to what is added [to the standard allowance]."

If one currently possesses many items that are not formally held (*parigṛhīta*), yet does not know which among them constitute an offense—thinking, for instance, that since the three robes and one bowl are by nature original prescriptions (*prakṛti-saṃvara*), they may be accumulated in excess without incurring the fault of a transgression—is this correct? Regarding the first case, these are indeed original possessions;

even if they are not formally held, there is no offense of "excess" (*atireka*). However, if they are of a color that conforms to the Dharma, they may be consecrated (*adhiṣṭhāna*) or [treated as] the substance itself.
If the robe is unlawful, or its color is improper, or if it was obtained through trade, begging, or by seeking it through improper means, then even if one possesses it, the act is not accomplished;

this case is similar to the rules regarding the keeping of the three robes. As for its actual use and the offense incurred in possessing it, these are the same as those for the alms bowl; the rest is as explained in the *Śāstra* commentary and within the ninety offenses.
In the first section of the following analysis, it is shown that one must apply the ritual of *adhiṣṭhāna* (empowerment), and it does not specify whether the material is felt or cloth;

this means that regardless of the quality of the substance—whether fine or coarse—one should simply take what is commonly used, empower it, and maintain it. As for the remainder, one should perform the rite of *viśuddha-sthāpana* (purification) before keeping them.

Now, the following passage refutes improper practices, while the subsequent section clarifies the correct meaning, namely, what the Patriarchs intended. First, it rebukes the practice of accumulating many items, as in the case of robes and bowls.
Since the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) is counted as one among the six requisites, and as it is identical in status to the robe and bowl, how could its multiple possession be permitted?
As will be explained below, this first demonstrates whether the matter is established or not; next, it clarifies the rules for its use.

Regarding "possessing [it] like the three robes," this refers to the regulation that it must be kept with one at all times. Regarding "the violation and maintenance being the same as the bowl," even staying overnight apart from it is permissible.
The *Fashilü yishu* (Commentary on the Vinaya Rules), Volume 2, the *Yiyeshu* (Exposition on Robes and Medicine), section 90, concerns the precept regarding exceeding the prescribed quantity.
[Vinaya Text] 16. The precept against carrying wool beyond the limit.
[Commentary]: The sixteenth precept concerns carrying wool beyond the permitted limit.
However, for one who has left the household life to personally carry wool while traveling along the road is conduct identical to that of worldly commoners;

it violates dignified decorum, invites reproach, and brings self-reproach, which is utterly improper. Therefore, this rule was established. As for the exceptions provided, they concern the maintenance of the body.

Aids to the Path are not things that can be dispensed with; yet, if one were to strictly prohibit them entirely, there would be no remedy for what is required, and seeking them elsewhere would lead to even greater exhaustion and disturbance.
Therefore, it is permitted up to three *yojanas*; beyond that, it constitutes a transgression.
Regarding the first section of the sixteen points on the intent behind the regulations, "fragmentary" refers to what is sought by petty people;

below this, it clarifies the intent of the allowances. "Must" (*yu*) means that when establishing a regulation, there must be an allowance; since every allowance must be followed by a regulation, the limit of *yojanas* is set, such that exceeding it constitutes an offense under the regulation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the four conditions for committing an offense, the first concerns "noble wool. The text excludes "base [wool]" because the allowance [for base wool] is made within the context of the head and leg hair.
Now, if one incurs censure, it does not matter whether the wool is noble or base; even carrying *vāla* (coarse hair) and the like constitutes a transgression of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).

However, since the basis of the rule lies specifically in [the use of] wool, the prohibition is established while the allowance applies to other materials. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One who makes it into an implement does not commit an offense. "Implement" refers to the characteristics of a robe.

This is also a general designation, as in the case where items such as knives, axes, clothing, or vessels are collectively termed "one's own property" (sva-dravya). There are four conditions for this offense:
first, it must be one's own property; second, one must carry it oneself; third, the distance traveled must reach three *yojanas*; and fourth, the object must be forgotten.

Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that even if one carries wool in a cloth bag while walking or circumambulating a stūpa, or if one forgets the object after traveling one and a half *yojanas* and returns, the offense of *pāyattika* is incurred once the total distance exceeds three *yojanas*.
Regarding the conditions for the offense, the first condition excludes those of low status, while the subsequent provision allows for exceptions;

now, according to the judgment of the lower meaning, the first case is judged as an offense based on the commonality of the censure regarding the carrying of wool and so forth—this summarizes the text concerning the allowance—and "transgressing the rules of decorum" constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor) offense. By reason of...
Because this is minor and base, it is not treated with the same gravity; rather, the following section clearly sets forth the meaning of non-offense.

Above, the original offense was described in detail, encompassing both prohibitions and allowances; therefore, the non-offenses are indicated as being outside the scope of those prohibitions and allowances.

Next, the initial passage from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited to resolve the textual characteristics. Following this, the names of the vessels are explained, such as knives, axes, and other various implements for use.
The term "receiving" (*de*) is used to designate the vessel (*qi*) in order to show that the name of the vessel is not restricted; it refers to clothing and other items.

From the passage "down to three *yojanas*" below, this is the fourth section of the text, though the numerical heading has been omitted. Below, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited to demonstrate the distinct characteristics:

first, it clarifies that although walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) around a stūpa is not travel on a road, it is nonetheless calculated in *li*; or, next, it refers to being on a road for one *yojana*.
If one forgets an object for half a *yojana* and returns after traveling three *yojanas*, and then goes again, one commits an offense for one *yojana*,
which calculates to forty *li*.
[Note] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the householder Bhaṇḍana obtained some sheep’s wool and carried it on the head of his staff as he walked.
[The Buddha] rebuked those who traded in wool; the bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.
[Commentary: Regarding the origin of the offense within the conditions for the precept, "transgression" refers to the act of trading.
In the explanation of the conditions for this precept, the words of censure are specifically cited to clarify that this precept is intended to prevent reproach.
[The Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a road, obtains wool and there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for up to three *yojanas*."
[Note] Whether on the road or at a dwelling place, if one obtains wool and requires it, one may take it; if there is no one else to carry it, one may carry it oneself for up to three *yojanas*.
If there is someone present, one should say, "I have this item; help me carry it" until reaching that destination.
If a *bhikṣu* does not assist in carrying it during this interval, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one causes the fourfold assembly of *bhikṣuṇīs* to carry it beyond [the limit], [it is likewise a fault].
If one carries wool for three *yojanas*, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one carries other garments, such as those made of hemp and so forth, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if one carries other items on the end of a staff, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
[Vinaya] If there is no one to carry it and one carries it oneself beyond three *yojanas*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

【Note】A *bhikṣuṇī* commits no offense (*agilāna*) if she carries [the items] for up to three *yojanas* or less than three *yojanas*, provided someone tells her to carry them partway and she does not assist; if the four groups of *bhikṣuṇīs* together carry them within three *yojanas*;
or if she carries woolen cloth (*vāka*), woolen thread (*sūtra*), or a cap or headcloth made of hair on her head.

[Commentary]: Regarding the five phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* [text]: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the section beginning with "while traveling on a road" which establishes the formal rule (*vidhi*)—the interpretation of the textual characteristics of these can be understood;
third, the section beginning with "if there is no one... clarifies the karmic nature of the precept (*śīla-karman*). The final two [sections] can be understood.

In the first section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the second phrase refers to the commentary. Within the commentary, the first part clarifies that one may take [the items] for oneself and maintain them until the limit is reached;
"if there is someone next" clarifies entrusting others to continue maintaining them; "if one causes" clarifies having other members of the assembly maintain them;
and "excluding" clarifies various light items.
[Commentary: Regarding the opening [of the rule] concerning hats and head-cloths, this refers to cases where the intention was formed before the materials were carried.

Next, regarding the non-offense for those who already possess hats and head-cloths—since there was originally no offense for them—the present opening [of the rule] refers to cases where one carries a small amount of wool with the intention of making [a hat or head-cloth].
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The seventeenth precept: Causing a non-relative nun to wash wool.
[Commentary] The seventeenth precept: Causing a nun to wash and card wool.

[Commentary] The intent behind the formulation of this precept and the conditions for its violation are the same as those for the precept on washing robes; since that [latter] was already established, this is a minor offense regarding new [wool].
Since this involves labor, both the new and the old are equally guilty.
Regarding the seventeenth name, "pì" (劈) is a corruption of the character "bò" (擘), meaning to divide or split; it was originally pronounced "pì," but is here a scribal error.

In the *Tongshì* (General Explanation), the initial reference is identical to this; furthermore, the three conditions for the establishment of the offense and the characteristics of its commission—whether combined or separate—are all as explained above.
The conditions for the offense differ only in that the third point specifies it is wool; this distinction can be understood from the following passage.
[Note: While the Buddha was at Kapilavastu, the group of six bhikṣus took wool and had a bhikṣuṇī wash, dye, and comb it.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Ābhiri, having stained her hands with the dye while coloring the wool, went to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and stood before him. The Buddha—
Knowing [the situation], he questioned her and rebuked her, thereby establishing the precept.

[Commentary]: Regarding the circumstances of this precept, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (*Duolun*) states that the reason for its establishment was to provide the monks with a superior rule (*adhika-dharma*).
Furthermore, if the community of nuns were to persist in performing the work of washing and dyeing [robes]...
If one abandons the cultivation of right practice, there will be no dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), and the supreme Dharma (*adhipati-dharma*) will be destroyed;
furthermore, because the sequential causes and conditions for ceasing unwholesome dharmas must each be purified, one does not sit. This is because women possess much reverence and apprehension;

moreover, the Buddha did not extensively preach the Dharma for the female assembly; and finally, when nuns arrive at the Buddha’s presence, they all stand as a means to stop the slanders of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Therefore, because women are vulgar and often subject to ridicule and suspicion, they do not sit [in the assembly].

Regarding the initial citation of the text and the inquiry into its intent within the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra-vibhāṣā* (or *Vinayavibhāṣā*), there are two parts. First, the explanation of the establishment of the precept has two points.
The first point, concerning the "superior dharma" (*adhi-dharma*) for bhikṣus, is that it arises because nuns’ engagement in [worldly] activities would disrupt their practice.

Regarding the ritual protocol: because the bhikṣu’s violation of the supreme dharma follows a sequence of mental applications (*smṛtyupasthāna*) toward unwholesome dharmas, and because one restrains what is light while guarding against what is heavy, the following section clarifies that one need not sit, explaining this through four points.

Second, since the preaching and listening will not last long, sitting is unnecessary; the remaining three points are easily understood. In the commentary, "aunt" refers to the nun Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. "Defiled" [refers to her state].
[The Buddha], seeing this with his own eyes, made a formal request and established the precept.
[Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
[Note] For a bhikṣuṇī, a *duṣkṛta* offense is established; the exceptions are as in the precept concerning the washing of old robes.
[Commentary] The remaining phrases can be understood by consulting them.
Since the precept text is the same as before, it is omitted here; however, the commentary on the text contains six points: first, the person; second, one who is not a relative;
third, the characteristics of the primary action, namely washing, dyeing, and beating; fourth, wool, which constitutes the object of the offense; fifth, relinquishment; and sixth, the offense itself.
[Vinaya] The eighteenth precept: Prohibiting the Possession of Money and Precious Objects.
[Commentary] The eighteenth precept: Prohibiting the Possession of Money and Precious Objects.

[Commentary] "Precious objects" (*ratna*) are one of the eight impurities (*aśuci*). First, by means of scriptural evidence (*hetuvidyā*), they are analyzed and distinguished; second, by enumerating them, their improper nature is made manifest; third, the conditions for their allowance and prohibition are set forth.
Third, the gravity of the offenses and the resulting transgressions; fourth, the transgression incurred through mutual exchange.
Within the eighteen sections of the detailed analysis, the chapter divisions state: "The eight impurities are also called 'impure speech'; though the names differ, the meaning is the same.
They are also called the 'eight venomous snakes,' named after a metaphor."
[Commentary] Regarding the initial enumeration of the numbers: various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras all speak of the "eight impure things.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, these are extensively discussed across more than ten passages as being subject to censure for their faults, yet the specific names are not listed there. Thus, that text states:

"If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) knows that a bhikṣu has broken the precepts and is impure in his acceptance and possession of the eight things, he should not provide them with gifts, nor should he give him the *kāṣāya*..."

Because of the causal conditions of the *kāṣāya*, if one performs prostrations and reverences [to others], or engages in communal affairs with the Saṃgha, one will fall into hell after death; this is explained at length as stated there.
Regarding the first section of the enumeration: first, there is a general indication of various scriptures; next, there is a specific citation from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Within that, the first part prohibits laypeople from showing reverence, while the subsequent part prohibits monastics from following the same practices.
[Commentary] Since there has been a tradition handed down from antiquity regarding eight categories [of forbidden items], one must know these eight types: 1. fields, houses, and gardens;
2. planted crops and seeds; 3. stored grain and silks; 4. domesticated servants and laborers; 5. caged birds and beasts; 6.
money, treasures, and precious objects; 7. woolen rugs and heavy valuables; 8. items that the Buddha did not permit, such as women’s articles and weapons.
In the sixth of the eight sections that follow, the current precept is properly addressed.
[Commentary]: There are five reasons why it is called "impure": first, because maintaining [possessions] increases greed, it is termed an "impure mind";

second, because its substance is defiled, it is termed "impure precepts"; third, because it contravenes the clear injunctions of the Sages, it is termed "impure teaching"; fourth, because it exceeds... [text fragment].

The fifth [aspect] is impure faith, which consists of disparaging worldly sentiments and seeking fame. The sixth is impure karma, which refers to being submerged in the three realms of existence and bound by the fetters of the three evil paths.
Among these three [categories], there are five [sub-factors]: intention, mind, precepts, teaching, and faith; since karma is itself practice, these five together constitute the eight entities.
Because they are defiled, they are all termed "impure. Furthermore, the mind of greed is the root that spontaneously gives rise to the four subsequent types.
Moreover, these four together collectively constitute the final karma. However, the teaching itself is not impure;
it is only designated as such because, by desiring to possess [the requisites], it defiles and disparages the holy word.

[Commentary: The remaining three sections are fully contained within the *Suijie shixiang chubaocai jiaochao* (The Commentary on the Precept Against Possessing Precious Things), where they are explained in detail.

Next, regarding the second section of the *Kaili jiaochao* (The Commentary on Permissible and Prohibited Matters), which is extremely extensive, it is stated in brief that the entire Saṃgha is permitted [to possess such things], with the sole exception of women.
As for individuals, there are cases where permission is granted and cases where it is not; for example, the room is permitted to be of standard measurement, as is money.
Regarding the third category, the light and heavy offenses concerning the declaration of purity (*śuddhi*) and so forth, the *Chao* states:

"If one possesses six or seven gold coins or a cotton mattress, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) because it violates the rules for pure gifts; [the mention of a 'cotton mattress' as being subject to the declaration of purity refers only to small ones]. The remaining six cases constitute *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), as the items possessed are of little value.

Regarding the fourth category, mutual exchange, the *Chao* states: "If one exchanges these eight items for clothing, one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), because clothing can be exchanged for precious materials such as silk or cotton mattresses."
Furthermore, if one discards [the bowl] and obtains another of the six types, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), and so forth.
[Commentary: The reason for citing the *Shan-chao* (Excerpts) in succession above is that it provides a detailed exposition, thereby sparing one the trouble of expending further effort.

In the third section, the general indication, because the preceding various precepts mostly refer to the *Chao* (Commentary), this is specifically indicated to make known the intent of the abridgment.

[The *Shu* (Commentary) says: To correctly explain the intent of the regulation: Now, one who leaves the household life does so for the sake of the Way; worldly wealth is not their concern, and even those of high integrity among the laity look back with envy.
If even those who have cast off worldly dust [cannot be expected to do so], how much less can those whose minds still cling to it?
When their fundamental purpose deviates from the essential meaning and they contradict their habitual practice by greedily accumulating possessions, they utterly violate the monastic regulations.

This is precisely why the Tathāgata established the precepts—not for laypeople, but because this one precept alone was specifically formulated for them—to cause them to extinguish greed and competition and to give rise to the characteristics of a teacher of the Way. If they do not comply...
The Dharma itself is a pitfall that ruins and destroys the vessel of the Path; what evil could surpass this? Therefore, the *Samantapāsādikā* states that there are three benefits to the regulations:
first, to cease slander; second, to extinguish strife and contention; and third, to establish the four noble lineages and the practice of frugality.

In the initial section of the current explanation regarding the intent behind the prohibitions of the precepts, the passage describing what is inappropriate cites secular scholars such as Wang Yan and Guan Ning, who viewed wealth as mere tiles and stones;
Cui Hong, who did not speak of trading goods nor handle pearls and jade with his own hands;

and the various worthies of the Jin dynasty, all of whom possessed little private interest or few desires, held their principles in high esteem, and renounced household life for the Way. How could [the monastic community] possibly...?
Conversely, since the meaning deviates from common practice, the terminology must differ from that of the mundane world. Next, the following section clarifies the specific faults;

below this, two citations are introduced as proof. First, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* is cited to provide evidence regarding the laity, specifically the introductory narrative of the precepts (*śikṣāpada-nidāna*) which speaks of "establishing the Way," meaning to cause the Sangha to perfect its virtuous characteristics so that worldly people may turn their hearts toward it. Second, three passages from the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* are cited.
This further proves that it accords with the initial practice of the Path, secondly because it severs commercial exchange, and thirdly because it fulfills the cultivation of few desires.

[Commentary] The four conditions that constitute an offense are: first, the object must be money or precious goods; second, it must be for one's own sake; third, there must be no intention to inform or entrust the matter to another; and fourth, the act of receiving constitutes the offense.
The third condition for the offense: because it was not possible to speak immediately at the time of receiving the gift, the intention is defined by first accepting and subsequently speaking.
[Note]: When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was a high minister who, for the sake of Upananda, set aside his portion of food for his son.

When Upāli took five coins for food and Baddhālī came to collect the money, he deposited it with a householder at a marketplace. The householders collectively resented this, and the bhikṣus reprimanded him.
The King discussed the matter with his ministers, and the Buddha extensively explained the causes and analogies before criticizing the conduct and establishing the precept.
[Commentary] Within the context of the conditions for the precept, the first section clarifies the origin of the transgression involving the taking of money at a marketplace.

The second section, beginning with "The two householders both felt resentment," clarifies how the king and his ministers discussed the matter, providing analogies, censuring the act, and establishing the prohibition. Thus, the Vinaya text states:
The Buddha told the great minister, "If you see a śramaṇa or son of the Śākya who, while taking me as his teacher, accepts gold, silver, coins, or treasures, then it is certain..."

Knowing that they are not disciples of the Śākya, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* further states: "If there are śramaṇas who accept and store gold and jewels, one should know that the five desires are all meritorious and pure.
The rest of the passage is the same as in the *Yao*. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"If one can distance oneself from the dharma of the eight poisonous snakes, this is called the pure field of merit of the noble assembly; such a person should be venerated by humans and devas."
The pure fruit of retribution is not seen by the fleshly eye, and so forth.
Because this is the first section of the text concerning the conditions for the precepts (*śīla-pratyaya*), the following citation and explanation has three parts. First, it cites the *Mūla-vinaya*:
during the time of the Buddha, kings and ministers gathered together and spoke these words: "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are permitted to handle gold and jewels. There was one great...
The minister, named Muktika, said to the other ministers, "Do not speak such words; I have heard from the Buddha that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are not permitted to handle gold or silver.
He then went to the Buddha and addressed him, saying, "Is what I have spoken to you not without error?
The Buddha replied [with the following words], which were the Buddha’s response: "Furthermore, Great Minister, you should know that the sun and the moon..."
There are four obstructions that prevent clarity and purity, namely: the asuras, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist. Śramaṇas likewise have four things that prevent clarity and purity, namely:
not abandoning the drinking of alcohol, sexual desire, the possession of gold and silver, and wrong livelihood.
Next, citing the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, [it says]: "The purity of a śramaṇa and the defilement of the five desires; gold and jewels are form, which is the fifth."

If one were to permit the acceptance and possession of even a single desire, would not the five desires, conversely, become pure? Third, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* first exhorts one to distance oneself from them.
The lower [passage] praises their virtue; the upper four lines praise the cause, and the lower two lines praise the fruit.
Because it is the outflow-free (anāsrava) retribution, it is not something seen by the fleshly eyes of ordinary beings.

[The Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu takes money (bearing inscriptions or images) in his own hand, or gold and silver, or instructs another to take them, or accepts them by placing them on the ground, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
[Note] Regarding "renunciation" herein: if there is a garden-keeper who has faith and devotion, or an upāsaka, one should say to them, "This is mine;

it is not yours; you should know this. If they take it back and give it to the bhikṣu, he may accept it for the sake of that person's property and instruct a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things permissible) to look after it. If he obtains pure robes or bowls, he should trade for them and accept them.
If one holds it as that upāsaka has taken it, and if he gives a pure robe or bowl to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should accept and hold it.
[Vinaya] This is a pāyattika.
[Commentary] For a bhikṣuṇī, the offense is the same. If she does not inform that person that this is for inspection, it is a duṣkṛta; otherwise, there is no offense.
If one speaks thus, "Know this and see this," according to the aforementioned method of relinquishment (*niḥsargika*), and if that person is unwilling to give back the robe, other bhikṣus should say:

"The Buddha has given instruction that for the sake of purification (*viśuddhi*) it may be given to you; you should return the object to him. If he still does not give it back, one should go in person and say:
"The Buddha instructs the bhikṣus to perform purification and give it to you; you should [give it] to the Saṃgha, the Stūpa, or a fellow practitioner (*sabrahmacārin*)."
This is because the preceptor and the original donor do not wish for that faithful offering to be lost. [Commentary:

Of the six phrases in the root text, (1) "a person" and (2) "grasping with one's own hand" constitute the action (*karma*) of the precept; (3) "money, gold, or precious gems" constitutes the object (*viṣaya*) guarded by the precept;
(4) "instructing another to receive it" is the same as the aforementioned action; the final two [phrases] are self-evident.

In the first section of the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, there are two parts: first, performing the act oneself; second, instructing others to do so. Although the self and the other differ, the actual performance of the act is no different;
therefore, they are treated as the same. Regarding the "upper" and "lower" sections, these refer to the relinquishing [of the offense] and the confession of the transgression, respectively.

[Commentary]: This refers to the precept against possessing precious objects; the ninety-first [precept] is the precept against handling precious objects. In the present text, the term "possessing" is not explicitly mentioned as it is abbreviated.
Whether one handles them with one's own hand or instructs another to do so—if the objects can be placed on the ground—the characteristics of receiving and possessing them are set forth.

Receiving is fundamentally for the purpose of possessing; thus, one incurs two offenses: one for handling and one for possessing. Handling is subject to the subsequent rule, while possessing is subject to this [present] rule. If one handles them but does not possess them, [the offense is determined accordingly].
Because one does not violate this precept until one violates the subsequent ninety [offenses], the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If one takes hold of gold leaf, a golden image, or the treasures of others—if one has personally purified the treasure through the ritual of *viśuddhi*—one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is also like this:
gold, silver, and coins, provided they are of the type used in the country and possess the requisite characteristics, all constitute a *pāyattika* offense."
In the first part of the section on "Avoiding Excess," two precepts are initially distinguished; now, the general textual characteristics are presented below.

Regarding the phrase "holding with one's own hand," former commentators claimed that this regulation for holding jewels was intended specifically to supplement the following rule; therefore, they have specifically separated and indicated them. First, the commentary on the text:

regarding the determination of offenses below, based on this, one should formulate four permutations. To possess [jewels] without holding them—as described in the text where they are placed on the ground—constitutes a single offense.

Regarding this precept, there are two cases of "taking" (*grahaṇa*) without "storing" (*parigraha*), as explained in detail in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. In the case of violating only the subsequent precept, there is both "taking" and "storing," as stated in the text.

In the case of the two precepts concerning taking with the hand, one commits both offenses. There are four combinations that are neither; for example, when instructed to take a golden image and so forth.

Below, the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* cites evidence from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, stating that "gold leaf" refers to objects used for gilding or coating, while the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* refers to money and treasures.
Whatever currency is used in a country—whether gold, silver, copper, or iron—if one takes hold of it when it has been fashioned into the form of coin, one commits an offense.

and so forth clarifies the method for abandoning the money: seeking a pure master to whom it may be entrusted. Third, "if that person takes it back and gives it to the bhikṣu," there is no offense.

The Buddha Dāśārha, for the sake of purity, caused him to receive [the items]; because he did not understand, he did not dare to accept them immediately, as this would have contravened the rules for pure giving.

Fourth, if the recipient takes them down and subsequently awakens to the intention, he may take them and return them to purity; therefore, no further exchange is required.
Regarding the text on trading:

the commentary explains that there are four correct interpretations and three incorrect ones. The failure to understand the intent of the giving arises from not having spoken beforehand and not comprehending the meaning of *śuddhikaraṇa* (purification).
By treating those objects as received, one causes the *śuddhikara* (the purifier) to perform the task; this is equivalent to receiving a deposit.
If one subsequently exchanges robes or alms bowls for other items, because the prior purification ritual was not validly established, the items obtained later remain impure;
thus, among the four cases, this refers specifically to the method of resolving through purification.
[Commentary] Question: Since the giving is identical for both parties, how can there be such a difference between delusion and awakening?

Answer: A śramaṇa must follow the teachings and speak so that others may understand. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "First, one seeks out a layperson who knows the Dharma and has them inform [the donor] of the bhikṣu’s rule against possessing money or jewels;
later, if [money] is obtained, it is purified through the donor. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the former case is due to delusion.

Therefore, since things are not yet accomplished when they are first seen, one must act toward them as such objects; later, if wealth is obtained, it must still be traded before one can formally accept and enjoy it.
The text is extremely explicit, so do not be surprised by this meticulousness.
In the question, the preceding two sections are restated to express the intent of the teaching. In the answer, first there is the direct response:

that because of speaking or not speaking, there are four divisions of delusion and enlightenment. Below this, the preceding passage on delusion is re-explained; the final two phrases are a caution against the concern that the text might become overly prolix.

[Commentary] Regarding the concluding summary of the offense, the sub-commentary states: "If one does not speak while looking at it" means that although one looks at the money or treasure, one knows it is not something I have made for myself;
yet, having purified it by giving it to you, how can one fail to speak? This constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) because of the loss of the Dharma. The passage beginning with "If he...
clarifies the signs of seeking treasure and failing to obtain it, as well as the manner of proceeding; the text is extremely clear and authoritative.

Next, the commentary on the section regarding the formal determination of the offense (*āpatti*) explains the notes within the text. The phrase "if not" clarifies that [the monk] did not instruct [the other] in the pure speech;

the phrase "if he speaks" clarifies that [the offense occurs] once the act has been performed and he requests the sign. In the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), the first part explains the preceding section: "If one sees with the eyes, one knows through the mind. How could it be otherwise than this?
This explains the meaning of the formal determination of the offense for failing to manifest [the purity]. The phrase "if he" explains the subsequent section.
Section. [Commentary]:
This is also something people frequently commit; yet, if one recognizes the offense upon committing it, there is a period for its cessation.

Although those within the monastic community (the *kṣetra*) often commit such offenses, few recognize their transgression. Therefore, I now exhort you to recognize them; once recognized, they may be brought to rest.
To commit an offense without awareness, while being greedy and stingy—how can such things ever be exhausted?
[Vinaya] The nineteenth precept: Trading Money and Jewels.
[Commentary] The nineteenth precept: Trading Jewels.
[Commentary: Because the mutual trading of precious objects increases greed, obstructs the Path, and invites worldly reproach and faults, it was thus prohibited.

The intent of the nineteenth rule primarily clarifies the middle section: first, it demonstrates the characteristics of the karma; "increases" and below briefly indicate the three faults, which are all ultimately subsumed [under this].
"Both are diminished.
[Commentary: This precept differs from the subsequent precept regarding the trading of robes in five ways. First, the persons involved differ:

the trading of precious objects is an offense for all seven classes of followers, whereas the trading of robes is an offense only for the two [classes of householders]. Second, both types of trading—whether performed by oneself or instigated in another for one's own sake—are equally offenses.

Except for acting as an intermediary for the Three Jewels when trading clothing, one does not commit an offense; this is the first instance where a prohibition is relaxed. Trading for oneself to obtain clothing is permitted.

Exchanging butter and oil is allowed. Regarding the forfeiture of robes and treasures, there is a difference between the monastic and the lay. Furthermore, returning the original capital is distinct from returning what was not the original capital.
Next, regarding the five specific points concerning the exchange of robes: first, the person; second, the action; third, the allowance; fourth, the relinquishment; and fifth, the restoration.
These collectively encompass the beginning and end of the two precepts; they have already been examined below in their respective contexts, so they will not be cited again here.

First, the statement that "robes received as gifts belong only to the laity" refers to the two groups of householders. Fifth, regarding "that which was originally not [a robe] becomes [one]," this means that when a robe is exchanged, it must be returned.

Because trading one's own robes for jewels and exchanging them with laypeople for pure items constitutes a non-original offense, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established to distinguish between the two precepts:
(1) exchanging robes for jewels; (2) exchanging jewels for robes; (3) exchanging jewels for jewels; and (4) exchanging robes for robes.
In cases (1) and (3), one commits this [first] precept; in cases (2) and (4), one commits the subsequent precept. This principle applies accordingly, depending solely on the object being traded.
The two categories of precepts do not distinguish between "possessing" and "trading. [Commentary]:
Furthermore, regarding the fourfold classification of "possessing jewels," the first category is "possessing but not trading," which refers to secular gifts of money or precious objects;
the second is "trading but not possessing," which refers to exchanging clothing for money or precious objects; the third is "both," which refers to buying gold with money and keeping it.
The fourth case, "neither," refers to the mutual exchange of clothing and goods.

Next, regarding the four propositions concerning the possession of precious objects: the first proposition constitutes an offense of the former [category]; the second constitutes an offense of the latter; the third constitutes both offenses;
and the fourth, when dealing with a layperson, constitutes an offense of trading for clothing.

[Commentary: Former scholars did not establish [the offenses] because they held that there were no two acts of relinquishing property and no double connection of offenses regarding the recitation; having heard these words, we dare not let them be lost.

However, our current view is not the same. Suppose one buys gold with money and then keeps it: the initial act of trading and the subsequent act of keeping have different causal characteristics (*nimitta*).
Why, then, should the offenses not be doubly connected?

In the first section of the "Refutation of the Ancients," the ancient view is presented: they claim that the third [offense] constitutes only the violation of trading for precious objects, but does not violate the preceding rules regarding hoarding or reciting.

The subsequent passage—"the property of the robe has no dual forfeiture," and so forth—refutes this by stating that one commits an offense regarding the robe-property, yet there is no further commission of the offense of "excess" (*atireka*).
This [ancient view] merely accepts the words and cites them erroneously, failing to realize that their application is distinct; therefore, it says, "one may recite [the rule]."
Regarding the statement "the discourse below now reveals the correct principle," the previous judgment merely cited a single instance of relinquishment;
however, when the conditions for repenting two offenses differ—meaning the causal conditions for violating the two precepts are distinct in their sequence—one must incur separate offenses.

[Commentary]: If that is so, then the sale of clothing and wealth should also be subject to the rite of *śuddhi* (purification). Answer: This is entirely different. The rite of purification (*śuddhi-dharma*) serves to delimit the object [of the offense], whereas the transgression does not depend upon the object.

Since both [the offense and the purification] are established as a dual bond within the resolution of this difficulty, there is the possibility that wealth acquired through a transgression may constitute an offense of "excess" (*atireka*); therefore, it must be purified.
The meaning of purity is as explained above. Regarding the ancient interpretation that establishes a response by clearly distinguishing [the cases] to refute the objections raised:

[The Commentary] states that this precept, taken at first glance, constitutes an offense immediately; it differs from selling goods, for one must relinquish them to a layperson, whereas they cannot be given to a śrāmaṇera, because even the latter must relinquish precious objects as well.

Among the three citations from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, this briefly demonstrates two distinctions regarding the subsequent rules on trading robes. First, it distinguishes them based on the nature of the offense:
this precept constitutes an offense at the very moment of receiving [the robe], whereas the subsequent precept on selling constitutes an offense only when one actually sells it;

thus, the timing of the offense differs. Second, it clarifies the distinction regarding the forfeiture of property: trading robes is not permitted among the laity, while trading jewels is not permitted among the monastics; therefore, the latter applies to the lower assembly (monastics).
Nor does one give it away.

[Commentary] The offense is established through five conditions: first, the object is money or treasure; second, there is mutual bartering; third, the price is settled; fourth, it is for one's own sake;
and fifth, it is accepted. These constitute the offense.
[Note] When the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, Upāli’s brother, Upananda, went to a marketplace and exchanged money for money.
A lay devotee criticized him, saying, "He is quite skilled at buying and selling. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept.

[Commentary]: Regarding the conditions for the precept, as for the exchange of money for money, this is based on the origin of the rule (*nidāna*). In this world, the use of counterfeit currency is not permitted;
yet, there were bhikṣus who exchanged high-quality coins for it with the intention of using them later. Thus, it was precisely such a person who fell into this transgression.

In the initial commentary on the conditions for the precepts, the text cites and explains the passage from the *Analects* expressing lamentation: "When Bo Niu was ill, the Master went to inquire after him.
Looking through the window, he took his hand and said, 'Alas! It is fate that has taken him. Such a man as this, and yet to suffer such an illness!
(The meaning is that a virtuous person should not be subject to such a malignant disease. Now, I borrow those words here, though the intended meaning is different."
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling.
[Commentary] This refers to gold that has been refined, gold that has not been refined, and both gold and silver that have been refined and those that have not;

furthermore, there are three types of coins, one type of exchange-coin, eight types of metal coins—namely gold, silver, copper, iron, white tin, lead, and pewter—and wooden coins, as well as foreign coins.
"Glue" refers to the eight kinds of currency.
[Rule: *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. [Commentary: For bhikṣuṇīs, this constitutes a common offense under the rules concerning forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*).
The provisions for relinquishing the object, as well as the allowances regarding the seeking of precious items and the methods of acquisition, are all the same as in the preceding precepts.

Regarding the offender: if one uses money or precious gems to trade for necklaces or ornaments, or exchanges money for money for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, this constitutes an offense.
[Commentary] The precept text consists of four phrases.
[Commentary] One person.
[Commentary: Regarding the second point, "various kinds," this refers to the actual nature of the offense: the mutual exchange of money, precious objects, or the seven types of currency.
The second phrase of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* indicates this briefly, as shown below in the notes.
[Commentary: The Prātimokṣa-sūtra merely mentions "various [precious objects]" without being explicit; if one does not provide an annotation, it would be impossible to know what these things are.
Therefore, regarding their characteristics, there are three *kārsāpaṇas* each for gold and silver, constituting a single category.
In the general introduction of the commentary, the first part explains the intent of the notes and proceeds to list the characteristics.

[The Commentary] states: As it was said in the past, "that which has not yet become gold" refers to ore mixed with stone. How could there be a mere lump of stone that clearly exhibits the characteristics of gold?
This is as explained in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā*, where the phrasing is transformed to mean "to act as. As for the term "accomplished" (*cheng*), it means already...
The "vessel" refers to ornaments such as flower-shaped hairpins; these are the completed forms. The "uncompleted" refers to the gold ingots themselves.
The "both completed and uncompleted" refers to those melted and cast into vessels but not yet refined into ingots. The same applies to silver.

Regarding these three types of coins, although according to principle there are only three kinds, because they have not yet been fashioned into inscribed images and are not in common use in the world, they are not considered precious objects.
Taken together, these form forty-nine phrases. Within the detailed explanation, there are two parts;
the first explains the three characteristics, which further divides into three sections. First, regarding "gold," it initially refutes the errors of past scholars.
Their delusion lies in identifying the character for "gold" as referring to gold ore that has not yet been smelted; therefore, he cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Sāmagrī-vinaya* as evidence.
Regarding the phrase "having already become gold": this is distinct from the current text concerning "unmade gold," which is why it is said that "it transforms and becomes made.

Since it is stated to be "unmade," it clearly refers to something that has not yet been fashioned into a vessel, rather than being stone or ore. Regarding the word "next" (*xià*), it indicates the correct explanation:
"ingot" (*tǐng*) refers to hammering and beating, while "smelting" (*yě*) refers to polishing and rubbing. The second explanation regarding the three types of silver is the same.
Above, the third section explains that money is exclusively already accomplished; thus, there is only one [category], as can be understood from the text.

Below, the subsequent section demonstrates the number of permutations: taking any one of the seven aforementioned types as the head—for instance, "exchanging already accomplished gold for already accomplished gold," and so on up to money—constitutes seven permutations. Furthermore, taking unaccomplished gold as the head...
It is the same when one uses "money" as the head of a phrase; thus, there are seven sets of seven phrases. In the commentary, "Hu-glue" refers to a substance similar to wax in this region.
[Commentary]: The remaining two phrases can be understood.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "opening for trading" below: if one takes hold of an object for the purpose of trading it for the sake of the Buddha or the Saṅgha, this does not constitute an offense against this precept.

The remaining two phrases explain the text within the commentary concerning the phrase "opening for non-offense. This is because taking hold of something with the intent that it not be for one's own use constitutes an opening (an exception).
However, at the actual time of trading, if one takes hold of it, it is not a non-offense; fearing that others might mistakenly assume this is a general opening, the text specifically points this out.

[Vinaya] The twentieth precept concerning buying and selling.
[Commentary] The twentieth precept concerns buying and selling.
According to this precept, one must distinguish three stages: namely, buying for the sake of profit, selling for the sake of profit, and bargaining.
To raise the price for the sake of profit is called "selling. To take [an item] for the sake of profit by reducing the previous price is called "buying."

To increase one's profit by raising the price through forceful means is called "selling. While the *Śīla-sūtra* (Precept Text) clarifies only the matters of increasing prices, decreasing them, and bartering, other Vinaya texts extensively detail the characteristics of buying and selling, as is analyzed at length in the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Commentary).

Regarding the twenty stages, the first stage of the beginning is shown generally as follows; the subsequent detailed explanations concern buying and selling, which both involve the exporting of goods, yet they are distinguished as two different categories based on whether one has previously received [the goods] or not. In the lower section of the precept, the extensive explanation merely clarifies matters such as increasing or decreasing [the price], as noted in the commentary;
it lists only the characteristics of selling and buying without mentioning receiving or trading. When the *Vinaya* speaks of "exporting," it refers to many instances.
The *Śāstra* states: "Among all offenses involving trade, this is the most grave. It would be better to be a butcher who harms only one life than to engage in trade that harms all beings.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "When storing medicinal herbs, one should form the thought: 'These shall become expensive later.
If one sells them subsequently, one commits an offense requiring forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). The text of the *Yīchāo* (Commentary) on this is very extensive and cannot be recorded in full.
[Commentary] Why was this established? Generally, those who have left the household life ought, as a matter of principle, to cease worldly affairs and sit in stillness to cultivate the Way.

How could one personally engage in trade, frequenting marketplaces and violating the majestic deportment, thereby inviting the ridicule and loathing of the world? Furthermore, once money and goods are exchanged, there is the possibility of committing a grave offense;
this is truly to be feared. For these reasons, it was necessary to establish this rule early on. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four meanings: first, for the sake of the Buddha...
First, because the Dharma is supreme; second, for the sake of ceasing strife and contention; third, for the sake of accomplishing the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*);
and fourth, for the sake of increasing faith and reverence so as not to slander [the teaching].

Regarding the first of these, the intention [behind the prohibitions], there are two aspects explained according to their meaning: first, regarding intentions that deviate from the Path, and second, regarding intentions that involve theft.
The first two lines of the citation present four meanings found within the treatise: first, maintaining and sustaining; second, eliminating evil; third, generating goodness;

and fourth, encompassing both. [Commentary]: There are six conditions that constitute an offense: first, being a layperson; second, a member of the assembly; third, exchanging goods; fourth, determining the price; fifth, acting for one's own sake; [and sixth...]
Regarding the six offenses involving bartering for the six types of food:
among the conditions for these offenses, it is sufficient to simply reverse the aforementioned six cases, as they constitute a deficiency in the necessary conditions;
thus, there is no need to elaborate further. [Note: When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Upananda went to a village without a permanent residence and exchanged ginger for food.

After he had finished eating, he took the food and departed. Śāriputra arrived later to beg for alms; when the donor questioned him regarding the matter of Upananda, he was so ashamed that he remained silent.

Furthermore, [Upananda] gambled with a non-Buddhist for a robe and regretted it, yet he could not get it back. When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently established a precept.

[Commentary] Within the section on the origin of the precept (*śīla-nidāna*), there are two parts. First, the occasion of the transgression arising from food and clothing; second, the subsequent censure and prohibition following the raising of the transgression. The first part is further divided into two:
first, up to the point where [the monks] remained silent out of shame, which clarifies the occasion of Baddhananda exchanging ginger for food;

second, his interaction with the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which clarifies the occasion of this person’s transgression of trading for robes. Within the former, it is due to Baddhananda’s exchange...
Regarding the practice of the *piṇḍapātika* (alms-gathering) bhikṣus, it was said that because their conduct had become lax and excessive, they were no longer considered true seekers of alms;
thus, when Śāriputra later went for alms, he was questioned about his previous behavior, which left the Venerable One speechless.
In the first portion of the text concerning the conditions for the precepts, the commentary first clarifies the condition regarding the exchange of food.

"A village without a dwelling place" means there is no monastery (*ārāma*). "Having eaten and taking it away" refers to taking the remaining food away. "Vulgar and excessive" (*vaipulya*); "vulgar" (*vaipulya*) here means mixed or impure.
When the time comes to beg for food, living purely is the duty of a bhikṣu; he [the donor] exchanges goods [for food].

To prevent the confusion and corruption of the Dharma, he used past events as a precedent to demand that goods be exchanged. Next, the *Vinaya* clarifies the circumstances regarding the exchange of robes:

A non-Buddhist practitioner brought a fine robe into Jetavana and sought to trade it for one belonging to Bāḍhananda. Bāḍhananda repaired his old robe so that it appeared as new and bartered it with him.
The non-Buddhist soon regretted the deal; however, Bāḍhananda refused to return it, whereupon the non-Buddhist reviled him and departed.

[Commentary] By means of *kālābhiṣeka* (medicines for the proper time) he exchanges for *kālābhiṣeka*, *akālābhiṣeka* (medicines for improper times), *saptāhika* (seven-day medicines), *yāvajjīvika* (lifelong medicines), or *pārikkāra* (miscellaneous items);
thus exchanging one for another, even up to exchanging robes for robes.

[Sūtra] Selling. [Commentary] This refers to repeatedly increasing or decreasing the price; for example, stating that an item worth one *kārsāpaṇa* is worth three *kārsāpaṇas*, or further increasing it by stating it is worth five *kārsāpaṇas*. The same offense applies to the buyer as well.

[Commentary] Regarding whether a bhikṣuṇī commits the offense or not when others do so: it is permitted for members of the fivefold assembly of renunciants to exchange [goods] among themselves.

They should examine the matter thoroughly and ensure there is no disparity in value, avoiding the methods of the marketplace. One must not trade with outsiders; rather, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") perform the exchange.
If one regrets having listened [to the teaching] and returns it, or exchanges it for ghee or oil, there is no offense.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "two kinds," the text does not explicitly clarify it. This distinction from the preceding precepts is not apparent in the wording and requires annotation to reveal that there are two separate precepts;
this was an error of the early translators. Even if these were the Buddha’s original words, they would certainly not have been compiled and transmitted in such a manner.
Rather, because the Buddha spoke so that people might easily understand, clarity is essential. Therefore, [the distinctions] are now mostly listed.
The various [aspects] are profound and difficult to comprehend.

In the second section, the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the initial passage clarifies that the translation of the text is confused and disordered; this "initial" refers to the fact that the original translation was not detailed.
Even if one were to push back to the source, it would not be so, for two reasons: first, because the Buddha’s words are clear and manifest; second...
Thus, because the compilation was conducted according to the circumstances, there could never have been any confusion or admixture; the citation below serves as proof.

For instance, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that when a bhikṣu preached the Dharma, the Buddha permitted him to cite essential phrases and elegant expressions to directly reveal their meaning. Therefore, we know that [the Buddha’s intention] was solely to make it easy for people to understand.
Since the current version is, on the contrary, difficult to understand, it is said that "it is profound and difficult to comprehend," and so forth.
[Commentary]: That which is listed in the commentary refers only to the specific circumstances of exchanging robes for medicine. If one purchases a robe with money, it falls under this precept;
conversely, the opposite case belongs to the preceding precept.

What was previously referred to as "merely concerning that which is traded" is here clearly demonstrated.
[Commentary] Regarding the term "selling," its characteristics have already been systematically explained above, as extensively cited in the *Chao*.

Next, in explaining the section on "selling" within the text, what was previously termed "systematic exposition" refers to the three divisions mentioned earlier; for the remainder, refer to the *Chao* in the section on "following the characteristics."
[Commentary]: In the introductory general explanation of the characteristics, it says, "The number of coins varies by one up or down," which refers merely to the different ways of selling.
"Selling at an increase" means originally asking a high price for what is cheap; "buying likewise" means buying cheaply what was originally expensive.
"Originally worth five coins, but reducing the purchase price to say it is worth three coins"—this refers to a heavy reduction in the purchase price where the original value was five coins.
"Qian" (錢) refers to a value of one *qian*.

In the commentary (*shìzhù*), the initial explanation of "one *qian*" states that it generally clarifies the characteristics (*xiàng*) because it encompasses the three subsequent positions. Next, regarding the numerical sequence, the commentary first explains the three positions;
within the explanation of "selling" (*fàn*), the terms "upper" and "lower" refer to increases or decreases according to the fluctuations of market prices at any given time.
Whether it concerns the price or the exchange and valuation between people, these refer precisely to the act of trade;
because their characteristics differ from those [of other acts], they are called "distinct. The sequence of selling first and buying later makes the manifestation of their characteristics very clear.

[Commentary] The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If there is no pure attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) who consents to this sale of goods, one should instead make them into bedding for the Saṅgha of the four directions.

Regarding those who have no formal grounds for suspension—such as one who has obtained a bowl, one suspended for five days, one who is insane or mentally deranged—it is said that although many days may pass, there is no offense;
once they recover, they may resume [the period], and if it is completed within the subsequent five days, they do not commit an offense. However, if ten days elapse, they do commit an offense.
It is further stated: "If one purchases another's bowl and the price has not yet been repaid, the acceptance is not valid. Even if the owner says, 'Just accept it,' although these words exist..."

Furthermore, it does not constitute an offense if the days have not exceeded [the limit] nor if the duration is not long; however, if the price has been paid and one informs a bhikṣu of the fumigation [of the bowl], yet the bhikṣu does not accept it and the days exceed [the limit], one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*).
If others know and inform someone who is not the owner of the bowl, there is no offense. Regarding the *Saṃghāṭī* bowl, one should perform the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*) with a friend;
if within ten days one discards the old and receives a new one, one may exchange them once every ten days.

The second condition for the offense is that it must be "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*); this excludes those who obtain it by means of trade or robbery, as there would otherwise be no fault regarding its surplus.

Third, as for its substance: it should be like a wooden bowl of the middle quality; it must not be like the precious bowls of non-Buddhists, the stone bowls of worldly people, or bowls that imitate the Tathāgata’s, as these are all contrary to the Dharma.

Regarding its color: it should be like the "oil-character" (*tailākṣara*) mentioned in the middle [text], which is pronounced with the final vowel elided; this refers to having coated the bowl with oil from *tóng* (Cinnamomum camphora) or *rèn* (sesame) and then burning it.

"Combined and fashioned into a *jiaon* (a polished vessel) means to rub and polish it until it reflects light. Regarding its measurement, various schools state that the dimensions are not uniform and lack fixed boundaries;

Among the five types of exclusion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), "expulsion" (*pīn*) refers to those whose minds are deranged or insane, thereby creating a legal separation from the community.

because it has not yet been assigned to oneself, even if one says it is not extra, it is an offense. The second is based on the robe already being returned;

when the owner reports it, it is an offense, whereas reporting it otherwise is not an offense, as the actual facts have not been verified. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, "near a friend" means...

The present citation of this text merely takes the point that the period must not exceed ten days.
[Commentary] The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* asks: "Regarding a white bowl that exceeds the limit, is it an offense? Regarding a white bowl that does not exceed the limit, is it an offense? The answer is:

Since dyeing robes necessarily results in a discolored (badha-varṇa) appearance, the principle of storage (*parigraha*) prevails; thus, even if a bowl is over-burnt and its color is ruined, its possession is not an offense. Question:

If a robe exceeds or falls short of the prescribed dimensions, it still constitutes formal acceptance (*parigraha*). Why is it the opposite for a bowl? The treatise answers: A robe can be cut or joined together, and therefore it constitutes formal acceptance [even when out of size]. A bowl cannot be altered in this way; thus, the case differs.
The almsbowl lacks these [two] meanings; it is established as a measure and established as something to be maintained.

Next, regarding the detailed analysis, in the initial question-and-answer section of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, it states that while dyeing a robe necessarily results in its being colored, fumigating a bowl does not necessarily result in its being [considered] "perfumed.

In the subsequent question-and-answer section, it says that if a robe has a defect, it may be cut out, and if it is diminished, it may be supplemented; however, this is not the case for a bowl, and therefore it is established [as such].
[This constitutes] no separate offense.

[Note: While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks kept alms bowls; they discarded those that were inferior and constantly sought out fine ones to keep, until their collection became numerous.
When a lay devotee went to visit them, he ridiculed them, saying they were no different from a potter’s kiln. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who then [prohibited it].
He rebuked [the offender] and established this precept.
[Commentary: Within the context of the causal conditions for the precept, the mention of the potter serves as the basis for the fault of derision.
In the causal conditions for the precept, the words of derision are merely explained; in the preceding note, it says that "bad" refers to setting aside those which are not well-made bowls.
Cast aside and unused, the potter borrows the sound [of the character] to form "Yáo" (姚), serving as a model for the earthenware worker.
[Precept]: If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl. [Commentary]:
There are six kinds: iron bowls, black bowls, red bowls, bowls from the country of Suma, bowls from the country of Uggara, and bowls from the country of Ouyue.

Regarding the *pātra* (alms bowl) of the country of Kāśi, there are two main types: the iron *pātra* and the clay *pātra*. The large [clay] *pātra* is three *dōng* (升), and the small is one and a half *dōng*.
These are the measurements for a *pātra*; it should be maintained and purified in this manner. It should be offered as a gift of purification (*pariṣkāra-dakṣiṇā*).

There are three types of distinctions regarding "extra" items (*atireka*) that clarify the regulation for the *atireka-pātra*. Specifically, one bowl is permitted for formal possession, while any beyond that is considered extra;
since this is not a matter of confusion, the original regulation is not explicitly stated.
In the second question of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, because the regulations for robes and bowls—both when they are extra and when they are permitted—are combined, various questions are raised.

the latter need not be discussed as it is merely a confusion regarding delusion.

[Commentary] Question: Furthermore, why does he open up the discussion on the *kaṭhina* robe and bowl, yet not mention the wearing of them? Answer: Because internal and external requisites for sustaining the body are distinct.
Because excess and benefit do not coincide, this precept does not include the *kāṣāya* (robe) as a separate category.
The intent of the subsequent question is also the same as before. Regarding the distinction between internal and external requisites in the response:

although both robes and bowls are external requisites, because the bowl contains food, they are treated as internal by association. "Excess does not coincide" means that surplus [robes] do not become subject to defilement [of the precept].
"If they do not mutually reach one another, then the *kāṣāya* will not be moistened.

[Commentary: If this is so, why does he not accept the *kāṣāya-paṭa* (the robe with three sections)? Because it is heavy to carry, the *guṇa-cīvara* (extra robe) is permitted for use while separated from one's regular robes.
Since the bowl (*pātra*) is singular and must always be used, how could he keep the *kāṣāya-paṭa* as a reserve?
Regarding the matter of the bowl, it is not permissible.

Among the various difficulties, the underlying intention is that since the benefit is not attained, it is only logical that each should receive [the bowl] individually. In the response, because of the gravity of the matter, an exception is granted;
this refers to the original circumstance. A single bowl is not considered heavy, and since there is no principle for separating from it, it cannot be compared [to the case of multiple bowls].
[Commentary] Question: For what reason is the month of Kārttika not opened? Answer: If the bowl has not yet been completed, there is no fault of excess;
if it has already been completed, one may open the limit for the declaration of purity (śuddhi)—why then would a full month be required?

Question three: "If the opening [of the period] for robes is like that of the *kaṭhina* bowl, it should also be so. Answer: "In the response, the limit for opening is stated as 'purification' (*śuddhi*), which refers to ten days.
[Commentary]: "If that is so, since the opening for robes is also ten days—just like the bowl—why is there a one-month period? Answer: "The robe has a fixed seasonal limit."

As the four seasons cycle and we have already entered autumn and winter, it is necessary to repair and wash the bowl; since there is no fixed time for this, what need is there to compare it with anything else?
It is difficult to provide a further explanation or resolution that would be easily understood.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the bowl, the mention of "six types" refers to the black and red colors according to the various countries and regions. This is the text.
What benefit is there in omitting the names of the countries? As for the *Sāndhīrgha-śāstra* (Three-Bushel Vinaya), it was translated during the Yao Qin dynasty;
its usage follows that of the country [of origin] extensively, as explained in the section on "Dwellings."

As for the two bowls—black and red—their country of origin is not specified, hence it is said that "the text is abbreviated. Next, regarding the measurement of the bowl, it is stated that the finger-width is according to the *fáng* (cubit) measure of the precepts;
this refers to the fact that during the Yao Qin period, the *dǒu* (bushel) measure of the Jī Zhou was used.

[Commentary: Now, if a bowl has fewer than five patches and does not leak, it is fit to support the body and sustain the path; thus, one should cease seeking further.

However, to now go about everywhere seeking extra bowls from those who are not relatives—driven by greed, obstructing the path, and troubling the donors—is unreasonable. For this reason, the rule was established.
In the twenty-second section on the regulation of intention (*cetana*), the first part shows what is appropriate; now, below, the state of transgression is set forth. [Commentary:

There are six conditions for committing this offense: (1) one has previously received and maintained an alms-bowl; (2) it has fewer than five patches and does not leak; (3) one subsequently begs from someone who is not a relative; (4) it is for one's own sake;
(5) one begs for a bowl that is in accordance with the Dharma; and (6) one accepts it. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if two people [are involved], there is an offense.
Because begging together for a single *pātra-gilā* measure is not in accordance with the Dharma, this is the fifth condition for an offense.
One must act according to the Dharma; having fulfilled the three aforementioned [conditions], the fifth is specifically illustrated below by citing the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
[Note] When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the householder Baṇanda possessed many alms bowls. Only after calculating his total did he realize he had received too many;
he then spoke with reproach, saying that monks never tire of receiving and taking. A monk reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently censured him and established the precept.
[Commentary]: Within the context of the conditions for the precepts, it is because one violates a single [precept] by begging for many things that one incurs censure and defamation.
This excerpt from the conditions for the precepts is intended to reveal the cause of such censure and defamation, so that one may recognize the fault and admonish oneself.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu possesses an almsbowl that has fewer than five patches (with each patch being one finger-width apart) and it is not leaking,

yet he seeks a new bowl for the sake of its beauty (if it has five or more patches and is not leaking, and he still seeks a new one, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense), this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
[Note] Regarding "renunciation" (*pratyākhyāna*) herein: having renounced the bowl before the Saṃgha at this dwelling place, one undergoes confession through a single formal motion (*jñapti*).
One then declares the name of the offense, its category, and its characteristics, generating a sense of revulsion and detachment. If the bowl is of good quality, it should be confiscated and kept;

taking the lowest and most inferior one, it is given [to the offender]. Then, performing a single formal motion, the bowls are exchanged sequentially with the elders, starting from the top seat, and the [newly acquired] bowl is held aloft.
The bowl of the presiding monk shall be given to the next-ranking monk; in this manner it is passed on successively until it reaches the lowest-ranking monk.
[Vinaya] This constitutes a *pāyattika* offense (the same applies to bhikṣuṇīs). That bhikṣu must go before the Saṃgha and relinquish the bowl that was received through succession;
he shall give the very last bowl to him and have him hold it until it breaks. He must hold it at that time.
[Note] The Saṃgha shall place the bowl before him with a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) and entrust it to him for his protection.
He must not place it where tiles or stones might fall, nor beneath a leaning staff, a sword, a hanging object, on a path, on top of a stone, under a fruit tree, or on uneven ground.
He must not place it inside a door or window, beneath a door-panel, on a threshold, or on a corner; except for temporary placement, he must not place it between two beds.

If, while standing, one causes the bowl to fall and break it down to its base, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense because it was done improperly, with the intent to damage it, or resulting in the loss of its function as a bowl.
There is no offense if it leaks after five patches have been applied; or if it leaks slightly and one seeks a new one; or if one asks a relative for one; or if one asks a renunciant for one;
or if one obtains it for another’s sake or for one’s own sake without having asked for it; or if one obtains it as part of a gift.
If one purchases an animal with its own price, there is no offense in any case.
[Commentary] The precept text consists of six phrases.
[Commentary] One person.
