[Commentary]: Regarding the two original alms-bowls that have not yet reached five patches, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one begs for another bowl like the aforementioned when the original has none up to four patches, it is also a *pāyattika*.
If one begs for a bowl with five patches, it is a *duṣkṛta*. According to the annotation, a patch is measured by the distance between two fingers;
based on this standard, even if the bowl has not been patched, if its size exceeds the limit, it is still not considered a violation.
In the second section of the *Prātimokṣa*, regarding the rule on "further requesting" as described above:

from having no patches up to having four patches—this refers to cases where the original [robe] exists and one subsequently seeks more, yet the total does not reach five; in such cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If one requests a fifth patch when the original is incomplete, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because the subsequent seeking completes what was originally incomplete. However, if the original already has five patches, there is no fault. Next, the commentary is explained.

If one measures using the Buddha’s fingers, two finger-widths (aṅgula) equal two inches, so five finger-widths equal eight inches; five [finger-widths] multiplied by ten [inches per span] equals two chi.
If one takes human fingers as the standard—where the width of one finger-face is one inch—then five finger-widths would only amount to five inches.

Although this is not explicitly stated in the text, the preceding and following sections frequently employ the Tathāgata’s extended fingers as a standard for measurement. Therefore, the mention here of "five finger-widths" should simply be understood in that sense.
The seams and markings measure approximately two chi; it is not strictly necessary to sew them together, which is why it says, "measure according to this," and so forth.
[Commentary] To seek new ones for a third time constitutes a violation of the Dharma.
[Commentary]: Regarding the fourth rule, "Renouncing through Restriction," the sub-commentary explains:

"Among the monks at this residence" means that because there are no many fine bowls [belonging to the individual], they are confiscated and kept in the monastery storehouse for the benefit of the original temple; thus it says "this residence."
In the fourth dwelling place, for the benefit of the original monastery, [the rule was established] because many people sought to damage it.

[Commentary: Question: Since begging for robes also causes much distress and likewise damages the monastery, why is this not the same as the case of the alms bowl? Answer: Because the utility of robes is broad, they must be returned to their owners and cannot be seized and entered into the communal property of the Saṃgha.
As for the alms bowl, there is no great need for many; obtaining one is sufficient. Any remainder beyond that is seized and entered into the communal property of the Saṃgha.

Question: Since begging for robes is not penalized and they are placed in the storehouse, why is this asked? Answer: Because robes are used for spaciousness, being changed according to the season, and thus are not limited to a single set.

[Commentary]: If that is so, what is the use of extra bowls? Why are they not entered into the communal storehouse? Answer: They may be obtained through personal trade, or given as offerings from those with sincere hearts.
Since there is no external affliction, it is not the same as begging.
In the midst of the "difficult-to-turn" [circumstance], since there is no great need, the previous rule regarding the long bowl does not apply to returning it to its owner.

In the response, the division of the long bowl—whether one begs for it or not—belongs to the preceding violation of the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (purification); therefore, it is returned to the owner. If one were to beg for it again, it would belong to the subsequent affliction.

If a donor commits an offense, he is fined and the amount is added to the Sangha; furthermore, because it does not diminish the Sangha, [the donor] requests that what would cause a loss [be returned].

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if a bowl is large and expensive, it should be sold; nine-tenths of the proceeds go into the Sangha’s kitchen, while one-tenth is returned to the owner.
Even if the price for the bowl is requested and added to the Sangha, one may directly purchase a bowl to return it to this bhikṣu.
In the introductory section, the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] initially states that when begging for a bowl, if one says it is "very expensive," this implies it has a specific value.
Because a single expensive bowl cannot be divided into two parts, one is instructed to exchange it for something of lesser value and return it to the owner.
When it is said, "ten bowls," this is merely mentioned as an illustration; next, it clarifies begging for the value to purchase a bowl, where the value returned is money or precious objects.

Because it cannot be returned, one follows this principle and does not perform the sequential method of exchange; rather, it is directly reconciled through harmony, as in the *Caturvargika-vinaya* below.

[Commentary: Regarding this abandonment and confession, it differs from other cases. First, it clarifies the single-announcement (*jñapti*) for receiving the confession of the primary offense. Second...

First, it is explained that the lowest-ranking person is given [the bowl] via a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation). Second, it is explained that [the bowls] are exchanged sequentially using a *jñapti-ekavācika-karman* (a formal motion followed by a single proclamation). Third, it is explained that [the bowls] are exchanged using a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
Fourth, it is explained that this lowest-ranking bowl is made to be held [by the recipient]; thus, there are four methods in total.
In the second part, the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*), first is the announcement for receiving the confession: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu so-and-so’s bowl was broken;
having fewer than five patches and not leaking, he sought a new bowl and thereby committed an offense of relinquishment (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me permission to receive the confession of this bhikṣu so-and-so. Having made this announcement in this manner, one next returns the bowl.

The initial motion (*jñapti*) of the *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one proclamation) is largely the same as above; however, after "the Sangha, please listen," it is changed to "grant this bowl to this bhikṣu.
The formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is performed according to the motion, with the following differences: in the second phrase, both the occasion (*nidāna*) and the basis (*mūla*) are recited;

in the fourth phrase, the occasion is omitted and only the basis is recited. (This method also appears in the *Guangjie zhu*; no further opinions are listed here. The sequence of the three [proclamations] follows.

The motion is stated as follows: "Venerable Sangha, listen. If it is the proper time for the Sangha and the Sangha consents, let the Sangha ask the Elder [the *upādhyāya*] in turn regarding this bowl;
the motion is made thus. This is the first of the four motions for the formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). First, the motion is stated: "Venerable Sangha, listen.
If it is the proper time for the Sangha and the Sangha consents, let the Sangha now bestow this lowest bowl upon the bhikṣu so-and-so for him to receive."
The procedure for holding [the precepts] up to their forfeiture should be performed according to the *karmavācanā* (as this method is explained in the subsequent notes).
The meaning of the first two methods applies to all forfeitures, whereas the latter two methods pertain exclusively to this specific precept.
[Commentary]: That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha and take the very lowest [portion] to be held; this is the method of descending in order from the bottom.
This is for the purpose of subduing his greed, proceeding from the top down.

Regarding the fifth section, the initial analysis of the text: the first point indicates that the textual characteristics fully contain two methods; taking the "lowest" refers to the *jñapti* (single motion).

Next, "changing" refers to the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one subsequent proclamation), which establishes the requirement for holding [the precepts]. This is intended to demonstrate the meaning of the punishment below.

[Commentary]: Within this, the establishment of the rule follows the measure appropriate for the Saṃgha; one may either return it to the original owner through reconciliation or exchange it according to the sequence of the Vinaya.

These two intentions are to be applied according to the timing and the specific circumstances. In the first section of the following division, it clarifies that the establishment of the rule is not fixed; "returning it through reconciliation" refers to cases where the situation is pitiable and the value of the robe is equivalent.
Regarding "returning" or "successive exchange," this refers to what is appropriate for subduing [the offender] and the necessity of punishment according to the Dharma.

The Vinaya provides the method for returning and further demonstrates the method of punishment; thus, it is said that both intentions are present. If one merely returns through reconciliation, only the first two methods are employed.
If there is a successive exchange, then three methods are used. This excludes the formal motion and notification (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) found in the text of the precepts.
The reason why the commentary on the *Mingci* (Explanation of the Sequence) only presents three methods, whereas the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) lists them all, is that there are indeed four.
Regarding the basis for the measure [of the offense], one must observe whether the offender is observant or negligent in their precepts, and whether their greedy intentions are heavy or light.

[Commentary: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that after the person distributing the bowls has completed the formal act of appointment (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), he proclaims: "Venerable sirs, each of you should come and receive a bowl.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that there are five things for which one should not give [a bowl]: if it lacks a bowl, or if it is too large, too small, perforated and broken, or if it is crooked and tilted. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"When the bowl is filled with water and circulated among the assembly, once it has been taken, one must not regret the choice; he who regrets it..."

An offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Among the three types of persons who may go for alms with a bowl, one must possess five qualities, namely: being free from attachment up to knowing what may and may not be given.
Regarding the appointment by formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), it says: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu so-and-so possesses the five qualities..."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and listening, authorize such-and-such a bhikṣu to act as the *pātra-cāraka* (the distributor of bowls).
The motion (*jñapti*) is made thus; the formal act (*karman*) is performed according to the procedure. Once he has been authorized, he shall announce it according to the text cited.

Based on this, including the preceding requirements, five methods must be practiced: two *ekajñapti*, three *jñaptidvitīya*, and one *jñapticaturtha*. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if these five matters are not granted, it constitutes an offense against the Saṃgha.

When walking among the community, one should not exchange vessels with those that are non-Dharmic—meaning they are either too large or too small in measure, perforated, useless, or crooked (meaning tilted)—as prescribed in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

When carrying water to show that it is free of leaks while walking within the Saṃgha, one who possesses the five virtues should hold the bowl up to the place where the Elder (Sthavira) is seated and ask:
"Is this bowl required? If he says it is required, one should give it to him and take [the other].

When the bowl is passed to the next seat, it should be done according to the same procedure as for the senior monk (*sthavira*). If the senior monk regrets his decision and requests back his own bowl, the Buddha said:
"It should not be given; [if so,] one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense."

[Commentary]: In the commentary following the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion with one announcement), it says to have him guard the bowl [he has received] lest he become angry and break it.

It states that while the previously received bowl is to be maintained according to the Dharma, the subsequent bowl is not to be formally accepted; one constantly keeps two bowls. When eating, one should hold both bowls, and this continues for the rest of one's life.

This demonstrates the fault of excessive desire. Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions for severing unwholesome dharmas, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "Because of [the bowl being] patched..."
A bowl is difficult to wash; it may take an entire day to finish. However, it must be washed thoroughly. If one finds this laborious, a knowledgeable teacher or monk may say:

"This virtuous bhikṣu is obstructing his sitting meditation, recitation of sutras, and practice of the Path because of washing the bowl. In such a case, there is no fault in having someone else break open the storehouse and retrieve it for him.
In the commentary, the first part explains the intention behind the *saṃgha-karman*: "breaking through anger" refers to harboring resentment and thereby destroying [the harmony] of many;

next, it clarifies the characteristics of punishing those who uphold [the rules], showing the fault of excessive desire and exposing prior transgressions. "Severing evil dharmas" means cutting off future faults.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the third part clarifies the conditions for permitting or prohibiting [actions]: fundamentally, there is the *saṃgha-dharma*, which must be based on harmony.
The Sangha must also observe conditions and not rely on or misapply them.
[Commentary] The meaning of the various texts can be understood; however, as for the practice, there is much repentance and little [observance], such that it is rarely seen in the末代 (final age).

In the initial section of this brief demonstration, the sub-commentary points out that because the preceding instruction regarding the protection of the bowl was intended to restrain others, damage to it does not constitute a violation of the bowl rule.

"Using what is auspicious" means that when one has extra items for future use, doing so does not constitute a violation. This is because purchasing and storing them oneself is not obtained through begging;
this also serves to clarify the meaning of the abbreviated [text]. [Commentary:

These all pertain to the observance and maintenance of the precepts (*śīla*). Since these practices are the very foundation of conduct, they are here enumerated. One who understands this will be able to recognize the principle of relinquishment (*tyāga*).

I repent: even those who study the words today say that the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) is not within one's own capacity regarding which mental states sever delusions, and such instances are numerous.
How much more so in this case, where it is indeed within one's own capacity—how could one not know? That one does not know is due to a lack of study; if one does not study, there is fault.
How could this be like the severing of delusions at the first stage, which is not a formal precept yet one must nonetheless know? Therefore, I again offer this admonition.
In the first part of the exhortation, the mode of practice is shown; now, the following section uses the distant to illustrate the proximate. This further has two parts:

first, regarding the reproach for failing to fulfill one's obligations, it states that those who merely speak of learning lack actual practice. Even the severing of afflictions at the first stage is not something known by ordinary people, yet they still engage in empty disputes.
How much more so regarding the precepts received upon the body—the very foundation of the monastic life—which one cannot possibly be ignorant of due to a lack of study.

In the future, when one is reprimanded for violating a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) that is not a formal precept (*prajñapti*), there is an offense because it contradicts the transformative teaching (*vinaya-śāsana*), yet it is not a formal precept and thus constitutes a "forced" transgression.
This does not mean that such knowledge is forbidden at the level of ordinary beings;

rather, it is said because in the world many people are fond of grandiosity and treat the categories of minor precepts with negligence, focusing exclusively on the literal words while rarely seeking actual practice. Therefore, this is a comparative censure intended to make them understand their own limits.

This is because it enables one to ascend to the distant from the near and to know the manifest through the subtle; it is for the reason that precept and wisdom support one another, so that both speech and action may be in accord.
[Vinaya] 23.
The Precept Against Asking for Thread to Have a Non-Relative Weaver Weave It.
[Commentary] The twenty-third precept: regarding having a non-relative weave cloth.

Now, although one already possesses the three robes sufficient to sustain the body, to now personally beg for thread and rely upon it for weaving is an excessive indulgence that harms one's practice and utterly contradicts contentment.
Since this both troubles and afflicts others and invites slander, it is a most serious obstacle to the Path.
Therefore, the Noble One established the rule for many reasons, primarily three: first, to eliminate unwholesome dharmas;
second, to stop slander; and third, to fulfill the four noble lineages.

23. Regarding the initial section on "Controlling the Mind": First, seeking through the meaning [of the teaching], one finds that excessive greed is an affliction (*kleśa*), harming one's conduct is karma (*karman*), and these three turn one away from the Path.
Thus, to deviate from contentment is to harm oneself; to distress others and incur slander is to harm others.

Since both of these involve out-flowing karma (*āsrava-karman*), they are able to obstruct the Path. Next, citing a treatise to corroborate the text, three points are listed to prove what has been stated above.
[The Buddha] knew. [Commentary: The offense is established through four conditions: first, personally begging for thread; second, the weaver not being a relative; third, not providing payment;
and fourth, the completion of the weaving constitutes the offense.

[Commentary] Question: Why is it that there are rules prohibiting laypeople from weaving, yet no such rule exists for making nuns weave? Answer: Laypeople are subject to official authority and often rely on their influence to weave;

nuns do not possess this capacity, and therefore there is no provision for them to weave. Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one causes any of the five groups of monastics to weave, one merely commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Moreover, since nuns are prohibited from weaving themselves, the possibility of their being made to weave is rare; even if an offense were committed, it would not constitute a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Therefore, regarding the initial question in the section on the conditions for offenses and the dialogue, since the censure of the fault is the same, one must address whether it is governed by a common rule or a distinct rule.

In the response, there are two parts: first, concerning reliance on power, there is [the offense] for the laity but not for nuns; this is clearly evidenced by the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, and in principle, it does not exist [for nuns].
Regarding the doubt raised below, this is next discussed in terms of the rules of prohibition (*pratikṣepa-dharma*). [The text notes that] for nuns, worldly conventions are rare. [Commentary]:

If this is so, why should the rule regarding washing robes be established for the laity rather than for those in the Path (the monastic community)? Answer: The teaching permits nuns to wash robes, yet the Great Assembly (monks) takes pleasure in creating obstacles to the nuns' cultivation of the Path;
therefore, it is necessary to establish the rule for the laity. This is the reverse of the case for monastics, ensuring that if they wash robes, they do not commit an offense.
The cost of weaving robes and the excessive labor required for their production are grave matters; therefore, they are treated with gravity.
Regarding the second difficulty, since the precept concerning the washing of robes specifically restricts nuns, the response states that there are two types of nuns who wash:

first, those who take pleasure in it, and second, those who obstruct their own spiritual practice. As for laypeople, the opposite is true; they reverse the two meanings mentioned above and do not fall under the restrictions of the prohibitions.
The objection is raised: "If there is no fault in having [a robe] washed, why is there a prohibition against having it woven?
This is clarified by the text. [Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Bāḍhananda sewed a saṃghāṭī. He requested thread and, having received a great amount, had it woven for himself.
While he was watching the weaving, a layperson criticized and disparaged him. A bhikṣu reported this transgression, and the Buddha, having rebuked him, established this precept.

[Commentary: Regarding the conditions for the precept, first, begging for thread to make robes and then hiring weavers extensively to spin and weave is contrary to the decorum of one who has left the household life;
therefore, it constitutes a transgression. Originally, the Buddha ordained that bhikṣus should stop as soon as they obtained what was needed.

Now, by violating the holy teaching and greedily accumulating, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* stipulates that begging for thread to make robes when one already possesses clothing constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Is this not because the act of weaving and making robes hinders the Path?

Regarding the first section on the conditions for the precepts, the term *sū* (pronounced *su* with a retroflex *ṇe* in the commentary, meaning "to wind silk onto a shuttle"—the character *shí* [pronounced *fú*] refers to the weaver’s shuttle) is explained as follows:

the Buddha’s regulation that one should stop once one has obtained what is needed refers to the practice of few desires, contentment, and the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), in its later sections, cites the text to clarify the faults involved.
【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu himself solicits thread (wherever he solicits thread, it refers to the thread for the ten kinds of robes) and has a weaver who is not a relative weave a robe for him.
[Note] If both the weaver and the provider of the thread are relatives, there is no offense. If the provider of the thread is not a relative, it is a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅).
To watch the weaving, to weave for oneself, or to spin thread constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
[Niḥsargika-pāyattika]. [Commentary]: Regarding whether a bhikṣuṇī commits the same offense or not:

if both parties are relatives, or if she weaves for herself a bowl-bag, a leather sandal-bag, a needle-case, a woolen mat, a meditation belt, a waistband, a hood, a sleeve, a heat-retaining cloth, or a cloth for wrapping leather sandals, it is permissible.
[Commentary] Regarding the six phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* [Sūtra]: first, the person; second, requesting it oneself; third, the yarn; and the following three [phrases] are self-evident.

[Commentary] In the annotation, the relatives are permitted because it removes the conditions for injury and slander. As for permitting weaving, it is only for minor and slight transgressions, as they are not profound;
yet even so, they are not without the potential to obstruct the Path, for they do constitute injury.

In the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, first the relaxation of the rule regarding relatives is explained, followed by the relaxation regarding minor matters; according to the precedent of "obstructing the path," this should be classified as a *duṣkṛta* offense.
[The Vinaya] states:
The twenty-fourth precept concerning exhorting a weaver to increase the amount of thread.
[Commentary] The twenty-fourth: The precept against encouraging a weaver to add thread.
[Commentary] When a layperson provides thread and sends a weaver to make a robe for a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu accepts it with a sincere heart free from duplicity;

this manifests integrity within his inner mind and ensures he does not trouble others externally—this is the natural order of things. Yet now, he encourages the weaver to add thread and increase the labor.
The prohibition was established because destroying one's own property and damaging that of others is of no benefit to either party.
Twenty-fourth, regarding the intent of the rule: first, it was stated that being at odds with those appointed for a task constitutes a transgression;

now, next, it clarifies that one should not destroy one’s own [reputation], meaning that deviating from the conduct of a bhikṣu and harming others gives rise to the censure and loss of faith among laypeople.
Regarding the phrase "it is of no benefit to either party" because it serves neither self-interest nor the interest of others:

[The Commentary] states that there are six conditions for an offense: (1) not being a relative; (2) having the purpose of having someone weave cloth from yarn one has prepared oneself—although the origin story (*nidāna*) of the precept text does not explicitly mention this, the *Vinaya* opens the possibility that there is no offense if it is a relative;

(3) having a fixed limit in one's original intention; (4) knowing that there is a fixed limit; (5) encouraging [the weaver] to improve the quality or increase the price; and (6) acting for the sake of...
Regarding the six offenses involving the addition of threads and the acceptance [of robes],
the first set of conditions for the offense follows the provisions below to resolve the *Śīlaskandha* (Precept Text): the first and second belong to the donor,
the fifth belongs to the weaver, and the remainder all pertain to the bhikṣu.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if one relies on the power of a previous precept to have a robe woven and it is completed, one immediately commits this offense; however, if one personally seeks and receives it, the offense is established at that point.

In the subsequent comparative analysis, the former case involves one's own property, so the offense is determined by the completion of the weaving; the latter case arises from what is bestowed by another, so it requires personal receipt.

[The offense of] receiving [the robe]. [Commentary]: Question: What is the difference between this precept regarding the damaging of thread and the previous two cases involving laypeople? Answer: In the former cases, one confronted the owner of the thread;
here, one secretly exhorts the weaver. Therefore, there are two distinct regulations.
The initial question—asking why two laypeople are also mentioned as being exhorted to increase [the offering]—requires an explanation of their distinction, which can be understood from the response.
[Commentary: Question: Since both the preceding and subsequent precepts involve a weaver, why are the distinctions drawn in the responses? Answer: There are four reasons.

First, in the former case, the damage to the weaver results in the acquisition of thread by the owner; in this case, the damage to the weaver does not result in the payment of wages. (The other three points follow this pattern.)

If one commits this offense of damaging the threads, and the owner provides the price, one incurs three of the preceding precepts; the subsequent precept regarding relatives is opened [as an exception], yet both offenses share the common meaning of "damaging.
In the fourth case, if it is one's own property that has been woven, one incurs the offense immediately; however, if it originally belonged to another, one incurs the offense only upon accepting it.
Next, the question regarding the different conditions for the two precepts can be seen; this inquiry is raised in order to provide a detailed analysis of how desire arises.
Within the response, the third point—that the latter precept is violated whether the object is a relative or a non-relative—refers to the weaver.
In the aforementioned list of conditions, the exclusion of relatives is based on the owner of the thread.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a householder provided thread to a weaver to have a robe made for Baddhananda.

Later, when he returned home, he selected the finest thread from his supply and gave it to the weaver to weave, while also promising him additional payment. The householder criticized and disparaged this, and the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
Consequently, the Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.
[Commentary: Among the conditions for the precept, the act of selecting a fine thread is precisely the characteristic of greed (*lobha*), serving as the source from which the transgression arises.

Regarding the two faults associated with the conditions for the precept: first, the selection of a fine thread; second, the permitting of payment. Because these activities give rise to [worldly] affairs, the rule was established on this account.
[The Vinaya] states: If a householder or a householder’s wife has a weaver weave a robe for a bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu has not previously received a formal invitation to do so;
[Commentary] If a layperson gives a monk a garment of high value, the monk—being content with few desires and knowing sufficiency—is permitted to request one of inferior quality as he pleases.
[Vinaya] He then went to the weaver and said, "Make this garment for me; weave it for me very well and make it wide."
"O you of great firmness, I shall give you some price. If that bhikṣu gives a price—even as much as the value of a single meal—and obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
[Note]: If one seeks clothing and does not obtain it, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding those who commit the same offense and those who do not:
[the offense is] reduced in cases such as seeking from relatives, seeking from renunciants, or seeking on behalf of another for oneself.

[Commentary: The precept text consists of seven phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the owner of the robe; third, the instruction to weave it; fourth, the characteristics of the offense beginning with "that bhikṣu" and so forth;
fifth, the formal determination of the offense if the robe is obtained—the latter two points are self-evident.
The phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* are distinct from one another.

[Commentary: Regarding the request for the *pravāraṇā*, this means permitting the acceptance of what is good and the rejection of what is bad; it does not mean seeking out what is fine out of excessive greed or to the point of destroying faith.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If lay brothers and sisters instruct one to go personally to manage the preparations so that one may quickly obtain what is good, this is permissible."

Regarding the characteristics of *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence/confession): In the commentary, the initial citation and explanation states that "self-indulgence" (*pravāraṇā*) means acting according to the will of the bhikṣus.

The passage from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* cited below refers to that text; it concerns one who is fundamentally free of offenses, and its purpose is merely to demonstrate the characteristics of *pravāraṇā*.
[Vinaya] The twenty-fifth precept: Taking the robe of a bhikṣu.
[Commentary] The twenty-fifth precept: Taking the robe of a bhikṣu.

[Commentary] Having made a plan with a companion to give him a robe was already a source of misconduct; since he later did not carry it out and took it back through conciliation, there was no offense. Now, however, it is done out of a mind of anger.
Because forcibly seizing and causing distress through deep-seated attachment is particularly contrary to proper decorum, the Noble One prohibited it. Master Daoguang stated:
"The precept against forcibly seizing robes that were previously given away without being shared.

Regarding the first two phrases of the twenty-fivefold intent for this prohibition: the former two describe the reason for giving them away initially, which was based on seeking [merit]; the latter two...
The phrases clarify that the principle must be harmonized; now, below, the faults are revealed because [the rules] were established to remedy violations of the ritual protocol.

"Protocol" (*yi*) refers to majestic deportment (*vīryāpatha*), while "sections" (*jie*) refers to the regulations of conduct. Later, Master Guang established these names to accord with the intent of the regulations. As for "not being clear," it means that whether [a rule applies] or not has not been definitively determined.
[Commentary]: There are five conditions for the completion of the offense. [Commentary]:

First, it specifies that this applies to a *bhikṣu* to distinguish him from the other four assemblies (*catur-parṣad*), as they are not of the same class. If one were to falsely accuse him, it would merely be a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

If that were so, why would those who are minor offenders be subject to the same formal suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*) as the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension) committed by the *saṃgha*? The answer is that the legal procedure of the *saṃgha* does not differ; since both equally violate the rule, they are treated alike. Second, the root [text].
Regarding the intent to take what is not given, there are four permutations based on the distinction between the uncertainty and certainty of both the object and the act of taking: 1.

Intending to take with one of the two *aniyata* (uncertain) factors, yet taking with certainty—this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense, as previously listed. 2. Intending to take with one *aniyata* factor and taking with another *aniyata* factor—this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. 3. Intending to take with certainty, yet taking with an *aniyata* factor. 4. Intending to take with certainty and taking with certainty.

If one seizes these two [objects] while intending them with certainty, it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*), because from the outset one has definitively relinquished one's own ownership over them.

Because it has already been determined, the text states: "Having given it back, one takes it again"; this refers to a double appropriation. Fourth, regarding taking it oneself or having another take it:

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four permutations—taking it oneself or having another take it—which all constitute an offense regarding robes; that is, if one seizes the three robes (*tricīvara*), one commits an offense, whereas if one seizes robes of less than the prescribed measure, one merely commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

Fifth, regarding the acquisition of robes belonging to oneself: according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four permutations; in the first case, when giving is appropriate, if one seizes them individually at the same time...
Regarding the offense of taking back a robe after having given it along with the three robes, one commits three *thullaccaya* offenses; the remaining phrases should be understood accordingly.

In the first enumeration of the conditions, this applies exclusively to the *bhikṣu* (Great Sangha). If that were so, an objection might be raised below based on the following examples, as within the ninety [offenses], both the *bhikṣu* and the *bhikṣuṇī* equally fall into the offense of complying with one who has been suspended (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*).
In response, it is said that because such an act violates the Dharma of the Sangha, the specific status [of the offender] is not distinguished among the three [categories].
First, the meaning of the conditions for violating the precepts is indicated; next, the subsequent phrases establish distinctions through exclusion.

Since the second phrase involves taking that which is not fixed, the resulting affliction is slight and thus the offense is light. The latter two offenses, being grave, belong to the preceding category of theft (*steya*).

This is because, once the renunciation is finalized, the object is no longer one's own property; this can be understood by citing the scriptural evidence. Among these four, the Sangha is cited as the witness.
First, to clarify the four permutations regarding oneself and others: (1) giving to oneself while having another take it away; (2) having another give to oneself while taking it away oneself;

(3) having another give to another while taking it away oneself; (4) giving to oneself while taking it away oneself. Next, concerning the distinctions of substance and reduction of measure for an offense of *dukkaṭa*:

since these do not constitute the three robes (*tricīvara*), there are five [cases]. First, regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika* rule on "giving and taking" and "separation and union," one also establishes four permutations. First:
1. Giving and taking separately; 2. Giving and taking together; 3. Taking away both together and separately—these two constitute one offense. 4.
Giving separately and taking separately—the same as the three offenses above.
[Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Nanda’s disciple was skilled at exhorting and converting, and he wished to join with Upananda.
While traveling, he first gave his robe to another bhikṣu, saying, "He is foolish and does not know how to recite the precepts, perform the *poṣadha*, or carry out the *karmas*.
Later, when that [other] bhikṣu departed and did not follow him, [the first bhikṣu] took the robe back. The bhikṣus censured him, and the Buddha, because of this, established the precept.

[Commentary: Regarding the four stages of the characteristics of delusion listed among the conditions for the precepts: the first two prevent non-virtue before it has arisen, while the latter two eliminate offenses that have already arisen.
Within the former two, "not knowing the recitation of the precepts" means one’s own practice is not yet proficient;

"not knowing the exposition of the precepts" means being confused regarding the ritual procedures of the assembly. Within the latter two, "not knowing the *poṣadha*" means not recognizing [the ceremony].

Regarding the mindfulness that serves as the antidote to offenses, those who do not know the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and do not recognize how to request the Sangha for the removal [of an offense] are all said to be "deluded" because they lack understanding in darkness.

Within the context of the conditions for the precepts, the characteristics of delusion are revealed; first, there is a general classification, followed by a specific explanation of the *poṣadha*, which is translated as "pure dwelling."

Therefore, this is explained by way of the confession of offenses (*pāpadeśanā*). Regarding the *poṣadha*, offenses committed against an individual are confessed before another person, while those concerning the various formal acts (*karmavācanā*) involving the Saṃgha are confessed before the assembly.
In both of these upper categories, the lower [offenses] are collectively included.
[The Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu, and subsequently, out of anger, either seizes it himself or instructs another to seize it back."
"I will not give you my robe. [Note:

If one seizes it out of anger, or instructs another to seize it, and then conceals it, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture); if it has not been concealed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

If it is placed on a tree, a rack, a bed, or any other location where it is left, and one moves it from that place, one commits the offense of *pāyattika*; if one takes it but does not move it from its place, there is no offense.
Dukkata. [Vinaya:
If she returns the robe or takes back the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. [Commentary: This offense applies equally to both nuns and monks.
As for when there is no offense: if one does not speak with anger, saying, "I regret it; I will not give it back; return my robe to me."

If that person comes and expresses regret in their heart, the robe may be returned immediately. If another person says, "This bhikṣu wishes to repent and return the robe to you," or if one has borrowed a robe from another to wear, there is no reason to seize it back;

to do so is not an offense. If there is fear of loss or fear of damage, or if that person has broken the precepts, broken right view, or broken proper conduct, or if they have been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) or expulsion (*pabbājana*), they should indeed be expelled. If, for the sake of this matter, one's life or *brahmacariya* (holy life) is at stake...
There is no offense in all cases where one takes back [the robe] from someone who does not store or keep it.
[Commentary: Of the five phrases in the root text, the first concerns the offender; the second concerns the robe given; the third, beginning with "in anger," clarifies the manner of taking it back;
the final two [phrases] are self-evident.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "seizes and conceals" in the annotation, this refers to seizing in the presence of another.

Because the concealment of one's intention and suspicion regarding ownership is not made manifest, the offense of *pārājika* (or *sthūlātyaya*, depending on the context) is established based on the act of concealment. Furthermore, it says:

"If [the object] is placed upon a tree," this means that even if not in the presence of another, as soon as it is lifted and removed from its place, the actual offense is committed; for there is no one present with whom to dispute, thus the offense is established. Subsequently, if one conceals it further...
This constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
In the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, it is noted that there are two ways this precept becomes an offense; therefore, it must be explained comprehensively.

First, the explanation of how the offense is incurred by "seizing and concealing"; next, the explanation of how the offense is incurred by "lifting and leaving. Each provides its respective rationale to clarify these two cases.

Regarding the concealment after separation: as previously established, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; however, because one fears the other might take it, one conceals it further—this is [the case for] *jīrṇaka*.
[Vinaya] Twenty-six: The precept against possessing seven-day medicine beyond the limit.
[Commentary] The twenty-sixth precept concerns the prohibition against keeping medicinal medicine for more than seven days.
Now, for one dwelling in this world, physical life is of primary importance; thus, clothing and food are required to adorn the internal and external person.

Although both are subject to regulations—medicines being strictly controlled and clothing being lightly regulated—it is because the afflictions of the mind take precedence that the rules are established according to the specific ailments. Herein, we shall further elaborate.
The doors and windows are intended so that the traveler may perceive the medicine according to the text for the purpose of verification and application.
In the twenty-sixth section, "Explanation of the Intent," the initial passage provides a general account of the two types of dwellings for the two kinds of sustenance.

Since physical life and vitality are of great importance, their preservation involves many accumulated tasks; thus, "adornment" refers precisely to the nourishment of these resources—food filling the interior and clothing adorning the exterior.

It is said that regarding the simultaneous opening and restriction of the *zhuāngyán* (adornment/decoration): in view of the four original reliances (*catur-niśraya*), it is an "opening" (*kāya*); yet what is established as the precepts now is a "restriction" (*niyama*).

Alternatively, within the precepts concerning food and clothing, each has its own openings and restrictions. Medicines are heavy and robes are light—meaning that while restrictions such as those against eating leftovers, touching [food with defiled hands], or cooking overnight apply strictly to medicine, they are less so for robes. This is because, as for the reason medicines are heavy, the afflictions of the mind take them as their primary object first.
Because craving is heavy, it is conformed to the illness; because the teaching is adapted to circumstances, it is now shown specifically below.

"The doors and windows" refers to the various gates mentioned below; "desiring to reveal the intent" means that by observing the text, one perceives the medicine—that is, knowing the methods of treatment.
"Raising questions for examination" means personally inspecting one's own transgressions.

[Commentary: Regarding this, the analysis of the general and the specific is divided into two parts. The specific [analysis] will be explained below; the general consists of three sections: first, listing the characteristics of the medicines;
second, clarifying the method of receiving them; and third, the proper and improper ways of administration.

[Commentary]: Regarding the first [section], there are four parts: 1) listing the number and explaining the names; 2) the different ways the names are derived; 3) the reason for establishing the four [categories];
and 4) defining the essential characteristics of the medicinal substances. [Commentary]: Within the first part, the listing of the number can be understood through common sense.

The first section, "Listing the Characteristics of Medicines," begins with a numerical enumeration that encompasses all medicines—those taken at the proper time, those taken at improper times, those for seven days, and those for life.
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the names, there are two aspects: the general and the specific.

[Commentary: In the Vinaya, there are three names: first, *pūjani*, which refers to medicinal food taken at the proper time (*kālabhojana*); second, *khādanīya*, which refers to medicinal food taken outside the proper time (*vikālabhojana*);
and third, *sāyani*, which refers to medicinal food for seven days (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*) and so forth. All are designated as "medicine" because they are nothing other than remedies for affliction.
In the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names), the general explanation contains only three names; among these three, it is said that "equality" (*sam*) should encompass all forms.

The specific names appearing above are all shown below as general designations. There are two afflictions: hunger and thirst constitute the primary afflictions, which are treated by the first two medicines;
the violation of the four great elements constitutes the secondary affliction, which is treated by the latter two medicines.

[Commentary]: Within the detailed explanation, although there are four names, when categorized according to time, there are only two types of medicine. These include beans, grains, milk, curd, cakes, fruits, rice, and vegetables;
these are permitted by the Holy Teaching to be consumed from dawn until midday. This accords with the Dharma and is called "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*).

Once midday has passed and before the appearance of the sun [the next morning], the Sage does not permit their consumption; to consume them would give rise to transgression, and thus they are called... [non-timely medicine].
Regarding the three other types of medicine that are not for [specific] times, they all constitute an offense when taken during the time or non-time periods;

however, since they are permitted for consumption at both times and non-times, they should be designated as "timely" (*kālika*). They are called "non-timely medicine" (*akālika*) only in contrast to the former category.

As for the actual substance of these medicines, there are strictly two types: the timely and the non-timely. The reason they are fourfold is that the timely medicine, within its own category, is singular and does not admit of further division.
At this time, because of the exclusion of the three [other categories], there are four.
Next, in the first section of the detailed explanation, the ancient interpretation is further divided into three parts. First, the general heading:

regarding the two types based on time, these refer to the two kinds of medicine—timely (*kāla-bhaiṣajya*) and non-timely (*akāla-bhaiṣajya*). Second, the specific explanation: first, explaining timely medicine; "past its time" refers to...
One must not arbitrarily designate "time" (kāla) alone; the following sections explain the three medicines, all of which constitute an offense when taken outside their proper time.

That [designation] means that within the [specific] time, they may not be consumed; however, since these three medicines are precisely what is permitted for consumption during the "non-time" (vikāla), they should be called "time.

Yet, in relation to the preceding "time-medicine" (kālabhaiṣajya), they are termed "non-time. If one follows the subsequent three [categories], this serves as a summary to demonstrate the inclusion and exclusion [of the classifications].

[Commentary]: If one interprets it in this way, I fear it is not the word of the Sage. Why is this? The designation and substance of "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*) and "untimely medicine" (*akālabhojana*) are restricted, as discussed above.
As for the remaining two medicines, once they have been accepted, they may be consumed both at the proper time and at improper times;
how could they be divided into three categories based on the distinction of "untimely"?

The next section consists of two parts: the first two lines briefly refute [the objection], and the subsequent portion investigates and demonstrates [the correct view]. First, it shows that the previous two [categories] are acceptable;

next, it clarifies that the latter two are not so. [Commentary]: Now, to re-explain the names: "timely medicine" (*kālabhaiṣajya*) is as described above. To clarify the various fruit juices and fermented liquors, one must explain their specific potencies and functions.
Regarding the general rule for drinking [medicines], they are only permitted during the non-time period (*akāla*). If a disease arises, they must be taken;

however, since there is no separate provision for opening this exception, it is designated by the time after noon. Furthermore, because there is no superior efficacy beyond that point, it maintains the designation "non-time.
As for substances such as ghee and oils, because the potency of these additive medicines lasts for only seven days, they are named according to their duration in days. Ginger and pepper are pungent.
Suffering is not something that non-humans constantly devour; rather, the power of medical treatment is slight, and it is only through long-term persistence that one can cure the illness.

Therefore, it is permitted to perform the ritual according to the form [of the ailment], and there are three such forms: first, the exhaustion of the medicinal form; second, the exhaustion of the pathological form; and third, the exhaustion of the retributive form. This is how it may be known.

Now, regarding the explanation of "medicines for the middle period" (kāla-bhaiṣajya), since the reference to the finger-tip is the same in both ancient and modern traditions, [the discussion] proceeds next to clarify "non-timely vessels," which refers to the mind and its objects (*nāma-rūpa*).
Since these possess no superior efficacy, they are of no use beyond the limit [of the current life] and are inferior to the latter two [categories].

Regarding "ghee" and so forth, thirdly, the "seven-day medicinal potency" means that generally, when medicines treat an illness, their efficacy is observed within seven days; if it does not manifest by then, they do not provide a cure.
The four flavors listed below—pungent, bitter, acrid, and salty—are two of the six flavors; the remaining four are sweet, sour, salty, and bland.

The three types listed below pertain specifically to the "exhaustion of the retribution" (盡報), which is why the *Liaolun* refers to it as "one period" (一期), "the end of one's life" (終身), or "the exhaustion of one's lifespan" (盡壽).

[Commentary]: Second, the names are applied at different times; "timely" (*kāla*) and "untimely" (*akāla*) are designated in relation to one another. The "seven-day" period refers to the duration of the efficacy, as explained in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*;
that it is "for the duration of life" refers to the maturation of the karmic retribution, which can likewise be understood.

Regarding the second point, it is called "the superior among the middle"; the two [preceding] points can be understood. As for the "seven days" being based on the duration of the medicine's potency, this is like the *Saṃghīti* [Vinaya]:
when the Buddha questioned a physician-monk about how many days a stored medicine would remain effective, he replied that its potency could be known to last for seven days.
The Buddha then said, "I permit you to store it for seven days. Since the "entire life" [limit] has already been clarified above, [the seven-day rule] is understood.

[Commentary]: Third, regarding the establishment of the four [types of medicine], there are two kinds of ailments: first, chronic ailments are easy to treat because they recur frequently; second, intermittent ailments are difficult to treat.
Because the chronic ailment is contrasted with the former [intermittent] chronic ailment, two medicines are established. Since the ailment of hunger arises, a single meal provides sufficient satiety;

as this extends through both day and night, the ailment is eliminated, and thus "timely medicine" (kālabhaiṣajya) is established. As for the ailment of thirst, it recurs frequently, and thus [medicine] is administered according to each occurrence.

Because the duration of their consumption is not restricted by specific times, "non-time" (vikāla) is established as a category; because they are intended for future illnesses, two types of medicine are established.
Because the efficacy of the seven-day medicine is strong while that of the lifetime medicine is weak, they differ in the length of their functional application.

Since the "time" (kāla) and "non-time" (vikāla) categories are each fixed at one period, and the seven-day and lifetime medicines both apply to both time and non-time, four types of medicine are established.
The first section of the third chapter of the fourth fascicle is divided into three parts. First, it demonstrates the two types of illness: constant illness, which refers to hunger and thirst;
and intermittent illness, which refers to the four hundred and four ailments. These are also termed "new and old" or "host and guest.

Constant illness is not a primary affliction and is thus easy to treat, as it arises regularly every day and therefore manifests frequently. Intermittent illness, being contrary [to the body's natural state], is difficult to treat; once treated, it may never recur.
Because there is no [fixed] occasion, they are always contrasted with the preceding two; next, the four medicines are explained. First, it clarifies the establishment of the first two medicines:

"殄" (jin) means to extinguish; they are contrasted with the subsequent two. Next, it clarifies the establishment of the latter two medicines: because their efficacy is strong for seven days, the limit is short;
because their power is inferior throughout one's life, the limit is long. This concludes the summary indicating the general and specific applications.
[Commentary]: If one relies on the measure of "clearly manifest" (vibhūta) medicines, there are five types: first, the measure based on time (*kāla-pramāṇa*);

second, the measure based on *yāma* (watches), which is another name for "non-time" (*akāla*); however, in that treatise, the day and night are divided into five periods, and medicine is taken according to the time;
since it revolves through the watches—such as from dawn until the second watch and so forth—it is called a *yāma*. Third, the measure based on seven days (*saptāha-pramāṇa*).
The fourth is the measure of a single lifetime, which refers to the duration until death. The fifth is the measure of great openness, referring to ashes, soil, water, feces, and urine.

These five are discarded by the people of the world and need not be accepted; therefore, they are called "greatly open. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are instances where these are permitted or prohibited.
The next section concludes the discussion on the five *pramāṇas*, which means "measures" or "limits. The measure of time can be understood;
as for the further measure, it takes these five [periods] as the limit and further subdivides them.

Regarding the division of the day into five periods, such as the hours of *yín* and *mǎo*, these belong to the calendrical systems of this region and cannot be directly correlated [with the Indian system]; rather, one simply divides a single day into five parts based upon it.
Regarding the five watches: receiving [the precepts] at the first watch (approximating seven o'clock) is like the dawn;

receiving them at the second watch is until midday; receiving them at the third watch is until the sun is high; receiving them at the fourth watch is until the sun is slanting; and receiving them at the fifth watch is until sunset.
If one follows the final watch of the night, it extends until the end of the night. However, according to our own school, regardless of whether it is early or late, they are all considered complete.

Regarding the five major openings during the night, there is nothing that restricts them. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when ash or soil is required by someone, if a person is present it is received, but if no person is present it is opened separately;
thus it is said that there are both passages and obstructions. The *Śāstra* on the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "These five encompass everything without exception."

[Commentary: Regarding the substance of the four types of medicinal preparations for concentration, as they are explained in detail in the *Jiyao* (Excerpts) according to their specific application at the time, I shall not elaborate further here.
Instead, I will provide a brief summary under three headings: first, the substance of the medicinal preparation; second, the substance of transformation; and third, the substance of combination.

Regarding the initial section on the classification of the essential substance of the four medicinal stabilizers (*catvāraḥ samādhi-bhaiṣajyāni*), the *Guangchao* (Extensive Commentary) further details six types of essential substances along with their transformations and combinations;
as that text is very extensive, the present work provides only a brief outline below.
[Commentary] This section is divided into two parts: first, establishing the essential nature; second, eliminating confusion and redundancy.

The first part further contains two sub-sections: first, a general introduction to the divisions; second, the two medicines both having two gates, with the lifelong [vow] specifically establishing the essential nature.

Regarding the term "confusion and redundancy" (*wulan*): it refers to how weeds mix with fine grain; by analogy, it describes how false explanations intermingle with and disrupt the authentic regulations.
[Commentary]:

Regarding the substance of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*), when speaking of "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*), there are two types of texts. First, *pūyāni* (soft foods), which refers to rice, parched grain flour, solid rice, fish, and meat.
If one eats even a single mouthful of these five kinds, it constitutes a formal meal (*bhojana*), which is the primary [transgression] and the basis [for the offense].
This is the distinction: the two types of *khādaniya* (solid foods) refer to branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and finely ground powdered foods.
These five, as opposed to the aforementioned [soft foods], are neither sufficient nor primary.

Within the section on the essential nature [of food], this first clarifies "primary food" (*bhojana*); being "primary" reveals that its substance is sufficient, while being "distinct" refers to the third chapter below.
The precepts restrict [the consumption of] formal meals; violating this next point clarifies the non-formal meal. The text states that it is contrary to the above, which should be understood as:
"neither formal nor sufficient, neither back-to-back nor separate.
[Commentary: To clarify the confusion regarding these very medicines: for instance, the substance and name of a single type such as rice do not change, and it is what is commonly used in the world.
If one treats the mixing of porridge with rice as identical [to other mixtures], it is not correct.
In the subsequent section, where distinctions are made to eliminate confusion, the example of mixing rice with porridge is judged according to the nature of the porridge.

[Commentary]: In the world, there are those who use items such as *gāo* (rice cakes) or *mí* (congee) that are not categorized as "rice" (*fàn*), yet they are like porridge when they emerge from the cauldron and form characters when drawn across the surface.
This is sufficient as a correct standard; one may seek to apply this principle to other cases accordingly.

Regarding the refutation of impropriety in the first section of the initial chapter, it first addresses the impropriety of *gāo* (sweet cakes) and *mí* (porridge): using rice to make *gāo* by steaming it until it becomes a mash (*mí*).

As determined below according to the text, the classification of *zhōu* (congee) into thick and thin is set forth in the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Shanjian lü piposha); here, the meaning is consistent with that of thick congee.

Correctly Included. [Commentary]: Furthermore, using rice cakes (*gao*) and biscuits (*bing*) is analogous to the case of cooked rice; these are categorized as "fine powders" and thus are not correctly included. If that is so, then parched grain flour (*chao*) and grain gruel (*jiang*), being fine powders, should likewise not be correctly included.
Answer: Their essential nature (*tǐ*) is fundamentally correct, but due to external conditions (*yuán*), they are not considered correct, just as in the previous example of porridge.
The meaning of the example is divided into two parts.

In the first section of the subsequent division, it is shown that "non-cake" refers to flour-cakes, wheat-cakes, and their like; what follows below points out the error, and the passage beginning with "If...
explains the objection, namely, that dry parched grain mixed with water constitutes a gruel-like liquid. In the response, this is categorized into two types based on the thickness of the porridge.

[Commentary]: Regarding the two types of fish and meat, the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) provisionally permits them, whereas both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles maintain strict prohibitions; this is explained in detail in the *Shuchao*.
Among the three [points], the first cites the words of what was abolished as a provisional opening, yet the matter does not end there. Furthermore, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, prior to...
Regarding those permitted to eat [meat], these are not actual sentient beings but merely manifested transformations. Next, I shall clarify the capacity to set aside [the prohibitions]:
the "Great" refers to the *Laṅkāvatāra* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, while the "Small" refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika* and *Dharmaguptaka* vinayas. The *Mahāsāṃghika* states:

"If meat has been killed for the sake of a bhikṣu, it must not be eaten by any of the seven classes of followers. The *Dharmaguptaka* holds that one may eat meat only when it is obtained from a household observing the ten wholesome precepts.

This indicates that the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings do not provide universal permission; for the details regarding the four medicinal substances, refer to the "Four Medicines" section in the *Śarīptra-vinaya-saṃgraha*.

[Commentary]: Second, explaining the substance of non-timely medicine (*vikāla-bhaiṣajya*): Among the eight types of syrups mentioned in the Vinaya, these were formerly consumed by sages free from desire;
therefore, they are permitted for those suffering from thirst. If the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is performed, they may be received at any time until dawn. If not...

Regarding the addition [of substances], the limit for consuming them as they are received is but a brief moment; the Vinaya provides no fixed determination, but the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states it thus.
Second, concerning the definitive substance of the "improper time" [food], the first section initially indicates its eight types of liquids:
1. pear, 2. sour jujube, 3. sugarcane, 4. parched grain fruit, 5. grape, 6. śāluka, 7. jambu fruit, 8. pomegranate.
Regarding the *lūka* fruit, the "sages free from desire" refers to those who are without greed. To clarify the temporal limits, there are two parts:

first, clarifying the limit of existing phenomena (*dharmas*), which refers to the period when darkness is fading and light has not yet fully dawned—specifically, the time when the night is nearly spent but before full daylight.
Second, clarifying the limit of non-existing phenomena (*adharmas*), which the *Vinaya* commentary below indicates by citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, stating it is "not the proper time."
Regarding the prohibition against placing received [medicine] on the ground: if it is received during the proper time (*kāla*), one may set it aside for a duration;

however, if it is received outside the proper time (*akāla*), one must apply the ritual formula (*adhivāsanā*) and may not leave it on the ground for even a brief moment. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, since it is clearly stated that if it is received outside the proper time, one should receive and consume it immediately without applying the formula, it is said that the *Mahāsāṃghika* rules are as follows.

[Commentary]: In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, regarding the purification of various fruits by fire, it states that if the juice within them is not purified by water, it is contrary to the Dharma and unfit for consumption.

In the subsequent section, the character "juice" (zhì) is transposed; following that [text], one should read "within the juice" (zhì zhōng). If it is not purified with water, it must not be drunk. The *Jiyao* states:
"Based on this, it applies to all four types of medicine; the purpose is to eliminate the taste and remove greed."

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, all beans, grains, and wheat that have not had their husks broken may be made into "non-time gruel" (vikāla-pāna) along with butter, oil, honey, and the juice of raw fruits.
According to the *Sudarśana-vinaya*, lotus roots may be made so by pounding them and clarifying the liquid; various leaves may be made so as well, except for leafy vegetables which are not permitted.
Various fruits may be made so, except for melons, which are not allowed.
Among the three types [of liquids], those such as *saṃkha* (mung bean) soup that have not been broken down indicate they must be clear and pure;

if they are broken down, they immediately become *yāgu* (gruel) and may not be drunk. The same principle applies to butter, oil, and so forth. According to the *Samantapāsādikā*, all substances must be clear and pure;

however, the two items—vegetables and melons—cannot necessarily be made clear, so they must be removed. (Some say that melons and vegetables are both "timely medicines" [*kālika*]; hence it is said here: beans, grains, lotus roots, and fruits.)
"Is this not a *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicament for the proper time)?

[Commentary] Next, to clarify what constitutes confusion and overlap: for instance, if the juice of dates or pear syrup is thick and turbid, undifferentiated from other substances, how can it be distinguished from *kālika-pāna* (beverage for the proper time)?
Yet, among various fruits, there are naturally clear juices; these are pure *pāna*.
If there are dregs and turbidity, it is because it is combined with *kālika* (timely) medicine; thus the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A patient may drink clear juice that is free of dregs.
Since drinking clear juice without the affliction of thirst already constitutes an offense, how much more so for turbid juice? Even in the case of illness, it constitutes an offense.

Next, in the section on distinguishing against erroneous interpretations, the first part indicates the confusion with thick syrups; "and furthermore" below clarifies the characteristics; and "therefore" below cites scriptural evidence. [Commentary]:

Regarding the claim that the non-seasonal consumption of apricot sprouts, human decoctions, powdered *fuling* (Pachyma cocos), various fine broths, and the like constitutes a permitted practice (*kai*), there is no formal textual authority for this.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is stipulated that apricot sprouts are for raw use and not for cooked consumption; therefore, the Vinaya strictly prohibits such practices.

Regarding those who are not permitted to eat [certain items], it is allowed for them to consume them throughout their entire lives for the sake of this present life. If something is not food when raw but becomes food when cooked, how can one continue to treat it as "throughout one's life" based on its original state, just as one does with ginger?
Refuting Excess in the First Section, Part One: First, pointing out that it is not the capital city, namely Jingzhao; the character "jiān" (煎) is pronounced with a departing tone.

Hereafter follows the decisive refutation of the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya). Below is the resolution of doubts regarding their adherence to the scriptural text, which generally takes the apricot seed (*xingren*) as the lifelong limit;
therefore, we now distinguish between the raw and the cooked to expose their error. As for the formal regulation of the Vinaya, the *Sifenlü* states: "All..."

Those that are salty, bitter, pungent, or sweet and cannot be used as food are called "medicines for the duration of life" (*yāvajjīva*). Their substance differs from [ordinary food]; for example, ginger, whether raw or cooked, is entirely [classified as] for the duration of life.

[Commentary: Therefore, in the *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā*, it is stated that among various trees and herbs, those whose roots, stalks, flowers, or fruits cannot be used as food may be taken for the duration of life.
The medicines are either all *kālika* (medicines for the time), or the fruits and kernels are *kālika* while the remainder are *yāvajjīvika* (lifelong).

Next, in the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, it first provides a general indication, stating: "One may take them for as long as life lasts"; here the text uses the character "medicine" (*yao*) instead of "fruit" (*guo*), which is a scribal error.
Or, below, there is a specific distinction: it says that there are trees and plants whose entire body is *kālika*, and there are trees... [text fragment].

Regarding fruits, heartwood, medicinal substances, and other items, they may be kept for as long as one lives; likewise, trees and entire trees may be kept for as long as one lives. This proves that "for as long as one lives" cannot be judged uniformly.

[Commentary: Taking this as a precedent, it is seen that the distinction between raw and cooked is not fixed; sometimes both raw and cooked forms are permitted, such as with rice, wheat, ginger, pepper, and so forth.
Some things are produced as *kālika* (medicines for the time) but mature into *yāvajjīvika* (medicines for the duration of life), while others are produced as *yāvajjīvika* but mature into *kālika*;

for example, apricot kernels, *śuṇṭhī*, taro tubers, and *kandamūla*. Thus, their transformation depends on the season and cannot be fixed. For instance, sugarcane is of one color [when fresh], yet it can transform into all four types of medicines;
how could it be that once it becomes stone honey (*śarkarā*), it is permitted only during the [specific] time? Such confusion is extreme; I have cited this as merely one example.

2. Regarding the first of the three [categories], it follows the aforementioned treatise by analogy: for the first phrase, rice and barley are both *kālāntika* (medicines for a limited time), while ginger and pepper are *yāvajjīvika* (lifelong medicines).
The second phrase is like rice, barley, sugarcane, and their ashes, and so forth. The third lists the characteristics.

It can be seen that since neither [of the two positions] is tenable, they cannot be established. Therefore, the following section on "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) demonstrates the fallacy of the "indefinite" (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding sugarcane, it applies to all four periods; as will be cited below, because it is originally a "timely medicine" (*kālabhaiṣajya*), if one takes its clear juice, it may be consumed at improper times;
if it is made into rock sugar (*śarkarā*), it may be consumed for seven days; and if it is burned to ashes, it may be consumed for the rest of one's life. Thus it is said.
"How could this be established?"—the following passage provides a brief indication.

[Commentary]: However, the burden of mouth and belly is a flaw shared by both the monastic and the laity; those who understand the teachings and exercise caution in their conduct are rare in the world.

Thus, Huiyuan of Jin died without drinking honey syrup, for he would not have opened [his mouth] unless it were permitted by the Vinaya. This was because the Vinaya texts required that one personally see [the substance] with one's own eyes.
When the search for [the truth] was nearly complete, he suddenly passed away. This person’s case may be recounted, while others remain beyond words.

One might occasionally eat rice at improper times and know it is not a sin that can be washed away; yet one cannot drink thin gruel when not ill, for to be deluded by false teachings makes it ultimately difficult to purify through repentance.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that sin is neither existent nor non-existent, precisely because of reliance upon a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*).

Among the four [sections], the first indicates the faults and afflictions of consuming [food]; the second clarifies that those who transgress frequently fail to study according to the teachings, and thus few are cautious in their practice;
and few are those who faithfully uphold them. Therefore, the following cites an actual event as proof:
in the twelfth year of the Yixi era, Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu suffered from a severe illness; senior virtuous elders urged him to drink fermented rice wine (*gǔjiǔ*).
Huiyuan did not accept the subsequent request for rice gruel, nor did he accept the later request for honey-water as a drink.
He instead requested that the Vinaya Master Yuanxing be summoned to resolve his doubts. The Vinaya Master said, "You may go," but Huiyuan replied, "I must see the Vinaya texts myself.

As soon as the Master opened the volume to examine them, Huiyuan had already passed away. This account appears in the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks). The Dharma Master was thus one who relied upon the four requisites.

The manifestation of these traces is by no means intended to obscure what is permitted or prohibited; rather, it is solely to demonstrate the necessity of careful protection, serving as a model for future generations.

If the masters of the present day do not even know that one should not consume [forbidden food], they are no different from the common run of people; how much less could they possibly reject or destroy the strict regulations?
Beholding these clear rules, how can one not reflect upon oneself? This passage below cites specific matters to issue a warning; the first sentence praises the distant [ideal].

The Master’s next phrase, “reproaching transgression as beyond words,” means that it is not even worth mentioning. He then provides an illustration: one who knows their error is like someone who realizes they have been eating inedible food;
because they know it is wrong, their offense can still be cleansed. One who drinks medicinal gruel while being ill is like one who drinks plain water while healthy;

because of their ignorance and delusion, their offense is truly difficult to repent. Therefore, he cites a scriptural proof below: when King Ajātaśatru sought from the Buddha the repentance for his sins, the Buddha immediately—

It is stated that "to have shame is not to be without it" (meaning that if one recognizes one's error, repentance is possible), and "to be without shame is not to be without it" (meaning that for those who claim they do not know [the truth], repentance is difficult). This is the essential meaning derived from the sutras.

[Commentary: Regarding the seven-day period for medicinal substances, the four types of medicine are recognized by the world, whereas the five types of medicine are permitted for seven days according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
These five medicines, along with fats, must be pure and free from any odor of food; they may be received all at once and consumed for seven days.

According to the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, this allowance is granted due to illness, and the duration is limited to seven days based on the measure of recovery. If one was originally not ill, or if one recovers within that period, [the rule does not apply].
Furthermore, there is no offense for eating at improper times when one is suffering from hunger or thirst; the same applies to fats and oils.

Regarding the seven-day medicines, the first section of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) lists five medicines as enumerated in the precepts. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Monastic Code of the Great Assembly) likewise states that the five medicines are the same as those in the *Dharmaguptaka*, adding "and fats.
This refers to when Śāriputra suffered from a wind-disorder and his physician instructed him to consume the five fats, namely bear... [and so forth].

Regarding bears, boars, donkeys, and fish: in the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra*, it first clarifies the opening of the limits [of storage], and below this, it demonstrates the restrictions.

For one who originally has no illness, the addition of the formal procedure (*adhikāra*) is not established; even if the simultaneous medicine (*sahagata-bhaiṣajya*) is determined to be within the limit, if one eats it despite having previously performed the formal procedure without cause, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense accordingly.
