Fatty substances (*vasā*) also fall under the category of the seven-day [medicine], and are judged according to the same principle as above; therefore, it is said.
It is likewise.

[Commentary: This clarifies that those who are confused and indistinguishable in the world—those who consume honey-marmalade or honey-ginger when ill, yet greedily devour it when not ill—are the same as those who violate the law.
How much more so for honey-lotus root and various decoctions; if one is driven by greed, the retribution of iron gruel will surely come.
This instance of covetous acquisition applies to all similar cases.
Next, regarding the first section which points out what is not to be confused with honey-based preparations: "medicated honey-gel" refers to a medicinal paste formed by mixing medicine with honey;
"honey ginger" refers to ginger boiled in honey; as for "honey lotus root," it is a *kālika* (timely) medicine and cannot be used to treat illness, so one must not take it unless one is ill.
Furthermore, the mention of "improper times" serves as an illustration of cause and effect for those driven by the messenger of greed;

since karma is produced by afflictions, the molten iron is likewise the fruit obtained by one who possesses greed, just as it was the cause. Thus, the preceding section has briefly cited examples, and all other cases are identical to this; therefore, it says, "such are the analogies."

[Commentary: Regarding the fourth category, "medicines for as long as life lasts," as stated in the Vinaya, those things that are salty, bitter, pungent, or sweet and unfit for ordinary food constitute "medicines for as long as life lasts.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is the same. As for "medicines without fixed times," it refers to a sick bhikṣu taking them for the remainder of his life.

The reason they are accepted is that having a body inevitably entails illness; the Buddha permitted the taking of medicine to protect the body of karmic fruition. While illness may be temporarily halted, there will certainly be [further] occasions [for its recurrence].
Because it is produced at the time [of eating], the dharma is not lost.
Among the four [points], the first indicates the substance of the medicine; the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* refers to its flavor, yet this does not exclude everything that is unfit for consumption.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* also refers to being free from the odor of a meal taken at the improper time, hence it says they are "the same. Following the word "see," the next section clarifies the intent of the allowance, which is indeed wholesome.

[The text] mentions the scriptural passage. [Commentary: Second, the section clarifying the gate of transformation. As stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "Sugar cane is [permissible] at the proper time; its clear juice is [permissible] at improper times; rock sugar is [permissible] for seven days;
burnt ash is [permissible] for as long as one lives. One should apply this principle accordingly, as explained in detail in the *Yaochao* (Digest).
Regarding the two types of transformation, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, sugarcane transforms into four kinds of medicine;

this is stated based on the case where a single substance, such as a "timely" (*kālika*) medicine, possesses all four qualities. For other substances, the transformations are indefinite, being either three or two.

Furthermore, that which is permissible for seven days may transform into "non-timely" (*akālika*) or "lifelong" (*yāvajjīvika*) medicines, such as honey transformed into a syrup, rock sugar, burnt ashes, and so forth—all of which may be used for life.
Regarding the transformation of substances, as previously mentioned for peaches, sweet potatoes, yams, and the like, only non-seasonal liquids (*akālika-pāna*) do not undergo such transformation.
As for rock honey (*śarkarā*), there are two types: black rock honey, which resembles this granulated sugar, and white rock honey, which is like rice syrup.

[Commentary: Regarding the "Gate of the Three Medicines Mixed Together," the *Vinaya* states that among the four types of medicines, those classified as "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*) must be consumed during the proper time; they may be taken throughout one's life, but it is strictly forbidden to take them outside of that time.

To take them according to their names [when mixed] would contradict this principle. As the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "When the four medicines are mixed together, they are to be consumed according to whichever is predominant.

For example, if clarified butter (*sarpis*) is boiled with meat broth, it becomes a "seven-day medicine" (*saptāhakalpiya*); if clarified butter is combined with milk, it is treated like mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*).
The lifelong observance is also as explained in the *Shuochao* (Commentary).

Regarding the three types of mixed [medicines], the first cites the original Vinaya, the Bhaiṣajyavastu: first, for the sake of *kālabhojana* (food at the proper time), one uses the lower three medicines mixed together to make *kālabhojana*, and receives it as such;
second, for the sake of *akālabhojana* (food at improper times), one uses the lower two medicines mixed together to make *akālabhojana*.

At that time, for the seven-day use, one should mix the lower-grade medicine with [the higher-grade] to make it for seven days' use; for life-long use, one should mix [the higher-grade] with the life-long medicine to make it for life-long use.
Since there is nothing below the life-long medicine that can be combined with it, it is said that "only one" [type] is used.

The text cites the beginning and the end; the middle two cases are to be understood by analogy. Regarding the statement that the lower [medicines] cannot be combined, this is a definitive textual clarification; it does not mean that at the initial stage, the *kālika* (time-medicine) may be combined [with others].
During the three lower periods of the day, one may take the three lower medicines, but they must not be taken concurrently with [medicines for] improper times;

therefore, it is said that such [concurrent use] is not permitted. As the following citations of scriptural evidence clarify, all four types of medicine are permitted to be mixed together and taken according to their respective names.

For instance, when clarified butter (*sarpis*) is boiled with meat broth, it may be taken during the seven-day period even at improper times; likewise, when clarified butter is mixed with milk and *jyotiṣmatī* seeds, it may be taken during the seven-day period... [and so forth].
If one asks whether the "temporary" and "lifelong" [medicines] do not mutually interpenetrate, the following refers to the four medicines; those in need should seek them therein.

[Commentary] The second section concerns the two modes of reception—by hand and by mouth—and their differences across ten gates: first, the intent of the regulation; second, the medicinal substances; third, the person who bestows them;

fourth, the ritual procedure (*vidhi*); fifth, purity and impurity; sixth, duration; seventh, strength and weakness; eighth, pervasiveness and restriction; ninth, purification or non-purification; tenth, the single [gate].

[Commentary on] the Repeated [Section]. [The Sub-commentary] states that the first two refer to receiving with the hand. The five types of mental intention are as explained below in the section on the precepts. Receiving with the mouth involves many types of mental intention.

This serves to prevent the fault of receiving with the hand at an improper time, and further prevents the two *pāyattikas* (defeats) and two *dukkaṭas* (wrongdoings) regarding: (1) not receiving [food], (2) eating leftovers overnight (*saṃnidhikāraka*), (3) food touched by an impure person (*duṭṭhullaphassa*), and (4) food stored indoors (*antarāgāra*).
The offenses that arise cannot be fully described, for their characteristics are too numerous to recite.
Regarding the second section, the ten gates on the method of receiving [food], the first gate has two parts. First, it clarifies the five intentions for receiving with the hand, as follows:

namely, the precept against eating food not formally received. Below, citing the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it says: "First, to sever the causes and conditions of theft; second, to serve as a witness for others."
The third [purpose] is to stop slander; the fourth is to accomplish few desires and contentment; the fifth is to give rise to a heart of faith and respect in others.
Next, the explanation of receiving [the teaching] orally has two intentions: first, to prevent receiving it by hand; second, to prevent various transgressions.
Briefly categorized, there are four types of transgressions, as will be clearly explained below. The latter two lines are entrusted to the lecturer to cite and expound upon later.

[Commentary] Second, regarding the distinction between the types of medicine: receiving [medicine) with the hand applies to all four types of medicine, as this serves to prevent the appearance of theft.

When clarifying "receiving by mouth," however, this applies only to the one type of medicine that is for immediate use (*kālika*); here, the two methods of receiving—by hand and by mouth—are mutually exclusive. As in other Vinayas, when "receiving by mouth" is added, this Vinaya states:
"There may be occasions where, due to certain causes and conditions, one receives [the medicine] by placing it on the ground. The details are as explained below in the section on the precepts.
Regarding the three medicinal substances, the ritual of oral administration is added.
Within the first section of the second [category], there are two parts: first, clarifying manual acceptance; next, clarifying oral acceptance.

For *kālika* (time-limited) medicines, if they are not intended for prolongation, there is only manual acceptance. However, if there are specific causes and conditions, the oral addition of the three acceptances serves as a substitute for manual acceptance.
Therefore, it is said that they do not mutually apply. As shown below by citing examples of oral acceptance (*mukha-paribhoga*) as found in various Vinayas:
in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, giving food to one with wrong views or food contained in a layperson’s precious vessel is both [orally accepted];

in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, when one does not understand [the language], and in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, when food is brought from a stable burned by fire and placed on the ground—these are all cases of oral acceptance according to this very Vinaya (*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*).

In this Vinaya account, a bhikṣu possessing supernormal powers went to the country of the non-Buddhists to beg for food; they resented the bhikṣu and, placing the food on the ground, abandoned it and departed.

The Buddha said: "Once [the food] has left the hand, it is already considered given. This clarifies that regarding the three medicinal substances, both forms of acceptance—the oral and the manual—must be performed;
first one must accept with the hand, and thus the two modes of acceptance are mutually interdependent.

[Commentary]: As the former interpretation stated: "Medicine taken at the proper time (*kālabhojana*) and medicine taken outside the proper time (*akālabhojana*) do not require the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), because 'time' does not involve the distinction between near and far.
Next, the previous judgment held that while this may apply to medicine taken at the proper time, it does not apply to medicine taken outside the proper time; therefore, it must be corrected.

"Near" (*jìn*) is a scribal error for "extend" (*yán*). That [former view] claimed that since medicine taken outside the proper time does not involve extending the duration of the day, there is no need to add [the ritual].

[Commentary]: Now, regarding the absence of scriptural authority [for this], it is insufficient as a basis for reliance. What we clarify here is that the division of the "timely medicine" (kālabhojana) is restricted to the period before noon;

there is no possibility of extending it further, nor is there any need for a formal ritual (karmavācanā). As for the "non-timely medicine" (akālabhojana), if the ritual of addition is not performed, even a brief moment after noon constitutes a lapse in its reception.
Therefore, one must establish a ritual of empowerment to enable it to be extended for a long duration. Thus, the text states: "It should not be [done]."

If one receives medicinal gruel today and sets it aside for the next day, because the limits of receiving the dharma have expired, it is no longer permissible as "timely" (kāla) once the full period has passed;
thus, it does not accord with the rules for the proper time. Regarding the latter two medicines, the ailment cannot be removed suddenly, and their efficacy is realized through gradual application;

therefore, by considering both the distance and proximity of the medicine's potency, the addition of the formal procedure (*adhikāra*) to the object allows for its consumption without fault. As the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "These three kinds of medicine may be kept overnight."

If one catches [the medicine] while not ill, it may not be received by hand but must be received by mouth; neither way is permitted for consumption. The opposite of the above constitutes valid proof of this.

Among the three [sections], the first refutes false views, while the following now correctly clarifies the original point. First, it clarifies that for *kāla-bhaiṣajya* (medicine for the proper time), there is no need to extend the duration; next, it clarifies that for the other three types of medicine, an extension is required.

First, it clarifies that although *vikāla-bhaiṣajya* (medicine for improper times) does not extend the day itself, it does require extending the specific time period; therefore, the following citation provides scriptural proof for this initial point.

The following citation clarifies the meaning of the text: since the non-appropriate time (*akāla*) is defined by the addition of the "non-time" rule, it is not permitted to take the medicine during the appropriate time on the following day.
Next, the subsequent passage explains that the efficacy of the seven-day and lifetime-long [medicines] gradually decreases;

this means that there are variations in the strength of the treatment for illness. Regarding the distance of the medicinal potency: because the potency of the seven-day medicine is strong, its duration is short, whereas that of the lifetime-long medicine is long.
Because the circumstances have changed, avoiding blame is itself a transgression, as the following cited passage clarifies that the three medicines may be either faulty or faultless;
thus, one must clearly understand the necessity of [determining] the improper time. To keep [medicines] overnight constitutes "stale" (saṃstaraka), and to handle them improperly is likewise faulty;
therefore, they are not permitted for those who are ill. Since there is no formal rite [for such cases], one does not receive them by hand or mouth.

[Commentary: Regarding the three types of transmission (*śāsana*), as for "transmission by hand," there are five meanings. Excluding those of one's own class, the remaining six groups of practitioners and the three realms of existence all constitute valid recipients of transmission.

Oral transmission is not like this; it must be of the same class. Only after first receiving transmission by hand may one subsequently receive the addition of the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*) regarding the Dharma.

Among the three [types of transmission], the first clarifies *hand-reception* (*pāṇi-saṃgraha*): it applies to all seven classes of practitioners, excluding those of the same category; it is restricted to the three realms of existence (*gati*) and excludes those who lack understanding, while for all other cases, it is universally applicable.

Next, *verbal reception* (*vāk-saṃgraha*) is clarified: this is restricted solely to those of the same category, as others cannot receive it. Since the essential substance (*ātman*) of both parties must be identical to allow for mutual bestowal, it is said that these constitute the "six harmonies" (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*).

[Commentary: Regarding the four methods of formal procedure (*karmavācanā*), although there are four types of medicinal substances, when the procedure is being performed, they must be correctly matched;

if they are confused or interchanged between the parties, the reception is not accomplished. This is as explained extensively in the *Karmavācanā-viniścaya* (Jie-mo-shu) and the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-ṭīkā* (Jie-mo-chao).

Among the four [sections], the first clarifies the understanding of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), meaning that both the giver and the receiver must each discern the substance of the medicine without error.
Furthermore, "below" refers to the detailed explanation.

[Commentary]: Fifth, regarding the distinction between purity and impurity: the single method of receiving with the hand prevents theft and serves as proof; thus, all four medicines require both purity and impurity.

Receiving [food] with the hands while reciting the oral dharma is not so; the holy teaching does not apply to what is impure, and thus it is not accomplished. As stated above in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one must first purify [the food] before it is obtained.

In the fifth section, "Clarifying the Correct [Procedures]," the first part clarifies that receiving with the hands applies to both pure and impure [food], serving as a proof to prevent theft and demonstrating the specific purpose [of the rule].

Therefore, the next section clarifies that oral acceptance must necessarily involve the selection of pure items; the reference to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) refers to the aforementioned passage concerning "storing overnight" and so forth.

[Commentary] Question: If the medicine is currently impure, the ritual of oral acceptance is not established because there are existing obstacles. Why, then, is the procedure of formal authorization (*karmavācanā*) permitted?
Answer: Even this [authorization] is likewise prohibited in such cases.

In the first of the question-and-answer sections, it says: "Even this is refuted; that is to say, if there are prior obstacles or difficulties, the formal act of *saṃgha-karman* (ecclesiastical disposition) is not established.

[Commentary]: If this is so, why does the text state that the *saṃgha*-disposition may have obstacles or difficulties, such as one *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) or two *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoings)? This is the answer to that.
In this case, the formal authorization (*jñapti*) is established first, and the obstacle (*vighāta*) arises later.

Regarding the resolution of the objection: if one were to explain it as above, it would contradict the Vinaya text, which states that (1) the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is for exceeding the measure, and (2) the *duṣkṛta* offense is for the obstacle.
In the response, it is said that the obstacle only begins to exist after the formal authorization has already been completed; it does not pre-exist.
[Commentary]: If that is so, then the verbal ritual for the robes excludes objects that are impure or exceed the proper measure; thus, even the three robes would not be validly received. Answer:
Because the robes are subject to restrictive regulations, while the medicine is permitted as an exception.

Next, regarding the inquiry concerning the three robes (*tricīvara*), since the procedure for receiving an additional robe exceeding the standard measure is permitted, this is cited as an example to pose a challenge.

In response, it is argued that while the regulation for robes must be relaxed for medicinal purposes, the allowance for medicine must necessarily be restricted; thus, the two teachings are established in mutual relation, the significance of which lies therein.

[Commentary: If that were so, then for laypeople (*avadātavasana*) as well, the addition of the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) should result in [the robes] becoming [monastic] entities; however, because their substance and appearance are identical to those of the laity, they do not constitute monastic attire (*mārgavastra*).

This can be understood from the response in the initial objection, which states that the addition of the white three-robes (*tricīvara*) does not result in [them becoming monastic]. The text of the response is clear.

[Commentary]: If that is so, then what of those robes that exceed the prescribed measure and are thus unlawful, which likewise deviate from the attire appropriate for the Path? Are they not subject to the additional formalities of acceptance (*parikarma*)? Answer:

Those that exceed the measure are permissible [in terms of material], yet their white color is particularly discordant. Next, it is argued that since both color and measure are non-conforming, there should be a distinction between what constitutes a valid robe and what does not. This remains to be addressed. In the answer, it is stated: [...]

Regarding the character "誤" (error), the ancient text reads "吉" (jī). This means that while exceeding the prescribed measure constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* offense, wearing [robes] with white showing on the outside is entirely forbidden;
hence it is said they are "utterly contrary.

[Commentary: Sixth, regarding length and shortness: because the hand-receiving [of robes] is restricted by time, it is termed "short"; the oral dharma (*mukha-dharma*) extends [the period], each having its own [rule].
The term "far" (*yuan*) refers to length.

Among the six types of hand-measured periods, when one receives the precepts, they are called the "stopping" (*zhi*) and "equalizing" (*qi*) periods; within these, there are three distinct "far" durations, as the time limits for each of the three medicines differ.
[Commentary]: Seventh, regarding the difference between strength and weakness: if one does not receive [the precepts] with the hand, the verbal dharma is not established; thus, the hand is strong.

Furthermore, if there is no verbal dharma, even if the hand is extended to receive them, they are lost as soon as it follows; thus, the mouth is strong. These alternating explanations show that the meaning is not fixed.

Among these seven, if one considers them in terms of mutual dependence, the mouth must depend on the hand; thus, the hand is stronger. If one considers them in terms of mutual succession, the mouth must precede the hand;
thus, the mouth is stronger. Since each is established according to a single principle, neither is fixed.
[Commentary]: Regarding the distinction between what is permitted and what is prohibited for the two types of acceptance—by hand and by mouth—as they relate to other bhikṣus:
some explain that acceptance by hand prevents theft; once accepted by one person, it may be shared among all bhikṣus. Oral acceptance is not like this:
if one declares the name [of the donor] and adds [the food], yet later gives it away to another, then because that [food] lacks the formal rite (*dharma*), it is not fit to be eaten.

In the first section of the eight [sections] on "Resolution by Others" (*paravādin*), the principles are established based on whether or not the name is invoked, thereby distinguishing between what is general and what is restricted.

[Commentary]: If that is so, when one has completed other legal acts (*dharmakarma*), how does it apply to the rest of the Saṃgha? The answer is: those acts merely perform the ritual procedure; they do not invoke the name [of the offender], and the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is resolved as soon as it is formed.

This is like the case of a patient’s remainder [of medicine]; therefore, it is general. The method for medicinal substances is not like this, for there one must specifically inscribe the name and add [the appropriate remedy].
This cannot be treated as a precedent.

Next, regarding the resolution of the objection within the section on the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa-dharma* (the rule for consuming leftover food): since one person having performed the rite allows it to apply to many people, this would contradict the aforementioned principle.
Therefore, in the response, the name is not mentioned; for in the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa-dharma*, one simply says: "Venerable sir, I have already eaten my fill."
Regarding this, the *Vinaya* states that the remnants of a sick person may be consumed by anyone without performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), provided they are not medicinal substances.
This is because the ritual for medicinal substances involves recording the name and designating the illness as belonging specifically to oneself.

[Commentary] Furthermore, another interpretation holds that while the flavor of medicine is a general rule for the mouth, the ritual for the mouth also applies generally. This is because the ritual for the mouth is added to the two general rules for medicine, thereby excluding them.

Because it does not violate the rule regarding speech with others, the Vinaya text states that when medicine reaches the seven-day limit, if it is not suitable for the bhikṣus, the Buddha would not have exhorted them;
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* expresses the same intent, so I shall not cite it further at length.

Now, regarding the initial establishment of the thesis in this commentary: because the medicinal flavor is common [to all], everyone may consume it; therefore, it is said that the manual reception (*hasta-grahaṇa*) is also common.
Thus, it connects with the subsequent text, meaning that although the name is invoked and the rite is performed, the substance inherently possesses two types of commonality.

Consequently, one is permitted to have another person take it. The *Shichao* (Commentary on the *Sifenlü*) explains these two types of commonality as follows: first, the commonality of the medicinal flavor; second, the commonality of manual reception. This is acceptable.

Having verified that the characters were erroneous, one no longer harbors doubt. Therefore, the scriptural evidence cited below—namely, the rule for relinquishing medicine on the seventh day, where it states that the medicine is to be relinquished and given to other bhikṣus for their use—is this not a universal application? When the Buddhist teachings command relinquishment, they are thereby exhorting [one to do so].
As for the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* being the same, it says: "If a bhikṣu has honey-candied sugar [that has reached] the seventh day," and so forth; the comparison is made accordingly.

The Buddha asked, "Do you wish to drink? and the monk did not answer, "I wish to drink. This is another clear proof that when a bhikṣu receives stone honey (*śarkarā*) without performing the *pariśuddhi* (purification) rite, it is permissible.

[Commentary]: Regarding the nine methods of purification, one may perform the "seven-day" rite for medicinal substances; however, if one performs the oral rite with a biased mind, intending the substance for oneself, one must declare it.

Regarding the purification of stored medicines: because they are precious, they tend to increase greed for their flavor; as they are substantial and correspond to serious illnesses, they are subject to the rule of relinquishment.

However, if one receives them with the hand alone and does not prolong the duration, there is no need for the formal purification (*pariśuddhi*). As for the other three medicines, the opposite of this applies; it should be understood that they do not require the declaration of purity (*śuddhikaraṇa*).

Among the nine [categories], the first clarifies that for seven days one must maintain *śuddhi* (purity); this means that once the seven-day limit is reached, one must declare it as pure (*śuddha*) before storing it.

The following section explains the reason for this: first, because its substance is precious; second, because its flavor is heavy. If one were to merely receive it with the hand, it would be considered a temporary intake outside of the proper time.

The subsequent part clarifies the three medicines; "contrary to the above" refers to the absence of these two qualities. This is stated in reference to the *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines restricted by time).
There are also cases where [an object] is considered precious, yet because it is subject to common mixing and is not long-lasting, it is not treated as such.

[Commentary: Regarding the ten grave prohibitions (*daśa-guru-dharma*), there is an opening for exceptions: for what is received by hand, one loses [the status of the object] with every touch and completes [the offense] with every reception;

thus, even if repeated, there is no fault. As for what is received by mouth, most treatises state that after two [days], if five days have passed or less, one adds seven days [to the period of storage].

If two days are added to the six days during which one may touch the medicine according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one must not add medicine again; as it approaches the limit of purity, it is due to the force of its potency.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The seven-day period can be understood by the continuity of the medicine's potency."

In the first part of the tenth section, which clearly elucidates the [rules on] receiving [medicine], the initial discussion clarifies the allowance for receiving by hand regarding heavy offenses; next, it clarifies the restrictions and allowances regarding receiving by mouth.

Regarding the loss of [the five-day] period due to contact, this is discussed according to the nature of the dharma: because there is no [allowance for] a second day’s dharma, one may not reach the sixth day.

On the seventh day, one must immediately perform the *śuddhi* (purification/declaration). This is because, following the potency of the medicine, there is no need to take more; the supporting evidence for this can be understood [from the scriptures].
[Commentary] Question: If one has already taken medicine for more than seven days and may not add more, but the illness has not yet been cured and there is a new medicine available, may one add it?

Answer: If it is the same medicine, it may not; however, if it is a different substance, it should be permissible—just as the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that after six days, contact with the medicine causes its loss of efficacy and prohibits further preparation.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the addition of medicinal properties is permitted through the exchange of raw and cooked butter, as their flavors differ.
In the question, because the ancient masters maintained that [the addition] could never be repeated, the question was posed to resolve this.

In the answer, it is stated that while identical substances cannot be added—just as honey cannot be used both before and after [another substance]—different substances may be so added, such as when honey is used first and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) afterwards.

As for the citations of authority provided below: first, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* is cited to prove that identical substances cannot be added; next, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is cited to prove that different substances may be added.
Just as when fresh butter (*navanīta*) has been received for seven days and is then boiled to become clarified butter (*ghṛta*), another seven days are added.
[Commentary] Third, regarding the determination of the distinctions in offenses, this is discussed in four sections: first, the prevention of offenses; second, the arising of offenses;
third, the lightness or gravity of their storage and use; and fourth, the quantity of the offense incurred through consumption.

[Commentary] Regarding the first section on the *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines taken at the proper time): receiving [the food] with the hand prevents two offenses; not receiving it prevents the offense of improper contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*). Even if one receives it by opening the mouth, it likewise prevents these two offenses.

In the third section, concerning the prevention of offenses through compliance or non-compliance: the initial rule for *kālika-bhaiṣajya* is that it is fundamentally to be received with the hand; however, there is an occasion where the method of opening the mouth is permitted.

Because the hand is the instrument of action, the objects to be guarded against are not distinguished; the three medicines mentioned below share the same protection as the hand, yet each differs from the protection of the mouth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the two offenses concerning non-timely liquids (*vikāla-pāna*) and the protection of the hand: one offense is committed when one goes to receive them without being permitted; the second offense is committed when one receives them without being permitted.
Regarding the simultaneous consumption of food while holding it with a bad touch, there are two oral defenses: first, the defense against losing the received [alms] due to the lapse of time;
second, the defense against the bad touch that causes one to lose the received [alms] when the time has passed.

Regarding the two oral defenses during the improper time: if the ritual addition (*adhikāra*) is not performed, then upon the lapse of time, the received [alms] are lost, and thus they remain unreceived.

The two offenses regarding improper contact with medicine. [Commentary]: Among the medicines for the twenty-one-day period, receiving them with the hand prevents the first two; as before, these two medicines are prevented by the oral method. The four are:

first, preventing the loss of the formal acceptance due to exceeding the time limit; second, preventing the loss of acceptance through improper contact; third, preventing the offense of having medicine remain overnight without being consumed.

Fourth, by guarding [the medicine] throughout the night, one avoids the offense of "storing within" (*antargṛha-sthāpana*). According to the Vinaya texts, while the offense of storing within is a transgression for as long as one lives, there is no explicit prohibition against keeping medicinal substances for seven days;
therefore, we know that they must be kept [in a secure place]. Thus, the oral tradition prohibits three things but does not prohibit storing within.

Consequently, when the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that a bhikṣu’s seven-day medicine may be kept in the same location as the community’s food, it is understood that this refers to being contained within a purified area (*śuddhasthāna*).

Regarding the oral ritual (karmavācanā) for the seven-day period, there are four points to be guarded against. First, according to the ancient judgment, it is said that during those seven days, one may keep food overnight (antarāśaya), provided it is the same as the first two cases above;
however, in the latter two cases, it is "overnight" (vāsita) because the oral ritual is added, yet there is no "leftover" (saṃsṛṣṭa) or "touched by impurity" (duṣṭasparśa).

Based on the latter [point], the following clarifies the present judgment: within the seven-day limit for "non-timely" (akāla) food prescribed in the Vinaya, only the "leftover" and "impure touch" are permitted.

Regarding offenses such as taking food at improper times, only medicinal substances for life-long use are permitted; internal overnight storage (*antarāvasatha*), internal cooking (*antarasvayaṃpāka*), and self-cooking are to be understood by analogy with this.
Since these are not permitted even under the seven-day rule, one knows that the oral dharma does not prohibit internal overnight storage, and thus only three offenses apply.
As for the citation of evidence below, since it establishes the use of a pure ground (*śuddhabhūmi*), it is certain that [the seven-day rule] is not permitted.

[Commentary]: Regarding the fourth category, medicines for life-long use: the protection of the hands is the same as above; the protection of the mouth concerns five offenses, namely: improper contact (*duṣṭasparśa*), not receiving [food], food kept overnight (*sthāpita*), food cooked inside [the monastery] (*antaḥsiddha*), and food cooked by oneself (*svayaṃsiddha*).

Among those for life-long use, the five offenses protected against by the mouth should be stated as six offenses, as the term "cooked overnight" (*antaḥsthāpita*) has been omitted from the text following "kept overnight."
The three [cases] prior to this fall under the three categories mentioned below.

[Commentary]: Regarding the second point, the arising of offenses: originally, there were no two types of receiving [the precepts], so no offense would arise; it is because of the addition of two types of receiving that the offense arises accordingly.

[Commentary: When discussing the timing of medicinal substances in relation to their administration: if received by hand, they become subject to the fault of "bad contact" after noon; if kept overnight until the end of the night, they become "stale";
and if received orally, the characteristics of the offense incurred are likewise the same.
Next, regarding the offenses incurred when taking medicine: because one loses the validity of the formal acceptance (*paribhoga*) after noon, an unwholesome contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*) arises;

and because it was previously accepted by hand, there is the offense of "storing overnight" (*sāyaṃpāta*). These two offenses apply equally to all three types of medicine; no further explanation is provided below.

[Commentary]: Receiving with the hand at an improper time (*akāla*) results in the fault of "improper contact" (*duṣṭasparśa*) after noon has passed; by the end of the night, the fault of "storing overnight" (*saṃnidhi*) arises. Three faults arise through speech:
all are the faults of "improper contact," "storing overnight," and "improper time," occurring when the light of dawn appears. These differ slightly from those involving receiving with the hand.

Regarding the three offenses of the mouth committed at an improper time (*akāla*): because it clarifies that the limit has been exceeded, one commits this offense at an improper time even while it is still within the proper time (*kāla*).

Because one has previously accepted [the food], there is the fault of "remaining overnight" (*śeṣa-rātra*); because one has lost the method of acceptance, there is the fault of "improper contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśana*).

However, since only the factor of "improper time" is added, it is said to differ slightly from [the offense] regarding the hand. According to the rule for receiving with the hand, if it were past noon, there would necessarily be [these faults].
The reason why this is not clarified at this time can be understood by reflecting upon it.

[Commentary]: Regarding the offense incurred by receiving [food] with the hand for seven days, it is the same as before. Regarding the four offenses arising from speech, all are incurred when the limit is exceeded:
first, eating at the improper time; second, keeping food overnight; third, committing a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture); and fourth, improper contact.
For seven days, one receives orally the three offenses as above, with the addition of one *pāyattika* (offense of expiation); this is the fundamental transgression. [Commentary:

Some establish five [offenses], claiming that taking this medicine constitutes an offense; however, our current interpretation is not so. If one takes it, there is an offense; if one does not take it, there is no fault.

This differs from the four mentioned above, where the offense arises even if one does not take it. Furthermore, some establish that the offense arises from "not receiving" [the instruction]; however, our current interpretation is not so.
Receiving [the medicine] is not included among the offenses.

The subsequent section has two parts: first, it refutes the five offenses; therein, it is said that if one consumes *niḥsargika* medicine without having relinquished it, an additional *duṣkṛta* offense is incurred.

Now, below, it clarifies that this is not the case. If that were so, would one also incur an offense for not consuming [the medicine] in the case of the aforementioned four offenses? The answer is: No.

Regarding the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, this does not depend on the consumption [of the medicine]; whereas for the other three offenses, because they arise from receiving [the medicine], the fault exists prior to consumption, and the offense is only formally established upon consumption.
Since the fault of consuming the medicine is not caused by the act of receiving it, even if one consumes it, the offense incurred is a distinct transgression;
one cannot say that the fault exists prior to the consumption. Next, he refutes the six offenses, asserting that there are further [distinctions].

"Not receiving [the medicine] once" is now set forth below to clarify that it does not refer to the fault of exceeding the time limit; rather, the substance of the medicine is lost by its own nature as it becomes "not received.
This differs from the "non-timely" (*akāla*) or "overnight-kept" (*śeṣa*) offenses, which are faults in their very essence. Therefore, it is said to be subsumed under "non-offense" (*anāpatti*).

Even if one consumes it without having received it, this offense does not arise because of the act of receiving; since this clarifies that the offense arises [from the consumption itself], it cannot be established [as being caused by receiving].

[Commentary]: Regarding medicines for life-long use (*yāvajjīvikam*), two offenses arise from [using them] with the hands, as can be understood from the above; no offense arises from using them orally because the Blessed One permitted their use through the application of the formal procedure (*vidhi*), and thus the legal status of the substance is not lost.

Within the category of life-long medicines, no offense arises orally because the oral procedure was applied specifically to prevent various transgressions, and the nature of the substance remains intact.

Because the limit is fixed, no offense arises; however, according to the *Shanbuji*, it is said that six offenses arise—five being the same as those for the seven-day period—with the addition of taking medicine while not ill, which still follows the ancient interpretation. What is clarified here, by contrast, is intended to be exhaustive of the principle.

[Commentary]: If this is so, why is it that when one is touched [by an unordained person], the *upasaṃpadā* need not be received again? The answer is that through the empowerment of the ritual procedure (*dharmakarma-adhiṣṭhāna*), although one is touched, the status is not lost.
This is like the case in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* where rock honey was given to laypeople; furthermore, the original method of bestowing it upon a bhikṣu is not lost.

We know for certain that throughout one’s entire life there is no way to lose the dharma, just as in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, where even if illness temporarily ceases, the original method is not lost; therefore, there is no mention of illness as a cause for loss in the Vinaya.
Wearing [the robe] merely as a pretext constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense because there is a formal rule; if one does not apply the formal rite (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it is equivalent to a *pāyattika*.

In the question, there is doubt that the fault of contact arises because it produces an unwholesome touch. Therefore, in the answer, the first interpretation is judged as follows, citing evidence from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
"Because of that, the bhikṣu gave honey-candies on the seventh day to an upāsaka, who then took them..."

If one obtains rock honey (*śarkarā-madhu*) on the same day as other bhikṣus and takes it without performing the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification), [the offense is incurred]; this refers to consuming it within a single day and not declaring it pure again while keeping it.
Based on this precedent of the seven-day limit, one should understand that according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there is no fault of "contact" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) within the seven-day period;
this differs from the calculation of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* cited above. Next, citing the *Sārmavidyā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, what remains regarding the method for treating illness?
Because of the fault arising from [improper] consumption, the subsequent sections follow the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

If one knows that taking [medicines] lightly when not ill applies throughout one's life, then the oral precept (*mukha-dharma*) is established once and remains for the rest of one’s life without being lost. Question: In the Vinaya, if one takes [medicine] while not ill, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;

is this not because the offense arises from the act of receiving [the precept]? Answer: This is due to the violation of the rule regarding consumption, not because the offense arises from the act of receiving [the precept]. As stated later in the fourth section on "Consumption" (*paribhoga*).
[Commentary]: Third, regarding the gravity of keeping [medicines] for use. [Commentary]:
Fourth, among the medicines, keeping them for seven days is grave, while the other three are all light. The reason for this is that ghee and oil provide sustenance...

The gravity of the offense regarding the storage of food arises because the mind harboring greed and hoarding is heavy; furthermore, it constitutes a violation of the sacred teachings by constantly maintaining the practice of *śuddhika* (purification) while remaining attached, thereby failing to perform the recitation (*āviṣkaraṇa*) when the time limit has expired.

This is why it is established as a grave offense. As for the one type of *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (food for the proper time), although its utility is strong and its physical manifestation is abundant, it does not persist for long.

Since there is no need to establish a rule for its purification, and since there would be the fault of failing to recite what ought to be recited, it is considered light and is not subject to the same restrictions as non-timely food.

As for fermented liquids (*jang*), because their physical substance is narrow and their nature is subtle, there is no intention to store them for long; even though they are medicines for life (*yixinshou yao*) that may extend one's life and treat ailments, the purpose of storage is slight and the intent to hoard is thin.
Since there is no greed in storing them, the requirement to perform the *shuo jing* (purification) rite does not apply, and thus they are considered light.
Regarding the three types of storage, first, concerning the storage of medicines, the initial section is divided into two parts. First, a general indication of the gravity of the offense:

a violation of the *pāyattika* (heavy) constitutes a *thullaccaya* (light), which results in a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Below this, there is a detailed explanation, which is further divided into two parts.

First, the explanation of the seven-day storage of heavy items, which has four meanings: 1. the gravity of the object; 2. greedy storage; 3. constant retention; and 4. contravening the teaching regarding time. Next, the explanation of the three medicinal substances.

Regarding light-time medicine (*laghu-kālika-bhaiṣajya*), there is only the first of the four meanings; the "non-time" (*akālika*) category lacks all four meanings; and lifelong medicine (*yāvaj-jīvika*) possesses only the third meaning.

However, as for the single category of non-time medicine, since it does not involve long-term storage, its discussion is not considered here; therefore, the text does not mention "light" [medicine] in this context.
Alternatively, because it may be permitted for temporary storage, it is explained by way of analogy.

[Commentary] Question: Since keeping extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) and medicinal requisites (*bhaiṣajya*) both constitute an offense of *pāyattika*, should begging for robes and begging for medicine also be considered identical offenses? Answer:

The nature and substance of medicine are versatile and differ from those of robes. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that they are equal; just as begging for fine food is subject to a heavy regulation, begging for measured robes should likewise be light.
In resolving the objection, it is stated that regarding possession, clothing and medicine are equally grave; however, regarding begging, clothing is grave while medicine is light.

Therefore, the response cites them as being equivalent. There are two explanations: first, an explanation based on their difference, noting that clothing is distinct because it belongs to a specific category;

second, an explanation based on their similarity, noting that although begging for regular food is light, seeking fine food constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense), whereas begging [for ordinary food] previously does not.

Although the robes may be heavy, if one begs for them beyond the prescribed measure, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; thus, it is known that because the weight and lightness cannot be distinguished, they are said to be "equal.

[Commentary] Next, regarding the principle that there are varying degrees of lightness and heaviness in their usage, the meaning is not fixed. For instance, the robes may be heavy while the medicine is light, as in the case of a layperson.

Regarding leftover medicine and the like, or when the medicine is heavy and the robe light—just as with leftover food—if one wears it, one commits an offense involving the forfeiture of the robe; the cases where both are heavy or both are light should be understood by analogy with the examples above.
Next, to clarify the application [of these rules], we shall formulate propositions based on the robes to specifically illustrate the [rules for] medicine. First, regarding the white three-robe set:

If one wears [the garment], one commits a *thullaccaya*; if one consumes the leftover medicine after it has been set aside, one commits a *dukkaṭa*. The relative gravity of the offenses in the subsequent phrases can be understood accordingly:

both are heavy when wearing a white robe while consuming leftover food that has been kept overnight; both are light when wearing a robe subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) while consuming medicine that has been set aside.
Therefore, it is said that this is explained by comparison with the former.
[Commentary: Fourth, an explanation of the gravity of the offenses incurred by consuming medicine.

Regarding the medicinal substances taken at the proper time (*kālabhojana*): with each swallow, one incurs seven offenses—namely, the offenses of *vikāla* (eating at the wrong time), *atirakta* (eating leftovers), *aparigrhīta* (eating what has not been formally accepted), *antarāvasatha* (storing within the monastery), *antarasvinnaka* (cooking within the monastery), *svapākya* (cooking for oneself), *duṣṭasparśa* (impure contact), three *thullaccaya* (grave offenses), and four *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoings).
This enumeration is stated in reference to those who possess [the full set of requisites]; it cannot be applied universally to all cases.

The four clarifications regarding the confession of offenses begin with the section on "Medicine Taken at Appropriate Times. Here, the number of offenses is first enumerated; below this, it is shown that their presence or absence is not fixed.
[Commentary]: Regarding "non-timely juice," if it is raw juice, there are only five offenses; there is no offense for cooking inside, cooking by oneself, or transformation.
Regarding the seven factors for maturation as mentioned above, this is based on the case where one eats immediately after the addition of the formal rite until the appearance of the dawn light;

in such cases, there are certainly offenses of eating at the improper time (*akāla-bhakṣaṇa*), eating leftovers (*vighasa*), and impurity through contact (*parāmṛṣṭa*), while other offenses such as eating what was stored overnight (*paryuṣita*) or what was cooked overnight (*pakva-paryuṣita*) depend on specific conditions and are not fixed.

In the section on "Improper Time" (*akāla*), the first part uses the categories of "cooked" and "uncooked" to demonstrate the number of offenses; the following part demonstrates the determinate and indeterminate [offenses].

[Commentary: The transgression of exceeding the seven-day limit is to be understood as above. If one adds the two offenses involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) and usage, there are then four *pāyattika* (or *pratideśanīya*) and five *duṣkṛta* (or *sthūlātyaya*).

Within the seven-day period, adding two offenses of *niḥsargika-pāyattika* constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for using [the medicine] prematurely; when added to the previous [offenses], they total nine offenses. [Commentary] Question:
Among the aforementioned arising offenses, there is neither arising nor receiving [of the transgression]; why then is there [a transgression] within this administration [of medicine]? Answer:

The arising [of offenses] is established by way of oral ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) based on two conditions. What is stated here concerns the administration itself, just as with the seven-day medicine (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*), where the ritual procedure (*adhikāra*) is added.

If one does not consume within the limited time, one merely incurs the offense of *atikrama* (exceeding the limit), which is a *dukkaṭa*. If one eats again, then there are offenses such as eating at the improper time (*vikāla-bhojana*), consuming food kept overnight (*sāyaṃ-vikāla-saṃsatta*), or touching food with impure hands (*appaṭiggahita*), as described above.

Next, regarding the "method for guarding against the arising [of offenses] by means of the mouth" discussed in the section on questions and answers: this refers to the fact that the method of the mouth can prevent one from receiving [an offense], but it cannot prevent the arising of what has not been received.
Therefore, while it is fully enumerated within the context of "guarding," it is not discussed within the context of "arising.

This clarifies that the categories of "use" and "non-use" are distinct and must not be conflated. To illustrate this further, we shall take the seven-day [medicine] as an example to clarify the distinction between using and not using it, and the resulting offenses.
"Different" means not wearing [the same robes]; "one mention" refers to the offense of transgression; "one instance" refers to the offense of acting immediately.
This constitutes two additional offenses appended to the preceding text as mentioned above; that which exists as such refers to the seven offenses previously mentioned.

[Commentary]: Regarding medicines for life-long use, if the formal ritual (*vidhi*) is performed, there is no fault. The meaning of "life-long" is that once the ritual of acceptance is completed, it is not lost;
thus, one may take them even when not ill, though doing so incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If the ritual is not performed, one incurs the full seven offenses: three *thullaccaya* and four *duṣkṛta*.
The further details of these characteristics are as explained extensively in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*), first, if one possesses the dharma, there is no fault because one has vowed to live by it; since the life-span is exhausted, there will necessarily be no further faults.
This is because once the physical form is lost, the meaning of possessing the dharma ceases, and thus there are no transgressions—there is only one auspicious outcome.

Next, to clarify that there are faults when the dharma is not possessed, the text below points to the root precepts, namely those concerning not receiving food at improper times, not consuming leftovers, and so forth.
[Commentary: Furthermore, for example, if one begs four kinds of fine foods together with five kinds of staple foods and leftover medicines kept overnight, there are nine offenses for each swallow;
yet, when repenting of these offenses, if one names all nine falls simultaneously, they are extinguished.
Next, regarding the four kinds of fine foods—milk, curd, fish, and meat—one must request them from others;

as for the five types of formal meals, if they have been kept overnight, each of the nine items constitutes a separate offense. To consume them together constitutes one *pārājika* (falling) offense per swallow.

If the following section clarifies that they may be confessed together because they belong to the same category, then each item is named individually, and the single method of repentance extinguishes them all.
[Commentary: What has been listed above is termed "prolixity. To distance oneself from this amidst such detail is entirely rare in the final age;

is it not because the affliction of craving is so grave that even excellent remedies cannot save one? Furthermore, it is because one suspects that the medicine of the Dharma is not sublime, hoping instead for a dual treatment of both the elixir and the medicinal pill. Thus it is said.

In the initial section of the *Jiegao*, it is first shown that the text is extensive; in the subsequent section, it clarifies that upholding [the precepts] is minimal. How is it that the following passage deduces the reason for not upholding them?

First, it clarifies that the delusions are heavy: although one’s disposition may be excellent, the affliction is incurable. Furthermore, the following section rebukes those who are negligent regarding the teachings:
although the medicine is most marvelous, they discard it and refuse to take it, and yet they do not fear the suffering to come—this is precisely what the mind craves like a drink.
"Maru" refers to two types of punitive treatment in the hells: molten copper and hot iron balls.

[Commentary] Next, regarding the meaning of the prohibitions and permissions according to the textual characteristics: when ordinary beings dwell in the world, the four great elements constitute their bodies. At the transition between late summer and early autumn, the seasonal energies contend with one another;
as the earth, wind, water, and fire differ in their essence and function, if even one element is out of harmony, all manner of illnesses arise.

As soon as one takes it up, it causes the abandonment of spiritual cultivation and the inability to remain focused on the holy task; therefore, out of compassionate pity, the Sage permitted its use to treat the suffering of the physical body.

However, because this leads to the expansion of hoarding and long-term greed, which destroys one's conduct and involves a profound transgression—offending externally against the precepts and internally betraying one's own conscience—it was established as a formal offense (*pāyattika*).

Second, regarding the separate explanation of the intent behind the regulations according to the text: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation. First, explaining the intent of the allowance (*anujñā*):

at the end of the summer retreat and the beginning of autumn, cold and heat are not in harmony, hence they are said to "compete. Although illness arises throughout the four seasons, it is most prevalent during two specific times.

Furthermore, as this is attached to the context of the precepts (*śīla*), the two periods—the conclusion of summer and the beginning of autumn—are cited. [The elements of] earth, water, fire, and wind...
Because wind pervades all phenomena, it is likewise termed "great earth. Water is heavy, while wind and fire are light and buoyant; thus, their essential natures differ.
Earth is that which is supported, whereas wind functions through agitation, water through moistening, and fire through maintenance;

thus, their functions differ. Regarding "binding karma," this refers to the binding of the mind to its primary karmic causes. Next, the intention behind the prohibitions is explained, namely, the *Piṅgala* [Sūtra].
"Externally violating" means harming others; "internally failing" means harming oneself.

[Commentary] Five conditions constitute an offense: first, the substance of the seven-day medicine has not been formally accepted by mouth, in which case there is no offense of prolongation; second, it is clear that the two acts of formal acceptance have been completed;

third, the rite of *viśuddhi* (purification) has not been performed; fourth, the limit has been exceeded or the conditions for its duration have expired; and fifth, there are no obstructing difficulties.

Regarding the offense: among the conditions for an offense, the four instances of exceeding the limit constitute the primary conditions for the offense. If the illness is cured and one immediately takes [the medicine], it corresponds to an offense of *duṣkṛta* (light transgression).

Fifth, regarding the "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*) in the *Wúzhēnàocháo*, it is called "without conditions" (*wúyuán*), meaning if [the substance] is lost or destroyed, or if one treats it as something other than medicine, and so forth.
There are eight circumstances under which one does not commit an offense regarding the *atirekacīvara* (extra robe).
[Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu suffered from a wind-disorder (*vāta-roga*) during the autumn months; his body became emaciated and sores broke out. The Buddha said:
"I allow those with the condition of illness to consume ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and fat, whether at the proper time or at an improper time. [The Buddha was] in Rājagṛha at the Piṅgala...

The assembly of *gaṇas* became greatly inflated and arrogant, leading both monastics and laypeople to criticize them. They reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established the prohibition.

[Commentary: Within the context of the causal conditions for the precept, from the beginning up to the section on "taking medicine at improper times," two instances of the Buddha being in Rājagṛha clarify the transgressions and the subsequent establishment of the rule.
Regarding the aforementioned medicines, some commentators explain that fat (*vasā*) is a "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*), unlike clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Regarding oil, it is now explained that this refers to a portion for seven days; both the *Mahāsāṃghika* and the *Pañcavargika* Vinayas likewise state that this refers to fat.
In the context of the causal narrative for the precept, because its initial allowance led to excess and invited public reproach, it was subsequently prohibited.

Since Pilindavatsa—whom everyone knew as the Buddha’s foremost disciple—caused his many followers to accumulate large quantities of it, we know that this was indeed a gift of faith (*śraddhā-dakṣiṇā*).

The root of the arising of transgressions lies in the mind; when turning toward the Path, be careful not to approach them. There are those who disparage the lower [traditions] and judge them as false, citing evidence for their current interpretation as previously detailed.
Those who say the two Vinayas are the same as the present *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part) Vinaya mean that those two codes are identical to the current *Dharmaguptaka*.

【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu is ill (meaning that a physician has instructed him to take a certain kind of medicine), he may consume the remaining medicines—ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar—for up to seven days.
(The eightfold phrasing and meaning are as previously stated in the rules on robes. If he consumes them beyond the seven-day limit, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
[Note] Regarding the method for returning medicine that was to be relinquished after it has been given to the Saṃgha and the offense has been confessed:

on the seventh day, one should relinquish it to a bhikṣu, who should then take it and eat it. If seven days have passed, ghee and oil are to be smeared on the door and the lintel; honey and rock sugar are to be given to the park-keeper.

If less than seven days have passed, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) to return it; the bhikṣu shall then take it to smear on his feet or to light a lamp.

Usage. [Vinaya] *Pāyattika*. [Commentary] Regarding the commonality and non-commonality of offenses for bhikṣuṇīs, these distinctions are as explained above concerning relinquishment, usage, and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the seven phrases of the *Prātimokṣa*: (1) one person; (2) illness; (3) the causal condition. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are four hundred and four types of illnesses:

one hundred and one each for water, fire, wind, and miscellaneous disorders. For wind disorders, oil is used; for heat disorders, ghee; for water disorders, honey; and for miscellaneous disorders, all three.
Thus it is said, "the physician instructs one to take [medicine]. (4) The three residual medicines: this enumerates their names and characteristics. (5) The limit of seven days.
Taking [medicine] daily according to the prescribed limit is the rule; taking it for more than seven days violates the Dharma. The following two cases can be understood accordingly.

In the second section of the *Śīlaskandha-vibhaṅga*, the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] is first cited to show "sickness" and "various sicknesses," which refers to the three types of wind-disorders arising together.
Below, the medical treatment is clarified, showing that the physician, knowing the illness, instructs that medicine must be taken. (4)
"Zhongji" (中給) means "to bestow. [Commentary] Question:

Since the *kāṭhina* robe is clarified in the section on extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), why is it not mentioned in this precept? Answer: Because the internal and external [categories of robes] are distinct;
thus, the benefits and losses do not extend to one another.
In the initial question and answer, it is stated that [the *kaṭhina*] prevents loss but does not cause defilement;

it prevents harm but does not provide moisture. [Commentary: Question: Since the original purpose of receiving the *kaṭhina* was to allow for the benefit of keeping extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) and medicine, why is it not permitted to receive them [as separate items]?

Answer: Regarding robes, the original regulation established that they must be kept and not separated from one’s person; thus, receiving the *kaṭhina* allows for staying apart overnight. However, this benefit extends to extra robes, whereas there is no such regulation regarding medicine.
Furthermore, since robes are limited in their utility, how could one be permitted to keep *kāṣāya* (robes) and medicine overnight?
The intent of the subsequent question is: why is it that *kāṣāya* must be formally accepted (*parigraha*), while medicine is not?

In the response, the first three lines clarify that robes must be accepted, while the final two lines clarify that medicine is not restricted [in its storage], as it can only cure illness; thus, it is said to be "limited in utility."

[Commentary] Question: Why is the *kārttika* month not mentioned in response? Answer: Regarding the use of robes, there is a fixed regulation for the four seasons; one may repair and wash them during the cool autumn.
However, the preparation of *kārttika* medicine must wait for illness before it is undertaken. Since its arrival cannot be easily anticipated, it is not required [at that time].
Therefore, the text does not mention the month of *kārttika* medicine.

Regarding the three questions on the non-opening [of the *kārttika* medicine-month], in the response, the first two phrases clarify that robes are permitted, while the last two phrases clarify that medicine is not permitted. [Commentary] Question:
The root text of the robe-precept states, "One may keep extra robes. Why does it not say here, "one may keep extra medicine"? Answer: The three robes are subject to formal regulation (*niyama*).

Since the storage of non-long-term items is contrasted with the non-long-term to clarify what constitutes long-term, and there is no such counterpart for medicinal substances—wherein only their storage is permitted—the text does not explicitly mention "long-term" in that context.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: although the word "long-term" is absent, because there are "residual medicines," one knows that the meaning is the same while the phrasing differs.

Within the four question-and-answer pairs, there are two meanings. First, the explanation based on their difference: it is said that while a robe may be considered "extra," medicine is not termed "extra.
Next, the explanation based on their identical meaning: the term *śeṣa* (residue/remainder) carries the same sense as "extra."
[Commentary]: If that is so, when one has not eaten for seven days and commits the offense of *atireka* (excess) on the eighth day, can this be called *śeṣa* (residue)? Answer:
Because both are viewed in relation to the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), they are both termed *śeṣa*. Thus, the text says: "If one obtains long-term benefits such as ghee, oil, and so forth..."

Regarding the difficult point raised concerning whether food may be termed "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*) when not eaten, the answer clarifies that among the four supports (*niśraya*), the practice of the superior conduct (*uttara-caryā*) and the fundamental observances (*mūla-dhāraṇa*) are all permitted as exceptions; thus, one should understand that the designation "extra" (*atirikta*) does not apply exclusively to clothing.
Therefore, the following citation from the section on the characteristics of receiving the precepts serves as proof.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the precept on robes, it says "to possess" (*tsū*) and yet uses the term "to wear" (*fuku*). Answer: The purpose of possessing is fundamentally for the sake of wearing; if one does not wear them, one does not possess them.
Therefore, the intent of possession is taken as the basis for listing this in the precepts. However, at the time one incurs the offense, it does not depend upon wearing them.
Furthermore, when discussing greed for robes, it is mostly for the sake of accumulation and storage, rather than for wearing them; thus, [the term "wearing"] is not listed.

Regarding the five questions on the mutual clarification of the rules for storing and wearing robes and medicine, in the initial response it is shown that the reason for the medicine precept is stated as "wearing," whereas the following section clarifies the robe precept by indicating the intent behind "storing. [Commentary]: Question:

Regarding the medicine precept, there is a limit on over-consumption, yet regarding robes, there is no mention of a limit on over-wearing. Answer: For robes, there is no fixed limit for wearing; for medicine, there is only...
Regarding the reason for the seven-day limit on wearing [medicinal cloth]:
when the sixth question cites the text of this precept as "if one exceeds seven days," the corresponding rule for robes should state "exceeding ten days.
The answer is that there is no time limit for wearing an inner robe, whereas medicinal substances have a limit for consumption; therefore, they cannot be treated as identical cases.

[Commentary] Question: In comparison with the precept regarding robes, there ought to be the practice of *viśuddha-dāna* (pure giving); why is it absent here? Answer: Because robes lack ambiguity, whereas medicines have external uses;

thus, there is a difference between wearing them and not wearing them. Alternatively, it may be omitted, as in the eight topical sections on the distinctions of *viśuddha-dāna* and so forth found in the commentary.

Regarding the seventh question on the precept concerning robes, it says: "If one accepts an impure gift [of medicine], keeping it for more than ten days should apply equally to medicine as well. In the initial response, the answer is given based on their differences:

since there is no confusion regarding robes because they serve only a single purpose, whereas medicine serves two purposes—internal use (which may be mentioned) and external use (which is unnecessary)—robes are worn while medicine is not.
Alternatively, in the subsequent response, the answer is given based on their similarities, as noted in the commentary.

The eight sections constitute a detailed explanation of the eighth of the eight precepts regarding pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*) and non-transgression; it is merely that the root text (*sūtra*) does not include the formal recitation (*saṃgīti*).
[Commentary: From "This should be abandoned" below, the characteristics of the purification of offenses are clarified, which is divided into three parts. First, up to "he should take that food,"...

This means that when the second day’s medicine reaches the house where the first day’s medicine was kept, it is precisely at the completion of the eighth *muhūrta* (period) of the seventh day; therefore, it is said to have "reached seven days.

Since there is no longer any fault of overnight storage (*sāṃstarika*), the rule regarding the mouth [of the vessel] still remains in effect, and permission is granted to give it as food to the Saṃgha.

Second, if it exceeds seven days, the limit of the first day has passed and various faults are incurred; because the owner is no longer permitted to eat it, it is given to laypeople. Third, it is reduced.
The "seven-day period" refers to the rule regarding the medicinal substances of the third day; it does not extend beyond the following day.

Once the limit has passed, one must return them to their owner and perform the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*). Beyond seven days, there is no further principle for consuming them. This regulation applies to external bodily use.

Within this context, those who discard [the medicine] on the fourteenth day through successive transmission, or those who discard it on the twelfth day while still combining it with the three uses—these all enter the category of "gardeners. You should reflect upon this yourself; do not merely recite it.

This is the section on the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Regarding the first sub-section of the second part within the commentary, it first clarifies the general meaning. The commentary states: "The one who administers the punishment makes the formal announcement to harmonize the Saṃgha;
the offender then recites the confession three times. This explains the three stages mentioned below, which refers here to receiving [the precepts] on the first day.

Regarding the medicinal substances, one may receive them for up to seven days; however, by the time the first day has passed and the second day has begun, all subsequent days constitute a transgression through mutual contamination.

Once they have been relinquished, they may both be returned to their original state. Therefore, in the threefold judgment within the text, the discussion is based on the case of relinquishment on the eighth day.
As for the substance obtained on the second day of the first stage, its essence does not exceed the limit, yet it constitutes a transgression due to mutual contamination.

Therefore, regarding the two periods during which the Sangha is permitted to eat: if the first day exceeds the limit, it constitutes a fundamental offense (*mūla-āpatti*), because the food has incurred the fault of being stored overnight (*supta-sparśana*) and so forth, and thus the Sangha is not permitted to consume it.
Consequently, it is given to the *ārāmika* (monastery attendant)—that is, those who oversee and protect the monastery. Regarding the three periods:

if one obtains [the food] on the third day, it likewise constitutes a defiled offense (*rañjana-āpatti*). Only by the eighth day does it become permissible; since six days have passed, it is permitted to be returned to its original owner.
Regarding the statement that one may return on the following day: previously it was said that long-term medicines do not necessarily require an overnight interval;

now, considering the matter carefully, this may apply to both cases, or one may simply follow the ancient practice. If one relies on the nature of the medicine itself, which lasts exactly seven days, it is logically appropriate to declare it "pure" (śuddha);
however, because it exceeds seven days due to the influence of the defiling factor, it must be used externally and cannot be brought into the pure area. Even so...
Regarding the recipient who accepts [the medicine] on the seventh day, even if it has passed one night, the judgment is the same as this.
Herein, "successive" refers to accepting the medicine day by day for seven days; on the eighth day, all become defiled by transgression simultaneously.

One may either abandon and repent on that very day, or until the fourteenth day—thus there are three judgments regarding the presence or absence of completeness. Therefore, both acceptance and abandonment are...

The ancient records concerning the seven-day period contain errors that are difficult for later students to understand; therefore, I have briefly provided a diagrammatic illustration. Regarding the term "successive transfer" (*kṣepa-krama*):

this refers to the fact that from the time one receives [the object] during the first seven days until the time one relinquishes it during the subsequent seven days, its three uses may shift and change.
For example, if one receives it on the third day and relinquishes it on the eighth day, one may return it to the original owner for use; however, if [one relinquishes it] on the ninth day...
If one relinquishes [the robe] on the tenth day, it is relinquished to the Sangha; if one relinquishes it on the eleventh day, it is given to the park-keeper (*ārāmika*).
However, if it is given to the park-keeper after the seventh day has passed, there is no longer the possibility of successive transfer. Regarding the statement "twelve days combined with three":

this refers to the five days starting from the eighth day onward, during which the relinquishment is combined with three uses. On the thirteenth day, there are only two uses; on the fourteenth day, [there is only one].
The sole purpose is as can be seen in the diagram. To the question, "Why does it only extend to the fourteenth day? the answer is:
those who leave thereafter are all judged in the same way, as they have already entered the enclosure; thus, the other days are not explained.
"One should reflect upon this" means to direct one's attention toward it. "Do not recite these words" is a warning against following them blindly.

[Commentary] Question: Why is it that while extra robes may still be worn as one's own, medicinal substances that have become "extra" cannot be used as one's own? Answer: Robes merely prevent the fault of excess;

once they are relinquished, that fault is extinguished. Medicinal substances, however, are distinct from robes in that they incur the fault of "overnight contact" (*sāmisadṛṣṭi*) when they become extra; therefore, they may not be used.

In the initial question of the *Guǎngwèndá* (Extensive Questions and Answers), it is asked: "Since the example of robes is cited, it would follow that medicine should likewise be permitted for consumption;
why then is it not the same? In the response, first the long robe (*cīvara*) is clarified, and next the long medicine is explained.

It is said that [medicine] is the same as the robe because once discarded, its transgression is extinguished; however, it is not the same as the robe because it still retains the impurity of overnight contact (*sūchù*).
