The topical outline (*arthamukha*) for the ninety *pāyattika* rules consists of seven sections. In the first section, which provides a general classification, it states "the three karmas" (*trikarma*), yet only body and speech are listed;
this is because the karma of the mind (*manaskarma*) is pervasive throughout them all.
[Commentary: Among the first thirty-one rules, which ones are those recorded by verse concerning the formal procedures (*dharmakarma*) of improper performance? Each shall be examined individually.
A woman who has not yet reached puberty; forcibly removing [the robe]; making a screen; giving [food] separately; an offense other than a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; not sitting outside; a screen and exposure;
four; three; an army; water; wine; striking; half-white; two; following; beating; a palace.

Next, regarding the section on bodily offenses (*kāyika-āpatti*), the phrase "individual enumeration of legal matters" (*dharma-kriyā-ekaika-gaṇanā*) refers generally to all the verses, as they encompass both dual observance and dual violation. Since the following verses cannot be indicated as pairs, [the text lists them individually]:

*nārī* (with a woman), *anupasaṃpanna* (with one who has not received full ordination), *balāt* (forcibly spreading bedding), *utkṣiptaka* (sitting on a bed with removable legs), *chādita* (roofing a house beyond three layers), *kṛta* (making robes for a nun), *rahasi* (sitting in private with a nun), and *datta* (giving...).

(1) Eating at improper times; (2) eating separately from the community; (3) eating more than three bowls; (4) eating at the wrong time; (5) eating leftover food; (6) eating food not formally offered; (7) giving food to non-Buddhists; (8) sitting forcefully in a house where people are eating;

(9) sitting in private with a woman; (10) sitting in the open with a woman; (11) receiving medicinal requisites for more than four months; (12) going to view military formations; (13) staying beyond the limit within an army;

(14) watching an army engaged in battle; (15) drinking alcohol; (16) playing in water; (17) striking another; (18) bathing more than once every half-month; (19) wearing white-colored robes; (20) [the twenty items].
(1) Following a suspended bhikṣu; (2) following a suspended śrāmaṇera; (3) striking (a bhikṣu); (4) assaulting (a bhikṣu); (5) entering the royal palace.
[Commentary]: There are twenty-one precepts that are offenses of vocal karma rather than bodily karma; therefore, the verse records them as follows:

"Destruction, two types of same-speech, speaking of women, difference, suspicion, censuring nuns, censuring the Dharma, terror, doubt, initiating desire, refusal, same-desire, groundless slander"—these twenty-one words constitute the retention [of the precepts].
Next, regarding the offenses, the first section concerns: (1) lying; (2) slander; (3) divisive speech; (4) reciting together with one who is not fully ordained;

(5) speaking of grave offenses; (6) claiming to have attained the Path; (7) preaching the Dharma to women beyond the limit; (8) using improper or false speech; (9) reviling the administrative officials; (10) instructing nuns arbitrarily; (11) disparaging those who instruct nuns;

(12) preaching the Dharma to nuns until evening; (13) intimidating bhikṣus; (14) causing doubt and distress to bhikṣus; (15) initiating disputes through the four types of litigation; and (16) communicating one’s consent (*chanda*) while stating it is not an obstacle.

(1) Refusing [to follow] the Path; (2) Refusing [to accept] exhortations to study; (3) Destroying the Vinaya; (4) Consenting to a *karmavācanā* and later regretting it; (5) Granting consent (*chanda*) and later regretting it; (6) Groundless slander regarding a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The final two characters summarize the preceding items.
[Commentary]: Formerly it was said that "receiving [the precepts] at a young age" constitutes an oral karmic offense; however, my current interpretation is not so.

According to the Vinaya, the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) is not the *śīla-ācārya* (precept teacher), because at that time the *upādhyāya* sat silently among the assembly and never spoke. Thus we know this interpretation is not what the Vinaya establishes.

As for the offenses of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) and *pāyattika* (expiation), these involve performing an action oneself while relying on the words of another, such as when one later acts for the sake of the Path.
Next, the refutation of what is not the Middle Way begins with the restatement of the ancient interpretation; this is followed by the actual refutation. First, the refutation based on the meaning;
next, the indication of the present judgment. As for the phrase "pointing as in the subsequent section," the text is found in the following chapter.

[Commentary: Third, regarding those pertaining to both body and speech, these are further divided into two categories. There are thirty-one precepts concerning the active functions (*karmapatha*) of speech that are transgressed through the conjunction of body and mind;
following these, there are seven precepts concerning the abstinent functions (*virati-karmapatha*) of speech that are transgressed through the conjunction of body and mind.
[Commentary] Regarding the preceding section, there are three divisions.
[Commentary] The first consists of nineteen precepts concerning offenses committed through verbal action that relies upon another’s body. The verse says:
digging, destroying, pulling, using, inciting, burning, hiding, drinking, killing, driving away, giving clothing, seizing, causing to fall, jewels, high beds—these seven precepts are all included.

Regarding the first section of the nineteen precepts within the three categories of body and speech: (1) digging the earth; (2) destroying living things; (3) dragging [someone out of a room]; (4) using water containing insects;

(5) urging [another] to eat until full; (6) lighting a fire in the open air; (7) hiding another’s robes or bowl; (8) drinking water containing insects; (9) killing animals; (10) driving [someone] out of a settlement; (11) giving robes [to a nun];
(12) taking hold of precious objects (due to picking up what was left behind); and (13) high beds—these seven precepts are all included [in this category]. (1) High...

1) Feet; 2) cotton-padded cushions; 3) needle cases made of ivory or horn; 4) oversized sitting mats; 5) wound-covering garments; 6) rain-bathing robes; 7) those equal to the Buddha’s robes—“equal” (等) meaning they are the same as these.
[Commentary]: Regarding this section on precepts, if one discusses the nature of one's own karma, violations involving only body and mind belong to the first category.

However, according to the principle that teaching another constitutes one's own violation—as previously stated regarding the instruction to dig the earth—the offense is not yet incurred until the actual digging by the other person has been completed;

it requires the physical act of digging and the destruction of living beings by the other party for the instructor to incur the offense. Therefore, it is said that while the verbal action is performed by oneself, the physical execution relies upon the body of another, which differs from the case of false speech.
Since there is no distinct matter [in the phrasing], the statement "upon completion" (*kṛta*) refers directly to the offense; the others should be understood by analogy.
In the section on discernment (*vibhaṅga*), because these various precepts constitute an offense whether committed by oneself or taught to another, they span both preceding and succeeding categories.

First, it was explained that they belong to the preceding category; now, next, it is explained that they belong to the succeeding category. First, the act of digging and destroying is cited to clarify that they do not fall below [the preceding category]. Furthermore, [it is] distinguished.
Regarding the phrase "the remainder of the individual words," this refers by example to the other precepts.

[Commentary]: If that is so, then as in the case of speaking deceptively to another—where the offense is not yet fully established until one awaits what is heard, and upon hearing it, there is an immediate bodily action—here we take "bodily action" (*kāyakarman*) in its specific sense as the movement that constitutes the performance of the act, rather than taking it in its general sense as the mere cognition of what is heard.

In resolving the objection, it is argued that since the offense is established through false speech, the case is identical to "borrowing from another," and thus this serves as the basis for the objection.

In the response, it is explained that the nature of the action differs: actions such as digging or destroying are termed "bodily" (kāyika) and are specific activities; whereas when the five sense organs encounter their objects and their functional application has not yet manifested, it is termed "mental" (nāman) and is a pervasive activity.
[Commentary]: Among the seven precepts regarding verbal actions, there is one that involves making a false claim by relying on the bodies of oneself and others.

For instance, in the case of making a prior appointment for travel, one must first agree together and later, when traveling along the same road and crossing a boundary, the offense is committed. The verse says: "In both private and public places, four types of appointments; requesting fine food."

Regarding the first of the seven subsequent precepts: it first demonstrates the nature of the action, and subsequently summarizes it in verse. [The offenses include: spreading out bedding in a secluded place;

likewise, regarding the four types of prior verbal instruction (the first being instructing another to spread bedding for oneself, the second being traveling with a nun in the same boat, the third being traveling with bandits, and the fourth being traveling with a woman)—if one requests fine food by first speaking to the donor, and the other person gives me food only after I have requested it, then I commit an offense.

[Commentary: Regarding the five subsequent precepts, one performs the action oneself while relying on another’s speech for its completion—just as when consuming *praśaṃsāhāra* (food praised by others), one relies on the speech of a *bhikṣuṇī* to complete the bodily act of swallowing;
the other cases are analogous. As the verse says: "Praising, admonishing, the two types of listening, and [accepting] those under five years of age.
For instance, regarding the violation of an admonition, there is also the refusal through speech; here, we shall distinguish their specific meanings based on a single characteristic.

Regarding the latter five precepts: first, the characteristics are shown; next, the verses summarize and praise them—[the precept on] eating with a nun (praising the eating of others), [the precept on] praising oneself for eating (because one eats for oneself), and [the precept on] admonishing (not accepting admonitions from others, while rejecting those who admonish me).

Second, regarding the two types of listening: (1) eavesdropping during the settlement of the four disputes, and (2) not covering one's ears while listening; both involve what is said by another. Regarding the granting of full ordination to one whose age is insufficient: the preceptor commits an offense by sitting in silence, whereas the act is completed through the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) performed by others.

Furthermore, below this, the precept on admonishing is specifically distinguished: if one takes up the words and rejects them, it should belong to the karma of speech; here, however, we clarify that it is not so.
Because this section on "Receiving Many" is discussed in relation to the body, it is said to have "one characteristic.
[Commentary] The second major section contains seven items concerning the verbal prohibitions against householders and the joint commission of offenses by body and mind. The verse says:
"Covering the back, the feet, the improper time, the householder, the true [nature], and not giving consent."
The second category, the "Speech-Stop" (vācā-virati), consists of seven precepts that all possess specific instructional methods;

this is because an offense is incurred when one acts with the body while refraining from speech. The verses include: concealment (of a grave offense), backbiting (successive eating), sufficiency (of food), untimely [entry into a village], visiting families [before or after a meal], true [alms-giving], and departing without having been granted permission.

[Commentary: Regarding the concealment of a single precept, various interpretations are not uniform. The *Karmavibhaṅga* states that the offense is completed through mental action; this refers to the primary factor.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states that an offense occurs through both body and mind when one sees or hears of another's transgression and harbors concealment without speaking of it;

this involves verbal action and its scope cannot yet be definitively partitioned. What is stated here—namely, that upon hearing of a fault, one speaks of it directly and thus has no personal offense—is intended to mean that the verbal act of non-disclosure is what constitutes the offense.
Because the mind harbors concealment (*mrakṣa*), it serves as the root of physical transgression; therefore, both are taken together.

In the separate explanation, first various interpretations of the *Gāthā* are cited: regarding the "mind," this refers to the general characteristic of the offense, which is difficult to manifest clearly and thus cannot be used in its entirety.

According to the *Jianlun* (Sūtra on Seeing), body and mind are raised together in their general and specific aspects; seeing and hearing pertain to the body, while harboring concealment pertains to the mind.

The *Xinju* states: "Since 'not speaking' is itself the cessation of speech, it generally pertains to vocal karma; however, because the text does not explicitly indicate this, one cannot yet distinguish it.

Below, we shall provide a definitive judgment: it actually pertains to all three types of karma. While 'abandoning' applies generally, when referring specifically to its ultimate destination, it is assigned to the physical and vocal [karmas] according to their respective categories.
Thus, it is said that both [physical and vocal] are taken, with the mental included therein; this can be clearly discerned."
[Commentary] Next, the second section is explained: the distinctions regarding offenses based on committing them oneself or instructing others.
There are twelve precepts where instructing another results in a concurrent offense; the remainder are minor. The verse says:

"Digging, destroying, pulling, using, urging, threatening, burning, hiding, killing, drinking, groundless [accusation], seizing, and dropping—these twelve precepts apply equally whether committed by oneself or taught to another. However, [the following applies]: "Treasure. [End of verse].
If one instructs another, even if they do not act for their own sake, it constitutes an offense identical to the original.

Regarding the first twelve precepts among the two categories of "acting oneself" and "instructing others," the remaining offenses are minor because there is no shared liability when instructing others;
thus, the meaning of the verse can be understood by comparing it with what precedes it.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, there are ten precepts that instruct others not to act for their own sake; regardless of the gravity of the intention, one incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). What are their characteristics? The verse says:
"In private or in public, [giving] robes to a nun, high beds," and so on, down to the seventh precept. These ten precepts instruct a *bhikṣu* to act [on behalf of another].

If he acts for his own sake, he can be instructed to incur a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) or a *pācittiya* (offense requiring confession); however, if it is not for his own sake, [he incurs no such offense].
If one commits a *thullaccaya* by acting as an agent, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* for instructing [another] to commit it.

Regarding the mutual relationship between light and heavy offenses within the subsequent ten precepts, the preceding heading specifies "not for oneself" merely to demonstrate the distinction from the aforementioned cases.
The characteristics listed below refer to the two types of spreading [the seat]: in private and in public. This concludes the formal section.
Clarifying the mutual transgressions between agent and object regarding light and heavy offenses.

[Commentary] If one seeks to understand this through its underlying principles, even the ninety rules of the *Prātimokṣa* do not fully encompass it. For instance, when striking or assaulting others, both self and other are equally afflicted;

why would they not be considered co-offenders? How could it be that only minor slanders, drinking water containing insects, and so forth, are exempt from definitive judgment based on the text alone? If there were no underlying principle, such cases would remain unresolved.
How could it be that what is equal does not exist? Therefore, we know that [the literal] meaning is not yet exhausted.

Seeking the meaning within the superior [text] is based on the phrasing; however, the phrasing is restricted to specific numbers, whereas this current [discussion] relies on the meaning. Since seeking the meaning is comprehensive, it is said to be "not exhaustive.
When the text mentions striking and beating, the rest may be sought out for oneself.
[Commentary]: Next, the third point, the meaning of "preventing the nature [of offenses]," is explained.

There are thirty precepts whose nature contradicts principle; when one regrets and commits an offense, even if the matter is purified and the accumulated karma has not yet been eliminated, one must first overturn the root of inverted views before the suffering can cease.
As for the remaining sixty precepts, they involve only a contradiction regarding the matter itself, as there is no lack of reproach or disgrace; thus, they merely violate the net of the teachings.

Regarding the three types of prohibitions that encompass the nature [of offenses], the first clarifies that the nature of precepts (*śīla*) applies to all three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.

Since the present discussion is restricted to the unwholesome, it speaks of "contravening principle" (*yukti*). Here, it is necessary to clarify the differences between transgressions and repentance according to the two teachings: the *vaipulya* (transformative) and the *vinaya* (disciplinary). Transgressing the transformative teaching contravenes principle;

transgressing the disciplinary rules contravenes the matter (*vastu*). When a bhikṣu violates a precept of essential nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), he contravenes both principle and matter. According to the Vinaya, this constitutes a formal offense.

Practicing repentance merely reverses the violation of specific matters, which is why it is said that "matters are purified"; yet because the violation of principle still persists, it is said that "karmic actions have not been dispelled.

If one follows the section on repentance and cultivates the three types of rational contemplation (*yili guan*), one can also destroy karma; however, this discussion proceeds from the perspective of ultimate realization, hence it says:
"To overturn the inversion of self, one must first destroy delusion. Once one has entered the stage of the sages (*ārya*), the delusions that can give rise to karma are eliminated.

Because karma can produce retribution, it is called the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). Next, we shall clarify the prohibitions regarding the *śīla* (precepts). These are established as offenses for specific instances; there is no contradiction in principle.
However, one must repent according to the Vinaya so that the matter may be rectified; otherwise, there will be no purity in the affair.

[Commentary] A detailed explanation of the refutation of their nature has already been set forth above; here we shall simply enumerate them to demonstrate their differences and then cease. Regarding the verse on the "evil nature," it says:

"Therefore, rejecting both views as different, out of strong resentment, one drags [the opponent] along; using sarcasm and admonition, driving away and frightening, concealing doubts, storing up [faults], drinking [of the poison], inciting speech, following along and following along, resisting and rejecting, desiring the same, not screening, striking and beating—these are absent [in our teaching]."
Next, regarding the summary shown at the beginning, "referring to the extensive explanation as previously set forth" refers to the categories (*arthamukha*) of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.

Now, the following verses provide the actual exposition: "desire" (meaning that [giving] consent does not constitute an obstruction); "same" (meaning regret after the formal ritual [*karmavācanā*]); "consent" (meaning regret after having given consent); "not" (meaning departing without having given consent);
"secluded" (meaning eavesdropping on the four types of disputes); and "baseless" (meaning slandering with groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* charges).
[Commentary] Next, the fourth section, the method for maintaining and violating the precepts, is explained.
Regarding the twelve precepts that possess both maintenance and violation, what constitutes the improper cases? There are seven stages in total:

first, because there is a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one may be charged with an offense; second, because of receiving a *guṇavatī-cīvara* (meritorious robe), one may accept an invitation and eat separately from the community; third...

Because there is the rule of entrustment (*anuparīkṣā*), one may enter another's house before or after the proper time; because of the four ways of making *kṛtānna* (prepared food), there is no offense of "having eaten enough" (*paryāpta*);

because of the five ways of performing the formal act with the mouth, there is no offense regarding the seven-day period or the remainder for life; thus, the aforementioned five stages constitute ten offenses.
Eleventh, regarding pure giving (*pariśuddha-dāna*), one asks the owner and then rises to grant consent (*chanda*) for the affairs of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the four clarifications on the dual maintenance of observance and transgression, in the first section: since the various matters of the precepts share the same procedural methods, they are combined into seven questions. [Question:
Why is it that while the *guṇavastuka-cīvara* (robe of merit) opens up five benefits, one who is separated from it alone is permitted to perform the act of "observance" (*dhāraṇa*)?

[Answer: In the preceding section, regarding long-term separation, there is already the *karmavācanā* for pure donation (*śuddha-dāna*); here, entering a village involves a separate procedure of formal announcement (*jñapti*). These three instances open up the allowance for the *guṇavastuka*.

Regarding the time for wearing robes, the shorter period is discarded and the longer is followed to clarify that the two precepts of "holding by both" (*ubhayato-dhāraṇa*)—namely, the separate precepts for the back and the sides—have no distinct rules for exemptions;

therefore, the *kaṭhina* robe is taken as the basis for the practice of "holding by action" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). If this is so, may the first three [precepts] also employ the *kaṭhina* robe as the basis for "holding by action"?
Answer: If one employs the *kaṭhina* robe, the original method is abandoned; thus we know that all three precepts equally incorporate both methods. Regarding this:
Because they were originally derived from the *Dīrghāgama*, they are not listed here. [Commentary:

These various precepts all have instances where the Buddha’s teaching permits their performance; performing them in accordance with this permission without transgression is called "observance through action" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*). Refraining from verbal misconduct is called "abstention from transgression.

When the body violates the matter, it is called "transgression through action" (*kṛta-āpatti*). Thus, these two types of transgression—abstention and action—are identical in essence but differ in name. This was the ancient tradition.

People say that because the restraint of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*) and the restraint of actions (*vastusthiti*) are called "restraint-and-maintenance" (*sthiti-dhāraṇa*), one knows that the names and entities of these two types of restraint are each distinct.
In the subsequent section on the ancient interpretations, the first three lines are listed to demonstrate that they are all equally accomplished through volitional effort (*abhisamskāra*);

subsequently, only *sthiti-dhāraṇa* is singled out to clarify that maintaining the precepts is not a matter of volitional effort. As for the claim that the entities of the two offenses are identical while their names differ, that...

This means that the meaning of "committing" (*kṛta*) encompasses both the commission of an offense and the cessation of such commission; while the names "cessation" (*niṣedha*) and "commission" (*kṛti*) differ, the substance of the volition (*cetanā*) is one and without distinction.

Second, regarding the offenses mentioned previously: the former represents an ancient interpretation, while the latter is presented as the definitive position, intended to demonstrate that the observance of prohibitions (*niṣedha-śīla*) is paramount.

Thus, the "dharma of cessation" and the "matter of cessation" refer to the fact that neither dharma nor matter involves any active engagement, which is termed the practice of "observance through cessation" (*niṣedha-samvara*). Conversely, "observance through performance" (*anujñā-samvara*) refers to the process of active execution.
"Stopping and maintaining" (*śīla*) are distinct in essence because one does not perform [unwholesome acts]. Question: What fault is there in the meaning explained previously? Answer:

That [explanation] only understands "stopping" (*saṃvara*) but does not recognize "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*). Since "maintaining" constitutes goodness, and goodness is itself karma, karma does not exist of its own accord but must be established through action.
Action is the mental activity of performing; there is nothing that is not a creative act. If one simply does not act...
Since this [neutral state] cannot constitute karma, it is clear that the ancient interpretation is fundamentally at odds with reason;
therefore, when lecturers and students encounter this passage, they must reflect upon it carefully, as the commentators have refuted it chapter by chapter.

[Commentary: My current interpretation is not as [previously] stated. Above, we extensively enumerated the observance and violation of precepts according to the teachings and in accordance with the rules, manifesting the characteristics of both.

As for the observance and violation of both types, it is as explained in the *Karmavācanā*: a gross offense that is committed while not transgressing the teaching is called "observance by abstention" (*virati-dhāraṇa*);

to speak without formal instruction (*avijñapti*) is "offense by commission" (*kriyā-āpatti*). To suppress the teaching and fail to seek it is "offense by non-abstention" (*avirati-āpatti*). Based on these characteristics, how could they not be clear?
The remainder may be understood by analogy.

Now, in explaining the middle four lines, they all refer to the act of commissioning; "referring to what was stated above" indicates the source regarding the observance and violation of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules according to the teaching;
"manifesting the characteristics according to the precepts" refers to the distinction between the dual and the single. As for example:

The following provides a brief indication of the names and essences of the two types of observance (*dhāraṇī*) and the two types of transgression (*āpatti*), each cited individually as an example; the remainder should be understood by analogy.
Furthermore, "suppression" (*niyama*) refers to being restrained such that one does not seek [permission], which is to say, one does not request the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).

[Commentary: When repenting of offenses, one relies solely on the two categories of transgressions—those based on the precepts and those based on the Dharma—which are not included within the general category of repentance. These are specifically prescribed and separately repented for: namely, the "transgression through lack of learning" (*aśikṣita*) and the "transgression through ignorance" (*ajñāna*).

Since these superior types of repentance differ from the ancient two-fold classification of offenses and their natures are distinct, it is necessary to clarify the characteristics of the expansion and contraction of the practice of repentance.

First, the primary offense is explained; second, the cessation of the offense is shown. Regarding the "two offenses," this refers to committing both simultaneously while in the midst of committing a transgression.
Alternatively, it may mean that this offense is not subsumed within the methods for repentance (*pratideśanīya*), as it is a distinct regulation and therefore requires a separate confession.
It is called a "distinct regulation" because it further increases the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

[Commentary]: As the former interpretation stated: "Medicines such as the seven-day [medicines] are completed by receiving them twice; because they prevent what is not timely, they are called 'maintained by action' (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*).
This current interpretation is not so. There is no such thing as a "seven-day medicine" that permits eating at improper times (*vikāla*).

Originally there was no limit, but because one transgresses the limit through the formal act of oral declaration (*mukha-karman*), the "improper time" arises from that speech. How could speech itself prevent the improper time? Therefore, we know it does not exist.
Regarding the refutation of the initial ancient interpretation concerning the "seven days" and so forth: the phrase "and so forth" includes the "entirety of one's life.

That [ancient] view held that once the *mukha-dhāraṇī* (oral authorization) had been conferred, one could take the medicine even at improper times (*akāla*). Next, the present interpretation is presented in two parts:

first, it clarifies that while the original opening for non-timely use was intended for temporary consumption, one thereby understands that the oral authorization does not prohibit taking medicine at improper times; second, it clarifies that exceeding the limit can give rise to transgressions.
If it were not the proper time, one would know that the rule regarding speech cannot serve as a preventive measure; thus, "knowing there is nothing" means knowing there is no sense of prevention.

[Commentary] To conceal the former interpretation and claim that it constitutes *dhāraṇī* (maintaining) is also incorrect. Is there perhaps a case where, in accordance with the teaching, one conceals [a fault] yet incurs no offense?
For example, entering a village at an improper time while acting in accordance with the instruction is no different from the original time of entry; therefore, it is said to be [permissible].

Regarding "performing and maintaining" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*): this refutes [the claim] within the section on concealment (*paticchādana*). First, it shows that what is called "confession" (*āviṣkaraṇa*) is not that [concealment]; rather, it is precisely "performing and maintaining. Below this, there is a counter-interrogation:
if one were to admit that concealment is spoken of while there is no fault, it could be named "performing and maintaining"; however, since such a principle does not exist, it is untenable.
The following analogy establishes that if the preceding twelve precepts were originally non-existent, then their violation would constitute an offense;
however, because there is a formal procedure for their suspension (*kṣānti-karman*), they are termed "observed" (*dhṛta*). Otherwise, the same logic may be inferred through this analogy.
[Commentary] Question: When instructing another to dig the earth to ascertain what is pure, is this not "active observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*)? Answer:

Because the twelve aforementioned [precepts] involve physical action in accordance with the teaching, they are termed "active observance. As for the instruction to ascertain purity, it merely involves directing another; since there is no personal performance of the act, it is not called "active observance."

In the section resolving objections, it is stated that because knowing purity, opening the dharma, and similar acts constitute *dhāraṇa-śīla* (observance), they must be distinguished; the response in the text is easy to understand.

[Commentary]: Next, there are two precepts consisting of *kriyā-dhāraṇa* (active observance) and *vāraṇa-vipatti-gopana* (concealment of transgressions through non-restraint); the remaining seventy-six are all *vāraṇa-dhāraṇa* (restraining observance).

Next, regarding the section on "Holding Individually," the first part clarifies that the two precepts are established through both "active observance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) and "cessation of transgression" (*niṣiddha-āpatti*). Since a transgression is incurred precisely because one does not disclose [the fault] and does not listen [to the instruction], it is asked:

how does this explanation of concealment (*pracchādana*) differ from that of the ancients? The answer is: the ancients explained it according to the formal rule (*dharma*), judging it to reside in the "holding of both" (*ubhaya-dhāraṇa*);

now, discussing it in terms of the actual matter (*vastu*), it is contained within the "holding of one" (*eka-dhāraṇa*). Although the wording is the same, the meaning differs; this is self-evident in the text. The remainder follows below.
Next, it should be understood that for the remaining precepts, one may know the offenses through commission (*kṛta*) and the observances through abstention (*virati*).

[Commentary]: Regarding commission, there are both offenses and observances; these were extensively detailed in the preceding section. Here, we clarify the offenses through abstention and the observances through abstention.
In the third section, "Extensive Classification of the Stages," the reference to the "upper volume" indicates the previously mentioned general meaning and the section on the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.

[Commentary] Regarding the term "restraint and observance" (*śīla-vinaya*): it refers to the Buddha’s established precepts and instructions that one must study and practice; I rely upon these to train, such that regarding the objects [of training], there is no...

Although the faculties of sentient beings vary such that they cannot be standardized as either sharp or dull, regarding the ten thousand objects of experience, because of the net of delusion and doubt,
the various grades of the nine levels of meditative concentration are provisionally divided into three stages based on their relative superiority and inferiority.
In the introductory section of the *Zhichi* (Observance of Cessation), first the source for establishing the teachings is indicated; next, "I" and below clarify the fundamental basis for study;

finally, "then" and below generate the stages of practice (*pinwei*). Regarding the mention of "the nine [categories] of all things," this is stated from a general perspective. Whether concerning phenomena (*dharma*) or matters (*vastu*), they do not exceed the two sets of nine propositions regarding what is learnable and what is unlearnable.

When discussing phenomena and matters specifically in relation to the precepts, those who maintain both [the precepts and the phenomena] or violate both constitute the phenomena and matters [under discussion].

If the two categories are distinguished separately, there are four sets of nine; however, regarding single dharmas and single matters, there are only two sets of nine. This refers to the offenses of transgression and addition, which include only the fault of failing to train in the teachings and practices.

As for the distinction between superior and inferior: in terms of the gate of observance (*dhāraṇa*), those who recognize [the precepts] are superior, while those who doubt them are next, and those who do not recognize them at all are most inferior.
In terms of the gate of transgression (*āpatti*), the order is reversed.

[Commentary]: Regarding the superior grade, "knowing the dharma" (*dharmajñāna*) refers to recognizing the offense, such as when receiving the *guṇavat-cīvara* (a robe with special qualities), one must know the application of the ritual procedure;

this is called "knowing the dharma. "Knowing the offense" (*āpattijñāna*) refers to identifying whether a transgression constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) or a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation), and determining the gravity of the offense—such as whether it involves the opening or closing of robes or the administration of medicine.

Other characteristics should be understood by analogy, though they cannot be fully set forth here. This is because there is no loss of the fundamental precepts, and furthermore, one is not ignorant regarding training and knowledge.
Dajiao is renowned as one who maintains the Vinaya at the highest level (*uttama*).

Regarding the first phrase of this highest level—“as with the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of special qualities)” and so forth—the subsequent section cites the preceding rule, separately opens up the method for its application, and provides a detailed explanation of its characteristics.

(There is a variant reading that says “having obtained the robe, one then applies the ritual to the white three-robes,” but this is incorrect; the white robe cannot be subject to the ritual of formal acceptance, nor can it be held as a dual possession. As for what is called “applying the ritual of acceptance” (*adhivāsana*), it means:
Regarding the three distinct functions that the person performing the *karmavācanā* must know, the *Chao* states: "It can induce many robes, and the robes will not deteriorate.
It further states: "Because the Sangha collectively accepts these robes, one thereby attracts the fivefold merit;
should there be any transgression, it is said that for accepting the *guṇavat-cīvara*, there are many prescribed rules: first, as for the timing, one must be in *varṣā* (the rainy season retreat)."

First, the determination of the substance and the method of manufacture of the robes; second, the determination of the recipient, who must be one currently observing the *pūrvavārṣika* (first rains retreat) within the same boundary and possessing the three robes;
third, the determination of the holder, who must possess the five virtues; if even one of these matters deviates from the Dharma, the acceptance is not valid.
Since the acceptance is not valid, to falsely claim that it is permissible to be separated from them constitutes a *thullaccaya* or a *pācittiya* offense for each respective precept.
Because the gravity of these offenses is not fixed, the word "or" is used. Regarding the opening or closing [of the rules] concerning clothing and medicine:

this refers to whether the precept against "backbiting invitations" (paccāsaṃsandanā) is applied alone—such as when there is an invitation for food or clothing—or combined—such as when there is an invitation for both food and clothing. Whether there is "backbiting" or not will be clarified later.

As for the determination of the degree of the offense: this refers to the various characteristics of the preparatory acts (*prayoga*) and the fundamental acts (*maula*), as well as their relative gravity, within the context of the two precepts mentioned below.
This is also as explained later: the remaining eleven precepts below are established by way of their lower status.

[Commentary: There are four middle positions: (1) being aware of the rule but doubtful about the offense; (2) being aware of the rule but not aware of the offense; (3) being doubtful about the rule but aware of the offense;

and (4) not being aware of the rule but aware of the offense. "Awareness" is to be understood as previously explained. Regarding "being doubtful about the rule," this refers to receiving a *kaṭhina* robe for use.

Regarding the Dharma, there are four types of doubt; if one cannot resolve these—saying, for instance, that one does not know the Dharma, being deluded and ignorant due to a lack of study, allowing one's conduct to be led by external circumstances, and leaving the determination of right and wrong to others because one lacks even a fraction of personal judgment—then such a person is mired in the darkness of doubt concerning transgressions. By analogy, this can be understood through other cases.
However, because even in a single matter one retains a degree of discernment, they are judged to be of the middle grade in upholding the Vinaya.

The middle section is divided into three parts. First, the enumeration of the clauses; second, the citation of the shared [rules] from below; third, the explanation that there are three [sections]. Regarding the first, "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers back to the preceding doubt.

As for the statement "four dharmas," they are: first, the single-announcement (*jñapti*) dharma for harmonizing the Saṃgha; second, the double-announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya*) dharma for appointing a person to hold the robes;

third, the dharma for formally receiving the robes; and fourth, the single-announcement dharma for distributing the *guṇavat-cīvara*. If one does not recognize these, one should proceed according to the nature of the object.
It is like a blind person who, having no measuring scale of their own, is unable to measure anything. A student clarifies the teaching; the teaching is itself the eye and the scale.
Having eyes, one can see the treacherous and the level; having a scale, one does not become confused regarding length and shortness.

If those of later generations hear this and still do not understand, it is because they are subsequently deluded regarding transgressions—meaning they harbor doubts concerning what constitutes a violation and fail to recognize them.

Following the above explanation, "darkness" (*tamas*) refers to non-cognition; however, regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) below, it is appropriate to speak of them as a single "dharma" or a single "matter" (*vastu*).
Alternatively, even if the term "matter" is used in a general sense, there is no fault.

[Commentary: Regarding the four categories of the inferior grade: first, doubting both the Dharma and the offense; second, doubting the Dharma but not recognizing the offense; third, not recognizing the Dharma but doubting the offense;

fourth, not recognizing either the Dharma or the offense. These are all classified as the inferior grade of upholding the Vinaya because, while the training is entirely obscured, there is still some recognition of the object.
The lower grade can be understood by listing the phrases and concluding with the stages.

[Commentary] Question: Since one is ignorant and does not study, how can they be called "upholding"? Answer: It is not that they do not violate the fundamental precepts that they are termed "stopping and upholding" (*zhi-chi*);
rather, it refers to stopping the mind within the framework of the teachings and practicing them. In relation to the objects of transgression, this involves the delusion of non-study.
Regarding the resolution of doubts: "Not violating the fundamental precepts" means that, in relation to the root, there is no offense, which is termed "maintaining";

whereas not studying or being ignorant constitutes an offense regarding the branches. Furthermore, one should ask: "If there are offenses regarding the branches, how can it be called 'maintaining'? The answer is:
"The offense is subsumed within the practice of the teachings, while the category of 'maintaining' refers only to the purity of the root."

[Commentary]: Since those of superior grade are wise people, they incur no offenses or faults. Those of middle grade have four [types], each accompanied by delusion and doubt, thus totaling eight offenses.
The names of these offenses are as follows: for each of the four phrases in the upper and lower positions, there are four distinct offenses;
being deluded regarding the Dharma constitutes sixteen offenses when one fails to study, which is also explained as above.
Regarding the indication of offenses, two fingers as described above correspond to the eight offenses of the preceding chapters:

four for not training in the upper grade (which are non-offenses), four for not training in the middle grade (two *pācittika* for ignorance and two *pācittika* for doubt), and two *pācittikas* for not recognizing [the rule].

This constitutes eight offenses. For the lower grade of not training, there are eight *pācittikas* for ignorance and four *pācittikas* for doubt, totaling sixteen offenses; this is the section on these gates.
In total, there are twenty-four offenses: eighteen *pāyattika* (light offenses) and six *pratideśanīya* (confessions).

[Commentary] Next, we explain the nine phrases regarding the cessation of offenses (*niṣiddha-āpatti*). This refers to the fact that because the practitioners' levels of clarity or obscurity regarding the teachings and their faculties for cultivation differ, nine phrases are established.
Some establish eight phrases; however, our current explanation reverses this by clarifying that the cessation of offenses consists of only eight, and one must not establish nine.
The ninth [point] concerns being deluded regarding both the teachings and the practice, such that there is no transgression of the two recognitions;

conversely, when one cultivates clarity and commits a transgression by relying on appearances, all nine factors are complete. As in the ninety cases: not performing the prescribed teaching is termed "cessation" (śīla), while acting contrary to it as soon as one acts is termed "transgression."

Next, the explanation of the cessation of transgressions (*śīlavipatti*) begins with the initial presentation of the intent for establishing this section. Following that, the ancient interpretations are shown:

the eight propositions of the ancient masters exclude the cognition of the rule (*dharma-vijñāna*) and the cognition of the transgression (*āpatti-vijñāna*), thereby including only the cessation of transgression due to a lack of learning (*aśikṣita*).

In the present master’s system, the eighth and ninth propositions are established as a pair, which includes both types of cessation of transgression. Below this, the correct interpretation is presented; the "reversal" (*viparyaya*) refers to the absence of non-learning (*aśikṣita*).
"Knowing the offense" refers to the cessation of transgression through the practice of the teachings; "reversing cultivation" refers to the various aspects of upholding the precepts.

"Reversing the offense" refers to the cessation of transgression regarding phenomena and matters; "reversing understanding" follows this. Within the first established phrase, since it clarifies the absence of lower-grade [transgressions], it is discussed in terms of delusion regarding the commission of offenses.
If one were not deluded, then how could the [offenses] exist within the subsequent nine phrases?

The reason for this response is that it possesses a fundamental basis, which is why it differs [from other cases]. Regarding the first phrase of the "Reversal of Cultivation" (*viparyaya-bhāvanā*), the term "relying on characteristics" (*nimitta-ālambana*) refers to the various characteristics of the precepts, such as citing the precepts to illustrate the four "immediate" (*sadyas*) offenses.

The term "immediate" (*sadyas*) summarizes the preceding twelve precepts. There are three types of immediate offenses: (1) entering a village without having received permission; (2) eating immediately [after the meal is finished]; and (3) six offenses regarding food: eating what has been stored overnight, eating what was set aside, eating what was not formally offered, and the two offenses regarding speech: speaking of one's own faults and instructing nuns.
"Taking [something] at once (without asking the owner) and acting accordingly" refers to committing an offense against the facts; "immediately violating" refers to violating the Dharma.

This demonstrates that although these two offenses occur simultaneously, their essential natures remain distinct. [Commentary]: One who understands the characteristics of the teachings will have no delusions or confusions. Regarding this, the single phrase for the lower grade and the four phrases for the middle grade are as explained above.
Since each item listed contains two offenses, there are eight in total. Regarding the four superior positions: first, not knowing the dharma and not knowing the offense;
second, not knowing the dharma but doubting the offense; third, doubting the dharma but not knowing the offense; fourth, doubting both the dharma and the offense.
Each of these phrases contains four offenses, and when combined with the confusion regarding the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), they total sixteen.

In the "Correct Enumeration," the three grades can be known by counting; as for those who speak of "learning and delusion," learning is actually non-learning and delusion is actually ignorance, which collectively subsumes both doubt and lack of recognition.

[Commentary] Regarding the gate of transgressions, the meanings are explained with many offenses ranked as superior; conversely, regarding the middle grade of upholding, these can be understood. This follows the sequence of upholding, explaining, and transgressing.
Why is it that one cannot attain [liberation]? Because reciting many texts causes one's own awakened wisdom to become obscured; thus, the inverted and wavering mind is troubled.
If one is clear and lucid, even amidst distraction there is no suffering, just as when a flock of birds flies together, they naturally distinguish their mates.

In the first section of the "Clarifying Errors," the primary purpose is to clarify the reversal of the "Holding" (dhāraṇī) gate. Regarding the interpretation of the meaning within this gate of holding, being free from transgression is considered supreme.

Furthermore, in the gate of transgressions, the clauses are arranged from the most serious to the lightest; thus, for the upper grade, the two instances of "lack of awareness" constitute the first clause, which stands in direct opposition to the practice of holding, as can be understood from the preceding discussion.
Following the sequence below, the intention behind the reversed listing is now set forth: "male and female" refers to the masculine and feminine.
[Commentary] Next, the fifth point is explained: the differences between monks and nuns.

Among the ninety precepts, sixty-nine are offenses committed equally by both monks and nuns; therefore, in the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, the core precepts (*śīla-mūla*) are listed individually, and the text does not elaborate on the points where they are identical to those of the monks.
Fifth, regarding the offenses shared by monks and nuns: first, the number is indicated; there are one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* rules for nuns.
For now, we shall clarify the similarities and differences by correlating them with the number of rules for monks.

Therefore, the citations from the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*—that is, the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa*—which correspond to offenses shared with monks, have their detailed accounts of the origins (*nidāna*) omitted; this is done to economize on the text.
[Commentary]: There are twenty-one precepts that differ from those for nuns, falling into three categories.
First, there are three instances where [the rules] exist for one but not the other: teaching and admonishing nuns, preaching the Dharma until sunset, and reviling those who teach and admonish nuns;
these do not apply to the sequence of non-teacher ranks.
Next, it is explained that these three [aspects] differ from the initial [category of] existence or non-existence. Within this Sangha, they are established in mutual dependence;

because the Bhikṣuṇīs occupy a lower rank and lack the status of being a "Sangha" in the technical sense, and because the latter two causes are absent, it is said that they are sequentially non-existent.
[Commentary]: Among these, the degrees of gravity differ, consisting of thirteen precepts. The verses state:

making robes, holding [food], sitting in concealment, the three periods, receiving food, encouraging [others to eat], fine food, [using] ivory or horn, exceeding the measure, and covering the three robes. Regarding their characteristics of offense, they shall be explained in the relevant passages.
Next, among the light and heavy offenses: making robes (making robes for a nun); possessing [robes] (possessing robes to give to a nun—some say this refers to *tūla* cotton, but it is not the same;

otherwise, one incurs the offense); sitting in private (sitting in private with a nun); the three periods (Period One: a nun traveling; Period Two: traveling on the same boat; Period Three: a woman traveling); receiving food through praise (eating food praised by a nun); encouraging [to eat more] (the meaning is clear);

fine food (seeking fine food—the *Śāstra* says this is a *duṣkṛta*, but because the formal definition of the offense differs, it is actually a *sthūlātyaya*); ivory or horn (needles and cases); exceeding the measure (the *niṣīdana* sitting mat); covering (the *vastra-āvaraṇa* wound-covering cloth).
Regarding the three robes (of the same measure as the Buddha’s robes) and those exceeding them, these all constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for a nun.

[Commentary] Regarding the five subsequent precepts, although the offenses are the same, the conditions differ. The verse says: "Refusing an invitation, being outside the boundary, a novice, and the rain-bathing robe—all these are said to be offenses;

they are identical in that they are permitted under specific conditions, yet the conditions differ. Therefore, in the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, separate rule-texts (*śikṣāpada*) have been established. Up to... [text continues].
The text further states:

"Regarding the three differences in conditions, in the section on 'refusing an invitation' (*pratyākhyāna*) and 'having eaten enough' (*paryāpta-bhakta*), the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Jieben) in both cases says: 'For a nun, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The commentary (*śu*) says:

'This refers to the establishment of different rules; because the two rules for nuns are combined in their formulation, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If one has previously accepted an invitation and [then eats] enough...'"*

Regarding "eating after having finished eating," this constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense (this refers to the distinction between separation and conjunction). Regarding "non-Buddhists," among the nuns, a layman in white robes also commits an offense;

however, for the monks, it is permitted. That root text states: "If one gives food with one's own hand to a layman or a non-Buddhist, it is a *thullaccaya*" (this refers to the distinction between the general and the specific).
Regarding "those of young age," among the nuns, it refers to girls of eighteen who have increased their training period by two years; for the monks, it is... [the text ends].

It is not so; the *Śīlaskandha* (Fundamental Code of Precepts) states: "If one has not been granted the two-year training in the precepts, even if they have reached twenty years of age, one must grant them the full ordination.
(This refers to the difference between existence and non-existence. Regarding the rain-bathing robe (*varṣāśāṭī*), although the excess of its dimensions is the same, its usage differs:
for monks, it is permitted for use during the summer months, whereas for nuns, it is permitted for constant use (the difference lies in the duration of its permitted use).

[Commentary: I venture to rely on the legal precedents to further seek the underlying principles. For instance, regarding the offense of dragging someone out of a room: if committed by monks or nuns during the spring or winter, they are equally guilty.

However, if it occurs in a summer room, for a nun it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), while for a monk it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Among the offenses of disparagement, nuns are liable for both categories, whereas for monks the gravity varies.
Regarding concealment, there are two grades of offenses for monks, while for nuns there are three levels. Since these various differences exist, how can one claim not to know them?

The "seeking the meaning" (*yìqiú*) section prior to this is based on the textual record; since this [section] arises from personal insight, it says: "I venture to rely on the monastic rules (*vinaya*). Regarding the three types of "leading out" (*qiānchū*): first, "separate leading out" (*biéqiān*) refers to cases where the conditions (*yuán*) differ;
second, "defamation" (*huǐ*) refers to the gravity of the offense; third, "concealment" (*fù*) refers to whether such concealment exists.

In the case of leading out from the *saṃgha*, there are three periods for the distribution of rooms. Regarding summer quarters, once they have been assigned to oneself, one need not avoid the senior monks (*sthavira*), as their leading out is infrequent and thus considered light. This applies to nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*) as well.

Regarding the *Pāyattika* (提): the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* states that during the *varṣā* retreat, once one has accepted the retreat, if one makes any effort to leave the boundary and exits, it is a *pāyattika* for each instance.

(This should be because women have weak constitutions; their place of residence must be fixed, and because the offense of causing distress is grave. Regarding censure (*kṣepa*), since a *bhikṣuṇī* censuring either the original assembly or the *saṃgha* constitutes a *pāyattika*, it is said to apply to both assemblies.
As for the *saṃgha*, it is a *pāyattika* for those of the same class, while for the four assemblies [of lay followers], it is a *duṣkṛta* (吉); thus it is so stated.

Regarding the concealment of offenses, light and heavy: for monks, because there are two *pārājika* offenses for concealment and three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses for concealment, it is said there are "two stages.
For nuns, because one *pārājika* is added, it is said there are "three grades. This concludes the summary with the lower category.
[Commentary] Next, the sixth section concerning the differences among the various schools is explained.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are ninety-one *pācattika* offenses; this [offense of] "not accepting admonition" does not exist there, but instead there is a separately established rule for "disrespect toward those who preach the Dharma.

Furthermore, the rule regarding "frivolous speech that disparages the Saṃgha during the *poṣadha*" resembles this [offense of] "causing provocation," yet that [latter rule] itself includes the offense of "not following questions."
Answer: Regarding the precepts, if one discusses the general numbers among the various schools, the *Vinaya* of the Mahīśāsaka and the *Dharmaguptaka* are the same;

the *Sarvāstivāda* and the *Mahīśāsaka* are the same, while the *Mahāsāṃghika* alone is different. Initially, the *Sarvāstivāda* lacks [certain rules] that the others have; these two differences are merely idle talk, referring to frivolous speech.

The "Waves" [commentary] also provides a brief clarification below, stating that not following the questions and answers constitutes *sparśana* (annoyance); it is clearly known that these are merely the "Waves" [author's] own independent assertions.

[The *Śāstra*] states: Among the ninety-one *pātayantika* rules of the five divisions, there is no such [rule]; however, drinking water containing insects or using water containing insects [is a transgression].

Regarding the establishment of individual precepts: (1) entering a nunnery and preaching the Dharma without authorization; (2) slighting the three masters; (3) diverting communal property to private individuals. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are two fewer [precepts] than the other versions, while three others differ.

"Preaching the Dharma without authorization" excludes cases where one is providing formal instruction (*śāstṛ-dharma*). "Diverting to private individuals" refers to the misappropriation of communal goods.
[The text] excludes those that do not enter one’s own possession.

[Commentary: Among the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, these two rules—receiving admonitions with fear and speaking the Dharma to nuns—are not included; they are established separately. Furthermore, there are four rules:
giving property belonging to the Saṃgha to an individual, failing to relinquish the three pure robes (*tricīvara*), and slighting the Saṃgha. These are also excluded.
The precept against causing distress is established separately from other verbal offenses.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four distinct categories rather than two; the first two are identical to the preceding five-part [Vinaya].

Regarding the rule on "not relinquishing what has been purified" (*śuddhaka-tyāga*), according to that Vinaya, when one has declared an object to be "purified by gift" (*śuddhaka-datta*) and wishes to take it for use, one must perform the rite of relinquishment, saying: "This robe is given as a purified gift."

"Whether [the robe] belongs to such-and-such a person or to me, having no fixed intention regarding it, if one now abandons it or does not abandon it, and makes it into the three robes, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;

if it is entered into a stūpa or used by the Saṃgha, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. Furthermore, regarding the offense of 'speaking apart from the truth' (*anyathā-vāda*): consulting the respective *Prātimokṣa* and the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, it is largely the same as the fourth category [of the Dharmaguptaka school];
it is simply one precept. If one says it is 'separate,' it would not accord with the great number [of offenses], and thus it should be counted as ninety."
The third [item]—[some versions read "two," which is an error for "three"]—the meaning of this is not yet detailed and awaits future scholars. [Commentary:

Regarding the ninety *pārājika* offenses, there are no other remaining [offenses]. As for the three precepts distinct from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: sitting in private with a nun; regretting after a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*);
and preaching the Dharma without permission in a nunnery, diverting monastic property to others, and lack of respect for the three [precepts].
There are three distinctions regarding liberation, which are the same as the five parts mentioned previously.

[Commentary] Among the ninety rules of the *Pinaiye* (Skt. *Vinaya*), there are five points of difference. Because of the dispute between the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) and the group of seventeen (Saptadaśavargika), the *Śīlaskandha* (Precept Manual) was established.

Regarding "one who is angry" (*pratigha*), it is a *pāyattika* offense. Because the group of six caused disturbance, the precept was formulated, stating: "If one strikes or agitates another to provoke anger..."
Regarding the *pācittiya* offense for going uninvited to trouble others: the root of the precept states that if one goes forcefully where not invited, it is a *pācittiya*.

An exception is made for matters concerning the Saṃgha, illness, or making robes. If a bhikṣu arrives first at an invited household and plays with small children, or makes a loud noise to disturb the people, it is a *pācittiya*.

The *Pi-nai-ye* (Sūtra on the Five Precepts) differs entirely from those of other schools, as can be seen in the text; "náo" (撓) is pronounced with the *nu* and *qiǎo* finals, meaning also "to disturb" or "to confuse.

The first four names differ, while in reality there are only six distinct items: 1. Disrespecting the preaching of the Dharma (*Daśabhāṇavāra*); 2. Slighting the Saṃgha (*Daśabhāṇavāra* and *Mahāsāṃghika*); 3.

Entering a bhikṣuṇī monastery to preach the Dharma (*Pañcavargika*, *Mahāsāṃghika*, and *Vimokṣa*); 4. Slighting the teacher (*Pañcavargika*, *Dharmaguptaka*, and *Vimokṣa*); 5. Diverting the property of the Saṃgha.
[The rules concerning] others (the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*’s *vimukti*) and the six non-abandonments of purity (*saṃghika*).

[Commentary]: This listing is not intended to be redundant; it is merely to demonstrate that there are similarities and differences, as well as variations in quantity, within the teachings. Not only those listed above, but there must be others as well.

In the first part of this brief summary, the intent of the enumeration is clarified; in the subsequent section, it is shown that the list is not exhaustive. This means that what was previously presented was based merely on what has been observed;
since the Vinaya and its commentaries (*śāstra*) are vast and extensive, there may be omissions, which is why it is said that "more exists."

[Commentary]: Next, the seventh [category], the *śrāmaṇera*’s spontaneous [karmic] meaning, is as explained in the first section—that is, within the second "Gate of Teaching Others" above—concerning the twenty-two precepts where one causes another to act before they have received them or commits an offense after having received them; among these three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), it refers to the karma spontaneously induced.

[Vinaya] First: The Precept Against Intentional False Speech.
[Commentary] The precept against intentional false speech is the first.

[Commentary] Regarding the intent of its formulation: for one who has left the household life, speech must accord with reality; even at the cost of losing one's body and life, one must not permit falsehood.

To act now with error, contrary to one's heart and thoughts, deceiving others and causing them to have false understandings while losing one’s own benefit for oneself—because such faults are profound and the affliction heavy, it is therefore prohibited.

First, regarding the intent of the prohibition, the initial section describes what ought to be done: even at the cost of one’s own life, because this is a fundamental transgression (prakṛti-sāvadya), it is appropriate [to refrain].

Because it must be urgently guarded, it is permitted [only] as a provisional measure (*yushi*). Now, following this, the characteristics of transgressions are enumerated next to demonstrate the necessity for regulation.

[Commentary on the Title]: To explain the terminology: that which does not accord with reality is called "false" (*wang*); that which manifests through the mouth is called "speech" (*yu*). Since there is no offense when it is not from the mind, it is designated by its name.

In the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names), it is said that the mouth is the instrument for creating [speech] and the mind is the root of karma; because one wishes to manifest the resulting characteristics, both are designated. [Commentary: Question:

Since deception constitutes a grave offense while frivolous speech constitutes a light offense, why is it that hiding another's property results in a *pāyattika* (offense of falling) in both cases? Answer: False speech is not necessarily a grave offense in terms of the affliction caused;

it is classified as a *pāyattika* based on the gravity of the intention. Frivolous speech, however, is immediately classified as a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). Regarding the concealment of property, the objective of the affliction is profound, and thus [it is judged accordingly].
Concealing [another's property] involves both light and heavy degrees of offense due to the shared factors of expectation, loss, and emotional affliction;

therefore, both result in a *pāyattika* (falling offense). Regarding the question: concealing another’s robes or bowl, joking, and so forth, differ from lying (*mṛṣāvāda*), and thus the question is explained accordingly.

In the answer, the five words form a single phrase; while lying is distinguished by its emotional intent, concealing objects is determined by the commonality of the resulting affliction. This concludes the preceding exposition.

Regarding the statement that lying constitutes a grave offense while the present case is said to be otherwise: the answer is that deceiving another by taking what belongs to them is grave, whereas this [present case], involving the concealment of property, is still relatively light.

[Commentary] Six conditions constitute the offense: first, it must be a human being; second, one must perceive them as a human being; third, one must speak in contradiction to that perception; fourth, one must know [the truth of the matter] oneself.
The five verbal transgressions contrary to perception and the six [mental] factors understood by others are listed.
Regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*), there are six; they do not appear as mental objects (*citta-viṣaya*) or words (*vākya*), yet they together constitute deluded karma.
[Commentary: Among the four karmas of speech, all are primary offenses (*maula-āpatti*); however, with respect to the object (*viṣaya*), there are degrees of gravity.
In the general exposition, the heading states that these are "actual offenses" because they constitute the sevenfold nature of karma. Regarding the gravity of the object:
it should be understood that the preceding sections distinguish between specific transgressions against different objects, with their respective degrees of severity arranged in descending order.

[Commentary]: Regarding the single karma of false speech, it follows the person and leads them to fall [into evil realms] together; because this fundamental falsehood flows on continuously and is difficult to sever, the Sage established a heavy precept to prohibit it.

Within the category of false speech, the first part indicates the offense. As for "following the person," it means that the object [of the lie] is not distinguished. This is because the following section explains the reason.
These are called "fundamental falsehoods" because they arise from the fundamental inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*) and increase in accordance with delusions; thus, they are difficult to sever.
Since the establishment of the teachings refers to them as "karmic offenses," they are termed "heavy precepts.

[Commentary: This differs from cases where two parties mutually disparage one another, which possess varying degrees of lightness or gravity. If it involves the same class of people, the emotional distress is grave, and it can obstruct the distribution [of the Dharma].

Because of this, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense; as for the remaining six groups [of monks], even if they should violate [the rules] with slight intent and minor dispute, it does not obstruct the Saṃgha, and thus they incur a *dukkaṭa* offense.

Regarding the two middle cases, the first two phrases are the reverse of the preceding [explanation]. Below, the text correctly demonstrates this: first, it clarifies that when the object is grave, it obstructs the *poṣadha*.
Among all dharmas, harmony is most precious; discord and vexation give rise to much contention. For now, I shall cite the *poṣadha* as a representative of all *karmavācanā* procedures.
Next, I will clarify the objects [of transgression]: "light" refers to contemptuous disparagement (*paiśunya*), which is the breaking of harmony through slander, thereby destroying both sides.

[Commentary]: Regarding the single karma of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), its fault lies in the agitation and distraction of the mind; it does not constitute a transgression of the monastic rules (*saṃgha-śīla*).

Generally, these are all minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*). The *Tattvasiddhi* states that among the three vocal karmas, they may sometimes be combined or separated, yet the single karma of frivolous speech is never dissociated from them.
This should be sought in the *Śāstra* (the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*) as found in the *Yi-chao*.

Regarding frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), the first section clarifies its gravity and lightness: since agitation (*auddhatya*) is a mental hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), it is said to "corrupt the mind. When directed toward the Saṃgha or regarding matters of pure dharma (*avadāta-dharma*), the offense is grave and constitutes a *thullaccaya* (serious offense).
If directed toward an individual, or toward the Saṃgha when the formal announcement has not yet been made, the object is light and thus constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).

The *Jie cheng lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Precepts) below indicates the combinations and distinctions; those who consult the *Chao* (Excerpts) should investigate them, as that work does not include the formulations for the combinations and distinctions of the three types of action (*trikarma*).
Because of frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*), one knows that the other three [unwholesome paths] involve both separation and conjunction, whereas frivolous speech involves only conjunction.

[Note: When the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, the Śākya son Hastibala was skilled in debate; when he debated with non-Buddhists, he failed to speak at the proper time and instead contradicted his own previous words.
When questioned within the Saṃgha, he again spoke inconsistently, leading the brahmins to criticize him for lacking the True Dharma.
A bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept.

[Commentary] Within the context of the causal conditions for this precept, we discuss how even when practicing wholesome dharmas, one may give rise to false deception; if this is so, what need is there to mention other miscellaneous matters?
How could such conduct establish trust? The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* also states: "I truly know that it is not shameful to fall into a position of defeat; what kind of words are these?"
Furthermore, the Buddha established the precepts to stop the inversion of self; now, you instead assist this "self" by further intensifying deluded habits—how can you hope for liberation?

Regarding the initial citation and explanation within the context of the precepts, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* specifically cites the method of debate as an analogy for other matters; the five parts [of the argument] are like an elephant.
Regarding the phrase "the power of confronting the Sangha," what kind of words are these? The commentators follow up with this reprimand to instruct future generations.

The Buddha’s subsequent narration of the regulations and exhortations to uphold them means that those who instead assist me are merely following their delusions. How can one escape and be exempted from this? There is no time for deliverance.

seeing, hearing, touching, and knowing; as well as not seeing, not hearing, not touching, and not knowing. Regarding "seeing," this ranges from what can be seen by visual consciousness up to what can be known by mental consciousness.
Regarding "not seeing," this excludes visual consciousness and refers to the other five consciousnesses. The same applies to the opposites.
[Commentary] The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

This differs from other schools, which take that [organ] as the basis of seeing. If one claims that whatever sensory objects are apprehended by the various organs constitutes "seeing," all such statements are false speech.

our own school (the *mūla-nikāya*) holds that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is capable of producing vision, whereas many other schools hold that the faculty (*indriya*) is capable of producing vision;
