For these reasons, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*) sets forth three principles for which it is appropriate to manage and protect the property of the Sangha from the four quarters—donations made by those of sincere faith—which provide vast benefits when used for the sustenance of the Sangha. Thus, one should manage and protect such resources so that they may support the body and facilitate the practice of the Path.

First, because they attain peace and happiness; second, because these two items are gifts of faith that one cherishes with a devoted heart, ensuring constant enjoyment and causing faith and respect to grow;

third, because once used, the monastic property is immediately returned so as not to cause damage, thereby allowing the merit of its enjoyment to instead benefit the donor and bring their roots of goodness to fulfillment.

In the first section of the fourteen points on "Restraining the Mind," the initial description of what is appropriate is given because it is beneficial and weighty, being utilized throughout the ten directions and continuing through the three periods of time.

However, the following two points [of the first section] reveal the faults of sentient beings. Regarding the subsequent three points, which cite texts to demonstrate the three meanings within the treatise:

the first is the intention of protection, the second is the intention of cherishing, and the third is the intention of concealment. The first [of these three] benefits oneself, while the latter two benefit others.

[Commentary]: The six conditions for this offense are: first, using a seat that is permanently established; second, knowing it is the property of the Sangha; third, being in an open space; fourth, having someone else spread it out;
fifth, having someone else fail to remove it; and sixth, departing from the site—this constitutes an offense.

The fifth section of the *Liejian* (List of Conditions) combines [the cases] and states: "Neither lifting it oneself nor having another lift it. When compared with the original text of the precept, one knows that the wording is inverted. [Note:
While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, an elder invited the Saṃgha; the group of seventeen bhikṣus took the Saṃgha’s sitting mats and spread them out in the open.
While walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), he waited for the time of the meal to arrive; failing to gather [the bedding] away, it was ruined by wind, dust, insects, and birds.
Having reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked him, the Buddha established the precept.
Regarding the context of the precept: when one walks in meditation upon an open space, one uses the bedding to cover the ground where one walks.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu takes a rope bed (of which there are five types: with curved legs, straight legs, bent legs, with crossbars, or legless), a wooden bed (also as described above),
bedding (used either for sitting or lying), a sitting cushion (intended for regular use), or a mat spread in the open air, and having instructed another to spread it,
departs without personally putting it away or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika.
[Note]: He hands over the property of the Saṃgha to the administrator, saying: "I now entrust this to you; guard and look after it.
If there is no one at all [to supervise], he should place it in a secluded spot. If there is no secluded spot, he must ensure that it will not be damaged;
he should cover the fine items with coarse ones on top. If he returns immediately, he should go back following the rain. If he can return quickly and in time, he should go. Next, he...
One should depart by employing such skillful means; if one does not do so, one falls into an offense the moment one steps out the door.

If one employs skillful means but then regrets it, it is all *dūṣkṛta*. If two people sit together, the junior person should withdraw [the bedding]; if they do not, they commit two offenses, while the senior person commits one offense of falling (*pācittiya*).
If neither withdraws it, both fall into offense. This also applies to other beds, stools, machines, and so forth, which are not withdrawn.

If one spreads bedding with both the inner and outer sides exposed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; likewise, if one enters a room for meditation after spreading out the Sangha’s property in the open air, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense if, when leaving after spreading the Sangha’s property in the open air, one informs those who have been residing there, the *karmadāna*, or the administrator so that they may take care of it;
through such expedients as these, there is no offense in any case.

[Commentary: Regarding the four clauses of the *Prātimokṣa*, there are four offenses: first, [misappropriating] a single person’s property; second, [misappropriating] the property of the Saṃgha; third, [leaving] on open ground; and fourth, abandoning and departing. [Commentary:

Within the explanation of the property of the Saṃgha, there are three types as mentioned above. In the case of misappropriating the property of the Saṃgha, if one takes it and subsequently returns it to the Saṃgha, the offense is only a minor one (*duṣkṛta*).
All other cases constitute a grave offense.
In the second section of the *Prātimokṣa*, three items are listed without distinguishing between their light or heavy status; therefore, they must be examined.
Third, regarding the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense), whereas the preceding two were merely *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), the commentary notes that there are five types of beds.

As for those with rotating legs, these are like worldly revolving frames or cross-legged stools. As for those with removable supports, these are like stools with detachable legs that are inserted as needed. The rest are as follows.
The three points that can be understood from the sutra regarding the four items of bedding and seating are that the offense is incurred upon the completion of even one item, not necessarily all four.

[Commentary] Within the section analyzing the characteristics of the offense, the first clarifies the signs of the preparatory act (*prayoga*) of detailed entrustment; this explains the text of the precept itself concerning "whether for oneself or another.

If one does not do so as stated below, it violates the teaching; thus, the offense is established. Regarding the two offenses committed while sitting together with two people, the second person is the one seated lower. One—
The phrase "not being in proper deportment" refers to the elder monk’s offense; the two [other offenses] regarding the precepts are as follows, while the remainder may be understood by oneself.
Regarding the first part of the fourth section, the text explains it from the perspective of the junior monk.

In the commentary on the latter part, the meaning of the first two lines—where the upper and lower [offenses] are mutually exchanged—is that the intention is to cause the junior monk to receive [the penalty], thereby making the elder monk superior; thus, it encompasses both offenses, as indicated in the sub-commentary (*śū*). Afterward...
"Neither receiving" means that they depart simultaneously, neither before nor after, because they do not wait for one another;
thus, there is one offense for each. The note states: "Returning quickly in the rain" refers to the intention formed at the time of departure.
*Mamati* is a Sanskrit term meaning a person in charge of administrative affairs.
[Vinaya] The fifteenth precept concerning the spreading of monastic property in a concealed place.
[Commentary] The fifteenth precept concerning the spreading of monastic property in a concealed place.
[Commentary] The intent of the regulation is the same as before.
Regarding the fifteenth [offense], although the property of the Saṃgha is the same, because the matters [of its use] are distinct, it is divided into two precepts.
[Commentary: Six conditions constitute the offense: (1) it is property of the Saṃgha; (2) one knows this; (3) it is a secluded place; (4) one uses it oneself; (5) one departs without returning it;
and (6) one exceeds the time limit. Thus, the offense is committed.
The sixth condition for the offense, "exceeding the limit," has two aspects as clarified below.

[Commentary: The reasons they are distinguished are: first, the difference between a secluded place (*praticchanna*) and an open space (*vivṛta*); second, the difference in the time when the offense is incurred. In an open space, it is incurred upon leaving the door; in a secluded place, it is incurred upon leaving the boundary (*sīmā*).

This involves a firm resolve to never return, similar to the aforementioned case of leaving the boundary. If it is temporary rather than permanent, and one exceeds three nights, the third offense is committed. Three exceptions are provided.
Regarding the different conditions for exposure: when both parties are relaxed, the prohibition applies for two nights.
In distinguishing the three types of separation, the division into two offenses arises because the speed of the object’s destruction differs;

thus, "exposure" refers only to leaving the door, while "screening" is divided into permanent and temporary, as can be understood from the text. Among these three, "exposure" is permitted when relaxed.
If it is urgent, one should entrust [the bedding] immediately; if it is not urgent, one should return even through the rain.
[Note: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a visiting bhikṣu spread out bedding in a peripheral room and went away without informing anyone.
The bedding became moldy, infested with insects, and its color faded. Upon seeing this, he informed the Buddha, who consequently established this precept.

[The Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu spreads bedding belonging to the Saṃgha within the monastic quarters—meaning rope beds, wooden beds, mattresses, sitting mats, pillows, floor coverings, or even down to the woolen rugs—and whether he spreads them himself or instructs another to do so, and whether he sits or lies upon them, if he fails to pick them up himself or instruct another to pick them up when he departs, [he commits an offense].
[Note] He should say to the resident bhikṣus: "Please lift me up securely.

If there is no one [to help], and he does not fear losing anything, he should move his bed away from the wall, prop the legs of the bed high, place pillows, bedding, and requisites inside, and cover them with other coarse items.
If he fears they might be damaged, he should take the bedding and other items and place them on a clothing rack, stand the bed upright, and depart. If he does not act in this manner...
If one leaves the boundary, it is an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*); if one intends to go but returns and regrets it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one returns immediately, stays outside the boundary for two nights, and on the morning of the second night, fails to go there in person or dispatch a messenger to take charge of the protection, one commits an offense of downfall.

[Pācittiya. [Commentary: Regarding non-offenses, as mentioned above, those cases where one was already outside the boundary, or where the path—whether by water or land—was cut off, or due to circumstances involving life or celibacy (*brahmacarya*), are permitted.
[Commentary: The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* are as explained above; the text for distinguishing their characteristics is easy to understand.

In the separate explanation, first the text of the precept is cited to distinguish the following points regarding non-offenses: "if the path is cut off by water or land," and so forth. This applies to returning within three nights;
because there are difficult circumstances, the previous precept is opened [as an exception]. Since there is no offense when departing from the gate, there is no mention of it in the text.
Section. [Vinaya] Precept 16: Forcibly Spreading Out a Seat.
[Commentary] The sixteenth precept concerns forcibly spreading out a seat.

[Commentary]: All things have limits and affairs are restricted by the distinction between self and other. When feelings are harmonious, the other becomes one's own; when there is a barrier of resentment, matters are viewed as contrary.

If one knows where another is staying but, failing to deliberate on the matter, forcibly spreads out bedding in the space between them to encroach upon and displace the other, this is not the deportment of one who has left the household life; therefore, it was prohibited.

In the first part of the "Sixteen Methods for Controlling the Mind," it is clarified that objects have their respective owners; in the subsequent section on "Sentiments," it is clarified that the human mind may be either open or obstructed.

Because that which is acceptable is granted, there is progress; because that which is unacceptable is rejected, there is refusal. Thus, the following section formally explains the intent of control, where "expelling" (*chi*) is defined as "driving away" (*zhu*).
[Commentary]: Five conditions constitute an offense: (1) having first borrowed a dwelling and settled therein; (2) knowing that another was already residing there;
(3) forming the intention to cause annoyance; (4) forcibly spreading one's bedding within it; and (5) lying down upon it—each of these constitutes an offense.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks and the group of seventeen monks were traveling along the same road to a place without a dwelling.
The group of seventeen monks sought a lodging for themselves, while the group of six, knowing they had found a place to stay, forcibly spread out bedding in the middle to sleep there.
A monk reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept.
Regarding the conditions for the precept: "having no place to stay" clarifies that there is no monastery where one may reside, and one is instead staying in a layperson's house.

[The Vinaya states: If a bhikṣu—whether knowing or not knowing—that a previous bhikṣu is already residing there, comes later and forcibly spreads bedding (such as a grass mat, a leaf mat, or even a ground mat or sleeping blanket) in the middle [of the space], or at the head, the feet, or both sides [of the bed], and stays there with the thought: "If he finds it cramped..."
If one should intentionally move away from another to create such a circumstance, and it is neither for any other reason nor due to a lack of decorum, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
[Note: This refers to cases where no offense is committed despite the mat falling as one turns over onto one's side. These include: if one did not know [the mat was there] beforehand;

if one remained after having spoken [to the other]; if space had previously been cleared; if the space was so wide that it did not cause obstruction; or if an acquaintance instructed one, saying, "Simply spread [your bedding]."
If one falls to the ground oneself, if one turns over due to illness, if one falls upon it while being carried by force, or if one is imprisoned— under these conditions,
even in the face of the two perils of life or the Dharma, there is no offense.

[Commentary: The five phrases of the *Śikṣāpada* are as follows: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the knowledge [of the situation]; third, the forceful spreading of the mat by one who arrives later; fourth, the intention to cause distress expressed in the words "thinking thus" and below;
fifth, the formal determination of the offense (*āpatti*).
The division of the text of the *Śikṣāpada* is easy to understand.

[Commentary]: "To act as the cause and condition and not otherwise" means that it is not otherwise that one does not commit an offense; rather, by looking at what constitutes an offense and what does not, this is the meaning of "offense.
As for "otherwise," it refers merely to not relying on non-offenses; thus, to harass others is not a matter of *īryāpatha* (proper deportment). How could this not be an offense?

The explanation of "not otherwise" within "not otherwise than this": "otherwise" refers to what is external; non-offense exists outside of offense, meaning that which is not an offense is precisely not a non-offense.

This clarifies that these are actual offenses. First, the text cites and indicates [the subject], and below it explains the remaining meanings; the following passage provides the combined explanation of the text.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Rule 17: Expelling Another from the Room.
[Commentary] The seventeenth rule concerns expelling a bhikṣu from his room.

[Commentary] However, as the monastic quarters for the Saṃgha of the four directions are held in common by all, it is logically improper to restrict them to a single individual; they must necessarily be shared for the benefit of all, even if previously...
Once the food has been properly prepared and settled, it is appropriate for the fellow practitioners who arrive later to enjoy it together.

To now harbor malice within one's heart and forcibly drag others out—this is the root of self-destruction, harming others, and inciting contention; since the harm caused is not slight, this rule was established.

Seventeenth: Regarding the initial clarification within the section on "Restraining the Mind" (*cittaviniyama*), it explains that the various objects [of the precept] generally apply to those who dwell together;

*zhan* (贍) means to provide or supply. Now, following this, the text proceeds to enumerate the transgressions to clarify the rules of the ordinance. The causes for offense are either the same as in the preceding precepts or have been omitted from the transcription. According to the *Chao* (the *Vinayavibhāṣā-viniścaya-upadeśa*), there are two [cases]:

first, regarding the monastic quarters for spring and winter (if one has already entered the summer quarters and drags them out, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense); second, regarding the prior establishment and settlement [of the dwelling].
Third, with an intention to cause disturbance; fourth, dragging [a monk] out [of the monastery].
[Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six and the group of seventeen were traveling together on the same road toward a small dwelling place.
The group of seventeen entered the monastery first, swept and sprinkled it to make it clean. Knowing they had secured a good location, the group of six drove them out and dragged the bhikṣus out.
Having reported this transgression to the Buddha, He then established this precept.

[Commentary]: Regarding the causal conditions for this precept, because [the monk] had previously forcibly spread out [a seat], the Buddha’s prohibition and the resulting offense arose. This was in a layperson’s home;
however, within a monastic monastery, the principle is that one must rely on the position according to the number of years since ordination (*kṣetra*). For this reason, he was dragged out.

The *Śaikṣa-vibhaṅga* (Exegesis on the Origins) states: "Regarding 'monasteries and so forth,' this clarifies the arrogance of the group of six [monks] based on their seniority; the order of the characters [in the original] is inverted.
[Sūtra]: If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu, personally drags that person out of a monastic dwelling or instructs another to do so...
"Dragged out.
[Note] If one does it oneself or instructs another to do so, for every portion dragged out, one incurs an offense as soon as it leaves the room.

If many people are dragged out through a single door, or if one person is dragged out through many doors, one incurs multiple *pārājika* offenses. If one person is dragged out [through a single door], [one incurs one offense].
If one falls [from the path] at the doorway, or carries out many objects, or throws them outside the door, or closes the door on others outside, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
[According to the Vinaya,] it is a *pāyattika*.
【Note】There is no offense in the following cases: if one departs in succession without a mind of malice; if one sends away someone who has not yet received full ordination;

if one departs because [the other] has violated the precepts, views, or deportment, or for the purpose of formal censure or banishment; and if one is driven out due to threats to life or to the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya). All such instances are permitted.

[Commentary: Regarding the four phrases of the precept text: first, the person; second, internal anger; third, it is a private area within the monastic compound and thus not an offense; fourth, leading [the person] out constitutes the formal offense.
The third phrase of the precept text applies exclusively to communal quarters; for all other cases, there is no offense.
[Commentary]: Regarding the analysis of the characteristics of the offense, the primary intent of establishing many rules is to restrain evil conduct so that it may be severed.
Nowadays, however, those who are attached to their possessions mostly guard their rooms and lock their doors; they do not permit others to enter and only begrudgingly allow them to be led out.
In the explanation of the transgressions, the first part clarifies the intent behind the establishment of multiple offenses; now, next, it indicates that such violations are rare in the末法 (mofa) age.
Regarding the note stating "one holds another's object and throws it outside the door," the intent is to cause that person to leave.

[Commentary: Regarding the opening [of the rule], one asks: "In the previous precept, the opening for relatives did not distinguish between pure and impure; why is this case restricted to those of pure conduct, excluding relatives? The answer is:
In the previous precept, it concerns secular family members who were the first to borrow [the space]; because there was no compulsion from relatives, it was opened.

This case concerns a monastic dwelling, which does not distinguish between the defiled and the pure, as it has the sense of being a residence for the Saṃgha. Those with evil precepts have no share here and are expelled.
This means that one does not violate the precepts.

Regarding the non-violation mentioned in the inquiry concerning the precept prior to midday: while the opening [provision] for relatives and old acquaintances does not list "breaking the precepts" or "wrong views," this present precept is the reverse of the former;

therefore, its intent is investigated. In the response, the first part explains that the opening provision for relatives in the previous precept extends to those who are impure, and the following section explains the current case.

Now, the prohibitions of the precepts clarify that purity is maintained by not permitting [the use of] what belongs to relatives; it is said here that since a monastic dwelling does not belong to oneself and yet belongs to a relative or friend, there is certainly no basis for taking it [as one's own], and thus it is not permitted as an exception.
[Vinaya] Precept 18: Regarding Sitting on a Chair with Detachable Legs.
[Commentary] The eighteenth precept concerns sitting on a chair with detachable legs.

[Commentary] In all matters one must be circumspect; regarding dangerous situations, one must be cautious. If the roof-covering of a house is thin and the chair has detachable legs, one should not cast one's body onto it.
Sitting or lying down may result in falling and injuring those below; because such places are not free from distress, this rule was established.
Regarding the eighteen rules of training, they are explained here according to their origins (*nidāna*) to set forth the formal regulations.
"Thin covering" refers to unstable floorboards, while "releasing the body" means sitting with unrestrained abandon.

[Commentary]: There are four conditions for an offense: first, it is a multi-storied building; second, the roof is thin; third, the legs of the bed are about to fall off; fourth, one sits or lies down, and thus commits the offense. [Annotation]:

When the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu was staying on an upper floor of a multi-storied building. While sitting on a bed with detachable legs, the legs fell off and landed upon the bhikṣu, injuring his body and causing him to bleed.
He looked up and cursed in anger. Another bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked him and established the precept.

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu, whether in a dwelling (meaning a communal monastery cell or a private room) or on an upper story of a multi-storied building (meaning standing such that his head does not reach the ceiling), sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with removable legs (removable legs meaning the legs can be inserted into sockets), it is a pāyattika offense. This applies whenever his side touches the bed or he turns over.
[Note] Excluding beds with removable legs, if one sits on a single-seated bed, a plank bed, or any ordinary secular bed, it is all *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

Those that do not constitute an offense are: sitting on a bed with swiveling legs, straight legs, curved legs, or no legs; if the supports of the bed are large; if removable legs are fitted with a narrow waist-piece;
if the bed is covered by a wooden floor in an upper story, or covered with carved woodwork in the shape of flowers, or covered with thick material, or covered with planks.
If a bed or seat has its legs detached, it is permitted to sit upon it.

[Commentary]: The four phrases of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra are: first, a person; second, a room; third, a multi-storied building; and fourth, sitting or lying down on a bed with detached legs, which constitutes an offense.
[Commentary]: "The foot enters the thigh" clarifies that liberation is not far off.
In the third section of the *Prātimokṣa*, "about to be liberated" refers to the foot moving and entering the socket.

[Commentary]: The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (the root text of the precepts) applies to both sitting and reclining; however, the detailed explanation (*vyākhyā*) and the Vinaya regulations apply only to reclining. When observing the conditions for the origin (*nidāna*) of the rule, one considers three points:

the root text applies to sitting, while the detailed explanation and the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) apply to reclining. Since it is specifically prohibited to lie on one's side with the feet dangling from the bed, we know that there is an offense for both sitting and reclining.

In the fourth [section], first there is the citation and presentation; below that, the reconciliation with the *nidāna* (origin story), the discernment of characteristics, and each of these constitutes one [part].

Since the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (戒本) encompasses two [aspects], the following judgment is made according to the commentary on non-offenses: regarding "installing a small waist [ornament] on the legs of a bed," this refers to things such as clasps and locks.

If it is a multi-storied building covered with wooden boards, this phrase serves as a general heading; the carving of floral patterns and thickness are specifically distinguished as the two characteristics, which are respectively the opposite [of the standard].
Because the precept text provides a brief covering, one does not incur an offense.
[Vinaya] Nineteen: The Precept on Using Water with Living Beings.
[Commentary] The nineteenth precept concerns using water containing living beings.

[Commentary: Generally speaking, the essential core of the Way lies in compassionately saving the lives of sentient beings. To knowingly consume water containing insects and thereby intentionally damage their lives violates the path of compassion.

If one persists in pursuing only one's own interests without any principle, it is profoundly contrary to the compassionate heart described by Master Guang, who held himself lightly and others as precious. Therefore, an urgent regulation must be established.

19. Regarding the "Regulating the Intent" section, the first part clarifies that the fundamental practice of a bhikṣu consists of the fact that the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the Way through compassion;
and that Bodhisattvas, setting aside their own benefit to profit others, have forgotten weariness throughout kalpas.

It is not that those of the Two Vehicles do not provide universal succor, yet because they do not manifest it to the same extent as the aforementioned [Bodhisattvas], it is called the "Essential Doctrine. As for the gentlemen of the Confucian school, they still harbor a heart of compassion and are broad-minded.

To practice charity and provide relief for the multitude by extending love to all things—how much more so for a superior person who has left the household life—to instead commit acts of killing is truly inappropriate.
Those who hear this should take it as a profound warning. Below, the faults are described; first, it clarifies how both self and others are harmed.

To claim that one should exist solely for one's own sake, asserting that harming others benefits oneself, is utterly unreasonable. Master Guang, in the passage below, cites what he himself holds in contempt, namely: [The text continues with the specific examples Master Guang finds despicable.]
Whatever one uses for personal enjoyment that is highly valued by others is, in fact, the very life-force of insects.

[Commentary] There are four conditions: first, the water contains insects; second, one knows there are insects; third, one does not employ a straining method; and fourth, one uses it accordingly and thus commits an offense.
If one filters a third time according to the listed conditions, there is no offense.

[Commentary]: The Tathāgata’s fundamental intention was one of compassionate rescue; while harming [sentient beings] is esteemed by ordinary people, the World-Honored One established treatments according to the specific ailment.

Initially, regarding non-sentient things, digging and destroying were universally prohibited; subsequently, regarding the procreation of life, the treatment was applied according to the specific ailment.

The precepts for both humans and animals have been extensively established and their regulations are already comprehensive; yet nowadays, those who delight in transgressing them proceed to drink and use [water] without regard, failing to perceive the gravity of the matter.

This is why they are called "Great Sages"—as stated in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Thus, many members of the present Sangha lack water-strainers (*parisrāvaṇa*), and whether walking or staying, they drink and use [water] without reflection on the injury they cause.
To call this "the Way" has never been seen as a valid principle; this is explained in detail in the *Shan-chao* (Commentary).

In the introductory section on the precepts, the initial part provides a general exposition on the differences between the minds of the noble and the ordinary; the following section specifically demonstrates the distinctions between the capacities of the practitioners and the teachings they receive.
This is divided into two main parts: first, it clarifies that while non-sentient things may be dug up or destroyed, the two [bodily] precepts remain to protect life;

second, it clarifies that regarding sentient beings there are four precepts: first, killing humans; second, killing animals; third, using water containing insects; and fourth, drinking water containing insects.
In the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, it is stated that there are four types of this precept against taking life, and this is the first to be established.
Since one was not permitted to use water containing insects, one would take it and drink it; because the prohibition was so restrictive, one would consequently deprive animals of their lives.

Furthermore, because the prohibition was so restrictive, one would consequently deprive human beings of their lives. This is manifested by the Teacher’s excellent knowledge of the capacities of his disciples.
The Holy Name [of the Buddha] has now been cited below to lament that those who study the later teachings, though they call themselves "men of the Way" (daoren), do not possess water-strainers;

thus, lacking such compassionate mindfulness, they cannot be said to possess the Way. Therefore, it is said: "Not yet proficient. The following refers to the author of the *Śāstra* (the *Shanfang ji*), who says:

"In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if insects are so minute that they remain even after three layers of filtration, one should discard [that water]. If one uses water, one must inspect it carefully every day until no insects are found."
Regarding the "five-part insects," these are those caught in the water-strainer and visible to the naked eye; without a strainer, one may not travel even half a *yojana*.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Two Garments* (*Dvīvastra*) that although the objects [of harm] may be minute, the consequences are immense;

the compassionate intent of the renunciant to provide relief lies precisely here. Now, if even those of superior grade and lofty conduct drink and use water containing insects, how much more so for others?
How can this be described? [Note:

When the Buddha was in Kauśāmbī, he instructed a house-builder to mix water with insects into the mud for plastering. An elder saw this and felt resentment, thinking there was no True Dharma as living beings were being harmed.
A bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.
[Sūtra]: If a bhikṣu, knowing—or if he does not know, there is no offense—that water contains insects, pours it onto mud or grass, or instructs another to pour it; [Commentary]:

If one throws grass or soil into water containing insects; or if one pours insect-infested curd-liquor (*mastu*), clear curd-liquor, or vinegar onto mud or grass—in all such cases, one falls into an offense.
This applies equally to instructing another to do so.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Pātayantika.
[Commentary] There is no offense if one does not know there are insects and perceives them as being absent; or if the insects are large and one moves the water with the hand to make them leave;
or if one strains the water and sprinkles it on the ground; or if one instructs another to strain the water—in all such cases, there is no offense.

[Commentary: The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* are: first, a person; second, knowledge [of the presence of insects]; third, the object damaged by insects; and fourth, the act of pouring water onto mud, which clarifies the offense.
[Commentary: Within the analysis of the characteristics, two modes are fully present: either using grass or soil mixed with insect-infested water, or pouring insect-infested water [onto the ground].
Even if there is a pond or a large body of water on grass or soil that does not turn to mud, if one throws grass or soil into it, insects and fish will die accordingly;
this constitutes an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*). This rule was established as a profound precaution against causing the loss of life.
If their lives are actually severed, it is governed by the precept on animals, resulting in exactly one offense of transgression; the details of other textual passages can be understood accordingly.

In the first part of the fourth section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the characteristics of offenses are clarified; there are two parts. First, it clarifies the offense committed when intentionally throwing water and earth at one another;
next, it clarifies the offense for casually tossing objects other than those mentioned above. Following this, it clarifies the formal determination (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) of the offense.

First, it clarifies how this specific precept applies according to the number of objects involved; next, it contrasts this with the different formal determinations for killing animals that follow; finally, it covers the remaining three [cases].
The brief indication that this does not constitute an offense and so forth can be seen by consulting the text.
[Vinaya] The twentieth precept on exceeding the limit when roofing a house.
[Commentary] The twentieth precept on exceeding the limit when roofing a house.

[Commentary: Generally, all things have their limits, yet when tasks are undertaken, greed leads one to lose measure. If one piles on more and more without ceasing, it will cause the house to collapse;
thus, one’s labor and effort are wasted, and one fails to honor the faithful offerings made by others. For this reason, the rule was established.

In the first section of the twenty rules concerning the intention (*saṃcetanīya*), it first clarifies what is appropriate for one who is greedy; next, it enumerates the characteristics of transgressions, which are the fundamental *nidānas* as cited in the commentary.
[Commentary]: There are four conditions that constitute an offense: (1) acting for one's own sake; (2) having another person conceal it; (3) not ceasing before the third stage is completed.
The section on the offense of being out of sight and hearing for three or four intervals is concluded.

Regarding the third point concerning the enumeration of conditions, it says "three intervals" (*tri-parvan*); some say this refers to three layers, such as a thatched hut in the world, while others say it refers to three rows, like the tiles of a roof.
The exact manner of roofing houses in the Western Regions (India) is not well known, so it cannot be definitively determined.

[Commentary] Question: Why is it that there is permission to look over [a roof] while covering it oneself is not permitted? Answer: Looking over does not constitute the offense of "appropriating" (paribhoga), whereas covering it oneself invites heavy censure;

therefore, its use is not allowed. Alternatively, this may be explained according to the *Pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) of the teaching: because the act was initiated by causing another person to do it, the precept was promulgated immediately upon that causal factor.

In the question, this refers to whether instructing another to inspect or cover [the bedding] constitutes an offense; it does not prohibit one from covering it oneself, hence the question addresses this generally.
There are two points in the answer, the textual structure of which is easy to understand.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, this room was one of the thirteen large rooms built for three hundred thousand coins, yet it collapsed immediately upon completion. It was then offered [as a gift].
The Lord spoke to the bhikṣu who was experiencing distress, saying: "Although this dwelling has collapsed, its merit is already perfected. While it was yet unruined, the Buddha came to this room;
thus it was utilized by the unsurpassed field of merit. Subsequently, a newly ordained bhikṣu entered it.
Whether one builds a chamber or a pavilion as majestic as Mount Sumeru, or maintains the precepts, once their use is finished, the grace [of the merit] is bestowed."
Because the precepts turn one’s back on worldly dharmas, whereas dwellings and the four requisites are worldly dharmas.

In citing the initial instance among the conditions, it refers to the original narrative of the collapse of a house which distressed its owner; in the "Thirteen Major Matters," the "large house" is specifically a house with an owner.

If one relies on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the causal condition is the cutting down of a sacred tree, which differs from this account. As for the "three hundred thousand," [it refers to the number of years].
Ten thousand makes ten thousand, which is three hundred thousand bhikṣus; this next section clarifies the words by which the bhikṣus provide explanation.
The preceding section clarified that the Buddha had previously made use [of them]; following this, it clarifies the use by newly ordained monks.
Those who turn their backs on the mundane rely upon the uncontaminated (anāsrava) and supreme dharmas, for the noble path is the fundamental basis that excels worldly dharmas.
[Note] When the Buddha was staying at Kausāmbī, a monk built a cell with multiple layers of roofing that did not stop until the house collapsed.

A lay devotee complained, saying, "Though the donor provides for the recipient, the recipient should know moderation. The bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.

【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling (using a great deal of wealth and materials), including doors, windows, and other decorative fittings (such as carvings and painted designs), and directs the covering with thatch (of two kinds:
longitudinal and transverse), exceeding two or three layers, [he commits an offense].
[Note] If that bhikṣu, while still in the process of directing [the act] through three stages, reaches a place where he is neither seen nor heard;
or if he does not reach such a place by the time the three stages are completed, he commits an offense of falling (pārājika).
[Pācittiya]. [Commentary]:

If one mutually relinquishes the place where [the offense] was seen or heard, it is a dukkaṭa. As for those who do not commit an offense, this is as explained above regarding the allowance for those who have been instructed to stay at a distance.
[Commentary]: 1) The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* constitute the first [section]; 2) from "one person" and "two dwellings" below, it constitutes the method of performance;

3) from "instruction" below, it constitutes the characteristics of maintaining [the practice] through its application; 4) from "if one exceeds" below, it constitutes the offense incurred for violating the teaching.
The third section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, beginning with the character "shàn" (苫), refers to thatching grass used for roofing.

[Commentary]: Regarding these three stages, although the Vinaya and the Abhidharma treatises discuss them interchangeably, they may also be cross-referenced according to their actual facts. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"In constructing a dwelling, there are three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—and the roofing for each has its own limit. If a middling or inferior dwelling uses the method prescribed for a superior one..."
Because it is covered with something heavy, one may use grass for each [section], and each shall be five parts high.
According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, if one covers it with grass, tiles, or wooden boards, there is no offense even if it exceeds the limit, as these are light materials.
Furthermore, when constructing a room, one should first measure out the foundation, steps, and building materials before covering it, lest it become excessive.
This is a treatise (*śāstra*).

Among the three [categories], because the first concerns origination, the following citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (or *Vinayamātṛkā*) shows that the three grades are distinguished according to the thickness or thinness of the expenses for the dwelling;
the middle and lower grades, as well as the upper grade, are covered [by this rule]. Thus, exceeding the limit is established; those [expenses] below five parts are all [permissible].

Regarding the differences in the characteristics of the objects involved, the draft manuscript of the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there is no offense because it does not contradict the aforementioned texts;

thus, the lightness of the object is applied as a general principle. Furthermore, the following section clarifies the weighing of the actual act versus the preliminary effort (*upakrama*), referring to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (the *Bahudhātuka-vibhaṅga*) as in the case of the two types of rooms.
[Vinaya] 21. Teaching the *bhikṣuṇīs* without being appointed.
[Commentary] There are twenty-one cases of teaching the *bhikṣuṇīs* without having been appointed by the *saṃgha*.
[Commentary] There are five underlying intentions for this regulation.

[Commentary: First, regarding the purpose of the Bhikṣuṇīs coming to request the Dharma: Mahāprajāpatī and the assembly, in order to show reverence for the Dharma, consulted [the monks] regarding their doubts and difficulties and practiced according to the instructions.
However, because the Bhikṣuṇīs were weak and lacked the opportunity for travel and study, they were confused regarding principle and practice, truly like those facing a blank wall.

Therefore, it was necessary for them to seek teachers and request the Dharma every half-month. The two Buddhas commanded the Bhikṣus to permit them to go; the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, specifically selected [this rule].

Virtuous and compassionate instructors should provide guidance and clarification to those who harbor doubts, causing them to give rise to understanding and practice so that they may achieve the benefits of the Path.

When requested, one may go before a separate assembly of monks for the sake of the nuns; however, unless it is necessary to open the way for them to go, it is better for both sides to remain in tranquility to avoid much labor.

Regarding the reception of the precepts, the opposite of the previous case is difficult; thus, the Sangha does not go [to the nuns]. The three regulations require that those possessing the requisite virtues must themselves be profoundly conversant with the Vinaya.

The practice of the Vinaya is like water and jade; its words are clear and its principles are refined. Who, possessing both virtue and the capacity to encompass all things, can transform the masses and rectify the Way?

There are those who are single-minded and upright yet possess shallow knowledge and are unacquainted with the rules of advancement; they do not lose themselves in their own confusion, but how can they guide others according to the intent of the teachings?

Or there are those who, though possessing some slight knowledge, do not act in accordance with the Dharma; in their every movement and action, they deviate from the ritual protocols. How can those who drown themselves in the long current lead others across?

Salvation arises from these conditions; therefore, one must possess virtuous conduct. (First, regarding being appointed by the Saṃgha: Although one may personally possess virtue, if there is suspicion of impropriety, one must be screened out.

Only when the Saṃgha has carefully selected and dispatched one who is fully endowed with virtue can one advance. Relying on the majesty of the assembly, one’s conduct and influence are universally accepted.

The recipient of such an appointment acts with profound reverence and ultimately attains the benefit of the Path. (Fifth, regarding the intent of the precepts: They are intended for those who act solely according to their own will and do not receive the commission of the Saṃgha.

They frequently go to provide instruction, yet they perform rituals in a perfunctory manner, deviating from the proper rules and failing to guide others toward the right direction. Their conduct causes the teachings to decline, while their own arrogance diminishes the Dharma;
since the damage caused by this failure to propagate the doctrine is grave, how can we not impose restrictions?
Twenty-one: Regarding the initial intention within the formulation of the rules, there are two parts.

First, the narrative concerning Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī—the Buddha’s maternal aunt and the one who initiated the teaching—and those who respectfully followed the Dharma, namely the eight weighty rules (*gurudharma*) which stipulated that she must rely upon the Saṃgha for the *poṣadha*.

Next, the following clarifies the necessity of requesting [permission]: regarding the practitioner who is deluded about principle, "principle" refers to that which is realized, while "practice" refers to...

These two practices that have been cultivated are both taught through the scriptures; because those who have not studied do not understand them, they are said to be "deluded. The phrase "facing a wall" is a metaphor from the *Analects* signifying a state of having no vision.

Regarding the section on listening to the [teachings] of others, there are two parts: first, the formal narration of the intent for listening, which distinguishes those of virtuous character as listed below;
second, the general application of the practice. Within the latter, there are two sub-sections to dispel doubts: first, the doubt that a *bhikṣuṇī* must come to study.

Why is it that the Sangha is sent to teach? It is because the ritual principles for instructing a teacher in the high tone (shangsheng) of the character "qiang" (to compel/force) dictate that it is not appropriate for [the Sangha] to go;
thus it is called "compelling. As for the subsequent section, one might wonder why the reception of the precepts is not treated similarly.

While one may go to provide general instruction to an individual, the matter of receiving the body of ordination is so grave that it requires the entire assembly; therefore, it is called "difficult. Among these three points:
First, the initial four lines—beginning with "Only one who acts in accordance with the Dharma should go"—collectively summarize the ten virtues mentioned later;

specifically, the first line subsumes the second, third, and fourth [virtues], the second line subsumes the first and ninth, the third line subsumes the fifth and eighth, and the fourth line subsumes the sixth, seventh, and tenth.

Following this, there is a further distinction regarding what is not in accordance with the Dharma; from the beginning up to "guiding sentient beings," these are the opposites of the first line above.
There is no [separate] "liberation" (vimokṣa); or, reading "ji-ba" (to rescue) below, it refers back to the preceding phrase to mean there is no "practice" (caryā).

Since there is neither liberation nor practice, how could one be able to preach the Dharma or possess complete virtues? The meaning of this can be seen in the fact that the text does not repeat the term.

From the following three concluding points, two intentions are shown within the distinctions of the four regulations: first, to prevent confusion regarding the teacher; second, based on the following two [points], for...

Because those taught are easily transformed and the transmission of instruction is unobstructed, it is called "universal practice" (*sāmānya-pravṛtti*). Because it is like the wind bending the grass, it is called "wind-like transformation" (*vāyu-vikṛti*).

Among the five [points], the latter four lines specifically reverse the initial intent of the preceding [section]; the final two lines reverse the subsequent intent of the preceding [section]. "Mí" (靡) means to comply.

Regarding the phrase "light[ly]" (*qīng*) at the end, it concludes the fault and reveals the prohibition: because they do not accept the Sangha’s command, it is said they "slight the Dharma" (*qīngfǎ*) and act willfully (*zhé*).
To act as a teacher and provide instruction is itself an expression of self-respect.

[Commentary] The treatise states that there are five conditions for an offense: first, the Buddha has opened the way by expounding the Dharma through the Eight Teachings; second, the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) was enacted to appoint [a teacher];

third, one does not go to assemble the community of nuns upon being commissioned by the Sangha—this specifically excludes cases where rooms are separate and teachings are given separately, which do not constitute an offense; fourth, the teaching of the Dharma; and fifth, the eight points of respect (*gurudharma*).
Regarding the second rule for the formal motion (*jñapti*) concerning the appointment [of a monk to instruct nuns], the text states: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let it appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. This is the motion. (The *karmavācanā* is to be understood accordingly).
[Note] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī came to request instruction. The Buddha ordered that they be sent according to the sequence of the Saṃgha;

Paṇḍaka went there and preached the Dharma for them. Subsequently, the group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) went there and spoke of worldly discourse (*lokāyatika*). Mahāprajāpatī informed the Buddha, who then performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to appoint [an instructor] and established the precept.

[Commentary]: Within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this section first clarifies the nun’s request; second, the dispatching of monks by the Saṃgha; third, the arising of faults due to the Ṣaḍvargika monks preaching worldly discourse (*lokayātra*);
and fourth, from the point of addressing the Buddha downward, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and the requisite virtues.

In the section on the conditions for the precepts (*śīla-pratyaya*), it is stated that those who propound worldly treatises (*lokāyatika*) are defined by the Vinaya as those who discourse only on kings, subjects, armies, horses, and the like. [Commentary] Question:

When Mahāprajāpatī came to request [the establishment of the Bhikṣuṇī order], why did she not request the Buddha to stop the debate among the bhikṣus? Answer: She requested the Buddha’s instruction because there was [a need for it].

There are two kinds of faults: first, it contradicts the teaching of the Eight Respectful Rules (*gurudharma*), for within those rules one is required to consult the Saṃgha; second, it contradicts the mental resolve made when undertaking the vow.
If one instead invites the Buddha, one incurs the two aforementioned losses.

In the initial question-and-answer section, the first part clarifies the invitation to the Buddha; both of these faults constitute violations of the respectful rules, though the former specifically violates the formal dharma of respect.
Below, this contradicts the intention of the text, because the substance [of the precepts] was obtained by following the eight *gurudharma*s from the beginning;
if it were "next," it would clarify the invitation of the *saṃgha*, as both versions exist, though the text reading "inviting the Buddha" (*pātimokkha*) is an error.
[Commentary]: If this is so, since the Buddha had already established among the Eight Rules of Respect that nuns must go to the monks once every half-month, why did Mahāprajāpatī seek out the Buddha?
The answer is: although the nuns had received the prohibition, the monks had not yet been commanded; therefore, she came to request that the Buddha command the monks to go and instruct them.

Regarding the difficulty [of why one should not request from the Buddha after he has already established a rule], it is because the nun Āryā Ānandā requested it of the Buddha; once the rule was established based on the Saṃgha, one should not seek it from the Buddha—the explanation of the text is clear.
[Commentary] Question: Why does the Buddha not teach [the rule] himself? Answer: There are many faults. First is the fault of narrowness: it would not apply to the three continents. Second...

The first minor transgression applies only to the Buddha; these three are shortcoming-transgressions that do not extend through the ages. For a bhikṣu who commits them, they are instead transformed into three benefits.

In the subsequent section of questions and answers, the first clarifies the decline of the Buddha’s teaching, while the second clarifies the benefits of the Sangha’s teaching—thus transforming the three [transgressions] into three benefits.
"Extensive" means vast and long.
[Commentary] Among those selected for the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), one must possess ten qualities: first, being fully endowed with the practice of the precepts; second, being widely learned;

third, having mastered the recitation of the two sections of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*; fourth, possessing decisive judgment free from doubt; fifth, being skilled at preaching the Dharma; sixth, being of noble lineage... [and so forth].
Seventh, her physical appearance must be upright and handsome; eighth, she must be capable of preaching the Dharma to nuns so as to bring them joy;

ninth, she must not have left the household life for the sake of becoming a Buddha [in order to gain worldly power], nor must she have committed a grave offense while wearing the three dharma-robes; tenth, she must have twenty or more years of seniority (*varṣa*).
If these ten qualities are not fully possessed, the appointment is not valid; therefore, they are briefly distinguished here.

Among those appointed as officials, the first list enumerates ten virtues; items 1, 9, 5, and 8 are termed "semblance-virtues" (*pratirūpaka-guṇa*) because they are liable to confusion with the preceding [general] and the following [specific] categories, which can be understood by dividing them accordingly.
Furthermore, the eighth and tenth virtues are restricted to the teaching of nuns and are thus termed "specific virtues" (*viśeṣa-guṇa*); all others are "general virtues.

Since this [text] merely lists the names and numbers according to the Vinaya without yet having the leisure for extensive explanation, it does not go so far as to exclude those that are not [included here].
This is a summary. [Vinaya]:

If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha has not been appointed (without having performed a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* within the Saṃgha) to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs (the eight rules which must not be transgressed, as set forth in full in the text), commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*.

[Note] If, during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, after questions and answers have been exchanged on the seat, that bhikṣu—whether appointed by the Saṃgha or invited by the bhikṣuṇīs—arrives at the appointed time, the bhikṣuṇīs must also arrive at the appointed time to welcome him.
If either side fails to do so, both commit a *duṣkṛta* offense. If they hear he is coming, they should go out half a *yojana* to welcome him and provide whatever is required;
failure to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. This applies unless the Saṃgha has not appointed him or it is not a time for instruction.
If one preaches the Dharma to a nun without being appointed to do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If one is appointed but the Saṃgha is ill, discordant, or incomplete, one should send someone to pay respects and inquire after the nuns' health; in cases such as illness, one should likewise send someone to pay respects and inquire.
If one does not do so, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For both the Bhikṣuṇī and other groups, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense for a Bhikṣu.
The nuns, having employed the aforementioned expedients, find that the paths by water and land are cut off and various obstacles arise such that they are unable to perform prostrations or inquiries.
All such cases are hereby exempted.
[Commentary] The precept text consists of five phrases: (1) one person, (2) the Saṃgha, (3) not being dispatched, (4) instruction, and (5) the formal conclusion of the offense.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the fourth section on the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), I refer to the root Vinaya text; fearing that those who seek excellence may not have seen the preceding and following sections, I shall briefly present this in three gates:
first, the intent of the original enactment and the enumeration of the characteristics; second, the sequence of the respects; third, the gravity of the offenses incurred.

In the fourth section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, under the initial heading, it says: "Regarding the reference to the *Vinaya-mūla*, this indicates that [the text] is abbreviated. This is because those who delight in the Dharma might fear [that the full text is too extensive]. [Commentary:

Regarding the initial formulation of the precepts, their essential nature knows neither noble nor base; rather, it is those who possess the Way who are honored. The formal rules and essential methods are not for the sake of the *saṃgha* alone.
Those who do not possess reverence for the Dharma and respect for persons must pay homage; when speaking with such reverence, every encounter becomes [an occasion for practice].

However, because these eight types of respectful rules (*gurudharma*) are particularly essential for governing *bhikṣuṇīs*, they were separately established. If one can truly practice them, the precepts will be pure and the Dharma will abide.

Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Because of the ordination of *bhikṣuṇīs*, the True Dharma was reduced by half; if the eight respectful rules are practiced, the Dharma will again be fulfilled for a thousand years."
If people propagate its meaning, they will not be deluded.

Regarding the second section on "Regulating Intentions," the first part provides a general exposition of the monastic virtues; because they possess the Way and the Dharma, it is necessary to pay them respect.

Following this, the second part correctly elucidates the Eight Respects (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), which is further divided into three sections: the first correctly clarifies [the principle], followed by citations of scriptural evidence. This is...
Ānanda first requested that nuns be ordained; the Tathāgata granted permission for their ordination, as recorded in the section on the formal procedures (*vidhi*) below.

[Commentary: In the subsequent listing of names: (1) a nun of one hundred years of seniority must pay homage to a monk who has been ordained for even a single summer; (2) she must not revile monks; (3) she should not initiate formal charges against monks;

(4) she receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the assembly of monks; (5) she confesses the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses before both assemblies; (6) she requests the fortnightly teachings (*poṣadha*) every half-month; (7) she establishes [the boundary].
Regarding the eight occasions for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination), one must in all cases rely upon the Saṃgha;
the names [of these occasions] may be seen [in the list].
[Commentary: Second, to clarify the sequence: the Dharma does not manifest itself; its guidance depends on the person. Therefore, the first three clarify compliance with the rules.

The Sangha is honored by people because of the Dharma; next, the fourth and fifth [sections] clarify the Dharma that is followed. Since this Dharma is obtained through invitation, the third section below clarifies the reception of repentance.
Within the clarification of the sequence, the first division shows how the three stages arise in succession; for now, they are categorized generally according to each individual stage.
Within this, there is a sequence as detailed below in the separate treatise; [note that] the character "huì" (悔) is an error for "huì" (誨), and the same applies hereafter. [Commentary]:
Within the first stage, the arrogance of bodily action is coarse, and thus it is explained first. Because the transgressions of verbal action are subtle, they must be explained later.

Between the two types of speech—those that violate the Dharma and those that accord with the Dharma—the former cause deep affliction, while the latter merely point out minor faults; therefore, they are listed in this order. Alternatively, one might expect...
This is a numerical enumeration.
Within the first section of the detailed exposition, there are two parts: first, physical homage; second, verbal abuse.

Since both physical and verbal conduct are coarse, verbal offenses are mentioned first and physical ones later, as the latter are subtle. Below this, there is further discrimination regarding verbal offenses, which has two interpretations. First... [text continues].
Regarding the two faults of the afflictive portion—depth and shallowness—there are hopes and counts.
[Commentary]: Within the practice of following the Dharma, one first receives the root precepts and subsequently repents for the branches.
Within this practice of following the Dharma, the sequence of receiving, giving rise to, and committing offenses can be understood accordingly.
[Commentary]: Within the context of receiving repentance, the ritual procedures are explained in general; since these must be initiated through formal petition, the instructions are first clarified.

Because practice arises in accordance with the Dharma, there follow the phases of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism). Subsequently, when the proper time arrives, specific terminology and supplementary refinements are added to ensure that the path is fully realized and its radiance expanded.
In the initial section of the instructions, the sequence is first clarified: one requests instruction beforehand because one must rely on it for practice;

furthermore, since the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) is performed after the summer retreat has concluded, they are said to follow one another in succession. Regarding the subsequent addition of "radiance" (*guang*) mentioned at the end:
"radiance" means to glorify and propagate the teachings so that they flow forth.

[Commentary] Next, regarding the three [sections] concerning offenses: among them, the first, fourth, sixth, and third all constitute *thullaccaya* (grave) offenses, as found in the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts.

Regarding the second [section], "Respect": insulting or slandering [a superior] is indeterminate; [if it constitutes] a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, or *duṣkṛta*. Third, "Accusing and speaking of faults" constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; obstructing an accusation constitutes only a *duṣkṛta*.
Fifth, "Regretting a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense without coming to the Saṃgha for confession" constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The remainder is easily understood.

Regarding the three types of offenses, the first clarifies the three factors that constitute a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). Second, because the meaning of reviling and slandering is identical, they are explained together.
The Vinaya states: "One must not revile a bhikṣu; one must not slander [him]," and so forth. These texts designate three offenses.

Slandering applies across all three categories of offenses as previously assigned. Reviling, however, consists of only two types: reviling for unwholesome dharmas constitutes a *pāyattika*, while reviling for wholesome dharmas is merely a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Regarding the three types of formal accusations (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), the *Vinaya* explains the characteristics of an accusation as follows: "What you have done is thus;
what you have done is not thus; and you must not do it. Regarding the offense of a *pācittiya* for self-assertion that obstructs an accusation, the *Vinaya* states:

"Obstructing another in their search for faults" (meaning to obstruct another when they are accusing one, preventing them from doing so). Regarding the fifth *pācittiya*, which concerns obstructing the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* or the *Pravāraṇā*, this matter should be rare.
The remainder refers to both the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony), for which one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

[Commentary: Regarding the determination of the offenses, the initial section clarifies the characteristics of extensive instruction; however, the Vinaya and Abhidharma state that this dharma has largely perished.
Even among those who practice the abbreviated version, there is still a lack of dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*).

The first part of the fifth section clarifies the extensive method, as indicated in the Vinaya-śāstra; that is, the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, which summarizes the essential points of the Vinaya texts into five items:
(1) the community of nuns sends a messenger; (2) they arrive at the monastery and rely upon the monks; (3) they make their request before the assembly;
(4) the Sangha performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of appointment; and (5) they must go when the time arrives. Next, the abbreviated method is shown because [the former] is absent.
Virtuous people merely transmit the admonitions of the Sthavira, which are contained in detail within the *Chao*; those who require them should seek them there.

As for those who still lack proper ritual, the *Yeshu* states: "Because those who do not study or possess learning occupy high seats as leaders and act without the rules of Dharma, they cause nuns to be sent back empty-handed, and they never respond to them;
those who understand this are all equally ashamed. This refers to the provisions [for nuns] mentioned in the commentary.
Regarding what is required, the Vinaya states that one should prepare a seating area, provide bathing requisites, and arrange various foods and drinks such as congee;
furthermore, for occasions such as when a monk is ill, the methods for prostrating and inquiring after his welfare are likewise abbreviated.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "not on a day of instruction" in the text: there is no such provision in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Sifen lü*). However, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (*Shengji lü*) lists eight factors in detail:
1. An improper time, namely the evening; 2. An improper place, meaning a concealed or exposed location; 3.
An excessive time, namely the twenty-ninth, thirtieth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day; 4. The time has not yet arrived, regardless of whether it is the waxing or waning phase of the moon.
Regarding the ten-day interval, one should go during the remaining days; other times are improper. The other four [periods] are omitted.

To explain why these days are improper: according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, eight periods are improper, yet the text specifically cites three or four to illustrate the nature of their impropriety.

This refers to the fact that each of the two halves—the bright half (*śukla-pakṣa*) and the dark half (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*)—consists of ten days. One may go during the first four days of the bright half up to the thirteenth day, and during the nineteenth day of the dark half.
Up to the twenty-eighth [precept], both the two subsequent days are designated as "past time" (atikrānta-kāla), and the three preceding days are designated as "time not yet arrived" (aprāpta-kāla);

those before and after these are all termed "improper time" (akāla). Regarding the other four abbreviated points, I shall now cite them in continuation: Fifth: If the bhikṣuṇīs are not in harmony, one should not provide instruction or admonition.

Sixth: One must not provide partial instruction; rather, one should instruct only after the entire community has reached harmony. Seventh: [The precept concerning] the improper time for visiting a layperson’s home.
One should not deliver a long discourse on the Dharma as Nanda did until sunset; one must welcome [the eight rules] when they arrive, and if one fails to welcome them, one incurs a *pāyattika*.

[Commentary]: As the ancients explained, "day" does not refer to the eight respectful rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*). Violating them constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Not appointing someone to preach the Dharma also constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the two offenses: two *pāyattikas* and two *dukkaṭas*.

The masters of the Ancient and Middle [Traditions] rely on the text as cited in the commentary; according to them, the former consists of two *dukkaṭas*, while the latter consists of two *pāyattikas*. [Commentary:

Our current interpretation is that since there is no distinction between light and heavy regarding the eight rules of respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) when teaching the Dharma, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "The instructor [commits a] *pāyattika*. This refers to the extensive [explanation].

Regarding the explanation that "one who speaks the Dharma" refers to the *tīrthika*, it is known that the meaning is the same. As for the formulation of the *duṣkṛta* offense, it merely states "not [waiting] until daybreak";

as for the formulation of the *pāyattika* offense, it merely states "not [waiting] until the appointment. Although the eight points of respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) are mentioned therein, the text simply lists them without further elaboration.
The characteristics of the completed offense clearly indicate that it refers specifically to going at will without having been appointed.

Now, regarding the first section of the middle commentary, there is no distinction between the two aspects: the *śīla-mūla* (root precepts) and the instruction. The detailed explanation of the eight points of respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) is as explained in the commentary, which cites itself.
Regarding the phrase "concluding with auspiciousness" (*jie ji*), the subsequent explanation clarifies the intent of concluding with the transgressions mentioned in the commentary.

Thus, one knows that if the day is not incorrect after having been dispatched, then preaching the Dharma and the eight points of respect both result in auspiciousness; however, if one goes without being dispatched, both constitute a *pāyattika* offense.
The Vinaya text merely establishes the two offenses of "assigning on a day" and "not assigning," listing them interchangeably; this leads to erroneous interpretations.
As for the phrase "the text contains no words," it means that the *Prātimokṣa* (Sūtra of Precepts) does not explicitly state the eight rules of respect (*gurudharma*) regarding preaching.

Regarding the phrase "establishing the characteristics," it means that when the *Prātimokṣa* establishes the offense by following the preceding rule against "not assigning," one knows that the downfall (*pāyattika*) occurs solely due to the failure to assign. Now...

Furthermore, let us construct a syllogism to determine the characteristics of the offenses so that there is not even a slight discrepancy: [Thesis] If one commits a single offense on the day of appointment, it constitutes one *pāyattika* (提);
if one commits two offenses on the day of appointment, it is not merely one *duṣkṛta* (吉); if one does not commit any offense on the day of appointment, it is neither [a *pāyattika* nor a *duṣkṛta*].

[Reason] Because the teaching and instruction regarding the eight *gurudharmas* (八敬法) are no different [in all three cases]. [Conclusion] For what reason, then, would you distinguish between light and heavy? It is certain that [your position] is incorrect.

[Commentary]: Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for a nun who teaches [the monks], this does not refer to the crime of teaching the monks arbitrarily; rather, it refers to teaching them without having been appointed by the nuns.
This is because even within the two assemblies of nuns, one must not go to a monastery to pay respects or inquire after others' welfare without being dispatched by the senior nuns.
In the first section of the *Śramaṇerikā-śīla*, regarding the offense of a *bhikṣuṇī* teaching [the nuns] on her own initiative: this refers to going there herself to request [instruction].

Regarding the subsequent two groups [of nuns], the meaning of "requesting on one's own initiative" is not different; therefore, while there are cases where merely performing prostrations on one's own initiative does not constitute an offense, it is only for the *bhikṣuṇī* community that the fault of not requesting [permission] is waived.
[Vinaya] Precept 22: Teaching the Dharma to Nuns until Sunset.
[Commentary] The twenty-second precept concerns teaching the Dharma to nuns until sunset.

[Commentary] Generally, there is a distinction between monks and nuns such that they reside separately and do not occupy the same place; when a Mahāsattva (Great Being) acts, he must avoid causing public scandal or reproach from outsiders.

Faith and reverence increase within, yet the expectation for the Path has declined today; as we gather together at dusk, external suspicions arise and our own conduct is compromised. Since the transgressions of our behavior are grave, they must be restrained.

Regarding the first of the twenty-two rules for restraining the mind, this section first describes the principles upon which one should rely, which bring benefit to both oneself and others. Now follows [the explanation].

Next, it is explained that one must not violate this rule, for doing so would cause harm to both parties; conversely, by not violating it, what would have been a loss becomes a benefit—this is why the precept was established.
[Commentary] There are six conditions for an offense: first, being appointed by the Saṃgha; second, the assembly of nuns arriving; third, the instruction and preaching of the Dharma;
fourth, reaching the evening twilight; fifth, knowing oneself [to be capable]; and sixth, continuing to speak when requested to stop. These constitute an offense.
Regarding the conditions for the offense, the first is that the Sangha has appointed [the monk]; if the Sangha has not appointed him, he commits the preceding offense. [Note:
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, after Nanda had been appointed by the Sangha to instruct the nuns, he remained silent. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī requested him again and again until evening.
When the nuns went out from Jetavana, they stayed overnight within the moat of the city and were criticized by the laity. The bhikṣus informed [the Buddha].
The Buddha then rebuked him and established a prohibition.

[Commentary: Regarding the circumstances of this precept, it was first established because of a transgression involving a nun coming to a monastery of monks to preach the Dharma; consequently, he prohibited her from going there.

There is no text to be found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), though I have previously seen such accounts in other schools (*nikāya*), which were forgotten due to my old age and failing memory.

In the *Nidāna*, it is stated that because monks from the Western Regions resided outside the city while nuns lived within it, when the city gates closed at dusk, they were unable to return in time and stayed overnight in a moat.
Consequently, the laypeople mocked them, saying: "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame and lack pure conduct;
they spend the entire night sleeping with nuns and release them only during the day. This refers to various schools.
The *Shanjian* (Sudarsana) states: "Initially, because women’s faculties were dull, it was permitted for [monks] to go to the nunnery to instruct them;

however, because they were criticized by others, it was subsequently opened up for five persons to go. Yet, as criticism still persisted, it was finally permitted for monks to go to the nunnery. If one explains it in this way, there is a significant contradiction:

since the previous section on the *Biqiujie jing* (Bhikṣuṇī-śikṣāpada-sūtra) already clarifies that those who are dispatched must be specifically selected, if this were the very first opening of such permission, it would not be the case.

If those listed later were placed at the beginning, it would again be difficult to determine their sequence as they have previously been appointed to advance or retreat; let students examine the following instructions carefully so that forgetfulness may serve as a warning for those who come after.

[Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha (1. *śāstṛ*—instruction; 2. *karmavācanā*—formal act), is to instruct a bhikṣuṇī (the appointment among the assembly is made by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*—a formal motion followed by one proclamation). Now...
