"Until sunset": [Note] He has been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; he should return before sunset, unless he is instructing, receiving the scriptures, reciting the scriptures, answering questions, or attending to other matters until sunset—excluding the case of instructing bhikṣuṇīs, or being with women, or other persons.
If one continues to receive the scriptures until sunset, it is all *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅).
[According to the Vinaya,] it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提).
[Commentary: For *bhikṣuṇīs* and others, it is *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if, while instructing the *bhikṣuṇīs*, one stops before sunset, excluding women.
It is permitted to listen to the Dharma if one has already heard it from others at a ferry crossing; or if one listens while preaching the Dharma to merchants at night;
or within a bhikṣuṇī monastery; or if one happens to hear it while being invited by someone else to preach.

[Commentary]: Regarding the four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* [Sūtra], the first concerns the individual; the second, the appointment by the Saṃgha; the third, the instruction; and the fourth, the formal conclusion of the offense at the end of the day.

In the commentary on the second phrase of the *Prātimokṣa*, it says "first, the instructor, etc."; the Vinaya states that within the assembly of monks, one is appointed through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation).
However, the difference from the previous rule is that the former did not involve an appointment and referred generally to two methods, whereas this case—since it...
Having already differentiated [the offenses] based on a single dharma.
[Commentary: In the detailed explanation, excluding the instruction (*avavāda*), regarding the remaining cases of reciting and receiving the sūtras until evening, why are they equally criticized?

Because instructing the Saṃgha is easy when the assembly of nuns gathers, it is considered heavy; as for the rest, there is no restraint over the coming and going of nuns who have been specially invited.
It is light because it concerns the Dharma.
Regarding the fourth [section], the initial inquiry is followed by an explanation. First, it clarifies that the gravity of the instruction lies in its being a communal rule (*saṃghadharma*);

next, it clarifies that the remaining cases are light because they concern individuals who have made a request. In the commentary on "no offense," the phrase "before sunset" means there is no [offense].
Regarding the transgression of violating the *vidyā* (knowledge/pledge), with the exception of women—meaning other men—there is no censure or suspicion.
As for crossing by boat, among the four types [of cases], three are permitted due to specific circumstances and are not intended exclusively for nuns. Third, regarding those within a nunnery:
since there is no fault in the location itself, it is "due to the request of a person," which is written in reverse order; the Vinaya states: "On the day of the *poṣadha*, [a person] comes."
One should listen when the instructor speaks upon being requested;
this is the rule. [Vinaya] Twenty-third precept on reviling the instructor of nuns.
[Commentary] The twenty-third precept concerning the reviling of those who instruct nuns.

[Commentary: However, one who is endowed with all virtues and has been appointed to instruct others out of a compassionate heart should have as their sole intent the preservation of the Dharma and not seek fine flavors.

Now, seeing others obtain profit, they inwardly give rise to jealousy and outwardly utter words of derision and reproach, thereby vexing and disturbing the virtuous and good. Should they fail in their mission because of this, it would sever the opportunity for universal benefit;
since the harm involved is no small matter, this rule was established.
Section Twenty-three: Restraining the Mind. Part One: An initial account of the transgressions committed, according to the Dharma. "Rich flavors" refers to fine food.

Now, next, the following section accounts for the arising of faults through slander. First, it clarifies the karma of the mind—namely, vexation, jealousy, and envy—as well as the karma of speech—namely, derision and reproach.
Following this, it clarifies the destruction of affairs; "ruined" means brought to ruin or abandoned. "To sever the means of universal succor" means to fail in benefiting others and to cause harm.
The following is the double summary. [Commentary]:

There are six conditions for committing an offense: first, being appointed by the Saṃgha; second, having the intention to act for the sake of the Dharma; third, conceiving envy within one's mind; fourth, speaking words of derision and reproach;
fifth, the completion of the verbal expression; and sixth, being heard and known that the offense has been committed.
In the enumeration of the conditions, one, two, and six [factors] constitute that which is censured, while the remaining three belong to the censors. [Note:

While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, he heard that the instructor of nuns had arrived and that she was being welcomed and provided for. The group of six [monks] became jealous and said, "She has no genuine qualities;
she instructs the nuns merely for the sake of food. A bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established the rule.
Regarding the precepts: among the conditions for the precepts, the group of six bhikṣus were subject to a regulation due to their transgressions;
because they lacked virtue and were excluded from the formal procedures, they harbored resentment within their hearts and consequently incurred censure.
【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus, "The bhikṣus are instructing bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink," it is a pāyattika offense.

[Note] If it is said that the offense is *kṣudrāpatti* (light transgression) for not speaking clearly, and that there is no offense for bhikṣuṇīs and others regarding the same, this is indeed the case.
There is no offense in any of the following: teaching [the Dharma] for the sake of providing food and drink; teaching recitation or receiving the scriptures for the sake of food and drink;
speaking while questioning, joking, or by mistake.
[Commentary: Regarding the three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* (the core of the precepts), the remainder can be understood.
As for the three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa*: first, the person; second, the censure; and third, the offense. In the note concerning "no offense," the facts are indeed as stated;
even cases such as reciting scriptures for the sake of food are all considered censurable but not erroneous, and therefore there is no offense.
[Vinaya] Precept 24: Giving Robes to a Nun Who Is Not a Relative.
[Commentary] The twenty-fourth precept concerns giving robes to a nun who is not a relative.

[Commentary] Generally, the status of monks and nuns differs; logically, there should be no interaction between them. Even if there is no formal cause for taking or giving, such actions still invite public censure and suspicion; how much more so when there is actual intimacy?
Because it leads to defilement, the corruption of the holy life, and is truly a great loss, this rule was established.
Twenty-fourth: Regarding the intent of the rule, first the categories are clarified; next, the provocation of censure is revealed.

"One who lacks the conditions for taking or giving" means that even one who lacks the conditions for taking or giving and merely associates with others cannot avoid censure, let alone one who holds robes.
If one engages in mutual contact and defilement, one often commits a grave offense; this clearly reveals the intent behind the regulation.
[Commentary] Five conditions constitute an offense: first, it is a bhikṣuṇī. The *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* states that for the three groups [of nuns], they fall equally under the Vinaya;
although there is no explicit text, the meaning should be the same. Regarding the washing of robes, it appears to be a light offense, as the gravity depends on the circumstances.

Regarding these two [cases], there is an offense when: (1) the person is not a relative; (2) one perceives them as not being a relative; (3) one acts [to give] with a sincere heart; (4) one gives a robe; and (5) the other accepts it. This is the first condition for an offense.
First, regarding the initial taking, the treatise resolves the Vinaya rules concerning washing; next, one compares the gravity or lightness of those offenses, as explained in that treatise.

If a junior member washes [the robe] together with others, they commit the same offense of *duṣkṛta*. If one were to compare this to washing clothes, the offense for a junior member should be lighter; thus it is said "it seems so.

However, one must grasp the underlying intent (*citta*) rather than applying the rule by mere analogy. Since the intent regarding washing is light while the gravity of the offense regarding the robe is heavy, the lighter case should follow the lenient rule and the heavier case must follow the strict rule.
Therefore, it is said that "according to the intent" and so forth. "To give with an empty mind" means to apply oneself with single-minded devotion.
Alternatively, it may be inferred from the following account of the *pratītyasamutpāda* that the bhikṣu’s attempt to give [the robe] was not done with sincere intent. [Note:

While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī begging for alms, a bhikṣu’s deportment was perfectly complete. When a bhikṣuṇī saw him, wholesome thoughts arose within her, and she repeatedly invited him [to accept a robe], but he did not accept.
Later, when the Saṃgha distributed robes, she gave a robe to the bhikṣuṇī; he immediately accepted it. She then felt resentment and reproached him.
The nun repeatedly spoke to others regarding the fault of the bhikṣu, and he reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked her and established this precept. [Commentary:
Within the context of the causal conditions for this precept, it first clarifies that the nun pushed aside the robe offered by the Saṃgha and did not accept it;

subsequently, when the Saṃgha attempted to give it again with the hope that she would share the same disposition as the monks, the nun suddenly accepted it. This greatly deviated from her original intention; therefore, it is categorized as a grave offense involving many complications.

The circumstances were as follows. Regarding the investigation into the conditions for the precept, it is said that one should speak with deference, saying, "Please accept. The Vinaya states: A bhikṣu thinks to himself, "The bhikṣuṇīs have repeatedly invited me, yet I did not accept.
If I now give this robe to them, they will surely not take it. [This refers to] the instruction regarding the fault of giving too little, as indicated by the finger.
The Imperial Decree states: Do not engage in excessive affairs.

[Vinaya] If a bhikṣu gives clothing (the ten types as explained above) to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative (as defined above), except in exchange (exchanging clothing for clothing, clothing for non-clothing, needles, knives, or thread, down to a single *liang* of medicinal herbs), it is a *pāyattika*.
[Note]: For bhikṣuṇīs and others, it is a duṣkṛta offense; there is no offense if one exchanges robes with a relative bhikṣuṇī, or gives them to a stūpa, to the Buddha, or to the Saṃgha.
[Commentary]: The precept text consists of six phrases: (1) the person; (2) the non-relative; (3) the nun;

(4) the robes and other items—the text does not specify their dimensions, yet both major and minor transgressions are equally classified as *pācittiya*; (5) excluding trade; and (6) the formal determination of the offense.
The fourth phrase of the *Prātimokṣa* merely refers to the substance of the robe; thus, one knows it is not restricted to robes of large or small size.

[Commentary: The reason why nuns incur a light offense for giving robes to the two assemblies (the monks and the nuns) is that the precept was not established based on the frequency of the occurrence, but rather on the basis of the fault of public censure.
Since the Sangha is the most venerable assembly, for a superior to personally offer [robes] to an inferior assembly invites deep public censure; therefore, the offense is grave.
It can be understood that the nun’s act of offering up to those above while disparaging and doubting them indicates a sense of lightness.

Regarding the offenses of nuns, the initial inquiry distinguishes them from the Great Sangha and śrāmaṇeras; thus it says "the two assemblies. Now, the following section explains how what is below applies to what is above.

In terms of human sentiment and principle, it is not appropriate for what is below to be offered to what is above; however, when the matter is accomplished through convenience, it is not the same [as the offense].
[The Vinaya] Twenty-fifth: The precept regarding making robes for a nun who is not a relative.
[The Commentary] The twenty-fifth precept regarding making robes for a nun who is not a relative.
[Commentary] The intent of the regulation is the same as before.
Regarding the twenty-fifth regulation, the intent refers to the absence of any non-censurable defilement.

[Commentary] There are four conditions for committing an offense: first, being a bhikṣuṇī (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that all three assemblies commit the offense equally); second, [the person] is not a relative.
The three [factors] of sending oneself [to the tailor] constitute the fourth factor of "acting in accordance with" the offense.
Regarding the conditions for the offense: the first three belong to the object confronted, while the fourth is the person who commits the offense.
[Note: While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, Kāḷodāyin had a great robe made; he then cut it into the shape of a phallus, and once it was finished...

[The Buddha] had a nun wear it at the rear of the assembly, which provoked the ridicule of the laity. The nuns reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept. [Commentary:

Regarding the causal conditions for this precept, the reason for creating an image of sexual intercourse is truly due to the gravity of afflicted passion; by entrusting the object [of the act] to another, the transgression is manifested.
The object [of this precept] must be severed. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Māyā folded her robe and spread it out to show the Buddha; he observed what she had done.

Regarding the initial explanation of the conditions for the precept: because the making of robes leads to the defilement of sentient beings, it is said that "the entrusting of objects reveals the fault.

Thus, one knows that although this precept concerns the making of robes, its true purpose is to sever desire. The lower section of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* cites and demonstrates this by means of the folding [of the robe].
[The Buddha] displayed his robe to the Buddha to reveal the fault, saying it ought to be regulated.
[The Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika offense. [The Commentary states:

For that bhikṣu, according to the amount of cloth cut by the blade and according to every single stitch sewn, he falls into an offense; this applies even if he merely inspects it while it is being worn.
If one pulls, drags, irons, or smooths [a garment] by rubbing it with the hand; or if one grasps the corners and pulls them to make it square and even;
or if one arranges the borders, or seeks thread, or joins thread—all these constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses, except in cases where there is no transgression.

There is no offense in making [garments] for a relative nun, or for the Saṃgha, or for a stūpa; or if one borrows [a garment], washes, dyes, or repairs it, and then returns it to the owner—all such cases are permitted.
[Commentary]: The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* can be understood by examining the text itself.
Regarding the four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa*: first, the person; second, one who is not a relative; third, a nun; and fourth, the making of robes. Below this, the offense is concluded.

[Commentary: Since one has already performed the acts of needle and blade, the *karmic bond* (*saṃyojana*) follows the actual execution; other means such as cauterization or massage are merely minor offenses.

Next, regarding the explanation of the transgression: because the knife and needle constitute the primary act while cauterization and so forth serve as auxiliary factors for its completion, they are termed "preparatory acts" (*upāya*).
[Vinaya] Precept 26: Sitting with a Bhikṣuṇī. [Commentary] Precept 26:
Sitting in a secluded or exposed place with a Bhikṣuṇī.
[Commentary] This is no different from staying overnight with a woman.
Twenty-six: The initial intent of the prohibition is the same as for not leaving overnight; there are two reasons: first, the influence of defilement;
second, the incitement of public censure. [Note] When the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, Kāḷodāyin and the nun Thullanandā were both of handsome appearance. Each...

There were those with lustful intentions who sat together outside the gate; the laypeople collectively disparaged them using the analogy of a *rūpāṅga* (a pair of mating birds). When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.

[Commentary]: In the narrative context (*nidāna*), sitting together outside the gate is merely subsumed under the rule concerning exposed places; since the core text of the precept (*śīla-sūtra*) clarifies "in private," it is known that both cases are simultaneously included in the formulation of the rule.
Next, regarding the section on the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra* (Jièběn) concerning the origin of the precept, the corresponding text clearly explains the distinction between secluded and exposed places.

[Commentary]: There are four conditions for committing an offense: first, when a *bhikṣuṇī* and one of the three other assemblies (*tri-gaṇa*) [are together], according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya*, both assemblies commit a *pāyattika* offense;

the same applies to the precept regarding traveling by boat or on land. However, if a laywoman is excluded, one does not commit this offense. Second, it concerns a concealed or exposed place. Third...
There is no third person; as for the "human form," according to the *Śāstra*, if four people sit together, one commits an offense.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu sits or stands while following a bhikṣuṇī as she rises and sits, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for each instance. The same applies when a bhikṣuṇī sits. If two people share the same seat, it constitutes a single *pācittiya* (offense requiring expiation) throughout the day.
Regarding the first condition for an offense in the *Catvāri-varga-śīla-sūtra*, as it refers exclusively to fully ordained nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), citations from other schools are used;
since they state that the community of nuns encompasses all three categories [of women], there is no doubt. Furthermore, the analogy of the "path" and the "boat" is judged in the same way.

As for the exclusion of secular women, because there is a separate regulation below, it is stated here that this constitutes no offense. Third, the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya-vibhāṣā* (The Commentary) cites the rule concerning sitting with a woman, which refers to monks.
Ji says: "If they are one's mother, sister, or a male or female attendant (kappiyakāraka), or if they are asleep, deluded, insane, infants, or otherwise incapable of being witnesses.
[Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī (one being a bhikṣu and the other a bhikṣuṇī) are in a secluded place.
[Note]: There are two kinds of "hidden places": those where one does not see due to dust, mist, smoke, clouds, or darkness;
and those where one does not hear, such that even the sound of ordinary speech cannot be heard.
[Sūtra] One who sits in a place obstructed [by a tree, a wall, a fence, a cloth, or any other object].
[Commentary] If a third person is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, or if they are standing, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
[Pācittiya. [Commentary: For nuns and others, it is a dukkaṭa. There is no offense if the bhikṣu has a companion;
or if there is a witness who is neither blind nor deaf; or if he falls while walking; or if he is ill; or if he is overcome by force or by the threat to his life.
The objections raised by Brahmā and others are all resolved.
[Commentary] The four phrases of the Pratimokṣa Sūtra.
[Commentary] A single person.

[Commentary]: Second, regarding making robes for a bhikṣuṇī: because there is no reproach of intimacy with the one who provides the robe, it is permitted to sit apart and walk together regardless of whether they are related or not;
however, if outsiders are unaware of this, it incurs reproach—this is the first point.

In the second section of the *Prātimokṣa*, it simply states "with a nun" without distinguishing between those who are related; therefore, this is contrasted with the preceding two precepts to clarify the underlying intent of the teaching.

[Commentary]: Regarding the third point, secluded places—as described in the Vinaya—there are two types of seclusion: those of sight and those of hearing, the characteristics of which are easily understood. Furthermore, there are cases where one party is blind and the other deaf.
Because it fulfills the conditions for proof, it is auspicious; because one sits [in violation] while the precept was established [for others], it is light.

Regarding the third [offense], the initial reference to the two "secluded" [factors] is explained in great detail, as in the section on the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules. Below that, the next part explains the third person;
below that, the three parts explain the standing and dwelling above as being a deficiency of faculties (*indriya*), while the following part explains the discordance of conditions (*ālambana*).
"And both commit a light offense. [Commentary:
The reason the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* is light is that when sitting together with those of superior rank, her will is not free; because the transgression is slight.

Regarding the first section of the fourth [chapter], it raises the question and indicates the reason the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* is light: it is because it was unintentional; or perhaps it is because if those of superior rank become intimate with those of lower rank, [the fault is minor].
It is easy to list what follows below, but difficult to refer back to what precedes above; therefore, although they sit together, their circumstances differ significantly.

[Commentary] Regarding the opening of the middle section, "not blind or deaf," this refers to the preceding phrase "blind but not deaf. The same applies to the subsequent sections listed below; the rest is self-evident.

In the subsequent section explaining the commentary, the two phrases beginning with "not blind" (*abādha*) are listed with their words inverted from their original order; furthermore, two phrases are mutually missing in the paired translation.
These are established as *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses), while the rest is understandable: the sequence of actions and the nature of the illness are both contrary to one's intention.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The twenty-seventh precept concerning traveling together with a bhikṣuṇī.
[Commentary] The twenty-seventh precept concerning traveling together with a bhikṣuṇī.
[Commentary] The details regarding transgressions of the established rule are the same as before.

Twenty-seven: The formulation is the same as the preceding cases because while the specific matters differ, the underlying principle is universal; thus, they are not cited again. Regarding staying overnight, traveling by boat, and the abandonment of defilements, there are no distinct categories;

rather, these actions are performed in accordance with their respective objects. Since the specific characteristics of these matters are diverse, the text provides only brief indications of their general intent, as follows.

[Commentary]: Regarding the six conditions for the offense, the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: (1) being among the three groups of the nuns' community; (2) having made a prior appointment, except when meeting by chance or when the appointment was not permitted or one did not leave the place where it could be heard;
(3) traveling along the same path; (4) not leaving the range of sight or hearing; (5) having no valid reason;
and (6) crossing a boundary while following [the nun]. These constitute the offense.
The second condition for an offense excludes those encountered by chance; this refers to the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*. It states in full:

"If one does not intend [to travel together] but happens to encounter another on the road, one should ensure they remain at a distance where their speech cannot be heard. If it can be heard, there is an offense.
If both parties have intended [to travel together] but neither has given permission, and their voices can be heard, there is an offense. In the text, this is not a case of being separated.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of hearing," both of the preceding two lines involve offenses of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), but because they do not constitute a *pācittiya* (offense requiring expiation), they are excluded from this specific rule.
[Note: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) and the group of six nuns (*ṣaḍvargikī*) were traveling through the countryside.
Householders criticized them, and when the monks reported these transgressions to the Buddha, he rebuked them and established the precept.

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī (saying, "Let us go together to a certain village, city, or kingdom") and travels along the same path (where there are delimited sections for travel between villages),
from one village to another village.
[Note] According to the respective limits, if one enters a non-village area— such as traveling through an open space— even for ten *li*,

it constitutes an offense (*pācittiya*). If it is less than a village or less than ten *li*, or if one travels between many villages within the same boundary, or if there is a common agreement regarding the preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
all constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.

【Vinaya】 Excluding other occasions, it is a *pāyattika* offense. "Other occasions" refers to traveling with merchants when there is suspicion (of being robbed by bandits) or fear (of being robbed by bandits); these are called other occasions.

[Note]: For nuns and others, there is no offense for a *duṣkṛta* in the following cases: traveling with a large group without prior appointment; traveling through places of suspected danger or fear; going because one will find safety there;
or being compelled by force or facing difficulties such as threats to life or the celibate life (*brahmacarya*). All such instances are permitted.

[Commentary: Regarding the five phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* [offense], their characteristics can be understood through a detailed explanation of their mutual relations: first, the person who commits the offense; second, making an appointment with a nun; third, traveling together on the same road; fourth, excluding special circumstances;
and fifth, the formal determination of the offense.

Regarding the re-explanations within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (the section on the precepts): this refers specifically to the explanation of the rule concerning different times. The causal narrative for the Vinaya rule is as follows:

because both monks and nuns wished to travel to the country of Vaiśālī, the nuns sought companions from among the monks. When the monks did not grant permission, the nuns proceeded anyway and were subsequently plundered by bandits.

Consequently, the rule permitting protection was established. Within that text, it is further permitted for two types of traveling merchants to accompany one another; likewise, there is no difficulty in having male companions, and even those who are suspected are permitted.

It is also permitted [for a nun] to travel without a companion when there are causes for fear or difficulty. [Commentary: If a *bhikṣuṇī* relies on the *saṃgha* as her support, the offense is minor because the transgression is slight;

furthermore, since traveling by road involves many hardships, it is permitted to sit down out of apprehension regarding fear—this is because sitting is a state of security, which is why it is not prohibited. However, regarding instruction, permission is granted from the third [situation] downward.

[The offense is] committed. In the first section of the commentary, it is explained that because a nun relies on a monk as her companion, and this is not due to reasons of suspicion or fear, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light) offense.

[The Sub-commentary] states: On a journey where the distance is vast, the risk of inviting public censure is great; even if there are many bhikṣus, a single nun still commits the offense, and it is necessary to have many [monks].
When the *bhikṣuṇīs* first open their seats and disparage [the monks], there are two cases where the presence of two *bhikṣus* constitutes no offense.

The next section provides a comparative analysis of the two grave offenses regarding the preceding rule on sitting; first, it distinguishes the circumstances of fear, wherein opening the seat is permitted while closing the seat is prohibited;
second, it distinguishes the conduct of the third person, wherein closing the seat is permitted while opening the seat is prohibited.
[Vinaya] Precept 28: The Prohibition Against Traveling in the Same Boat as a Bhikṣuṇī.
[Commentary] Precept 28: The Prohibition Against Traveling in the Same Boat as a Bhikṣuṇī.
[Commentary] This was established because of criticism regarding traveling after midday.

[Commentary] The treatise states that there are six conditions for committing this offense: first, being a nun or one of the three other assemblies; second, having made a prior appointment; third, being on the same boat;
fourth, intending to travel upstream or downstream; fifth, having no valid reason; and sixth, both feet entering the boat—upon these conditions, the offense is committed.
The Fourth Condition for the Twenty-Eighth Offense: Explaining that traveling up and down a river current is not a direct crossing.
[Note] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus traveled on the same boat upstream and downstream with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs.
Laypeople collectively resented this, and the bhikṣus reported the transgression to the Buddha. Consequently, he established this precept.

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to board the same boat to travel upstream or downstream (or enters the boat or employs other such means), it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
except for crossing directly across, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
[Note] For nuns and others, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; there is no offense in the following cases: if one does not make a prior appointment; if one simply crosses to the other shore;

if one enters a boat and the boatman loses control of the crossing; if one travels upstream or downstream; if one goes to the other shore and cannot reach safety; or if one is held by force or under circumstances involving danger to life or the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*).
[Commentary: The four phrases of the precept text are: 1) a single person; 2) making an appointment with a nun; 3) traveling on the same boat; and 4) the formal establishment of the offense.
The division of these phrases in the precept text is easily understood.
[Commentary: Question: Why is it not prohibited to travel on the same boat with a laywoman? Answer: There must be a boatman as a third person.

Therefore, it is unnecessary to establish a separate rule; rather, nuns and women are subject to the same regulation, and both incur the offense of a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), as in the *Vihāra-vatta* (Rules for Monasteries).

When the Buddha permitted traveling in a boat with a laywoman, he stated that this applied only to crossing directly across. Thus, we know that traveling not directly across constitutes an offense without doubt.
This precept is [thus] summarized.
In the question-and-answer section, there are two interpretations. First, it is explained generally that there is always a third person present;

next, it is briefly explained according to the text that the censure and doubt are no different [from those regarding monks]. Below, the Vinaya is cited as evidence: since the direct crossing [of water] has been prohibited, it is verified that the regulations for nuns are the same as those for monks above and below [the waist].
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Precept 29: Receiving Food Praised by a Bhikṣuṇī.
[Commentary] Precept 29: Receiving Food Praised by a Bhikṣuṇī.

[Commentary] There are four reasons for the establishment of this rule: first, to prevent those bhikṣuṇīs from praising one's own virtuous conduct and physical appearance in order to seek profit and increase gains.

First, because the fetter of greed destroys right livelihood; second, because it causes partiality and crookedness of mind, praising those currently in one's affectionate circle and thereby inviting external censure and not slight harm;
third, because it causes others to provide offerings and service based merely on words despite a lack of virtue—this is the impairment of giving;
since there is no practice toward such a field of merit, by what means could the merit of a reciprocal gift be obtained? Fourth, because it involves disparaging good people and praising the base.
The command was issued because failing to show reverence toward superior objects constitutes an affliction of all the worthy and holy ones;
it is for this reason, involving these various faults, that the rule was established.
Regarding the four intentions: first, it increases craving; second, it invites public censure; third, it diminishes the merit of giving; and fourth, [it leads to rebirth in the lower realms].

Disturbing the Saṃgha: first, it harms oneself; second, it harms both oneself and others; third and fourth, they both harm others. Regarding the first point, "sending away a bhikṣuṇī," this is based on the *nidāna* (origin story);

according to the present rule, it constitutes an offense even if she is not actually sent away. Among these three cases, since one has already received [teachings] from those without virtue, one conversely fails to honor and serve those who possess the Path.
Having lost such a superior object of refuge, there will be no meritorious reward. This concludes the general summary of the lower [offenses].

[The offense is] established. [Commentary: The offense is completed through four conditions: first, a nun of the three assemblies praises and obtains food; second, knowing it is contrary to the Dharma; third, receiving and obtaining it;
fourth, consuming it—each swallow constitutes an offense.
The conditions are fourfold: the first is that which can praise, while the latter three are all those being praised—namely, persons who have committed an offense against the precepts.
[Commentary]: As for the others sitting together who are not being praised, there is no fault in eating with them, because praising occurs in private rather than in the midst of the assembly;

thus, there is no fault of failing to censure when one ought to censure, unlike the case of Tiṣya, who conferred [the precepts] privately before the Saṃgha and failed to censure immediately, thereby involving the entire assembly.
If one conceals [the offense] such that no instruction is given and does not permit eating, it is clarified in the *Prātimokṣa* (Skt.:

*Pratideśanīya*) that the initial explanation of this precept applies only to individuals and is not extended below [to the community]. Next, it is shown that the *Pratideśanīya* is a regulation applicable to the entire assembly;
however, regarding the instruction by a nun, it is restricted to a single person. If there is no one to reprimand her, then those sitting together with her shall be made responsible.
Because one may not eat food that has not been specifically assigned to them, it is said, "causing [the offense] by not being assigned," and so forth.

[Commentary: Why is there no exemption for the sick? It is because praising the healthy does not incur an offense, whereas praising a sick person as virtuous will inevitably lead to the healthy being disparaged;
since this constitutes a transgression, no exemption is required.
Briefly stated, even within the context of illness, this is clarified through reference to Tiṣya to demonstrate its difference from the initial inquiry. This consists of two parts:
first, the clarification that there is no opening [of the precept]; second, the clarification that if one were to open it, there would be fault.
It is said that "a good person is slandered" because the presence of virtue in one who is ill implies the absence of virtue in one who is not ill.
[Commentary]: Why are the seven conditions for forming a separate group not opened up? The Noble Ones established the precepts with allowances and prohibitions to prevent transgressions.

This particular precept, however, involves praising one's own lack of virtue, which causes profound harm to the Dharma; since it applies universally without exception, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"If one praises one's own virtues in a biased manner, whether one is a worldling or a noble one, the eater [of the food] falls into an offense."

Distinguishing the various cases within the assembly: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation, which is further divided into two parts. First, a general indication of what is permitted and prohibited for those acting as a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

If one acts as a separate assembly where it must be prohibited, one fails to gain the benefit [of the precept]; if one permits it where it should be prohibited, there is transgression. Permissibility and prohibition depend on the circumstances and cannot be treated uniformly.

Below this, the specific reason why this particular precept does not permit acting as a separate assembly is clarified: making offerings to those of virtue is planting seeds in a fertile field for the cultivation of merit.
This is contrary to what the Buddha taught; therefore, it is said that "probing for faults" is inferior. This subsequent citation serves as an illustration:

if one knows that even sages may still commit such offenses despite their praise, how much more so those without virtue? The fact that sages never commit such offenses is stated here as an extreme admonition for ordinary people below.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a householder invited Śāriputra and others, having prepared excellent seats in the open air.

When the nun Thullanandā saw this, she spoke falsely, saying: "Those who have been invited are all of low birth. Had I been invited, I would have had Devadatta and others—the dragons among dragons—eat [there].
She then returned and related this in detail to the Buddha. Consequently, the Buddha rebuked her and established this precept.
[Commentary: Regarding the "dragon among dragons" within the context of dependent origination, the following explains the reasons for his descent and clarifies the censure of the fetters.
Within the causal conditions of the precepts, after Nanda-ni had thus offered praise, and when Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana arrived, the nun spoke to the householder, saying:
"The dragon among dragons has already arrived. The householder then said: "You previously called me a person of low birth."
How can you now say he is the "dragon among dragons"? From this day forward, do not come or go to my house again;
therefore, it is said that Devadatta and the others spoke falsely. The phrase "Devadatta and the others" refers to his four remaining companions.

[Commentary]: The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) states that one should invite Śāriputra, Kāśyapa, and others who possess: (1) those capable of bestowing merit in the present life; (2) those who have entered the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*);

(3) those who have attained the great extinction of knowledge (*jñāna-kṣaya*); (4) those who have entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); (5) those who rely on the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); and (6) those who practice the conduct of non-contention (*araṇā*).
Each of these characteristics is explained in detail as cited in the treatise.
In the first section of the "Requesting Merit" (*ming qing fu*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains the virtues of those being requested, briefly listing their names and numbers;

for details, one should refer to the treatise itself. Here, I have extracted and annotated a portion: "Entering the Vision of Truth" (*ru jian di*). [This means] now, having realized the vision of truth, all beginningless false views are entirely eliminated without remainder.

The "unimpaired faith-vision" (*bu huai xin jian*) is now first accomplished. There are two kinds of vision: that which is severed by false views is affliction (*kleśa*), while that which is constituted by faith-vision is wisdom (*jñāna*). "Truth" (*di*) refers to the principle (*tattva*); because one realizes the true through wisdom, it is called "vision of truth. "Entering" (*ru*) is synonymous with "realizing" (*zheng*); this is the initial stage.

[The Fruit] (2) The Knowledge of the Exhaustion of Outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*): Now, having attained the knowledge of exhaustion, the three defilements of beginningless ignorance, craving, and pride are forever exhausted. This "exhaustion" is itself cessation; cessation is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), which is *nirvāṇa*. The wisdom that realizes this is called the "knowledge of exhaustion.

This refers to the person who has attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) by severing the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*). (3) The Person Emerging from the Meditative Absorption of Cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): According to the treatise, there are three meanings [to their emergence].

First, even upon emerging from the absorption of cessation, they cause sentient beings to obtain merit in the present life. Second, it is said that emerging from the absorption of cessation is exactly like coming forth from *nirvāṇa*. Subsequently, because a musician from Rājagṛha had previously invited bhikṣus for a meal, on the following day, when the city held a festival, various laypeople brought [offerings].
When various bhikṣus had finished eating the food they had received, they then went to the invitation of a musician and were unable to eat much more;

the musician then criticized and disparaged them, leading to the establishment of this precept (this is the second circumstance). The commentary divides this into three sections: the first two separately cite two circumstances regarding receiving food again after having already eaten;
the last one summarizes the previous two circumstances because they returned to their original invitation, which is why it is said that the single regulation applies universally.
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika* recitation of verses when eating gruel, it says: "Maintaining pure precepts, one is honored by others;

with respect, gruel is offered at the proper time. It brings ten benefits to the practitioner: physical strength, vitality, longevity, happiness, clarity of speech, eloquence, the removal of indigestion and wind, and the quelling of hunger and thirst.
This is called medicine as taught by the Buddha. Those who wish to attain long-lasting happiness among humans and devas should [offer it]."
Regarding the offering of gruel to the Sangha, the first verse clarifies the purity of the field (*kṣetra*) and the five benefits such as physical health;

the subsequent verses clarify what is to be eliminated, such as the consumption of leftover food, while briefly omitting mention of the regulation of excrement and urine. The following verse clarifies the retribution received in future lives.
If one does not understand this and constantly recites it, one will remain deluded. Therefore, [it must be understood].
In the introductory verse, the first part is the actual citation; "Now, below" introduces the subsequent commentary. Regarding the phrase "desire not," this indicates the underlying intention.

Within the commentary, the first verse is combined as follows: the first half-verse corresponds to the preceding two lines. The upper line clarifies the virtue of that which is given, while the lower line clarifies the mind of the giver.
The section beginning with "form and so forth" explains the middle four lines; the first of these lines provides a general heading for the ten benefits. *Rāo* (benefit).
"Benefit" (*anuśaṃsa*) has the meaning of "advantage. Regarding the practitioner who receives the offerings of the Saṅgha, the next two lines separately list ten advantages;

however, to complete the metrical verse, there are only nine types: 1. complexion (the luster of the countenance); 2. strength (vitality and robust health); 3. longevity (the extension of life span); 4. happiness (the comfort of the limbs and body); 5.
clarity of speech and eloquence (clear and distinct speech—this is divided into two, which is incorrect); 6. digestion of food; 7. wind (*vāta*).

(These two are both removed) by the eighth [removing] hunger and the ninth [removing] thirst (these two are thereby eliminated). Tenth, as in the commentary, the final phrase concludes the explanation:
because it sustains the person’s body and removes illness, it is called "medicine" (some say "excellent medicine" is incorrect). Regarding the latter half of the verse below:
the first line indicates the retribution, while the second line exhorts one to give (some say "long life and happiness" is incorrect).

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu partakes of food (such as boiled rice, parched grain, or dried rice) by passing it around from one person to another—this refers to an invitation, which is of two kinds: an invitation according to the monastic order or a private invitation—except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The "appropriate times" are: when one is ill; when one is unable to eat a sufficient amount of good food in a single sitting; and when robes are being distributed.
[Note] After the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded, there is one month [for the robe] if no *kaṭhina* robe has been spread; there are five months if a robe has been spread;
furthermore, there may be other gifts of food or robes.
[Vinaya] This is called "the proper time."
[Note] If one does not relinquish a previous invitation and accepts a subsequent invitation, there is an offense of *pācittiya* for every swallow.

If one does not relinquish a subsequent invitation and accepts a previous invitation, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* for every swallow. Exceptions where there is no offense include: when one is ill; when robes are being distributed;
or if, within a single day, one receives many invitations and accepts only one while giving the remainder to others, saying: "Venerable sir, I must go there; please give this [invitation] to me now."
If you are given non-food, or if there is insufficient food, or if there is no invitation to eat, or if you receive more food after having already eaten,
or if there is both a prior meal and a subsequent meal at the same location— in all these cases, it is permitted.

[Commentary]: The precept text consists of six sections: 1) the person; 2) the mutual invitation; 3) the meal; 4) the opening of the conditions; 5) the determination of the offense; and 6) the detailed explanation.

Regarding the explanation of the mutual invitation, it simply mentions "inviting. Since both types of invitations are listed, there is an offense of transgression (*pācittiya*) for both; if one accepts the invitation...
If one has already eaten a thick gruel, or eats one's own food, or eats the food of the Saṃgha, there is no offense even if it causes slight distress.

However, if one first gives consent and later violates it, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) for the transgression. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one eats regular food or food from a separate room, there is no offense."
In the first commentary on the second section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, only two invitations are listed without clarifying the process of successive transmission;

however, in the subsequent passage, the distinction is made that if one partakes of two meals provided by the Sangha itself, one incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*), whereas it constitutes a formal transgression only when both meals are provided by two different hosts.
Therefore, the following citation of scriptural evidence establishes that "regular meals" refers to food provided by the Sangha, while "separate rooms" refers to food provided for oneself.

[Commentary]: Regarding the third of the five interpretations of "proper food" (*bhojana*), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Various vegetables, cakes, parched grain flour (*maṣa*), and fruits are not 'food at all times' (*sarvatra-bhojana*).

Within this third category, the term "parched grain flour" (*maṣa*) is a general designation for proper food; here, it specifically excludes that which is improper, such as the flour of wheat, beans, and the like.

[Commentary: The reason for permitting [the consumption of] what is unwholesome is that the donor understands the suffering and affliction of the sick person; if it were not permitted, their physical life would be difficult to sustain.
Since this is not a matter of personal preference, no time limit is set.

Regarding the opening of the section on illness, the initial intent of the opening has already been shown. "Manifesting the constant" means that what is not sentient is not something the practitioner desires.
"Not setting a time limit" distinguishes this from the provision of robes for one month or five months mentioned below.
[Commentary: There are two reasons why the giving of robes is permitted: first, to provide relief for bhikṣus whose physical needs must be met;

if one does not accept them at the time they are offered, they may become difficult to obtain later, leading to unreasonable begging that harms one's own practice and disturbs others. Second, to benefit the donor, who gains both the merit of providing clothing and food, thereby receiving a reciprocal reward.

Regarding the two benefits within the giving of robes: the first is to relieve oneself, and the second is to benefit others. As for "obtaining a reciprocal reward," this is because the dual giving of food and clothing brings about great merit.

[Commentary] Within the text, regarding the one-month or five-month period, if there is a remainder, according to the ancient interpretation, it was only permitted through a formal act of temporary donation (*āśraya-dāna*). Now...

This does not mean that the giving of robes applies universally to both appropriate and inappropriate times; rather, when it says "the rest," it refers to food and clothing in relation to time, which are indeed permitted at the proper time.
Among the "rest of the food" (atireka-bhojana), accepting an invitation in advance is permitted, whereas accepting [an invitation] for robes is not.
Since it is not only food and clothing that are permitted, but all such items are allowed, it is called "the rest."
Next, the remaining types of giving are explained. First, the introductory section reiterates the ancient commentary; below that, it cites the interpretations of past scholars.

They maintain that during the [restricted] period, one normally does not open [the practice], but rather waits for the occasion of receiving clothing before opening it; therefore, they speak of "one month" or "five months" as times when there is "remaining giving.

In our present interpretation, the first part refutes this incorrect view by asserting that during the [restricted] period, the practice is generally opened regardless of whether clothing is being given; if clothing is indeed being given, there is no such limitation.

Regarding the phrase "during the proper time" (*kāla*), it is said to encompass both the proper time and the improper time (*akāla*). Now, for the explanation below: first, *kāla* (time) is explained in contrast to food and clothing;
because these are obtained outside of the [prescribed] time, they are called "residual" (*śeṣa*). Second, regarding clothing and utensils, they are explained in relation to food;
since the original rule permitted turning away from food while clothing and utensils remained external to it, they are called "residual."

[Commentary] The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: If one accepts an invitation for food from the first house and an invitation for both food and clothing from the second house, it is permitted to go back [to the second house]; there is no offense. 1.

If one accepts an invitation for food from the first house and an invitation for clothing from the second house, and takes the clothing toward the first house, there is no offense. 2. If one does not go toward the first house and fails to eat for the entire day, this violates the promise and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅).
3. If one accepts invitations for food from both houses and goes back [on one], one commits a *pāyattika* (提) offense. Furthermore, there are three cases regarding the former...

Regarding the second case: if one accepts clothing and food from the former family while accepting only a single garment from the latter family, as in the first two clauses, there is no offense for refusing [the former].
Regarding the third case: if one accepts clothing and food from the former family but accepts only food from the latter family, one commits a *pāyattika* offense by refusing [the former].
In the "Liaojian" (Discrimination), the first three phrases of the two sections both follow the former school’s practice of requesting food alone;

the latter three phrases both follow the former school’s practice of requesting both food and clothing. Regarding the initial and final sections of the latter school, both apply to both single and multiple [offerings].

The middle phrase states, "not eating is auspicious," which means either eating monastic food or one's own food. In the first phrase of the latter section, since the preceding and following parts are identical [to the former], [the interpretation remains consistent].

How could there be no offense? It must be because the robes differ in quality, quantity, or both; thus, the next phrase refers to "as before," meaning whether one has already accepted or not yet accepted.
Regarding the offense of "refusing an invitation" (*pratikṣepa*), its establishment occurs within the subsequent six phrases concerning households.

Of these six phrases, four concern invitations for robes where there is no offense—these constitute the permitted exceptions (*anujñāta-pratyaya*). Two concern invitations for food which constitute a grave offense, as they directly contravene the original rule.

[Commentary]: Regarding the seven conditions for eating separately from the assembly, only two are permitted as exceptions while the others are not. In the cases of traveling on a road, by boat, or at a great assembly, these are permitted because food is difficult to obtain and a donor has invited them.
Since these two [other] cases permit the consumption of extra food, it would foster greed and bind one to afflictions; furthermore, they provide benefit to non-Buddhists and lack a donor.
Therefore, if this were permitted, one would turn one's back on the Buddha’s disciples, accept invitations from non-Buddhists, destroy faith, and cause distress.
Because it is profound, it is kept closed. When making robes, the month can serve to clarify both [the prohibition and the allowance].
In response to the initial point in the *jian* (memorandum), "only two" refers to the opening of the prohibition regarding illness and the distribution of robes.

The remaining points below indicate the differences: the first group collectively demonstrates three types; those were allowances during times of scarcity, whereas these are not for reasons of scarcity. To explain the latter, the text next clarifies the śramaṇa.
Giving to them is for the purpose of receiving those from other paths; this is done out of fear that those who have attained right faith might lose it.
"Buddhist disciples" refers generally to both monastics and laypeople. Regarding the phrase "the three lower types of knowledge," the principle for making robes is likewise permitted.

As for the mention of "time and months," the subsequent precepts also refer to a period of one month or five months. This was explained previously: during the time when robes are offered, they may be collected and made into robes; therefore, it is said "may."
Because this was also clearly explained, it was included in the revised and finalized precepts as "making robes.
[Commentary: Regarding the section on non-offenses, there are four points: 1) illness, 2) the gift of robes, 3) the relinquishing of invitations, and 4) the time for robes;

these are to be understood as explained above. As for "if the invitation provides what is not food," this refers to things such as twigs, leaves, or *makarasaṇika* (soft foods), or those that are insufficient.
This refers to not being fully satiated; or, if there is no one requesting food, it is said that there is no offense.

Or, if after having finished eating one receives food again, it is only when one has finished eating at the previous house and then accepts food from another house that it constitutes an offense for exceeding the limit (*pūrṇa*), but not for turning back (*pratyāgamana*).

Or, if one does not break one's seat, one may still accept it. Or, if there is food before and after at a single location, since the host is the same even though the food is different, it is likewise [permissible].
"One who is without backsliding offenses will certainly not violate the deportment, nor will they transgress the rules regarding the feet.
Regarding the section on non-transgressions, the first division consists of the preceding four items; within the commentary, three characteristics are listed.

In the context of giving robes, these are further divided into four categories, as the category of "robes given at an improper time" is inclusive, whereas the category of "robes given at a proper time" is restricted solely to that specific occasion.

If one requests [the recitation] using a lower-ranking document, it may be explained according to the latter five pairs of texts; these can be understood. Third, regarding the statement that there is no offense if one does not request the recitation:

this is not an opening provision (an exception), as the scriptural text lists it redundantly, similar to how previously mentioned cases where one possesses extra robes beyond the permitted days are also termed "non-offenses.

Regarding the fourth and fifth types, both may involve an offense; however, for the "sufficient" [category], one must rely on whether the deportment is impaired or not—there is no offense if it is not impaired.

[Vinaya] The thirty-third precept concerning eating in a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa-bhojana*).
[Commentary] The thirty-third precept concerns eating in a group apart from the community.

Generally, when the monastic community is on the road, their fundamental intention is to nurture others with compassion; internally they purify the inversion of self, and externally they extricate themselves from worldly entanglements.

However, since solid food is limited, it is difficult to provide for all universally. When there are few people, it is easy to supply them; but when there are many, resources will be exhausted. Furthermore, this would involve sacrificing what is of great benefit for something of little value.

It is not for the sake of saving the world that these two [rules] exist. If one were to permit common sympathy while eating separately, it would constitute forming a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*) and thereby disturb the Sangha.
Because there is this twofold benefit in order to gather those who are difficult to discipline, the Vinaya establishes these regulations.
The thirty-third section, "Regulating the Mind," consists of three parts: first, a general exposition of the aspiration for renunciation, clarifying that harmony is essential;

second, a specific illustration of the two types of loss, which formally presents the intent of the teaching; and third, an explanation of the loss of worldly ties, which itself contains two further points.
The first four lines clarify the loss of wealth, as communal expenses increase due to the consumption of food; based on this, the underlying intention is revealed.
It causes people to diminish [their merit], as in the passage cited below: "You should simply invite three people; we may not form a separate assembly. Regarding "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*):
because it possesses color, fragrance, flavor, and tangibility, it has a physical form and substance (*kavaḍa*). Furthermore, the following two points clarify how it diminishes merit:

first, because it differentiates [the recipients] and disrupts harmony, those who are differentiated fail to gain benefit; second, because it weighs heavily upon the mind of the donor, the resulting merit is not universal. Thus, it is said that [such food] diminishes [merit].

Because it is not superior, it is called "sharp" and "light. Second, explaining the impairment of the Path: this refers to the conditions for the formal precepts, as cited in the commentary regarding Devadatta and others.
Because they vied with the Buddha in his ministry and their natures were difficult to subdue, they were called "Hard-to-Tame" (*Durdānta*).

Now, by regulating the separate assemblies so that they become one with the ocean-like Sangha, they are thereby included. Below, the third part is the summary: because this precept was established, it reverses the impairment.

The first is the "Prosperous Assembly" (cheng-sheng-yi), which refers to saving the laity; the second is the "Harmonious Sangha" (seng-he), which refers to what is called below "compassion for white-robed [laypeople] and the gathering of those who are difficult to tame.

[Commentary]: In the second section, the explanation of names, it is simply by means of the person who distinguishes [the group] and the place where they eat that the assembly is established; it is through the assembly that one distinguishes them from others.

The shared flavor also indicates that because there is a separation regarding the food of the Dharma, one incurs an offense in a communal setting. How could the distinct location not be considered a "community"?
However, since the Vinaya refers to the person who makes the distinction, the text says: "Regarding 'eating separately from the community,' it means four or more people.

If one were to speak according to the literal meaning, it should be called "eating separately from the community"; yet, taking the original intent, it is simply called "separating from the community. (3)

Because [an assembly] of fewer than two people would result in a double loss—both for the person and the Dharma—the text states: "One should simply invite three people to eat; we may not form a separate group.

The explanation of the names is divided into two parts. First is the formal explanation of the three people; second is the exclusion of those below that number. Within the first part, there are three sections: from the beginning... [text truncated].

The offense arises from the "distinguisher" (the *nirdeśaka*). To judge whether a transgression occurs, one must determine that the distinctions are not shared; specifically, this refers to the distinction between food and profit (*lābha*), which are incompatible.

Since the phenomenon (*dharma*) is manifested through the matter (*vastu*), there is also a divergence within the phenomenon itself; thus, because of the incompatibility between precepts (*śīla*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*), it is said that "phenomenon and food are separated.

Regarding the "distinguished" (the *nirdiṣṭa*), the following two sections distinguish the confusion between the "distinguisher" and the "distinguished," citing scriptural evidence where the logic of the text is manifest. If...

Regarding the statements from the three lower assemblies, those who discuss the linguistic conventions of the discourse find it convenient to treat them as the subject and object; however, if one grasps the original intent, it is because Devadatta’s original karmic conditions involved separating himself from the true assembly.
Consequently, the middle section distinguishes what is not [the case], while the upper section explains the intention behind the prohibition due to the dual harm [caused by his views].

Thus, the lower section cites evidence that this is not a separate [rule]; this refers to when the Buddha had already established the precepts, a donor came to invite the bhikṣus, and they responded accordingly.

[End of] Exegesis. [Commentary]: The treatise states that there are seven conditions for committing this offense: (1) there is a donor, thereby distinguishing it from eating monastic food or eating alone;

(2) there is a separate invitation and a separate begging; (3) it occurs during the proper time; (4) the place of eating constitutes a formal assembly; (5) one knows there are virtuous companions within the boundary.
The six [factors] of the Bhagavān; the seventh is the offense regarding swallowing food.

In the first enumeration of conditions, "distinguishing monastic food" means that because it is shared by those from the ten directions, if people do not assemble or do not establish the formal signs (*saṃketa*), it is all considered stolen property, yet one does not commit this precept.
Third, the combined demonstration of the two conditions is fivefold, following the analogy of the virtuous.

The Master [Kāśyapa] stated that one does not become a person who has committed a grave offense; the commentary below says, "This excludes only those with evil precepts. [Commentary: The explanation of the seven conditions for the precepts provides an extensive analysis of their pathways and ultimate purposes; these may be understood as the points regarding conditions as set forth in the *Chao*.

If one were to list them all here, it would merely result in a double effort, fearing that one might not see the essential sections summarized in the *Chao*. Therefore, I have briefly cited the essentials.

The "Pointer" (*biaozhi*) refers to the first among the [five] pointers; "broad paths" (*guangxi jing*) and "small paths" (*bingxiaolu*) both refer to minor routes. The *Chao* (Excerpts) clarifies ritual practices by following conditions and demonstrating their characteristics.

[Commentary: Here, "eating separately from the assembly" (biezongshi) is explained in terms of constituting a formal assembly at the place of eating; this is divided into three cases.

First, if one is invited to a household as part of the monastic rotation (*saṃghakrama*) but does not assemble there, an offense is committed. Although this was originally a monastic procedure, when the time for eating arrives and monks within the boundary (*sīmā*) are present but do not eat together, this very instance of the monastic rotation is termed a "separate invitation" (*bipin*). Second, if it was originally a separate invitation and monks arrive at the time of eating...

Since there is no restriction or exclusion, this specific invitation is termed "monastic succession" (*saṃghakrama*). Regarding other types of individual invitations—whether for a single person, a group, or a specific request—it does not matter whether there are monks within the boundary;
as long as the place where the meal is taken constitutes a formal assembly, an offense is incurred.
If the wooden gong is struck to signal the gathering, or if one person is summoned by voice, it is not an offense. One must clearly understand these three conditions, and then act accordingly.

There is a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*); later, it clarifies that by reversing this separation, one becomes a *saṃgha*, at which point there is no longer a separate group.

From here on, the explanation of the two types of separation is easy to understand. Regarding the statement "there is no offense against the *saṃgha*": this refers to cases where one previously obstructed others and then departed at the time of the meal;
