[Commentary] There are three conditions for committing the offense: first, it concerns the four kinds of medicine; second, taking them oneself without authorization; third, swallowing them constitutes an offense.
[Note] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, people, for the sake of their parents and others, [offered food] at crossroads, even within temples.
A bhikṣu who subsisted on rag-robes and begged for alms took for himself food that had been offered as a sacrificial gift;
the laypeople collectively censured him and reported his transgression to the Buddha, who then established this precept.
[Commentary]: Regarding the conditions for this precept, it was established because a *dhūta* bhikṣu would take and eat sacrificial offerings set out by laypeople for the deceased.
The conditions for the offense and the conditions for the precept itself can both be understood [as explained above].
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu does not receive [it]. [Commentary] Regarding "not receiving" food:
that which has not been received constitutes receiving; there are five ways of receiving: receiving from hand-to-hand when given by hand;

receiving by holding an object when given by hand; receiving by hand when given by holding an object; receiving by holding an object when given by holding an object; and receiving when an object is passed over from a distance.

The recipient knows both that there is no obstruction or contact between them in the interim and that the object has fallen into their hands; this is one way. Furthermore, there are five types [of receiving]:

giving with the body, with clothing, by bending the elbow, with a vessel, or returning it; these are the aforementioned four ways of receiving. If there is a specific cause or condition, placing it on the ground to give constitutes the fifth type.
[Vinaya] Food. [Commentary] *Khajja* food refers to roots up to fine flour; it is also called rice, parched grain, dry rice, and so forth.
[Vinaya] Or medicine.
[Commentary] *Seyyani* food refers to ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.
[Vinaya] Placing it in the mouth.

[Commentary] If one takes and places it in one's own mouth without being given food, swallowing it at each gulp constitutes an offense of *vikālabhojana* (eating at the improper time) for seven days; if the limit is exceeded, [the offense is incurred].
Furthermore, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense to consume medicinal substances that should be taken for life without receiving them when there is no valid reason [to do so].
[The Vinaya states: "Except for water and tooth-sticks, it is a *pāyattika* offense. [The Commentary notes:
Those who do not commit an offense are those who take pure water or tooth-sticks; or, if they receive clarified butter (*sarpis*) or oil for nasal administration, it is as if it were saliva.
There is no offense in discarding what remains. If a bhikṣu begging for alms has food carried away by a crow, or if it is blown into his bowl by the wind, he may remove that food;
there is no offense in removing even as much as a fingernail’s worth, provided the remainder is discarded.
[Commentary]: The precept text consists of five phrases: 1) the person; 2) not receiving [the food]; 3) medicinal food; 4) excluding water; and 5) the formal determination of the offense.

Regarding "not receiving," before explaining what it means to not receive, one must first explain the characteristics of receiving, which differ in ten ways. There are circumstances where food is placed on the ground;
as stated in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, although the hand does not touch the mouth, one must perform three acts of receiving (*tri-saṃgraha*) before one may eat.

Regarding the first point in the second section of the *Śīlaskandha-vibhāṣā*, "first explaining 'equally,'" this refers to the opposite of these ten methods, which constitutes non-reception [of food].

As for "placing on the ground with a specific intention," as cited in the *Vinayakṣudraka-vibhāṣā*, it refers to a non-Buddhist who, intending not to give food to a bhikṣu, makes a mark on the ground and places his bowl therein;
when the bhikṣu is about to eat, the non-Buddhist says three times, "I accept [this]," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding food or medicine that has entered the mouth but not yet been swallowed, the textual evidence for the formation of an offense is based on the fact that once one intends to eat, it must pass through the mouth. However, according to the treatise, the actual formation of the offense occurs only upon swallowing;
while the preparatory act (*prayoga*) within the mouth results in a mere *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

Regarding the first part of the third section, the text is obscure because the *Prātimokṣa* merely states "swallowing with the mouth," which suggests that the offense is incurred even without swallowing;
however, the meaning of the subsequent commentary can be understood.
[Commentary]: Regarding the exemption from offense when using water or *yāñcī* (willow twigs), this is stated as a general principle for clarity.
However, concerning the five types of *yāñcī* involving earth and water, there is no textual authorization in any of the Vinayas; thus, one may act according to one's own discretion.

In the fourth section, the first part restates the text; the following is a detailed explanation of the first three phrases. Regarding the phrase "excluding water," the term "one characteristic" (*eka-lakṣaṇa*) indicates its brevity;

thus, it refers back to the *Vinayavibhaṅga* (Liaolun), which is likewise brief. [The text notes that] excrement, urine, and ash are all broadly permitted. The latter two phrases explain the *śīrīṣa* twig (*yángzhī*):

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if an ulcer develops in the mouth or if one must swallow saliva from the throat, one may receive [the twig]; however, if one accidentally swallows it, [it is not permitted].
Since this constitutes an offense, there is no allowance [for it]. Now, if one swallows the broth, one should follow other Vinayas; if one does not swallow it, one must conform to our own school.
Therefore, it says: "it is left to one's discretion.
[The Vinaya] states: The forty rules concerning the prohibition against seeking fine food.
[Commentary: The forty precepts concerning seeking fine food. [Commentary:

A monastic of noble standing ought especially to be pure and incorruptible; now, to indulge in and crave exquisite flavors, to seek out fine food, increases greed, ruins one's character, invites derision, and leads to the loss of the Way; therefore, this rule was established.

In the first part of the forty rules for regulating the mind, the fundamental basis of practice is shown; now, the following section reveals the characteristics of transgressions. Regarding the passage beginning with "increasing greed," it refers to the two types of harm.
In the commentary on the conditions of the precept, it says that "mixed food" refers to using the four kinds of fine delicacies to mix with rice and parched flour;
this is considered a rich flavor according to the local customs of the Western Regions.

[Commentary]: Regarding the five conditions for an offense: first, it must be fine food; second, one must beg from someone who is not a relative; third, it must be for one's own sake; fourth, there must be no occasion of illness;
and fifth, the offense is committed upon swallowing the food.

In the listing of these conditions, the first item fully encompasses four types [of food], while the second clause does not distinguish between relatives and non-relatives; according to the underlying principle, there is no fault in this.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, Upananda took a merchant as his *dānapati* (donor). He told him, "I wish to have some mixed food.
The merchant asked, "What ailment do you have that you think of this? He replied, "I have no ailment; it is simply my desire.
The merchant censured and disparaged the bhikṣu, reporting the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha then rebuked him and established a precept.
【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu obtains fine food— such as milk, curd, fish, or meat— and if that bhikṣu,
being free from illness (except in cases where one cannot finish eating during a single sitting), seeks such fine food for his own sake, it is a pāyattika.
[Note] For nuns and others, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; there is no offense in the following cases: when one begs for oneself while ill, or begs on behalf of one who is ill and eats what was obtained;
or when one acts for another or another acts for oneself; or when something is obtained without having begged for it.
[Commentary: The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* are as follows: first, the presentation of the four kinds of fine foods added for a bhikṣu, which appears alternately in the Vinaya texts;
second, "if a bhikṣu" refers to the person who incurs the offense; third, from "in such a case" onwards, it clarifies the condition of being without illness; fourth, the conclusion of the offense.
In the text of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the first phrase clarifies the food while identifying the bhikṣu as the one who receives it;
the subsequent passage identifies the bhikṣu as the one who incurs the offense. Therefore, it is said that they are presented alternately.
[Commentary]: It is generally said that they are called "delicious foods" because they are expensive, difficult to obtain, and effective in curing illnesses.
Delicious food is not necessarily a medicinal elixir; milk, curd, and ghee are medicinal elixirs but not delicious foods. Fresh ghee and oil are both [delicious food and medicinal elixir].
Fish, meat, and dried meat are both [neither delicious food nor medicinal elixir]. The harītakī fruit is [a medicinal elixir].
In the first section of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the initial part presents the names, while the following three phrases explain them through three meanings.

Regarding "exquisite food" (*praṇīta-bhojana*), the second part distinguishes and clarifies it through four phrases: the first phrase concerns milk and curd, which are "timely food" (*kālika-bhojana*);

ghee (*sarpis*) is fundamentally a "seven-day medicine" (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*), but here, because it can serve as a supplement to food, it is also termed "exquisite food. The second phrase concerns fresh butter (*navanīta*).
Because it cannot be consumed directly, it is merely called a "medicine"; since fish and meat are both foods, and these are further boiled with ghee, they possess both names.
Regarding those that are neither [food nor medicine], although the harītakī is a medicine for the duration of one's life, it is not considered a pleasant substance for a seven-day period.
Thus, while the categories of medicine and food are discussed in general, this current analysis is based on what may be regularly used as food.
That which is permissible is called food; that which is impermissible is termed medicine. [Commentary]:

The *bhikṣuṇīs* establish light offenses because the physical retribution and strength of the great *saṃgha* (monks) are powerful; they take pleasure in begging for fine food to sustain their bodies, and thus it is strictly regulated.
For *bhikṣuṇīs*, begging for fine food is a minor offense, as such things are rare and considered a taboo among women. This is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Regarding the different offenses for these bonds, she actually commits a *pāyattika*.
This explains the intent behind the initial classification of gravity and lightness within the offenses of nuns; next, it demonstrates the differences in the formal charges of the offense.
Among the eight *pāyattikas* for nuns, this refers to begging for the eight kinds of fine foods—namely, ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, milk, and curd—without being ill.
Regarding "fish and meat," because monks and nuns each gather separately, it is said they are "not the same.

[Commentary] Question: What offense constitutes this "not being the same" for a nun? Answer: "Not being the same" is not itself an offense; rather, it indicates that the precepts regarding what is "not the same" are established according to the specific circumstances of the preparatory acts (*prayoga*), thereby making the two assemblies distinct. The remainder is easily understood.
In the question, since this *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) is not an actual offense, it would logically result in a false accusation; therefore, the question asks, "What is the offense?

In the answer, the first part clarifies that it is not an offense because it is not a formal transgression (*sāpattika*). Next, it indicates the essential nature of the offense. The final phrase has a double meaning:
it may refer by analogy to the various preceding and subsequent precepts, or it may refer to the notes concerning non-transgressions (*anāpatti*) and so forth.

The forty-first precept concerning giving food to non-Buddhists.
[Commentary]: The forty-first precept concerning giving food to non-Buddhists.

[Commentary] Because there are three faults: First, those of other schools have hostile dispositions and are generally distant and aloof, making it difficult for them to become intimate with the Dharma;

even if one bestows gifts upon them, they do not appreciate the kindness and instead give rise to slander. Second, those with false views deviate from the fundamental tenets and are not true fields of merit;
if a donor gives food offered with faith to such outsiders, the donor will feel particularly indignant upon hearing of it, and furthermore, the merit of the gift will be diminished.
Because one does not receive a reciprocal reward for giving to those who are not fields of merit, [the Buddha] personally served food three times and gave it to the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

This allowed outsiders to give rise to deluded and inverted views, claiming that the non-Buddhists were superior and the bhikṣus were inferior. Due to these various faults, he established this prohibition.
Section Forty-One: Restraining the Mind (Three Parts). First, inciting slander by others, as in the *Nidāna* [Sūtra].

Second, not being a field of merit, which further has two points: first, vexing the donor’s mind; second, damaging the merit of the gift. Third, deceiving the common people. The following section provides a summary.
[Commentary: There are six conditions for the commission of an offense. First, it concerns those who have left the household life, as opposed to non-Buddhist practitioners;

whereas for householders, such acts constitute only minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*), because it is difficult to distinguish between the true and the false based on their shared status as renunciants, which would give rise to confusion and delusion among people, and therefore [the offense] is grave. Second, knowing that the person is not a relative;

this excludes parents. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is permitted to employ a pure attendant (*śucipuruṣa*) when giving to one's own parents, brothers, or those who have left the household life as non-Buddhists.
If one speaks with someone who has nothing, one should let them take it themselves; if they object, one should reply: "You have left the household life and may not [take it] yourself;

this is prohibited by the Buddha's precepts. In such a case, if one does not eat, one may do as one pleases. Fourth, regarding food: except for giving clothing, to give it oneself constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

Fifth, giving food with one’s own hand is generally improper; however, because eating alone or placing food on the ground might cause others to feel resentment or misunderstanding, these are permitted as exceptions.
Sixth is the offense of receiving [a gift].

Among the enumerated conditions, regarding the first condition—the minor offense of a householder—it refers to the offense of defiling a family (*kuladūṣaka*), which is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* does not exclude relatives in this case;
rather, they must still be sent away. Why is this cited here? First, to demonstrate the distinctions between the schools (*nikāya-bheda*); second, to ensure that [the rule] is applied universally.

This was intended to subject him briefly to humiliation, hoping that he would turn away from his heterodox ways; furthermore, since those who partake of the flavors of the five midday meals may still be capable of mutual salvation.
[Note: The Buddha, leading his disciples, traveled from Kośala to Śrāvastī, where the Buddha and the assembly of monks received a great quantity of cakes.
He had Ānanda divide the food and give it to other beggars; he then gave the sticky rice cakes to a woman.
Furthermore, because a non-Buddhist ascetic who received food was called a "shaven-headed householder," the Buddha assembled the Sangha, and based on what he had heard, he established this precept.
[Commentary: Regarding the origin of this precept, it was first established because [a monk] approached a woman and later ate with a man, thereby becoming subject to derision and mockery.
There are two origins for these precepts; regarding the first, concerning women, the Vinaya states that she was the daughter of a naked ascetic (nirgrantha), whose countenance was...

The *Duānduǎng zhù* (Commentary on the *Duānduǎng*) states: Regarding the "stuck cakes," when Ānanda was distributing the cakes, he gave each person one or two cakes that were stuck together, saying they were a single cake.
When this woman asked for more, he said to the other beggars, "She has had illicit relations with him;
why should she not receive two?"
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu [associates with] male heterodox practitioners or female heterodox practitioners.
[Commentary] Those who are naked ascetics and followers of heterodox paths, such as the Pāśupatas and Pārāśaryas, are those who have gone forth outside of this [Buddhist] community.
[Sūtra] Regarding giving food with one’s own hand: [if one wishes to give, one may place it on the ground or have another person give it].
[Commentary] As for *khajja* (solid food), this includes food from roots up to fruits, as well as food consisting of finely ground powders;
these five types are also as explained above.
[Pācittiya. [Commentary: For nuns and others, it is a dukkaṭa.
There is no offense if she gives it away by placing it on the ground; or if she causes another to give it;
or if she gives it to her parents, to a stūpa, or to the laborers of a separate dwelling; or if she gives it as payment for food; or if it is forcibly seized through power. There is no offense.

[Commentary]: The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* are: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the non-Buddhist male or female practitioner; third, giving food with one's own hand; and fourth, the formal conclusion of the offense.
[Commentary]: The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-śāstra* states: "The non-Buddhists originally had only six masters. Each master taught fifteen disciples, and each received [the teachings]."
Regarding their differing practices and views, the six teachers each possessed distinct doctrines and followers; including both the teachers and their disciples, they numbered ninety-six.
Thus it has been transmitted through generations, continuing without interruption.
In the second part of the *Śīlaskandha-vibhāṣā*, citing treatises to demonstrate the number:
if one follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it merely states there are ninety-six paths, with the Buddha-path situated among them; thus, the ninety-five would belong to non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).

This is simply according to their respective origins and need not be reconciled. However, in this region [of China], it refers only to the followers of Li and Zhang, whereas in the south, many more [non-Buddhist schools] exist.
The "house of Māra" refers to the transgression of the boundary; the note on the "naked ones" indicates one type, though in reality there are many classes.
*Pāṣaṇḍa* is a general term for non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the specific translation of which remains uncertain.

In the commentary on the third line, nine types of improper [eating] are first listed; as they are similar to the aforementioned "sufficient eating," they are mentioned here only briefly. Regarding "food," the following section clarifies this.

Since, among the five offenses of the preceding section on the conditions for transgression, only that concerning clothing constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (light offense), we know that this precept’s regulation applies universally to all four types of medicinal substances.

[Commentary: The nun’s offense is likewise a *pāyattika*, but here it is defined as a *duṣkṛta*; this is merely to account for the preparatory stage (*upakrama*) and to distinguish it from other rules.
The *bhikṣuṇī* commits an offense under the intermediate *bhikṣuṇī* precepts; because this also restricts laymen, whereas the rules for monks (*bhikṣu*) differ, it is called a "distinct precept.
[Vinaya] Forty-second: The precept regarding visiting the homes of others before or after meals.
[Commentary] The forty-second precept regarding visiting the homes of others before or after a meal.

There are three faults for which this is prescribed: first, because worldly affairs are manifold, it is difficult to cease one’s own household duties to devote oneself exclusively to the cultivation of merit at a religious assembly;
yet, having already accepted an invitation from another, one goes to their home and then encounters some unexpected matter that causes extreme distress. Second, since... [the text continues].
When there is a place where food is being served, one who seeks rest, cultivates the path, or wanders about without purpose may neglect their practice;

furthermore, if three monks together accept an invitation from the Sangha but enter a village separately, causing the donor to see that they have not assembled, the meal will ultimately not be prepared, and by delaying the assembly of monks, they prevent them from being fully satisfied.
Because such a situation is a source of affliction and is not a minor matter, this rule was established.
Among the three types of offenses involving the forty-two rules of intentional conduct, the first is the offense of annoying laypeople; the second is the offense of excessive busyness;

and the third is the offense of annoying the Saṃgha by failing to provide them sufficiently—meaning that the time was too short and they did not get their fill of food. Among these, the latter intention constitutes the original *nidāna*.

[Commentary] The treatise states that there are five conditions for committing this offense: first, having previously accepted another's invitation; second, not having made an announcement (*anujñāpana*); third, entering a village;
fourth, being without a valid reason—excluding cases of illness or the time for robes; and fifth, the offense is incurred the moment one enters the gate.
Regarding the four conditions for the full assembly, three types of exceptions are as listed in the precepts.
[Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a householder prepared a meal for the Saṃgha on behalf of Baddhananda.

At that time, monks who were traveling and arrived late found there was insufficient food after the others had finished eating. Furthermore, a high minister in Rājagṛha obtained fruit and [sent it] to Baddhananda...
After the food had been distributed among the *saṃgha*, [the monks] went to other households; the Buddha established this dual precept because he was informed of these two transgressions.
[Commentary: Within the context of the causal conditions, it is first explained that before the meal, the monks wandered about and the food for the *saṃgha* was insufficient.
After the meal at Rājagṛha, they proceeded as usual, yet ultimately failed to attain the fruit; this constitutes the condition for the offense.
Regarding the two sections on the conditions for the precept, it says that one who does not receive the fruit [of the meal] is as follows:

A minister held the fruit and waited for Upananda to return so that it could be distributed among the Sangha; however, he had already eaten and went to another house, returning late and thus causing the time to pass.
This refers to the period before noon (*pūrvāhṇa*); if it occurs after noon, then one commits the subsequent offense.

[The Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu, having already accepted an invitation, visits another household (the residence of men and women) either before the meal (from the appearance of dawn until the time for eating) or after the meal (from the time for eating until noon), he must inform another bhikṣu.
[Commentary]: If one is alone in a single room, one may entrust [one's bowl] to a neighboring resident who dwells within the same boundary.

[Vinaya]: Except at other times, it is a *pāyattika* offense. "Other times" refers to: when one is ill (as described above), when making robes (also as described above), and when robes are being offered.

[Note]: After the *pravāraṇā*, there is one month when robes are not permitted and five months when robes are permitted; excluding these periods, it refers to those times when one encourages others to prepare food and offer robes as alms.
【Vinaya】 This is called "the proper time.

【Commentary】 Having previously accepted an invitation, if one enters a gate to eat before or after [the meal] without having announced one's arrival, one commits a *pāyattika* offense; for other preparatory acts, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense in cases where the aforementioned exemptions apply, or when one has announced one's arrival to a bhikṣu; or if there is no bhikṣu present and one enters without having announced one's arrival.
If one goes to a storehouse, to a dwelling on the outskirts of a village, to a nunnery, or to a house where one has been invited;
or if many people have spread out sitting mats and invite a bhikṣu—these are permitted in the event of difficult circumstances.
[Commentary: The precept text consists of six phrases: first, that it concerns a bhikṣu who has previously accepted an invitation; second, regarding the time before and after the meal;

third, not having informed [another monk]; fourth, excluding other times; fifth, the formal determination of the offense; and sixth, the subsequent detailed explanation of the exceptions under "other times."

[Commentary]: Regarding the explanation of "eating," it is divided into "before" and "after," which are mutually dependent. Since the *Vinaya-sūtra* (Jīng) states that the meal must occur precisely within the designated time, this constitutes the "time for eating.

In the second section of the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, it says: "The 'meal before' and the 'meal after' should be spoken of together as 'before and after the meal,' based upon [the time]."
Regarding the time: from dawn until before midday, the period is divided into two halves; thus it is called "the middle of the time," meaning the interval within the time.
According to this reckoning, it corresponds precisely to the hour of the Dragon (辰時). This is as the sutra says:
"At the time of eating, he put on his robes and took up his bowl."

[Commentary]: In the section on entrustment (*anujñā*) within the Vinaya, it is stated that if one is within the same boundary (*sīmā*) and living together, and there is no one else easily available to seek out, one need not announce [the matter] to those who are not part of the shared invitation (*pavāraṇā*), nor is it necessary to allow for indirect transmission. In cases where the timing differs, it suffices merely to inform those who are aware.
Regarding the first part of the third [section], it explains that the precept and the meditative concentration must belong to the same boundary (*sīmā*).

If there is no one else to seek out—meaning that seeking someone of equal standing for the invitation is difficult to obtain—then one who is not of equal standing may not be informed, nor may one entrust another to inform by means of a succession of messengers.
If one receives the invitation alone and there is no one to whom one can report it, this falls under the exception; it is distinguished from the subsequent precept below.

At that time, when entering a gathering, one need only announce the matter for everyone’s knowledge; it does not matter whether one is within or outside the boundary, nor whether the invitation was formal or informal.

Success is achieved simply by making the announcement. This rule is restrictive regarding the former case, while the latter is general; thus, there are two distinct differences in terms of observance and violation.

[Commentary: Among the permitted circumstances (*kṣaṇa*), three are listed; when the white [robe] is added, they become four. This explanation regarding the time for robes clarifies that it is permitted outside of the prescribed time.
If, during a non-time period, one has already received robes or food through the prior good intentions of donors, this is already considered permitted.

However, if a bhikṣu has not yet conceived the intention, but is exhorted by others to prepare food or offer robes for the sake of the Saṃgha, it is permitted because it brings great benefit. It is not permitted to do so for oneself, as it would result in surplus.
Greed is a ruinous path subsumed under wrong livelihood.
In the first part of the sixth section, there is a general indication; from "opening the allowance for robes" (*kāṭhina*) downwards, there is a specific explanation regarding the giving of robes.

First, it clarifies that when a donor gives personally, they must necessarily [follow the rules]; next, it clarifies that a bhikṣu may exhort and convert others to open up the monastic regulations for individual cases, as these points can be divided according to the text.

[Commentary: Regarding "not committing an offense concerning bedding and requisites belonging to many families," this means that when many families assemble together and wait for the Saṃgha at various locations, whichever family the monks arrive at first is considered the place of invitation.
Regarding the non-offenses, the commentaries explain that there are many cases; however, this discussion is limited to whether the invitation is for the same assembly or not.

Furthermore, according to the note, a storehouse or a side room within a *bhikṣuṇī* monastery does not constitute a "household. Thus, according to the Vinaya, once one has performed the formal entrustment (*anujñā*) and arrives at such places, the previous authorization is lost.

In the case where one informs others again to seek permission to go, this is not an offense, as it concerns a household where no entrustment is possible. Since this is not a violation, it is included among the non-offenses.
The remaining cases may be understood accordingly.
[Vinaya] Precept Forty-three: Forcibly Sitting in a Layperson’s Home.
[Commentary] Precept Forty-three: Forcibly Sitting in a Layperson’s Home.

[Commentary: Generally, those living in the secular world are constantly accustomed to marriage ceremonies; when they leave home to study wisdom, they must understand the proper conduct of bowing and rising.

If they do not contemplate these conditions and remain for a long time without departing, it obstructs the pursuit of others' desires and leads to mutual resentment and reproach. Since this is logically improper, [the Buddha] established this regulation.

Forty-third: Regarding the initial section on the intention behind the regulations, it first describes how worldly people are often habituated to defilement; next, it clarifies that monks do not know what is appropriate, thereby giving rise to transgressions.
As for "pressuring and expelling," it is as described in the *Karmavācanā* (Causes and Conditions of the Precepts):
Kāla forcibly sat down, and his husband gave him food; though he was repeatedly sent away, he would not leave. The husband, in a fit of anger, abandoned him, saying, "Do as you please."

[Commentary: Regarding "a house where food is being eaten," as explained in the *Chao*, this refers to a house where edible food (*āhāra*) is present. This is because: (1) the eye is directed toward visible forms;
(2) the husband and wife constantly reside in a secluded place; (3) there is no fourth person present; and (4) one commits an offense by sitting within arm's reach of the door.

Regarding the four conditions for committing an offense discussed in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*: first, "contact as nutriment" (*spraṣṭavya-āhāra*) refers to the meeting of the sense faculty and its object, which facilitates thought and sustains the spirit;
thus it is called contact-nutriment. Fourth, "the hand does not reach the door" is stated based on the fact that the body is inside [the house].

[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, there was a former lay friend of Kāḷudāyin whose wife was a devout female lay follower (*upāsikā*). Both were exceptionally beautiful and took mutual interest in one another.
Later, when they went to her house, the wife adorned herself, and her husband, who was deeply devoted to her, watched as the bhikṣu finished his meal and sat there.
The husband then became angry and departed. The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha consequently established the precept.

【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu sits down forcibly in a house where food is being served (where men are the "food" for women and women are the "food" for men, as described above), and where there are precious objects (such as *śaṅkha*,
*musāragalva*, pearls, amber, gold, or silver), he commits a *pāyattika* offense— provided he is able to reach the door with his outstretched hand [he may sit].

[Note: If a blind person and a deaf person are together, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense, yet there is no violation [of the rule against eating alone] in the following cases: if one is at a house where food is being served and reaches out for a jewel;
if one sits near the door; if there are two bhikṣus acting as companions; if there is a person capable of identifying [the situation];

if a guest is present in the same place; if one is not blind or deaf; if one passes by from a previous location without stopping; if an illness breaks out and one falls to the ground; or if one is held by force or is bound.
One does not commit an offense because of being commanded by a Brahma-farer or due to difficulty.
[Commentary] The precept text consists of three phrases:
first, the person; second, the family where one eats twice; third, sitting down forcefully. One commits an offense through these three.
[Commentary]: The explanation of "food" (āhāra) is that it is so called because the male and female mutually receive and accept their passions.

Regarding the statement "possessing jewels," as explained in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, it is because when one wears jeweled garments, they are light and bright, illuminating the interior of the body and manifesting desire.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, both males and females together do not constitute a violation, as this is not considered a "household where food is served."
In the explanation, first the meaning of "food" is clarified; next, "possessing jewels" is explained as referring to items for a woman’s adornment.

In the section on the *saṃgha*, the text is cited to distinguish against confusion and define the characteristics. Regarding the note stating that being blind and deaf respectively constitutes the fourth case:

because each lacks one faculty and is not fully qualified as a witness, there is no offense. "One who recognizes the person" refers to someone with whom one has long-standing acquaintance and with whom one faces [the accused].
A guest of lower status is not one with whom one has long-standing acquaintance.
[Vinaya] The forty-fourth precept concerning sitting in a secluded place at a layperson’s home.
[Commentary] The forty-fourth precept concerning sitting in a secluded place with a woman.
[Commentary: The intent of the regulation is the same as before; the difference lies in the absence of a fourth person.
Within the intent of the forty-four finger-breadths, the previous [case] addressed husband and wife, hence it discussed the fourth person.

This case does not address the husband, but rather lacks the third person; thus it is said to be different. Question: Since it does not address the husband, why is it called "eating in a family"? Answer: Truly...

The Tathāgata’s ruling is difficult to establish; however, based on the same conditions as the preceding case, it is formulated by following the sequence of the school’s tradition, as designated in the commentary, which constitutes the correct understanding.
[Commentary] There are four conditions for committing an offense: first, a secular woman; second, a secluded place; third, the absence of a third person; and fourth, being within arm’s reach.
If one sits so that it does not reach the door, one commits an offense.
The sequence of the conditions can be understood [as follows].
[Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Kāḷodāyin, mindful of the previous precept, sat with his hand reaching toward the place of the door.

[The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. A certain bhikṣu sat and conversed with a laywoman (*upāsikā*) who had come for the fast-day meal behind a door-panel. When other bhikṣus heard their conversation, they criticized and disparaged him, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
Consequently, the Buddha rebuked him and established the precept.

[Sūtra: If a bhikṣu, while in a household where there is wealth (as detailed in the previous precept), stays in a secluded place—whether it be behind a tree, a wall, a fence, a shelf, or obscured by clothing or other objects—[and engages in such conduct], [he commits an offense].
If one sits [in such a manner], it is a *pāyattika*. [Note:

If, while in a house where food is being served, one extends the hand to the door so that a *bhikṣu* seeking alms may see it, this constitutes another indication; the conditions for the exemption are the same as those in the preceding precept.
[Commentary: Regarding the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the interpretation is as in the preceding precept.

In the subsequent section, which points to the brief account of the conditions (*pratyaya*) for the precept, the phrase "behind the door leaf" means that because the hand does not reach [the object], there is no offense.
Based on the sequence of conditions listed above, this case is identical to the preceding precept: if the hand does not reach the door, the offense must occur when the hand is behind the door.
Although the characteristics [of the offense] and its basis in dependent origination are the same, it should likewise constitute an offense.
[Vinaya] 45: The precept against sitting alone with a woman in an open space.
[Commentary] The 45th precept regarding sitting in an open space with a woman.
[Commentary] The intent of the regulation is the same as before.
[Commentary] There are four conditions: first, it is a secular woman; second, it is an exposed place; third, there is no third person present;
fourth, one sits within arm’s reach—then an offense is committed. The rest is explained in the *Chao*.

Regarding the fourth section on the conditions for the forty-fifth [offense]: since this occurs in an open space, one need only consider the reaching of each other’s hands and the internal limit of the transgression as indicated in the *Śāstra*.
It cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which states: "If one sits in an open space with a woman, for every time he rises and then sits again, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense for that number of times.

If they are within the distance of one *vyāma* (a fathom), it is an offense; if within one and a half *vyāmas*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. (This "within one *vyāma*" is equivalent to being within arm's reach.)
If it exceeds two *vitasti* (spans), there is no offense. [Note:
When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, Kālodāyin sat on the bare ground with a female lay disciple (*upāsikā*) who had observed the fast.

A bhikṣu who was begging for alms saw this and, disapproving of it, reported the matter to the other bhikṣus. They brought the transgression to the Buddha's attention, whereupon he established the precept.

[Sūtra] If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman (a human female possessing intelligence and whose life-faculty is not severed) in an open space (meaning in a place where one is within sight or hearing but out of view)—it is a pāyattika.
(The definition of the offense and the allowances for its commission are as in the preceding precept.)
[Commentary: The phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* are categorized into four parts:
first, the person; second, solitude; third, the object; and fourth, sitting in the open air.

Regarding this precept on sitting in the open, why is it explained in the commentary by reference to the two types of "secluded places" (*praticchanna*)? Answer: Because when one is in the open air, one is separated from the sight and hearing of others.
Only then does it constitute the characteristic of an offense, differing from the previous case where one asks about a secluded place within a room;

for what boundary does this rely? The answer is that it must depend on the preceding person being free from both seeing and hearing. Thus, because the Vinaya prescribes a *duṣkṛta* offense for mutual blindness or deafness, we know that when these two conditions are mutually absent, one cannot yet judge the offense as grave.
[Vinaya] Precept 46: Expelling Others from a Settlement.
[Commentary] The forty-sixth precept concerning expelling others from a settlement.
[Commentary] When a renunciant has previously promised food to another but ultimately fails to provide it, and then, with an evil intent, expels them once the time limit has expired.
Because it causes others to go a day without food, distressing their empty stomachs and not treating them lightly, this rule was established.
Regarding the intent of the forty-sixth rule: first, the capacity for transgression—the improper time;
next, the harm caused by the expulsion—the exhaustion of provisions throughout the entire day, hence the term "empty stomach" (虛齋).

[Commentary] The transgression [of this rule] is established through five conditions: first, a *bhikṣu*; second, having previously consented to eat; third, not being given food; fourth, expelling [the person] with an evil intent;
and fifth, departing beyond the range of sight or hearing. This constitutes the offense.
Regarding the initial exclusion of the lower assemblies from the conditions for an offense, it stops at the minor offense of *duṣkṛta*.
[Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Bāṇanda fought with a bhikṣu and harbored resentment in his heart; he then led him into the city to a place where there was no food.
Knowing that they had arrived at Jetavana when the time for the meal had already passed, he said, "You are a great evildoer who has caused me..."

"One must not eat [and then] depart quickly; that person must not eat [if they have left]. Because a bhikṣu, having become utterly exhausted, raised this fault, the Buddha reprimanded him and established the precept.
[Commentary: Among the causal origins, the one who harbored resentment and quarreled with him was the same bhikṣu who had seized the robes from among the thirty [cases]. Since...
It was not permitted for him to travel; furthermore, he was humiliated and left to suffer from hunger and exhaustion, which is why this precept was established.

Regarding the circumstances of the rule, the details are the same as in the previous section concerning the seizure of robes and the failure to go [to fetch them]. How could there have been a driving back [of the monk]?
It must surely have been at a later time that he again repaid his old resentment.

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, let us go together to a village (there are four kinds of villages as mentioned above) and provide you with food (at the proper time for eating)," yet that [first] bhikṣu does not actually instruct [the other] to give food to that bhikṣu, but instead says:
"Go away; I do not enjoy sitting or talking in your company; I prefer to sit alone and talk alone. This is an offense.
This is the causal condition.

[Note: If one abandons the place of seeing through skillful means and goes to the place of hearing, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; the same applies to doing so by way of hearing. If one avoids both seeing and hearing, only then does one incur the *pāyattika* offense.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] To dismiss another by means other than [the prescribed] expedients constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

[Commentary] There is no offense in the following cases: dismissing [a person] by giving them food; if they are ill; if they are a person lacking proper decorum whom others would not be pleased to see;

if one personally delivers food to them; if they have broken the precepts and so forth; or if one employs expedients due to life-threatening or *brahmacarya*-threatening dangers, and not out of malice or resentment.
[Commentary]: The precept text consists of five phrases: 1) one person; 2) permission to provide food; 3) intending to enter the village to prepare food;
4) "that bhikṣu" and below, the means of driving him out; 5) the formal determination of the offense.
In the phrase of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the remainder of the words constitutes the second clause; "Venerable Sir" (*bhadante*) and below constitute the third clause.
Regarding the term "village" (*grāma*), it refers to the residence of laypeople (*avadātavasana*). This is annotated as being the same as [the definition of] a village mentioned above;
however, this precept determines the offense based on whether one is out of sight or hearing, regardless of the threshold of a door.

[Commentary: To explain why it is not otherwise: it is not that there is no occasion for transgression. For example, if one sees a person lacking dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) and does not take pleasure in them, one sends them away or has food brought [to them];
if such circumstances do not exist, yet one acts precipitately out of an evil mind, then it constitutes a transgression.
The explanation of "not otherwise" refers to the various circumstances below where there is no offense; the remaining cases regarding offenses are largely the same as the previous explanation.
[Vinaya] Forty-seventh: The precept concerning medicine requested beyond the limit.
[Commentary]: Regarding the forty-seventh precept on receiving medicine beyond the limit of what was invited.

Now, when a devout layperson prepares excellent medicine and invites the assembly of monks with a reverent heart to provide offerings, although their intention to give is limited, one ought to protect oneself by accepting only what corresponds to that gift.
To now take more than this at will is to increase one's own greed and cause mental agitation.
Because a donor’s defeat of their virtuous faith results in no small degree of harm, it is necessary to establish restraints.

Regarding the forty-seventh restraint, the first part explains the prior intention behind giving; the subsequent part clarifies that taking what is not rightfully one's own causes harm to both self and others, and is therefore not a minor matter.

[Commentary]: The treatise states that there are six conditions for committing an offense: first, the request for medicine; second, the donor having already fixed a time limit; third, knowing the limit; fourth, receiving it beyond the limit;
fifth, having no valid reason [to exceed it]; and sixth, swallowing it—only then does one commit the offense.
The second condition for the offense is the fixed time limit, which is four months. [Commentary:

Regarding the initial request for medicine, as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "If one receives food during the period exceeding four months, it is a *pāyattika*; if one requests other things, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Once the four months have passed, requesting [medicine] for seven days or for the rest of one's life is also a *pāyattika*; for non-timely medicine, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This case is the same as that."
If even receiving more than one meal at a single place is a grave offense, how much more so for the four-month period? Why then would one not incur a *pāyattika*?
To explain the first part of this passage, in order to clarify the subsequent text, it is necessary to state the underlying intent:

because the characteristics of the offenses in the *Vinaya-mūla* were not clearly defined, ancient rulings held that exceeding the limit for medicinal substances resulted in a *pāyattika*, while exceeding the limit for the night resulted in a *dukkaṭa*. Therefore, these [distinctions] still persist in the *Shan-chao*.

Regarding the ancient meaning and the present commentary, I wish to overturn the old interpretation by establishing that the night [offense] is grave while the medicine [offense] is light; thus, I cite clear evidence to reconcile these contradictions.

Examining this in detail: first, within the determination of the offense, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) is cited to clarify the four types of medicine and their violations, all based on exceeding the time limit.
Regarding "eating at the proper time" (*kāla-bhojana*), other matters are deemed minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*); these refer to other items such as robes and so forth. The following three...
Regarding the phrase "auspicious at non-proper times" among the medicines, it means that the medicinal flavor is light. The following section provides a corroboration;

since the current *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* does not clarify the category of "timely medicine," this passage is cited to prove the present point. By taking the example of the precept against giving more than one meal, it establishes that the current offense applies to all four types of medicine.

[Commentary]: If that is so, regarding the case where one gives a single meal, why is clarified butter (*sarpis*) and oil (*taila*) considered light? The answer is: because the sense of using them externally for the body is rare, they are light;
whereas in this context, because the sense of using them internally is frequent, they are heavy.

In the initial refutation within the commentary, by reconciling the internal and external requisites and harmonizing what precedes and follows, we know that while the preceding precept regarding internal requisites must be strictly observed, this precept concerning external requisites is relatively light.
[Commentary] Question: As listed above, since the penalty for seeking medicine is heavy, it is clear that the root precept itself does not permit taking medicine after the prescribed time has passed.
Regarding the subsequent question, those items listed above refer to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (*Shisong*).

Since the transgressions have already been clarified in the preceding text, there may still be confusion or dogmatic attachment leading one to seek a theoretical treatise; therefore, the present text follows upon the previous section to interrogate the current *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. This hypothetical objection is intended to provide the basis for the forthcoming response.

[Commentary] The answer is that this precept is established according to the nature of the offense: seeking a light substance when the limit for a heavy one has been reached. Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:

"If one gives oil but requests ghee, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense); this shows it is a light case. The reason for this is as follows: initially there was a virtuous intention to provide medicine for four months; once the period has expired, the intent to offer ceases.
To accept more than that and place it in a location where it will spoil and be ruined causes deep harm. Furthermore, it is based on...

Regarding the previous statement that "the person who accepted the invitation is heavy because they exceeded the day," the initial response establishes the definitive rule: since the words of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* are obscure and its principles require resolution through meaning, it is said that seeking [clarification] according to the meaning makes a light offense heavy.

This overturns the ancient interpretation to correctly demonstrate the present judgment; therefore, the following citation of the text serves as proof for the aforementioned point that seeking [clarification] makes a light offense heavy.
The following summarizes the meaning to demonstrate the faults of exceeding limits. The heading above follows the sense, which is made manifest here;

the text lists two faults to show that one must act with restraint. First, regarding the violation of giving, the affliction is profound; furthermore, the latter two follow this momentum, acting out of delight.

[Commentary]: If this is so, why was it prohibited because of requesting medicine from among the requisites? The answer is that requesting [anything] beyond the limit constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;

furthermore, since the definition of the characteristics below specifies that the offense is incurred by exceeding the limit, and since the root text of the precept also states "receiving beyond [the limit]," it is clear that the four-month restriction refers to the boundary of the night, not the characteristic of requesting medicine.
The initial objection concerns the causal conditions for the precept regarding begging; it was established because [the monks] exceeded the limit, and the judgment of the offense is based on this.

In the response, the first sentence is a concession (*yongs su gtoṅ ba*), as the original motivation actually arose from the act of begging. However, the subsequent section refutes this, for the textual passages concerning the three ways of seeking are identical in two instances;

thus, one must not insist that the characteristics of the offense are determined solely by the specific circumstances. This is explained in detail in the commentary, which quotes: "The division of night-medicine."

In the fourth month of the summer retreat, those who receive [the medicine] and the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*—that is, from the fourth month and the medicine, up until "if it exceeds" (the limit)—both texts conclude with a double summary. [Commentary]:
If this is so, and the night has no fixed limit while the medicine does have a fixed limit, why are they listed together? Answer: They are treated the same as the initial request for medicine.
This clarifies that the offense for seeking [medicines] beyond the limit is merely a *duṣkṛta* (light transgression).
Regarding the subsequent objection, the Vinaya divides it into four cases: (1) there is a fixed limit for the night, but no fixed limit for the medicine;

(2) there is a fixed limit for the night, and there is a fixed limit for the medicine—these two cases should be received during the four months of the summer retreat; (3) there is a fixed limit for the medicine, but no fixed limit for the night.

[The phrase] "without limit" (in the commentary, it is asked: this line merely lists [the items] in reverse order). There are two types of medicine without limit: medicine for four nights and medicine without limit.

These two should be received according to the time of their distribution. The difficult point of the meaning is as follows: if one says that the broad explanation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* concerns the formation of an offense based on the night, rather than the offense being incurred by seeking [the medicine], then the third line should not have been listed. This is because the Vinaya texts do not definitively establish the gravity [of the offense].

Regarding these difficult-to-answer points, the first two lines clarify the reason for the sequence in the Vinaya; because they follow from the preceding discussion on "staying overnight," it says "the same as the initial offense" and so forth.
The subsequent section determines the nature of the transgression based on the meaning, as explained above.

Now, to provide a general judgment of the four lines in the Vinaya: the first two constitute a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation); the third constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing); and the fourth involves no offense.

[Note] When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, Mahānāma invited the Saṃgha to provide medicine. Because the group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) were dissatisfied, they sought out medicines that were difficult to obtain.

He [Mahānāma] went to the market to procure them, whereupon they reviled him and cut off the supply of medicine for the Saṃgha. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.

[Commentary: Regarding Mahānāma among those who took refuge, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that he was the son of the Buddha’s paternal uncle; born one month after the Buddha, he attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
Furthermore, because he was of the Śākya clan, he drowned himself in water [to end his life].
In the section on the conditions for the precepts, first, the *Dṛṣṭānta-śāstra* (Jian lun) is cited to demonstrate his lineage and the stage of fruition at the time of his birth:
he was the son of the Buddha’s paternal uncle, King Droṇodana; born one month after [the Buddha], he was thus the Buddha’s elder brother.

Next, the *Mūla-vinaya* is cited to demonstrate his aspirations and conduct; within the section on clothing and dharma, it says that King Virūḍhaka of Śrāvastī mobilized his troops with the intent to...
He annihilated the Śākyas of Śrāvastī, having them buried up to their waists in pits he had dug and then having great elephants trample them to death.
At that time, Mahānāman—the maternal grandfather of King Virūḍhaka—addressed the king, saying: "I pray that you permit me to enter the pond;
whenever the Śākyas emerge from the water at the appropriate moment, do not kill them. The king, reflecting upon this, did not wait long and eventually granted his permission.
Even though he entered the pond and bound himself with his hair to the roots of a tree to die, the minister took him and showed him to the king, who immediately conceived a heart of compassion.
The king said, "Mahānāma, for the sake of your kinsmen, you have not spared even your own life. He then issued an edict to release all the Śākyas.

[The Vinaya] states: If a bhikṣu is invited to receive medicinal requisites for four months (the summer retreat), he who is free from illness (one who is ill is permitted to take medicine as prescribed by a physician) may accept them;
if he accepts more than that, it is an offense.

[Note] If the night-medicine has a fixed limit, it should be accepted during the four months of the summer retreat; if the night-medicine has no fixed limit, it should be accepted whenever it is offered, regardless of the limits of the medicine.

【Vinaya】 Excluding the following types of invitations: (1) a permanent invitation (where the person says, "I shall always provide medicine"); (2) a subsequent invitation (inviting again after a previous supply has been exhausted); (3) a shared invitation (bringing the medicine to the monastery and distributing it);

and (4) a lifelong invitation (saying, "I shall provide medicine for as long as I live")—these constitute *pāyattika* offenses. There is no offense in cases where the exemptions previously mentioned apply.
[Commentary: The six clauses of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra are as follows: 1. The text enumerates the period of four months within the summer retreat; 2.

according to the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, one commits an offense whenever there is a transgression during the three periods of the month or half-month; 3. the provision of medicine clarifies what has been requested; 4.
"if it exceeds" and below distinguish the characteristics of the violation; 5. this clarifies the conditions for exemption; 6. the conclusion of the offense.
Regarding the second phrase of the *Prātimokṣa*: the *Dharmaguptaka* school restricts it to the four months of the summer retreat because it arises from specific conditions;
the *Mahāsāṃghika* school clearly judges it by the limit of the gift, applying it generally across all three seasons with no fixed duration.

Regarding the third phrase, according to the Vinaya, it simply refers to "conditions of invitation," meaning the conditions of the donor’s invitation; the commentary distinguishes this from other types of invitations, hence it specifies "invitation for medicine. Fourth.
In the commentary, the first of the four phrases from the Vinaya can encompass the second [case]; subsequently, the citation of the latter phrase also subsumes the third.

The section beginning with "without distinction" below resolves doubts. The judgment regarding the aforementioned transgressions concerns the limits of the night according to the *Upasampadā-śāstra*; this is the present meaning.
The commentary briefly indicates this, while the details are found in the *Śū* (the sub-commentary).

[Commentary]: Regarding the distinction between "constant" (*nitya*) and "until the end of life" (*yāvajjīva*) within the context of the conditions for opening [the invitation], this is distinguished based on the capacity [of the donor].
In explaining "opening," "constant" refers to the inviting patron (*dānapati*), as it is not restricted by time;
"until the end of life" refers to the monks being invited, as it excludes only death. As for those who invite again, the commentary states that Mahānāma again formed this thought: [text follows].
"I would rather, for the sake of one person, sever the community's supply of medicine; having severed it, if one requests it again, this is not a case of receiving what is improper.
Therefore, the Buddha permitted it, and there is no offense, as explained previously. This refers to the aforementioned four exceptions.

[The Vinaya] Precept Forty-Eight: On Observing Military Troops.
[Commentary]: Regarding the forty-eighth precept on observing military arrays:
according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are three reasons for its establishment: first, out of respect for the Buddha-dharma; second, to eliminate slander;
and third, to cease all evils and increase wholesome dharmas. It was established because of these three benefits.

Among the forty-eight rules for restraining the mind, this precept was established because a certain bhikṣu observed an army, thereby violating the Buddha-dharma, inviting the derision and reproach of others, and habitually giving rise to ferocity; thus, by reversing such faults, one achieves benefit.

[Commentary: Regarding the three conditions for committing this offense: first, there must be a military array; second, one intentionally goes to view it; and third, upon seeing it, the offense is committed.
As for the second condition, "intentionally going," this is permitted if it was not done intentionally.
[Note] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the people rebelled. The King led his sixfold army to suppress them.
While observing the battle array, Prasenajit was displeased and offered a package of honey to the Buddha, while also holding the name [of the Buddha] and prostrating.
He went to the Buddha’s location and fully recounted these circumstances; consequently, the Buddha censured him and established the precept.

[Commentary] Regarding the causal conditions: the initial cause was when King Seniya Bimbisāra sent an envoy bearing a letter to pay homage to the Buddha; this is the foundation for the establishment of the precepts. As for the causal condition for the precepts:

King Seniya dispatched [the envoy] with the intention of inviting the Buddha, desiring that the precepts be established. The group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) did not know [of this] and went [to the palace], whereupon they encountered reprimand and the establishment of the precepts.
In the commentary, it is noted that "six armies" refers to twenty-five hundred men per army, and that a son of heaven (devaputra) should employ [this number].
The "six armies" consist of fifteen thousand men.
[Vinaya] If a bhikṣu goes to observe an army formation— whether it be a military display or a battle (an "army" includes even a single horse, a single chariot, or a single soldier)—
except under specific circumstances (such as needing to report a matter or being summoned), it is a *pāyattika* offense.

[Note] If one does not avoid [the path], it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). From the lower path to the upper path, from the main road to a non-road, if one does not see [the person], it is a *duṣkṛta*;

the same applies to not seeing [them] due to skillful means (*upāya*). If one sees [them], it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of falling); there is no offense in the following cases: if one goes for a specific purpose; if one has been invited to go; if one is led away by force;
if one was already on the march and arrives later, thus stepping off the road to avoid [them]; or if it concerns water or land routes.

There is no offense if one does not go on the road due to the danger of wild beasts, thieves, or floods; if one is bound by forceful power; or during calamities such as those involving the Brahma-world.

[Commentary: Regarding the four phrases of the precept text: first, the person; second, observing the army; in the note, both "true" and "mocking" constitute offenses; third, excluding the conditions, as follows.

The textual characteristics of the offenses for the latter four [rules] are understandable at a glance; failing to observe them constitutes the transgression of allowing the lower path (sexual misconduct) or avoiding theft through sight.

In the second phrase of the *Śīla-mūla*, the offense is identical because the underlying mental state regarding fighting and games is the same. Third, excluding the specific conditions as explained later, this is the next rule.
Regarding the fourth [rule], the first part refers to the text; "not descending" indicates the intention, and "that which is called 'identical'" means following the teaching.

There is no offense [in this case]. The *Śīla-sūtra* (Precept Text) establishes that one should observe by means of a "thief's glance"; though one may avoid [the danger] through such a glance, what benefit is there?

[Commentary: In this context, if the five weapons do not arise, then that is that; but once they have arisen, they will surely strike the person. Since the King has no choice but to provide for them, the Bhikṣu has no reason to look upon them arbitrarily.

Therefore, when the kalpa of swords and spears arises, it depends entirely upon whether one’s own mind is in opposition or accord with [the Dharma]. To maintain [the precepts], one must hold fast to this.
Regarding the offense of establishing [wrong] views:
in the first part of the "Exhortation to Uphold," the intent of the military is described. As for the "five weapons," these are the five types of armaments wielded in military formations.

The *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou) commentary states: *go* (a leveled-headed halberd), *shu* (pronounced *shū*; a bludgeon without a blade used for striking and thrusting), *ji* (a three-bladed halberd), and *qiú-máo* (pronounced *qiú*, with the initial *qiu* reversed).
(The *changmao* is a long spear; the *yimao* should be the shorter one. If the infantry lack *yimaos*, and they add bows, then when [the enemy] rises up, [the infantry] will surely be struck.

This means that [the enemy] would inflict harm upon the person, the family, and the state. They established these [weapons] to manifest their majesty and employed them to settle chaos because there was no other choice;
thus it is said, "I have no alternative. The passage below on the bhikṣu’s admonition to go and observe first shows that such [actions] are inappropriate.
Therefore, the following clarifies the kalpa of weapons (śastra-kalpa) that is experienced as a result [of karma].

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, when the human lifespan is ten years, those who are tall are one chi and five cun, while those who are short are one chi. At that time, the calamity of weapons arises for seven days and seven nights;

the earth becomes covered with thorns all like sharp blades, and whatever grass or wood people grasp in their hands turns into swords and halberds. They desire only to kill one another. If a person...
It was because he had previously observed the precept against killing that he avoided meeting this calamity.

The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that this occurs because such a person constantly harbors anger and a harmful intent toward others, lacking a heart of compassion; thus it is called the "kalpa of weapons. Therefore, it is said that [the calamity] arises in the mind.

This explains the characteristics of transgression and observance below: if one turns one's eyes away from the mind, one immediately violates the precepts and incurs an offense; by adhering to the regulations, one remains humble.

The term "mou" (gaze) refers to the act of looking with compliance and success; thus it is called "establishing the view. Regarding the section on offenses and transgressions, there are two parts in the commentary.
The first clarifies the gravity of the offense: avoiding auspicious places constitutes a violation of the disciplinary regulations. Moving from below to above means ascending to a high vantage point;

moving from the path to a non-path means selecting a convenient location. If one intends to look but does not see due to a deficiency in conditions, the offense is light; if one actually sees, it is grave.

Among the offenses, the first section opens with the allowance for having a valid reason; the next clarifies compliance with the teachings; and the final section opens with allowances for urgent difficulties, such as those involving water or land travel.
[Vinaya] The forty-ninth precept: regarding staying overnight within an army.
[Commentary] The forty-ninth precept concerns staying overnight in an army.

[Commentary] The treatise states that there are four conditions for committing this offense: first, the condition of being invited to stay in an army; second, having already stayed for two nights; third, on the third night, not remaining within range of sight or hearing;
and fourth, the appearance of dawn, at which point the offense is incurred.
Regarding the forty-ninth [offense] and the subsequent rules of restraint, because their underlying intent is the same as before, they are not repeated here.
Within the circumstances of the offense, "having been invited" refers to being summoned by a knowledgeable donor (*dānapati*).
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks had a reason to go and stay overnight in a military camp.

A layperson said to them, "We have these [weapons] because of our desire; what do you śramaṇas do with these? The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, whereupon he established the precept.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu has a legitimate reason to go into an army camp, he is permitted to stay for two or three nights; if he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika offense.

[Commentary] There is no offense if he stays for two nights and leaves by dawn on the third night; or if, while at the third night, the path—whether by water or land—is cut off, or there are dangers to life, to the celibate life (brahmacarya), or other such difficulties, and he cannot leave. In these cases, there is no offense.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if this were not permitted, one would be accused of slandering the monks by saying that they come uninvited when they have something to seek, yet do not come even when invited when they have nothing to seek.
Therefore, it is permitted to go [to them] in order to preach the Dharma and cause them to realize the fruits of the Path.

Next, the explanation of the "allowance" (*kṣepa*) begins with the prohibition against monks who are subject to reproach and slander seeking [gain]; "seeking" here refers to soliciting material offerings.
Below that, it is for the sake of benefiting others. That treatise further states: "Also because it increases faith and respect; and because the monastic and the secular require one another.
Regarding the commentary on "not committing an offense," the first part follows the teaching, while the section below provides the allowance for difficult circumstances.
[Vinaya] Precept 50: Regarding the Prohibition Against Watching Armies Engage in Battle.
[Commentary] The fiftieth precept concerns watching an army engaged in battle.

[Commentary] Since the transgression is no different from the preceding cases, if one has a reason to go there, one should sit and preach the Dharma; subsequently, if one watches the battle engage, one will be struck by a blade.
The offenses in the middle are the same as those at the beginning.

Regarding the intent behind the fifty precepts, the initial reference to the transgression is the same as before because it involves observing an army. Since the following section correctly narrates the present precept, the character "zhōng" (中) in the phrase "struck by a blade" (*rèn suǒ zhōng*) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùhū*).
This is because, as in the origin story (*jiè yuánqǐ*) of the precept, it was due to seeing a transgression that the statement says they are "the same."
If one sees an army without a valid reason, one immediately commits the preceding precept; only when observing a battle for a valid reason does one commit this precept.

[Commentary] Four conditions must be met for it to be established: first, being within an army; second, engaging in combat; third, employing the means of looking; and fourth, seeing it—then one commits the offense.
The third factor for the offense is "preparatory action," which refers to the mental intention (*manasikāra*).

[Note: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks had a reason to be among the army; while observing their combat prowess, one man was struck by an arrow and his companions carried him away on a cloth.
A lay devotee saw this and was astonished. When the bhikṣus heard of it, they informed the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.
【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu stays within an army for two or three nights, or at any time observes battle formations, or observes the strength and power of the troops,
elephants, and horses, it is a pāyattika (the remainder is as explained in the preceding precept).
[Commentary]: The core text of the precepts (*śīla-mūla*) is easily understood.
In the detailed explanation, regarding the first offender of the core text, there are two points: (1) being within an army, which shows that this precept was established based on the preceding one;
and (2) observing a battle, followed by (3) the formal definition of the offense.

[Commentary: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one is staying in a city and bandits come to besiege it, the King orders the bhikṣus to all go up onto the city walls to manifest the appearance of a large multitude.

There is no offense in looking [at the enemy] intentionally; however, if one looks with a preparatory effort (*prayoga*), it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. This is established as the criterion for maintaining or violating the precept;
therefore, one should know that closing one's eyes is precisely what constitutes 'maintaining' the restraint."

In the first section of the following analysis, since there was no intentional act, there is no offense; however, regarding the offense of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), it is because one intentionally looked [at the woman], and thus this constitutes the root of the karma.
Below this, the maintenance of the precepts and their violations are demonstrated as previously explained.
[Vinaya] Precept 51: On Drinking Alcohol.
[Commentary] The fifty-first precept concerns drinking alcohol.
[Commentary] Alcohol is a poisonous water; its consumption brings about affliction, causing one's will and nature to become deranged and giving rise extensively to all manner of transgressions.
Since it obstructs and ruins right practice, incurs reproach and fault, and is the very root from which calamities arise, how could it be permitted without prohibition?
Of the fifty-one [verses] regarding the intent of the regulation, the first two lines indicate the substance of alcohol;

because it can harm people, it is called "poisonous water," as stated in the *Eight Teachers Sūtra* (*Aṣṭācārya-sūtra*). "Calamity" (*huan*) refers to faults and afflictions. The following four lines enumerate the four faults in detail to explain the above.
First, it becomes a source of affliction when one’s disposition is deranged, meaning that being unable to maintain self-control, one engages in reckless acts.

Second, it extensively gives rise to various transgressions. As the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "Alcohol gives rise to immeasurable faults. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, thirty-five specific faults are enumerated:
first, the depletion of wealth and property; second, it serves as the gateway for all manner of illnesses; third, it leads to strife and contention.
1. One becomes naturally naked and shameless; 2. one acquires five kinds of ugliness and an evil reputation; 3. one’s wisdom is obscured and extinguished; 4.
one fails to obtain what ought to be obtained, and even what has been obtained is immediately lost; 5. one reveals all secret matters to others; 6.
one’s undertakings are abandoned and remain unaccomplished; 7. intoxication is the root of sorrow; 8. physical strength gradually diminishes; 9. the complexion of the body deteriorates.
13–20. Disrespecting one’s parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
21. Associating with wicked people; 22. Keeping distance from the virtuous and good; 23. Committing violations of the precepts;
24. Being shameless and lacking remorse; 25. Failing to guard the six sense faculties; 26. Indulgence.
27. Indulgence in sensual pleasures; 28. Being detested by others; 29. Being cast out by one’s kinsmen;
30. Practicing unwholesome dharmas; 31. Abandoning wholesome dharmas; 32. Not being trusted by others;
33. Being far removed from nirvāṇa; 34. Engaging in the karma of madness and delusion; 35. Falling into [lower realms] at the end of life.
The thirty-five hells and the future calamities of madness and folly are thus described;

seeing these holy instructions, how could those who have now left the household life not feel shame for their own indulgence? For three reasons—first, because it obstructs and ruins right practice and causes the mind and spirit to become darkened and deluded;

second, because it invites reproach and fault, which is unsuitable for one who has left the household life—one must generate [the resolve for renunciation]. The final two lines conclude by indicating this necessity.
The Vinaya Rule:
[Commentary] There are three conditions for committing this offense: first, alcohol; second, the absence of a grave illness; and third, swallowing it.

Regarding the second condition—the allowance granted in cases of grave illness—it shall be adjudicated later as specified. Regarding the third condition, the offense of swallowing, one must discuss the act of swallowing itself.
[End of section].
[Note]: While the Buddha was in the kingdom of Cīda, Sāgata, acting as the Buddha’s attendant, went to the chamber of a matted-hair Brahmin (*jaṭila*) and stayed the night there.
