At night, he subdued the dragon (*nāga*), and at dawn, he showed it to King Kauśāmbī. Later, while traveling through that country, he encountered [the one] with black...
The Buddha, having explained the ten faults of being intoxicated while lying in the road, established the precept.

[Commentary] Regarding the origin story (*nidāna*), the reason given is that even for such a holy one as an Arhat—who possesses the majestic power to subdue dragons—drinking alcohol brings about public censure and damages the Path;
how much more so for other ordinary practitioners? Therefore, it was prohibited lest they should recklessly partake of it.
When one has grass dripping from the mouth, what need is there to mention bowls and cups?

In the "Preface to the Commentary on the Vinaya" (*Jieyuan zhu*), the first section recounts the origins of the Dragon-subduing Birth and its transgressions; the subsequent section, "Traveling Through That Country," correctly clarifies the violation of the precepts.
The initial explanation of the preceding segment specifically cites the Sage’s virtue as the causal occasion (*nidāna*), intending to cause the vulgar and base to recognize their errors.

"Far removed" refers to using the noble as a standard to illustrate the ordinary; thus, the subsequent section explains this by citing a drop of grass-juice in the mouth to illustrate the few as a metaphor for the many.
As the Vinaya states: "If one takes me as their teacher, they must not even place grass or wood within wine to take a sip.
The commentary lists ten faults: first, an ugly complexion; second, diminished strength; third, impaired vision.
First, one does not understand the four present signs of anger; second, the resources for livelihood are destroyed; third, diseases increase; fourth, quarrels and litigation multiply;
fifth, one lacks a good reputation; sixth, wisdom is meager; and seventh, at the end of life, one falls into the three evil realms.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol. [Commentary] This includes liquor made from wood,
rice wine made from non-glutinous rice, rice wine made from other types of rice, barley wine, or any other substance processed to produce intoxicating liquor.

[Pācittiya]. [Commentary]: Whether it be actual liquor or something that is not liquor but possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of liquor; or whether it be something that is not liquor but possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of liquor—neither may be drunk.
If one consumes liquor that has been boiled or mixed into food, in all such cases it is a *pācittiya*. This applies equally to drinking sweet-flavored liquor or sour-flavored liquor.
Regarding the consumption of fermented yeast, wine dregs, and all similar substances: in the three cases involving the perception or suspicion of a *pācittiya* offense, one falls into an offense.
There is no offense if one has an illness that cannot be cured by other medicines and thus uses wine as medicine; nor is there any offense if one applies wine to a wound.
[Commentary]: The precept text consists of three phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the object of the offense; and third, the formal determination of the transgression.

Regarding the "wood-wine" mentioned in the commentary on the second phrase of the precept text, this refers to that which is fermented from plants or wood. The phrase "and other methods" encompasses all such cases in general.
[Commentary: Regarding the characteristics of intoxicants, even if they are not mixed with medicine or food, drinking them results in an offense;

therefore, the "Wangmu" (Net of Precepts) cited in the *Chao* (Excerpts) is extremely comprehensive, being so detailed that nothing is omitted, ensuring that all who transgress the prohibitions fall into punishment.
In the first section of the subsequent analysis explaining the characteristics of alcohol, the text first provides a general indication;

below, it refers to the detailed exposition, stating that according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if it is indeed alcohol—even if made from grasses or wood—one commits an offense. It further cites the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*:

"If one drinks what resembles alcohol, sour alcohol, sweet alcohol, dregs, or medicinal yeast, provided they can intoxicate a person, for every swallow one falls into an offense. Therefore, it says "all."
"Falling into punishment is an offense; though sparse, nothing escapes it"—this is from the *Laozi*, as cited previously. [Commentary:

Regarding the three phrases concerning "objects" (*viṣaya*) and "conceptions" (*saṃjñā*), all being grave offenses, other masters say that these are established by regulating the mind according to the objects.

My own view differs. The Sage’s regulations have their reasons; the text is not lacking in meaning. How could there be a wise person who has never smelled [something] yet mistakenly drinks the gruel? It is impossible.

Regarding the *Skt. pāyantika* offense: this refers to a grave case where one has previously prepared the means, intending to drink this alcohol, and having already lifted it toward the mouth, one then develops the thought that it is not alcohol, or harbors doubt;
in such cases, based on the subsequent state of mind, there is only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), as the prior preparatory act is not rendered grave.
How is it that in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* there is this explicit teaching?

Next, regarding the section on the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*), the first part cites the Vinaya with five propositions: (1) alcohol perceived as alcohol; (2) non-alcohol perceived [as alcohol];

(3) non-alcohol perceived with doubt—these three cases all constitute a *pārājika* offense, as there is no exemption for confusion or forgetfulness; thus both perception and doubt are grave offenses. (4) Non-alcohol perceived as alcohol;

(5) non-alcohol perceived with doubt—these two cases constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the various interpretations of the "below" [the text], there are two judgments from ancient and modern times. First:

The ancient [commentators] demonstrated their judgment based on the scriptural texts (*vinaya*), asserting that because the mind follows the object, it is identical to sexual misconduct (*maithuna*) and no other [offense] is permitted; this is the "ancient" view presented first. Next, there are three parts:

the first sentence clarifies that the Sage’s original prohibition was universal; the second sentence points out the deficiency in the compilation (*saṃgīti*); and the phrase beginning with "How could...

cites specific cases to show that one must weigh the circumstances and cannot follow the letter of the law (*yathā-sūtra*) alone, as the offense arises from the underlying intention (*cetanā*). This concludes the explanation of the general intent of the Vinaya, as stated below.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is a formal principle which states: "It was established [as a prohibition] because, fearing that cold-induced ailments might arise, one would provide wine mixed with other liquids and give it to someone who drinks it immediately without examining it—this refers to a case where the object and the mind correspond (*citta-viṣaya-samāna*).

However, if one examines it and knows it is not [wine], yet it is [wine], then its consumption is permitted—this refers to a case where the object is fixed but the mind errs (*viṣaya-niyata-citta-bhrānti*).
Based on this, the allowance for those who are deluded accords well with the present judgment. "Cheng" (誠) means reality or truth; "zhi" (致) refers to the underlying principle or rationale.
[Commentary]: Regarding the opening of the section on other medicines, the statement that wine is not treated as a medicine does not mean that one may drink it whenever one is ill;
rather, one must first treat the ailment thoroughly with other medicines, and only if it is not cured should one then consume it. This is explained in detail in the *Chao*.

Regarding the three cases mentioned above, there is a concern that one might suddenly consume medicine recklessly based on a physician’s instruction; therefore, the meaning of the text is shown to not permit such arbitrary or excessive application.

As explained extensively in the *Shan-chao*, it quotes the *Pañcaśata-praśna-sūtra*: "If a physician says, 'It will certainly be cured,' you may obtain and take the harmonized medicine, but you must not take it on an empty stomach."
[Vinaya] Precept 52: Playing in Water. [Commentary] The fifty-second precept concerns playing in water.
[Commentary] According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are four reasons:
first, the Buddha-Dharma is held in high esteem and ought to be respectfully honored; now, by entering the water to play, one causes damage [to this principle].

Regarding the two reasons for condemning the act of disrespecting others: first, one's deportment should be dignified and orderly; to enter the water for play violates this decorum and invites the reproach of the world.
Second, the three bhikṣus harbored thoughts that ceased their meditative objects while practicing the Path; entering the water for play obstructed and abandoned their primary spiritual work.
Fourth, one should cultivate right mindfulness; entering the water for play causes the mind to become distracted and leads to the loss of right mindfulness.
Master Guang said: "The nature of water is turbulent and cannot be kept shallow; if one plays and laughs within it, the current above will suddenly surge, endangering one's life.
Among the fifty-two rules for restraining the mind, four meanings are discussed: first, damaging and disgracing the Buddha-dharma; second, violating the majestic authority...

[The transgressions are: (1) violating the ritual procedures; (2) neglecting one’s duties; (3) agitation and loss of mindfulness; (4) causing harm to life, as added by Master Daoguang, which applies to the preceding cases, making five in total.

[Commentary] Regarding the three conditions for committing an offense: first, concerning water, it does not matter whether it is deep or shallow; even playing with water in a bowl constitutes an offense within the water.
Regarding the second [offense], one commits it through three types of playful activity without a causal basis.

As for the first causal condition for the offense: it consists simply of the substance being water, regardless of its location. Regarding the second, "absence of a causal basis": if there is a lower opening or a passage for water and other such conditions, then one does not commit the offense.
[Note: While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, the group of seventeen monks was playing and splashing water in the Ajiravatī River.
King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā, seeing this from atop their palace, the King said, "Look at those you serve!
The Queen replied, "These are newly ordained; they may be foolish and ignorant. She then offered some stone honey to the Buddha, who immediately rebuked them.
The Precept on Restraining Blame.

[Commentary: Regarding the conditions for this precept, as stated in the other three Vinayas, the group of seventeen monks all attained the stage of *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning) yet incurred the fault of worldly censure for playing and laughing in the water.
Why does this text mention ordinary people? It cites the superior sages to serve as a standard for comparison with ordinary, inferior beings.

Regarding the three *vinayas* within the conditions for the precepts, these are the fifty *jīvas*. In the commentary, the first part clarifies the transgressions committed by seventeen young, newly ordained monks who formed a faction;
their conduct was similar to that of the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*), as can be understood from the preceding account.

Following the section on King [Bimbisāra], the next part clarifies the origin of the formulation of the precepts: the King saw [the monks] with disdain, and the Queen, fearing the King might become disrespectful toward her, [intervened].

Furthermore, it was caused by the offering of honey to the Buddha, which led to the establishment of regulations; this great expedient for protecting the Dharma and the initiation of this teaching is not something that can be conceived by ordinary beings.
[Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu sports and plays in the water.

[Note]: "Acting with unrestrained license, moving from here to there, against the current or with the current, sinking here and emerging there, drawing patterns on the water with the hand, splashing it about, and even playing by filling the bowl with water."
[Pācittiya]. [Commentary]: With the exception of water, if one plays with anything else—such as buttermilk, sour gruel, or malt juice—within a vessel, it is a dukkaṭa (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense in cases such as when traveling on a road and crossing water, whether going from this shore to the other shore, or when water carries along bamboo, wood, mats, or rafts.
If one is carried along by a current upstream or downstream; if one picks up stones or sand; if one loses an object and sinks into the bottom of the water; if one surfaces here and submerges there;
or if one has learned the method of floating and raises one's arms, strokes the water, or splashes it—there is no offense.
[Commentary: The textual form of the three phrases in the *Prātimokṣa* is easy to understand. Regarding "entering [the water]" to wash, it is difficult to avoid the fault of playing.

The three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* are largely the same as the preceding precept. "Entering below" refers to the admonition to be cautious; in this land, those who enter the water in the south are rare.

However, because the nature of water is clear and cool, many people enjoy playing in it. According to the above, those who play with water in their alms bowls all commit an offense. This is the annotation.
Regarding "not committing an offense," the characters *bó* (簿) and *bēi* (卑) are pronounced as *pái* (牌); *zhuó* (擢) is combined with *diào* (掉) to mean "to shake" (*diàozhèn*).
[Vinaya] Precept 53: Prohibiting the Annoying of Others.
[Commentary]: The fifty-third precept concerns pinching or poking.
Although the act itself is a minor transgression, it can lead to grave consequences. Small people lacking resolve often take pleasure in doing this;
it is extremely base and vulgar, greatly undermining one’s physical dignity and harming the Way and social customs. Since there is no loss greater than this, the rule was established.
Fifty-three: "Tickling" refers to using the hand to tease the armpits to induce a sensation of itching and provoke fear.
Regarding the first two phrases of this section, they indicate that the transgression is grave; the next two phrases clarify that taking pleasure in it constitutes an extreme offense.

The subsequent passage describes the characteristics of the transgression: "vile" means contemptible and base; it refers to the debasement of the grand performance of monastic deportment, which damages one's dignity.
The high reputation of such a person is diminished, which is considered a disgrace to the Buddha-dharma; it harms social customs and ruins the work of transformation and guidance.
Thus, it can be seen that while the offense may appear minor, its gravity is profound.

[Commentary] There are four conditions for committing this transgression: first, the person must be a *mahābhikṣu*; second, one must have the intention to treat them with frivolous mockery; third, [one must use] the ten fingers of the hands and feet; fourth, [the act must be completed].
The fourth [category] constitutes an offense immediately upon attachment.

Regarding the first condition for the offense: it excludes the lower classes of practitioners, for whom it would be a *dukkaṭa*. Regarding the second: it excludes cases where the act was unintentional, in which case there is no offense. Regarding the third: it excludes other types of objects, for which one incurs a light offense.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, one member of the group of six struck one member of the group of seventeen so severely that he nearly died.
A bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept.
[Commentary]: Within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the characteristics can be explained in detail.
Regarding the note within the *Pratītyasamutpāda*: "How many die?"—the term "how many" (*ji*) also implies "nearby" (*jin*).
[Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu strikes or tickles another with his fingers (referring to the ten fingers of the hands and feet), it is a *pāyattika* offense.
[Note] Excluding the hands and feet, if one strikes or pokes another with a staff, the handle of a fly-whisk, a door-key, or any other object, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense if it was not done intentionally; if one touches another while sleeping to wake them; if one touches another while entering or exiting, walking or coming;
or if, while sweeping the floor, one accidentally touches another with the tip of the broom.
[Commentary: The characteristics of the *Prātimokṣa* may also be understood accordingly.
Since the first section of the *Prātimokṣa* text distinguishes its characteristics through three phrases that are easy to understand, it is shown here only briefly. [Commentary:

The reason other objects result only in a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) is because the distinction lies in the gravity of the mental state; if the mind is heavy, it constitutes a *pārājika* (defeat), whereas for other non-sentient objects, it is otherwise.
Therefore, the offense of the mind should also be light and need not necessarily persist until the end.
In the commentary on the subsequent section, it is stated that for offenses such as using a whisk handle or a door key, one incurs only a minor (jī) offense;
thus, it is necessary to clarify the principle of the Way of Sentient Beings—that the offense of the mind should likewise be light—and "dāng" (should) here means "to receive."
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Precept 54: Refusing Counsel.
[Commentary] The fifty-fourth precept concerns refusing counsel.

[Commentary] Generally speaking, the fundamental purpose of leaving the household life is to abandon evil; this is the essential core of the training, which depends upon spiritual friends mutually admonishing and instructing one another. However, because...

His passions were so deluded that he was about to commit a transgression; another admonished him with reason, yet he would not comply. He persisted in his improper conduct, causing harm that was no small matter;

therefore, this rule was established. Regarding the intent of the fifty-fourth rule: at the outset, it describes how those who seek the Way rely on friends for mutual refinement and polishing. However, below...

Next, the explanation clarifies that because one persists in delusion, one commits an offense; because one knows it is wrong yet acts intentionally, it is termed "shameless" (*gaqie*). [Commentary] Five conditions constitute the completion [of the offense]:
first, the intent to commit a sin; second, another person admonishes according to the Dharma; third, one knows that what one has done is wrong and that the other person’s admonition is correct;
fourth, one rejects the admonition and does not accept it; fifth, one proceeds to commit the fundamental transgression. Because this violates the admonition, the offense is finalized.
*Thullaccaya*.
Regarding the fifth factor for an offense (*āpatti-paccaya*), the first violation is merely a *dukkaṭa*;

it becomes a *thullaccaya* only when one persists in the act. [Note: When the Buddha was at Kammāsadhamma in Kauśāmbī, a bhikkhu who was about to commit an offense was admonished by others, saying, "Do not harbor such an intention."

"If one should act thus and not follow the admonitions of others, one immediately commits various offenses. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha; consequently, the Buddha rebuked him and established the precept.

The circumstances of the precept are the same as those for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* [offenses], with the sole difference that whereas the former involved refusing the Saṃgha in a formal assembly, this involves refusing an individual in private.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika.

[Commentary] If another person restrains him, saying, "Do not do this; you should not act thus," yet he nevertheless persists in doing so, he commits a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) because he does not follow the instruction;
it is a duṣkṛta. If he knows for himself that what he has done is wrong, yet he nevertheless persists in doing so, he commits a fundamental offense because he does not follow [the advice].
Speaking [thus] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. There is no offense if: a person lacking wisdom comes to admonish you and you reply, "You should ask your teacher or preceptor;
further study, recitation of the scriptures, and knowledge of the methods of admonition are required"; or if one uses the admonition appropriately;
or if speaking in jest, speaking alone, speaking in a dream, or intending to say this but saying that instead. These cases do not constitute an offense.
[Commentary]: The three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* are the same as before. [Commentary]:

Within the section on discerning the characteristics, there are two phrases; the first concerns minor offenses where one’s deluded mind takes [the fault] as one's own, which is the aforementioned admonition for oneself.

Because insentient objects are subtle, an offense against them is merely a *śuddhaka* (minor fault), which does not obstruct [the path]. However, as one engages in actions according to circumstances, offenses may range from light to heavy.

An offense committed later that is considered "heavy" refers to knowing that one has already transgressed; it is not the same as the previous admonition. Because this constitutes a violation of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) with grave error, it is not considered light.
In the first section of the "Discerning Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*), the two sentences correspond to the two segments of "lightness and heaviness" within the commentary on offenses.

First, regarding the explanation that committing a light offense does not preclude performing [the rite] according to its lightness or heaviness: this means that what one performs pertains to all seven classes of transgressions (*sapta-āpatti-nikāya*). Next, the following section explains the commission of heavy offenses.
[Commentary] Question: Since the text lists "that which is done" (*kṛta*) as the object of admonition, if there is an offense for doing [the act], what would constitute an offense for stopping [it]?
Answer: If one rejects exhortation regarding the training precepts, the violation of that admonition is termed an offense for stopping.

While the prohibitions of the various precepts are not all enacted by oneself, this particular precept—regarding the desire to commit [an offense]—is such that because the karmic factors are manifold and cannot be gathered by a single person, the Saṃgha must be assembled.

Because one person is appointed to offer admonition, it is required that this individual travel everywhere to provide counsel; knowing that a transgression is imminent, they must intervene to stop it.
Since a violation results in a *pāyattika* offense, one should understand that this regulation is of vital importance and must not be exceeded.

In the initial question-and-answer section, the first question consists of five-character phrases; this is intended to introduce the subsequent precepts, hence this inquiry is raised. Within this dialogue, the initial citation of the subsequent precept constitutes the formal response.

This serves to reject [the notion that] one need only study the preceding rules; it refers to the seventy-first precept below. Furthermore, the subsequent sections contrast this with the remaining precepts to demonstrate its essential importance.

Moreover, there are three parts: first, clarifying the specific regulations; second, indicating the underlying intent (as seen in the passage beginning "But below"); and third, showing how the Sangha’s admonition becomes difficult to fulfill.
Because it is easy for [the offender] to persist in their refusal despite the separate admonition, the text concludes with a lament below.

[Commentary]: Question: Regarding the violation of the Sangha’s admonition, is one guilty immediately upon the completion of the admonition, or does one wait until the act is accomplished? This [specific] admonition does not constitute an offense until the act is accomplished; as for the offense of violating the admonition, the answer is:

In the case of an admonition within the Sangha, the life of the community is of great importance, and the transgression of defying their will is profound. Consequently, [the offense is determined by the act].

Regarding the offense incurred through the formal act of admonition (*jñapti-karman*), this single case of admonition is the opposite of the previous [case] and can be understood accordingly; it requires that the formal act be completed before the offense is established.
If the action is not performed, then the exhortation itself constitutes the acceptance [of the offense];

therefore, it is not the same as the former. In the subsequent question, two differences are raised in contrast to the previous case of the Sangha’s admonition and the establishment of the offense, which are addressed by the answer. In the response, the first part provides an indication.
When the *saṃgha* offers admonition, one immediately commits this offense. The following two sections clarify that individual admonition awaits its completion. [Commentary:

If this is so, then within the section on "Exhortation to Study," there is likewise a single person; since there is no *saṃgha* dharma, why does one commit an offense immediately upon the conclusion of the admonition?
The answer is: that admonition ceases the offense because the person was previously one who did not study, yet spoke out to reject the admonition once the path had already been set forth.

Training (*śikṣā*) refers to the meaning of committing an offense by violating a formal admonition; this constitutes an actual offense (*karmasamutthāna*) once the act has been performed. Although one may have spoken words of refusal when being admonished, this is not yet the commission of an offense;

the violation of the admonition is not established until the act itself is carried out, for it is only then that the sense of violating the admonition is complete. Therefore, these two states do not coincide.

Regarding the difficulty in the transition [of the offense]: because one is exhorted to study by an inferior [person], both being distinct individuals, the offense is incurred immediately upon the completion of the admonition; this would contradict the principle stated above.

In the response, however, regarding the admonition to desist (*pratiṣedha*), since it is due to the cessation [of the act], and because it is an exhortation, the desisting comes first; whereas regarding the admonition to perform (*pravartana*), since one desires to perform it, the performance itself occurs immediately, thus the performing comes later.
Therefore, for the admonition to desist, the offense is established at the very moment of the admonition, while for the admonition to perform, the offense awaits the completion [of the act].
[Commentary] The remaining characteristics may be understood.

Regarding the "remaining characteristics" mentioned in the brief reference, they concern non-offenses; as the text is identical to that in the section on the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, they will not be explained again here.
[Vinaya] The fifty-fifth precept concerning monks who cause fear.
[Commentary]: The precept against intimidating others is the fifty-fifth.
[Commentary]: It is the proper principle for those who have left the household life to mutually protect one another and refrain from causing disturbance;

yet, by using the characteristics of the six sense objects and so forth to intimidate others, causing them to give rise to terror and anxiety, they abandon the cultivation of right practice. Because such affliction is deep and the transgression grave, this rule was established.

Fifty-fifth, regarding the initial exposition of what is appropriate within the "Regulating the Mind" section: now, below, the manifestation of transgressions is revealed. The six sense objects are explained as follows.
"Huangju" (惶懼) means to be terrified; "ji" (悸), pronounced *qi* with the fourth tone, describes the state of the heart being startled and agitated.

[Note] When the Buddha was in the country of Pāṭaliputra with Nāgapāla attending on his left and right, it was the constant practice of all Buddhas that when they were walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), those providing offerings would stand at the head of the path. At the beginning, middle, and end of the night, [Nāgapāla] informed the Buddha and requested him to return;

however, the Buddha turned back and put on his outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) in reverse. Frightened by this, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha the following morning and, because of this incident, established this precept.

[Commentary]: Regarding the precept on fearing the Buddha, this is intended to clarify that even those who slight the Most Holy One and fear Him still encounter retribution; how much more so for others of lower status? The meaning requires that one must eliminate such traces.
Furthermore, it reveals that the Buddha has no mind of fear, as fear resides in the "fearer. This is discussed in terms of common human characteristics;
whether one fears or does not fear, both are classified as grave offenses (*duṣkṛta*).

Regarding the two [sections] within the "Conditions for the Precepts" (*śīla-pratyaya*), the first explains by means of an analogy based on the citation [of the Buddha]; "eradicating traces" (*miejì*) refers to what must be regulated and severed.

Furthermore, the next section explains by means of a judgment regarding the offense (*āpatti*); that is, within this precept, the Buddha is cited as the condition to clarify that this offense does not depend on what is feared, because the Buddha is without fear.

[Commentary]: If that were so, one might also kill a Buddha as the causal condition [for a transgression], and whether death or non-death occurred, both would constitute a grave offense. The answer is:

No. The precept regarding killing ordinary persons takes an ordinary person as its causal condition; it is by way of clarifying the breaking of the Saṃgha that it subsequently clarifies the killing of a Buddha, but the Buddha himself is not taken as the causal condition for that specific precept.

In the explanation of the objection, it is argued that the case of fear should not be treated as distinct from the case of killing, because the conditions (*pratyaya*) in the narrative origin (*nidāna*) are different;
thus, they cannot be used as an analogy. In the commentary, *nāgapā* is the name of a bhikṣu who was a donor and also an attendant;
he informed the Buddha, requesting him to return to his chamber. *Kuccha* refers to animal hide.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu frightens another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
[Commentary] If one uses forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects to frighten a person, whether that person is actually frightened or not, each instance constitutes a *pāyattika*.

If the person does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one speaks of the six sense objects—forms, sounds, and so forth—to frighten someone, and the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* offense for not being clear; a *dukkaṭa* offense for not being clear. There is no offense in the following cases: if it is dark and there is no light;
if one mistakes a place for defecating or urinating for a place inhabited by wild beasts and becomes terrified; if one is terrified by sounds such as footsteps, coughing, or the sound of contact;

if one shows someone colors and so forth without the intention to cause fear; or if such signs actually exist, or if one sees them in a dream, [thinking], "I shall die" or "I shall renounce the path."
If one loses an object, or if the parents of a preceptor are gravely ill or have died, it is no offense to inform them of this, whether done in jest or by mistake.
[Commentary] The precept text consists of three phrases.

[Commentary]: Within the section on the characteristics of transgressions, first the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are presented to people to demonstrate the gravity of the offense; subsequently, the six sense objects are explained to people in terms of what is heard and known, thereby establishing the lightness or gravity of the resulting sin.
In the analysis of the characteristics of transgressions within the *Prātimokṣa*, there are two parts. First, regarding the six sense objects shown to people, the Vinaya states:
"Fear of forms" refers to such things as the shapes of elephants, horses, or ghosts; "fear of sounds" refers to such things as the sounds of conch shells, drums, or weeping;

"fear of odors" refers to the fragrances of tree leaves, flowers, and fruits, as well as foul smells; "fear of tastes" refers to sour, sweet, bitter, and astringent flavors that cause one to taste them.

Regarding "fear of touch," the objects that cause fear through contact—namely heat, cold, heaviness, lightness, roughness, fineness, smoothness, and harshness—are the phenomena that cause fear when touched; "the one who fears" refers to the person.

As for the speech [of others], it means saying things such as "you will die" or "you have abandoned the path. Regarding the gravity or lightness of the karmic bond, it is determined by whether [the victim] was aware or unaware [of the intent].

Next, concerning the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), the person spoken of is the same as the six aforementioned characteristics; however, when explained separately, the determination of their gravity or lightness is likewise the same.
[Commentary] Within the section on the characteristics of non-offenses, one may understand the analysis by fully applying it to the objects of the sensory realms (*viṣaya*).
In the introductory note to the non-offenses, the first point concerns a person’s own doubt; this briefly cites two objects, namely form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*).

What follows clarifies that these are not intentional acts, fully demonstrating all six objects; thus it says "form, etc. Alternatively, cases such as dreams or death are cited separately as specific instances of the Dharma.
Dust. [Vinaya] Precept 56: Bathing more frequently than once every half-month.
[Commentary] Precept 56: Bathing less frequently than once every half-month.
The title of the fifty-sixth precept states: "Bathing once every half-month; exceeding this limit constitutes a transgression.
Because the phrasing is somewhat obscure, the commentary (*śāstra*) provides an easy-to-understand explanation, making the characteristics of the rule very clear.
[Commentary]: In the desire realm, the body sustained by solid food consists largely of impure matter; thus, bathing is required to increase the Path and generate wholesome qualities.

However, if one merely seeks to appear exceptionally clean beyond the ordinary, such that the body’s luster and physical appearance become objects of attachment, this contradicts the very spirit of renunciation.
Therefore, it must be regulated so that one bathes once every half-month; to bathe less frequently than this constitutes an offense.
In the initial section of the *Zhìyì* (Exposition of the Meaning), it describes the opening of the intention: "Lump food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is also called "segmented food.
Because one consumes this food, its fatty grease flows outward and accumulates as dust and grime, thereby becoming impure. Those who bathe wash away these [impurities]. This is a distinct term;

as in secular dictionaries, washing the head is specifically termed "bathing" (*mù*). Here, however, we take the general sense of the word rather than restricting it to the body or head, meaning to cleanse the person and remove [impurity].

Because one perceives [the body] as a source of affliction, one can increase the Path; because there is no external defilement, one can give rise to goodness. However, regarding the second and third [stages], the intention for restraint is explained:

frequent washing involves two faults. First, becoming attached to the physical marks is to delight in the mundane world. Second, being without the mind of revulsion and turning away [from desire] is to contravene the Path.

[Commentary: Regarding the five conditions for committing this offense: first, one has already finished bathing previously; second, less than half a month has passed since that time; third, there is no valid reason for bathing again;
fourth, one bathes more than half the body; and fifth, the act is completed.
Within these conditions for the offense, the third and fourth conditions have lost their numerical indicators in the text; the third, "having no reason," is as stated in the main precept.
Because there are circumstances that permit it, these four cases constitute further bathing; the fifth case, where more than half the body is submerged, is the limit for an offense.
[Note: When the Buddha was at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, there was a pond. King Bimbisāra permitted the bhikṣus to bathe in it regularly.
One night, the group of six entered the pond to bathe late in the evening. The king, accompanied by his court ladies, went to the pond and encountered them. The king did not bathe at all.
The minister, feeling resentment toward the bhikṣu, reported the matter to the Buddha; consequently, the Buddha rebuked him and established the precept.
Regarding the "Bamboo Grove Pond" mentioned in the context of the origin of this rule, it should be located near the royal palace grounds.
[The Vinaya states: If a bhikṣu bathes once every half-month, a bhikṣu who is not ill must accept this [limit] and may not exceed it (that is, bathing within the half-month).
[The offense of] *pāyattika* [is incurred] except at other times. "Other times" refers to: the time of heat (the forty-five days following spring and the first month of summer);

the time of illness (down to the point where the body emits a foul odor); the time of work (down to sweeping the ground in front of one's house); the time of wind and rain (down to a single whirlwind or a single drop of rain falling on the body);
and the time of traveling on a road (down to half a *yojana*, whether coming or going). These are the [permitted] times.

[Note] If one washes excessively such that the entire body or half the body falls [into the water], it is an *upāya* (preparatory act); if one subsequently regrets it, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and there is no offense.
This applies to cases where washing frequently is permitted due to specific circumstances, or when one is forced by another’s superior power to wash.

[Commentary]: Regarding the four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa*, one person may bathe once every half-month, but must not exceed this limit. If, according to the literal phrasing, one bathes outside of the half-month period, it constitutes an offense.
Now, since we are dealing with an offense of omission (ūnam-vadya), what is the meaning of saying "exceeding"?

Because the Buddha established the precept that one shall bathe once every half-month, if one bathes fewer times than required, it exceeds the holy regulation; thus it is called "exceeding. "Exceeding" (*atīta*) is a term used to denote the transgression of the formal rules of instruction.
There are three points regarding the offenses and four regarding the exemptions.
The character "guo" (transgression) in the second phrase of the first section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is explained in detail because its usage is ambiguous. [Commentary:
The remainder is fully and extensively presented in the *Shuchao* (Explanatory Notes), from which it should be consulted.

The subsequent section points out that the details are as explained in the *Śāstra* (Commentary), specifically in the passage concerning the "Opening of the Conditions" (*kaiyuan*) and so forth. Regarding the six conditions for the "hot season," the commentary states:
"The forty-five days after spring" refers to the period from the first day of the third month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month;

"the first month of summer" refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, totaling seventy-five days. For the remaining five [conditions], one incurs an offense.
The text concerning non-offenses is as explained in the commentary and is easy to understand.
[Vinaya] Precept 57: Burning Fire on Open Ground.
[Commentary] Precept 57: Burning Fire on Open Ground.
[Commentary]: The nature of fire is to burn fiercely and its transformations are constant; there may be instances where it spreads uncontrollably, so it must be restrained.
Furthermore, when fires gather together, they often lead to many worldly entanglements and the neglect of one's duties, causing self-deprecation. How could one not exercise control over them?
The fifty-seventh regulation regarding the intention has two parts: first, to prevent the spread of fire to other areas;
second, to avoid the neglect of one's duties.

[Commentary] There are four conditions for committing this offense: first, the presence of fuel; second, an open space; third, grass or wood with flames; and fourth, the act of burning itself constitutes the offense.

Regarding the second condition for the offense, it is restricted to being in the open air; if one is inside a building, there is no offense. Three factors must be present: there must be flames, whether with or without smoke, in which case the offense is light;
however, if it occurs on ground where plants grow, or among living grasses and trees, the two offenses of "digging" and "destroying" arise.
[Note] While the Buddha was at the City of the Wilderness (Kalandaka-nivāpa), the group of six monks said to one another, "We shall not speak as we please in the presence of the Elder.
They then went out onto the open ground, gathered firewood and grass, and lit a fire. A venomous snake that had been dwelling within a tree stump was driven out by the heat of the fire;

it leaped up in alarm and threw itself into the flames, burning down the Buddha’s lecture hall. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established a precept.

[Commentary]: Within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), because one is unable to speak according to one's own will, one goes outside the assembly and toward [the fire], which then burns the lecture hall;
thus, a light offense leads to a grave harm, so one must not fail to be cautious. In the world, that which is destroyed most often suffers damage by fire;

otherwise, it would endure for a long time. The world is likewise: fire is something that ordinary people crave and yet cannot touch. This is the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); how could one become attached to it?

In the initial section of the "Conditions for the Precepts" (*śīla-pratyaya*), the text first cites the scriptural injunctions to exercise caution; subsequently, it demonstrates the faults and exhorts one to abandon them. First, it points to present phenomena, saying, "In the world," and so forth.
Next, it cites the calamities of the kalpas, saying, "The world is likewise. For example, when the three great calamities arise, the fire-element destruction reaches up to the First Dhyāna Heaven.
Furthermore, the nature of the third [calamity, water] is fierce; even in the cold months, though one craves tactile contact, one would be dissolved by it.

The essence of this refers to the practitioner of contemplation who, by observing how fire can cause transformation and decay, realizes the impermanence of the world and thereby gives rise to revulsion and renunciation.
Alternatively, it may be because sutras and śāstras frequently employ it as a metaphor— either comparing the three realms to a burning house, or the world to impermanence,
or instructing one to distance oneself from evil as one would avoid a pit of fire, or stating that a mind of anger is more fierce than a raging fire.
These instances are very numerous; I have cited only one or two as examples.

[Vinaya]: If a bhikṣu, being without illness (unless it is for the purpose of treating a disease or for bodily convenience), lights a fire in the open air for the sake of warming himself, or instructs another to do so, he commits a *pāyattika* offense under the same conditions.
[Note: If he sets fire to anything in an open space—whether grass, wood, branches, leaves, hemp, *kṣauma* linen, cow dung, husks, chaff, or ashes—it is a *pāyattika*.
If he places fire among grass, wood, or even chaff, it likewise falls under this offense.
If he throws half-burnt or scorched materials into the fire, or if he ignites charcoal, it is a *dukkaṭa*, provided he does not first inform the person concerned.
To know this and to look at this is also a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), yet there are cases where one does not commit an offense. This refers to saying, "Know this" or "Look at this.
Furthermore, if a patient naturally causes another to do so, or if there is a specific occasion or condition—such as when a caregiver is boiling gruel, porridge, soup, or rice;
or if one is in a kitchen, a bathhouse, or performing acts such as fumigating bowls, boiling dyes, lighting lamps, or burning incense—in all such cases, there is no offense.
[Commentary]: The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Jieben) distinguishes the characteristics [of the precepts] with extreme clarity, making them easy to understand.
Within the *Prātimokṣa*, the characteristics are indicated only in brief; however, in the commentary (*zhù*), they are divided into two parts:

offenses and non-offenses. Within the offenses, there are again two types: grave and light. Regarding the grave offenses, the first involves lighting a fire with an object, and the second involves throwing fire into an object.
At the beginning, *cīrama* is a Sanskrit term that is also the name of a grass; its translation is unknown. *Taṇḍula-kaṇa* refers to rice husks; *pāṃsu* refers to sweepings;

*yava-khala* (the character [麥*戈], pronounced *yi*) refers to barley chaff, which is the skin of barley. Next, regarding light offenses: "half-burnt" refers to the aforementioned grasses, trees, and so forth that have previously been exposed to fire.
As for charcoal, it is light because it lacks flames, and thus there is no offense. "Mí" (porridge) is also *yōu* (congee).
[Vinaya] Precept 58: Concealing Another’s Clothing or Utensils.
[Commentary] Precept 58: Concealing Robes.
[Commentary] The virtuous class of eminent renunciants, whose conduct is as mature as the aged, have forever severed worldly play; yet now they engage in jesting.

It is noisy and distracting; wherever one goes, it brings affliction and distress. When hiding another’s robes or bowl, they may not be found at the time of need, causing the owner to panic and suffer deep anguish—this is truly loathsome.
Furthermore, since one hides another’s property, a mind of theft may arise; when the situation becomes critical and grave, the fear is extreme.

Moreover, even if no theft has occurred, one may be slandered, and when one is pure and innocent, it is difficult to clear one's name. How can one extricate oneself from such a state? Because these many faults are present, [one should avoid it].
A single regulation must be established.

Regarding the fifty-eight regulations, there are three underlying intentions: first, the intention to distress others by slighting oneself, which combines the dust of sensory objects with a state of panic—meaning alarm and fear—and aversion—which means loathing;
second, the intention to deeply guard against serious theft; and third, the intention to avoid slander and the difficulty of distinguishing [the offense].
The final summary is provided below.

[Commentary]: There are three conditions for committing this offense: first, being a *bhikṣu* possessing robes and bowl; second, having the intention to cause alarm or disturbance; and third, taking the hidden items—by these means, one commits the offense.
The First Section on the Conditions for Offenses, Distinguishing from the Lighter Offenses of the Lower Assembly.

[Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a householder invited the Saṅgha. The group of seventeen monks took their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases and paced back and forth on one side, looking about.
At that time, the group of six monks, watching for their backs turned, took their belongings and hid them. The others...
Jiǔchá (丘察) recognized his transgression and reported it to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked him and established the precept.
In the context of the Vinaya, the term "pángyáng" (彷徉)—where "páng" is pronounced "biàng" and "yáng" is pronounced "yáng"—describes the manner of walking with slow, deliberate steps.
[The Vinaya states: If a bhikṣu conceals another bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case—whether he conceals them himself or instructs another to do so.
Down to those who do so in jest, it is a *pāyattika*.
[Note] There is no offense if one picks up the object knowing its characteristics and substance; or if one picks it up because it has been blown away or soaked by rain in an open space;
or if one stores it away for the sake of admonishing a property owner who neglects their belongings and leaves them in disarray; or if it was borrowed from another.
If one folds the robe because it might be lost if left unfolded, or if one lifts it up for this reason, or if one conceals the robes, bowl,
or other articles due to life-threatening dangers such as those from non-Brahmins and the like, there is no offense in any of these cases.
[Commentary]: Regarding the three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra, the second phrase specifies the object concealed, ranging from mere joking up to causing fear or loss of composure;
the third phrase defines the offense. The remainder is as cited in the *Śāstra*.
Because the first phrase of the *Prātimokṣa* is easy for practitioners to understand, it is not listed here; those who require it should seek it in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Regarding the "non-offenses" (*anāpatti*), there are five distinct categories, the first four of which are all divided by the character "if" (*cet*): (1) knowing the nature [of the object]; (2) fearing damage or destruction;
(3) desiring to alarm others; and (4) fearing loss or theft. The first three refer to the property of others, while the fourth refers to one's own property.
Alternatively, the fifth difficulty regarding the conditions may be seen in the text.
[Vinaya] Precept Fifty-nine: Taking a robe for pure offering without authorization.
[Commentary] Precept Fifty-nine: Taking a robe for pure offering without authorization.
[Commentary]: Generally, the method of pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*) is intended to eliminate attachment. Although the practice is gradual, its ultimate aim is to approximate the great conduct.

Once the robe has been entrusted to another, it must be asked for when one wishes to take it back; to take it without asking is equivalent to not having given it at all. This currently violates the prohibitions of the Sage, as it fails to relinquish what was once offered.
Furthermore, because the object is no longer in the possession of the original owner, the resulting distress is profound; therefore, this rule was established.
The fifty-ninth [section], "Regulating the Mind," has two parts. First, it addresses how one initially deviates from the pure dharma;
by first explaining the intention of giving, one gradually abandons attachment and ultimately fulfills the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), hence it says, "far resembling great practice.

Next, below the section on clothing, it clarifies that taking things at will and using them as one pleases is equivalent to claiming ownership; hence it says, "unable to sever and discard," meaning the mind of possessiveness is not yet cut off. Furthermore, below...
Second, it vexes the pure owner because, by not speaking, one causes them to believe their property has been lost.

[Commentary] There are four conditions for committing this offense: first, it must be one's own property; second, one must perform a formal act of purification (*visuddhi*); third, one must not inform the owner; and fourth, upon taking it, the offense is incurred.

Regarding the second condition for an offense, there are two types of pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*). If one entrusts an object to another person and has them hold it as a custodian, it is called "true purity" (*bhūta-śuddhi*).

If the object remains with oneself but one merely regards it as belonging to another, it is called "successive purity" (*paramparā-śuddhi*). This present regulation is established for the purpose of true purity.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a group of six monks took the robes of a monk with whom they were intimate after he had already given them away, without informing the owner.
When the monk who had been deprived of his robes reported this transgression to the Buddha, the Buddha rebuked him and established the precept.
【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī,
and later takes it back and wears it without informing the owner, it is a pāyattika offense.
[Note] There is no offense if it is a gift of truth, if the donor takes it for themselves, or if it is taken at will by one who has received it through a series of transfers.
[Commentary] The four phrases of the precept text are: 1) the person; 2) the two types of giving to the fivefold assembly; 3) taking and using; and 4) the formulation of the offense.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Jieben) can be understood as follows.
[Commentary] Question: As explained in the section on the meaning, regarding the ritual for the pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*), the two assemblies [of monks and nuns] do not perform it for one another.

Why, then, does the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* list them together? Answer: This is to clarify that all five groups of practitioners possess the characteristics of transgression; although they differ in gravity, the ritual of the pure gift applies to all.
Because the meaning is the same, the names are listed collectively; as for the pure dharmas, they follow the Vinaya rules.
Within the section "Resolving Doubts," under the explanation of the meaning, it refers to the detailed exposition of the two divisions, namely the Vinayas of the two assemblies of monks and nuns.
The Vinaya states that the five groups of true practitioners may not act for one another because they are not of the same class. In the response, it is clarified by means of the pure [dharmas].

The rules for giving are generally restricted to the five groups of monastics; however, because there are distinctions in the nature of the offenses, it is said that they differ in terms of gravity. When it comes to pure giving (*viśuddha-dāna*), each group is considered in relation to its own members;
therefore, it is said that one follows the specific regulations of their respective Vinaya. In the commentary on "not committing an offense," both types of purity are listed in detail:
when the speaker of truthful words acts in accordance with the teaching without contradiction, and when things are passed along according to one's will, there is fundamentally no offense.
[Vinaya] The precept on wearing new robes (the 60th).
[Commentary] The 60th precept concerning new robes.

[Commentary] Generally, one dyes robes with austerely colored (kasāya) dye so that the monastic attire serves as a sign; internally it eliminates attachment to clothing, while externally it fosters faith and respect. Now, [this precept concerns...]
This was established as a prohibition because [clinging to] dyed garments is contrary to the banner of the Noble Path; it increases greed, invites reproach, and causes ruin.
Regarding the intent of the sixty rules, the first section describes the physical appearance and internally dispels attachment, for one does not crave beautiful forms.

Externally, it fosters faith and respect, so that others may know this person is one who has attained liberation. Now, the following passage reveals the faults concerning the body of a bhikṣu and the sacred Dharma.

Those who assemble [in robes] but wear the outer dharma-garments while their inner conduct is inconsistent with them—since these outward signs of the banner of the Noble Path are thus discordant—it is said they are "not [proper].

[Commentary: There are four conditions for committing an offense: first, it must be the three robes; second, it must be one's own property; third, it must not be stained or damaged; and fourth, it must be worn.
Offense. Regarding the fourth condition for the offense: it is committed based on wearing [the garment]; if not worn, it should be considered a minor offense.
[Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks wore white garments while walking about, which caused the laypeople to criticize them, saying they lacked the True Dharma.
As the King’s minister, a bhikṣu, reported the transgression to the Buddha, the Buddha consequently established this precept.
[Commentary] The origin story is clear; in the section of the precept on dyed robes that distinguishes its characteristics, it says: "Because new robes have not been worn out."
In the section on the conditions for the precepts, three locations are cited in total to mutually clarify their characteristics: that "new clothing" is not spoiled refers specifically to white cloth.
[The Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu obtains new clothing (whether the substance itself is new or first obtained from another), he should apply one of the three types of discoloration;
within each color, he may choose as he wishes to spoil it—either blue, black, or madder."

[Note] The Vinaya Commentary states: "Regarding this term 'purified' (*kappiya*): if it is dyed with color, one says it is purified; if it has already become a colored cloth, it is a purified garment.
One should mark a single spot by folding over a piece of different-colored material. Therefore, it is said to be 'purified.

From here on, if it is a robe or not a robe, and it is an item that is not for personal use, one must entirely mark it with a sign and keep it as 'purified. Regarding what is called 'heavy': it refers to woolen rugs, carpets, and so forth."
This refers to what is most important among robes.
[The Vinaya states: If a bhikṣu wears any other new robe without having dyed it with one of the three types of disfiguring colors—either blue, black, or madder—he commits a pāyattika offense.

[Note]: If one wears a garment that has not been made into three layers, it is a *pācittiya* offense; if one wears a heavy or light robe that has not had the *kappaka-paṭṭa* (marking) applied, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.

If one keeps as one's own any item that is not a robe—such as a bowl-bag, a sandal-bag, a needle-case, a sewing-kit, a meditation belt, a waistband, a cap, socks, a heat-retaining cloth, a head-wrap, or a sandal-wrapping cloth—without having performed the ritual purification (*parikamma*), it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. This also applies to an undyed robe.

Regarding the offense of a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅) for entrusting [garments] to a layperson's house, there is no violation in the following cases: obtaining a garment from a layperson and dyeing it in three colors;
other matters of light or heavy offenses; and keeping a cloth (*mukhapuñchana*) after it has been purified.

[Commentary: The section on the precept text is divided into two parts. First, the establishment of the rule consists of three phrases: first, "a bhikṣu"; second, "obtaining a new garment"; and third, "it must be [dyed in] three [colors]."

The three phrases of the root precept on discarding the original color to assume the marks of a śramaṇa consist of: first, the person who commits the offense; second, not discarding [the cloth] with the three [proper] colors;
and third, the formal conclusion of the offense.
In the second phrase of the initial section on establishing the rule within the root precept, the commentary indicates the characteristics of new clothing by means of two types.

In the third commentary, the sub-commentary on the Vinaya is again cited and divided into two sections. The first explains "purification through processing" (*kappiya-kāraka*), which is further divided into two parts:

first, purifying by dyeing as it is; second, purifying by folding after it has been dyed. Following this, the next section explains "purification by marking" (*chidda-kappiya*), which also consists of two parts:
first, light offenses; second, heavy offenses; both must be purified.
[Commentary]: Regarding the offenses incurred, first, if one does not spoil new garments with the three colors, it constitutes a heavy downfall;

if one does not apply spots to heavy or light robes to change their color, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). All other small or fine items must likewise be purified by applying spots. This does not refer to towels or sandals.
To dye these with the three colors would further alarm the laity and be most ridiculous.

The three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* distinguish the characteristics [of the offenses]. The commentary divides this into three parts: first, it clarifies the actual commission of the offense, whether grave or light;

second, it clarifies the purification by marking (*parikarma*), such as dyeing; third, it clarifies the entrusting of items to a layperson’s house, because when items are mixed with those of a layperson, they cannot be distinguished.
The text of the sub-commentary explains the aforementioned two sections; as for other minor details—such as various bags and towels—they are not what is being excluded here.
Nowadays, there are those who, upon hearing that the Vinaya states all items should be dyed the color of a *kāṣāya*, indiscriminately dye everything from clothing to socks and shoes;
they have not seen this text and thus do not realize how excessive their error is.
[Vinaya] Precept 61: Killing Animals. [Commentary] The precept against killing animals is the sixty-first.

[Commentary] According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are three reasons why those who have left the household life should embrace the four immeasurables and compassionately save the lives of sentient beings; for this reason, it is added here.

First, because harming others violates the path of compassion and lacks pity; second, because self-destruction and the affliction of others are the very root of birth and death and obstacles to the Path that constitute evil karma, it is therefore prohibited so as to eliminate such evil karma; third, for the sake of increasing faith and respect and bringing an end to slander.

Sixty-first: Regarding the three points concerning the regulation of intention—first, the four "etceteras" (慈、悲、喜、捨)—because they universally encompass all objects of perception, they are collectively termed "etcetera.

Second, among these, the karma of killing violates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and is the foremost of all karmas; because it causes one to wander through saṃsāra, it is called the "root of birth and death," and so forth.
Third, as with the case of dependent origination, this was established as a precept due to criticism.
[Commentary] Five conditions constitute the offense: first, it is an animal; second, one perceives it as an animal; third, there is the intent to kill;
fourth, one initiates the means; fifth, its life is severed.
[Note] When the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, Kāḷodāyin, being displeased with a crow, shot and killed it with a bamboo bow, thereby committing a grave offense.

When the householder [堆/積] (Ji) paid his respects, he saw that the bhikṣus were being disparaged together; the bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.
In the context of the causal narrative for the precept, the character 藉 (jiè) is pronounced with the initial *zǐ* and the final *zhì*, meaning "to gather."
[The Vinaya] states: "If a bhikṣu intentionally... [The Commentary] states:

The Buddha said: "If one does not know [that they are insects], there is no offense."

【Vinaya】 To kill (whether by one's own hand or by commanding another to kill) an animal (one that is incapable of transformation) constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for taking life. (The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs;
the exceptions are as in the precept on killing humans.)

[The Vinaya] Precept Sixty-two: Regarding the Drinking of Water Containing Insects.
[The Commentary] Precept Sixty-two: Regarding the Drinking of Water Containing Insects.

[Commentary: The intent of this regulation is the same as that of the preceding precept. That [preceding] precept was established within the category of "limiting portions" and required the actual severing of life; this [present] precept is established within the category of "profound prevention.

It is intended to protect the lives of sentient beings: if one knows there are insects present yet drinks or uses the water, one incurs an offense regardless of whether life has been severed. If life is actually severed, it falls under the scope of the preceding precept.

The first phrase of the sixty-second rule on the regulation of intention indicates that it is the same as the preceding [rule], while the subsequent portion reveals its distinction. This precept was established to prevent the killing of animals.

[Commentary] There are five conditions for committing this offense: first, water containing insects; second, knowing [it contains insects]; third, not employing the method of straining; fourth, drinking; and fifth, using [the water].
Regarding the offense according to its causes:

this is the third condition for the transgression—failing to employ the method of straining with a filter. If one strains, there is no offense; furthermore, this refers only to what is obtained by means of a strainer and what is visible to the naked eye.

[Commentary]: If insects and water were identical, they should have been combined into one; however, because they destroy living seeds and involve internal and external prohibitions, they are classified as heavy offenses, for life follows the act of using [the object].
Thus, the distinction between the two internal and external fetters can be seen through their respective intentions.
The next section contrasts the preceding rule on water containing insects to distinguish between their combination and separation. First, it clarifies the principle of what is appropriate:

regarding the prohibition against destroying living beings for food, within this same regulation, "internal" refers to internal sustenance and "external" refers to external use; this is for the subsequent purpose. Second, it clarifies the intent of the separation:
if the rule were applied solely to use, there would be no fault in drinking [such water]; therefore, a separate regulation is required, the intent being to preserve life and the seeds of life.
The offense is light because the circumstances were minor.
[Note: While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks took water containing various insects for drinking. A layperson criticized and disparaged them;
the bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established the precept.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu knows that water contains insects [he commits an offense].
[Commentary] Apart from water, drinking or using fermented insect-infused liquids, bitter vinegar, clear curd-liquor, or barley-water mixed with insects constitutes the same offense.
[Sūtra] To drink water containing living organisms constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

[Commentary] The same applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*. There is no offense if one did not know it beforehand, if there was no perception of organisms, if the organisms were so large that they moved away upon contact with the water, or if one drinks water that has been strained.

[Commentary: The five phrases of the precept text are: first, the person who commits the offense; second, knowing [the water]; third, that the water contains insects; fourth, drinking and using it; and fifth, the resulting offense.

[Commentary]: The precept against causing doubt and distress is the sixty-third.

[Commentary]: Those who have left the household life have set their aspirations on a distant goal; they dedicate their minds to honoring the Path until the end of their lives and the exhaustion of their lifespans.

Now, if one causes others to harbor doubts by using such things as one's age to distress them, it ruins their correct cultivation. Since the harm caused by such distress is so great, how could this not be prohibited?

second, because of the thirteen *antarāyika-dharmas* (obstructing factors) discussed in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*; third, because of a mad *bhikṣu*; fourth, because of a *bhikṣu* who has committed a *pārājika* offense; and fifth, because of a *bhikṣu* who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Regarding the six-night *parivāsa* (probation) for one who has committed a *śikṣamāṇā* offense, the four formal acts (*karmavācanā*), and the mutual suspicion between monks and nuns: these all constitute the intrinsic nature of a *pārājika* offense.

Second, there is the intention to cause doubt and vexation. Third, the six matters are recounted as they occurred. Fourth, the verbal expression is clear and distinct. Fifth, the person addressed hears and understands them.

Regarding the first [section on] the conditions for transgression, it excludes those of the lower three groups; furthermore, according to the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya*, it excludes those who have committed the thirteen *pārājika* offenses, those who lack the essence of the precepts, and those who are insane or have lost right mindfulness—thus these two categories are both subject to light *śikṣādattaka* penance. Those below this [category] are the opposite of the above and are therefore subject to heavy *śikṣādattaka* penance, which constitutes a grave offense.
This involves six nights of separate residence (*ṣaḍrātra-parivāsa*) for one who has performed the confession for a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, followed by four formal acts (*catvāraḥ karmāṇi*).
That is to say, those such as those who have been rebuked possess the essence of the precepts by virtue of their inherent nature;
although those who are insane possess it as well, because their minds are deranged, they do not know for themselves that they are bhikṣus.
[Commentary] Question: Regarding the offense incurred upon hearing and knowing, why does the root text of the precepts state, "if for even a short time one does not find joy"? Answer:

It is not that one must wait until one finds no joy before the offense is committed; rather, it is established with respect to the intention of the one who causes distress, down to the point of intending to cause them to find no joy. This is for the sake of the Dharma. [The Vinaya] states: "If one does not take pleasure [in the practice] for even a moment, it is a *pāyattika* offense. [Commentary:

Fearing that he might later feel doubt or regret, [the Buddha] said to him who had been receiving offerings from others and receiving the prostrations of great bhikṣus without cause:
"You were not born at such a time; you were born like other people. I know that you were not born at such a time. The matter was indeed so.
Fearing that he might later feel doubt or regret regarding his receiving of offerings and respectful service from others, [the Buddha] said to him: "You have no such [age]."
If he has been permitted for as many years as other bhikṣus know him to have reached, yet he is not actually that many years old— if his age is less than twenty—

and if within the boundary there is a separate assembly (nānāsaṃgha) fearing future doubt or regret regarding the acceptance of offerings and reverential salutations, and they speak to him so that he may know [the situation] and return to his original place to receive the precepts again—
this matter is indeed true; the motion (*jñapti*) is not accomplished, the formal act (*karman*) is not accomplished, it is contrary to the Dharma, and it is a separate assembly.

Fearing that they might later harbor doubt or regret regarding the acceptance of material offerings and reverential salutations, he speaks to them to make it known [that they must] return to their original place and receive the precepts again;

for such is the fact, and he commits a *pārājika* offense, or even down to an *dukkaṭa* (wrong speech). [Vinaya] Precept 64: Concealing the Offenses of a Bhikṣu.
[Commentary] The precept on concealing offenses is the sixty-fourth.

[Commentary] Those who have left the household life share the same Dharma; if one sees that another has committed a grave offense, it is appropriate to immediately reveal it so as to manifest the purity of one’s own mind and also cause the former...

If one refrains from transgression after others have already ceased, then both self and others will benefit, and the Dharma of the community will remain pure; this is the natural principle of the Dharma.

Therefore, we should mutually conceal one another’s faults without any thought of exposing them. This prevents the roots of sin committed by those who have gone before from spreading and becoming inexhaustible.

Furthermore, it prevents one from corrupting one’s own mind and conduct when about to commit a transgression, thereby averting harm to both self and others and the ruin of the communal Dharma. This is the way to avoid such faults.

Because it is light, it is established as a *śikṣāpada*. Regarding the sixty-four *śikṣāpadas*, the initial exposition of the three benefits within the intent consists of: first, for oneself; second, for others; and third, the purification of the communal Dharma.

As for the mention of "committing a grave offense," this generally encompasses both the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* categories; this is the natural principle of the Dharma (*dharmatā*), meaning it is so by the very nature of things.
Next, the three types of damage are explained; by their opposites, they may be understood. "Increasingly vast" means that it spreads and expands without limit.

[Commentary] There are six conditions for committing an offense: first, being a *mahābhikṣu* (great bhikṣu), excluding the three lower groups; second, committing a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), excluding the lower offenses.

If one discloses as described above, yet maintains the intention to conceal the offense—this is the fifth [factor], non-disclosure—and if a night passes, one commits the remaining offense."

Regarding the second condition for an offense—concealing an offense of the three grades below [the pārājikas] which constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* (light) offense—it is excluded from the [standard] three conditions.

If the cooperation has already been revealed as described above, one should act according to the aforementioned method. "Below" refers to the *Shō* (Commentary), which states:

[Note] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Upananda frequently committed offenses with which he was intimate; however, he did not speak of them to anyone so that they would not be known.

[Prātimokṣa Vinaya] If a bhikṣu, knowing— or even if he does not know— that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (one of the four *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*), conceals it, [he commits an offense].
[Note] If one knows that another has committed a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), one may speak of it after the morning meal if one learns of it after the meal;

If one learns of it until the last watch and desires to speak of it but does so before the appearance of the "characteristic marks" (*lakṣaṇa*), it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
This excludes the concealment of a grave offense for other offenses, and the concealment of one's own offense. This excludes the case of [concealment by] inference.
If a bhikṣuṇī conceals the offenses of others, it is always a *duṣkṛta* (transgression); according to the *Vinaya*, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). [Commentary:

Regarding whether a bhikṣuṇī commits the same offense or not: if she previously did not know [of the offense], or if she did not perceive it as a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), or if she speaks to someone but there is no one [to hear her], she does not commit the offense.

As previously stated, if one has already resolved to leave the household life and has already manifested the characteristics of renunciation, there is no offense even if faced with the two hardships of [losing] one's life or [losing] one's Brahmanic status.
[Commentary: The three phrases of the precept text are clear; below, the distinctions of the characteristics are analyzed in detail, without further subdividing them into separate categories.
In the first section of the separate explanation, the initial part presents the text; below this, the second sentence of the commentary contains four points:

first, clarifying the timing of the commission of the offense; second, concealing other offenses; third, self-concealment; and fourth, concealing [offenses] from those of lower standing in the assembly—hence it says, "the distinctions of the characteristics are clearly delineated," and so forth.

[Commentary]: The reason why concealing [the offenses] of others is grave while concealing one's own is light is that concealing the offenses of others is designated as grave yet the punishment is light, whereas concealing one's own is designated as light yet the punishment is grave.
Furthermore, when concealing the offenses of others, there is an original gravity; the rule was established to compel disclosure so that one may purify oneself through the precepts.

Since one’s own concealment fundamentally destroys [the integrity of the precepts], there is no need for a further regulation. Moreover, concealing the offenses of others involves three types of harm, whereas concealing one's own involves only two; therefore, it is lighter, as in the case of the *Daśa-varga*.

It is called "light" because it is auspicious; it is "heavy" because it conceals [the fault] for the duration of a day. Furthermore, the following section explains concealment based on the purity or impurity of the precept-substance (*śīla-ātmabhāva*).
