According to the Vinaya, if a bhikṣu—whether knowing it or not—confers the full ordination upon one who is less than twenty years of age, this person does not obtain the precepts.
That bhikṣu is to be rebuked for his folly; it is a pāyattika offense.

[Note] If the candidate for ordination knows that they have not reached the required age, and the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the Saṃgha likewise know this, yet among the assembly they ask, "Have you reached the age?
and the candidate replies either that they have or have not, or if they are doubtful, or do not know, or remain silent,
or if the Saṃgha does not ask— regarding these four cases, whether [the candidate] knows or is doubtful— the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense and the Saṃgha commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is claimed that there is no offense for not knowing [the transgression], yet the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) commits a *pāyattika* once the three *karmavācanās* have been completed;

or if it occurs during the interval, or while the formal motion (*jñapti*) has not yet been concluded, or when he is performing the preparatory rites, or when shaving the hair, or when the assembly of monks has gathered—the preceptor incurs a *duṣkṛta* in all such cases, and the same applies to the community of monks.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, this constitutes a *pāyattika*. There is no offense if one received the candidate in good faith without prior knowledge.
If the testimony of a bystander is given, or if one trusts the words of one's parents, or if one has doubts after receiving the precepts, the Buddha said:
"One should count the months of the pregnancy and the intercalary months; if one counts all the fourteen-day periods of the *poṣadha* as years, it is permitted when the number of years is complete."
[Commentary] The section on the *Prātimokṣa* is divided into two parts: first, establishing the rule; second, the formal text itself. It consists of three points: 1) the person; 2) knowing the year;

and 3) if the age is less than twenty, bestowing the ordination results in a *pārājika* offense. [Commentary] Regarding the first point, those whose middle age is under twenty are incapable of enduring suffering; the specific conditions are listed in full in the text.
Regarding the enumeration of items as they appear in the text within the "Explanation of the Pratimokṣa Sūtra" concerning the establishment of the rules:

there are ten matters in total. These are: (1) cold; (2) heat; (3) hunger; (4) thirst; (5) wind; (6) rain—these constitute six; (7) mosquitoes and gadflies; (8) harsh speech and suffering; (9) maintaining the precepts;
and (10) eating only one meal a day. One who can endure these ten directions is fit to receive full ordination.

[Commentary]: Regarding the reason for the censure within the *Prātimokṣa* itself: it is because the original recipient’s intention was to induce the preceptor to perform the function of bestowing the Dharma;

yet, knowing that [the requirements] were not fulfilled, they forcibly received [the precepts]. Consequently, they caused the Saṃgha the trouble of bestowing the ordination [in vain], and since there was no principle by which they could obtain them, their ignorance was extreme.
What fault could there be greater than this? Therefore, they were made to be censured.
In the first section of the main text, the initial passage describes the preceptor who is capable of receiving [the transmission]; next, it clarifies the faults of the teacher’s bestowal.
As for what constitutes a fault, the character "guo" (fault) should be pronounced with a level tone.
[Commentary: Within the analysis of the characteristics, there are also two broad categories; by reading closely and dividing them finely, they can be understood.

In the commentary on the offenses, I have provided only a brief indication; now, for the sake of detailed classification, I shall divide them into two parts: first, the *bhikṣu* saṃgha, and second, the *bhikṣuṇī* saṃgha. Regarding the first part (*bhikṣu* saṃgha), there are two sections:
first, clarifying offenses and non-offenses by means of questions and answers; second, clarifying the gravity of the offense by means of formal procedures (*karmavācanā*).

Within the first section, regarding the *bhikṛ* questioning another and their response, there are four possibilities: full and not full, which are combined with the categories of knowing, doubting, and not knowing.
Regarding the four types of silence where no question is asked, this does not constitute a formal response; this is the initial determination of the offense.

Within the two methods of formal procedure (*karmavācanā*), the first clarifies that the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) may incur either a grave or a light offense, while the subsequent section clarifies that the remaining monks invariably incur only a light offense.
[Commentary]: Regarding the non-offense, among those who have received the precepts through faith, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one should inquire even of one's parents.
If the parents do not know [the age], one should consult the birth-year register; if there is none, one should observe their physical appearance.

For a child from a wealthy and prosperous family whose physical form is large but whose years are few, one should observe whether the hands and feet are fully developed. If they still do not know, one should ask: "Under which king, in what year, was the land abundant?"

Regarding the seasons of scarcity, drought, and flood, one does not violate the first section of the middle [rules]. According to the sequence of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four steps: first, inquiring of the parents; second, examining the birth-year board.
In the royal laws of the Western Regions, whenever a son or daughter is born, their birth year is immediately recorded upon a wooden board. In this land [China], it is similar.
In antiquity it was likewise so. According to the *Zhou Li*, the Superintendent of the Population (*Siming*) maintained the census of ten thousand people;

from those who had reached the age of dentition upward, all were recorded on wooden tablets. Boys attained dentition at eight months and girls at seven months. In the present day, one must wait until reaching adulthood before being entered into the official registers.
One observes three aspects of their physical appearance and interrogates them four times regarding the era, the name of the sovereign, the reign title, and the conditions of abundance or scarcity.
Droughts and floods can both be calculated; thus, "lào" (澇) is also written as "lǎo" (潦), with the phonetic component "láo" (郎到反), meaning to be submerged or inundated by water.
[Commentary]: If one receives a subsequent doubt, one should count the months spent in the womb to clarify the signs of the opening [of the womb].
Next, the calculation for opening [the period] is explained.
[Commentary]: As the former interpretation stated, when receiving the precepts, both the secular years and the days and months are fewer;

the "opening" occurs only when the secular years are full but the days and months are not yet full. Our current interpretation states that one simply counts the months of gestation until twenty secular years are reached.
There is no offense in not completing [the full age].

Regarding the first section of the ancient [commentary], "ancient" refers to the view that one must be a full year of secular age before the calculation of years may be increased; however, our Master maintains that the increase is permitted for all who have reached the full number of calculated years.

[Commentary]: It is further stated that this country uses a calendar in which an intercalary month is added every three years by subtracting from the "small months" (deficient days) to form the intercalation;
thus, it is also inconsistent with the reduction of the "great *poṣadha*. This is not the correct theory and does not accord with common practice.

If one examines other calendrical systems, the remainder of the days (*divasāvaśeṣa*) and the remainder of the intercalations (*māsāvaśeṣa*) must be calculated separately; only after thirty-two or thirty-three months does a single intercalary month occur—how could it be restricted to every three years?
Such statements as these are merely verbal assertions.
Regarding the first of the two [points], there are four ancient traditions cited: (1) one intercalary month every three years; (2) reducing the small months to form an intercalary month;

(3) reducing the large months, which refers to taking the *bimāsa* (double-month); and (4) the method of the *poṣadha*. The latter maintains that the last two methods are not appropriate for extraction and reduction.
The phrase "simultaneously rejecting" (並下斥) constitutes a general refutation of the first point; it does not extend to a specific refutation of the intercalary months.

When examining other calendars, this refers collectively to the various schools of Yin-Yang calendrical arts and their calculations of daily remainders (*ri-yu*). The term "daily extraction and reduction" (*ri-betsu chūgen*) refers to the subtraction of days on a daily basis.

As for the phrase "not only small months," it refers to the occurrence of three or two intercalary months within a three-month period; that is, when the accumulation of months results in an intercalation, there may be a double intercalation within five years.
"How could it be that only after three years, as detailed in the subsequent text, does one finally see the error of the past?

[The Commentary] further states: "It must be that after receiving the precepts, one only then resolves their doubts; there is no room for prior resolution because of one's youth. Now, this case is also not like that opening [of the precepts].

Obtaining the precepts does not mean that the substance of the precept (śīla-skandha) is attained only when the calculation [of years] is completed; rather, it is the karma at the ordination platform itself.

Since it arises at the time of the formal motion with three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*), one knows that the accumulation of months—including intercalary months—constitutes a year; this is because the principle is based on reaching the full count. Therefore, it is said that one obtains the precepts.
Now, first calculate [the date] to ensure that one deeply understands how to maintain them without impairing the precepts.
Regarding the three cases, "that" refers to the original acceptance; if one was unaware at first and later harbors doubt, the calculation is opened.

If it was known beforehand that the number was incomplete, then it is not opened. Now, below, the error is refuted: first, it clarifies that once accepted, the calculation is opened to resolve prior doubts;
next, it clarifies that even if not yet accepted, calculating in advance is equally valid according to principle.

[Commentary: Therefore, one first consults various schools to extensively clarify the characteristics of receiving [the precepts], and only then relies upon the methods opened up in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
In the present explanation, the heading states "consulting various schools"; "consulting" (*fang*) means to investigate and seek out.

[Commentary]: In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one is under twenty years of age and considers oneself to be so, or forgets and does not know [one's age], and when the Saṃgha asks whether one has reached the full age, answers that one has, one obtains the precepts;

if one has not reached it, one does not obtain them. If one is twenty years of age, whether one knows it or not, or even if one doubts, and answers the Saṃgha that one has reached it, one obtains the precepts;
if one answers that one has not reached it, one does not obtain them. If one answers "I do not know" or expresses doubt, in all such cases [the precepts are obtained].
Regarding the offense of *duṣkṛta* incurred by the Saṃgha when conferring the precepts due to a lack of careful examination:

first, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are two responses concerning those who have not yet reached the required age; next, according to the [other] Vinayas, there are four responses concerning those who have reached the age.
Whether one obtains [the precepts] or not can be seen from this.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the case where one knows they are not yet twenty years old but answers that they are, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* explains: "Because they do not wish to receive the precepts, the ordination master forcibly confers them;

therefore, it is said they are 'not full [of years]. However, if one does not know or has forgotten, even if they answer that they are not full, they still obtain the precepts, because this follows the truth."
In the question, since he knows for himself that he is full [of years], how could the answer be that he is not full? Furthermore, if he is actually full, why would he not attain [the precepts]?
Therefore, citing the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it resolves the previous recitation.
[The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*] states: "In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one is less than twenty years old, 'full' refers to being free from offense, while 'half' refers to being not full."

Regarding the proposal that both [conditions] must be fulfilled for full ordination (*upasampadā*): if either is not met, it is not called receiving full ordination. Even if one is twenty years of age, if both conditions are not met—meaning both are incomplete—it is not called receiving full ordination.
"Both" refers to the two requirements; alternatively, it may mean that the latter takes the secular age as being twenty.
Tenth, it must be that the years of seniority (*saṃgha-ratna*) are complete; hence the term "two. This is explained in detail as follows:

being born in winter and receiving [the precepts] in winter (such as being born after the sixteenth day of the eighth month and receiving them after the sixteenth day of the eighth month in the twentieth year);

being born in spring and receiving [them] in spring (such as being born after the sixteenth day of the twelfth month and receiving them after the sixteenth day of the twelfth month in the twentieth year); and entering the *pūrvavāsa* retreat and receiving [them] during the *pūrvavāsa* retreat (such as being born after the sixteenth day of the fourth month...).

(For one born after the sixteenth day of the fourth month and receiving the precepts after the twentieth year: Receiving [the precepts] during the later retreat (*paścimā varṣā*) while born during the later retreat (e.g., for one born after the sixteenth day of the fifth month and receiving them after the sixteenth day of the twentieth year).
These four cases are all termed "incomplete" (*aparipūrṇa*) as they have not yet completed a full retreat.

If one is born in winter, or born in spring, or born during the earlier retreat (*pūrvā varṣā*), and receives [the precepts] after having completed the earlier retreat (until the tenth day of the seventh month...)

Regarding the "six cases of receiving [ordination] later": receiving after the *paścimikā* retreat (i.e., receiving after the conclusion of the *paścimikā*, from the sixteenth day of the eighth month onwards) is all termed "having completed twenty years" (referring to the completion of the twenty years of secular age).

Regarding the "completion of twenty years in both ways" (referring to the completion of the twenty years of monastic age): in the text, the first part clarifies whether one may receive it if incomplete;
"half" refers to the case where the ordination is received while half of the ten-member *saṃgha* is unaware, and thus there is no offense. This concerns the "half of the *saṃgha*."

If one commits an offense out of knowing [the rules] yet accepts them, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), though it does not obstruct the attainment of the precepts. (According to the majority view, if the number is full, one attains the precepts without doubt; according to the minority view, if the number is full in meaning, one should not attain them.

"Both" refers to when the number is not full. If the entire assembly knows this collectively, then the precepts are not attained. Even if the preceptor or the *saṃgha* has committed an offense, although it is ranked lower, next we clarify that for those who are "full," there may still be cases where they do not attain them—this refers to cases where, upon thorough investigation, they were unaware [of the deficiency], or where their subjective perception was that the number was not full, and their intention was insincere.
If one forcibly accepts [the precepts] without having received them, one incurs an offense.
[Commentary: The remaining [explanations] from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Mātṛkā* are the same as the fourfold classification in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Regarding the three types, that which is called "the remainder" refers to those such as the womb-born and moisture-born, which are the same as the fourfold classification. In the three types, the "remainder" refers to the womb-born; the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* has three, namely: the womb-born...

The intercalary month is [a matter of] the fruits of the śramaṇa (for one who has attained the dharmas superior to the fruit of arhatship attains the precepts regardless of the year). Regarding the intercalary month in the womb, it is the same; however, there is no *poṣadha*.

The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that the three positions are entirely identical. The *Commentary on the Meaning of Our Own School* says: "Although the master of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* does not maintain the fourteenth day, this is the case according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* and the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*."
[Commentary]: Now, within this text, first we count the months in the womb, then we count the intercalary months, and then we count all fourteen days as constituting a month and a year.
Next, among the four sections, the first part marks the three positions of the text; following the listing of the fourteen days, it is appropriate to add an explanation.
[The character for] "Precepts" (jie) is read here.

[Commentary: For now, let us calculate based on the minimum case: a śrāmaṇera born on the last day of the twelfth lunar month who, upon reaching twenty years of age, receives full ordination (upasaṃpadā) at dawn on the first day of the new year.
Calculating from the actual year of birth, this person would be eighteen years old when receiving the two-day [preliminary] ordination.

In the ancient methods, the first section of the masters of old required that one must be of full age according to secular reckoning before the calculation of additional years (*vassa*) could be permitted;
therefore, I shall first set forth the method of calculation based on that tradition. Subsequently, by means of that calculation, I shall demonstrate the present meaning:

on the final day of the twelfth month, one is born on the first day, which counts as one year; on the first day of the New Year’s morning, one receives [the precepts], and that single day of reception counts as one year within the term.

Eighteen months [in the intermediate state] corresponds to twenty years in common reckoning; even calculating from the shortest possible duration, there remains an additional five days, let alone those who exceed this. [Commentary:

Next, regarding the calculation of the period in the womb, the reception of the vital breath is not fixed, as in the case of Rāhula, who underwent the suffering of birth and death for six years, or the bhikṣu who remained in the womb for six years.

There are also cases where one is born after being in the womb for ten months plus five days; however, these cannot be taken as the standard rule. Generally, according to the scriptures of both the clergy and the laity, [a fetus] remains in the womb for nine months.
As stated in the *Pañcarājopama-sūtra*, the fetus undergoes a transformation once every seven days; thus, it becomes a fully formed human after forty-nine days (seven times seven).
In total, there are thirty-eight such transformations, each lasting seven days, which amounts to a total of two hundred and sixty-six days.
For six days prior to this, his vital energy was the same as that of his mother; for the subsequent four days, as he was about to emerge from birth, his vital energy became distinct from hers.
Calculating by the standard lunar month, this amounts to nine months and four days; including the preceding eighteen years, it totals eighteen years, nine months, and six days.
Next, within the section on the method of entering the womb (*garbhāvakrānti*), first it is shown that [the timing] is indefinite;

Rāhula was conceived when the Buddha entered the mountains and born when he attained enlightenment. Regarding the suffering of birth and death, the Bhikṣu—namely the Venerable Pārśva—was already white-haired at birth.
Below this, there are two major sections based on certainty, and further, three parts: first, the general indication; below this, the enumeration of the five.

The *Rājanīti-sūtra* states that the Buddha spoke this for the sake of the five kings: regarding the formation of the human being over seven times seven days, on the first seven days it is like thin curd;
on the second seven days, like thick curd; on the third seven days, like solidified butter; on the fourth seven days, like a soft lump of flesh; on the fifth seven days, like a firm lump of flesh;
on the sixth seven days, the five swellings open out; and after the seventh seven days, the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are fully complete. Thus it is said.
Up until the thirty-eighth seven-day period, there is a wind that blows upon the embryo every seven days, causing it to gradually transform;

thus it is called "turning. As explained in detail in the *Dàodì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Path), thirty such turnings amount to two hundred ten days, and eight turnings amount to fifty-six days;
when combined with the four additional days for the separate vital energies (*vāyu*), the total is two hundred and seventy days.
Thus, within nine months there are four small intercalary months (small *kṣaya* days), leaving a remainder of four days; these, together with the three [days] below, total the aforementioned number.

[Commentary]: Next, regarding the method for calculating intercalation: in the secular calculation of intercalary days, one separately sets aside a remainder of one thousand six hundred from the total.
When the accumulated intercalary months reach three dozen (thirty-six) or thirty-three months, they complete one intercalary cycle;
this cannot be fully described, but roughly speaking, nineteen years constitute a *zhāng* (a major period), within which there are seven intercalary months.
Thus, there is one intercalary month every three years, and in some five-year cycles there are two, making a total of seven. This accounts for the preceding ten [years].
On the sixth day of the ninth month of the eighth year, two months were lacking; on the twenty-fourth day, it was not yet nineteen years.

There should have been six months and twenty-seven days of intercalary months included within the preceding nineteen years, reaching back to the third day of the fourth month. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"From what point is a year counted? It is counted from the mother's womb, including all intercalary months."

Next, in the section on intercalation, the initial description of the method of intercalation refers to what is called the "secular" system, namely the various schools of Yin-Yang calendrical systems.
Regarding the daily remainder (*riyu*), this means that each day consists of thirty-two *fen* (units);
the first and last days of the month are fixed, while the twenty-eight days in between have a daily remainder of half a *fen* because the sun's motion is rapid. Thus, over one month...
The remaining twenty-eight half-months constitute fourteen parts; together with the minor omitted days (*kṣayadina*), they collectively total sixteen hundred intercalary units.
As for the "external" [units], they are not yet detailed and await consultation with a master of calculation (*gaṇaka*). Regarding the accumulation of thirty-two months:
each month yields fourteen parts, so thirty-two months together yield four hundred and forty-eight parts. [Using three...]
One hundred and twenty units constitute ten days, and one hundred and twenty-eight units constitute four days;
together these amount to fourteen days. Furthermore, in three twelve-month periods, there is one half-month of a short month, which amounts to sixteen days.
When added to the above, this makes thirty days; thus, one intercalary month is obtained. Alternatively, in thirty-three months, one again obtains half a day, but—
Because there are occasional major [intercalary] months within the minor and medium periods, the number of days is not fixed. To provide a general illustration of the calculation method:
there are three instances of an intercalary month every three years, namely at the beginning, middle, and end;

and there are two instances of an intercalary month every five years, specifically in the two intervals. Calculating over ten years, this amounts to one full cycle less two months and twenty-four days.
Combining the three days obtained by extraction with the remaining days, one obtains four *śata-bhāga*s (fortieth parts) of a day, which amounts to one day and eight *bhāga*s.

Since there is a minor intercalary month (*kṣaya-māsa*), this corresponds to one additional day; thus, rather than being unable to obtain three days as previously deducted, because the six months and twenty-seven days extracted have a remainder, it is said that "there should be" [an extra day].
This concludes the general synthesis below, while the section following "Ga" provides scriptural evidence.

[Commentary: Next, regarding the calculation of the *piṇḍa* (intercalary) months, there are no textual records in the various Vinayas; however, the calendars of this region do contain such calculations.

If one were to calculate them, the small months would increase excessively, and how could there be seven small months in a year? How then could they be subtracted from the large months? The *poṣadha* is used to complete the year, yet it does not exist [as a formal category] in accordance with the Dharma.
For the time being, following what we have studied, let us attempt a brief calculation.
Regarding the second [section], "Frequent and Great," within the first part: first, it indicates what is produced; next, it clarifies that which is irrational.
There are seven minor sections, but only five major ones. Below, the classification takes up six major points. Regarding the *poṣadha*, there are certain inconveniences;

furthermore, below, the method of calculation is presented in accordance with those who study, meaning it is the instruction bestowed by the teacher. Because these methods of calculation all appear in the *Shoushu* (Initial Commentary), they are thus recorded in the *Yichao* (Explanatory Notes).
This refers to the initial heading and its explanation.
[Commentary]: This generally sets forth the method by which the preceding years total two hundred thirty-two months, with three "great intercalations" (da) occurring every three days;
forty-nine months constitute one chapter, and each chapter contains three great intercalations. In the first two periods of seventeen months, there is one great intercalation each; subsequently...

Every fifteen months there is one "great" [intercalary] day; thus, as the cycle repeats, using the previous one hundred and ninety-six months, four chapters are formed, each consisting of three days, totaling twelve days.
The remaining thirty-six months yield two further "frequent" great days, sufficient to complete fourteen days.
When calculated together with the previous period, this totals nineteen years, four months, and seventeen days.
Next, regarding the initial section: extending years into months under the "Frequent Great Dharma" (頻大法) correctly demonstrates the method of calculation.

Forty-nine months constitute one chapter; each chapter consists of three "frequent great months. Once a chapter is complete, it returns to the beginning once more, revolving and connecting in succession;
hence it is said that "it cycles and begins again," etc., which summarizes the total count below.

[Commentary: Next, calculating by taking fourteen days for a *poṣadha* as one year without an intercalary month, and according to the standard where half-months are small or large, there are eighteen major *poṣadhas*.
Subtracting eighteen days, the total calculation over nineteen years yields three hundred and forty-eight days.
If twenty-eight days are taken as a month, this amounts to three hundred and thirty-six days.
One day constitutes one year; with twelve remaining days within the intercalary period of Ti-pin and seventeen residual days, this completes one month.
Counting from the preceding total, it amounts to the first day of the fifth month in the twentieth year.
Regarding the three *poṣadha* periods, first it clarifies that the method for determining the dates applies generally to the subsequent ones;
next, it demonstrates the calculation by deducting one month from the total, leaving only twenty-eight days. Therefore, the calculation presented here is based on these twenty-eight days:
the twelfth and seventeenth days together account for twenty-nine days, leaving twenty-eight [for the remainder].
Because one day constitutes one month, when this single day is added to the preceding period, it totals one year; when added to the preceding period, it becomes twenty years.
When one month and one day are added to the preceding four months, they become five months and one day.
[Commentary]: Calculating this, twenty full years are equivalent to twenty years plus five months and one day. [Commentary]:

Now, if there is a śrāmaṇera who was born at the end of the twelfth month and is nineteen years old, and receives the precepts in the eighth month, they may take the first day of the fifth month as the starting point to complete the twenty years; this is also permissible.

Next, regarding the first category within the current system: those who have reached nineteen years of age by the end of the twelfth month (the *laba* month) are those for whom both the year and the month are not yet complete.
To "connect" them with the first day of the fifth month means that they intend to receive the precepts in the eighth month;
however, because their age actually becomes full in the seventh month, one uses the calculation of the "excessive" days to connect them, treating them as being eighteen years and two days old.
It is said that one may calculate based on a twenty-year period; this need not necessarily be in terms of actual secular years, as it must be fulfilled. Thus, it is said that "it is also permissible.
This is merely borrowing those "empty days" as a method of calculation; when it comes to the subsequent filling in, one adjusts downward according to the actual [days].
[Commentary: However, these five months have all been subject to reduction through the accumulated method for forming the month; according to actual reality, they are thus deficient.

Since one intends to receive the precepts in the eighth month, the preceding month has not yet arrived and was originally not permitted [to be omitted]. How can it be arbitrarily abbreviated? Now, it must be restored by filling it back in. How is this done?
Within the five months, seven days are deducted from each of the seven *poṣadha* assemblies, and further, the weak remainder of the intercalary month is deducted.
Five days were further reduced, and the frequent, great weakness lasted for half a day; totaling the days reduced by weakness amounts to thirteen days.
Subtracting these from the previous period of five months and one day, in reality, only four months and eighteen days remain.

Next, in the initial section of this rubric, the intention is stated: since the previous month has not yet arrived—that is, the seven months of the novice period have only just been completed and the eighth month has not yet begun—the month is not yet present;
therefore, it is said that [the reduction] was originally not permitted. Since the meaning requires the period to be fully satisfied, how could one arbitrarily abbreviate it?
Below, the method for making up the deficiency is explained: on the first day of the fifth month, one actually proceeds from the tenth day of the fourth month.
The eighth day was drawn out on the thirteenth; now, by filling in that very thirteenth day, the actual number is restored.
First, calculating the *poṣadha* days for the fourth month, there are two large months and two small months, which yields six days;
adding one day from the middle of the eighteenth day, they total seven days. Next, restoring the intercalary remainder, there are six days remaining from the four months and the eighteenth day.
In fifteen parts, one obtains two days; within this, there are two small intercalary months (*kṣayamāsa*), which together amount to four days and one part of a day.
Since this does not yet constitute five full days, it is considered "weak. (The Ancient Record states: "In one month, fourteen parts shall constitute one day;

that five days are obtained in five months are all 'weak' gains—since thirty-two parts already do not even constitute half a day, how could they constitute a full day? Furthermore, these five months are themselves empty months; how can one say that five days are obtained in five months? Now...)

Regarding the "Weak Attainment" (*nyūjaku toku*): taking four days and dividing them into one hundred twenty-nine parts and five-fifths, breaking them down results in twenty-six parts for one day, though it lacks one part. As for the three cycles of the "Great *Bimbin*" (*hindaibō*):
with the Great *Bimbin* method, it takes about one and a half years to reach one day, and only after seven or eight months does one attain half [a day].
Today is the eighteenth day of the fourth month; since it is not yet half a day old, it is considered weak. Calculating the total, there are thirteen days;
however, even including the half-day of the frequent "great weakness," it should still count as one full day.
In reality, only eleven days and some ten odd *fen* (minutes) have been obtained. This is why, in the *Chao*, only eleven days are returned until the tenth day of the eighth month is reached.
Regarding the present agreement, one receives much more than was originally due; however, when returning what has been withdrawn, one must ensure that the increased amount is paid out.
Thus, even if the calculation based on the *Chao* (Commentary) results in a shortfall of two days, one must expand upon it as extensively as possible.

As for the actual date of the fourteenth day of the fourth month, once the repayment has been settled and the calculation completed, one must immediately reduce the total; this is the essential point.
This statement means that, according to the actual calculation of the eighteen years and two days by the ancient masters of former times, it corresponds to the fourteenth day of the fourth month;
whereas, according to the conventional calculation, it corresponds to the first day of the fifth month.
[Commentary]: According to this, for one born at the end of the year who has reached nineteen years of age, they should be permitted to receive [the precepts] on the twelfth day of the eighth month;
however, if the intercalary months fall frequently, they may receive them on the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month.
Among the three [methods], the first indicates the current fixed limit: from the day of birth until the end of life, one day is treated as one year;
thus, for one who received the precepts at eighteen years and eight months, the actual duration is seventeen years plus seven months and thirteen days.
Based on this actual number, one should calculate correctly using the four categories, including the fetal period and intercalary months.
If one has reached twenty years of age, the month of birth need not necessarily be fixed; it is sufficient to take this as the standard and calculate according to the individual.

Once the time is full, one is fit to receive the precepts without further doubt. As for the subsequent instruction regarding the frequency of the ceremony, the previous statement that "it should not be retained" was made because it was not what was opened up by the orthodox teaching, fearing that doubts might arise; therefore, both versions have been presented. If...

However, if one does not apply this [correction], fourteen days must be added to the actual year; thus, it is only on the twenty-sixth day that one is permitted to receive [the precepts]. (An ancient record states:

"On the eighteenth day of the fourth month, fourteen days are subtracted from the 'frequent large' [days]. Now, we ask: since the 'frequent large' days are already included within the total count of 'large' days, why would they be subtracted on the eighteenth day of the fourth month?
This contains a grave error, which we shall not cite here for fear of prolixity.)

[Commentary: Regarding the specific characteristics within this context, those who still harbor doubts take the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) as a definitive example of "not being fulfilled.
Among the four [types of calculation], there is still fear that one might cling to the old secular reckoning of years as not yet complete; thus it says, "those who still harbor doubts.
Even if one suspects they are not yet fulfilled, there are clear precedents; therefore, the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is cited as previously quoted.
[Commentary]: Some rely on the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* to calculate the actual lunar months as nineteen years; however, following the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this accords with secular reckoning.
As stated in the "Six Dharmas for Bhikṣuṇīs": "An eighteen-year-old girl studies the precepts for two years; when she reaches twenty, she receives full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Based on this, being eighteen does not necessarily mean the year has fully elapsed; reaching the morning of one's eighteenth year constitutes the completion of the age.

If one receives the six *dharmas* immediately upon following the instructions at eighteen, and only then begins the two-year study at nineteen—how could one not be twenty on the first day of the new year the following year?
Following this precedent, even for the youngest possible case, if one receives the *dharma* at the end of the year, that single day shall count as a full year;
thus, when one fully practices the next year and receives the full ordination on the first day of the first month, how could one not be twenty?

If it were not so, one would have to wait until reaching eighteen or nineteen at the beginning of the year to receive the six dharmas, and only at age twenty the following year could one begin training for one year;
once that year of training was completed, one would have to wait until the next year, at age twenty-one, to finally receive full ordination.

Furthermore, since there is no scriptural authority (*vinaya*) for such a prolonged delay, we know that the common secular age must be used as the definitive standard. As for the other textual passages [that suggest otherwise], they are merely explanatory elaborations.
By what means could it be exhausted?
Regarding the first of the five [points], he cites that false attachment from the *Mahā-śāstra*, which states:

"Because it is not truly fulfilled up to nineteen years, it is therefore not opened" (meaning that if it is not fulfilled at nineteen, one may receive [the precepts] once it is fulfilled). That [text] claims that nineteen refers to actual months.

This corresponds to twenty years according to secular reckoning. Now, taking an example from below to refute [the objection] and establish the meaning of receiving [the precepts] at nineteen secular years in the eighth month:
the first two phrases provide a general indication based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

As for "being the same as the secular," this means that when discussing age in secular society, one also takes the span of time across the months rather than counting only the actual months, as follows:

The citation of examples is further divided into two parts: first, presenting textual evidence and showing the number of years below; second, first, establishing the present meaning by reconciling overlapping dates with the teachings, stating "if it were not so" and so forth;
next, demonstrating the errors of the past by contrasting actual months with the texts, stating "therefore" and so forth;
finally, determining the remaining points based on these, and pointing to the extensive details below.
[Vinaya] Sixty-six precepts on the arousal of the four types of disputes.
[Commentary] There are sixty-six precepts concerning the arousal of disputes.

[Commentary] Whenever the four types of disputes arise, they deviate from principle, violate the Dharma, and disturb the monastic community; since these matters must certainly be extinguished, it is necessary [to establish these rules].

When one’s virtues are fully prepared and one’s disposition is measured, such that the monastic community is settled and at peace, it is only then that one may cultivate the path and its practices. Now, you have suddenly incited [conflict], further increasing its ferocity;

by assisting evil and fanning the flames, you have caused it to spread until it has ruined the assembly and vexed the monks—this is the gravest of transgressions, and therefore this rule is established.

In the first section of the sixty-sixth rule concerning the governance of the mind, it is stated that the four types of disputes have already been extinguished: *vāda* (contention over principles) refers to that which deviates from reason; *adhikaraṇa* (legal dispute) refers to that which violates the Dharma;

and *anuvāda* (accusation regarding an offense) refers to the three types of disputes being brought to an end. This constitutes "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*). It is called "possessing virtue" (*guṇavat*) because it pertains to a person of virtue.

"Measuring the situation" (*pramāṇa*) means observing the minds of the assembly. "Peaceful settlement" (*samatha*) means bringing about harmony so that [disputes] cease. *Samatha* is composed of *sama* and *tha*; *tha* is glossed as "tranquility" (*śānti*).
Next, the following passage further clarifies the metaphor of the rising waves to illustrate how assisting in evil is like the wind stirring the water;
as the waves surge and toss, they become increasingly vast and pervasive—*mi* (瀰) being a term describing the appearance of great waters spreading far and wide.

[Commentary: There are five conditions for committing an offense: first, there must be one of the four types of disputes; second, the Saṃgha has extinguished it in accordance with the Dharma; third, one knows it has been extinguished in accordance with the Dharma;
fourth, one initiates [the dispute] again; and fifth, the words are completed and the offense is finalized.
The conditions for the offense are easily understood.
[Note: While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, after the legal settlement of a dispute involving the group of six monks, they subsequently re-ignited the conflict.
Because a bhikṣu reported their transgression to the Buddha, he established this precept.

【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu, knowing that a legal dispute (of which there are four types: disputes concerning speech, disputes concerning investigation, disputes concerning offenses, and disputes concerning matters) has been settled according to the Dharma through confession in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, should raise it again, he commits a pāyattika offense.
(If he did not know [that it was settled], and it was settled according to the Dharma, there is no offense.)

[Note] To speak indistinctly constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Excluding this dispute, if one initiates other forms of quarreling or verbal abuse, or if such quarreling has already been initiated and one further incites it—whether involving two groups or other persons—one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense in all such cases. Regarding what constitutes a non-offense:
if one did not previously know [the facts], or if one perceived something as such while intending it to be so, or if the matter was indeed as stated but the speech was improper, there is no offense.
If one speaks out of observation, jesting, or error, there is no offense.

[Commentary]: The four phrases of the precept text are: (1) a person; (2) the four types of disputes, which distinguish these from other quarrels that cannot undermine the Saṃgha; (3) resolving them in accordance with the Dharma;
and (4) the formal conclusion of the proceedings.

Regarding the second section of the *Prātimokṣa*, the remaining disputes cannot undermine the Saṃgha because the four types of dispute must be extinguished through the legal procedures (*dharmakarma*) of the Saṃgha;

however, if they are repeatedly raised and brought forward, this constitutes undermining the Saṃgha. Among these four, "initiation" (*utthāna*) refers to the fault of the action (*karmavastu*), while "binding" (*saṃyojana*) refers to the characteristic of the offense (*āpatti-lakṣaṇa*).

[Commentary]: To speak of "repentance according to the Dharma" (yathādharma-pratikarma) refers precisely to the expression of mutual apology. It follows the precedent of two parties apologizing to each other while facing the ground, as if covering it with grass.
It need not necessarily involve actual offenses; disputes that are not offenses may also involve offenses.
In superior cases, such as when grass covers mud, disputes over offenses are extinguished together. This will be explained further below.

In the commentary, the first section has two explanations. First, the explanation based on the mutual cessation of conflict: regarding the case where two factions dispute over covering the ground with grass, the strife persists for years and is difficult to extinguish;
however, when a person of virtue performs the ritual, the two assemblies face one another and both prostrate themselves in submission.

Taking this as an example, in all other cases of settling disputes, the meaning necessarily involves mutual cessation. This clarifies that the term "repentance" (*sāṃghāvaśeṣa*) in the text does not mean...

Because one confesses offenses, it is said that "not necessarily" there is an offense; for among the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), when seeking the transgression, two disputes may involve an offense—namely, disputes regarding teachings and principles (*dharma-vivāda*) and disputes regarding formal procedures (*karma-vivāda*). Thus, it is also possible that there is no offense. Next, regarding the confession of offenses, the "dispute involving an offense" refers to the dispute of an actual transgression (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*);
specifically, a grave transgression (*uttarimanuṣya-dharma*) is extinguished through the *tṛṇastāraka-vinaya* (the method of covering over with grass).
As with offenses regarding grass or mud, there is the principle of repentance for transgressions; this will be explained extensively in the subsequent section, and is therefore referred to here.

[Commentary] Regarding the category of non-offenses: "if one observes the action but does not observe the perception," "observing" means to deeply penetrate the medicine and the illness, as well as their arising and ceasing.

Regarding the method: those who now raise a dispute do not know that it has been settled according to the Dharma, and they claim it was settled contrary to the Dharma; therefore, they raise it immediately without offense.
For the most part, there is no need for further explanation.
In the commentary on the next section, first the minor offenses are listed; once a dispute has been raised, others assist in raising it because of that dispute. The rest [is as follows].
"Dispute" refers to the three lower assemblies; next, regarding "not committing [an offense]," first, "not knowing" excuses those who are confused or forgetful.

Regarding "observing" and "not observing," this refers to a discrepancy in perception (*saṃjñā-viparyaya*). In the commentary (*śū*), only the phrase "discrepancy in perception" is explained. First, the text cites the passage; then, the meaning is explained below.
First, the character "observing" (*guan*) above is explained as the person capable of resolving [the dispute], who extinguishes it according to the Dharma. Now, below...
Next, regarding the explanation of "not contemplating": this refers to the actual opening [of the precept] for those who incite disputes;
the rest are not explained here as they are already covered by the preceding and following annotations. [Vinaya] Precept 67: The Precept on Agreeing to Travel with Thieves.
[Commentary: The precept regarding traveling with bandits is the sixty-seventh.
[Commentary: Severing depravity and prohibiting what is improper is the law of kings; since one knows these individuals are bandits, it is right to avoid them in secret. How can one travel together?
Their conduct is the same, yet their hardships differ, which invites censure and ruins the Way. Because this is a grave matter, the rule must be established.

67. Regarding the formulation of the precept, the first part describes the nature of the fraudulent intent; the subsequent section reveals the characteristics of the offense, showing that it is difficult to distinguish from other cases because the person cannot be identified.

[Commentary] The offense is established through six conditions: first, the thief; second, knowing [the person is a thief]; third, a mutual agreement; fourth, traveling together on the same path; fifth, not departing [from the group].
Regarding the six transgressions involving crossing boundaries through seeing or hearing:
the circumstances for these six offenses are both found in the commentaries on the Sūtras. [Note:
When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a large number of bhikṣus arrived at Vaiśālī; some merchants there crossed the customs barrier by private means and did not pay the toll.
A king’s tax collector, traveling with a bhikṣu, was seized by a border guard and taken before the king; the offense merited death.
The king censured the bhikṣu in secular terms, and the bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established this precept.

In the context of dependent origination, if merchants cross a frontier pass without paying the king’s tax, they are equivalent to thieves; it should be understood accordingly that violating the precept does not necessarily require actual robbery.

[Vinaya] If a bhikṣu knows—or even if he does not know—that he has entered into an agreement with a bandit (whether the bandits have already returned from their raid or are about to depart) to act together as accomplices, [he commits an offense]. (If he did not know, or if no such agreement was made, there is no offense.)

Regarding the "path" (the essential point being any path leading to a city or a village, including every path between villages): [if one travels] even as far as one village interval, it is a *pāyattika*.
[Note] If one travels from village to village along various paths until reaching a single path, one commits an offense;

if one travels ten *li* together through a desolate, uninhabited area where no boundaries exist, one commits an offense. If one travels half-way between villages, less than ten *li*, within a village, or makes a prior agreement for the journey but does not go, all such cases constitute a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
This applies equally to both [the teacher and the disciple]. As for those who do not commit an offense: if...
If one proceeds step by step with stability toward a destination, and if it is due to the power of fate, Brahma, or forceful compulsion, there is no offense.

[Commentary] The five phrases of the root text are: first, the person; second, the thief; third, the mutual agreement; fourth, traveling together on the same path; fifth, the determination of the offense.
The detailed explanation of these characteristics can be understood from the full commentary.

In the second sentence of the separate explanation (*pṛthag-vyākhyāna*), the commentary notes that when two parties—one who has already returned and one who intends to go—meet, they both incur an offense regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
"Meeting" (*saṃgama*) refers to their coming together. The note states that "reaching the city" refers to the designated destination, while "village road" refers to the path traversed;

it is by meeting at these points that the offense is incurred. For a detailed analysis of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one should consult the initial explanation provided within the subsequent commentary.

In a village setting, because an offense is determined by the boundaries of the settlement, the conditions for the rule state that "transgressing the boundary constitutes an offense," which corresponds to the precept regarding traveling with a nun;
this applies according to the extent of the various divisions, and one falls into an offense for each individual boundary. Next, it clarifies the case of no village:
since there are no boundaries, a limit of ten *li* is established. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
[Vinaya] Precept 68: Proclaiming that desire does not obstruct the Path and thereby defying the admonitions of the Saṃgha.
[Commentary] Precept 68: Proclaiming that desire is not an obstruction to the Path and thereby defying the admonitions of the Saṃgha.
[Commentary] There are three intentions behind the formulation [of this rule].
First, regarding why the Vinaya does not permit it: desire as a source of affliction is precisely the root of birth and death and the central obstacle to the Path.
Since one can speak of it with the mouth yet inevitably act upon it with the body, one becomes submerged in the ocean of desire, never finding the way out; thus, it constitutes an obstruction.

Because it is profound, it is established as a precept. Regarding the first of the sixty-eight intentions for establishing the precepts, there are two parts. First, to demonstrate that desire is the root of birth and death, by which one revolves in saṃsāra;
thus, it obstructs the source of the Path, and there will be no time of liberation. Having explained this, next follows the clarification of why the precept must be established.
Reversing those two afflictions: first, severing birth and death; second, entering the Noble Path. [Commentary:
The second interpretation explains the intent of the admonition: because it was spoken for the sake of laypeople, it states that one's own wife is not an obstacle to improper conduct.

Relying upon this teaching, some have claimed that practicing desire while ordained does not constitute an obstacle. Since such verbal expressions and their actual reality are difficult to distinguish, the Saṃgha must establish [the rule].

Admonishing them to clarify their intentions so that they may comprehend the intent behind the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings— hoping thereby to lead them to abandon delusion, cast off evil, and embrace the good,
so that the heterodox and the orthodox are distinguished and right and wrong are made clearly distinct— the method of admonition was established.

Next, one must admonish their intent. The initial explanation has two parts: first, it shows that the teachings for engaging with the mundane world—which rely on [merit] and lead toward goodness—are for the purpose of generating merit;

therefore, they do not obstruct the correct renunciation for the sake of the Path, which requires the simultaneous severing of both [afflictions and merit] to give rise to wisdom and eliminate delusions.

How can one conflate these and speak [of them as identical]? Second, it clarifies the establishment of admonitions by distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox: what they teach is heterodox, whereas the Buddha’s teaching is orthodox.

[This] is correct. [Commentary: Another interpretation states: "Desire" refers to that which is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*). Where, then, is the meaning of "excessive" (*prasaṅga*) to be applied? The Noble Ones distinguish between the obstructions to the Path (*mārga-āvaraṇa*) and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) according to their strength and weakness.

Those of the highest grade obstruct the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while those of the lowest grade obstruct the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Therefore, although one has attained the first fruit (*phala*) through the Path, desire still remains.
The *Vastusamgrahaṇī* cites this scriptural passage to state that [the afflictions] do not constitute obstacles; while the words are the same, the meaning differs.

Therefore, it is necessary to list the scriptural authority stating they are not obstacles, because the categories of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are distinct, and they are eliminated by their respective antidotes. Since the obstacles specific to each stage are removed, these are not what is severed here.

Thus, there are those that are not obstacles for me, which does not mean they do not obstruct others. If one develops a profound understanding of this, the afflictions of such conceptualization will be exhausted.
Now, there is a persistent attachment to the general statement that "the nature of desire is not an obstacle," yet the divergent paths of the heterodox and the orthodox rest upon this very principle;
thus, the Saṃgha must provide admonition to reveal what is right and what is wrong.

Next, in the commentary, the first two phrases pose a question: because these [actions] are coarse, evil, and indiscriminately confused, they have no basis for being established—hence it says, "How can [it be so]? (安).
In the section "Pointing Out the Nature of Attachment," there are three parts: first, identifying the characteristics of confusion; second, clarifying the reason for partiality and attachment;

and third, concluding with the necessity of admonition. Regarding the first part, when the Sage distinguishes those who obstruct the Path, he does so specifically in terms of the four fruits [of the śramaṇa].

As for the statement that "the fetters have strength and weakness," "fetters" (saṃyojana) refers to the underlying tendencies (anuśaya); they are not limited to ten types, as greed is included among them.

The five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśāḥ*)—anger, ignorance, pride, doubt, and the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśāḥ*)—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—these ten are called "afflictions of insight" (*darśana-heya*) because they obstruct the vision of the truths. They are termed "coarse" and "strong" because they are of the highest grade.

Furthermore, the four [remaining] afflictions, beginning with greed (*rāga*), which obstruct meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), are called "afflictions of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*). They are termed "subtle" and "weak" because they are of the lowest grade. First...

Although the fruit [of the first stage] merely destroys the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), because the defilement of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) has not yet been extinguished, it is said that "one still possesses desire.

Only from the second fruit onward does one sever the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), and only upon reaching the fourth fruit can one truly become free from desire. As stated in the *Saṃghīti*, the two nuns Sūṣā and Susīlā experienced pleasure while being violated;

furthermore, according to the Vinaya, even those in the family of those who have realized the Truth (*dṛṣṭasatya-kuṭumbika*) still have husbands and wives, and there are also those at the first fruit who still possess lustful thoughts.

"Because they arise, they abandon the precepts and return home; desiring to be satiated, they return again," and so forth. This means that those [who claim] the sages who have attained the Way still engage in sensual desires do so to demonstrate that such acts do not constitute an obstruction;
thus, this false statement was raised. As for the necessity of listing [these points], it serves to introduce the subsequent text.

Second, explaining the reason: the words of the Sage state that [desire] is not an obstruction. This refers back to the preceding passages. "The methods of cultivation differ" refers specifically to the severance [of afflictions] and the realization [of the fruits].

Because this wisdom has degrees of depth, the shallow cuts through coarse evils while the deep removes subtle obstructions; thus it is said they are "antagonistic. Regarding "removing what pertains to its own level":

as with the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one can only remove [the afflictions of] views but cannot yet sever [those of] cultivation; therefore, it is said that these are distinct from what is not to be severed.

As for "there being obstructions that are not the self," this refers to those who possess volitional activity; provided they are merely able not to obstruct the views pertaining to their own level, [they are not considered obstacles].
The Path is not without obstacles, for one has not yet realized the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);

it is only when profound understanding arises that one enters the Path of Cultivation, continuing until the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*), which is why it is said that "delusions and thoughts are exhausted. This serves as a counter-illumination to clarify that defiled desires obstruct the Path; this is evident.

Below, the text correctly demonstrates that what is "relied upon" or "confused with" is generally stated to be non-obstructive, which is not like the previous detailed distinction. Thus, the two views regarding the "false" and the "correct" arise.
Because this arises from that, it is said that "the principle resides herein. The third [point] concludes the demonstration; it may be understood accordingly. [Private Commentary:
Many Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras contain such expressions. For example, the *Acaranga-sūtra* (Wuxing jing) states: "Lust is itself the Way; so too are anger and delusion.
Within these three dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas are complete. This points to the meaning that delusion is itself reality (*tathatā*), thereby causing one to...
To return to the source: those who lecture in this world claim that while the Hinayana constitutes an obstacle to the Path through desire, the Mahayana does not obstruct anything at all.
Thus they gloss over their own depraved conduct to deceive and entice later generations, leading immeasurable people into the Avīci Hell.
By slandering the sutras and reviling the sages, they have no hope of escape and delude the masses for all time; in accordance with the principle of justice, they deserve this punishment.

[Commentary]: Third, the intent behind the formal determination of the offense: Since the Saṃgha has already established the method of admonition and the characteristics of the situation are manifest, yet [the monk] stubbornly clings to his delusion and refuses to follow the exhortation, thereby openly defying the command of the Saṃgha, it is appropriate to determine a *pāyattika* (offense of falling) for him.
Among the three types of formal offenses (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), stubbornly persisting in opposition to the Saṃgha constitutes a fault of the mind;

therefore, an offense must be established. [Commentary] There are five conditions for committing this offense: first, a person with evil views; second, having already offered private admonition; third, not accepting the private admonition;
fourth, the Saṃgha performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) according to the Dharma; and fifth, the commission of the offense upon the third such instance of opposition.

Regarding the first condition for the offense, although it is categorized under "wrong views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the specific term "evil" (*akuśala*) is used here to distinguish this particular transgression.
[Note: While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, Ariṣṭa gave rise to an evil view and said, "I know that the Buddha’s teaching is such that practicing sexual intercourse does not obstruct the path.

Although the bhikṣus admonished him with parables, he still did not abandon it. He informed the Buddha, who, after he had made his own declaration, ordered the Saṃgha to perform the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations).
He rebuked him as he was offering this admonition and established the precept.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, because the disciple of the Tīrthika Liṭa was exceptionally intelligent, he was sent into the Buddha’s Dharma with the intent to cause confusion and disorder.
However, that person soon mastered the Tripiṭaka; thus, when he attempted to subvert the teachings, his wisdom and eloquence were exhausted, and he could not succeed in establishing [his own views].

Among the conditions concerning the precepts, those who promote confusion and disorder seek to destroy the True Dharma. Although the Buddha’s worldly teachings were powerful, even when people possessed the wisdom of ultimate knowledge, they did not believe or accept them;
thus, they could not prevail. In the final age, however, Māras are strong and, conversely, many people place their trust in them, leading to the destruction of the orthodox teaching.
Tracing back from the present to the past, is this not to be lamented?

【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu speaks thus: "I know that the Dharma taught by the Buddha states that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path," that bhikṣu should be admonished by the others, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One. It is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One did not say such a thing. The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, has declared that committing sexual misconduct is an offense."

Sensual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path. When a bhikṣu admonishes another bhikṣu regarding this matter, if the latter persists and does not relinquish it, the former bhikṣu may admonish him up to three times to cause him to relinquish that matter.
If he relinquishes it after two or three admonitions, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a pāyattika. (The offense for a bhikṣuṇī is the same as for the saṃgha;
the rest is as in the *Pravāraṇā-sthāpana-śikṣāpada*, with the exception that the name of the offense is adjusted according to the rank.)
[Commentary: Regarding the seven phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* (Sūtra of Precepts), they are as explained above;

the difference lies in the name of the offense, which is categorized under the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Residual Offenses). Within the seven phrases of the *Prātimokṣa*, "as in the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa*" refers to three pairs and one single case.
The matter of the admonition—beginning with "if the person being admonished by a bhikṣu speaks as follows"—is the first pair. That bhikṣu then offers this admonition:

First pair: When a bhikṣu privately advises another against violating the Buddha’s word, and that person, because their karma is heavy and their obstacles are deep, does not abandon [the misconduct] despite the advice, this is unwholesome;
thus, the second pair concerns rejecting private advice when a bhikṣu firmly persists in it. Third pair:

When a bhikṣu—even down to the lowest members of the Saṃgha—performs a formal act of admonition and the person still does not abandon [the misconduct], this is rejecting the admonition of the Saṃgha. Thus, the third pair.
The offense is also defined as a *pācittiya*. The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) notes that this refers back to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* [offense], indicating the relative gravity of the offenses.
[Vinaya] Rule 69: The Precept on Following the Suspension of a Bhikṣu.
[Commentary]: The precept against associating with those of wrong views (the sixty-ninth). [Commentary]:

There are three reasons for the formulation of this rule, of which one must be cited. However, this bhikṣu erroneously clings to the teachings of the Holy One, asserting that sensual desire is not an obstacle;
he defies the three admonitions of the Saṃgha and stubbornly persists in his refusal to relinquish his perverted mind, thereby creating an obstacle on the path of training within the Buddha-dharma.

Because there is nothing therein that can be increased or benefited, it is necessary to raise up and discard the mind of dualistic attachment to views; if one does not raise up and treat it, there will never be a reforming of faults or repentance.

To follow the good, the Sangha must collectively raise up [the offender] and impose the "thirty-five matters" of harsh discipline as punishment, subduing both body and mind so that they may reflect, believe, and reform their faults.
This brings the benefit of entering the Path, and because it accords with human sentiment, many people will place their trust in it.
Regarding the suspension and expulsion from the assembly such that one no longer counts as a member of the Saṃgha and their spiritual guidance is suspended:

among the three primary intentions of the sixty-ninth [precept], the first is to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish and increase; the second is to cause [the offender] to reform and enter the path of humanity;
and the third is to eliminate the heterodox and manifest the orthodox.

[Commentary] Second, it clarifies that there are three faults in complying with another's wishes: (1) If one complies with another’s view, believing it to be correct, that view will increase and intensify until one is forever unable to follow the Path;

this constitutes a failure in the transformation of others. (2) Since one has already complied with another’s view, one will inevitably share that same perspective, becoming defiled by and attached to sensual matters until the integrity of one’s mind and conduct is utterly destroyed.
(3) When the Sangha formally censures someone, the community prohibits speaking with them; yet now, [the monk] willfully complies with [the censured person].
Because they disobeyed the Sangha’s command, they are equally culpable.

Regarding the next three points of meaning: first, it reveals the increase of evil and the harming of others; the character for "transformation" (*huà*) is a scribal error. Second, both are defiled and destroy conduct;
since this *pārājika* offense leaves no remainder, it is said that [the conduct] is "completely destroyed. Third, it is to disobey the Sangha and obstruct the Dharma.

[Commentary]: Regarding the third point, the explanation of the light and heavy [offenses] is presented together because their significance is equal. Why are there two light and one heavy? The answer is:

to say that desire is not an obstacle is a verbal expression that superficially resembles the principles and teachings, yet it leads to the destruction of the True Dharma. Furthermore, it ruins one's own conduct and obstructs the path of training;

moreover, it accords with human sentiment, as people generally delight in compliance. As for the other two clauses, although they involve errors such as being wrong or failing to extinguish the Dharma, [the gravity differs].
Because those who follow [the path] while destroying it for themselves are rare, whereas there are many who do not destroy it, the offense is classified as light.

Regarding the subsequent discussion of light and heavy offenses, the initial section first presents the inquiry: since one does not see [the fault], does not confess, and continues to follow [the wrong view], both are auspicious;

however, because holding a wrong view constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), it is said that "two are light and one is heavy. In the response, the first part clarifies the reason why the wrong view is heavy, which contains three points; the first concerns its confusion with [other categories].

The teaching further states: (1) the second and third [categories] involve harming oneself; (2) the third involves harming others; and (3) the remaining [categories] clarify the other two types of light offenses.
Regarding the three meanings above, only the subsequent meaning is fully present here.

[Commentary: There are four conditions for committing an offense: first, holding wrong views; second, identifying the person; third, knowing [the nature of the act]; and fourth, following along in compliance.
Each matter is tied to its respective offense.
Among the conditions for transgression, the first refers to the object followed (*anuśrita*), while the latter four refer to the agents who follow (*anuśrayin*).

Within these four, "following the same matter" means that regarding matters such as the ritual of providing services (*karmavācanā*) and so forth—as listed in the text—one commits an offense by following even a single instance, without waiting for all factors to be complete.

[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the evil view of Liṭṭha arose; although the Saṃgha admonished him, he did not relinquish it. The Buddha ordered that he be formally charged through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

When the monks who performed the *karman* together with the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) provided him with his necessities, the monks reported this transgression to the Buddha. Because the Buddha rebuked them for this reason, he established this precept.

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu knows that such a person (if he did not know at first, there is no offense later) has spoken thus (saying, "I have heard the World-Honored One teach that practicing sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path"),

and has not undergone the formal procedure (if he has been suspended and has not yet been rehabilitated), and holds such a wrong view (holding the view that what the World-Honored One taught regarding the Dharma is not an obstacle to the path),
and does not relinquish it (the Saṃgha admonishes him with censure, yet he does not relinquish his evil view), and [the bhikṣu] provides him with his necessities.

[Note] There are two kinds: the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth. The gift of Dharma consists of teaching and training in the higher training of ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), the higher training of mind (*adhicitta*), and the higher training of wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), as well as instruction in study and recitation of the scriptures.
The gift of material wealth consists of providing clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.
[Sūtra] One may stay overnight together with others for communal *karmavācanā* (such as the recitation of the *Poṣadha*).
[Commentary] A dwelling has four walls that are either entirely enclosed and covered, or entirely covered but not entirely enclosed,
or entirely enclosed but not entirely covered, or neither entirely covered nor entirely enclosed.
[The Vinaya] states: "Regarding speech.

[The Commentary] states: If a bhikṣu enters a house first and another person enters later, or if that person arrives first, or if they enter together, for each instance where he lies down with his side touching the ground, he incurs an offense.
[Pācittiya. [Commentary: The same offense applies to a nun.
As for when there is no offense: if one does not know; or if the building is entirely roofed but lacks four sides, or has half-sides, or few sides;
or if it is entirely enclosed but lacks a roof, or has a half-roof, or a small roof; or if it has a half-roof with sides, or a small roof with sides.
There is no offense if one is obstructed by an open space, or if one is ill, imprisoned, or facing a life-threatening danger or a threat to the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya).
[Commentary: The ten phrases of the precept text are: 1) a person; 2) knowing; 3) a person who speaks according to the Dharma; 4) not having performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā);
5) such a wrong view; 6) not relinquishing it; 7) providing support; 8) sharing the same Dharma; 9) staying overnight; 10) the incurrence of the offense.
In the third phrase of the first section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the character "yǐfǎ" (如法) is an error; it should read "rúshì" (如是).

Regarding the eight types of offerings (*saptavidha-upasthāna*), the note at the beginning provides a general indication of the rules, while the subsequent sections provide specific explanations. "Yìzhì" (意智) refers to the mental wisdom of the mind.

In the eighth [section] on "common dharma," the note states that "preaching the *Poṣadha* and so forth" includes all other *karmavācanā* and communal legal procedures. In the ninth [section] on "staying overnight," the note...

There are four types of rooms: (1) those where both the walls and the roof are all-pervasive; (2) those where the roof is all-pervasive but the walls are not; (3) those where the walls are all-pervasive but the roof is not;

and (4) those where neither the walls nor the roof are all-pervasive—such as a room with three walls and an opening in the wall above. The term "not all" or "not exhaustive" refers to the obstruction being incomplete;
thus, if one side is missing, it is simply that one side is absent, and if the roof is only partially open, it is simply that a small portion of the room's characteristics is revealed.
Because [the offense] is accomplished, there is an infringement; regarding "not infringing thereafter," this refers only to cases where the amount is one-half or less.
Although the characteristics listed in both places are clearly distinct from one another, because the wording here is brief and not explicit, the following point asks:

"How does this differ from the allowance (*anujñā*)? (The *Gujì* states: "It is an error to say that the former concerns an infringement due to knowledge, while the latter concerns an allowance due to ignorance. The words in the Sūtra are annotated below to clarify this.
In entering the room together or staying overnight, there must inevitably be mutual conversation and exchange between them.

[Commentary: Regarding the analysis of these characteristics, as such matters are rare in the text, I have not cited them extensively. Furthermore, using "staying overnight" (*zhìsù*) to manifest the characteristic is not a good translation;
