[Vinaya] Precept 71: Refusing Encouragement to Study.
[Commentary] Section Seventy-one: Refuting [Those Who] Discourage the Study of Precepts.

In general, spiritual practice does not achieve itself; it must rely on instruction and guidance to be able to spur one forward toward the cultivation of goodness and the benefit of entering the Path.

A "Good Spiritual Friend" (kalyāṇamitra) is the primary condition for the holy life (brahmacarya). If one does not rely upon and look up to such a friend, there is no way to exert self-motivation. Thus, for all sentient beings...

Regarding those with the aspiration for enlightenment, they may be briefly divided into three categories: The superior class, having attained realization, does not depend on external conditions to achieve their goal and serves as a model for all beings.

The inferior class, though exhorted, finds it difficult to follow such counsel. As for those of the middle class, who persist in worldly habits, they must rely on the guidance of friends; if they follow this principle, they will surely ascend toward purity, but if left to their own devices, they will succumb to base avarice.
Yet nowadays, those with deluded minds and indolent natures refuse to practice or study; when hearing the admonitions of others, they reject them and will not accept them.

Because there is no internal resolve to advance oneself and no external will to follow what is good, one violates the holy teachings; since the transgression is grave, this rule is established. (71) Regarding the intent of the rule:

[Note: While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, one member of the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) realized he had committed an offense just as the *Poṣadha* was being recited.
Fearing that his transgression would be exposed, he first went to a pure monk and said, "I have only now become aware of this rule recorded in the *Prātimokṣa*."
[The Buddha established this precept because] a bhikṣu who had come from among those reciting the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* every half-month during the confession ceremony pointed out his transgression.
[Vinaya: If, at the time of the recitation of the precepts—whether reciting them oneself, having them recited by another, or while chanting the precepts—a bhikṣu speaks thus:
"I have only now learned that this rule is contained in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month; other bhikṣus already knew this."

If a bhikṣu sits during the recitation of the *prātimokṣa* precepts—whether it be two or three times, let alone more—and yet remains ignorant and lacks understanding, if he has committed an offense, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma;
furthermore, he incurs an additional offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*). (If the heavier penalty of a *pāyattika* is not imposed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. One should say to him:
"Venerable sir, you have gained no benefit and have acted unskillfully. When the *prātimokṣa* was being recited, you did not apply your mind to it (you did not attend to it with focused reflection)."
If one listens to the Dharma with both ears while the other is single-mindedly focused, it is a *pāyattika* offense because of that lack of mindfulness.
[Note: Nuns commit the same offense. There is no offense if: one has not previously heard the detailed exposition and hears it for the first time; or if it was spoken in jest;
or if it was spoken by mistake.
[Commentary] The precept text consists of six phrases.
[Commentary] First, the individual.
[Commentary] Second, regarding the time when others recite the precepts: according to the Vinaya, when one recites them oneself, there is nothing that is not included.
The ear has indeed heard false speech, yet although one has known it for a long time, one says, "I only know it now.
Regarding the second phrase of the root precept, as cited in the commentary, the Vinaya is the same as in the preceding precept where both self and other are listed together;
however, since there is no principle for a self-accusation in this particular precept, it must be resolved that one commits the minor offense of false speech mentioned previously.
[Commentary: Third, there are those who are deluded regarding the teachings; they recite them without understanding the words, and only then do they realize the nature of this Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "deluded regarding the teachings," this refers to being deluded about what can be learned—that is, ignorance of the teachings.
[Commentary]: The passage beginning with "The other bhikṣus... serves as evidence that he had heard [the precepts] long ago; how could he have only now come to know them?

If the offense were attributed to him for the second or third recitation of the *Poṣadha*, what need is there to mention more than that? Examining this point, there would be no way for him to escape the charge. If he had previously heard the precepts, he already knew them long ago;
to say he "only now knows" them and thus incur the *pāyattika* offense of lying is untenable. If he lacked understanding, he would merely incur the offense of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).

Regarding the first of the four [sections], the explanation of the text and the attribution of the offense to that person: because there was a prior transgression and one feared the Sangha would raise it for punishment, one says, "I only now know.

The underlying intent is that previously one was unaware and thus did not commit an offense; now that the Sangha collectively testifies and one has repeatedly heard the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, how can one say "I only now know"?
When the offense for a prior transgression is attributed to that time, how could there be any room for such prevarication and deception? This concludes the section below.
To show the essential point: if one has actually known for a long time but says "I only now know," this is a lie, which falls under the preceding precept.
Even if one has attended the recitation of the precepts, if one truly lacks understanding and yet says "I only now know," one commits the actual offense of this specific precept.

Since one commits both offenses simultaneously, it is said that there is no way to escape the fault. It should be understood that this precept applies solely to cases of ignorance, as in the following example:
The judgment regarding the offenses in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā) becomes even more evident.

[Commentary: The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one says, 'I have only now come to know this dharma,' it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) due to a distracted mind or a confused mind when listening to the precepts;

if one speaks after the recitation is finished, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense). This refers to cases where one actually knew beforehand but claims to have "only now come to know" it, thereby committing the offense of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). The Vinaya root text establishes that this constitutes a lack of single-mindedness.
This is the offense of listening to the Dharma.

Next, regarding the citation of scriptural evidence from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Daolun): at the beginning of the oral recitation, one only realizes that the ear was not included in the act of listening;

therefore, as long as the recitation of the precepts has not been completed, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). Once it is completed, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession). This actually indicates a distinct offense below [the general category], while the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Jieben) below provides a specific distinction.

One must certainly observe this precept; the characteristics of its transgression have been difficult to adjudicate between ancient and modern scholars. Based on this, it is evident that there are distinct boundaries [between what constitutes a violation and what does not].
Let students reflect upon this.

[Commentary] Fifth, from "That bhikṣu... onwards, the faults are further clarified because [the Buddha] did not permit [the action], because they did not recognize the characteristics of the precept, and because they lacked...

Understanding arises from non-understanding; when encountering conditions, it arises rather than being destroyed by its own mental formations. Therefore, it is said: "If one commits an offense, one shall be dealt with according to the law.

Among the five [categories], the faults are emphasized again because, due to his previous statement that he wished to avoid prior transgressions, it is necessary to demonstrate once more that such offenses exist.
All offenses are to be treated [accordingly].

[Commentary: Sixth, further increasing the gravity of the offense below by concluding on the characteristics of multiple transgressions. One cannot escape by claiming ignorance, for the facts can be recognized;
therefore, one must further increase the charge of the offense of ignorance. Regarding the root offense, because the conditions were not fully understood, no further conclusion is reached.
Because it is done intentionally, it is said that the offense is further increased; because it is done through ignorance, the offense is a *pāyattika*.
"Not giving" refers to not giving to a virtuous person who is listening together; for one with a distracted mind, the offense is a *duṣkṛta*.
In the sixth section, the "Explanation of the Further Increase," the initial phrase "not by means of [the text]" indicates the intent of the concluding summary; the phrase "it should be further...
clarifies the meaning of the "further increase. The subsequent notes indicate that those who listen together are not to be penalized, meaning they shall not be subjected to reprimand or punishment.

[Commentary] Question: Why does the *Śīla-sūtra* mention "one mind" and "two ears"? Answer: The *Abhidharma-piṭaka* is for the adornment of the body, while the *Abhidharmakośa* is for assisting the formation of consciousness;
therefore, it is explained in detail therein.
In the subsequent section, the question is raised: "Since *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* are one and the same faculty (*indriya*), how can there be two? In the response, there are two explanations.
The first cites the *Abhidharma*—specifically the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* (The Heart of Scholasticism)—which clarifies the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). A question is posed:
"One should distinguish twenty-one elements, because within the eighteen elements, the six faculties—the eye, ear, and nose—are each divided into two. The verse answers: "Two are shared."
It is said that one realm [of the eye] exists for the sake of making the body beautiful. The commentary explains:

two eyes, two ears, and two nostrils arise in order to adorn the body, because people do not hold those with only one eye in affection or respect (the same applies to the ears and nostrils). Next, it cites the *Abhidharmakośa*, which establishes two positions;
the first position is the same as above, while the second position refutes it, saying: "This interpretation is not correct. If it were originally thus..."
[Objection: What is the purpose of these [beings], such as cats, raccoons, and starlings, being born with two eyes, ears, and noses?
[Response: It is for the sake of assisting the accomplishment of consciousness. For instance, when a person closes one eye, their perception of forms is not clear;
the same applies to the ears and noses respectively. [The purpose is] to adorn consciousness so that it may be fully accomplished.

[Commentary] Question: Previously, it was explained that violating [the rule] through negligence constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* (light offense), yet now you say that through ignorance one commits a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

Answer: This has already been explained above. Why do you forget what was said before? Did I not state that regarding the actual act, the offense may pertain to any of the four categories (*catur-varga*), whereas regarding the training itself, it pertains only to the fifth category?

Among the three [sections], the initial question was previously explained as the general meaning mentioned above regarding the rules for upholding and violating the precepts; therein, failing to train in them all constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
Now, this "lack of knowledge" corresponds to an offense not subsumed under the specific precepts, which is grave and increases due to ignorance. This is addressed in the subsequent questions.

In the response, first there is a reprimand and a further inquiry regarding the gravity of the matter, followed by the formal answer. However, the previous section did not provide this explanation, but merely stated the opposite.
"Clarifying the cessation of non-learning offenses refers to those not yet studied; clarifying the cessation of non-learning through corrective cultivation refers to specific matters.

This means that from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down, one possesses both observance and violation regarding specific matters. Since the cessation of non-learning for each article applies only to cases where the four grave offenses (*pārājika*) are excluded, it is said to 'pervade the four articles.
Because the cessation of non-learning for what has not been studied is universally a *duṣkṛta*, it is restricted to the fifth category."
[Commentary] Question: Why is it that in this case, the addition of ignorance results in the formal offense of *pārājika*? Answer: The offense for failing to train is merely a *dukkaṭa*.

However, whether ignorance, delusion, or doubt constitutes a light or heavy offense depends on the training and the circumstances of the matter, which may be clear or obscure. Thus, within the category of "perception regarding the object," doubt contains the lighter [offense], while perception harbors the heavier.
Here, being deluded and failing to recognize the object is precisely what is subsumed under the *pārājika* offense, as can be understood from the text. Regarding this:
This concerns the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.

Next, the question is raised that since the offense is increased through repetition, it should not be treated as identical to the root offense; thus, in the response, first it is clarified that "not training" applies exclusively to the latter [repetition], while secondly it is clarified that "ignorance" applies to both.
Furthermore, there are three parts: first, clarifying the reason for the division into two categories; second, explaining why doubt constitutes a light offense (*duṣkṛta*).

Because one who trains has clarity regarding the object of the offense, their delusion and downfall are grave; because one who does not train is entirely ignorant of the object, [their fault is otherwise].

Therefore, the two examples cited below illustrate that when there is a mistake in the perception (*saṃjñā*) regarding the object, doubt (*vicikitsā*) is grave while perception is light; when there is a mistake regarding the object itself, perception is grave while doubt is light.
Now, taking the latter two cases as examples, the following three sections correctly demonstrate the offenses here, which are absent in the former case.
Knowing that the offense is also due to not fully understanding the matter as a conditioned phenomenon, it is said that "the offense is settled according to the facts.

[Commentary] Regarding the fact that both assemblies are deemed non-offending (*jī*) in the Vinaya, this is because there were occasions when even their own recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* was not permitted due to certain conditions.

Regarding the first section of the commentary on the *Śāstra*, the note states that the *bhikṣuṇī*s share [the same offense] as those below, and that there should be three groups in total for whom this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
This text appears to be a scribal omission, or perhaps it was not cited because it refers forward to the *Vinaya* text; thus it says, "In the *Vinaya*... and so forth.
Since the lower three groups do not share the same legal principles (*dharma-artha*), it is explained according to their specific rules, as is explained at length in the *Shan-chao*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "never before heard" in the section below, this refers to those who have received the precepts but have not yet participated in the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.

Regarding "never before heard in detail," this refers to those who may have heard the three-word formula, the mental recitation (*manasikāra*), or the abbreviated recitation, yet did not clearly understand the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the precepts; thus, it is said that they now hear them, while the remainder can be understood.
Next, the section provides an explanation to clarify what has not yet been heard. First, the three meanings are listed: (1) hearing nothing at all; (2) hearing specific teachings;

and (3) hearing abbreviated teachings—all of which involve not hearing the extensive [teachings]. Regarding the reference to "others" below, this refers to things such as jesting and the like, as these are not intentional.
[Vinaya] 74. The precept on regretting after a collective *karmavācanā*.
[Commentary] The 74th precept on regretting after rewarding someone according to the communal dharma.

[Commentary] Generally, when communal property is shared among a group whose sentiments are not uniform, once they have collectively reached a harmonious consensus and performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to reward another person for their service as an administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*), one must not—acting arbitrarily—[revoke it].

Consequently, they regretted it and instead slandered the Saṃgha; following their own attachments, they agitated the minds of the multitude, giving rise to joy in strife and mutual affliction, so that they could not dwell in peace while cultivating the Path.
For these three reasons, as explained in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bahudharmaka-śāstra*, the rule was established.

74. Regarding the initial section on "Restraining the Mind," first it describes those who follow the same Dharma; next, it clarifies those who slander [the Dharma] and cause alarm; finally, it demonstrates their faults: first, they give rise to contention;
second, they mutually afflict one another; third, they abandon the work of the Path. The *Mahā-śāstra* explains these three points as follows:
"It is for the sake of extinguishing strife and contention; for the sake of extinguishing suffering and affliction; and for the sake of attaining peace and happiness in the practice of the Path."

[Commentary] Regarding the four conditions for committing an offense: first, it concerns property belonging to the Saṃgha. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* state that items offered to the "present Saṃgha" (*pratyutpanna-saṃgha*) are to be divided;
thus, one knows they are not permanent endowments (*akṣaya-nīvī*). Second, regarding the recognition of those who perform administrative duties (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) by their peers:

the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* frequently states that when the entire Saṃgha is in harmony, one need not inquire whether a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed or not; if there are diligent and virtuous persons who are impoverished, one should give to them in harmony with the assembly.

If one has already rebuked another, it is also a *thullaccaya* offense; if one repeatedly [rebukes] and then immediately regrets it, it is four [offenses]; if the verbal expression is complete, it constitutes an offense.
Regarding the first category of the conditions for the offense, three Vinayas are cited together to distinguish the objects to be rewarded, fearing that they might be used indiscriminately.

Among the four types of monastic property (*saṃghika-vastu*), two types—those currently present—are suitable for reward. Regarding the two types of administrative officers (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*), the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or *Mahā-saṃghika-vinaya*) takes only those from the monastic community.
The "harmonious" (saṃmodana) need not be a formal act of the Saṃgha (*karmavācanā*). One who takes charge of those undergoing hardship is one who manages the affairs of those undergoing hardship.

[Commentary: Why is it that one who does not admonish is already considered to have conformed to the monastic law? If the Saṃgha has attachment, he likewise has attachment; since there is no confusion [between them], it is unnecessary.

In the first part of the following section, the initial inquiry asks why this constitutes slandering the Saṃgha; from "according to the rules, one should add a formal admonition" onwards, the explanation clarifies that it is not necessary [to do so]. [Note:
When the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, the son of Ṭhapa Māra, who managed the affairs of the Saṃgha, did not attend the distribution of external offerings because his robes were worn out.

After the destruction [of the robes], the monks obtained precious garments; they then performed the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act with one motion and one announcement) to give them to the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*). Later, the group of six felt regret. The monks informed the Buddha, who rebuked them and established the precept.
Regarding the causal conditions for this precept: "not attending an external offering" means not attending an external invitation, resulting in a lack of robes for replacement.
【Vinaya】 If, after a formal legal act (*kamma*) has been performed together, a bhikṣu should say:

"The bhikṣus give the property of the Saṅgha (the property of the Saṅgha refers to items such as robes, alms bowls, needle cases, sitting mats, down to drinking vessels and water containers) to those who follow their friends" (meaning those with whom they sit, rise, speak, and are intimate, such as their *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*), he commits a *pāyattika*.
[Note]: If it is said that there is no offense for one who speaks indistinctly, this is indeed the case;
however, giving monastic property to a relative out of affection, or doing so in jest, or speaking erroneously, is all permitted.

[Commentary: The precept text consists of five phrases: 1) the person; 2) the commonality of the Dharma; 3) subsequent slander; 4) the distribution of communal property and below, which clarifies the characteristics [of the offense];
5) the conclusion of the offense.
In the separate explanation of the text, regarding the third point—slander—it says "in accordance with friends and relatives," meaning that the Sangha follows private sentiments.
The order can be understood. [Commentary:
Regarding the four types of monastic property (*saṃghika-vastu*), the theft of these was already explained above in terms of their spatial location and temporal status; they are now presented again.

Within the explanation of monastic property, the first section distinguishes two types of permanent property (*sthāvara*) based on location, and two types of current property (*jaṅgama*) based on time.

[The preceding section. [Commentary: First, regarding "the Saṃgha present before one" (*pratyakṣasaṃgha*), as in the case of giving ponds, wells, and so forth within these precepts, the gift is directed toward specific persons; it belongs to those present before one.
Regarding the "Saṃgha present in the twenty directions" (*viṃśatidig-pratyakṣasaṃgha*), such as the property of a deceased monk, it extends from the highest sages down to the śrāmaṇeras.
Third, regarding the "permanently established" (changzhu): because it pertains to the pure dwelling of the site, it extends throughout the three periods of time;
being fixed and immovable, it likewise cannot be divided. Fourth, regarding the "presently established permanently" (xiànqián chángzhù):
as when preparing cooked food intended for the monastery's monks, the intention encompasses both residents and guests, and it is not permitted to take it outside.

Therefore, among the explanations listed, the first concerns the acquisition of material goods for the purpose of rewarding people; thus, it refers here to the precept regarding the giving of ponds and wells.

As for the Vinaya’s statement that one constructs ponds, wells, and so forth, and then gives material goods as a result, this is shown below to clarify the meaning of the term. Among these two points, the first clarifies...

The meaning of "the ten directions" (*daśadig*) refers to the ultimate holy ones, namely those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), down to the novices (*śrāmaṇera*); it encompasses the entire assembly of both noble and ordinary beings, as well as the Great and Small Vehicles.

Regarding the term "present" (*pratyutpanna*) used below, within the three types of [monastic] assemblies, the first three phrases are restricted to specific locations, while the last phrase differs in that it is not divided by location;

alternatively, it may be named by combining both aspects. In other contexts, this is also called "the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions" (*caturdiśasaṃghadravya*), and "Pure Abode" (*viśuddhavāsa*).

"Ga-lam" (Skt. *saṃghārāma*) is another name for this; among the four types [of property], it is also called "permanently established for the ten directions" (*śāśvata-dig-vihāra*), meaning that it is not permitted to be taken outside—this indicates its specific name.
[Commentary: Among these four kinds, the first substance is harmonious and can be shared; the second principle is general, while the latter two are complete in themselves.

Closed. In the *Jianpan* (Brief Judgments), the first two [categories] are both classified as "divisible" (*sabhāga*), while the latter two are entirely "closed" (*asabhāga*) because they are permanent.
—From *Xingzongji*, Volume 4, Part 1, of the *Sifenlü Hanzhu Jieben Shu* (Commentary on the *Sifenlü Hanzhu Jieben*).
*Commentary on the Essentials of Practice of the Annotated Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Four-Part Vinaya*, Part 4, Section 2 of the Lower Volume.
[Vinaya] Precept 75: The Precept Against Not Granting Consent.
[Commentary] The precept against not granting consent is the seventy-fifth.

[Commentary]: In all matters that accord with the Dharma, it is appropriate to follow them collectively and permit no discord or competition. Now, those who arbitrarily abandon the formal procedures (*karman*) of the Saṃgha when they are being suspended act with a lack of harmony;
because such obstruction of monastic affairs and the resulting distress to the community are not minor matters, this rule was established.

Of the seventy-five rules for regulating the mind, the first section provides a general introduction to the monastic laws; the following section clarifies the arising of transgressions and their cessation.

[Commentary] There are five conditions for committing an offense: first, it must be a formal monastic matter conducted according to the Dharma; second, one must know it is conducted according to the Dharma; third, one has not granted one's consent (*chanda*); fourth, one rises and departs abruptly;
and fifth, one steps both feet across the threshold of the door. This constitutes an offense.

The first section on the conditions for an offense: Distinguishing the lawful from the unlawful is without offense; this is determined by the following rule. Furthermore, the settlement of disputes is restricted to the specific methods for resolving contention and excludes other legal procedures, as these are merely minor matters.

[Note: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a great assembly of bhikṣus gathered to discuss the Dharma and Vinaya. The group of six bhikṣus said to one another, "Let us observe the other bhikṣus..."
The Buddha, who was as if performing a *karmavācanā* for us, rose from his seat and departed. A bhikṣu called out for him to stay, but he continued on his way.
When the matter was reported to the Buddha, he rebuked him and established the precept.

[Sūtra] If a bhikṣu, while the Saṃgha is engaged in a formal act (*karmavācanā*)—such as the recitation of the *Poṣadha* (one *śīlaskandha*) or the settlement of a dispute—and the matter has not yet been concluded (there being eighteen matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha, ranging from what is legal to what is illegal, up to what should be spoken and what should not be spoken):

If one departs without having given consent (except when attending to monastic affairs, temple affairs, or caring for the sick, in which cases giving consent is permitted), it is a *pāyattika*. [Note:

If the legal proceeding has not yet concluded and one moves a foot outside the door, one commits a *pāyattika*. If one foot remains inside the door while making the effort to depart but does not actually leave, it is a *duṣkṛta* (or *pāyattika*).
There is no offense if one has given consent, or if one departs by means of verbal consent.

If one remains silent during an illegal *karmavācanā*, or if one departs without having granted consent (*anumati*) when it would cause harm to the Saṃgha, a stūpa, a monastery, an upādhyāya, an ācārya, or one’s fellow students, [the offense] is incurred. [Commentary]:

This refers exclusively to the cessation of the four types of disputes. One who does not grant consent incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation); for other matters, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This is as stated in the *Śīlaprakīrṇaka-viniścaya*.

Regarding the explanation: in the initial section of the "Discriminative Judgment," the formal discrimination is as follows. As indicated in the commentary on the *Saṃkṣipta-śīla-pratyaya*, the *Dharmavinaya* refers to the settling of disputes.
As for the six groups of monks addressing one another, it was because they had committed many transgressions that doubt arose within them, and from this, [the dispute] originated.

In the commentary on the six phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* regarding the three matters of "severing" (*chedana*), it states: "The eighteen dharmas are cited here by way of example through verbal disputes; the other three cases follow this pattern.

Regarding the fourth [dharma], "not giving consent" (*anujñāna*), the commentary briefly sets forth the conditions under which one may give consent. According to the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*, six conditions are fully permitted:

when the Three Jewels are ill, when one is tending to the sick, and when one is making robes—all these permit the giving of consent. This is further clarified in the subsequent commentary on the "explanation of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Going out of doors" refers to occupying a hall or chamber; the meaning is detailed in that one must certainly have no doors or windows and must depart from both seeing and hearing.
One does not violate the character *jin* (禁), which is pronounced as the opposite of *kan* (噤)—meaning the closing of the mouth.
[Vinaya] Precept 76: Regretting the Granting of Consent (*chanda*).
[Commentary] Precept 76: Regretting the Granting of Consent.

[Commentary] In all matters of the Sangha that accord with the Dharma, one must follow the proper principle; having previously granted consent, if one then sees that the treatment of one's companions was biased due to partiality...

To agree to something and then immediately regret it, conversely claiming that the agreement was not reached, or to disparage the Dharma and disturb the assembly—because these acts are grave, they are thus prohibited.

Regarding the seventy-sixth rule, the first part of the intent explains that when one expresses a desire for a practice and it is appropriate, one should grant that desire; following this, the subsequent section clarifies the matter of subsequent regret.

[Commentary] There are four conditions for committing an offense: first, a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) that is contrary to the Dharma; second, granting consent (*chanda*) in a manner contrary to the Dharma; third, immediately repenting and reversing one's position;
and fourth, the completion of the verbal formulation.
Regarding these conditions, both [the first and second] exclude what is not in accordance with the Dharma.
[Commentary]: According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, regarding matters other than those concerning the Saṃgha, if one reconciles with others and later regrets it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The next section of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* treats other matters such as verbal reconciliation.
[Note]: While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks feared being formally censured; thus, the six men followed one another, finding no way to act, until they did so at a later time.

While the monk was being summoned to receive the *chanda* (consent), the Bhikṣus performed the formal act of suspension (*ukṣepa-karman*) against him. Later, the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) said, "I gave my consent regarding that matter;
the Bhikṣu has committed an offense. The Buddha, because of this, rebuked them and established the precept.

Because the six groups of monks followed one another in forming a sangha, people did not dare to challenge them; yet when the sangha challenged the companions of the six groups regarding their consent (*chanda*), they regretted their previous granting of consent.
[The Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu, having already granted his consent, subsequently regrets it..."
[Note] To speak thus: "The *karmavācanā* you have performed is an illegal *karmavācanā* and is not established;
I grant my consent (*chanda*) for that matter, but not for this one," [is a] *pāyattika*. [Vinaya] *Pāyattika*.
[Note]: If it is said that when one declares an indeterminate offense (*aniyata*), the same applies to whether there is a shared or non-shared offense, this is indeed the case;
however, if one incorrectly declares "this" or "that," it is permitted [to correct it].
[Commentary: Regarding the three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, for the three lower assemblies (*tṛtīya-parṣad*), there is a residual offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) following remorse.

In the initial section of the separate explanation, two phrases are briefly indicated for the lower assemblies; the second phrase is presented in the annotations with the words of that subsequent remorse, while the rest clarifies the characteristics [of the offense] and is thus understandable.
[Vinaya] Precept 77: Listening in Secret to the Four Disputes.
[Commentary] Precept 77: Listening in Secret to the Four Disputes.

[Commentary] Generally, public discourse reveals the principle, whereas secret speech follows personal sentiment; now, walking slowly to eavesdrop and transmit what one has heard from one side to the other follows such sentiment.
Because the faults of harboring malice, causing destruction, and creating disorder are extremely grave and not to be taken lightly, this rule was established.
Regarding the seventy-seventh rule, the initial general introduction concerning speech has now concluded; below, the text specifically clarifies the act of eavesdropping.

[Commentary] For an offense to occur, five conditions must be met: first, there must be the prior initiation of one of the four types of disputes; according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, most disputes involve going to listen to them.
This is grave because it can destroy the Buddha-dharma and cause the Saṃgha to split into two factions. Second, to evaluate others in private;
third, to harbor intentions to cause strife while pretending to mediate, yet not following this Vinaya oneself; fourth, to go and listen without letting them know;
fifth, to commit an offense as soon as one hears their words.

Regarding the first cause for transgression: according to the *Sarvāstivāda Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, all disputes are comprised within the four types of disputes (*catvāro adhikaraṇāḥ*). The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* clarifies that because these manifest faults, they universally bring ruin to the Triple Gem;

thus, among the three [types of monks], those who act as mediators to reform themselves do not engage in strife or discord. Since it is permitted that there is no offense in such cases, this Vinaya states that one need not apply [the rules] here.
[Commentary]: If this is so, why does it say "one listens to what is said to them"? The answer is that the intention of the listener is such that the offense is incurred merely by hearing it;
if one were to wait until the words are spoken to them, it would fall under the category of divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
In the initial portion of the question-and-answer section, the citation of the precept text raises a challenge regarding the fifth condition;

the response text is easily understood. [Commentary] Question: This permission [to listen] immediately follows the prohibition against divisive speech (*paiśunya*). Does it wait for a mediator? Answer: Prior to this, there was no dispute, so listening did not necessarily arise;

it was only upon hearing the words that this [prohibition] first occurred. Since there was already a dispute when one went to listen, the offense would certainly have arisen. Therefore, why wait for that [mediator] when the previous prohibition was already established?

[The text] explains this. Next, in order to resolve the difficulty regarding the intention behind the formulation of the two precepts concerning offenses, the response first clarifies that double-tongued speech necessarily depends upon the transmission [of words];
hereafter, it clarifies that for this particular precept, one commits an offense at the very moment of hearing or speaking, and thus states that it is "deeper" than the previous prohibitions.
[Note] While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks permitted various bhikṣus to fight and then reported it to others, causing the disputes within the Saṃgha to remain unresolved.
When the bhikṣus reported this transgression, the Buddha consequently rebuked them and established a regulation.

[The Vinaya] states: If a bhikṣu, after having engaged in a dispute with another bhikṣu (there being four types of disputes: verbal quarreling, seeking faults, litigation, and contention), listens to these words and reports them to the other party.

[Note: As for "listening," it refers to eavesdropping on the speech of others; that is, listening to their words by going from the path to a non-path, or from a high place to a low place, or conversely, as described in the preceding sentence, going toward them to overhear.
[Pāyattika]. [Commentary]: If one does not hear [the call], it is a duṣkṛta;
if one intends to leave through some expedient means while having made a prior appointment, it is a duṣkṛta in all such cases;
if two persons converse in a dark place, or converse in a secluded spot, or converse while walking ahead, or if one does not snap one's fingers or cough [to signal departure], [it is a duṣkṛta].

"Those who are startled [by this] all commit a *duṣkṛta* offense, the same as the offense for the Saṃgha; those who do not commit an offense are those who, wishing to know [the truth], listen to the performance of an unbeneficial and illegal *karmavācanā*.
[Commentary]: The *Prātimokṣa* text consists of three phrases: (1) "one person," (2) "having previously disputed together," and (3) "listening to these words. Below this, the offense is defined.
The commentary on the third phrase of the *Prātimokṣa* explains the opposite of the preceding phrase regarding going to listen [to the recitation].

From "an improper path" to "a proper path," and from "low" to "high," these constitute three offenses. The sub-commentary states that "not hearing" constitutes a deficiency in the requisite conditions (*pratyaya*).

If one intends to leave and makes a prior appointment [with another], both are considered preparatory acts (*prayoga*). If two people [agree] such that they do not alarm others and thus violate the teaching, it is an offense.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one hears that others harbor enmity and desire to kill or harm [the community], or hears that bandits are coming intending to steal the property of the Saṃgha, the administrative officer (*karmadāna*) shall inform the Saṃgha, and each person shall prepare themselves for alarm, saying: "I have heard an evil sound."

Next, regarding the section on the *Saṃghāṭi* [robe] and the situation of life-threatening danger: it is permitted to stay [in such a place] without incurring an offense, provided one is prepared for a surprise. This means that one has been previously alerted and has made prior preparations.
[The Vinaya] states: "The seventy-eighth precept concerning striking a *bhikṣu*."
[Commentary]: The precept against striking a bhikṣu is the seventy-eighth. [Commentary]:

Having left the household life to cultivate loving-kindness, one ought to be able to endure humiliation and provocation; yet now, on the contrary, one harbors resentment and strikes the person before one.
This destroys oneself and afflicts others, and the harm is no small matter; therefore, it is proscribed.
In the first part of the seventy-eighth section on "Controlling the Mind," the fundamental basis of practice was initially described; now, next, it clarifies the violation thereof:
harboring anger and meager virtue is self-destruction, while encountering a beating and bearing pain is the affliction of others.

[Commentary: There are four conditions for committing this offense: first, a fully ordained bhikṣu; second, the arising of a mind of anger; third, the intentional act of striking; and fourth, contact with the body, at which point the offense is committed.
The remaining details are extensively cited in the section on the specific precepts.
The First Section on the Conditions for Offenses: Distinguishing the Lesser Assembly; Auspiciousness; the Remainder; the Lower;

Referring to the Extensive [Vinaya]. [Commentary]: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, one member of the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) struck one member of the group of seventeen (saptadaśavargika) out of anger.

The victim cried out loudly, and his fellow monks heard him. Upon investigating the matter, they reported the transgression to the Buddha. Consequently, the Buddha rebuked them and established the precept.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu (whether with the hand, a stone, a staff, or other such implements), it is a *pāyattika*.

[Commentary] With the exception of using a staff, the hand, or a stone, if one strikes with a door-key, a curved hook, the handle of a whisk, or the handle of an incense-burner, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
This offense is committed equally by all. There is no offense in cases where one must strike due to illness, or when striking the spine is necessary to cause food to swallow.
If one does not hear when speaking together, but touching makes it heard; or if, while sleeping, one’s body leans against another;
or if, while coming and going or walking in meditation, they touch one another; or if, while sweeping the floor, the tip of the broom accidentally touches [another]—these cases are permitted.
The three phrases of the precept text are: first, [anger]; second, hatred; third, striking. In the analysis of the characteristics, the character *chì* (挃) is pronounced *zhǐ lǐ* (陟栗);
it means to strike. There is no offense in various circumstances where these are not due to anger or affliction.

The signs [of the offense] are very clear.

In the initial section of the commentary, it says "profoundly guarding" means to guard against the previous offense of striking so as to prevent its commission.

If one raises a hand as a "knife" toward many bhikṣus, each individual case constitutes an offense.

Among the three categories, the definition of the term can be seen in the Vinaya-mātṛkā; here, "hand-knife" means using the hand as a knife, and "each individual case" refers to the formal determination of the offense according to the specific object involved.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks struck the group of seventeen monks with their hands. Those who were struck raised a loud cry.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the precept.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu with his hand, it is a *pāyattika*.

[Commentary] If he strikes him with both hands, he commits a *pāyattika*; if he strikes him with anything such as a door-key or the like, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This applies equally to all members of the Saṃgha regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not.
If there is a necessary reason to raise one's hand to ward off or beckon someone, there is no offense.
The enumeration of the causal factors is the same as in the previous precept. Regarding the commentary on the definition of the offense: "the two hands" refers to raising either one hand.
Among the non-offenses, raising a hand to ward off a beckoning, whether it be warding off or beckoning, is all permitted.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The Eighty Saṃghāvaśeṣa Offense of Groundless Accusation.
[Commentary] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks, out of malice, groundlessly accused the group of seventeen monks of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
When they reported this transgression to the Buddha, he rebuked them and established this precept.

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu, out of anger, slanders [another] with groundless [charges]—as explained in the preceding categories—regarding a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*. [Commentary] The same applies to a bhikṣuṇī;
there is no offense in three cases: if one speaks the truth to cause [the other] to repent, if one does not slander, or if it is said in jest.
If one speaks erroneously:
[Commentary] The offense of groundless slander is the eightieth precept.
[Commentary] The regulation regarding the commission of this offense is no different from the preceding precept on slander; the only distinction is that this one is lighter.
In the extant portion of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, only the objects of censure and the offenses committed are distinguished; therefore, it merely provides a brief indication.

Now, I shall cite and explain the underlying intent of these regulations. The *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* states: "First, to protect one's own practice and cause the Dharma to endure for a long time;
second, to stop slander and allow those who lead the holy life (*brahmacarya*) to practice the Path in peace, so that their primary task is not hindered. Thus, the regulations were established.
The conditions for the offense are eight: first, it is a bhikṣu; second, one perceives him as a fully ordained bhikṣu;

third, there is a mind of malice; fourth, the charge is groundless; fifth, it is done even before a single bhikṣu; sixth, one slanders him by charging him with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; seventh, the words are finished;

eighth, the other hears and knows the five phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* text. Second, the persons involved: the offender and the one who is the object of the malice. Third, the absence of grounds. (Note: This refers to the commentary.)

The preceding section concludes with the four characteristics of slander and the fifth point on the determination of the offense; the comparison of these characteristics can be understood by referring back to what precedes.
[Vinaya] Eighty-one: The precept concerning entering the gate of a royal palace.
[Commentary] The eighty-first precept concerns the offense of intruding into a royal palace.
[Commentary: Kings possess sovereign power and are often prone to luxury and indulgence; they seek sensual pleasure rather than righteousness and must be observed and restrained.
Now, this bhikṣu has abruptly entered [the palace] and, having already pressed and rebuked [the king], both parties feel ashamed; such conduct is profoundly inappropriate.

Furthermore, the splendor and excess of a royal palace can disturb the ordinary mind and give rise to defiled attachments, thereby ruining and disordering the Path. Because the transgression is so grave, it was thus prohibited.
The eighty-first [offense], "Entering Unannounced," refers to entering without having informed [the residents]. There are two aspects to the regulation of the mind.

First, regarding the obstruction of others, the explanation of the meaning requires careful observation and inspection: a bhikṣu wishing to enter must first examine whether he will cause disturbance or displacement;

"displacement" (chì) means to drive out or expel, as seen in the *Nidāna* (Origin Stories). Second, next, regarding harm to oneself, the explanation: "yàn" (豔) means floral splendor, and "yì" (逸) means extravagant indulgence.
Because it is valued by the foolish, many give rise to attachment.
[Commentary] Regarding the four conditions for committing an offense: first, when a Kṣatriya king is in the same place as his consort; second, when the king has not yet hidden his treasures;
third, entering through the threshold of the gate—these offenses are indeed rare.
Regarding the second condition for an offense: it is rare for a king to commit this alone while in the company of his queen;

furthermore, it is rare for such an offense to occur because in the Western Regions (India), where the Dharma is upheld, bhikṣus are permitted to enter and exit the palace precincts, whereas in this land (China), strict guards do not allow them to enter at will.

[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, Queen Mallikā made offerings to the Buddha and, out of faith, encouraged the King to have confidence and listen to the bhikṣus entering the palace without obstruction.
When Kālodāyin arrived and entered the palace, the Queen brushed his seat and caused him to lose his robe, leaving his body exposed.
The bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked him and established the precept.
Regarding the *mālī* fruit mentioned in the context of the precepts, this is translated here as *nài* (the *jambu* or rose-apple).
[The Vinaya] states: "If a bhikṣu [approaches] a Kṣatriya king of the 'water-sprinkled' lineage.
[The Commentary] explains: "Water-sprinkled" refers to taking water from the great ocean and using the left horn of a white bull to collect the seeds, which are then placed upon a golden carriage.
The minor kings carry the great Brahmin on a palanquin and pour water upon the king’s crown;

because he is thus established as a member of the Kṣatriya caste, he receives this name. Even if one from the Vaiśya or Śūdra castes is established in this manner, it is likewise called "consecration" (abhiṣeka).
[Sūtra] The king had not yet departed (meaning the women had not yet returned to their original places), and the treasures had not yet been concealed.
[Commentary] Gold, silver, precious pearls, carnelian, agate, crystal, lapis lazuli, shells, jade, and various other jewels, as well as necklaces,
had not yet been gathered up and hidden away.
[Sūtra] If one enters and crosses the threshold of a palace gate, it is a *pāyattika*.
[Commentary] If one foot is outside the threshold and one foot is inside, and one forms the intention to depart, it is all a *duṣkṛta*, except for the case of a king;
for other minor kings, petty rulers, or the households of wealthy elders, entering their thresholds constitutes a *duṣkṛta* in all such cases. For *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is likewise.

Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not: if one has submitted a petition, been summoned, or is under the circumstances of a threat to life or a *brahmadanda* (monastic penalty), all such cases are exempted.
[Commentary: The first six phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* are: 1) a person; 2) a Kṣatriya; 3) a king who has not yet stepped out [of his palace]; 4) jewels that have not yet been stored away.

Although the *Vinaya* lists the jewels, it does not explicitly define their characteristics. As the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (*Manyi lun*) states: "When entering the inner quarters to attend upon the women, one causes them to wear jeweled garments within."

Externally, it is observed that this bhikṣu has now suddenly arrived here; having entered the palace gate—which is deeply guarded and restricted—and having already committed the first offense, how much more so for seeing the jewels, which constitutes the sixth offense?
The second phrase of the *Prātimokṣa* refers to one of the four castes, the Kṣatriya royal lineage, specifically those who have had their heads sprinkled with water (*abhiṣikta*).
The translation of this term is somewhat literal; it refers to a consecrated king (*mūrdhābhiṣikta-rāja*), as cited in the commentary.

Although the Brahmins and others mentioned in the commentary do not belong to the royal caste, their consecration is no different, and thus they incur the same offense upon entry. "The three kings have not yet emerged" means they have not yet left the women’s quarters of the palace.
Since they have not yet returned to their original locations and are still within the royal palace, this is based on the original *nidāna*; it refers specifically to the bedchamber.

Here, however, it simply concerns the inner court of the king’s quarters, where the boundary is established as soon as one enters the gate. Among the four [types of boundaries], the first point is obscurely noted in the text;
it merely lists various jewels without clarifying the meaning of "not hidden," as will be shown below: namely, that the ladies-in-waiting attending the bedchamber all wear light [robes].
The fine jeweled robes have not yet been put away, which manifests his distress and constitutes an offense of transgression.

Regarding the identification of the characteristics [of kings], with the exception of the four Universal Monarchs (cakravartin), all other rulers of minor kingdoms are called "scattered grain" kings (*kṣullakarājānaḥ*); this means they are so numerous that they cannot be counted.
[Vinaya] Precept 82: Taking Precious Objects.
[Commentary] Precept 82: Taking Precious Objects.

[Commentary] Because precious objects bring great profit, many people are greedily attached to them; since the worldly affairs of śramaṇas are severed from such greed, this constitutes the thirtieth precept concerning hoarding.
Since it is already an offense to tie up even a domestic animal, how much more so for bodily contact; truly, this is not in accordance with the monastic code.

Therefore, merely seizing [an object] constitutes an offense of falling (pācittiya). Now, this bhikṣu, failing to reflect upon the noble prohibitions, impulsively seized the lost treasure and was instead slandered;
as purity and turbidity were thus indistinguishable, this precept was established based on these circumstances.

Of the eighty-two rules concerning mental intention, the first section describes the fault of possessing wealth and valuables beyond their proper measure; how much more so when one actually takes them into one's own hands. Next follows the clarification of the fault of grasping or seizing.

Regarding the case of one who is falsely accused based on the original *nidāna*: *Note: The term "過直" (guò zhí) refers to exceeding the proper value or measure. "本緣起" (běn yuánqǐ) refers to the original narrative context or causal origin of the rule.*

[Commentary: Former masters have traditionally transmitted that this constitutes an offense against the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination). However, according to the explanations in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* across various schools, one commits an offense simply by taking hold [of an object].

Why, then, do they discuss "picking up what was left behind"? Thus, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* initially lists the rule: "Taking hold of precious objects is an offense. It excludes only two specific conditions;

otherwise, it permits the collection of temple requisites. Since there is no separate provision for such cases, how can it be said that taking hold of precious objects incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)?
Regarding the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as clear as a mirror and not obscure, as listed according to the characteristics in the *Guangru chao*.

In the initial section of the "Refutation of Errors," he first cites the opponent's position based on the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, which holds that one commits only a *duṣkṛta* for merely grasping [the object], whereas the *Shiyi* (The Omission) states that one commits a *naiḥsargika* only when [the object] has been abandoned. Now, following this, the text formally refutes [that view].

First, it judges the nature of the offense; then, it cites and demonstrates the original rule (*śikṣāpada*). First, it shows that the *Vinaya-mātṛkā* excludes two conditions, namely those found in the *Gāthā*.

In the *Lan su chu* (Blue Lodging), it states that opening a stūpa repository does not constitute an offense; however, apart from these three conditions, there is no other text that permits the handling [of gold].
It says that handling it constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). In the *Guang* (Extensive Commentary), the specific details are pointed out.

That text, based on the clear textual evidence of various schools, states "clearly evident" and so forth. It cites the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, stating: "If one handles gold leaf or a golden image, or if one handles..."
If one takes another's property or claims as pure what is not pure, one falls into an offense;

furthermore, citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it states that if a person knows of property belonging to the Buddha or the Saṃgha, they must not take it themselves—even gold, silver, stupas, or images—having instead have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) hold them. Such cases are not instances of committing an offense for picking up lost items.

[Commentary] Regarding the four conditions for committing this offense: first, it must be a precious object; second, it must not be an ornamental implement belonging to a stūpa or monastery; third, it must not be due to other circumstances; and fourth, the offense is committed as soon as one takes hold of it.

As for the second condition regarding the offense, according to our own school, taking ornamental implements is permitted and does not constitute an offense; this is also the view of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.

The permission to seize the notes depends on whether there are pure persons present, so as to reconcile the two texts. Regarding the "three non-conditions," this refers to the lodging place within a monastery.
[Note: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, some heterodox practitioners were traveling on the road; they stopped to rest, forgot a thousand ounces of gold, and departed.
The Buddha saw this and had him take it away; he then returned the gold to him, but the king remarked that the gold was insufficient and punished him by confiscating the gold for the state treasury.
The bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who then rebuked him and established this precept.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] "If a bhikṣu [touches] treasure.
[Commentary] "Treasure" refers to gold, silver, pearls, amber, musaragalva, agate, vaidūrya, shells, jade, and wrought or unwrought gold and silver.

【Vinaya】 Regarding precious ornaments (those adorned with various jewels using copper, iron, lead, tin, or white wax): whether one holds them oneself or instructs another to hold them, this is prohibited, except within a monastery.

[Note] At that time, Visākhā’s mother removed her precious robe while listening to the Dharma at the Buddha's presence. A bhikkhu, mindful of the Dharma but having forgotten the robe, informed the Buddha that he wished to take it up for safekeeping so as not to lose this durable possession. The Buddha granted permission.
[Sūtra] And regarding the place where one stays overnight.
[Commentary] At that time, a bhikṣu traveling on the road stayed overnight at a goldsmith’s house. There were both finished and unfinished gold pieces laid out before him;
he remained awake all night guarding them. He informed the Buddha, who said: "For the sake of security, you should collect and store them away."

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Pāyattika (the same offense for nuns as for monks): If, within a monastery or at a lodging place, one takes hold of precious objects or ornaments made of precious materials—whether taking them oneself or instructing another to do so—one should maintain this intention: "If there is an owner who recognizes [them], they shall take them."
[Note: If one obtains treasure at two locations, one should grasp it in a bag or vessel, noting its characteristics and counting how much there is.
If anyone comes, give it to those who are appropriate; to those who are not appropriate, say, "I did not see it.
If one does not know the characteristics of the bag or vessel—such as whether it is tied or wrapped, its shape, whether it is new or old—all such instances constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
[The Vinaya] states: "This is the specific cause and condition, and no other.
[The Commentary] states: There is no offense if one stays overnight in a monastery and employs the aforementioned methods of grasping and lifting;
nor is there any offense if one securely collects and lifts up the ornaments and furnishings of a stūpa or temple for the purpose of making offerings.

[Commentary]: The precept text consists of six sections: (1) the individual; (2) the two Jewels; (3) taking [food] oneself or instructing another to do so; (4) the exception where there is no offense; (5) the formal conclusion of the offense;
and (6) the detailed explanation following the exception.

In the fourth section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, regarding the two conditions as explained in the commentary, there is concern over losing another’s property; thus, taking it up to secure it is permitted.

This does not mean that within a monastery grounds (*ārāma*), one is permitted to handle other types of precious objects. The sixth heavy offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) in the commentary clarifies the manner of picking up and returning such items.

[Commentary] Question: Since the Buddha prohibited one from personally grasping precious objects, how is it that there are those who commit an offense by having another person grasp them? Now, this is explained: it is not that [the act] itself is non-dharmic;
rather, both self and other commit the offense equally. Therefore, in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), having another person grasp them is also an offense.
There must be a specific allowance where grasping them oneself is without fault, as listed in the precepts.
Regarding the third section, the initial question is explained because the text on the precepts states that both taking [an object] oneself and commanding another to do so constitute an offense;

therefore, it is asked and explained here. Now, the following passage explains this generally: it means that for a bhikṣu to command a fellow practitioner to take hold of something is an imprecise and illegal act.

Thus, the text below points to the evidence in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* (Duolun), which says: "If one commands a bhikṣu to take hold of precious objects, one also incurs a *pārājika* offense. This is certainly what follows below.
The reason for opening [the storage] as listed in the precepts is to retrieve what was left behind at two locations and to collect the ritual implements.

[Commentary]: The reason it is permitted is that if one does not take hold of them oneself but leaves them for another to carry away, and a later seeker comes looking for them, even though the bhikṣu is in the same place, he cannot avoid slander.
Therefore, it is permitted to take them, pending their return to the owner, in order to quell the fault of public censure. Is this not so?

[This section concerns] the benefit. Regarding the first sentence of the subsequent section, it interrogates the text: why is it that in two instances the grasping [of an object] is permitted without offense? The following passage clarifies the intent:

according to the text, this merely indicates that one may pick up [an object] to avoid censure; yet in terms of the actual matter, it can also resolve false accusations and ward off harm—the benefit is thus evident.
[Commentary]:

To act through these specific causes and conditions and not others means that there are no other occasions for transgression. That is to say, when one unintentionally returns the item to its owner and stores it away oneself—whereas a transgression would otherwise have been expected—one does not commit a transgression.
This constitutes a case where what would otherwise be a transgression is, in fact, non-transgression; there are no other [circumstances] remaining.
Among the three [sections], the first restates and explains: "As mentioned above, to pick up and return [an object] in accordance with the teaching is non-offense; it is not an offense.
The subsequent section, which provides a counter-explanation, is easy to understand. [Note: The remaining characteristics are easily understood.
The brief commentary on the section concerning non-offenses is explained as above.
[Vinaya] Precept Eighty-three: Entering a Village at an Improper Time.
[Commentary] Precept Eighty-three: Entering a Village at an Improper Time.
[Note] Generally, when one has left the household life to cultivate the Way and has severed all worldly distractions, one must travel back and forth for the sake of sustaining life.

Since such travel occurs at an improper time and without a valid reason, entering [a village] arbitrarily abandons the Path and invites derision; the harm and ruin it causes are not few. Therefore, this rule was established.
83. Regarding the intention of the precept: First, it is stated that wandering about for amusement and dissipation is improper and should be strictly prohibited.
However, during the proper time, one must enter for alms to sustain life; once having gone out, one relies upon the bowl.
[Note] There are five conditions for committing the offense: first, it is at an improper time; second, there is no prior announcement or invitation; third, there is no formal entrustment;
fourth, one is heading toward a layperson’s house; and fifth, upon entering the gate, the offense is incurred.

The second section on the conditions for an offense: if one announces, summons, or enters [a place] without being instructed, there is no offense; however, the latter three cases constitute a violation of the Dharma. [Note:
The *Vyākhyā* on the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "If, due to such circumstances, I must go to a certain place, I announce it so that the Venerable One may know."
It is said that "listening" refers to the white dharma (*śukla-dharma*) for two reasons: first, to avoid obstructing monastic affairs;

fearing that when a *karmavācanā* is being performed, others might require their cooperation for other matters, and if it is unknown where they have gone, it would cause distress to the community of monks. Second, to prevent them from entering the homes of laypeople without restraint.
If five or three persons follow one another into a village, they should likewise announce [their presence] after ten or nine years of ordination.

If the juniors report minor matters while the seniors report major ones, it is auspicious; this is intended to demonstrate a lack of autonomy. Since the seniors entrust matters to the juniors, how could the juniors possess independent authority?
Within their own respective domains, the seniors and juniors inform one another of both major and minor affairs.
The *Vinayavibhaṅga* first indicates the necessity of the formal motion (*jñapti*), and subsequently shows the purpose for which the motion is required: 1.

Regarding monastic affairs that are generally obstructed by the fact that the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) cannot be performed within the same boundary (*sīmā*), or those legal matters that require the participation of others and may involve delays—it is necessary to inform them of one’s location so that they may be summoned to attend.
2. To ensure that those who lack autonomy may examine their own conduct; this is explained below.

Regarding the initial clarification of the "white" (announcement) within a village: the term "large white" refers to the formal announcement made at the home monastery, while "small white" refers to the announcement made again upon arriving in the village.

If the small white were performed before the large white, it would violate the established rule and thus constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the sequence from superior to inferior, if there is no corresponding person below to whom one may announce, one may open the announcement from the superior to the subordinate;
this is the primary rule. Next, regarding those situated within the boundary (*sīmā*), mutual announcements are permitted among their respective groups. Thus it is now explained.

Our school merely requires that a formal announcement (*jñapti*) be made; it does not distinguish between the primary boundary (*maṇḍala*) within the village, nor is there a regulation requiring another announcement upon reaching the village.
Now, if one performs the ritual, one should simply follow our own school’s tradition.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, Upananda entered a village at an improper time and played dice with a householder, winning.
Because the householder was stingy and jealous, he reviled and disparaged him. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked him and established this precept.
[Commentary]: "If a bhikṣu [eats] at an improper time.
[Note]: "Proper time" refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until midday; "improper time" refers to the period from after midday until the dawn light has not yet appeared.

if one is engaged in matters concerning the Saṃgha, a stūpa, or illness, or if one entrusts the matter to another bhikṣu, or if the path passes through [the village], there is no offense.
