[Commentary]: According to the *Vidyāmātra-śāstra* (*Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*), the reason for permitting entry during the "white" period is as follows: to observe faults at the place where the deceased are;
to protect the Dharma; to receive formal reliance (*niśraya*); to preach or listen to the Dharma; and because of invitations to meals.
Because it is beneficial, one is permitted to go to that place; however, one must avoid temples, shops, prostitutes, and female renunciants of non-Buddhist sects, observing them from a distance.

Next, having completed the preliminary section of the treatise, which first clarifies the permission to go, the five conditions are enumerated. Regarding the first condition, the faults of a deceased person are as follows:
Regarding the two rules for protecting the Dharma against impermanence and impurity: the third and fourth items concern the Three Jewels as causes and conditions;

the fourth item concerns monasteries, or perhaps that school [of thought] relies on entering cities and towns, in which case one must announce it. This school, however, holds that an offense is incurred based solely on relying on a lay residence.
Fifth, regarding accepting invitations: if it occurs during the proper time, it falls under the preceding precept; if it is a distant invitation separated by days, one should first...
The preceding belongs to this precept, which must be clarified below by avoiding improper places; "improper places" refers here to the quarters of nuns, namely the *ārāma*.
[Vinaya] The eighty-fourth rule concerning beds exceeding the prescribed measure.
[Commentary: The precept concerning bed-legs exceeding the prescribed measure is number eighty-four.
Generally speaking, high beds and arrogance are not the proper conduct of the Way; matters must follow the Dharma and may not exceed the limits.
To transgress them is to increase greed and violate the holy teachings; therefore, this regulation was established.

In the first section of the eighty-four rules concerning the underlying intention (*adhyāśaya*), the initial part describes matters that are inappropriate; the subsequent part clarifies compliance with the teachings; and the following section reveals the characteristics of transgressions.

[Commentary] There are five conditions for committing an offense: first, it must be a bed; second, it must be made for oneself; third, it must exceed the prescribed dimensions; fourth, one must either make it oneself or cause another to do so.
Regarding the fifth offense of "making" (kṛti), one commits a *pāyattika* for each instance of sitting upon it as it is being constructed.

According to the second fascicle of the *Fenbie chui*, this refers to sitting on a monastic bed; however, as cited below from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this specifically concerns the initial manufacture of the item.

In the present case, since the seat is already completed, one should be judged to have committed a *duṣkṛta*. Thus, the fifth offense of "making" constitutes a transgression immediately upon its completion.
The act of manufacturing [the furniture] also constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya* (提) for the maker alone.

[Commentary: According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, for laypeople observing the eight precepts, high beds are likewise measured by eight finger-widths (*aṅgula*), with one finger-width being two *cun*.

This is based on the *zhou* (周) foot, which is approximately one foot and three inches by current standards. Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the dimensions of the monastic bed that constitute an offense are as detailed in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (鈔).
Within the fixed measurements, the eight precepts for laypeople are also the same as the monastic regulations.
One *zhou* foot and six inches corresponds to one foot and three inches of the present day; this is the Tang foot.

Taking twelve inches as one Tang foot, thirty-six *fen* are counted as three inches, with an additional four *fen* remaining; thus it is said "permitted. The following refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, although...
If one constructs this monastic bed using materials that also belong to one's own share, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense;

for others, it should be a *dukkaṭa*. [Note] When the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, Kālodāyin, having foreknowledge that the Buddha would come along this path, spread out a high and fine bed in the middle of the road and said, "Look at my bed and seat! The Buddha said, "You should know, foolish man, that you harbor evil within."
The Sangha was assembled and he was rebuked; consequently, this precept was established.

Regarding the origin of the precept: first, Kāla invited the Buddha to visit him, which served as the cause for its inception; next, the Buddha rebuked him and established the rule to prevent future transgressions.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu makes a corded bed or a wooden bed (the five types as mentioned above), and the legs exceed the height of eight fingers of the Tathāgata—
excluding the portion inserted into the mortise holes— at the top, having finished the cutting, it is a pāyattika offense.

[Note]: If one performs the action oneself, instructs another to do so, or causes it to be made, it constitutes an offense of *pācittiya* if completed; if not completed, or if done for another’s sake, all such cases constitute *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding whether there is an offense or no offense: if the height is eight finger-breadths or more, or if it is less than that, or if another has given a piece of wood which was cut and used, or if the feet are detached—[in these cases, there is no offense].

[Commentary]: The precept text consists of three phrases: first, "a bhikṣu"; second, "instructing the bhikṣus to use the method of measuring with a cubit"; and third, "if it exceeds [the limit]," which concludes the offense.

Regarding the second phrase of the precept text, the five types [of materials] are annotated as above; that is, they are excluded from the aforementioned precept concerning the spreading of bedding in the open air, specifically excluding the insertion of crossbars.

Regarding the phrase "the hole above," this refers to the entry point into the *kǒngxùn* (mortise-head); it is not included in the count. "Cutting to completion" means reaching the ultimate fulfillment of the task. [Commentary:
The reason one cannot rely on human measurements using the *chǐ* (foot) is that the laws of various countries differ and local customs vary.

Therefore, we take the Buddha’s standard as the definitive measure; by using this as the fixed standard, there will forever be no discordance. The rest is as explained in the section on the precept concerning the *fáng* (bed/chamber).

The Buddha’s explanation regarding the various measurements of countries—meaning that there are differences in the length of cubits and spans—is intended to prevent disputes arising from worldly attachments where each person clings to their own single perspective.
However, when following the Buddha’s standard, one relies solely on the Buddha’s own body, for His stature is eternally fixed and serves as a definitive benchmark;
therefore, in all preceding and subsequent precepts, the span of the Buddha’s finger is consistently taken as the measure.
[Vinaya] Precept 85: The Prohibition Against Storing Cotton in Mattresses.
[Commentary] Precept 85: The Prohibition Against Storing Cotton in Mattresses.
[Commentary] Because such mattresses harbor many small and minute insects that may harm living beings, they violate compassion and destroy one's practice.
It was established as a precept because it leads to immeasurable faults.

Regarding the eighty-five rules, they were established because faults arise within the mind due to external objects; thus, they must be prohibited and severed. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), there are four reasons:

first, what is possessed by persons of high status; second, what is despised by others; third, the generation of insects; and fourth, that after lying upon something soft and warm, one becomes incapable [of maintaining mindfulness].
Because it is coarse and hard, it is now appended to the section on dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as merely one illustrative point.

[Commentary] There are five conditions for an offense: first, *tūla* (cotton); second, stuffing a mattress; third, for one's own sake; fourth, doing it oneself or having another do it; fifth, the completion of the act constitutes the offense.
Regarding the first [type of] material, *tūla*: in Sanskrit this is translated as "frost-cotton.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that *tūla* is a general term for the cotton-like fibers of plants, flowers, and grasses; it is as listed in the commentary.
[Note] While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the six groups of monks used cotton wool as bedding. A householder criticized them for killing living beings and lacking a compassionate heart.
A bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established the precept.

【Vinaya】 If a bhikṣu makes a corded bed or a wooden bed (both of which have five types as mentioned above), or a large or small mat (for the purpose of sitting or lying down), once it is completed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
(Whether he does it himself or instructs another is as stated above; the same applies to the bhikṣuṇīs regarding the offense and non-offense, as well as the permitted exceptions.)

[Commentary]: According to the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya, one should shake out [the robe] until it is completely free of dust; if it is not entirely clean, one should moisten it with water, rub it with the hand until it is finished, and then perform the confession (*pratideśanā*).

First, the opening of the substance and its distinctions; next, the opening of the making of other items; then, the enumeration of the names and characteristics of the eighteen items, as explained in detail in the *Shu* (Commentary) and *Ji* (Record).
[Vinaya] The eighty-seventh precept concerning the oversized *niṣīdana* (sitting mat).
[Commentary] The precept on oversized sitting mats is the eighty-seventh.
[Commentary] Regarding the four subsequent precepts concerning what is not permitted to be oversized: these all concern the acceptance and use of offerings from the faithful;
they should accord with the Dharma so that the original merit may increase boundlessly. This is the method for a bhikṣu to sustain his body; now, to make them oversized is an excess.

Because greed causes the loss of the merit of giving through useless expenditures, and because it leads to the ruin of the Path and the increase of karmic faults and calamities, these [precepts] were established.

Among the four precepts concerning the intention within the eighty-seventh [section], they are presented collectively because they all stem from excessive [desire]. First, there is a general exposition of what is appropriate, which has two parts:
first, that receiving offerings must be in accordance with the Dharma; second, that for the sake of the Path, one should act in accordance with conditions. Below this, the faults are revealed.

Regarding the offense of violating the two aforementioned intentions, according to the *Chao*, it requires five conditions: first, making a sitting mat; second, exceeding the prescribed dimensions; third, making it for one's own sake;

fourth, making it oneself or having another make it; and fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as it is completed. The following four cases are identical, differing only in that the first condition is modified accordingly.
[Note] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, it was the constant practice of all Buddhas that, if they did not accept an invitation, they would tour the dwellings.

Seeing that the monks’ bedding had been spread out in the open air and defiled by impurities, he addressed the bhikṣus: "Even for non-Buddhist seers who have abandoned desire, such a thing does not occur.
To provide protection for robes and bedding, I allow the making of the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat). However, the group of six [bhikṣus] made them excessively large.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.

[Commentary: Within the account of the origin (nidāna), the initial [restriction] was for the purpose of preventing defilements and obstacles to listening; the subsequent [restriction] was because it had become a great matter, and thus he established the limit.
In the commentary on the *Pratītyasamutpāda*, the initial passage describing the act of entering a room and witnessing an offense records the Buddha’s words of reprimand;

the section following "listen" establishes the formal rule; and the passage following "the group of six" describes the origin of the transgression. Regarding the latter two points concerning those who are subject to defilement and leakage, these refer specifically to the obstruction of robes and the obstruction of bedding.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana* (a sitting mat for use while seated), it must be made according to the prescribed measurement. The measurement therein is:
two spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and one and a half spans in width.
[Commentary] At that time, Kālodayin’s body was large and his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) was small; he reported this to the Buddha, who then permitted it to be enlarged.
[Vinaya] If one increases the width or length by more than half a *vitasti* (span), or if it exceeds that limit after being finished, it is a *pāyattika*.

[Note] If the length and width both exceed [the prescribed measure], or if they mutually exceed [the limit], one commits a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) for making it oneself or instructing another to make it;

there is no offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). For making it on behalf of another, there is no offense of *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in cases where [the garment] is reduced in size, or where it is folded such that another may cut it down.
[Commentary] The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
[Commentary] The first person.
[Commentary] Second, the instruction for the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) and below, which sets the limits and restrictions for the bhikṣus to perform it.
The second section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states that the length is two spans (*vitasti*), which is four feet, and the width is one and a half spans, which is three feet.
[Commentary] Regarding the "three further increases," these are allowances under specific conditions (*pratyaya*). These are added separately outside the original limits;
however, if one were to adopt them as the standard measurement, it would be the unrighteous teaching of the Vātsīputrīyas spreading throughout the world.
Regarding the first section of the three, the commentary cites the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* concerning the explanation given to the Buddha:

"to further increase by half a *vitasti* each" means that the length and width are each one *shaku* (one chi); thus, it is five [units] long and four wide. From ancient times, people have added [the measurement] only to one side and one end;
however, according to the *Gantong* (Responsive Transmission) based on what was shown by a celestial deity from Central India, the addition began with all four sides. This is stated in the text.

The initial summary and explanation of the opening conditions for the original regulation are extremely clear. (Some claim that the increase constitutes the regulation; this is because they are ignorant of the teaching.

This means that first, one relies on the original regulation to cut the length to four [units] and the width to three, completing the trimming and the sewing of the border. Subsequently, five inches are added to each of the four sides;
thus it is said that "one again increases separately outside the limits of the original regulation. If the following passage reveals what is improper, it may be that some do not perform the cutting.
To simply take a measurement of five spans in length and four in width is already contrary to the *vatsa* rule, which was abolished during the Seventh Council;
nowadays, all such practices are likewise unlawful, even if one cuts away its face and adjusts its base.

[Commentary: However, speaking of the ways of the world, people take pleasure in the vastness of their clothing and seating, and they delight in the abundance and luxury of their food, drink, and enjoyments.

When it comes to matters of austerity—examining and scrutinizing body and mind, or managing wealth and affairs—their conduct is as vast and unfathomable as the Milky Way. How could such people subdue their minds?

Their actions only serve to provoke the conceit of "self" and "other," seeking faults in the paths of others while using them to justify their own failings. Knowing this, one understands the nature of the human world.
Because this is a treasure, it causes the sitting mat to be entirely inconsistent with the teachings.

Within the subsequent admonitions, there are again four parts: first, an account of indulging one’s passions; next, an explanation of how ignorance of the teachings leads to such behavior; third, an explanation of how delusion and obscuration cause this;

and fourth, an explanation of how the ignorant do not recognize their own faults. Following this, there is a request for others to seek the Way, which includes a lament that wise people are difficult to find and a request for them to seek the path from others.

"Transgression" refers to the instruction of teachers and friends used for self-examination and correction; "self-reproach" means holding oneself accountable and confessing one's faults. Because the character *zì* (自) is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùhū*), the following four lines clarify that what is currently being done is not the Dharma.
Nowadays, people act according to their own whims and compose extensive treatises, yet they do not measure them against the standard nor eliminate their increasing views.

Instead, they perform acts based on the Dharma only to provoke derision. This is what the Patriarchs meant when they said: "In a lifetime, there has been nothing like sitting in accordance with the Dharma."
Facing these compassionate instructions, one should quickly reform their delusions.
[Commentary: The details are as found in the *Chao* (the *Shishi Yaolan*).

The reference below to the *Chao* concerns the two types of robes; therein it instructs that one should first follow the original regulations by cutting the cloth and then attaching the border (*yuan*).
If one sits down and the body cannot be accommodated, one should first rely on the method of expansion as described extensively therein.
[Vinaya] The eighty-eighth precept concerning the oversized garment for covering sores.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu suffered from a sore from which pus and blood flowed out, defiling the monastic bedding; the Buddha permitted him to use a large [garment].
A monk covered a sore with a valuable robe and put on his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) when visiting the home of a layperson. He said, "I am ill;

you should lift up your *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* so that I may cover this sore with it. The group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) then acted excessively. The other monks reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] If a bhikṣu makes a garment for covering sores (to be used for covering the body when one has various types of sores or diseases), it must be made according to the prescribed measurement.
The measurement herein is four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width. Should he finish making it exceeding these dimensions, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

[Note] If both [the donor and the recipient] exceed the limit, or if one exceeds while the other reduces it, yet the robe is completed by the recipient’s own work or by instructing another, the offense is a *pāyattika*.

If it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If it is completed for another, it is a *dukkaṭa*; if it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa* for the nun (*bhikṣuṇī*). As for cases where there is no offense: if the material is reduced to the proper measure and the robe is completed, one should cut it down to the correct size and fold it to make it fit.
[Commentary] The precept concerning the oversized wound-covering robe is the eighty-eighth.

Within the text of the eighty-eighth, the underlying intention for the prohibition and the conditions for its violation are not explained; these are identical to those in the initial account of the origin story (*nidāna*).
Regarding the phrase "the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, that is, the inner skirt, [worn] when going to the homes of laypeople," this refers to either proceeding to attend an invitation.

First, having informed them, he explained that the six groups of monks had committed the offense of rising from their seats; thus the fundamental rule was established. The four lines [of the verse] are the same as above;
the dimensions are eight chi in length and four chi in width, with the characteristics of the markings being identical.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Precept 89: Regarding Rain-Bathing Robes Exceeding the Proper Measure. [Commentary] Precept 89: Regarding Rain-Bathing Robes Exceeding the Proper Measure.

[Note] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Viśākhā, Mother of Mṛgāra, presented him with a rain-bathing robe. The Buddha said: "It shall not be divided; it should be treated according to the superior [category]."
[The Buddha] established this precept because the group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) made robes excessively large, and other monks reported their transgression to the Buddha.
[Vinaya]:
If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bath robe (varṣāśāṭī)—so called because it is worn while bathing in the rain—he must make it according to the prescribed measure. Herein, the measure is as follows:
If it exceeds six spans in length and two and a half spans in width after being cut, it is a *pāyattika*. [Note:
Whether one acts for oneself or instructs another, if both exceed the measure or either falls short, it is the same as the preceding precept; this is the exception for *bhikṣuṇīs*.
[Commentary: The characteristics and limitations can be investigated by oneself.
In the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, the brief indication regarding the regulation of the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) is the same as that for the *Pratītyasamutpāda*.

Regarding the vow made by the mother of Viśākhā to constantly provide robes for the monks and nuns, the "Six Groups of Great Monks" (the makers) refers to those who, using the cloth and materials, caused her to have them made herself.
Because they do not rely on measurements, the root precepts are also fourfold, all as above; [the robes] are one zhang and two chi in length and five chi in width.

[Commentary]: Regarding the three precepts here where the nuns' offenses are light and the monks' are heavy, and the one precept regarding rain-clothing where the regulations for monks and nuns are identical—this is the answer concerning women.
Because human bodies are subject to external impurities and because nuns take pleasure in wearing large rain-cloaks, their offenses regarding these items are the same as those for monks;

however, since the other three [types of robes] are always used as basic requisites, and nuns prefer small robes while exceeding the prescribed measurements only rarely, these offenses are treated more lightly than those for monks.

Next, among the monks and nuns, the four precepts regarding rain-clothing are collectively distinguished: [violations] of these fall under the category of *pāyattika*, whereas for the remaining three, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

Because the underlying intent of the teaching must be understood, they are all interrogated together. In the response, first the gravity of the rain-clothing rule is clarified, followed by the explanation that the remaining three are minor offenses.
[Vinaya] The ninety rules concerning the three robes exceeding the proper measure.
[Śāstra] The ninety rules concerning the measurement of the Buddha’s robes.

[Śāstra] According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, because the Buddha’s body was sixteen feet tall while ordinary people were half that height, the measurements of his robes were all half those of Nanda, who was shorter than the Buddha.
Because there were not many old robes, they reduced the length by one foot and the width by four inches. Among those born of the *Saṃghāṭī*, Nanda and Māyādevī possessed thirty marks;
the color of their robes was different from that of the Buddha, whereas the robes of the other bhikṣus were the same color as the Buddha's.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw this, they assumed the measurements were also the same, and consequently made their robes identical in size.

Regarding the first of the ninety rules (*navati-śikṣāpada*) concerning the circumstances of the origin: according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the Buddha’s body and robes were equal in measure to those of an ordinary person, as will be seen in the subsequent explanation.
Since Nanda was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha—which is eight inches—it is said that he was "not much [smaller]," meaning not by much.
The robe was one zhang and seven chi in length and one zhang, one chi, and six cun in width; a single person could not manage two.

The Arhat Nanda, who had usurped the status of a Buddha, was inferior to the Buddha by two marks: he lacked the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra-cakra*), both of which belong only to a Buddha.
Regarding the color of his robes, while the Buddha ordained that Nanda wear black robes, other bhikṣus did not wear them so as to avoid confusion with the Buddha;
thus, they were the same as the Buddha’s. The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks, being unable to discern the difference, made robes of equal measurement to those of others.
This was for the purpose of instigation.
[Note] While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, Nanda—who was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha—was seen from afar by a bhikṣu who went out to welcome him, thinking it was the Buddha;

only upon reaching him did he realize his mistake, and each felt shame. Consequently, the Buddha ordained that Nanda should wear black robes, and that the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) should be equal in size to the Buddha.

Whether making robes of standard measurement or exceeding the standard measurement, a bhikṣu who makes them so incurs an offense. Because the Buddha was criticized for this, he established the precept.
In the *Nidāna* (the account of the origin), first Nanda’s robes were confused with those of the Tathāgata, and subsequently the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks exceeded the proper measure.
[The Vinaya states: If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to that of the Tathāgata, or makes one exceeding that size, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).
Regarding the measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe among these: it is nine *vitasti* in length and six *vitasti* in width; this is called the measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe. [Note:

If the width and length are correct but the other dimensions are incorrect, one commits an offense. This applies equally whether one acts for oneself, instructs another, or has a nun act on one's behalf.
As stated above, there is no offense if one obtains a finished garment from another that has been cut to the proper measurements; nor is there an offense if it is folded into two layers.

[Commentary]: The four phrases of the precept text are: first, clarifying the person; second, clarifying the giving of a robe equal to those of the Buddha; third, concluding with the offense; and fourth, providing further details.
The fixed measurement for a Buddha’s robe:
according to the second phrase of the *Prātimokṣa*, one has already committed an offense if the robe is equal to the prescribed measure, let alone if it exceeds it.

[Commentary] Question: While the other three precepts establish their limits for measurements based on the Buddha’s span (*vitasti*), why does the single precept concerning the three robes merely follow along?

Regarding those who do not have a fixed measure for their own bodies, the answer is that others—those who are not śramaṇas—may use robes of external appearance regardless of whether they are large or small;

therefore, there is a fixed measure. These three dharma-robes are the outward symbols of the monastic vocation. If the measure were fixed, some people would be too tall or too short, which would not accord with dignified deportment;
externally, it would fail to inspire goodness, and internally, there would be no standard for conduct. Therefore, [the robes] should conform to the dimensions of the individual's body.
Regarding the indefinite measurement for making robes, because it is indefinite, there is the fault of making them equal in size to the Buddha’s robe.
In the question-and-answer section, the initial question concerns all three precepts as being established by the standard measurement for bhikṣus;

however, this particular precept only prohibits making them equal to the Buddha’s robe, and thus the bhikṣu’s robe does not exceed the fixed measurement. In the answer, first the fixed measurements for the other three are shown.
Next, regarding the fact that the dharma-robe is not indefinite: externally, it does not give rise to goodness, meaning that one might harbor arrogance regarding one's secular appearance;

internally, there is no standard for conduct, meaning that the Way would lack a rule for emulation. By showing this below, [the author] indicates the fundamental cause of the subsequent precepts. If there were a fixed regulation, it would not allow for equality with the Buddha.
If this is so, why does the *Shuochao* (Commentary), in the section on the two robes, cite various Vinaya texts to demonstrate the dimensions of the three robes? Why does it say...?
Question: Is this indefinite? Answer: It is merely established as a standard by citing the Dharma; it differs from cases such as the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), which one may never exceed.

The private interpretation that the precepts concerning the Buddha’s robes and so forth constitute the fixed regulation for a bhikṣu’s three robes implies that everything within them is universally permitted to be exceeded.
How could this not be a fixed regulation? Therefore, the precept is specifically designated as "the precept on exceeding the measure of the three robes."

[Commentary] Question: Within the *Prātimokṣa*, there are instances where the length is ten *tala* or nine *tala* finger-breadths; by what textual authority is this determined? Answer: Nine *tala* constitutes the length of the robe.

According to the Zhou cubit, this is one zhang eight chi in length and one zhang two chi in width. Thus, in terms of the current [Han] system, it is nine chi and six chi respectively. Therefore, the robe—
Regarding the doubt concerning usage: if one takes ten *zhè* as a *dù*, that constitutes two *zhàng* and a half, which corresponds to eight *chǐ* in the present system.
According to the measurement of five *zhǒu*, it is seven feet and five inches; therefore, this is set forth so that one may adjust it according to one's own judgment.
Next, a question is raised regarding the fact that some versions of the precepts originally state "ten spans" (*vitasti*); this is resolved through the following response.

First, it is shown that the Buddha’s body was twice the size of a human's; therefore, the ten spans were halved. Next, it clarifies that those who harbor doubts because ten spans seem too narrow are merely adding to the measure out of their own deluded human sentiments.
According to the Zhou *chi*, this would be twenty feet; if halved, it would be ten feet for an ordinary person.
The "eight chi" of the present day is the *Táng* (Tang) chi. According to the standard, it measures eight chi and four cun;
however, taking the full number as five *zhǔ* (cubits), we further cite nine chi to calibrate against the *Táng* chi. One *zhǔ* equals one chi and eight cun; thus, five *zhǔ* equal nine chi.
Taking the Zhou measurement of eight chi and four cun as seven chi plus six cun of the *Táng* measurement, we round the six cun down to five cun; hence, the conclusion below.
[The text] indicates that because there might be attachment or contention [regarding robes], no fixed limit is established for them.
[Commentary (Sū)] Question: Why is it that while the regulation of robes sets a maximum size, such a limit is not set for the alms bowl? Answer: A robe is a Dharma-robe;

it must not have a fixed measurement, as its dimensions must correspond to the physical needs of the wearer. Therefore, a limit is set for it. As for the bowl, it is used solely for food; since there is no variation in the size of the food itself, a fixed limit is established for it.

Question: Since the matters regarding robes and bowls are similar, why is there a partial restriction? Answer: In the first part of the response, it clarifies that robes must be restricted because they are permitted to be carried on one's person;
thus, restrictions are imposed on excesses and so forth. Next, it clarifies that bowls do not require such restrictions, as their three grades are permanently fixed and no excess is possible.

[Commentary]: If this is so, what is the fixed measure for the Buddha’s robes? Answer: For his disciples, there is no limit, as they cannot be fixed by a standard; however, because there is only one Buddha in the world, his robes are fixed.

Furthermore, it is explained that regarding the transgression of exceeding the size of a robe, cutting [the excess] is common, whereas regarding the transgression of exceeding the size of an alms bowl, cutting [the excess] is rare; therefore, [excessive robes] were prohibited, while [excessive bowls] were not.

In the response to the first of the two difficult questions within the "Turning Difficulties" section, there are two interpretations. First, it is explained by way of the teacher and disciples being one or many.
Next, it is explained by way of cutting off the number of hopes.
[Commentary]: If this is so, why is the bowl not made equal in size to the Buddha’s? The answer is that because the substance of the robe is the same, there would be faults such as those mentioned.

Because the substance of the bowl differs, it cannot be the same [as that of the Buddha]. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Zhidu lun) states: "The various Buddhas of the Dharma keep celestial bowls and human robes;
these two serve as fields of merit for the two realms. Because celestial stone is fine and capable of being maintained, bhikṣus are not permitted to possess it.

The stone of the human realm is coarse and incapable of being refined; because their merit and virtue are shallow, they do not attract celestial bowls, and because the power of their physical substance is inferior, they cannot [use them]."

Because he felt compassion for the bhikṣus who must inevitably experience fatigue and hardship while carrying it, [the Buddha] did not permit its possession; this was unlike the case of the Buddha himself, who possessed the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
Ānanda’s strength was great enough to roll a stone forty *li* in circumference, yet as an attendant to the Buddha, he did not consider it heavy.

In the initial response to the objection, it is first explained that while the substance (*dravya*) of the robe is the same, its quantity may overlap; however, since the substance of the bowl is distinct, there is no such overlap.
My personal interpretation is that for robes, the substance is not restricted, so the quantity is restricted; for bowls, the quantity is not restricted, so the substance is restricted.
A bhikṣu must not possess a stone bowl; thus, one should know that there is no overlap between the two cases of robes and bowls. (From *Zhìxià*).
To demonstrate the distinct nature [of the bowl], since the Buddha kept a stone bowl, the initial section clarifies the Buddha’s intention for keeping it.
It states that on the four mountain peaks of the Four Heavenly Kings, stones were produced spontaneously; these stones were fine-grained and did not retain grease.

The *Benqi jing* (Sutra of the Origin of the Buddha) says that the Four Kings each took one and offered them to the Buddha, who accepted them all together, holding them in his left hand while pressing them with his right; thus they were divided into four sections at the edges.
The explanation follows. There are three reasons why a bhikṣu cannot hold [the bowl]: first, the stone is coarse; second, there is no resonance; third, the body lacks the requisite weight.
This differs from the following [case] which resolves doubts: since it is said that the body lacks the requisite weight, why did the Buddha hold it?

Even if the Buddha possessed such power, Ānanda, as the Buddha’s attendant, would also have been able to hold it. This explanation clarifies the general principle and demonstrates that the bhikṣu was indeed unable [to do so].
One may keep the Kṣānti-nārāyaṇa—here translated as "Vajra" or "the wrestler with the hook and chain.
[Vinaya: "Venerable sirs, I have already recited the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas. Now I ask the venerable sirs:
