[Sūtra] It is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense to walk with arms swinging (swinging the arms back and forth while entering the house of a layperson). [Commentary] There is no offense in the following cases:
if one has an illness; if one raises the hand to ward off someone who is striking another; if one raises the hand to ward off a wild beast or a person being carried by or pierced by a stake;
or if one uses the hand to beckon a companion while crossing a canal by swimming.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] 17. It is an offense of wrong-doing (śikṣākaraṇīya) to swing one's arms while walking into the house of a layperson.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] 18. The precept regarding being naked in the house of a layperson.
[Note] While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks entered the homes of laypeople with their bodies improperly covered.

Lay devotees criticized them, saying, "The robes they wear do not properly cover the body, like those of Brahmins. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established a rule.
[Sūtra] To enter the house of a layperson with the body poorly covered (or, if in a village, with parts of the body exposed) is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
[Commentary] There is no offense if one is ill, or if one is bound, or if the wind blows the robe away from the body.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Nineteenth Śikṣākaraṇīya: Sitting in the house of a layperson while properly covering one’s body.

[Commentary] Among these nineteen rules, if any part of the body is exposed, one should employ skillful means to have someone take hold of it; if it is a woman who does so, one should rise and move away.
The nineteenth asaṃkhyeya kalpa refers to when, while among the assembly, one sees someone with their body exposed who intends to take an object;
one wishes to alert that person, yet the woman—referring here to a bhikṣuṇī—intentionally exposes her body.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The twentieth precept concerning looking around while entering the house of a layperson.

[Commentary] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks looked left and right as they entered the house of a layperson. A householder criticized them, saying, "They are like thieves.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the rule.
【Vinaya】 One must not look left and right (even while looking about here and there within a village) when walking into the house of a layperson; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense.

【Note】There is no offense in cases where one is ill; or when observing the time of day or the seasons; or when facing the two difficulties of life or the Brahma-faring (i.e., threats to life or loss of chastity);
or when seeking a way to escape by fleeing through various nearby routes.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] 21. It is an *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense to sit in the house of a layperson while looking left and right. [Prātimokṣa Sūtra] 22.
It is an offense regarding the house of a layperson to speak in a loud voice.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople shouting loudly. The householders criticized them, saying, "They are like Brahmins;
they have no sense of shame and possess no True Dharma. The monks reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the precept.

【Vinaya】 Entering the house of a layperson in silence— within this context, if one does not remain silent by shouting loudly, making a great clamor, giving instructions, or calling out loudly while offering food, it is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
【Note】There is no offense in cases such as: being ill; being deaf and unable to hear [the instruction]; needing to speak loudly when giving instructions; speaking loudly while offering food;
or running at a loud voice due to the two dangers of life or the Brahma-faring life.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] 23. The training rule concerning sitting in silence in the house of a layperson (*śikṣākaraṇīya*). [Prātimokṣa Sūtra] 24.
The training rule concerning laughing and joking in the house of a layperson.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople while laughing and joking. A householder criticized them, saying:

"They have no shame; they laugh and joke like monkeys. How can there be true Dharma in such bhikṣus? The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established a rule.
[Sūtra] It is an *śaikṣa-dharmā* offense to enter the house of a layperson while laughing or smiling with bared teeth.
[Commentary] There is no offense in cases where one is ill, or where the lips are painful and the teeth cannot be covered, or where one laughs out of joy while recollecting the Dharma.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] 25. One must not sit in a laughing or joking manner in the house of a layperson; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
[Commentary] Regarding the twenty-fifth [offense], in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, it is stated that when faced with something laughable, one must not bare one's gums and laugh "ha-ha";

rather, one should endure it by contemplating the thought of impermanence and death. Furthermore, if it cannot be endured, one should cover the mouth with one’s robe. If the body is not composed, one should move the hands [to signal restraint].
He tramples upon grasses and trees.
During twenty-five *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, his gums—that is, the flesh at the roots of his teeth—were subjected to the teaching of suppression and the dharma of patience;
furthermore, he was taught skillful means and concealment in order to avoid the ridicule of the world.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Precept 26: Receiving Food Without Careful Attention.

[Commentary] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a lay devotee invited the Saṃgha to provide an offering. The group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) received food without careful attention, casting away the soup and rice.
The lay devotee criticized them, saying: "These śramaṇas have no sense of moderation; their greedy hearts cause them to receive as much as during times of high grain prices."
The Buddha, having cited the fault, prohibited it.
[Vinaya]: To receive food with improper attention (if one does not pay attention, the soup and rice are discarded) constitutes a *śikṣākarani*.
[Commentary] There is no offense in cases such as when one has such an illness, or when the bowl is small and rice is discarded during the meal, or when it falls back onto the table.
[Sub-commentary] Twenty-sixth:
With the left hand held steady and the mind focused, lift the bowl while supporting its rim with the right hand.
26. The characteristics of the underlying intent as shown in five parts.
[Vinaya] 27. The precept against receiving food with an overflowing bowl.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, a householder invited the Saṃgha; the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks received food with overflowing bowls, discarding the soup and rice. They resided...

The laypeople criticized him, saying he was shameless and insatiable, like a starving person greedily seeking more. Because the bhikṣus reported his transgression, [the Buddha] rebuked him and established the precept.

[The Vinaya states: One should receive food with a level bowl (a "level" bowl means one that does not overflow). This is a *śaikṣakaraṇīya* (a training rule). There is no offense if one is ill at the time, or if the bowl is small, or if the food falls onto the table.

[Commentary]: The *Āgama* recited by the twenty-seven [schools] states: "One should not receive food such that it overflows the bowl. This clarifies the meaning of the term "level bowl" (*sama-pātra*).
A certain master, following the literal sound of the word, annotated the precept, saying: "The term 'not level' refers to avoiding the fault of partiality or tilting."
The twenty-seventh recitation clarifies the characteristics [of the practice]: because one is not permitted to receive food until the bowl overflows, it is called "level bowl";
and because there is a lower censure for those who do not hold the bowl upright, it is called "free from partiality and deviation."
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The twenty-eighth precept: Receiving soup with an overflowing bowl.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a lay devotee prepared an offering. The group of six monks took such an excessive amount of rice that there was no room for the soup.
The lay devotee criticized them, saying they were like hungry, greedy eaters. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established this rule.
[Sūtra] Receiving soup with a level bowl [so that it overflows and causes staining] is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
[Commentary] There is no offense in cases such as when one is ill, when the bowl is small, when food falls onto the table, or when receiving [the soup] in a level manner.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Rule 29: The Precept Against Unequal Receiving of Food.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a lay devotee prepared an offering. He personally served the food, and having first set down the rice, he went inside to fetch the soup.

Upon his return, the rice had already been finished; when he gave him the soup, the rice was gone. He returned again for more rice, and by the time he returned, the soup was finished. This led to censure as being comparable to such behavior.
Because a starving bhikṣu raised this fault, [the Buddha] reprimanded him and established the precept.
[Vinaya]: When eating rice and soup together (if they are not equal, it means the rice is finished before the soup), it is a *śaikṣakaraṇīya*.
【Note】 There is no offense if one is ill; or if one requires only soup and not rice, or likewise requires only rice and not soup; or if the time for eating is about to expire;
or if one eats quickly due to the two difficulties of life or the Brahma-faring (i.e., threats to life or to the religious life).
[The Vinaya] Precept 30: Regarding Receiving Food Out of Order. [Commentary]:
While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, a householder prepared a meal offering and personally served the food. The group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) took their portions out of order.
The householder criticized them, saying: "They have no sense of satiety; they are like pigs, dogs, oxen, donkeys, camels, crows, or birds. The bhikṣus reported this transgression.
The Buddha, because of this, rebuked and established a rule:
[Vinaya] One should eat in proper sequence (if one does not eat in sequence, it means taking food from various places within the bowl to eat); this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense.
[Note] There is no offense in cases where one is ill; or when the rice is hot and one picks out a cool spot; or when the time for the meal is about to pass;
or when there is an urgent need regarding life or the holy life (brahmacarya); or when eating quickly due to such difficulties.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Rule 31: The Precept Against Scooping Up Food from the Alms Bowl.

[Commentary] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a householder prepared an offering and personally served the food. The group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) accepted the food and began scooping it up from the bowl to gaze at the empty space within.
The householder criticized them, saying: "You never tire of receiving food; you are just like oxen, donkeys, horses, camels, and pigs."
The Bhikṣu Śvāna addressed the Buddha, and as a result of his reproach, the precept was established:

[Vinaya] “One must not scoop up food from the center of the bowl (by pushing it toward the four edges and then scooping from the center down to the bottom) while eating; this is a *śaikṣakaraṇīya* offense.”
[Note] There is no offense in cases where one has an illness and is permitted to cool hot food by opening it; or where the time for the meal is about to expire;
or where one eats from the middle of a vessel due to the two difficulties of life or the holy life (brahmacarya).
[Note] The thirty-second [precept] concerns begging for food for oneself.
[Note] While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the householder provided an offering, yet the group of six monks begged for food on their own behalf as if they were starving.

The householder criticized them, saying, "How can there be true Dharma when you accept offerings without satiety? The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the rule.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] When not ill (if one is ill, it is permitted to seek food for oneself), one must not seek out soup or rice for oneself; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
[Commentary] There is no offense if one is ill, or if seeking for another, or if another seeks for oneself, or if one obtains it without having requested it.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The precept on covering soup with rice with the three fingers.

[Commentary] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a householder prepared an offering. The group of six monks received the soup; the householder recognized their turn and took the soup, but the bhikṣus followed behind and covered the soup with rice.
The householder censured them, saying: "In receiving and taking, you have no satiety; you are like people suffering from famine."
There was a bhikṣu of the True Dharma who reported a transgression to the Buddha;
consequently, the Buddha rebuked him and established a precept: [Vinaya] "One must not cover the soup with rice while hoping to obtain more; this is a śaikṣa-dharma."
[Commentary] There is no offense in cases where one is ill, or has been invited to a meal, or when soup is specifically required, or when rice is specifically required at that time.
[Vinaya] The thirty-fourth precept concerning looking at a fellow monk with a look of disdain.
[Note] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a householder prepared a meal. The group of six monks received a small portion, yet they asked their fellow monks for a larger share.

They said to the householder, "You have invited the Saṃgha to partake at will; how much do you intend to give? The householder, being partial, replied, "We are giving this to the monks who point out faults.
The Buddha, on account of this, established the precept.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] It is an *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense to look into the bowl of a neighboring seat [to see who has more or less food].

[Commentary] There is no offense if the neighboring seat is ill, or if one’s own eyesight is dim; or if one looks to see whether food may be taken or not, whether it is pure or impure, or whether it has been formally accepted or not;
or if one is oneself ill, it is permitted.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The thirty-fifth precept: Not eating with the bowl unrestrained.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a householder prepared a meal. After the group of six monks had received it, they looked left and right;
unaware, their neighbor took their bowls and hid them. A bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who, having rebuked them, established this precept.
[Sūtra] One should eat with the thought that the bowl is tied [to one’s person] (meaning one does not look left or right); this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.

[Commentary] There is no offense in the following cases: when one is ill; when the neighbor to one's seat has impaired vision and one uses the aforementioned expedient means; when one observes the time of day;
or when, due to the two difficulties of life or the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one looks left and right in order to escape.
[The Vinaya]: The thirty-sixth precept concerning large mouthfuls of solid food.

[Commentary]: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a householder prepared an offering. The group of six monks took such large mouthfuls that their mouths could not close. The householder criticized them, saying, "They do not know moderation;
they are like pigs, dogs, camels, donkeys, oxen, crows, or birds. When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, established the rule.
The Precept on Taking Bites of Food. [Vinaya]: One must not take a large mouthful of food that cannot be accommodated by the mouth; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*. [Commentary]:
There is no offense if one is ill, or if there is a danger to life or to the holy life (*brahmacarya*) as the time for eating is passing, and one eats quickly.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The thirty-seventh precept on waiting for food with the mouth wide open.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, a lay devotee prepared a meal offering. Before the bhikṣus had arrived, he opened his mouth wide. The lay devotee criticized him, saying:
"He is shameless and insatiable, like a pig, a dog, a camel, an ox, or a donkey. The bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked him and established this rule.
[Sūtra] One must not open one’s mouth wide to await food (opening the mouth wide before the morsel has arrived); this is a *śaikṣakaraṇīya*.

[Commentary] There is no offense in cases such as when one has a certain illness, or when the day is about to end, or when there is a life-threatening or *brahmacarya*-threatening emergency, and one eats quickly.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The thirty-eighth precept concerning speaking while chewing food.

[Vinaya] While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a householder prepared a meal. The group of six bhikṣus chewed their food while speaking to the householder, disparaging him with similes such as pigs, dogs, camels, and crows.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the rule.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] One must not speak with food in the mouth (for when food is in the mouth, speech cannot be articulated and others will not understand); this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
[Commentary] There is no offense in cases where one has an illness, or is choking and asks for water, or makes a sound while eating due to the two perils of life or the Brahma-faring life.

[Commentary]: Regarding the thirty-eight *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, if a monk asks whether the sound [of the recitation] should differ, one answers that it should not; otherwise, having swallowed [the food], one answers.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when distributing supplementary food (*vighasa*), one must determine whether it is required or not.
Regarding the thirty-eighth point, the monks asked: "If the sound is not different, why is it that although there is food in the mouth, the speech is still distinct?
It is not the case that the sound is different; rather, because one may or may not need to speak when approaching those who benefit from the five practices, the speaking is permitted."
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The precept against tossing thirty-nine morsels of food into the mouth.

[Commentary] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a householder invited the Saṃgha and personally served them. The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks tossed morsels of food from a distance into their mouths.
The householder criticized them, saying, "They are shameless and insatiable, just like illusionists. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established this rule.
Precept. [Vinaya] One must not take morsels of food and toss them into the mouth from a distance; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
[Commentary] There is no offense if one is ill, or if, being bound, one tosses food into the mouth while eating.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The forty-first precept on the dropping of food.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a householder prepared a meal. The group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) held lumps of rice in their hands and chewed them halfway while eating.
The householder criticized them, saying, "You accept food without satiety, like pigs, dogs, camels, donkeys, oxen, crows, or birds. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha.

[The Buddha] prohibited it because of [this incident]. [Vinaya]: It is a *śaikṣakaraṇīya* offense not to drop food while eating (with half already in the mouth and half remaining in the hand). [Commentary]:
There is no offense in cases of illness when eating thin cakes, parched rice, or melons; or when eating sugarcane, vegetables, pears, fruits, or lotus roots.
"Regarding the peach blossom, leaf, and heart [of fruit]:
[Commentary] If one divides forty *saṃkhyeya* kalpas' worth of flour cakes into individual morsels of appropriate size, there is no offense regarding fruits, melons, and the like.

Many people do not understand this precept, thinking that if one holds an object in the hand and bites it so that half enters the mouth, while the other half remains in the hand, [it constitutes an offense]."

For this reason, it is said that the text has been omitted; the citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that "piece by piece" means cutting with the hand until the pieces form a mass suitable for being placed in the mouth.
Regarding fruits, melons, and the like, the rule is relaxed; in general terms, whatever can be cut constitutes an offense, while whatever cannot be cut is permitted.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Rule 41: The Prohibition Against Cheek-Filling Food.
[Commentary] While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, a householder provided a meal offering. The group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) ate with their cheeks full. The householder, feeling resentment, said:
"These śramaṇas have no sense of shame; they eat like monkeys. A bhikṣu reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established this precept.
**[Vinaya]** One must not eat with cheeks puffed out (resembling the appearance of a monkey); this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense.
**[Commentary]** There is no offense in cases where one is ill, when the time for eating is about to expire, or when there is danger to life or to the holy life, and one eats quickly.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Precept 42: Chewing food while making noise.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, the householder was providing a meal for the Saṃgha. The group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) chewed their food while making noise.

The householder criticized them, saying, "They are like pigs, dogs, camels, oxen, donkeys, crows, and birds. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established this rule.
**[Vinaya]** One must not eat making noise while chewing food; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
**[Commentary]** There is no offense in cases of illness when chewing dry cakes, scorched rice, sugarcane, melons, fruits, grapes, walnuts, chestnuts, peaches, pears, or windpears.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The forty-third precept on slurping while eating.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a householder provided a meal offering. The group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) ate with loud slurping sounds, which the householder detested, saying:
"They have no sense of shame; they eat like pigs, dogs, camels, oxen, donkeys, crows, or birds. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who, having rebuked them, established this precept.
[Sūtra] One must not take large mouthfuls of food (opening the mouth wide to call out and gulp down food); this is a *śikṣāpada*.
[Commentary] There is no offense if one is ill, or if there is pain in the mouth, or if one is eating soup, or milk, curd, whey, *pīlu* juice, or sour vinegar.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The forty-fourth precept concerning licking while eating.

[Commentary] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a householder prepared an offering. The group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) protruded their tongues as they ate, causing the householder to express his resentment, saying:

"They have no sense of shame or modesty; they are like pigs, dogs, camels, oxen, donkeys, crows, or birds. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established this precept.
【Vinaya】 One must not lick food with the tongue (licking morsels of rice with the tongue); this is a *śikṣāpada* offense.
【Commentary】There is no offense if one has an illness, is bound, or if the hands are soiled with mud or grease such that one licks them to take the food.

[Commentary: For forty-four *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas, the monk who directly supervised the distribution of food would, in order to know whether the food was cooked or raw, salty or sour, place it upon the palm of his hand and lick it with his tongue.
Because this was done during the time of the original regulation for receiving food, it was permitted as an exception based on those circumstances.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The forty-fifth precept: Eating while shaking the hand.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a householder prepared an offering and personally served the food. The group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) shook their hands as they ate.

The householder criticized them, saying, "There is no true Dharma here; it is like that of kings and ministers. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established this precept.
**[Vinaya]** One must not shake one's hand while eating; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* offense.
**[Commentary]** There is no offense in the following cases: if one has an illness; if there is grass or insects in the food and one shakes them off; if the hand is impure and one shakes it off;
or if the hand has been defiled by touching food that has not yet been formally received (*paribhoga*) and one shakes it off.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] The forty-sixth precept: Regarding eating scattered food while holding it in the hand.

[Commentary] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, a householder prepared an offering. The group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) ate with their hands grasping the scattered rice. The householder spoke with displeasure, saying, "They eat like chickens or birds.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established the rule.
【Vinaya】 One must not eat by hand while scattering the rice (scattering refers to discarding the rice); this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.

【Commentary】 There is no offense if one has an illness, or if there is grass or insects in the food, or if it is defiled by impurities, or if one discards food that has not yet been formally accepted (*parigṛhīta*).
**The Vinaya:** The forty-seventh precept concerning holding a drinking vessel with hands soiled by oily food.

**Commentary:** While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, a householder prepared an offering. The group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks held the vessel with hands soiled by impure, oily food. The householder expressed his displeasure, saying, "There is no Dharma here;
it is like that of kings and great ministers. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established this precept.
[Sūtra] One must not hold a drinking vessel with soiled hands (such as hands stained with greasy rice); this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
[Commentary] There is no offense in cases where one has an illness, or receives [the vessel] upon grass, or receives it upon a leaf, or receives it after having washed one's hands.
[Commentary]: During the forty-seven *kalpas*, he received drinking vessels; he was not permitted to hold them deep in his mouth.
If they touched his forehead or nose, he was not allowed to drink them dry, but must leave a small amount remaining and discard it at the level of his mouth, giving it to those of lower rank.

Forty-seven: For forty-seven *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one must not touch the drinking vessel to the forehead or nose, nor discard it while it still contains a small amount of liquid for fear of staining or defiling it;
one should wipe the rim of its opening.
[Vinaya] Forty-eight: One must observe the precept against discarding bowl-washing water at the homes of laypeople.
[Note] When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks discarded the water used for rinsing their bowls while eating in a layperson's home, leaving the food in disarray.
A householder criticized them, saying, "They receive so much as if they were starving beggars. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently established the precept.
**[Vinaya]** A *śikṣamāṇā* must not discard bowl-washing water (which contains mixed rice-water) inside the residence of a layperson.
**[Commentary]** There is no offense if one has an illness, or if at that time the water is collected in a vessel or a basin, and it is carried outside to be discarded.
[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] Precept 49: Regarding defecating or urinating upon living grass.

[Commentary] While the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, the group of six monks defecated, urinated, spat, and snotted upon blades of grass. When householders saw this, they reviled them, saying, "They have no shame or modesty;
they are like pigs, dogs, camels, oxen, and donkeys. The bhikṣus reported this transgression to the Buddha, who consequently rebuked them and established this precept.
【Vinaya】 One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate upon living grass, except in cases of illness (if one is unable to avoid it due to illness, it is said that there is no offense).
This is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*.
[Commentary] There is no offense if [the excrement] falls onto the leaves of living plants, or if it is carried off by a bird and dropped.
[Vinaya Rule] The precept regarding the discharge of feces, urine, mucus, or saliva into water (50).

[Prātimokṣa Sūtra] "Venerable sirs, these seven principles for the settlement of disputes come from the half-monthly recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Whenever a dispute arises among the bhikṣus, it should be settled immediately."

[Note] The Buddha stated that there are four kinds of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*): disputes concerning speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*), disputes concerning search (*anveṣaṇa-adhikaraṇa*), disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*), and disputes concerning matters (*kṛtya-adhikaraṇa*).

Disputes concerning speech are settled by means of two methods: the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (settlement before the eyes) and the *yadbhūyaḥ-kalpa* (decision by the majority). Disputes concerning search are settled by means of four methods: the *pratyakṣa-vinaya*, the *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by memory), the *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one who is not insane), and the *tatsvabhāva-avasthāpana* (settlement by the nature of the case).

Disputes concerning offenses are settled by means of three methods: the *pratyakṣa-vinaya*, the *pratijñā-kāraka* (settlement by confession), and the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (settlement by covering over as with grass).
Regarding the settling of disputes through cessation (*nirodha*), all forms of cessation are used to settle the three types of dispute.

Each is divided into three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—making nine types of disputes in total when combined. One type of dispute passes through each of the three [preceding] disputes, resulting in nine grades accordingly.

Among the five methods of settlement (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), one should skillfully observe and understand how the three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—are applied as medicines according to the specific afflictions (*vyādhi*).
[Commentary] The eighth section of the main body of the text, following the previous explanation, concerns the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha*).

Regarding these seven methods for settling disputes, there are specific therapeutic prescriptions for each, corresponding to the particular ailments and applied according to the capacity of the practitioner through skillful means and ritual protocols; it would be impossible to explain them all exhaustively here.
The *Vinaya-mātṛkā* (Basic Collection of the Vinaya) occupies a single chapter alone, and while various masters have followed it with some degree of brevity, as for the specific articles...

That the tradition has rarely emerged from its fundamental path is truly due to the fact that the textual characteristics are so fully developed that their interpretations have become indistinguishable.

Now, I shall briefly cite their characteristics to demonstrate the methods for treating and extinguishing them. This is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the four types of dispute as the source from which affliction arises;
second, listing the seven medicines as the methods for their eradication.

In the eighth section, "An Exposition of the Seven Methods for Settling Disputes," the first two lines set forth the intent of the chapter: the four types of disputes are like diseases, and the seven methods are able to eliminate them like medicines.
"Contemplation" (dṛṣṭi) refers to the ability to sever [disputes]; one must examine this with precision. "Confrontation" (pratipakṣa) means that the medicine and the disease must not be mismatched.
"Appropriate application" (yathāyogam) refers to wisdom and strategy; "expediency" (upāya) refers to using or setting aside [methods] as the occasion requires. This chapter is thus brought forth.

Observing conditions and adapting accordingly, the application of medicine to eliminate disputes is merely a skillful means for harmonizing the assembly. The next two phrases demonstrate the breadth of the matter;
the final two phrases point to the source in the Vinaya: the *Bhikṣu-vibhaṅga* (the Collection of Fundamental Laws), specifically the *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (Khandhaka on the Settling of Disputes).
Regarding the section on "Various Masters," the initial part describes the past: the first two phrases point to what was lost—namely, negligence—which refers to a lack of detailed investigation.

"Mutual succession" means that there is no pervasive transformation; it follows the sequence. The next two phrases clarify what is lacking: "principles" (*tiao*) refers to systematic order, and "pervasion" (*guan*) refers to comprehensive integration.
Because within the original text the medicines and illnesses were intermingled and disordered, they must be systematically organized so that each has its own fundamental path.
Since this was previously unclarified, it is said that [such works] rarely appeared. The final two phrases demonstrate the reason for this mutual succession through the text.
"Phenomena" (xiàng) refers to the two introductory sections of the *Khandaka*; these two points reverse the previous two meanings: first, not being restricted solely to following old traditions;

second, demonstrating the path of the school's tenets. As shown below, the demonstration of phenomena, the classification of chapters, the presentation of remedies in correspondence with ailments, and so forth, all possess systematic order. This is it.

[Commentary]: Regarding the first point, if a dispute arises and it is immediately eliminated, this is because the ordinary mind has received the Way, yet the inversion of self has not yet been overturned.
When living together, one frequently gives rise to perceptions of fault; if these faults are not eliminated, old habits will only increase further.

If one investigates and examines [the situation], harboring delusion leads to contention. Once contention is in full swing, where is the harmony of the Sangha? Therefore, the Buddha established regulations so that [disputes] must be eliminated immediately.
If one suppresses [conflict] without reflecting upon it, the Great Dharma will eventually be subverted; there is no reason why the Three Jewels would not perish in this world other than through this.

Thus, the cause for the outbreak of strife in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī and the subsequent extinction of the Dharma both occurred in this very country. First, one must recognize the "disease. What constitutes strife?
Briefly, it is divided into three parts: first, recognizing its names and characteristics; second, distinguishing its categories and degrees; third, the methods for its pacification and eradication.

In the initial clarification of the four types of disputes (*caturvivāda*), within the section explaining the underlying intent, there are first two parts concerning the harm caused by the arising of disputes:

first, up to the point "further increasing old habits," which refers to the damage to oneself; second, up to the point "the harmony and peace of the Saṃgha are established," which refers to the destruction of the communal Dharma.

Below these two, the section explains the benefits of establishing rules to extinguish disputes: "even if one does not reflect" means that even if one indulges in deluded attachments and fails to reflect upon them, [the rules] will cover and suppress such transgressions.
The Dharma and the Buddha—these two jewels—rely upon the Saṃgha for their endurance; if the meaning of the Saṃgha is lost, how can the Buddha-Dharma remain?
To provide proof, the following passage from the *Kauśāmbī* episode is cited: The Vinaya clarifies that when the Buddha was in that country, the bhikṣus were quarreling with one another.
The Buddha personally exhorted them, saying: "You have left the household life to pursue the Way, studying under the same Teacher. You should be like water and milk blending together."
"Do not engage in such quarreling," he said three times; yet they still did not desist.

The Buddha did not speak further, but taking his robes and bowl, he returned to Śrāvastī by means of his supernormal powers. This was because of an event that occurred while the Tathāgata was in the world, namely:
"The arising of disputes. As for the subsequent extinction of the Dharma, the *Māyā-sūtra* states it will be after fifteen hundred years.

In the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, the Tripiṭaka Master and his Arhat disciples killed one another; evil Māras and non-Buddhists vied with one another to destroy stūpas and monasteries and slaughter bhikṣus.

[Commentary] Regarding the first passage, the Buddha stated that there are four kinds of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*).

First, "dispute by speech" (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*) refers to the evaluation of the right and wrong of the characteristics of the Dharma; one must discern the false from the correct, yet when each party clings to their own view, a dispute arises.

Because the dispute originates from speech, it is called a "dispute by speech. Second, "dispute by seeking" (*anveṣaṇa-adhikaraṇa*) refers to a *bhikṣu* who has committed an offense... [the principle].

One must establish the removal of offenses (*āpattivyūpaśama*). There are three roots and five virtues for bringing forth [a case] before the Saṃgha to investigate prior offenses so that they may be eliminated.

Because one brings forth [the case] to evaluate the commission of an offense, a dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) arises; since the dispute originates from this investigation, it is called a "dispute arising from investigation" (*mṛṣādhikaraṇa*).

As for a "dispute arising from an offense" (*āpattyadhikaraṇa*), when a transgression remains within one's mind, it ought to be purified through confession. However, because the characteristics of the offense are difficult to discern, various opinions become confused and contentious, thereby giving rise to dispute.

Because these [disputes] arise from transgressions, they are called "disputes arising from transgressions" (*āpatti-araṇa*). Regarding "disputes concerning matters" (*kṛtya-araṁṇa*): when a formal ritual procedure (*karman*) is applied to a matter, the intent lies in its clear and correct execution;

yet if there is even a slight deviation, the objective is not accomplished. Since human nature tends toward tolerance, it is easy to reach harmony, but it is difficult to resolve when each party obstinately clings to their own view.
Thus, the success or failure of a matter or a rule leads to dispute. Because such disputes arise due to a specific matter, they are called "disputes concerning matters."

Regarding the term "contention" (*adhikaraṇa*) used here: it refers to disputes over the characteristics of the Dharma, such as the eighteen matters of legal dispute (*vinaya-adhikaraṇa*), with other types of disputes following this pattern.

*Quarrelsome dispute* (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) arises from others raising charges against one; its resolution depends on whether the charge is established. *Dispute over offenses* (*āpattyadhikaraṇa*) arises from the confession of an offense;

its resolution depends on whether the offense is grave or light. *Dispute over business* (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) pertains solely to formal monastic procedures (*kamma*); all matters that are not formal procedures are subsumed under the aforementioned three types of disputes.

Regarding the formation and destruction of phenomena (*dharma*): the "matter" (*vastu*) is that which is formed, while the "phenomenon" (*dharma*) is that which forms it; furthermore, this includes both the person who performs the act and the realm (*dhātu*) upon which it relies.
These four factors—matter, phenomenon, the agent, and the realm—are all present during both formation and destruction, as well as during non-formation and non-destruction.
[Commentary: Above, the names and characteristics were briefly explained; next, the classification of the sections is clarified. [Commentary:
Using seven medicines to treat four types of disputes results in eighteen divisions of dispute; thus, apart from the medicines, there are likewise eighteen.

In the second section, "Showing the Number by Measure," the seven types of medicine and the four types of disputes each have eighteen [subdivisions]; these are merely variations resulting from the combination and separation of general and specific categories.

[Commentary: As for what constitutes the "wrong speech" (*vitathavāda*), when the disputes regarding offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*) are each divided into three grades—namely superior, middling, and inferior—they are thus divided into nine.

Regarding the category of *adhikaraṇa* (legal disputes), there is one type which, when subdivided, becomes nine grades. To speak briefly, each instance of seeking out an offense gives rise to a *adhikaraṇa*.
Within the section on the classification of grades, the first part first clarifies how the three types of *adhikaraṇa* together constitute nine grades;

it then clarifies that among these, the nine grades of *vastu-adhikaraṇa* (disputes concerning matters) are those where the aforementioned three types of *adhikaraṇa* involve formal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) and are all subsumed under the category of *vastu*.

[Commentary: How is this to be understood? Within the context of disputes over doctrine (*adhikaraṇa-śāstra-vivāda*), if one evaluates the right and wrong of the principles of the Teaching, this is termed a "dispute over doctrine" (*dharma-vivāda*).

If one evaluates the right and wrong of formal procedures (*karma*) yet remains undecided regarding delusion or awakening, this is termed a "dispute over matters" (*vastu-vivāda*) within the context of a dispute over doctrine.

If one evaluates the clarity or turbidity of the three faculties and the openness or obstruction of the five virtues, this is termed a "dispute over seeking" (*anveṣaṇā-vivāda*). If one evaluates the application of legal methods for formal accusation, [this is termed a dispute over litigation].

When investigating the reality of whether a matter is true or false, it is termed a "dispute over matters within a dispute for litigation" (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*). Among the five classes of offenses, when there is confusion regarding confession and evaluation, it is termed a "dispute over matters within a dispute for transgression" (*adhikaraṇa-āpatti*).
Determining the gravity of an offense through an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act) is termed a "dispute over matters within a dispute for transgression.
These are divided into nine grades according to the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior inherent in the original disputes.
Next, the categories are arranged in sequence to contrast the three types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) with the dispute over matters (*vastu-adhikaraṇa*).

Only by dividing each of these into two parts can the four disputes be seen as distinct and without confusion. Regarding those that follow the original classification of disputes: this means that this dispute over matters, like the preceding three disputes, constitutes nine grades.
[Commentary] Regarding the methods for the threefold pacification and cessation:

these are the three methods of pacifying and ceasing that correspond directly to the illness, with the application of medicine alternating between preceding and following. The traditional accounts of the "pacification of disputes" (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) are difficult to understand;
this present section clarifies them through diagrams so they are as clear as looking at one's own palm. If one examines these diagrams, then from—
The difficulty of [the offense] arising is such that it may suddenly become easy in a single morning.

Among the types manifested before one, those common to the three kinds of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) encompass nine grades; excluding the lower grade, regarding the confession of an offense (*āpatti*), if one does not perform the *karmavācanā*, there are only three methods.
For the remaining seven, the *karmavācanā* is added, and all are complete with five factors. The method of self-accusation (*svayaṃ-vāda*) is restricted [to specific cases].

The subsequent offenses and disputes are treated collectively across two categories, while the remaining five types correspond individually to one category each. As stated above, the seven medicines and four types of disputes are each divided into nine grades;

regarding the nine grades of the medicines for the four disputes: there are two medicines for disputes arising from speech (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*), four medicines for disputes arising from accusations (*adhikaraṇa-anuvāda*), and three medicines for disputes arising from offenses (*adhikaraṇa-āpatti*), which together constitute the nine.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding verbal disputes (*vāda*), they are divided into three grades.

[Commentary: A dispute of the lower grade is extinguished by the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) of three grades: first, the presence of the person, wherein both parties assemble together and each expounds their own doctrine and reasoning;
second, the presence of the Dharma, which involves adjudication according to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka; third, the presence of the Vinaya.
The previous teaching was clear and explicit, whereby doubts and obscurities were naturally dispelled.

Regarding the discussion of the "lower grade" (*hīna-pakṣa*) within the *Vādavidhi*, the three factors present therein overlap with the five factors mentioned later. First, regarding the exclusion of persons:
among the three [factors], the agent and the object are discussed together because both are distinct individuals; among the five, the "person" (*pudgala*) refers only to the agent of the dispute.
Regarding the two methods of exclusion within the subsequent category of the Saṃgha: the former refers to the instructional text, while the latter refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

Regarding the three types of exclusion in the *Vinaya*: the first pertains to resolving delusions and bringing them to rest; the fifth is based on selecting those of virtue for collective deliberation. Thus, while these three names are common [to both], their specific functions are restricted;
as for the two categories of "Saṃgha" and "boundary," both name and substance are restricted.

[Commentary]: Regarding disputes of the middle grade, they are extinguished through five types of presence (*pratyakṣa*). First, the presence of one person requires that each party state their own intent regarding the dispute.
Second, the presence of the two *dharmas* (the Dharma and the Vinaya) requires that the Saṃgha perform formal procedures (*karman*) to conduct a detailed evaluation.

Third, the presence of the *vinaya* requires the use of formal procedures (*karman*), wherein those with virtue participate in the joint evaluation while those lacking virtue are censured and expelled. Fourth, the presence of the Saṃgha involves the precepts, views, livelihoods, and the three types of action (*trikarma*).
There must be no discord; those gathered together form a single assembly. When the five elements are present, one must gather all monks within the designated boundary; none may remain hidden.
Regarding disputes of the middle grade, among the three types of *vinaya*, one must employ *karmavācanā*—specifically, the *jñapti* motion—to select and assemble those who possess wisdom.
Because those who do not recite the precepts and others are sent away by means of a formal motion (*jñapti*), it is said that they are "deprived of virtue" and "degraded.

Regarding the presence of the fourfold assembly, at least four persons are required; regarding the presence of the five boundaries, this is restricted to the specific delimitations established for the performance of the ritual act.
[Commentary]: Regarding the settlement of serious disputes concerning verbal contention (*adhikaraṇa*) through the method of "the majority opinion of those present" (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*):

when a virtuous person has adjudicated the matter in private according to the Dharma and concluded it, the individuals who instigated the dispute, not seeing him, believe there is concealment or deception.

Therefore, the Tathāgata established the rule that both assemblies must gather together face-to-face and cast ballots (*śalākā*). Whichever side is in the majority is the Dharma, as explained in the analogy of medicine.

In the superior grade, "manifest before the assembly" (*sammukha-vinaya*) is as previously explained regarding the "words of many. Having first described the settlement through private deliberation (*tatsvabhāva-vinaya*), this follows upon the *sammukha-vinaya*.
This lower section clarifies the regulation for those who cast many voting sticks (*śalākā*). This is what is called the "words of many.
The method is as explained in the "Medicine" [chapter]; it is pointed out below in the commentary on the text.
[Commentary] The preceding explanation of *vāda-vivāda* (contentious speech) is concluded.
[Commentary] Next, it clarifies that the three grades of *anuvāda-vivāda* (disputes over offenses) are extinguished by four remedies:

the lower grade is extinguished by the remedy of *smṛti* (mindfulness) through the manifestation of the five dharmas; the middle grade is extinguished by the remedy of *amūḍha* (non-delusion) through the manifestation of the five dharmas.
The previous section on the locus of offenses explains the pacification of the *uttarimanuṣyadharma* (superhuman state) dispute by means of medicine.
[Commentary] Next, it clarifies the three grades of disputes arising from transgressions: the lower grade is pacified through the presence of three dharmas and the confession of one's own words;

the middle grade is pacified through the presence of five dharmas and the confession of one's own words; and the upper grade is pacified through the "covering over with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) procedure, also involving the presence of five dharmas.
Regarding the disputes concerning offenses: the application of medicines for seeking out and identifying offenses can be understood by consulting the diagrams.

[Commentary] As for "disputes concerning matters," there are no separate medicines; rather, one relies on the three grades as previously described, applying the medicine according to each respective category.

Regarding "extinction" (*nirodha*), the text states: "By means of all extinctions, one extinguishes within the text. This fully encompasses the three grades of disputes, each further divided into three grades.
The "lower" refers to the division of disputes; the "establishment of medicine" refers to the characteristics of their treatment and extinction, as explained above.

Regarding the disputes over matters (*vastu-vivāda*), first it is shown that the categories of dispute are the same; that is, within each of the three types of disputes over matters, they are further divided into grades as explained above, hence it says "based on these three grades.
As will be clarified below, the application of the remedy is the same for each respective case. "Respectively" means according to the differences between the disputes.
"Identical in cessation" means that all return to total pacification. Below, the cited text serves as proof; the term "all" comprehensively encompasses everything.

[Vinaya]: "If the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) should be granted, one must grant the *saṃmukhavinaya*."
[Commentary: Next, the second medicine is explained, first by presenting the general outline and subsequently by providing the detailed exposition.

"First presentation" refers to citing the text of the precepts, while "subsequent exposition" refers to the annotated commentary that follows.

[Commentary]: The phrase "should be granted to those present" means that since the Dharma teaching relies upon signs and requires face-to-face presence, any private deliberation or secret determination will never cease to harbor lingering doubts; this is the intended meaning.
In the commentary, the first section is easily understood.
[The Sub-commentary] states: "Vinaya" is translated here as *lü* (vinaya). *Lü* means "to divide" and "to record.

This refers to the necessity of deliberation and measurement according to established standards, because it is like the division of breaths in the musical scale (*lüyǔ*). Furthermore, it is like the worldly law that relies on punishments and regulations to define the Way.

The Dharma is likewise: it relies upon the faculties and is attached to the teachings, each having its own distinctions and gradations that must not be transgressed; therefore, it is called "Dharma" (*dharma*).

As for the character for *vinaya* (律), it is composed of "peace" (*an*) and "pen" (*yù*). "Pen" refers to a writing brush. One must carefully examine the teachings and verify the facts through the pen before making a decision;
because such judgments are rendered face-to-face, it is called *vinaya*. This is as explained at the beginning.
The next section translates the names to demonstrate their meanings; that is, the following specific explanations first clarify the meaning of "division" (*fen*).

One year consists of twelve months: odd-numbered months are called *lü* (律), and even-numbered months are called *lǚ* (呂). *Lü* represents Yang, and *lǚ* represents Yin. Each *lü* and each *lǚ* possesses two qi (vital energies);
thus, the six *lü* and six *lǚ* together constitute the twenty-four seasonal nodes (*jieqi*). Therefore, the present metaphor is based on these measurements for the purpose of judgment.
To eliminate any ambiguity, the following section explains the meaning of the term "pen" (*bi*). First, explaining it according to secular law, the *Shangjuan* (Upper Scroll) states:

"The pen is the symbol of the legal authorities. This refers to the administration of punishment; "criminal name" (*xingming*) refers to the codified regulations, that is, the specific articles and statutes (some editions erroneously read "according to form" [*juxing*] and "according to hearing" [*youting*]).

"Relying on the roots" refers to the three roots [of offense], and "adhering to the teachings" refers to the text of the Vinaya. Thus, the term "pen" used below in the Vinaya precisely accords with this meaning, as it follows the person.
The character *yù* (聿) represents a person holding a writing brush. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The *yù* is that with which one writes. In Chu it is called *yù*;

in Wu it is called *bulü* (because one writes of the ruler's transgressions); in Yan it is called *fú*; in Qin it is called *bǐ*. Regarding the examination of instruction, it means to scrutinize the details of laws and regulations, weighing their gravity;

regarding the verification of circumstances, it means to investigate the depth of intent. In the common parlance of legal adjudication, it refers to the finalizing of the sentence upon the stroke of the pen.
Moreover, when the Vinaya vehicle is used as a standard for judgment, one determines a case by taking that instance as an analogy for this one; thus it is said, "in such a manner.
The term "face-to-face" (*pratyakṣa*) carries the meaning of being "present before one's eyes," as in the initial explanation which points to the aforementioned five or three types of presence.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "it should be granted," since the three factors and five factors have been established, it is evident that one must follow the teachings and practice in order to settle disputes;

hence the term is used. Among the three [sections], the first traces back to what preceded regarding what "should be granted. The subsequent section provides the formal explanation of "should be granted"; here, "must" (須) carries the meaning of "should" (當).
[Note] When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Kālodāyin was bathing in the river with the group of six monks.
Kālodāyin mistakenly took one of their robes and departed. Later, the group of six monks claimed he had stolen it;

they then performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against him without his presence. Kālodāyin reported these circumstances to the Buddha, who rebuked them and consequently established this rule.
There are three kinds of *dhamma-sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement by presence of the Dhamma), and there are five kinds of persons for whom there is *dhamma-sammukhā-vinaya*.
There is also the *saṃgha-sīmā* (the boundary of the Saṃgha). What is the presence of the Dhamma? It is the settling of disputes through the Dhamma that is upheld. What is the presence of the Vinaya?
It is the settling of disputes through the Vinaya that is upheld. What is the presence of persons? It is the exchange of dialogue and discussion. What is...?

What is meant by "the Sangha being present"? Those who ought to come must come; those who ought to give their consent (*chanda*) must give their consent; and those who are entitled to censure must not censure.
What is meant by "the boundary being present" and "proclaiming the *karmavācanā* while establishing a restriction"? This method of presence applies universally to all *karmas*.
If it is a case for an individual, a face-to-face (*saṃmukha*) procedure, or a mental recitation (*manasikāra*), these three types of presence are sufficient. If there are four or five [monks]...
Regarding the monastic legal procedures (*saṃghadharma*) for a community of more than one person, if one performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*), five conditions must be present before it;

this is because the formal act necessarily arises within a designated ritual boundary (*karmabhūmi*), with the sole exception of the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*) established by the delimitation of a sacred precinct (*sīmābandha*).

[Commentary] Regarding the section on "Resolution," it is divided into two parts: first, the conditions (*pratyaya*), and second, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Concerning the first, because [the act] is performed in a secluded place to carry out the *nihsargika-pāyattika* dharma, one does not summon the offender.

When asked about the intention regarding the taking of the object, the person is not [the subject of the inquiry]; this is called "substantiation. Therefore, the regulation requires that the discussion be conducted face-to-face.

The meaning of the two characteristics—namely, the three and the five—is as explained previously. Furthermore, it is said that this *sammukha-vinaya* (resolution in the presence of) applies to all *karmas*.
By applying this principle analogously, the textual structure can be understood.

In the commentary, the first two phrases divide the text: from the beginning up to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) constitutes the narration of the circumstances regarding Kātyāyana’s petition to the Buddha;

what follows is the enumeration of the characteristics, which is further divided into two parts for specific explanation. First, the explanation of the "circumstances of the cessation of the dharma," which refers to cessation itself.

Since the mind is taken as the basis of the act of formal exclusion (*pabbājanā*), one must necessarily inquire into the mental concomitants (*cetasika*); the subsequent explanation of their characteristics refers back to what precedes and can thus be understood.

Furthermore, the later text points out that while the original rule was established for the purpose of extinguishing disputes, it concurrently encompasses all types of communal and individual *kamma*; therefore, it is said to "extend laterally" (*paccantika*) and so forth.
[Prātimokṣa-sūtra] "If the Smṛti-vinaya (the discipline of recollection) should be granted, one must grant the Smṛti-vinaya.

[Commentary] When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, the son of Ṭhappa (Ṭhapaka-mālava-putra), who served as the administrator for the Saṃgha, became the object of malice from among the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika).

Because he received a poor room and bedding and an inferior invitation, they gave rise to anger and slander, claiming he was possessed of attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; they subsequently accused him of a sexual offense.

When the Buddha asked the assembly whether the slander against Upāli was true or false, he replied, "From birth until even in my dreams, I have never committed sexual misconduct, much less while awake.
When the Bhikṣus questioned the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) regarding this matter, they said, "Upāli is pure; such a thing has never occurred.

The Buddha said, "Upāli is one who is free from attachment and does not intentionally violate the precepts; a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) should be performed [to clear him]."
This concerns the method of formal recollection (*smṛti-vinaya*).

[Commentary: Second, it clarifies that for one who practices formal recollection, the Dharma serves as a witness to prove that there was no offense. Only an Arhat such as Aśvajit may employ this method;
other ordinary persons of inferior capacity must not rely upon it, nor is it appropriate for them to practice it.
The second [section] follows the previous pattern and likewise divides the text into two parts; the latter five [sections] are also thus. First, there is a brief indication of non-attachment;
below that, there is the exclusion of confusion. Within the commentary, first is the *nidāna* (origin story), which refers to the occasion for the two preceding precepts against slander;

[The Karmavācanā. [Vinaya] One who should be granted the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who was not insane) must be granted the *amūḍha-vinaya*.
[Commentary] When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, the bhikṣu Nanda contracted leprosy and became insane; he wandered about, coming and going, entering and exiting [the monastery].

A bhikṣu who, while conforming to proper decorum, frequently commits many offenses, is questioned and says: "I committed offenses when I was deluded; now that my illness has been cured, I shall not do so again.

He reports this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "There are three kinds of those who are deranged or deluded: first, one who always remembers the *poṣadha* and always comes; second, one who does not remember the *poṣadha* and does not come;
third, one who sometimes remembers and comes, or sometimes does not remember and does not come. This person should report [his condition]."

The fourth [rule] concerning the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the legal act for one who is no longer insane) was established because when a transgression is committed during a period of illness, if the person does not commit it again after recovery, they should be considered pure by the Saṃgha and thus count toward the quorum. [Commentary:

Third, regarding "one who is no longer insane": since a crime committed while insane is not held in the mind, the teaching does not regulate such cases; rather, it is regulated once the insanity has been resolved.

If one has not committed [an offense], it cannot be proven through formal disciplinary action; yet, because there was no prior transgression, one performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (four-part motion) to certify that the act was committed out of ignorance and thus constitutes no offense.

Regarding the procedure for those who are insane, one performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (two-part motion). Because disputes over right and wrong are somewhat difficult to resolve and eliminate, this method for those who are insane employs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

The third [section] consists of two parts. First is the formal explanation: "delusion" (*moha*) refers to a state of madness and mental derangement; "resolution of delusion" (*mohavimukti*) means that once the illness of madness has ceased, one attains the resolution of the Dharma.
This indicates that for those who have previously committed an offense but now harbor doubts regarding others, they are not granted the same Dharma.

Thus, the *karma* (formal ritual) for resolving madness and the method of resolution both employ the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the motion followed by one proclamation). This serves to distinguish [this case] from other forms of madness.
There are two intentions: first, to distinguish it from two other dharmas; second, to manifest a distinct meaning.

In the commentary, the initial section regarding the matter reported to the Buddha concerns the description of the three types of insanity. First is the inferior grade, second is the superior grade—these two do not require the application of the dharma—and third is the middle grade, for which the dharma must indeed be applied.
[The Vinaya] states: "If one should be dealt with according to their own confession (*pātimokkha-thapanā*), one should be dealt with according to their own confession.

[Commentary]: When the Buddha was in the city of Campā on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon during the Sangha’s recitation of the *Pātimokkha*, the Buddha sat among the assembly in silence and did not recite the precepts.
Once the first watch of the night had passed, Ānanda requested that he speak them. The Buddha said: "I wish to cause the Tathāgata to remain in a state of impurity..."

It is not possible for one who recites the *Prātimokṣa* among the assembly [to do so] while such a person is present. It was likewise when, during the middle watch and the latter watch of the night, he was invited to respond.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana used his divine eye to observe those who had violated the precepts; they were not far from the Buddha, appearing outwardly pure while inwardly rotten.
He then took them by the hand and brought them out, saying to the Buddha: "The assembly is now pure; the *Prātimokṣa* may be recited. The Buddha said: "From now on..."
From now on, one should not administer the *pātimokkha* by means of a formal confession (*sammukhavinaya*).

[Commentary: Regarding the fourth, *sammukhavinaya* (settlement by confession): because the offense arises from oneself and must be confessed by oneself in the presence of the assembly, it is called "confession" (*svavacana*).
Because the circumstances of the offense are stated without concealment, it is called "settlement" (*vinaya*). Within this context...
Because one fears that if they do not accept their own statement, pure persons might later be indiscriminately expelled, this medicine [of confession] was established;
it likewise possesses three methods and five methods of self-accusation, which can be understood from the aforementioned cases of *pratyakṣa* (presence).
The fourth section begins with the explanation of the text’s context; following the context, the characteristics can be understood by following the sequence of the words.
[Vinaya]: "Where a formal rebuke by many should be given, a formal rebuke by many shall be given."

[Note] When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus could not cease their disputes over eighteen matters; consequently, they brought the matter before the Saṃgha for adjudication, yet it remained unresolved.
They reported this to the Buddha, who said: "The *yadbhūyaś-cittotpāda* (the method of seeking the majority) should be applied.

Those who speak according to the Dharma and those who speak contrary to the Dharma should be gathered in one place, and a bhikṣu should be appointed to distribute *śalākā* (voting sticks). There are three kinds of distribution: first, the open (*prakāśa*); second, [the secret]; third, [the half-open/half-secret]."
There are three types of concealment: first, concealing by means of a formal act; second, concealing by means of a secret whisper;

and third, if the Elder who serves as the leader, the wise one, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), or the teacher (*ācārya*) abides in a state of accordance with the Dharma, they should perform the *śalākā* (voting sticks) openly. If, however, they abide in a state contrary to the Dharma, they may perform the two lower methods of procedure.
If those who speak contrary to the Dharma are numerous, one should cause a disturbance and depart. Therefore, this Vinaya text says: "Seeking out the offense."
The intention behind the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) is also the same.

[Commentary: Regarding the fifth, "the speech of many people," because there are differing interpretations when evaluating the characteristics of the Dharma, two factions are summoned to a common location to settle the matter face-to-face by casting lots.
