[Note] This Buddha’s appearance in the world is identical to that of the previous kalpa; when human life expectancy was seventy thousand years, seventy years prior [to its end], he spoke these concise verses, after which he subsequently expounded them in detail.

[Commentary] Regarding the third section, the concise verses clarify the two practices of cessation (*śamatha*) and application (*pragraha*) for the purpose of teaching at that time; we shall first address the initial four lines.

The characteristics of the accomplishment of the practice of restraint through clearly observing the precepts of body and speech are followed by a half-verse concerning the accomplishment of the practice of diligent exertion in cultivating goodness. [Commentary:
Regarding the first part, there are two sections: the first half-verse concerns the absence of transgressions in speech, and the subsequent half-verse concerns the body’s freedom from transgressions.
[Commentary: To examine one's conduct while living together and to speak in accordance with the individual's faculties is called "not slandering.

Furthermore, to explain in accordance with the Dharma without error is called "not speaking what is not the teaching of the Sages. Thus it is said, "not slandering. When seeing others' fame and profit, to have no words of ridicule or destruction is called "not being envious.
Since these two faults lack principle and undermine the foundation of practice, one should uphold the precepts.
Regarding the third Buddha’s initial practice of non-slander during the first half [of the section], there are two interpretations of the initial explanation of "not slandering":

the former explains it in terms of accusing others of offenses, while the latter explains it in terms of teaching the Dharma. To hold inverted views and what is not noble is precisely called "slandering the Dharma"; how could one not be cautious when lecturing from a high seat?
Following the phrase "see below," the next part explains the practice of non-envy; its root refers directly to the precepts.

[Commentary]: Regarding the detachment from the body, there is a method for receiving and accepting [sensations] such that internal suffering does not arise; therefore, one knows the state of cessation (*śamatha*).
In a place of clamor and confusion, one remains as tranquil as a sage; therefore, one delights in emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
In the latter half of the verse, it is because of moderation in eating, dwelling in seclusion, and the conditions for the Path. [Commentary]:
Since the body and speech above have already been established in accordance with the Dharma, wisdom must necessarily be renewed daily; therefore, it says "the mind is settled and delights in vigor.

The wisdom that encourages cultivation is precisely the four types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Because the Dharma is not something transmitted by ordinary people, it must be received with profound and careful attention; therefore, it says...
This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
In the practice of cultivation, one follows what precedes to give rise to what follows; that which preceded was the karma of body and speech, while this is the karma of mind.

Furthermore, that which preceded was the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), while this is the dual training in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, there is daily renewal and daily progress. To exert oneself in the cultivation of wisdom is as follows:
Regarding the four types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*) are cited to explain the aforementioned diligence:
(1) to eliminate evil that has already arisen; (2) to prevent the arising of evil not yet arisen; (3) to bring about the arising of goodness not yet arisen;

and (4) to increase the goodness that has already arisen. The following section explains the subsequent phrase; this passage is restricted in its wording to what follows, while its meaning summarizes what precedes it. The person who can teach is mentioned first.

The prose having already been shown, the verse that follows does not require further commentary. *Vipaśyin* is also called *Viśvabhū*; terms such as *Vibhu*, *Śubha*, and *Vipaśyin* are merely variations in transliteration.
This is translated as "All-Knowing" (*Sarvajña*). His lineage is the same as the previous one.
He attained Buddhahood beneath a *sāla* tree and, during two assemblies, preached the Dharma and delivered 130,000 people.
【Vinaya】 Just as a bee gathers from flowers, Without damaging their color or fragrance, But taking only their nectar to depart;
So too should a bhikṣu leave a village, Not interfering with others' affairs, Observing neither what is done nor what is left undone,
But observing only his own conduct— Whether it be right or wrong.
[The Vinaya] This is the Sūtra on the Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda.

[Note] This Buddha was the first Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa; when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, he constantly recited this verse for sixty years before subsequently expounding it in detail.
[Commentary] In the fourth section, the practices for benefiting oneself and others, or practices solely for one's own benefit, are explained.

[Commentary] The initial explanation is divided into two parts: the first verse clarifies the method of practicing for the benefit of others, while the subsequent verses clarify only the practice for one's own benefit.

[Commentary]: Regarding the preceding verse, the first three lines constitute the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*), while the subsequent section beginning with "the bhikṣu" constitutes the application to the metaphor (*dārṣṭāntika*).

In the initial [section], the practitioner who employs provisional names (*prajñapti*) relies on food to sustain the body, just as bees reside within a cluster. Seeking alms is like gathering worldly flowers;
because one gathers the four sense-objects (*catur-viṣaya*) to produce the function of a responsive fruit, they are called "flowers. The donor likewise...
The harmony of these four factors is called giving (*dāna*), for they necessarily share the function of producing a corresponding result, just like a flower.

Furthermore, when a bee gathers from a flower, it does not merely take its flavor; it also takes its color and fragrance. Yet, because it takes them with extreme subtlety, it does not damage the flower’s capacity to produce fruit.
Thus it is said that it "does not destroy the color and fragrance. The bhikṣu is likewise: he must never seek much, lest he destroy the worldly [order].

Faithfulness and integrity are like the color and fragrance of a flower, which do not decay; because one seeks a small amount to sustain the body for the sake of cultivating the Way, it is said, "one takes only its flavor and departs.

Regarding the fourth Buddha-verse, the first two lines explain the benefit of oneself, while the following explain the metaphor of benefiting others; herein, the first part explains the preceding line regarding begging for food.

The phrase "gathering words of world-transcending excellence" introduces the analogy of the four sense objects—namely, fragrance, form, flavor, and touch. The section beginning with "the donor" below applies the analogy.
Furthermore, the subsequent section explains the following line; first, it presents an analogy, and then the passage beginning with "the bhikṣu" applies the analogy.
[Commentary: In this text, the bhikṣu is compared to the aforementioned bee. "Emerging from the assembly" means that he is about to go among the laity to beg for food;

thus it is said he "emerges toward the village. He is like the bee, hence the comparison. Furthermore, "emerging from the assembly" means that having entered the village and obtained food, he emerges and proceeds to the monastery (saṃghārāma) to eat, thereby not harming the sentiments of the laity—just as the bee takes its nectar from the forest and departs from the forest.

Returning [to the village] is why it is called "going out. Furthermore, there is a precept text concerning those entering a village, which states that when a bhikṣu first enters, he must observe himself using the analogy of a bee.

Within the formal application of the dharma (*dharmayojanā*), the initial citation and explanation has two parts: first, it is explained in relation to the initial act of going out to beg; next, it is explained in relation to... (the subsequent part).

Having finished the request, he departs and returns to his original state; furthermore, there is a lower dot [indicating a variant], which differs from the initial explanation where one observes oneself as before.

[Commentary: The following verse clarifies the practice of self-cultivation (*svayam-carita*). The upper portion clarifies that one does not externally contravene [the Dharma], while the lower portion clarifies that one is solely cautious within.

"Not contravening" means that the various practices do not conflict with one another. "Not observing what is done or what is not done" means that others are not involved. Indeed, those who delight in...

Evil arises from purity and impurity, and love and hatred must necessarily originate from these; thus, ordinary beings end up with acceptance and rejection, which ultimately leads them to fear falling into greed and anger.
It is necessary to discard both extremes to achieve equanimity and protection. As for the subsequent "contemplation of the internal," it is explained as usual.
In the initial general division of the "Practicing for Oneself" section, there is no contradiction with the subsequent specific explanation. First, the first half [of the verse] is explained:

since both types of assemblies belong to others, the assembly cannot be contravened; as for the individual, there is no need to observe contravention—*li* meaning to deviate or oppose—and *yu* meaning to discern or distinguish.
Below this, the intention is revealed: because conduct is pure, it is "good"; because one practices filth, it is "evil. Regarding "views," if they are good, one loves and adopts them.
Seeing evil, one must loathe and abandon it; yet as ordinary beings, one’s choices often do not accord with the Way.
When love arises from greed and hatred emerges from anger, it conversely becomes a source of self-entanglement. Therefore, one must dispel both love and hatred and equalize the mind;

thus it is said that one achieves the protection of equanimity (*upekṣā*). The phrase "the lower part" refers to the latter half [of the verse], meaning that one must discipline oneself and rectify one's conduct.

If one's maintenance [of the practice] is not upright, one must correct it; this is the essential art for acting as a person, practicing the Way, dwelling among the multitude, and establishing oneself.

[Commentary: Furthermore, these can be interpreted generally as the practitioner’s own conduct. The first three phrases are metaphorical text, while the subsequent sections are all explained through the Dharma (the teaching). The practitioner is like a bee.

Furthermore, entering among the assembly to learn the rules of conduct is like gathering flowers; when the pure dharma of the assembly is perfected, it serves as the fruit through its transformative power, acting as the blossoms.

To practice according to the Dharma without violating the net of the community is called "not breaking" [the rules]. Gathering the teachings of the Dharma to provide sustenance for the spirit is called "taking the flavor.
The bhikṣu corresponds to the upper part of the character for "bee" (蜂). Entering the assembly to gather is like the upper part of the character for "flower" (花) being gathered.

The verse beginning with "Violating [the precepts]" and so forth combines with the preceding section on not spoiling color and fragrance; the section beginning with "But observing for oneself" combines with the preceding section on taking flavor.

Next, within the practice of one's own conduct, there are two parts: first, the general explanation of the initial [verse], and second, the detailed explanation of the subsequent lines. First, the explanation of the simile:

this refers to entering the assembly to study the Dharma as "gathering," and practicing in accordance with the teachings as "taking flavor. The section beginning with "The bhikṣu" explains the application of the Dharma.
"Entering the assembly" (*praveśa-gaṇa*) refers to joining the multitude;

the rest may be understood accordingly. [Commentary: Furthermore, the first verse clarifies one's own practice (*svācāra*). Physical existence requires material support; thus, one relies on worldly conventions to sustain the Path. Receiving and accepting [offerings] must follow proper ritual (*vidhi*).

As in the first verse, practice depends upon the assembly to achieve its power. Since one cannot yet provide universal salvation, one remains silent according to the occasion to avoid disturbing the Sangha.
Because it concerns ritual decorum, the "external protection" is precisely the subsequent verse.

Next, regarding the explanation: the first verse concerns the retribution that serves as the support for one's own practice, while the second verse concerns protecting the Sangha when among the assembly. This is largely the same as the previous explanation;
it is merely categorized broadly rather than being subdivided further.

[Commentary: Second, regarding the conclusion on the speaker: during the formation of the Bhadrakalpa under Krakucchanda, when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, he constantly recited this verse for sixty years;
only after that did he speak extensively. Both the preceding and following sections must be explained by drawing analogies from these facts.
He who was able to preach [the Dharma] was Krakucchanda—also called Kāla-kūṭa or Kanaka, translated as "Golden Sage"—the ninth Buddha of the present Bhadrakalpa during the aeon of decrease.

He appeared when the human lifespan decreased from eighty thousand years to sixty thousand years, preaching the Dharma at a single assembly to deliver forty thousand people; this count includes both those above and below.
The explanation for this is already clear in the commentaries on the sutras; therefore, I shall not cite them again. [Commentary] Question:

At the beginning of a kalpa, human life spans were immeasurable; why did the Buddhas not appear then? Answer: There was no fault of negligence, yet even if they had appeared, people would not have received their true transformation.
As the treatise says: "Buddhas arise during the decrease of the kalpa; Wheel-turning Kings arise during the increase."
In the question, the phrase "humans transformed" (*puruṣa-nirmāṇa*) refers to the period at the beginning of the kalpa when humans were mostly transformed from the heavens.
In the answer, the first part explains this according to its meaning, while the latter part cites a treatise as proof; it is not yet clear which treatise is being cited.

Regarding the "Wheel-turning King" (*cakravartin*), the *Bhūmivastu* (or *Dharmasaṃgraha*) states that a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) acts as a Wheel-turning King who rules over the four continents, transforming humans through the ten wholesome paths of action during the beginning of the kalpa.

[Sūtra] Do not be heedless in mind; you should diligently study the noble Dharma. In this way, free from sorrow and grief, with a concentrated mind, you shall enter Nirvāṇa. [Vinaya] Do not be heedless in mind; you should diligently study the noble Dharma. In this way, free from sorrow and grief, with a concentrated mind, you shall enter Nirvāṇa.
[The Vinaya: This is the Sūtra of Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni.

[The Commentary: During this Bhadrakalpa, as the second Buddha when the human lifespan was forty thousand years, he constantly recited these verses twenty years prior [to his parinirvāṇa], and only thereafter did he preach them extensively.
[Commentary] The fifth section clarifies the conduct of negligence and heedlessness. The manifestations of negligence are extremely numerous;

essentially, whenever one’s traces are scattered among worldly customs and the mind follows after suffering or pleasure, it is called negligence, as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as being like frost and hail for the most excellent practices.
Dividing the verse into two parts: the first half clarifies the causal practice, and the second half clarifies the fulfillment of the result.

In the fifth section, "The Buddha’s Verses on the Marking of Divisions," the first part demonstrates the characteristics and traces of negligence (*pramāda*). It refers to conduct that is not pure and being scattered among worldly customs;
it refers to a mind that follows suffering and pleasure, meaning one's resolve is neither firm nor upright.

As will be cited below, negligence is shown to be capable of destroying wholesome conduct, just as frost and hail can destroy living things; therefore, this analogy is employed. The thirteenth fascicle of that sutra states: "All..."
Good son, it is through heedfulness that one is able to give rise to both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
If there is anyone who wishes to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should diligently cultivate the dharma of heedfulness. As for those who are heedless, there are thirteen karmic retributions:
first, delighting in performing worldly tasks; second, delighting in speaking useless words; third, always delighting in sleeping for long periods.
1. Excessive sleep; 2. Delighting in speaking of worldly matters; 3. Constantly taking pleasure in associating with evil friends;
4. Laziness and indolence; 5. Constantly being despised by others; 6. Forgetting what one has heard as soon as it is heard;
7. Delighting in dwelling in remote borderlands; 8. Being unable to subdue the sense faculties; 9. Not knowing moderation in eating. 12. [The twelfth item].

Not delighting in meditative stillness and having thirteen types of incorrect views—those who are heedless, even if they draw near to the Buddha and his disciples, are still said to be far away from them. [Commentary]:

To allow the mind to roam among sensory objects and become defiled by attachment according to conditions is what is called "heedlessness. If one can restrain the mind and engage in correct contemplation, [one is not heedless].

Because it is associated with being free from the faults of all conditions, it says: "The mind must not be negligent. Since negligence pervades the body, speech, and mind, and because the mind is the primary basis for karma, the text points specifically to the mind.
This clarifies that by abandoning faults and advancing in practice to accord with the truth, one possesses the cause of liberation;
this is called the "Noble Dharma," which one should diligently study.
In the first half-verse, the initial explanation of the first line first restates and explains that "heedlessness" (*pramāda*) extends to both body and speech, which constitutes its end;

it is "mind" (*citta*) that serves as the fundamental karma, which exhaustively traces its beginning. Below this, the second line is explained: following upon the previous departure from faults, the dharmas to be cultivated are introduced.

[Commentary]: "Thus" refers back to the establishment of the preceding causes. Because one enters the stage of *adhimātra-kṣānti* (superior patience) by practicing the noble Dharma, suffering and karma are forever extinguished;

hence it is said, "there is no sorrow. Because the mind is pure and wisdom is luminous, all forms of existence (*bhava*) are forever severed; hence it is said, "the mind is settled and one enters nirvāṇa."

In the first half-verse, the initial explanation of the preceding phrase concerns the stage of "increased patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), which is the third stage among the "inner ordinary beings" (*prthagjana*).

Regarding the phrase "the karma of suffering is forever extinguished," this is stated with reference to the causes and effects of the three miserable realms (*apāya*); for at this stage of patience, one does not regress and thus does not fall into the evil paths.
Next, the following phrase, "all existence is forever severed," refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the ultimate state of sainthood; this is mentioned above as a contrast.
The "Venerable One" has forever departed from the three evil realms; the following passage mentions that the "Supreme Sage" has forever transcended the triple world.

[Commentary]: This was the second Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa, who appeared in the world when the human lifespan was forty thousand years. For thirty years prior to his parinirvāṇa, he constantly recited this verse.
The one capable of teaching among humans was Kanakamuni (translated as "Golden Sage"), who in a single assembly preached the Dharma and delivered thirty thousand people.
[Vinaya] Do no evil whatsoever; practice all that is good; purify your own mind.
This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
[The Vinaya states: This is the Sūtra of Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa. [Note:
This was spoken twenty years before the Buddha of this Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years. After he spoke these verses...
The Vaipulya teaching.

[Commentary] The sixth section clarifies that while there may be minor transgressions regarding the practice of the three trainings, one should cultivate wholesome deeds. The verse is divided into two parts:
the first three lines clarify the practice of the teachings, and the final line points out what is not to be confused with such discourse.
[Commentary: Regarding the first part, there are two phrases: the former clarifies the cessation of evil, and the latter clarifies the cultivation of goodness.

Next, there is one phrase that clarifies that the root of both the practice of cessation and performance arises solely from the mind; one should contemplate this "will" (*zhi*). When the mind has a governing focus, it is called "intention" (*yi*);
when it is steadfast and difficult to uproot, it is called "will" (*zhi*).
In the first half-verse of the sixth Buddha-gāthā, the phrase "the mind" (*citta*) and the phrase "the intention" (*manas*) are distinct in their textual punctuation and semantic meaning.
[The Commentary] states: This is the true precept (*saddharma-śīla*), not some other heterodox technique; therefore, it is called "the teaching of all Buddhas."
The subsequent explanation of the latter phrase is easily understood.

[Commentary: During the third eon of the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world and constantly recited this verse twenty years prior to his parinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa, who can thus speak, is here translated as "Drinker of Light" (Yinguang). In this single assembly, he preached the Dharma and delivered twenty thousand people.
[The Vinaya: Guard well your speech; Purify your own will and intention; Commit no evil with the body.
When these three paths of action are pure, And one is able to practice in such a way, This is the path of the Great Sages.

[The Vinaya] states: This is the Sūtra of the Precepts (Śīlasūtra) which the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, spoke for the sake of the Saṅgha of those free from worldly affairs (*anavassutasaṅgha*) during twelve years; from this point onward, it is explained in detail and analyzed.
[Note] This brief teaching of the Buddha constitutes the essential core of the abridged version. At that time, he addressed those of sharp faculties who would not commit the offense again;

however, because they later committed the grave transgression once more, the Buddha ceased his preaching. He then entrusted both the extensive and the abridged teachings to his disciples to propagate.

[Commentary] The seventh section clarifies the gate of harmonizing the three karmas to transform beings during this time. The verse is divided into two parts: first, one line clarifies the purity of the three karmic actions;
second, it clarifies the fulfillment of these actions and their convergence with the Correct [Path]. Regarding "this is the path of the Great Seer (Maharṣi)":

the Buddha acts as the guide for the world, bestowing names upon things according to their nature. Because "Seers" (Ṛṣis) are those who delight in the worldly net, the Buddha established his teachings based on them, referring to them as "lesser seers."
It is said thus because one cannot avoid the three evil realms, whereas the Great Sages are forever free from the nine abodes.
Regarding the first section of the seventh Buddha-verse, this is the initial citation and explanation;

first, it indicates the reason for the name, and next, it clarifies the distinction from ordinary sages. The Sarvāstivādins say that among worldly beings, the Bhagavat is the most honored and supreme.
Therefore, because he is superior to the sages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he is called the "Great Sage" (Maharṣi). Consequently, those of the two vehicles are also termed "Lesser Sages.
In this present text, however, since the comparison is made specifically against ordinary sages, it is said that they have not yet escaped the three evil realms and the nine abodes;
that is, the three realms—counting the Desire Realm as one and the Form and Formless Realms each as four—are collectively the dwelling places of sentient beings.
It is said: "The Nine Dwellings.
[Commentary] This refers to the fourth Buddha of this Bhadrakalpa who was able to preach this [teaching]. The meaning should be divided into three parts:
first, this identifies Śākyamuni as the one who preached it; second, below this, it clarifies the person for whom the abbreviated teaching was intended; and from this point onward...
The "extensive explanation" clarifies that the concise teaching extends to the extensive.

Among those capable of teaching, Śākyamuni—translated as "Capable One" (Nengren)—and Muni—translated as "Silent Sage" (Jimo Ren)—appeared in the world to preach the Dharma during a time when the human lifespan was one hundred years;
he did not calculate the assemblies or the number of people he saved, yet for twelve years he constantly recited this verse.
The headings and divisions can be understood.
[Commentary: Regarding the term "monks without business" (*avastuka*), Master Guṇabhadra explained that they are called "without business" because they have not yet committed their first offense.

Another explanation states that although a first offense may occur, they are called "without business" because they are not present in the assembly when the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) is performed. My own explanation, however, is as follows:

According to the Vinaya, when the five-year rule was established as a broad teaching, there were those who violated it; however, because there had been no violation at the very beginning, it was termed "without incident.
It was not until the twelfth year that a re-violation occurred. As the Buddha stated in the Vinaya: "From this day forward, I shall not recite the precepts;
you yourselves shall now recite them."
In the initial section of the commentary and explanation, there are three interpretations. First, Master Guang explains extensively based on offenses that had not yet arisen.

Second, another master explains based on the view that offenses committed in private do not obstruct the recitation of the precepts. He asserts that because the Buddha only began to prohibit offenses committed within the assembly, it is known that prior to this, offenses committed outside the assembly were all termed "non-matters" (avastuka).
In our current interpretation, the fact that an offense occurred during the five-year period [of the first council] directly refutes the first explanation.

If one does not commit an offense at the outset, it is already a "breaking" [of the precept]; only when one subsequently commits a grave offense does it truly constitute a "matter. As seen in the cited scriptural evidence below regarding the settling of disputes through cessation (*nirodha-adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).

[Commentary] Question: Why did the Buddha not speak for those who have committed offenses? Answer: Because there is no "matter" that is not understood, and no "time" in which one is not trained regarding offenses.
If one does not answer when asked three times by others, there will inevitably be the suffering of having one's head shattered; therefore, [the Buddha] did not do so.

Regarding the matters in the initial question-and-answer section of the next section, it refers to the time of practicing his conduct: even regarding the ocean of the Perfectly All-Knowing Ones of the three periods of time, there was nothing he had not mastered thoroughly.
As for the "suffering of having the head shattered," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that five hundred *vajra*-beings constantly followed behind the Buddha.
Question: When he did not answer and they vied with one another, they raised their vajras and smashed his head, as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Is this also a manifested transformation and not a reality?

[Commentary]: Question: Since both the Buddha and the Saṃgha are said to be for the sake of those who practice purity, why is it that in one case there is openness and in the other closure? Answer: The Buddha...

The eye does not fail to observe; only those whose conduct is pure may accord with the monastic regulations. To receive the three faculties of retribution, one must manifest purity and then recite the precepts.
Next, it is asked: "Is it that within the Saṃgha there is the opening of impurity, while for the Buddha alone there is the closing of the pure realm? The answer is as found in the text.
This is an explanatory report. [Commentary] Question:

Regarding the claim that [the bell] can open and close [the gates], this is still obscure; please explain its meaning. Answer: If the Buddha’s teaching is ineffective, then the divine mallet would destroy it;
if the monks’ teaching is ineffective, then there would be no divinity to be damaged. Thus we know that in the Dharma-ending age, purity and impurity are the same.

As for dwelling [in such conditions], it merely involves preaching to those who oppose the Pure Land assembly; though one enters the correct path amidst impurity, even if one is among the masses, one does not destroy the Dharma of the Sangha, but only ruins one's own practice, and there is a distant prospect of escape.
Because the previous meaning was not yet exhaustive, he questions again; in the response, he returns to using the initial principle in two ways.

This explains and clarifies the following passage, which reveals the benefits and harmonizes with the capacities of the assembly to enter the "correct" [path]. "Correct" refers to the correct path (*samyag-mārga*).

Regarding those who have a distant prospect of liberation, it means they lack immediate benefit; as the *Yèshū* (業疏) states: "They act for their own sake and cultivate habits [for the future]. This is precisely what is meant.
【Vinaya】 Those bhikṣus who delight in the Dharma and the joy of being śramaṇas, and who possess a sense of shame and dread of blame while delighting in the precepts, should train therein.
(This refers to the concluding section of the brief teaching.)

[Commentary] The third section, beginning with "The various bhikṣus," clarifies the circulation of the abbreviated teaching. "Those who act for themselves" are those who have individually transcended worldly desires.

"Those who delight in the Dharma" are those who practice the teachings of goodness. "Those who delight in the śramaṇa life" are those who cease from evil conduct. "Those with a sense of shame" are those who remain hidden and do not give rise to transgressions.
"Those with a sense of remorse" are those who externally commit no violations. "Those who delight in training in the precepts" encompass all five of the aforementioned types.
This constitutes the foundation for accomplishing these practices; those who study within it should understand that the aforementioned brief teachings serve as the basis for practitioners.
By receiving and following them, there will certainly be accomplishment and salvation.

Regarding the circulation of these three brief teachings: first, they are presented in general; below this, they are explained through citation and enumeration, while the selection of individuals is omitted for brevity.
If a transgression occurs, one should immediately go to a secluded place; "outside" means that there is no violation in an exposed area.

These five points above collectively encompass the practice, for it is only by possessing these five that one can truly uphold the precepts; thus they are called the "foundation of accomplishing conduct. What follows below explains the exhortation to study.
That one may receive [the teachings] and follow them means that the instruction is not bestowed in vain. That there must be those who achieve success means that the practice is not performed in vain.
[Commentary] The third major section clarifies the general circulation text for both the extensive and abbreviated teachings, which is divided into five parts:
first, from "To clarify the person" down to "the Dharma of all Buddhas," it clarifies the benefits of practicing the extensive teaching and exhorts faith and circulation;

second, from "If there is one who acts for their own sake" down to "entering quiescent nirvana," it clarifies the benefits of practicing the abbreviated teaching and the exposition of faith and compliance.
The third section on circulation, from the time of the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa down to his entry into final nirvana, clarifies that the precepts are the teacher of all practices;
it shows how those who practice purity must guard them well, and it clarifies the entrustment for their long endurance to establish this circulation.

The fourth section, beginning with "If one does not uphold these precepts," consists of two verses that clarify that violating the Buddha’s final injunction will inevitably result in the fault of falling into ruin.

Section Five: Encouraging Faith, Reverence, Compliance, and Dissemination. Having already recited the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, this section concludes the preceding discourse and dedicates the merit to clarify the dissemination.

Regarding the third part, the "Dissemination Section" (*parīndanā-bhāga*) consisting of two teachings, the text is divided into five sections; one must employ the topical headings (*ko-yǔ*) to correspond them individually with the sūtra text.
To see the intent of the Sūtra:
[The Vinaya states: A wise person who can protect the precepts Shall obtain three kinds of happiness:
Fame and material gain in this life, And upon death, rebirth in the heavens. One should contemplate such a state; The wise should protect the precepts.
With purity of precepts and wisdom, one attains the foremost path.

Just as the Buddhas of the past and those yet to come, as well as the World-Honored Ones of the present—who are able to overcome all sorrows—all together revere and honor the precepts; this is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
[Commentary: Regarding the first section, it is divided into two parts. The first consists of two verses that directly manifest the benefits of the precepts and exhort one to contemplate them;
the second consists of one and a half verses beginning with "As did the Buddhas of the past," which cite the benefits of the practice universally observed by those of the three periods of time.

[Commentary]: Regarding the preceding section, there are two parts. First, one and a half verses clarify that when upholding [the precepts], one does not expect worldly retribution, yet through profound resonance, one obtains [benefits].

Second, the remaining half-verse clarifies that the goodness of upholding the precepts and wisdom support one another so that the Way is perfected; this is the far-reaching benefit of transcending the characteristics of existence, known as the "Supreme Path.
The explanation of the text can be understood [by the reader].
First, the extensive teaching exhorts faith; this section on the beginning of the beginning divides the text, with the final phrase indicating the concise summary.

Now, the first half-verse of the initial verse provides a brief outline: the first phrase identifies the holder of the teaching as necessarily a wise person, hence the term "enlightened one" (*vidvat*);
the following three phrases first cite worldly retribution to entice those of dull faculties—the first line provides a general heading, while the subsequent two lines provide specific illustrations.

Fame and profit are the retribution of the present life; birth in heaven is the retribution of the future life. Of the two lines below, the first exhorts one to contemplate, and the second exhorts one to uphold [the precepts].
"In such a place" refers to the three joys mentioned above; "possessing wisdom" summons those who have faith and devotion.

The latter half of the verse next demonstrates the supramundane fruit, universally connecting both the sharp and dull faculties; that is to say, by virtue of revering the precepts, one generates meditative concentration and wisdom, thereby destroying [afflictions].

Because one realizes the holy through the eradication of delusions, it is called the "first path. The preceding phrase clarifies the cultivation of causes, while the subsequent phrase reveals the realization of the fruit.
[Commentary] Second, since the teachings on extensive practice cited above must necessarily have a person who correctly expounds them, this passage generally clarifies the three Buddhas.
Since they are all equally liberated from fetters and collectively observe the Dharma of precepts, reverently upholding them in this manner is the Dharma of all Buddhas.

In the next section consisting of one and a half verses, the first verse has three lines in its upper portion that specifically cite the meaning which applies universally throughout the ten directions;
the final line reveals its virtue, for since noble wisdom extinguishes delusions and the suffering of birth and death, it is said to "be able to overcome all sorrows.
The latter half-verse means that since [the Buddha] is revered by the three periods of time, this reveals him to be the Dharma of all Buddhas; and since he is the Dharma of the Buddhas...
All should uphold this together.
[Vinaya] If there are those who, for their own sake, desire to seek the Buddha-way, they should revere the True Dharma;
this is the teaching of all Buddhas. The Seven Buddhas, as World-Honored Ones, have extinguished all fetters and afflictions.
By reciting this Sūtra of the Seven Precepts, one attains liberation from all bonds and enters into nirvāṇa, where all worldly play is forever extinguished.
This was taught by the Honored Great Sage; it is the virtue praised by the noble ones, practiced by his disciples, leading to the entry into the tranquility of nirvāṇa.

[Commentary] The second section, "The Brief Teaching," is divided into three parts: first, one line clarifies the passage where the Master of the Vinaya cites the brief teaching to exhort [the practitioners];
second, one and a half lines cite the brief practice taught by the Seven Buddhas for crossing over the world;

third, the verse beginning with "Honoring the Practice" explains how the sons of the Seven Buddhas received and followed the holy teachings to likewise cross over the world, clearly demonstrating that faith and compliance with the brief teaching are efficacious.
This is not merely for the sake of admonishing those who fail to grasp the meaning.
Second, regarding the three and a half verses on the brief teaching of faith and compliance, the first section clarifies the intent for those of inferior capacity.
Within the first line, the first two phrases summon those whose own bodies are weary of the suffering of birth and death and who desire to seek Buddhahood.
The Way aspires to the bliss of *nirvāṇa*. The following two lines exhort faith in the True Dharma; this constitutes a brief teaching.

Regarding the phrase "This is the Buddha-teaching," it means that the Ultimate Sages all conform to it. Within the subsequent half-verse, the first three lines cite the teachings of the Seven Buddhas.
Of these, the first two lines praise their virtues, while the last line expounds the Dharma. The final three lines clarify the practice for crossing over the world, both above and below.

The two lines clarify the destruction of hindrances, while the middle line clarifies the entry into the Path. Within the section on destroying hindrances, the upper line refers to the "various fetters," which are the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
the lower line refers to "conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*), which is the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). The subsequent verse concerns the disciples' practice:

the first line shows their obedience to the Teacher’s instruction; the second line praises the concise Dharma. The term "Sages and Worthies" (*ārya*) generally refers to all disciples; the following two [lines]...
The preceding phrase clarifies the cause, while the subsequent phrase demonstrates the fruit.
[Vinaya] When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he gave rise to great compassion; he gathered the assembly of bhikṣus and bestowed such instructions and precepts:
"Do not say that because I have entered parinirvāṇa, those who practice purity will be without protection."
I now recite the Sūtra of Precepts, And have also well expounded the Vinaya.
Although I have entered parinirvāṇa, you should regard it as if I were still the World-Honored One. If this sūtra abides long in the world, The Buddha-dharma will flourish and blaze forth.
Because of this blazing radiance, One shall enter into nirvāṇa.

[Commentary] The third section, concerning the time of the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, is divided into three parts: first, one line [of verse] introduces the ritual for transmitting the final instructions at the time of the Buddha’s entry into the precepts;
second, from "Do not say that I have entered nirvāṇa" to the end of one and a half lines, it correctly clarifies the method of entrustment;
and finally, the last three lines clarify that this sutra shall long abide in the world, showing that by practicing in accordance with the teachings, the Buddha-dharma will increase and expand.
Because practicing in accordance with the teachings is no different from when the Buddha was alive, one attains entry into parinirvāṇa.

Third, regarding the entrustment for circulation, there are three and a half lines; within the first line, the instruction to assemble the assembly and teach the precepts at the time of nirvāṇa refers to the re-establishment of the Vinaya in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which is a precious legacy for venerating the Prātimokṣa; this [text] now extracts that portion.

I consider that within the first one and a half lines of the verse, the first two phrases preclude the doubt or fear that the Buddha must protect [the Dharma] while he is present but will not protect it after his parinirvāṇa.
In the following section, I demonstrate for people that the maintenance of the Dharma and the person are analogous.

The first two phrases point to the teachings spoken, namely the precepts (*śīla*) and the discipline (*vinaya*); the latter two phrases cause one to contemplate the Dharma as being like the Buddha—this is the *Śāsanāntima-śāsana* (The Bequeathed Teaching).
It says, "You should know that this is your Great Teacher. Furthermore, the Sūtra states, "He who sees the Dharma sees my body," and so forth;
all such passages share this same intent. In the subsequent line, the merit and benefits of the teaching are praised:

the first two phrases clarify the benefit of its preservation—when the teaching exists, people revere it, the Sangha provides guidance, and practitioners cultivate causes to realize the fruit, ensuring that the Three Jewels endure for a long time. Do not... [omitted].
The following two lines clarify the benefits of attaining the Path:
[The Vinaya states: "If one does not uphold these precepts In accordance with the prescribed Uposatha, It is like the world falling into total darkness when the sun sets;
Therefore, one should guard and uphold these precepts As a yak protects its tail."

Fourth, regarding the passage "If one does not uphold these precepts," etc., which clarifies the harm resulting from violating the teachings, the text is divided into two parts. First, the verse cites the harm:
it causes the sun of wisdom to set and all practices to sink. Therefore, it is likened to the setting of the sun, whereby the world falls into darkness. Hereafter...
The verse [on] "observing harm" exhorts the upholding of the precepts; "preventing the yak's attachment to its tail" constitutes the excellence of upholding the precepts.
"Harmonizing as taught" constitutes the excellence of acting as one should.

Regarding the fourth section on "respectful compliance and circulation," there are two verses; in the first verse, the upper half is an exposition of the Dharma, with the character "if not" (若) extending through the subsequent portion.
The first two lines state that failing to uphold the precepts ruins one’s own practice, and failing to perform the *poṣadha* extinguishes the Dharma of the assembly;
since these two have perished, sentient beings are ignorant and dark, seeing nothing, just as when the sun has set. The latter two lines provide a simile, which corresponds to the subsequent verse.

The first half of the verse exhorts the cultivation of one’s own practice through the aforementioned method, while the latter half uses the metaphor of the yak (*gaurī*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: [definition of the character for yak].
The ox with long hair (*máo*) is the beast of the Southern Barbarians (*yī*). (This means it originates from the lands of the barbarians; *máo* refers to its tail.

According to tradition, the tail of this ox is long and red, and because the ox cherishes and guards it, it is frequently cited as a metaphor in the teachings. The second half [of the verse] exhorts the practice of various dharmas;

because the Buddha himself originally taught this to have one emulate the former sages, it says "as the Buddha has taught. Alternatively, it may mean that one should comply with the Buddha’s regulations.
The fortnightly observance is performed again, as arranged in the commentary.
[Vinaya]: I have recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; the Saṃgha has completed the Poṣadha.
May the merits spoken of in this recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra now be bestowed upon all sentient beings, so that together we may attain the Way of the Buddha.
[Commentary]: The fifth section, "What I Have Already Explained," is divided into two parts. The first verse concludes the preceding extensive and abbreviated texts;

the latter half of the verse clarifies the benefits of expounding the precepts. It asks: how could it be that these benefits apply only to those seated here? Rather, this karma is redirected to reach all sentient beings who possess a mind;
therefore, it says, "to attain the Buddha-way."

The fifth dedication and circulation consists of one and a half verses. In the first verse, the upper two lines conclude the two teachings previously explained, while the lower two lines collect the merits of practice from beginning to end.

In the latter half-verse, the upper line indicates that the objects of giving pervade the entire Dharma-realm, and the lower line indicates that the intended benefit extends all the way to Bodhi. [This concludes] the preliminary homage.

The final verse of all Buddhas has been honored equally throughout the three periods of time; those who seek the Buddha-way and bestow [merit] so that sentient beings may achieve Buddhahood have uniquely established this school, which transcends all other sects.
This ensures that practitioners have a place to which they can turn for study and that their practice is not in vain.

As stated in the *Yezhang* (Commentary on the Essentials): "Therefore, one must focus the mind upon its object"—the intent of this teaching lies precisely here. The text says: "If there is a mind, then..."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, "All who possess a mind shall become Buddhas," which is precisely this point. [Note:
This text was composed by the Venerable Dharmarakṣa as a general circulation for both the extensive and abbreviated teachings.

Now, I have annotated and expounded upon it rather than composing a new work, wishing to contribute as much as a speck of dust or a drop of dew to the great oceans and mountains, so as to illuminate and propagate it for future generations and those who share the same vessel.
To maintain this firmly is precisely what you must do.
[Vinaya] *The Bhikṣu Precept Manual with Explanatory Notes on the Four-Part Vinaya* (Part 2).

[Commentary] It is also permissible to further analyze the text according to its specific meanings; however, if one intends to deliver a comprehensive lecture for the sake of leading and guiding the assembly, and if the congregation has long been accustomed to the practice, one may proceed as follows.
Because many have become indolent and negligent, it is sufficient to provide a concise summary that points directly to the essentials so as to awaken the minds of the multitude.
[Commentary] *Sifenlü hanzhujieben shu*, Fascicle Four (Part Two).

The first two lines of the middle section briefly indicate that [the teaching] is not exhaustive, while the latter two clarify the intent behind the abbreviation. The first two lines explain the speaker’s intention:
having concluded the discourse, he guides [the listeners] as if speaking in haste, desiring to reach the end quickly. The next two lines clarify the mindset of the audience:
they harbor arrogance. The final two lines conclude by showing that this preceding simplification is well-suited to their capacities.
*Commentary on the Annotated Precept Manual of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya: Record of the Practice of the Essential Principles*, Volume Four, Part Two, Section Three (End).
[Commentary]: I, [the author], have risked my life to join the assembly of the True Dharma.

Since childhood, I possessed faith, yet lacked the opportunity for guidance until I reached the age of fifteen, when I was finally able to seek out a teacher. At sixteen, I began reciting the scriptures; at seventeen, I shaved my head.

During the Dali era of the Later Liang, I received full ordination (*upasampadā*). At that time, the Buddha-dharma was obstructed and the gates of the monasteries were constantly closed; thus, regarding the Vinaya teachings, there was no place to seek a teacher.

I merely adhered to the literal texts, remaining ignorant of what constituted an offense or its non-occurrence. When the Great Tang dynasty took control of the world, it encountered a period of scarcity and austerity;
though I initially desired to attend lectures, my will was not free to do so. It was only in the fourth year of Wude that I was finally able to participate in the lectures. Scarcely had I begun...

After hearing it once, he wished to practice seated meditation. The Master instructed him, saying: "Only when the precepts are pure will concentration be clear, and only then will wisdom have a foundation.

You have only just begun to listen; you are not yet familiar with what constitutes an offense or its non-violation. How could you know this? For now, focus exclusively on listening; I myself shall attend to your monastic duties. He then went to listen to the Vinaya ten times.
His mind delighted in meditative reflection, never forgetting it day or night. He became thoroughly versed in the points regarding what constitutes an offense and its non-violation.

I had not yet investigated the meaning of the words and phrases; moreover, I wished to practice seated meditation. The Preceptor said again, "Listen ten more times, and you may then fulfill your heart's desire.
I then went to the assembly for the Vinaya, taking my seat and attending to my duties. At that time, the Chief Vinaya Master personally commanded me to recite the text from memory.

Looking back at myself, I was ignorant and dark; the words and phrases were missing. As for the underlying principles, I merely chanted them according to the literal text, which was not yet from the heart.
Having realized that he could not bear to listen to a lecture being given by a subordinate, he did not dare to attend for twenty rounds; this period lasted six years.

At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he traveled among various lecture halls in search of renowned masters, whether in the mountains or in the world. Consequently, based on his own understanding, he composed three fascicles of a sub-commentary (*chao*).
Before he had even finished revising it, people began copying it. In the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, Yuan Guan passed away in the borderlands, and [the author] traveled north to Bingzhou.
When the Jin dynasty reached the territory of Wei, there was Master Li, who at that time relied upon distant peaks and valleys to seek out and study the texts.
After only one month, he suddenly passed away; the pain of my heart at this is beyond words.

I then returned to the mountains of Qindu for Master Ze, where he further produced three volumes of a commentary (*chao*), refining and polishing the previous edition so that its structural logic became fully integrated.

Furthermore, he produced one fascicle of the *Karmavācanā* with deletions and additions, two fascicles of commentary thereon, one fascicle of the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* (Precepts Manual) with annotations, and three fascicles of commentary thereon.
At that time, his mother was still alive; she repeatedly sent messengers to summon him, her longing for him never ceasing.

Consequently, he returned to Xilie, where those who shared the Dharma with him followed him in great numbers, reaching as many as thirty. They stayed together by the riverbank for one summer, engaging in discourse. He also produced [other works].
The *Nizhu Jieben* (Commentary on the Bhikṣuṇī Precepts) in one fascicle was subsequently separated from the original; only the abridged copy (*chao*) remained, while the rest flowed eastward.

Having traveled across the Xihu Lake and reached the capital, within sixteen years her mother passed away. By nature she did not seek the clamor of crowds but delighted in dwelling among mountains and wilds;
thus, due to these circumstances, she went to the Southern Mountains, where she finally attained the joy of seclusion in a rocky cave by the twentieth year.

Regarding the *Śīla* (Precepts), I have already sought them out and expanded upon their textual details; constrained by the circumstances, I further produced four fascicles of the *Karmavācanā* along with its commentary.
At the beginning of the Yonghui era, my earnest desire could not be restrained, and I again produced four fascicles of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* together with its sub-commentary and glosses.
However, encountering illness, my work was suspended, and my mind became despondent; my memory has failed me in many ways.
Seeking this with unceasing diligence, I finally completed the commentary on the nineteenth day of the ninth month in the second year of the Yonghui era.

I have roughly succeeded in clarifying its major principles; its decisions and applications can be followed as a standard. Now that I am in my final years, with life depending on every morning and evening, I have taken the time to compile it, so that there may be a definitive record for when my pen is laid down.

In the postscript to the *Jieben shuji* (Commentary on the Sūtra of the Essential Precepts), it is recorded that he once heard the celestial drum sounding spontaneously, yet he also heard bells and drums waiting for the mallet before they would ring.
Is the Vinaya not likewise? By its very nature, it speaks of itself without being questioned; as for prohibitions, it speaks in response to the capacity of the occasion. These two are thus...

It is for this reason that the Samyaksaṃbuddha has caused it to be so. On the first day of the first month of winter, during the year of the Jupiter star and the *wùwǔ* (earth-horse) cycle, there arrived a guest who was tuning the *liǚ* musical scales.
He knocked at my thatched gate; when I opened the door and looked out, I saw one who possessed the fragrance of orchids and the spirit of cutting through metal.
After the greetings were concluded, the guest folded his hands and changed the subject, saying: "Since the Buddha-dharma gradually spread to the East..."

The orthodox current of the Southern Mountain (Nanshan) overflows into the four seas. The Vinaya teachings have flourished, and the distinctions between what is observed and what is transgressed, as well as what is permitted and what is prohibited, have become brilliantly renewed.
Throughout all under heaven, who among the monastics and laypeople of the Śākya school would dare not to reverently uphold them?

Furthermore, the legacy texts of Zhongnan consist of three major works: namely, the *Śīlaparivarta-ṭīkā* (the *Chao*) and the two commentaries (*Shu*). Among these, the sections on Precepts (*śīla*) and Karma (*karman*)—
The commentaries on the beginning and end differ in their volumes; let the talented and sagacious among later generations pause to examine and collate them.

Now there was a Vinaya Master named Chanlong (Chanlong), who firmly held to the single word of authority and widely launched the vessel of the four immeasurables. In his practice of *shendu* (cautioning the solitary self), he modeled himself after the "grass-tethered" [ox];
in his love for all things, he compared himself to the "goose and pearl. To relieve the labor of his students, he once convened a *kaṭhina* ceremony.
[The author] wrote the *Moshuji* (Commentary on the *Karmavācanā*), which has circulated throughout the world, and so forth.

I privately remarked to the guest, "Is this the venue where you and that Master Longgong have met? The guest replied, "It is. I asked again, "Why has the Vinaya Master not yet compiled a commentary on the *Karmavācanā*?
The guest said, "I do not know what his intention is. I remarked, "Would it suffice merely to hope for the convergence of the original texts? It seems not."
"Is this acceptable? The guest said, "As I have reflected upon it, Master Zhi’s *ke-wen* (sectioning) and the *shu-wen* (sub-sectioning) are not part of the original text itself.
Why was this done? I replied, "What harm is there in its being so? Moreover, let us cite an example: for instance, the *Fahua hui-ben* (Collected Editions of the Lotus Sūtra) of Tiantai.
The *Wenju* (Textual Phrases) sectioned the sūtra according to its textual divisions, while following the *Jingxi* (Jingci) sectioning to further subdivide the phrases. Now..."
He also cited one thousand followers. Relying on the commentary (*shu*) to collate the sub-commentary (*zhu*) and the precepts (*jie*), he analyzed and explained them according to the records.
He divided and synthesized the text of the commentary; for while the *Chao* (the *Zongchao*) is a commentary on the school’s principles, how could it possibly synthesize the *Jieben* (Precept Text)?

The *Shu* (the *Jieshu*) is a commentary on the sub-commentary; it should cite and synthesize the original text rather than adhering to a single standard. The guest said, "Only this. With these few words, he inscribed his work upon the girdles of all scholars. The guest withdrew.
For the time being, it is said: "The current commentary on the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) lacks this section; it must be compiled here.
One must create this division and integrate it into both the commentary and the precepts. I say: To begin with, the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) is profound and subtle;
its virtuous function is inconceivable. Is it not lofty? It transcends the great void. Is it not deep? It is compared to the vast ocean—vast indeed, and resplendent indeed, far beyond compare.
To speak beyond the realm of the phenomenal is like this: now you would take up a short rope to peer down into a deep well, or hold a narrow tube to gaze at the vast heavens.
I fear that by failing to recognize your own measure, you will invite calamity from the Great Way and incur the censure of future generations.
How much better it would be to set aside your virtues, remaining silent and odorless! For petty wisdom is the thief of virtue.

Names are the guests of reality. If one merely seeks empty reputation, one will only exhaust those of like mind. If one’s words do not enter through the proper gate to reach that profound depth, it is impossible for them to succeed.
To dally in mere literary composition while ultimately losing the pure essence—do not accept such talk.

The guest advanced to his seat with indignation and, with a look of suppressed resolve, struck his palms together, saying: "Since the *Jiaochi* has been compiled and the *Yeshu* has also been completed, there remains only this single book that is incomplete.
Now that you have taken up the task of benevolence, how could you allow others to take the lead? Arise and spur me on;
I am as eager for this as the Emperor of Wei was for his noble younger brother. As for one of my humble capacity, though I am not worthy of being esteemed by foot, I shall beat the drum."
When the drum was struck, though he wished not to sound it, how could he possibly avoid doing so? He thus gave a hollow assent. Retreating, he pondered deeply:

from the time he first entered the monastic life as a novice to shave his head and dye his robes, and since setting his mind on the study of the Vinaya, he has long been sustained by the vast grace of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Having bathed early in the Dharma-water of the Three Studies, he truly knows that this kindness is immeasurable. How could he dare not express his gratitude? This, moreover, was not brought about by some prior causal condition.

Indeed it is so. Moreover, the precepts are the very foundation of concentration and wisdom; they are the single path through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend to the road of sublime adornment.
If one’s feet of precept are incomplete, how can one set out upon the journey? If one wishes to make the feet of precept complete, how could one ever abandon them?

How magnificent is the virtue of the precepts! They provide the initial sustenance for the commencement of practice. This is as explained by the analogy of the blind and the lame in the *Śata-śāstra*, and as stated by Mouzi regarding the resolution of practice.

What can be done? If one merely clings to a single corner and firmly declines, how could one ever cause the selection of the *Huigǔ* (Mirror of Wisdom) to illuminate the path of correct practice for all living beings? Therefore, I have sharpened my tools and devoted myself to this task.

Although the textual segments of the *Jieben zhushu* (Commentary on the Precept Text) are interlocked in more than one layer—almost as if they were intended to fit together perfectly—I have relied upon a careful exegesis to arrange them section by section.

The commentaries and records follow the structural divisions and harmonize the threads of the sequence. Now, by emulating that which completes the curves, the five sections—derived from the *Tian-di* and *Yi-jian*—are brought together.
A single glance shall make them universally accessible. As this labor reaches completion, I have further collated it against variant editions;

yet I still fear there may be errors, as the divine mirror is vast. I respectfully await the refinement of future sages; I do not presume to claim credit for this over my predecessors. It is merely...

This serves as a small repayment for the Buddha’s kindness and a modest response to the virtue of the Patriarchs. It is hoped that this subtle merit, arising from the realization of one's true nature, will be woven ever more deeply into the Dharma-realm, so that the Sun of the Buddha may increase in brilliance and the life-span of the Dharma be inexhaustible.

Thus it is said. Written on a sunny day at the inner chamber of the Jōjaku-ge (Tranquil Pavilion) by the Śramaṇa of the Śākya clan, Ren-gō, at the Vairocana-kō-in quarters of the Reishiji temple in Sannin.
